works_verified.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models (arXiv); published as 'GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs', Science 2024
works_verified.authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
works_verified.year: 2023 (arXiv v1 17 Mar 2023; v5 21 Aug 2023); Science online 20 Jun 2024, issue 21 Jun 2024
works_verified.what_measured: Whether each O*NET task or Detailed Work Activity (DWA) is 'exposed' to LLMs. The dataset has 19,265 tasks and 2,087 DWAs. Labels: E0 means no or minimal time saving at equivalent quality, or a loss of quality. E1 means ChatGPT/Playground access can cut task time by at least 50%. E2 means the LLM alone does not reach 50%, but software built on top of it could, at equal quality. Labels are rolled up into occupation shares: alpha = E1, beta = E1 + 0.5*E2, zeta = E1 + E2.
works_verified.method_plain: Annotators applied a rubric to task descriptions. The authors labeled the DWAs that clearly need physical work or manual dexterity. Contracted annotators did the rest; they had reviewed GPT-3/3.5/4 outputs for OpenAI's alignment work and were not workers in the occupations. Separately, an early GPT-4 was given a slightly modified rubric, tuned to agree better with a set of human labels, and labeled every task-occupation pair. 'Equivalent quality' means a third party, typically the recipient, would not notice or care that an LLM helped. Tasks are aggregated to occupations with core tasks weighted twice as heavily as supplemental tasks. Time spent per task is not used; a robustness check with O*NET importance weights reportedly changed little.
key_numbers: Abstract/text: 80% of US workers are in occupations with >=10% of tasks exposed, and 19% are in occupations with >50% of tasks exposed. Both use beta exposure, so they are shares of TASKS, not time saved or jobs lost.
Abstract: about 15% of all US worker tasks could be done significantly faster at the same quality with LLM access alone; 47-56% with LLM-powered software.

Table 3, occupation-level means: alpha 0.14 (human and GPT-4); beta 0.30 (human) / 0.34 (GPT-4); zeta 0.46 (human) / 0.55 (GPT-4). The text rounds these to 'over 30%' and 'surpasses 50%'; the human zeta is actually below 0.50.
Human labels: 2.3% of occupations are alpha-50 exposed, 21.6% beta-50, 47.3% zeta-50 (Figure 3 uses equal task weights).
GPT-4 (Rubric 1) vs human agreement (Table 2): 80.8% for alpha (Pearson 0.223), 65.6% for beta (0.591), 82.1% for zeta (0.654).
Science version (per GovAI summary page): about 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces, and 'just over 46%' once complementary software is counted.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: This is the canonical extensive-margin measure. E1 is a threshold indicator: 1{believed potential time saving >= 50%}. It does not measure the size of the saving. If you trust the labels and weight tasks equally, a service line with E1 share alpha_j has theta_j somewhere between 0.5*alpha_j and 0.5 + 0.5*alpha_j, which is too wide to use. Even that bound assumes the labels are accurate, and they are judgments, not measurements. The labels are gross: review cost (rho), rejection of output that passes checks (q) and AI running cost are not netted out. The authors say they chose a high threshold because they guessed the real-world time reduction would be lower than their estimates. The 0.5 weight on E2 is a discount for needed complementary investment, not a time fraction. Task weights are core/supplemental, not hours, so they give neither f_j nor w_j. The labels are a single snapshot of early GPT-4.
works_verified.limitations: Labels are subjective, and the annotators were not workers in the occupations. GPT-4 labels depend on prompt wording (Rubric 1 vs 2 agreement on beta is only 76%). No time-use weighting and no task-length (h) dimension. Labels are ordinal. Single snapshot. Gross of review. Based on US O*NET tasks.
works_verified.corrections: Added the Science volume, issue and pages from the Crossref record of DOI 10.1126/science.adj0998: 384(6702):1306-1308. Corrected the summary statistics. 'beta >0.30; zeta >0.50' repeated the paper's prose, but Table 3 shows human beta = 0.30, human zeta = 0.46 and GPT-4 zeta = 0.55; the key number now gives the table values. Clarified that the 80%/19% figures refer to workers in occupations. Clarified that the authors labeled the DWAs needing physical work or dexterity, and that the human annotators labeled DWAs plus a subset of tasks. All other numbers matched the PDF text.

works_verified.title: Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses (AIOE); follow-up 'How will Language Modelers like ChatGPT Affect Occupations and Industries?'
works_verified.authors: Edward Felten, Manav Raj, Robert Seamans
works_verified.year: 2021 (SMJ, December 2021); follow-up arXiv March 2023 (PDF dated 18 March 2023)
works_verified.what_measured: An AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) score for each occupation. Industry (AIIE) and county (AIGE) versions aggregate it.
works_verified.method_plain: Ten AI application areas come from the Electronic Frontier Foundation's AI progress statistics: abstract strategy games, real-time video games, image recognition, visual question answering, image generation, reading comprehension, language modeling, translation, speech recognition, and instrumental track recognition. A crowdsourced (mTurk) survey rates how related each application is to each of O*NET's 52 human abilities. Ability-level exposure is the sum of those relatedness scores. Occupation exposure is the average of ability exposure, weighted by O*NET's prevalence and importance of each ability, and is then standardized. The 2023 language-modeling version sets every application weight to zero except language modeling.
key_numbers: 10 AI applications x 52 O*NET abilities, applied to the 800+ occupations O*NET tracks.
The LM-AIOE correlates 0.979 with the original AIOE.

Most exposed occupations under LM-AIOE: telemarketers, then post-secondary teachers of English language and literature, foreign languages, and history. Most exposed industries: legal services, and securities, commodities and investments.
The score is a standardized relative index with no natural units.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Ordinal and relative only. It ranks occupations by how much their abilities overlap with AI applications, and says nothing about time saved, review cost or failure rates. The application weights can in principle be updated over time. In practice, the language-modeling reweighting barely changed the ranking (correlation 0.979), so the index has little power to track capability change. It is at most a cross-check on relative exposure across IT occupations. It cannot give a theta level.
works_verified.limitations: Built on abilities, not tasks. Based on crowd judgments of relatedness, not observed performance. Standardized units. Deliberately 'agnostic' about substitution versus augmentation. Reweighting changes rankings very little.
works_verified.corrections: No substantive errors. Filled in the full list of 10 applications and the SMJ DOI. Added the 0.979 correlation from the arXiv paper, which weakens the record's claim that the index can usefully vary over time.

works_verified.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market
works_verified.authors: Michael Webb
works_verified.venue: Working paper (Stanford; SSRN 3482150; NBER conference draft)
works_verified.what_measured: How exposed occupations are to AI, and historically to software and robots, measured by text overlap between patents and O*NET task descriptions.
works_verified.method_plain: Verb-noun pairs (e.g. 'diagnose disease') are pulled from patent titles and from O*NET task descriptions. Each task is scored by how common its verb-noun pairs are in the relevant patents. Scores are averaged to occupations, with weights that average O*NET task frequency, importance and relevance. The method is validated on historical cases: occupations scored as highly exposed to software and robots saw employment and wage declines. Those fitted relationships are then used to project AI's effects.
key_numbers: Unlike software and robots, AI is directed at high-skilled tasks; exposure peaks around the 90th percentile of the wage distribution.
Assuming historical patterns of long-run substitution continue, AI will reduce 90:10 wage inequality but will not affect the top 1%.
Exposure scores are relative (percentile-style), not time fractions.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: It measures where inventive effort is aimed, not how much labor is saved. Its use for this project is methodological: it validates exposure scores against realized employment changes, which is the same kind of check as comparing a bottom-up S(t) with the top-down 2.3 pp/yr. It does not give theta, p, q or rho.
works_verified.limitations: Uses pre-LLM patents. Verb-noun matching misses meaning. Scores are relative only. Assumes past substitution patterns carry over.
works_verified.corrections: No errors. The SSRN date (6 Nov 2019) was confirmed by search; the SSRN page itself returned 403. Added that the weights average frequency, importance and relevance, not only importance and frequency.

works_verified.title: What Can Machines Learn, and What Does It Mean for Occupations and the Economy? (Suitability for Machine Learning, SML)
works_verified.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Tom Mitchell, Daniel Rock
works_verified.what_measured: A Suitability for Machine Learning (SML) score, rated at the DWA level and mapped to 18,156 O*NET tasks and on to occupations.
works_verified.method_plain: The rubric from Brynjolfsson and Mitchell (Science 2017) is applied to O*NET Detailed Work Activities. Its items cover features that make a task learnable by supervised ML, such as a clear input-output mapping, available data, and tolerance for errors. Brynjolfsson's 2020 slides describe 2,059 DWAs, a five-point 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' scale, and 10 different raters per DWA. Scores are mapped to tasks and to occupations weighted by task importance. The replication files (HITRubric.docx, cf_report_DWAS_input.csv, cfProcessor_AEAPnP.py) and a later replication paper point to CrowdFlower as the crowd platform. I could not confirm the platform from the paper text itself, because the PDF would not download.
key_numbers: 18,156 O*NET tasks (paper abstract). The author's slides give 2,059 DWAs and 18,112 occupation-specific tasks, so counts differ slightly across sources.
Ratings on a 5-point Likert scale, 10 raters per DWA (author slides, 2020).

Findings: (i) ML affects different occupations than earlier automation waves; (ii) most occupations have at least some SML tasks; (iii) few occupations are fully automatable by ML; (iv) realizing the gains usually requires redesigning jobs.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: An ordinal suitability score from before LLMs. Its items on error tolerance and verifiability of outputs are conceptually close to our q and rho, so they could suggest extra dimensions to code for each IT task. The score is not a time fraction. Its central finding, that partial exposure within occupations is the norm, supports building S as a sum over tasks, S = sum w_j theta_j.
works_verified.limitations: Built for supervised ML (circa 2017), not LLMs or agents. Ordinal. Not time-weighted. Rubric item count is unclear: the MIT IDE page says 21 items, a later replication paper says 23 factors.
works_verified.corrections: Added the rating details from the author's own 2020 slides: 5-point scale, 10 raters per DWA, rated on about 2,059 DWAs rather than on task statements directly. Flagged CrowdFlower as likely (from replication file names) but unconfirmed in the paper text. Noted the 21 vs 23 rubric-item discrepancy. Confirmed the replication package (openICPSR 114436) and listed its files. Raised bibliographic confidence to high.

works_verified.title: Beyond AI Exposure: Which Tasks are Cost-Effective to Automate with Computer Vision?
works_verified.authors: Maja S. Svanberg, Wensu Li, Martin Fleming, Brian C. Goehring, Neil C. Thompson
works_verified.venue: MIT FutureTech working paper (also on SSRN); I found no journal version
works_verified.what_measured: For tasks exposed to computer vision: the accuracy required (from a survey of workers on Prolific), the cost of building a system that reaches that accuracy, and whether that system beats the human wage bill at a given deployment scale.
works_verified.method_plain: An end-to-end cost-benefit model. Workers familiar with each task state the accuracy needed (about 9 responses per task on average; 80% of tasks have 5 or more valid responses). Scaling laws turn required accuracy into data and compute cost, and 35 case studies supply further cost data. The model assumes a 5% real discount rate and compute costs falling 22% per year. Automation is called economically attractive only when the deployment exceeds the 'minimum viable scale'. A task's share of an occupation's compensation is set by O*NET task-importance scores.
key_numbers: Only 23% of worker compensation paid for vision tasks would be attractive to automate at today's costs. This is a share of compensation within vision-exposed tasks, not a share of jobs or of tasks.
36% of jobs in US non-farm businesses have at least one vision-exposed task. Only 8% (23% of them) have at least one that is economically attractive to automate.
Vision tasks are 1.6% of US non-farm compensation, and 0.4% is attractive to automate.
Robustness to cost parameters raises the 23% to at most 33%. If AI delivers twice the human worker's value, it rises to 30%.
A 'bare-bones implementation' (free data, free compute, minimal engineering) raises firm-level attractiveness only to 49% (0.79% of compensation).
If one system could serve the whole national economy (AI-as-a-service), AI already has a cost advantage for 88% of vision task compensation.
Example: checking food quality is roughly 6% of a baker's duties.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The clearest example in this stream of moving from exposure to a net economic test. It nets out the cost of the AI system and uses required accuracy, a cousin of p and q. But it gives a yes/no decision per task, not the fraction of labor time saved. Its use of O*NET importance as a stand-in for time share is a known weak point, and it is exactly the w_j/f_j measurement problem we face. The fixed-cost scale logic matters less for off-the-shelf LLMs, and for very large firms like TCS and Infosys.
works_verified.limitations: Computer vision only. Assumes large fixed costs for custom models. Uses importance scores as a proxy for time. Required accuracy is self-reported by workers. Working paper.
works_verified.corrections: The record attributed the 49% (0.79% of compensation) to AI-as-a-service scale. In the source, 49% is the firm-level 'bare-bones implementation' scenario (free data and compute). The AI-as-a-service figure is 88% of vision task compensation at national scale. Added the 30% result for AI that doubles the worker's value. All other numbers matched the PDF.

works_verified.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140); updates Gmyrek, Berg & Bescond (2023), ILO WP 96
works_verified.authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kamiński, Filip Konopczyński, Agnieszka Ładna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Rosłaniec, Marek Troszyński
works_verified.what_measured: A continuous 0-1 GenAI automation-potential score for each task: 0 means the task cannot be automated, 1 means it could be done without a human operator. Occupation-level mean and SD of task scores are mapped to exposure gradients 1-4.
works_verified.method_plain: (1) GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5 score the 29,753 tasks in Poland's 6-digit occupational classification. (2) A survey of 1,640 workers in Poland rates a representative sample of 2,861 tasks on a 0-100 slider, giving 52,558 data points. (3) International experts review the scores through a survey and Delphi-style rounds. (4) An LLM assistant built on the adjusted scores predicts scores for ISCO-08 task descriptions. Gradient 4 means mean >= 0.6 and mean minus SD >= 0.5. Gradient 3 means 0.5 <= mean < 0.6 and mean plus SD >= 0.5.
key_numbers: Globally, one in four workers is in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment is in Gradient 4; the 2023 'automation' category was 2.3%.
Gradients 1-3 combined: 20.5% of world employment, versus 29.2% for 2023's 'augmentation' (13%) plus 'big unknown' (16.2%).
Exposed share of total employment: 11% in low-income countries vs 34% in high-income countries.

Appendix Table A1 (ISCO-08 4-digit, mean / SD): Web and Multimedia Developers (2513) 0.60 / 0.08, Gradient 4. Applications Programmers (2514) 0.57 / 0.08, Gradient 3. Database Designers and Administrators (2521) 0.57 / 0.08, Gradient 3. Systems Administrators (2522) 0.57 / 0.05, Gradient 3. Software Developers (2512) 0.53 / 0.07, Gradient 3.

Highly digitized occupations (web and media developers, database specialists, finance and software-related occupations) had higher mean scores in 2025 than in 2023; the authors attribute this to multimodal and agentic capabilities.
The 2025 estimates are described as the 'upper threshold' of exposure.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Among the main exposure indices, it is one of the few with a continuous 0-1 task score; the 2023 WP96 version already had one. It is still not time saved. It is perceived automatability, with no definition of quality, review or cost. It could serve as a rough upper-bound proxy for gross theta. With the 2023 and 2025 vintages it gives crude time variation. India's NCO-2015 classification is aligned with ISCO-08, which helps. But public PLFS microdata appear to record occupation at only 3 digits (per microdata.gov.in variable listings seen in search). In that case PLFS cannot separate 2512, 2513 and 2514, which all fall within 251.
works_verified.limitations: Perceived automatability, not measured time savings. Review is not netted out. The task base is the Polish classification. Respondents are not task-specific experts. LLM scoring is hard to reproduce. The scores are an upper threshold of exposure, not impact.
works_verified.corrections: Database Designers and Administrators (2521) is 0.57 / 0.08 in Table A1, not 0.55 / 0.04. Added Systems Administrators (2522). Toned down 'the ONLY major exposure index with a continuous 0-1 task score': the 2023 ILO version also had one. Noted that the pgmyrek.github.io page is an interactive tree visualization, and I could not confirm a downloadable task-level file there. Flagged the 3-digit PLFS coding limit, which I took from search results and did not open directly.

works_verified.title: Generative AI and Firm Values (a March 2024 draft circulated as 'The Labor Impact of Generative AI on Firm Values')
works_verified.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang (NBER cover). Bledi Taska is a co-author on the 2024 drafts and on the Internet Appendix of the January 2026 revision.
works_verified.what_measured: Firms' workforce exposure to GenAI: Eloundou-style task labels aggregated by each firm's occupation mix, split into exposure through core tasks and through supplemental tasks. The paper relates this to stock returns, labor demand and profitability after ChatGPT's release.
works_verified.method_plain: GPT-3.5 Turbo, given few-shot prompts, labels all 19,265 O*NET tasks with an Eloundou-style rubric: direct exposure = 1 (ChatGPT cuts time by at least half), indirect = 0.5, none = 0. Occupation exposure is aggregated to firms by their occupation employment mix. The authors treat the LLM as a 'research assistant' applying categories the researchers defined.
key_numbers: 14% of the 19,265 tasks are classed as directly exposed.
On average, 77% of occupations' exposure comes from core tasks and 23% from supplemental tasks.
The 'Artificial-minus-Human' portfolio earned 44 basis points higher daily returns in the two weeks after ChatGPT's release, about 5% over the two weeks (NBER abstract).
Occupations exposed through core tasks (e.g. proofreaders, web developers) point to substitution; exposure through supplemental tasks points to complementarity.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: It reuses the Eloundou 50% threshold through GPT-3.5, so it has the same extensive-margin limitation. It shows LLM labelers can apply the rubric at scale. Its useful addition is the core/supplemental split, a rough stand-in for whether saved time turns into lower headcount. The firm-level template (occupation mix x task labels) carries over to TCS/Infosys if their role mix is available.
works_verified.limitations: Ternary labels from GPT-3.5. Nothing on the size of time savings. US public firms. Core/supplemental is O*NET's designation, not a time share.
works_verified.corrections: Title and authorship history clarified. The 'Labor Impact...' title appears on a March 2024 four-author draft (UW Foster copy). The current NBER revision (January 2026) is titled 'Generative AI and Firm Values' with three authors on the cover and Taska on the Internet Appendix, so 'later drafts' is not accurate for the latest version. Added the 14% direct-exposure share. All numbers verified.

works_verified.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works_verified.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works_verified.what_measured: The 10-year gain in total factor productivity (TFP), meaning output per unit of all inputs combined. It is computed as (GDP share of tasks affected within 10 years) x (average cost saving on those tasks).
works_verified.method_plain: A task-based model using Hulten's theorem: the aggregate gain is roughly the GDP share of affected tasks times the average cost saving on them. Exposure comes from Eloundou et al.: the wage-bill-weighted share of exposed occupations is 20%. Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate (23% profitably automatable) is applied to all exposed tasks, giving 4.6% of tasks affected within 10 years. The labor cost saving per affected task is 27%, the average of Noy and Zhang (2023) and Brynjolfsson et al. (2023). Multiplying by the exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535 gives an overall cost saving of 14.4%.
key_numbers: 20% of US labor tasks exposed (wage-bill weighted, from Eloundou et al.).
0.23 x 0.20 = 4.6% of tasks affected within 10 years.
27% average labor cost saving x 0.535 labor share = 14.4% overall cost saving on affected tasks.
TFP gain of no more than 0.66% over 10 years (about 0.064% per year), or under 0.53% after adjusting for hard-to-learn tasks.
Adding Peng et al.'s Copilot estimate raises the labor cost saving to 36% and the overall cost saving to 0.193, which gives a TFP gain of 0.89%.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Clear evidence that exposure measures alone do not give the intensive margin. Acemoglu has to bring in a separate per-task saving (27%, from experiments) and multiply it onto exposure and the 23% feasibility share. Structurally that is S = sum w_j x 1{exposed_j} x feasibility x saving, the product our recipe replaces with a capability-based theta_j(t). His 27% is a gross experimental saving on short, well-defined tasks. It is not net of review and does not change with capability.
works_verified.limitations: Assumes static capability. Applies a computer-vision feasibility share to LLMs. The intensive-margin number comes from a few short-task experiments. US economy-wide.
works_verified.corrections: The record said 'an alternative exposure value of 0.193 gives 0.89%'. In fact 0.193 is an alternative overall COST SAVING (36% labor cost saving x 0.535, after adding Peng et al.), not an alternative exposure. The 20% exposure comes from Eloundou et al. alone; Svanberg et al. supply only the 23%. Made the 0.535 labor-share step explicit. Economic Policy citation verified on RePEc.

works_verified.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works_verified.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works_verified.year: 2025 (November; the page shows 25 Nov 2025 while its suggested citation says 2025-11-05)
works_verified.what_measured: Model-estimated time per task WITHOUT AI and WITH AI, for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro and Max tiers) mapped to O*NET tasks. This gives a continuous time-saved fraction for each task.
works_verified.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a professional would take without AI and how long the task took with AI. Estimates are aggregated to O*NET tasks by the median for each task, and valued at May 2024 OEWS wages. Validation uses self-consistency across prompt variants and 1,000 open-source JIRA tickets with tracked times. The report extrapolates to economy-wide productivity using Hulten's theorem (labor share 0.6), assuming universal adoption within 10 years and capabilities fixed at today's level.
key_numbers: Headline: Claude speeds up individual tasks by 'about 80%'. The text gives a median saving of 84%, and a figure caption gives 81%; the report does not reconcile them.
The average task would take about 90 minutes without AI per the overview; the key findings say 1.4 hours on average for complex tasks. These are not reconciled.
Implied: +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth over the next decade (about 1.1% per year in TFP), under universal adoption and current models.
JIRA validation: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 (log Pearson 0.46) vs actual times; developers' own estimates 0.50 (0.67). Claude overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones.
Stated limitation: it cannot account for time outside the conversation, 'including validating the quality or accuracy of Claude's work'.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The only large-scale source in this stream with a continuous time-saved fraction per task. The roughly 80% figure is GROSS: it is not net of review (rho), of output later rejected (q), or of failed attempts. It is also selected, because people bring AI the tasks it is good at, so it is closer to an upper bound for the tasks used than an average over f_j(h). The 'time without AI' estimates give a rough task-length distribution. The January 2026 Anthropic follow-up (added below) adjusts these figures for task success.
works_verified.limitations: Times are model-estimated and only moderately validated (Spearman 0.44). Ignores verification time. Selected on tasks people bring to Claude. Consumer Claude.ai sample. Not net of AI running cost. Not peer reviewed. Task-level estimates do not appear to be publicly released.
works_verified.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Added the date discrepancy, OEWS wage source, labor share of 0.6, log-Pearson values, and the direction of Claude's bias. Removed 'more compressed' as a paraphrase and replaced it with what the source says (overestimates short tasks, underestimates long ones).

works_verified.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works_verified.authors: Tejal Patwardhan et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works_verified.what_measured: Expert-graded win/tie rates of frontier models against industry professionals on 1,320 tasks from 44 occupations in the top 9 US GDP sectors. It also gives speed and cost multipliers that include an expert's time to review the work and redo it when it fails.
works_verified.method_plain: Experts averaging 14 years of experience write realistic tasks and produce human deliverables. Other experts blind-grade model output against human output. The speed analysis has three scenarios: 'naive' (human time vs model sampling time), 'try 1x, then fix it', and 'try n times, then fix it yourself'. The last two add review time and the cost of doing the task by hand when the model fails. Review time R_T is the observed time each expert took the first time they graded a task, from task-monitoring software. It is grading time, not production code review.
key_numbers: Gold subset (220 tasks, open-sourced): average human completion time H_T = 404 minutes (cost $361); average review time R_T = 109 minutes (about $86).
Best model on the gold subset: Claude Opus 4.1, 47.6% wins or ties vs experts.
GPT-5 (39.0% win rate): speed 90x naive, 1.12x try-once, 1.39x try-n. Cost 474x, 1.18x, 1.63x.
o3 (35.2%): speed 161x, 1.08x, 1.28x. GPT-4o (12.5%): speed 327x, 0.87x, 0.46x, so with GPT-4o, using the model is slower than doing the task yourself.
Authors: 'When incorporating time to review and redo work, the payoff from using a model shrinks.'
No cost estimates for Claude, Gemini or Grok.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The closest thing in this stream to our NET theta formula, though it comes from the benchmark literature, not the exposure literature. R_T/H_T = 109/404 ≈ 0.27 is an empirical rho for long (about 7-hour) knowledge-work tasks, but it measures grading time. The win rate is roughly q*p. The paper's appendix defines win rate as 'rated better', while the headline 47.6% counts ties, so the two uses differ. A try-n speedup of 1.39x means about 28% time saved for GPT-5; GPT-4o's 0.46x means negative savings, which our max{..., kappa} floor would rule out. The fall from 90x to 1.39x shows how far gross measures overstate net savings.
works_verified.limitations: 44 US occupations, with software only partly covered; Software Developer tasks were excluded from the automated grader. Tasks are one-shot deliverables, not maintenance of existing code. Review time is grading time. Cost data are missing for non-OpenAI models. Produced by a model developer.
works_verified.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the o3 multipliers, how R_T was measured (grading time from monitoring software), and the ambiguity in how 'win rate' is defined.

works_verified.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
works_verified.authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, Siddharth Suri (Microsoft Research)
works_verified.what_measured: An occupation-level 'AI applicability score' built from about 200k anonymized US Bing Copilot conversations (1 Jan to 30 Sep 2024) mapped to O*NET Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). It separates the user's goal from what the AI itself did.
works_verified.method_plain: An LLM pipeline classifies conversations into IWAs and rates completion (whether the AI completed the user's goal) and impact scope (counted when moderate or higher). An IWA counts only if its activity share exceeds 0.05%. Scores are weighted by O*NET relevance and importance and aggregated to 785 SOC occupations. The final score averages the user-goal side and the AI-action side; the AI-action side counts only nonphysical tasks. The data are two samples of about 100k conversations each (uniform and thumbs-feedback).
key_numbers: About 200k conversations; 785 SOC occupations covering 149.8 million workers.
The most common and successful AI-assisted activities are information work ('the creation, processing, and communication of information').

works_verified.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works_verified.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simón Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. works_verified.what_measured: Expert-graded win rates of model deliverables against industry experts' deliverables, on 1,320 tasks (220 gold) from 44 occupations in 9 sectors. Also time and cost to complete, review and redo.
works_verified.method_plain: A benchmark, not an RCT. Experts (on average 14 years of experience) wrote real tasks and deliverables, and other experts blindly compared model and human outputs. The authors then compute expected time saved if you try the model, review it, and do the task yourself if it fails (once, or repeatedly n times).

Win rate (strictly better) and speed-up: GPT-4o 12.5% (naive 327x, try once 0.87x, try n times 0.46x); o4-mini 29.1% (186x, 1.02x, 1.06x); o3 35.2% (161x, 1.08x, 1.28x); GPT-5 39.0% (90x, 1.12x, 1.39x).

E[T] = MT + RT + (1-w)HT maps onto theta = w - RT/HT - MT/HT, with w (strict win rate) as the accept probability (like q*p) and RT/HT as rho (about 0.27 for multi-hour tasks). For GPT-5 trying once, roughly 61% of HT is spent redoing failed tasks and 27% on review. So the collapse from the naive 90x to 1.12x comes mainly from redoing failures, not from review alone. The rising speed-ups across model generations give a second, non-experimental capability slope.
works_verified.limitations: Benchmark, not a field experiment. RT is graders' time on pairwise comparisons, not workplace review. Win rate counts only 'better than expert'. Task hours self-reported. works_verified.corrections: All numbers match Table 2 and Appendix A.2.1. Completed the author list. Corrected the interpretation: the drop from the naive ratio is driven mainly by the redo term (1-w)HT, not just review cost.

works_verified.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
works_verified.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
works_verified.what_measured: Time to finish one fixed greenfield coding task (write an HTTP server in JavaScript) with vs without Copilot. Completion = first commit passing all 12 tests in a provided suite; participants could see the tests but could not alter them.
works_verified.method_plain: Randomized experiment on Upwork, 15 May to 20 June 2022. 166 offers sent, 95 accepted; 45 randomized to Copilot, 50 to control. The paper says 'Thirty-five developers from both the treated and control groups completed the task and survey', which is ambiguous between 35 per group and 35 in total. Success rate 7 pp higher with Copilot, not significant (95% CI -0.11 to +0.25).
Participants were mostly aged 25-34 and from India and Pakistan. Median income was $10k-19k/yr, average coding experience 6 years, and they reported about 9 hours of coding per working day.
Self-estimated gain averaged 35% in both the treated and control groups, below the measured 55.8%.

Heterogeneity (Table 1): less experienced developers (p = 0.063), developers coding more hours per day (p = 0.017) and those aged 25-44 (p = 0.030) benefited more. The experience result is significant only at the 10% level.

Time saved = 1 - 71.17/160.89 = 0.558, so it maps directly to theta for that narrow task type with 2022 autocomplete. It does not measure review cost (rho) or acceptance (q), because passing the tests was the acceptance criterion.
works_verified.limitations: One toy greenfield task. No maintenance work and no code review. Freelancers, not firm employees. 2022 Copilot model. Time is measured only for those who finished, so selective completion could bias the estimate. The sample (mostly India/Pakistan) is demographically close to the Indian IT labor pool, but the work setting is not.
works_verified.corrections: Number of finishers: the paper's sentence is ambiguous, so do not cite '35 in each group' as fact. Added that self-estimates (35%) came from both groups, that five treated participants did not have Copilot active, and that the experience effect is significant only at the 10% level. All other numbers were confirmed in the PDF text.

works_verified.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Refined the method description (median per task; log differences with Hulten weighting by time share and wage-bill share; OEWS May 2024 wages; JIRA subset of 1,000 tasks) and added the Pearson validation figures.

works_verified.title: Growth Accounting with Intermediate Inputs (source of 'Hulten's theorem')
works_verified.authors: Charles R. Hulten
works_verified.what_measured: A theory result, not a measurement. In an efficient economy, to first order, the aggregate productivity effect of a small productivity gain in one sector equals that sector's sales share of GDP times its own productivity gain.
works_verified.method_plain: An accounting result based on the envelope theorem. To first order: aggregate TFP change = sum over sectors (or tasks) of (sales/GDP share) x (cost saving). Acemoglu (2024), Aghion-Bunel (2024), the OECD work, PWBM and Anthropic's Nov 2025 estimate all apply a version of it to tasks. The growth models in this stream (GATE, Erdil-Besiroglu, Korinek-Suh) use CES/growth models instead.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers. As Acemoglu (2024) writes it: TFP gain over 10 years = GDP share of tasks impacted by AI x average cost saving on those tasks (e.g. 0.046 x 0.144 = about 0.0066).
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: This is the aggregation step S = sum_j w_j theta_j. Hulten weights by sales or GDP share. The project weights by labor-time share, the labor-only analogue. It says nothing about where theta_j comes from; it takes the task-level saving as given.
works_verified.limitations: Valid only to first order, for small shocks in an efficient economy. AI savings of 30-80% on a task are not small (see Baqaee-Farhi).
works_verified.corrections: Fixed the URL: the record's '/r/' URL is the RePEc 'cited by' page, and the article page is '/a/'. The article page I opened lists Charles R. Hulten as author, with the same journal, volume, issue, pages and year. Removed the claim that 'every AI macro paper below uses this formula': the growth models in this stream do not.

works_verified.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Microeconomic Shocks: Beyond Hulten's Theorem
works_verified.authors: David Rezza Baqaee, Emmanuel Farhi
works_verified.what_measured: Second-order (nonlinear) corrections to Hulten's theorem. These come from elasticities of substitution, network linkages, returns to scale and factor reallocation.
works_verified.method_plain: Theory plus calibration. When goods are complements, a sector whose costs fall sees its share of spending shrink over time, while low-growth bottleneck sectors gain share (Baumol's cost disease). So nonlinearities shrink the effect of positive shocks and magnify negative ones relative to the first-order Hulten formula.
key_numbers: Nonlinearities that underpin Baumol's cost disease account for a 20 percentage point reduction in aggregate US TFP growth over 1948-2014 (abstract; this is a cumulative figure over the period, not per year).
In a business-cycle calibration, nonlinearities almost triple the estimated impact of the 1970s oil shocks on world aggregate output (abstract).
Average output losses from short-run sectoral shocks are an order of magnitude larger than Lucas's (1987) welfare cost of business cycles (abstract).
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Warns that the weights w_j are not fixed. If AI makes one task type much cheaper, its share of labor time changes, so S(t) computed with today's w_j can misstate later replacement. At firm level this is tied to the eps*phi demand channel. Suggestion: report both a first-order version and a reweighted version of S.
works_verified.limitations: Macro and sectoral focus, with no AI-specific numbers. Only the abstract page is open; the full text needs a login.
works_verified.corrections: None to the citation. Added the DOI and a third abstract number. Clarified that the 20 pp figure is cumulative over 1948-2014.

works_verified.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works_verified.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works_verified.venue: NBER Working Paper 32487; Economic Policy 40(121): 13-58 (2025), doi 10.1093/epolic/eiae042
works_verified.what_measured: Ten-year TFP and GDP effect of generative AI and computer vision in the US.
works_verified.method_plain: Hulten-style formula: TFP gain = (GDP share of tasks impacted) x (average overall cost saving). The impacted share = wage-bill-weighted exposure from Eloundou et al. (20%) x Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate = 4.6%. The labor cost saving is the average of two experiments: Noy & Zhang writing at about 40% and Brynjolfsson et al. customer service at 14%, giving 27%. Peng et al.'s 55.8% Copilot result is used only as a robustness check. Multiplying by an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535 gives an overall cost saving of 14.4%. Tasks are then split into easy and hard, with hard tasks given a 7% labor saving.
key_numbers: 20% of US labor tasks exposed (wage-bill-weighted, from Eloundou et al.)
23% of exposed tasks profitably automatable (Svanberg et al., computer vision)
0.23 x 0.20 = 4.6% of tasks impacted within 10 years
Average labor cost saving 27% (average of Noy-Zhang and Brynjolfsson et al.); adding Peng et al. gives 36% and an overall cost saving of 0.193, i.e. a TFP gain of 0.89%
Overall cost saving 0.27 x 0.535 = 0.144 (unadjusted labor share 0.576)
TFP gain no more than 0.66% in TOTAL over 10 years, about 0.064% per year

Easy/hard split: 72.6% of wage-bill-weighted exposed tasks are easy; easy exposed tasks are 3.3% of GDP and hard ones 1.3%; hard tasks get a 7% labor saving (half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s 14%), giving a TFP gain of about 0.53% over 10 years

GDP = TFP x about 1.75 (= 1/(1-0.43), capital share 0.43): 1.16% over 10 years, or 0.93% with hard tasks; with the Acemoglu-Restrepo investment response, up to 1.56% (no easy/hard split) or 1.4% (with the split)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The standard 'exposure x cost-effective share x saving' decomposition. The 27% is an intensive-margin number: experimental speedups on easy, well-defined tasks with 2023-era models, taken as given and held constant. It is not modeled from capability. It is net of review only to the extent that the experiments' measured time included checking. The 7% hard-task value is a judgment call. For theta_j, this is the template to beat. The 23% cost-effectiveness share comes from computer vision, not LLMs, a point the paper itself flags.
works_verified.limitations: Savings are frozen at early-2023 levels. Two or three experiments stand in for the whole economy. The cost-effectiveness share is borrowed from a different technology.
works_verified.corrections: Added Economic Policy pages 13-58 and the DOI (from the NBER page). Removed the claim that 'the April 2024 draft said 0.71%': I could not confirm it (search budget exhausted). Removed the claim that a footnote says displacement cannot be observed in experiments: not checked. Split the 1.4%-1.56% GDP range correctly: 1.56% without and 1.4% with the easy/hard split. All other numbers were checked against the May 12, 2024 PDF.

works_verified.title: GATE: An Integrated Assessment Model for AI Automation (plus 'AI and explosive growth redux')

works_verified.what_measured: Simulated paths of the automated share of tasks, compute investment and output growth.
works_verified.method_plain: Tasks lie on a continuum. The automated share f(C) stays at an initial level, then rises log-linearly in effective compute between a lower threshold and the full-automation threshold (the gap is the 'FLOP gap'), then equals 1. Tasks below the cutoff are automated; tasks above it are not. Automated tasks get digital workers = runtime compute allocated / runtime compute required. A CES across tasks (default rho = -0.65) creates bottlenecks, inside a semi-endogenous growth model with investment and adjustment costs.

Default simulation: 23% per year world output growth in 2027, which the redux essay calls 'extremely unlikely'

Redux essay: growth may exceed 20% per year at about 30% task automation; explosive growth (>30% per year) needs about 50-70% automation; with three dampening factors, about 12% growth at 40% automation
Epoch announcement: compute investment may exceed 10% of world GDP; growth elevated 2-20x relative to the historical ~3% per year, over roughly a decade
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive margin: a task is automated or not, with no partial labor saving per task, no review cost and no failure rate. The runtime-compute requirement is a cost-of-running term (part of the project's 'net of AI running cost'). The mentor, Andrei Potlogea, co-wrote both the GATE paper and the redux essay. GATE's f(compute) is the macro analog of 'which h-bins have p(h) high enough', so the project's integral could supply a partial-automation version.
works_verified.limitations: Built for qualitative insight, not forecasts (Epoch's own caveat). Assumes AI can substitute for human labor across all tasks. No industry detail.
works_verified.corrections: Authors were given as 'Epoch AI team'. The arXiv abstract lists nine named authors, including Andrei Potlogea (the mentor), so he co-wrote GATE itself, not only the redux essay. The 23%-in-2027 figure comes from the redux essay, not the GATE paper; I did not find it in the arXiv PDF. rho = -0.65 is confirmed in the paper's appendix. Added the essay's 12%-at-40% figure.

works_verified.title: Explosive growth from AI automation: A review of the arguments
works_verified.authors: Ege Erdil, Tamay Besiroglu

With f = 10% of tasks unautomated and rho = -1, output rises 100-fold

f = 25% of tasks unautomated with an elasticity of substitution of about 1/3 could plausibly block explosive growth

works_verified.title: Scenarios for the Transition to AGI
works_verified.authors: Anton Korinek, Donghyun Suh
works_verified.what_measured: Output and wage paths under different speeds of automation toward AGI.
works_verified.method_plain: Work is a set of atomistic tasks of varying complexity, and automation moves to ever more complex tasks. Wages depend on a race between automation and capital accumulation. If the complexity distribution has a heavy enough infinite tail, wages can rise indefinitely; if it is bounded and full automation occurs, wages collapse.

Paper: 'baseline AGI' (full automation in 20 years) reaches steady-state growth of about 18% per year after wages collapse
Paper: 'aggressive AGI' (full automation in 5 years), with wage collapse after about 3 years and an earlier growth take-off

Acemoglu (2024, footnote 1) characterizes the paper as predicting 'baseline' GDP growth of 100% over 10 years and an 'aggressive' 300% increase. This is second-hand, and I did not find these exact figures in the paper's text.

works_verified.corrections: Opened the arXiv HTML full text and added the paper's own scenario numbers (2%/yr business-as-usual; about 18%/yr steady state under baseline AGI). Acemoglu's '100% over 10 years / 300%' description is not stated in the paper text I read, so it should not be cited as the paper's result. Confirmed NBER WP 32255 and CEPR DP 18928 via RePEc. Raised citation confidence to high.

works_verified.title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
works_verified.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works_verified.what_measured: Theory, not measurement. A task-based growth model. Automation moves a range of tasks from labor to capital (the 'displacement effect'). Creating new labor-intensive tasks moves work back to labor (the 'reinstatement effect'). In the full model, capital accumulation and the direction of research are endogenous.
works_verified.method_plain: Tasks lie on a line. Tasks below a threshold I can be done by machines, and labor does the remaining tasks up to the newest task N. Automation pushes I up; new tasks push N up. In the static version (fixed capital), automation lowers employment and the labor share and can lower wages, while new tasks do the reverse. In the dynamic version, automation makes labor relatively cheap, which discourages further automation and encourages new tasks, so a stable balanced growth path can exist (unless the long-run rental rate of capital relative to wages is low enough, in which case all tasks are automated). Companion paper: Acemoglu and Restrepo, 'Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor', JEP 33(2): 3-30, Spring 2019 (abstract opened). It splits labor-demand effects into displacement, productivity and reinstatement, and its abstract says automation always reduces the labor share in value added.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers; a theory paper

JEP 2019 companion: abstract gives no figures; it attributes slower US employment growth over the last three decades mainly to faster displacement (especially in manufacturing), weaker reinstatement and slow productivity growth
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Here theta is binary at the task level: a task is either automated or not, so the 'replacement rate' of a task bundle j is the share of its tasks below the threshold I. That is a pure extensive margin. A continuous theta_j (fraction of time saved) would correspond to the hours-weighted share of j's subtasks crossing the threshold, which is what the integral over f_j(h) does if each h-slice is treated as a 'task'. The productivity and reinstatement effects sit outside theta, in d and eps*phi or in new-task creation. Speaks mainly to w_j (task composition shifting over time) and theta_j-direct.
works_verified.limitations: In an automated task, capital is assumed cheaper than labor, so labor stops doing it. There is no partial or assisted mode (no kappa) and no verification cost (no rho or q). Tasks are ordered exogenously. No calibration to AI or to services.
works_verified.corrections: None of substance. Bibliographic details and abstract claims for both the AER 2018 and JEP 2019 papers match the AEA pages. Small wording fix: the record said labor is 'useless' in automated tasks. In the model labor could still do them, but capital is cheaper, so it does not.

works_verified.title: Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality
works_verified.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works_verified.what_measured: How much of the change in the US wage structure from 1980 to 2016 is explained by 'task displacement', meaning the loss of tasks in which a worker group specialized, in industries that automated.
works_verified.method_plain: They build a task-displacement measure for each demographic group from the group's initial specialization in routine tasks combined with industry-level automation signals. They then relate changes in group wages to this measure and use a general-equilibrium model to compute aggregate effects. Construction details are beyond the abstract and were not checked.
key_numbers: Between 50% and 70% of changes in the US wage structure over the last four decades are accounted for by relative wage declines of worker groups specialized in routine tasks in industries that automated rapidly (abstract)
Automation accounts for most of the task-displacement effect, with offshoring playing a smaller role (abstract, qualitative)
Large changes in inequality can coexist with only modest productivity gains (abstract, qualitative)

That has the same structure as S = sum_j w_j theta_j, with w_j as a group's wage-bill share in task j. Realized displacement is measured top-down from industry signals, not bottom-up from capability, which matches the project's split between the filing-based 2.3 pp/yr and a capability-based theta.

The abstract says market power, markups and deunionization do not appear to be major drivers. No intensive margin or review cost. Details beyond the abstract were not verified.
works_verified.corrections: None. Venue, year and the 50-70% figure match the NBER page, which also lists the published Econometrica 90(5): 1973-2016 version.

works_verified.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works_verified.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works_verified.url_opened: https://www.nber.org/papers/w32487 ; full text of the April 5, 2024 version read from https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2024-04/The%20Simple%20Macroeconomics%20of%20AI.pdf
works_verified.what_measured: An upper bound on the 10-year TFP and GDP gains from AI, built as (share of tasks impacted) x (average cost saving per impacted task).
works_verified.method_plain: A Hulten's-theorem argument: to first order, the aggregate productivity gain equals the sum over tasks of each task's GDP share times its cost saving. He takes Eloundou et al.'s task exposure (which does not separate automation from task complementarity), weights occupations by wage bill, and gets 19.9% of tasks exposed. He extrapolates Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate within 10 years, giving 0.23 x 0.199 = 4.6% of tasks impacted. He takes 27% labor cost savings (the average of Noy-Zhang 2023 and Brynjolfsson et al. 2023) and multiplies by an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.57, giving total cost savings of 0.154. TFP gain = 0.046 x 0.154 = 0.71%. He then treats 'hard' tasks separately, with 7% labor savings (0.040 total cost savings).
key_numbers: 19.9% of US labor tasks exposed to AI (Eloundou et al., aggregated to occupations and weighted by wage-bill share)
23% of exposed tasks feasibly and profitably automatable within 10 years (Svanberg et al., computer vision, extrapolated), so 0.23 x 0.199 = 4.6% of tasks impacted

Average labor cost savings 27%; total cost savings 0.27 x 0.57 = 0.154 (15.4%). Adding Peng et al. (GitHub Copilot) raises labor savings to 0.36 and total savings to 0.205, giving 10-year TFP of 0.94%
April 2024 text: 10-year TFP gain at most about 0.71% (about 0.07%/yr); GDP about 1.1% (0.92% with hard tasks); 1.6-1.8% if there is a large investment boom

NBER/published abstract: TFP gain 'no more than 0.66%' over 10 years, and 'less than 0.53%' after the hard-task adjustment. The April 2024 abstract instead says 0.71% and 'less than 0.55%'. Quote the version you cite
Hard tasks: labor cost savings assumed 7% (half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s 14% customer-service effect), giving 0.040 total cost savings
If computer-vision costs fall 10%/yr (Svanberg scenario), the profitable share rises from 23% to about 30%, about 6% of GDP impacted and about 1% TFP over 10 years
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing analog to S(t) = sum_j w_j theta_j. In effect, theta is a product: (share of tasks impacted) x (cost saving on impacted tasks). The intensive margin (27%) is borrowed from 2023 RCTs rather than derived from capability, and it does not rise with capability; only the extensive share responds, in the GPU-cost scenario. His easy/hard task split is a crude two-point version of f_j. He says explicitly that it is unclear whether the RCT savings come from extensive-margin automation or task complementarities, and that the distinction matters less for productivity. That is the claim to test for employment, where it does matter.
works_verified.limitations: Intensive-margin numbers come from 2023 RCTs (writing tasks, call centres, Copilot) with pre-agent models and only measure speed, ignoring quality. No review-cost term. No link to capability growth beyond the GPU-cost scenario. Svanberg's computer-vision profitability share is extrapolated to all AI. Uses cost shares rather than hours shares.
works_verified.corrections: All numbers checked against the April 2024 full text and the NBER abstract. Added the April version's hard-task bound (0.55%), its hard-task GDP figure (0.92%) and the Peng-inclusive TFP figure (0.94%). New work shifted from middle-paid production and clerical jobs (1940-1980) to high-paid professional jobs and, secondarily, low-paid service jobs (since 1980) (abstract, qualitative)

works_verified.title: Trading Tasks: A Simple Theory of Offshoring
works_verified.authors: Gene M. Grossman, Esteban Rossi-Hansberg
works_verified.what_measured: Theory of how a falling cost of offshoring tasks affects home factor prices. Identifies a 'productivity effect' that benefits the factor whose tasks are easier to offshore.
works_verified.method_plain: Low-skill tasks i in [0,1] are ordered by how costly they are to do remotely. Doing task i abroad takes t(i) times as much foreign labor, with t rising in i. Firms offshore every task below a threshold I, where the wage gap just equals the remote-work penalty: w = t(I) w*. The unit cost of the low-skill tasks becomes w * a_L * Omega(I), with Omega(I) = 1 - I + [integral from 0 to I of t(i) di]/t(I). Omega(I) is below 1 when I > 0. Cheaper offshoring works like labor-augmenting technical progress for the low-skill workers who stay at home.
key_numbers: Threshold condition: w = t(I) w* (eq. 1, February 2008 version)
Cost factor Omega(I) = 1 - I + [integral_0^I t(i) di]/t(I) (eq. 3); Omega(I) < 1 for I > 0, so 1 - Omega(I) is the share of low-skill task cost saved
No empirical calibration in the paper
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: A useful structural template, not an identical model. Tasks are ordered by a single 'hard to hand off' index, a threshold separates delegated from in-house tasks, and the saving integrates a per-task penalty t(i) over the delegated range. Replacing the offshore worker with an AI agent, t(i) with (review + redo cost)/(human cost) at task length h, and I with the h at which delegation stops paying gives something close to the max{.} integral over f_j(h). Unlike the draft, though, GRH's penalty is deterministic, with no failure probability. The productivity effect is the warning: savings raise the effective productivity of the workers who remain, so theta need not translate one-for-one into job loss. The model also describes Indian IT services itself, as a destination of offshored tasks.
works_verified.limitations: Task characteristics do not depend on location (foreign and home tasks are perfect substitutes, per the paper's footnote). One-dimensional ordering. The small-country, price-taking assumptions drive the shared-gains result. No quality or error dimension. Equation numbering is from the February 2008 version; the AER version's notation was not checked.
works_verified.corrections: None of substance. Equations 1 and 3 match the February 2008 PDF, and the AER page confirms 98(5): 1978-97, December 2008. The 'mathematically the closest template' language is softened in the relevance note.

works_verified.title: Artificial Intelligence: The Ambiguous Labor Market Impact of Automating Prediction
works_verified.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works_verified.url_opened: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.33.2.31 ; companion NBER WP 24626, 'Exploring the Impact of Artificial Intelligence: Prediction versus Judgment' (May 2018; published in Information Economics and Policy, 2019), https://www.nber.org/papers/w24626
works_verified.what_measured: Conceptual framework. AI is a fall in the cost of prediction, and the paper asks how that interacts with human judgment (knowing the payoffs) and with decisions.

The JEP abstract gives examples where automating prediction ends up automating whole decisions and examples where it instead helps humans decide better. The WP 24626 abstract adds three points: cheaper prediction enables riskier decisions, which raises observed productivity and may raise variance; better prediction moves the returns to different kinds of judgment in opposite directions, so not all judgment complements AI; and humans may delegate decisions to machines even when human input would do better.

Only abstracts were verified; the body text (exact list of channels) was not opened

Fully delegated decisions correspond to the q*p(h) branch, and AI 'enhancing' a human who keeps judgment corresponds to kappa. Judgment (knowing the client's payoff function) is what review (rho) is for, so tasks where judgment cannot be codified should have high rho or low q. Conceptual only.

works_verified.title: Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production
works_verified.authors: Luis Garicano
works_verified.what_measured: Theory of why knowledge-based hierarchies form. Front-line workers learn the common or easy problems, and specialist problem-solvers handle the rarer or harder ones, because matching problems to solvers is costly.
works_verified.method_plain: Problems vary in difficulty. Each agent can solve problems up to some knowledge level, and unsolved problems are passed up the hierarchy, costing the solver time to help. The optimal organization trades learning costs against helping costs, which produces a pyramid. The abstract confirms the common/easy versus rare/hard division. The helping-time mechanics are standard in this literature (Ide-Talamas restate them) but were not read in Garicano's own text.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers in the abstract (full text paywalled)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Describes the structure of Indian IT delivery pyramids: many juniors, and a few leads who handle escalations and review. Helping time per referral is the economic analog of the review cost rho. Whose time is saved matters: if AI removes junior work but leads must review it, the saved hours are cheap junior hours and the added hours are expensive senior hours, so an hours-weighted theta_j and a cost-weighted theta_j can differ. This application to IT services is the stream's own interpretation, not something the paper does.
works_verified.limitations: Only the abstract and bibliographic details were verified. Stylized: one-dimensional difficulty and a homogeneous time cost of help.
works_verified.corrections: Added the DOI and month. Noted that the helping-time mechanism was not read in the full text.

works_verified.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy
works_verified.authors: Enrique Ide, Eduard Talamas (also spelled Talamàs)
works_verified.venue: Journal of Political Economy (DOI 10.1086/737233; volume, issue and pages not verified); earlier CEPR Discussion Paper DP19135 (2024)
works_verified.what_measured: Theory. How AI with a given knowledge level changes occupational sorting (workers vs solvers), wages and output in a Garicano-style hierarchy, comparing 'autonomous' AI (can do the work itself) with 'non-autonomous' AI (copilot only).
works_verified.method_plain: Humans have knowledge z in [0,1], the fraction of problems they can solve. Problem difficulty is Uniform[0,1] and independent across problems. Each referral costs the solver h units of time, so a two-layer team satisfies h * n(z) * (1 - z) = 1. AI turns compute into agents with fixed knowledge z_AI. Autonomous AI can act as worker or solver; non-autonomous AI acts only as a copilot.
key_numbers: Team time constraint: h * n(z) * (1 - z) = 1 (Section 3.1)

Prop. 2: AI is always used for independent production; the compute rental rate r* = z_AI; if z_AI is in the pre-AI worker range, AI is used as a worker. The post-AI wage function is continuous, strictly increasing and convex
Prop. 3: 'basic' AI (z_AI in the worker range) displaces humans from routine work into specialized problem solving; 'advanced' AI (z_AI in the solver range) displaces in the opposite direction

Prop. 5: there are always winners at the top, and winners at the bottom exist only if z_AI exceeds a threshold. Section 5.2 text: the individual with knowledge z_AI always loses, and gains are concentrated at the extremes of the knowledge distribution

Prop. 6: with non-autonomous AI the compute rental rate is 0, and overall output is strictly higher with autonomous than with non-autonomous AI. The abstract says autonomous AI primarily benefits the most knowledgeable and non-autonomous AI the least knowledgeable
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The most direct theory of the delegate-vs-assist distinction in the theta formula. Autonomous AI corresponds to the q*p(h) branch and copilot AI to the kappa branch. z_AI plays the role of p(h,t), the fraction of problems AI solves alone, and h (helping time) plays the role of rho. Implication: as capability rises, which pyramid layer is displaced changes. Basic AI pushes humans out of routine work; advanced AI pushes solvers down into routine work. A single theta_j per service line therefore hides which layer shrinks.
works_verified.limitations: AI is a perfect substitute for a human of equal knowledge (no q < 1 acceptance problem). Compute is abundant. Problem difficulty is uniform and one-dimensional. No calibration.
works_verified.corrections: Prop. 5 was mischaracterized. The record said Prop. 5 shows wage effects are non-monotone in z_AI and that the z_AI human always loses. In fact Prop. 5 states winners at the top always exist and winners at the bottom exist only above a z_AI threshold. The z_AI-human-always-loses statement is in the Section 5.2 text, and the winners-at-the-extremes pattern is across the knowledge distribution, not 'non-monotone in z_AI'. Added Prop. 2's wage-function properties and Prop. 6's r* = 0. The JPE venue is confirmed only through the DOI linked on arXiv and a Nature Index listing (the journal page returned 403), so volume and issue are unverified.

The abstract says these effects differ from those of changes in task quantity, and for employment they run in the opposite direction

works_verified.title: O-Ring Automation
works_verified.authors: Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works_verified.what_measured: Theory of automation when tasks are quality complements: output depends on the product of task qualities, and the worker splits a fixed time budget among the tasks that remain manual.

Because qualities multiply, automating one task changes the value of automating others, and the worker shifts freed time to bottleneck tasks (the 'focus' mechanism).
key_numbers: No numbers in the abstract

Abstract claims: task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete; adoption is discrete and may need bundling even when automation quality improves smoothly; labor income can rise under partial automation; exposure indices that add task-level risk linearly overstate displacement when tasks are complements

works_verified.title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation
works_verified.authors: Mert Demirer, John J. Horton, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier, Peyman Shahidi
works_verified.venue: NBER WP 34859 (February 2026, revised September 2026); arXiv 2606.15960 (v1 14 June 2026, v2 2 October 2026); accepted to the 27th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation (EC '26)
works_verified.what_measured: Theory plus empirical tests of how AI is assigned to sequential workflow steps: manual, augmented (human prompts and verifies each step), or automated in contiguous 'chains' verified only at the end.
works_verified.method_plain: Production is a Leontief sequence of steps. AI succeeds on step i with probability q_i = alpha^{d_i} (alpha = AI quality, d_i = step difficulty), independently across steps. A chain succeeds with probability alpha raised to the sum of its steps' difficulties, and a human verifies once at the end, retrying until it succeeds. The firm picks the cost-minimizing split of steps. Empirically they use O*NET tasks (ordered by GPT-5-mini via Expected Parrot) with Eloundou et al. exposure labels and Anthropic Economic Index execution labels. They validate the ordering with the APQC Process Classification Framework and eight 4TU.ResearchData process-mining logs.
key_numbers: Augmented step expected time = t^A / q (retry until success)
Chain expected time = t_r^A / product of q_i; verification happens once per chain
Three-step worked example (Section 4.1): optimal chaining costs 15.6 vs 35.4 under comparative-advantage assignment (model time units)
Two-step example (Section 4.3): below alpha = 0.5 no AI is used; between about 0.5 and about 0.92 only the easy step is augmented; above about 0.92 the two steps are chained
Fragmentation index: (1/8)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT in general; (1/4)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT if every manual time is at least 1

Empirical samples: about 18,000 O*NET tasks in 850+ occupations; 10,708 tasks across 1,748 Detailed Work Activities (Prediction 2); 872 occupations (Prediction 3); APQC PCF 13,482 steps in 525 process groups

Results: mean AI chain length 1.45 (O*NET) and 1.16 (PCF), above randomized placebos; an AI-executed adjacent step raises a step's execution probability by about 0.04-0.11; fragmentation coefficient negative and significant in PCF (about -0.26 to -0.35), small and insignificant in O*NET
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The most directly usable 2026 model for the theta formula, and it does derive expected labor time as a function of a capability index alpha, net of verification. q_i = alpha^{d} with additive difficulty has the same compounding logic as METR's logistic-in-log(h) p(h,t). It treats failure as 'retry and re-verify' (expected time t^A/q), whereas the draft treats failure as 'a human redoes it with kappa assistance', and these give different theta. Review cost is per verified chunk, not proportional to h, which challenges rho as a constant share of h. theta_j depends on how AI-able steps cluster within j, not only on f_j.
works_verified.limitations: Step failures are independent, and verification at the end of a chain is perfect (no undetected errors). The O*NET task ordering is LLM-generated. works_verified.title: Delegation and Verification Under AI
works_verified.authors: Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi
works_verified.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306: 48039-48071; arXiv 2603.02961 (v1 3 March 2026, v2 25 June 2026); Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper 2500
works_verified.what_measured: Theory of a rational worker choosing how much to delegate to AI (d) and how hard to verify (s), and how this affects quality as judged by the employing institution.
works_verified.method_plain: Success probability p(d,s) = (1-d)p_w + d*p_a + d(1-p_a)phi(s)p_w, where p_a = AI success, p_w = worker success, and phi(s) = chance of catching an AI error at verification effort s (e.g. 1 - e^{-alpha s}, or 1 - 1/(1+alpha s)). Expected cost = (1-d)C_w + d[C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]: delegate, pay to verify, and redo the caught failures by hand. The worker's choice jumps between manual work, pure delegation (no checking) and verified delegation.
key_numbers: Cost of verified delegation = C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)*phi(s)*C_w versus manual cost C_w

Theorem 3.1: three regimes (manual; pure delegation; verified delegation) with sharp boundaries in verification reliability alpha and execution efficiency beta, which the authors call phase transitions
Theorem 3.5: quality improves over the no-AI baseline if and only if alpha exceeds a threshold psi(beta); low-verification workers over-delegate and lower institutional quality

Calibration on Collab-CXR clinician data: C_v(s) = 118.1*s and C_w(beta) = 262.3*(1-beta) (maximum observed verification and execution times), giving p_w = 0.447, p_a = 0.368, C_w = 172.5 and cost of verified delegation 116.8
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Gives a micro-foundation for the theta integrand. Time saved per task = 1 - [C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]/C_w, so rho = C_v/C_w, p = p_a, and AI running cost is C_a/C_w. The difference from the draft is that missed errors (1-phi) are silently accepted: they cost quality, not time. The draft's q captures 'passes tests but would not be merged'. This model adds undetected failures, which suggests adding a quality-loss term or treating verification effort as chosen jointly with rho.
works_verified.limitations: A single task with binary success, and failures of worker and AI treated simply. The calibration comes from a radiology (chest X-ray) setting, not software or BPO. The institution-vs-worker objective is stylized.
works_verified.corrections: Venue details confirmed: PMLR 306 pages 48039-48071 (43rd ICML) and Cowles DP 2500 (the Yale repository's own sequence number is 2924; the CFDP number is 2500). Added the v2 date and the calibration values that the record said were 'not extracted'.

Separately, Anthropic Economic Index measures split AI use into 'automative' use (AI does the task) and 'augmentative' use (AI helps a person). Table 3, Panel A (March 2025 AEI release): automation coefficient for ages 22-25 is -0.098 (s.e. 0.018), as a fractional percent change in employment per SD. It shrinks with age to -0.006 for 50+. The complementarity coefficient is +0.024 (s.e. 0.010) for ages 41-49. Panel B (pooled later releases): -0.084 for ages 22-25.
Earlier versions headlined regression estimates of a 13% relative decline (July 2025 data) and 16% (September 2025 data). The 19%/15% figures are a different, purely descriptive metric.

The gap is a reduced form of roughly s(1 - eps*phi) times the exposure difference. Inverting it would need the theta gap between quintiles in hours, an assumption that demand shocks are common across quintiles, and an eps*phi correction. The automation-versus-augmentation split is only a rough occupation-level proxy for delegation (q*p) versus assistance (kappa). It is not a direct measure of theta or kappa.

They note some pre-existing divergent trends, strong attenuation when education is controlled, and larger gaps in ADP than in national surveys. Exposure is occupation-level and static. works_verified.corrections: No errors in the citation or numbers. Within firms, employment in highly exposed occupations (90th percentile of pay) falls about 3.1% relative to the least exposed. This is mildly reversed once firm growth is counted.

key_numbers: Reasonable alternative fits cut recent models' 50% horizons by up to 35% and raise their 80% horizons by up to 100%
For Opus 4.6, reasonable methods vary by about 1.5x at 50% and about 2x at 80%

Opus 4.6 on private-only tasks: the 50% horizon falls 40%, from 11h59m to 7h11m
The fixed-slope logistic, one slope shared by all models, performed best on both cross-validation metrics
The logistic model is very sensitive to performance on very easy tasks. This tends to give shallow slopes, which lower 80% horizons and raise 50% horizons
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: theta_j integrates p over the whole task-length distribution, so it depends on the slope and the curve shape, not only on the 50% point. The note shows that the high-reliability region moves by up to 2x across reasonable methods. Implication for the recipe: fit one shared slope, and report theta_j under at least the logistic and constant-hazard (or Weibull) curves.
works_verified.limitations: A research note, not peer reviewed. Software tasks only. No doubling-time estimates.
works_verified.corrections: Minor: the SIMEX 80% effect has a stated range of 0-50%. The note attributes shallow slopes to the logistic model in general, not only to per-model fits. The '35%/100%' figures come from 'reasonable alternative fits', which include more than curve shape.

works_verified.authors: Toby Ord (Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, University of Oxford)

works_verified.method_plain: Overlay a one-parameter exponential decay, p(h) = 0.5^(h/T50), on Kwa et al.'s per-model success curves and compare it visually with their log-logistic fit. Then derive the implied high-reliability horizons. Ord does no formal statistical comparison and says one should be done.
key_numbers: T80 ≈ 1/3 T50; T90 ≈ 1/7 T50; T99 ≈ 1/70 T50; T99.9 ≈ 1/700 T50 (each additional nine divides the horizon by 10)
Assuming a 7-month doubling time, T80 reaches a given length about 1 year after T50 does, T90 about 2 years after, T99 about 4 years after and T99.9 about 6 years after
Kwa et al.'s 80% horizon for Claude 3.7 Sonnet was 0.25 of its 50% horizon (15 vs 59 min), close to the constant-hazard prediction of 0.322
Human success decays more slowly than constant hazard predicts: still above 20% at 12 h, against a predicted 6.25%
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Gives a one-parameter, interpretable alternative form for p(h,t) and makes the reliability tails explicit. The record's own derivation was checked and is arithmetically correct: a logistic in log h with T80 = T50/5 implies T99 ≈ T50/207, against T50/70 under constant hazard.

works_verified.corrections: Clarified the method: Ord fits an exponential curve and compares it with the log-logistic by eye; he runs no formal model comparison. All key numbers match the PDF text.

works_verified.title: Estimating time spent on work tasks

The abstract also notes that 'recent work suggests weighting tasks by time spent', so prior work is not uniformly count-weighted.
