works_verified.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works_verified.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (lead authors); Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
works_verified.venue: Anthropic research report (data on Hugging Face, Anthropic/EconomicIndex, release_2026_01_15)
works_verified.what_measured: Five 'primitives' for sampled Claude conversations from Nov 13-20, 2025 (1M Claude.ai Free/Pro/Max conversations and 1M first-party API transcripts): task complexity, human and AI skills, use case (work/personal/education), AI autonomy, and task success. It also has Claude-estimated human time for each task without AI and with AI, which gives a speedup.
works_verified.method_plain: Claude classifiers label privacy-protected transcripts. Success is Claude's own judgment of whether the task was completed. The human-time estimates reuse Anthropic's earlier productivity method, which had shown Claude's time estimates correlate with actual time on software tasks. For Claude.ai, the new classifiers were checked against a human researcher's labels on a small set of transcripts with user feedback. For the API they were checked on internal and synthetic data. The authors call the classifiers 'directionally accurate' and say no single number should be treated as exact. Speedup = estimated time alone / estimated time with AI. Task-level speedups are then aggregated into a macro labor-productivity calculation, with and without a success adjustment.
key_numbers: Task success (Claude-judged): 67% on Claude.ai, 49% on the 1P API, 61% for software development requests

API success falls from about 60% on tasks under 1 human-hour to about 45% on tasks of 5+ human-hours. It crosses 50% at about 3.5 hours. On Claude.ai, a linear extrapolation reaches 50% at about 19 hours.

Mean estimated human-alone time: 3.1 h (Claude.ai), 1.7 h (API). Mean human-with-AI time: 15 min (Claude.ai), 5 min (API). Software development: about 3.3 h alone vs about 15 min with AI. All are Claude's estimates, not measured durations.
Speedup on Claude.ai: about 9x for tasks needing 12 years of schooling, about 12x for 16 years

Implied US labor productivity uplift: about 1.8 pp/yr over the next decade. Success-adjusted: 1.2 pp (Claude.ai) and 1.0 pp (API). With CES sigma = 0.5 (tasks are complements): 0.7-0.9 pp unadjusted, 0.8 pp (Claude.ai) and 0.6 pp (API) success-adjusted.
API traffic: 74% work-related and 64% directive. Claude.ai: 46% and 32%.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The closest public field analogue to p(h): success conditioned on estimated human task length, from real deployment. The time-alone vs time-with-AI ratio gives a crude theta or kappa per task. Adjusting for success cuts the uplift by roughly 33-44% (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp), which is the same logic as multiplying by p. It separately identifies neither review time (rho) nor reviewer acceptance (q). Both success and time are model-judged, so the figures are gross of human verification. The report acknowledges validation costs could reduce gains but does not net them out.
works_verified.limitations: Success and times are Claude's estimates, not observed outcomes. 'Time with AI' is Claude's estimate of collaboration time, not a measured duration of the whole workflow (integration, testing, review). The sample is selected: users bring tasks they expect AI to handle. Data are conversation-level, not hours-weighted task shares, so they are not f_j(h). There is no India or firm breakdown. Classifier validation used small samples.
works_verified.corrections: All key numbers confirmed on the report page. Clarified the sampling window (Nov 13-20, 2025; 1M + 1M transcripts) and the validation details. Added the unadjusted CES figure (0.7-0.9 pp). Reworded the limitation: 'time with AI' is a Claude estimate, not measured interaction time. Removed f_j from params, because the record's own limitations say these data are not f_j(h).

works_verified.title: Many SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged into main
works_verified.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works_verified.what_measured: Whether active repo maintainers would merge AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests. This is the gap between 'passes checks' and 'accepted by a reviewer'.
works_verified.method_plain: 4 active maintainers (2 scikit-learn, 1 Sphinx, 1 pytest) reviewed 296 grader-passing AI patches from 5 models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Old), Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. The 3 repos cover 95 of the 500 SWE-bench Verified issues. To measure noise in their own merge decisions, maintainers also reviewed 47 original human 'golden' patches, a random half of the golden set. Results are normalized to the golden merge rate.
key_numbers: About 68% of human golden patches were merged by maintainers (the noise baseline)
Golden-normalized, grader pass rates exceed maintainer merge rates by about 24.2 pp (SE 2.7). The summary says roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged.
Raw (unnormalized) gap: 34.9 pp (SE 2.2). Raw maintainer merge rates are roughly one-third to one-half of grader pass rates (Appendix A4).
Normalized trend: maintainer merge rates improve about 9.6 pp/yr less than grader scores (SE 5.5). The authors call this weak evidence. The raw trend difference is 15.5 pp/yr (SE 4.6).
Claude Sonnet 4.5's 50% time horizon is about 50 min under the grader vs about 8 min under maintainer merge decisions, roughly a 7x overstatement
By repo, level gaps are 18.3 pp (scikit-learn, SE 4.6), 23.3 pp (Sphinx, SE 4.1) and 43.1 pp (pytest, SE 5.2)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The source of q of about 0.5. The horizon shrinking about 7x, not 2x, suggests acceptance falls with task length, so q is better modeled as q(h). That is an inference from the horizon refit, not a directly reported q-by-length curve. A cleaner method is to refit p(h) with maintainer acceptance as the success criterion rather than multiplying by a scalar q. The trend evidence on whether q drifts over time is weak and differs by repo (it reverses for scikit-learn).
works_verified.limitations: Agents got one attempt, with no feedback or iteration. There was no CI (no linting or tests) during review. The study covers one benchmark, one harness and 3 Python OSS repos. Issues are small: golden patches average about 17 changed lines. The newest model is Sonnet 4.5. The setting is not enterprise maintenance work.
works_verified.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the SEs by repo, the raw trend difference, the 95/500 issue coverage, and the fact that maintainers reviewed a random half of golden patches. Flagged that 'q falls with h' is an inference.

works_verified.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works_verified.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth (Beth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works_verified.what_measured: The causal effect of allowing AI tools on completion time for real issues in developers' own large repositories.
works_verified.method_plain: A randomized controlled trial at the issue level. Each of 246 issues was randomly assigned 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed', and completion times were compared. Developers mainly used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. 'AI allowed' means developers could use AI as they chose, so the estimate is the effect of permission, not of any single usage mode.
key_numbers: 16 experienced developers on repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code
Issues averaged about 2 hours. Pay was $150/hr.
Allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (95% CI +2% to +39%, as restated in METR's Feb 2026 post. The GitHub README gives 0.188 with CI of about 0.013 to 0.395.)
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and believed afterward that AI had sped them up 20%
The page now carries a banner saying the results are out of date
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Causal evidence that the AI-assisted speedup could be negative in early 2025 on about 2-hour tasks. It is not a clean measure of kappa, because the treatment mixes assistant and delegate use (and non-use). Converted to the project's units (fraction of labor time saved = 1 - T_AI/T_alone), the estimate is about -0.19, not -0.16. The figure -0.16 is the change in output per hour (1 - 1/1.19). The perception gap (about +20% believed vs -19% measured, roughly 39 pp) warns against building theta from self-reports.
works_verified.limitations: Small sample of elite OSS maintainers on familiar codebases, unlike Indian IT services staff on client code. Early-2025 tools. METR itself labels the result out of date. The public data include initial and post-review implementation times for part of the study, so review time is only partially separable, not entirely absent.
works_verified.corrections: Citation and headline numbers confirmed. Corrected the relevance claim: time saved in the project's units is about -0.19, not -0.16. Noted that the treatment is 'AI allowed', not pure assistant mode. Softened the claim that the study does not separate review time: the dataset has post-review implementation time for part of the sample. The CI is not shown on the July 2025 blog page itself; it was confirmed via METR's Feb 2026 post and the GitHub README.

works_verified.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
works_verified.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)

key_numbers: Returning developers: -18% time (negative = speedup), 95% CI -38% to +9%
New developers: -4%, 95% CI -15% to +9%
30-50% of developers said they did not submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI
Pay was cut from $150/hr to $50/hr
Data: github.com/METR/Measuring-Late-2025-AI-on-OSS-Devs (public)

works_verified.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works_verified.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simón Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. Kim, Patrick Chao, Samuel Miserendino, Gildas Chabot, David Li, Michael Sharman, Alexandra Barr, Amelia Glaese, Jerry Tworek (OpenAI)
works_verified.what_measured: Blind expert comparisons of model vs human-expert deliverables on 1,320 real work tasks in 44 occupations across the top 9 US GDP sectors. Also expert completion time, monitored expert review time, and the implied speed and cost of a 'model, then human review, then human redo if it fails' workflow.
works_verified.method_plain: Professionals (average 14 years' experience, minimum 4) wrote tasks from their real work. Other experts graded model vs human outputs blind. Human completion time was self-reported and checked by reviewers. Review time was observed from task-monitoring software. 'Try 1 time': expected time = model time + review time + (1 - w) x full human time, where w is the win-or-tie rate. 'Try n times': resample and re-review up to n times, then the human does it. Speed ratio = human time / expected time. All speed and cost figures are computed on the 220-task gold subset.
key_numbers: 1,320 tasks in the full set; 220-task open-sourced gold subset
Best win-or-tie rate vs experts: Claude Opus 4.1 at 47.6% (gold subset)
Average expert completion time 404 min at $361 per task (gold subset)
Average expert review time 109 min ($86) per deliverable, about 27% of completion time
Speed multipliers, Try n times: gpt-4o 0.46x, o4-mini 1.06x, o3 1.28x, gpt-5 1.39x. Cost: 0.53x, 1.22x, 1.47x, 1.63x.
GPT-5 (win rate 39.0%), Try 1 time: 1.12x speed, 1.18x cost
Software Developers is an included occupation (Professional, Scientific and Technical Services)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The 'try' formulas are structurally close to the project's delegate branch: success probability (w, the expert win-or-tie rate, standing in for p*q), review cost (rho about 0.27 on tasks averaging about 6.7 h), and a fallback to full human redo. They have no partial-credit or assistant term (no kappa): a failure means the whole task is redone. Implied time saved for GPT-5 is about 1 - 1/1.39 = 0.28 (try n) or 1 - 1/1.12 = 0.11 (try once), on this task mix. It is the best public template for measuring rho directly.
works_verified.limitations: One-shot, self-contained deliverables written by recruited experts, not an hours-weighted sample of real work (not f_j). Speed and cost tables cover OpenAI models only. Footnote 9 says the try-n calculation over-penalizes the model. 'Win' includes ties with the human, a lenient acceptance bar. Grading is preference-based. There is no Indian IT services mix.
works_verified.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the full 19-author list, the try-once GPT-5 figures (1.12x speed, 39.0% win rate), and the facts that the speed/cost figures are on the gold subset and completion times are self-reported while review time is monitored. Softened 'structurally almost identical to the integrand' to note there is no assistant (kappa) branch.

works_verified.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 version)
works_verified.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
works_verified.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper. Accompanying news post: 'No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%' (Aug 12, 2026).
works_verified.what_measured: US employment by age and AI-exposure quintile, using ADP payroll data through June 2026.
works_verified.method_plain: Occupations are ranked into AI-exposure quintiles (the Eloundou et al. GPT-4 'beta' measure, plus alternatives). Usage data split occupations into automating vs complementary AI use. The 19% headline is a simple descriptive 'kept-pace' gap: how far young exposed workers' employment is below where it would be had it grown like less-exposed peers. Earlier versions headlined regressions that adjust for firm-level shocks. This is descriptive, not causal.
key_numbers: Employment of workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations is 19% below the kept-pace path (June 2026), up from 15% at the July 2025 data vintage (same descriptive measure)
Nov 2022 to Jun 2026, ages 22-25: employment fell about 11% in the top two exposure quintiles and grew about 10% in the bottom three

Earlier versions headlined a different measure, a firm-shock-adjusted regression: 13% relative decline on July 2025 data and 16% on September 2025 data. Do not mix these with the 15%/19% descriptive figures.

No evidence of economy-wide displacement. The adjustment runs mainly through reduced hiring, not separations. Declines are concentrated where AI use substitutes for tasks, with flat or rising employment where it complements. So far it shows up in employment, not base pay.
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Measures outcomes downstream of theta, using extensive-margin exposure scores plus an automation/complementarity split. It does not measure labor time saved, which supports the working hypothesis. Useful as a validation target: the realized effect is on hiring and concentrated among juniors, which matters for w_j and the pyramid structure in Indian IT.
works_verified.limitations: Descriptive, not causal. Gaps shrink with education controls. Some divergent trends predate generative AI. Gaps are larger in the ADP sample than in national survey benchmarks. Specifications that account for firm hiring became more sensitive after data-pipeline changes. US only. No task-level time-saved measure.
works_verified.corrections: (1) The 16% figure is from September 2025 data, not a 'Nov 2025 version'. (2) The 13% and 16% are firm-shock-adjusted regression estimates, a different measure from the 15%/19% descriptive kept-pace gap, so mixing them is a measurement mismatch, not just a vintage issue. (3) The method description wrongly said the headline controls for firm-level shocks; the 19% headline is the simple descriptive divergence. (4) Replaced the news-post URL with the paper PDF and gave the paper's exact title ('Six Facts about').

works_verified.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
works_verified.authors: Maithra Raghu, Katy Blumer, Greg Corrado, Jon Kleinberg, Ziad Obermeyer, Sendhil Mullainathan
works_verified.what_measured: Diagnostic error on diabetic retinopathy grading under three regimes: human doctors only, the algorithm on every case (full automation), and per-case triage, where some cases go to the algorithm and the freed human effort goes to the rest.
works_verified.method_plain: A CNN grades fundus (eye) photos. A second model predicts, for each case, how likely the algorithm and the doctors are to be wrong. Cases are ranked by this 'triage score'. The easiest share goes to the algorithm, and the human budget (several doctor reads per case) goes to the hardest cases. Main evaluation is on an adjudicated gold-standard set; an appendix repeats it on a noisier holdout set.
key_numbers: Error rate: about 5.5% for human doctors, about 4% with full automation, about 3.5% with optimal triage (introduction, not the abstract)
On roughly 40% of instances the algorithm has zero errors (adjudicated set)
Triaging by model uncertainty finds a zero-error subset of 35% of the data; a separate error-prediction model raises this to 44%; both averaged over 3 training repetitions (adjudicated set)

On the noisier holdout set (appendix) the zero-error shares are smaller, roughly 10-24% depending on method and on one repetition that makes two errors; total error there is about 10% vs 4% in the main text
There is a nontrivial mass, about 5%, of cases where human experts have lower error probability than the model (Figure 3)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the automation ceiling depends on predicting algorithm (and human) error for each instance, not on the average error. For the draft, this argues for an instance-level p_i rather than p(h). Because max{.} is convex, the average over instances of max(q p_i(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa) is at least the max evaluated at E[p|h] (Jensen's inequality). This is an ORACLE bound: the gain actually achievable depends on how well p_i can be predicted in advance, and the paper's holdout results show that gain shrinks with noisier labels. The idea that the zero-error slice needs near-zero review (rho close to 0) is the record's inference, not a result of the paper.
works_verified.limitations: Medical image classification, not generative or agentic work; 2019 CNN; outcome is error, not labor time; the human-effort budget is stylized (number of doctor reads); preprint; zero-error shares are much smaller on the noisier holdout set.
works_verified.corrections: Numbers confirmed in the PDF text. Clarified that the 5.5/4/3.5% figures are in the introduction, not the abstract. works_verified.title: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology
works_verified.authors: Nikhil Agarwal, Alex Moehring, Pranav Rajpurkar, Tobias Salz
works_verified.venue: NBER Working Paper 31422 (July 2023, revised August 2026); pre-registered AEARCTR-0009620
works_verified.what_measured: Accuracy and active time of 227 professional radiologists reading chest X-rays with or without AI predictions and with or without clinical history (2x2 information design). Also estimates how radiologists weight the AI against their own signal, and the optimal case-level delegation among AI alone, human alone and human+AI.
works_verified.method_plain: A randomized information experiment. A structural model of belief updating is estimated by GMM. Its weights show whether people over-trust AI (automation bias) or under-trust it (automation neglect). A delegation policy then routes each case, based on the AI's predicted probability, to minimize (dollar cost of a false negative x decision loss) + human time cost. In the main analysis human time with and without AI is treated as equal; an appendix uses a radiologist wage of $3.6 per minute with heterogeneous time.
key_numbers: 227 radiologists; recommendations match the diagnostic standard in 73.2% of patient-pathology pairs; 2.79 minutes per patient on average (2.8 in the delegation section)
AI predictions do not improve average performance, although the AI tool performs better than about three-quarters of radiologists

AI assistance slows radiologists by about 4% (about +5.9 seconds, s.e. 2.3, on a base of about 154 seconds of active time, Appendix Table C.6); the authors treat human time with and without AI as similar in the delegation model
Weight on the focal AI signal b = 0.26 (s.e. 0.02) vs weight on own information d = 0.88 (s.e. 0.01) in the selected model, i.e. automation neglect
48% of radiologists improve on average with AI assistance

Optimal delegation: AI decides almost all cases if a false negative costs less than $100. Using observed behavior and a high false-negative cost, humans are involved in 51% of cases, mostly without AI assistance. For a Bayesian decision-maker even at $10,000, 21% of cases go to AI alone
Moving from the unassisted radiologist to the frontier can reduce decision loss while saving $4.9 per case in time costs
Radiologist wage of $3.6 per minute (footnote / Appendix C.8.2)
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that kappa, the assistant-mode speedup, can be zero or slightly negative: AI slowed experts by about 4% with no average accuracy gain. It also shows that, given observed (biased) human updating, the best design is either/or routing by case. For the draft, kappa should not be assumed positive, and with biased reviewers the max{} should compare 'delegate to AI' with 'human alone'. Note that for a fully Bayesian reviewer the optimal policy does use human+AI, so this depends on reviewer behavior.
works_verified.limitations: Classification of X-rays, not generative or coding work; the AI gives a probability, not a draft artifact; an experiment on retrospective cases, not production; radiology has liability and regulatory constraints unlike IT services.
works_verified.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the August 2026 revision PDF. Added the s.e. and source table for the 4% slowdown. Added the nuance that the main delegation model sets human time with and without AI equal, and that $3.6/minute is used in a footnote and appendix variant. Clarified that b is the weight on the focal AI signal.

works_verified.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas Malone
works_verified.what_measured: Whether human+AI teams beat the better of human alone or AI alone ('synergy'), and whether they beat the human alone ('augmentation'), across published experiments.
works_verified.method_plain: A meta-analysis pooling standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g: difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation, with a small-sample correction), with moderator regressions by task type and by which party performs better alone.
key_numbers: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes
Synergy (human+AI vs best of the two alone): g = -0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07)
Augmentation (human+AI vs human alone): g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.74)
Decision tasks: synergy g = -0.27 (95% CI -0.44 to -0.10); creation tasks: g = 0.19 (95% CI -0.09 to 0.48, not significant, n = 34)
When the AI alone beats the human: synergy g = -0.54; when the human beats the AI: g = 0.46
Only 3 experiments (4 effect sizes) used a predetermined delegation of separate subtasks; synergy g = 0.22 (95% CI -0.42 to 0.87), not significant
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Generalizes the Agarwal result. Where AI outperforms people, adding a human to the loop tends to make results worse than AI alone, so the max{} rule should often choose pure delegation or pure human. Creation tasks, which are closer to code, show positive but imprecise synergy, so kappa for generative work may be positive. Outcomes are quality, not time saved, so this bears on the sign of kappa only indirectly.
works_verified.limitations: Outcomes are quality or accuracy, not labor time; lab and online experiments with a mix of crowdworkers and experts (e.g. doctors); few coding or agentic tasks; heterogeneous metrics.

works_verified.what_measured: Review logs for about 9 million reviewed changes (Jan 2014 to Jul 2016) from more than 25,000 authors and reviewers. About 13 million comments (Sep 2014 to Jul 2016). Reviewer time from logged tool interactions over five weeks starting in October 2016. Also 12 interviews and a survey sent to 98 engineers, with 44 valid responses (45% response rate).

A 'review session' is a run of interactions on one uncommitted change by someone other than the author, with no more than 10 minutes between interactions. Session hours are summed and averaged per user per week. Users without data for all 5 weeks are dropped.
key_numbers: Reviewer time: mean 3.2 hours/week, median 2.6 hours/week, spent reviewing changes (from logs, not self-report). The paper contrasts this with 6.4 hours/week self-reported for open-source projects (Bosu & Carver 2013)
Median developer authors about 3 changes/week (80% author fewer than 7). Median developer reviews 4 changes/week (80% review fewer than 10)
Median change size: 24 lines modified. Over 10% of changes modify a single line. Over 35% modify one file and about 90% modify fewer than 10 files
Median wait for first feedback: under 1 hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large changes. Overall median latency of the whole review process: under 4 hours (elapsed time, not effort)
Fewer than 25% of changes have more than one reviewer, and the median reviewer count is 1
Average comments per change rise with lines changed, peaking at 12.5 comments/change for changes of about 1,250 lines

Cited from Rigby & Bird: median time to approval 17.5 h (AMD), 15.7 h (Chrome OS), 14.7/19.8/18.9 h (three Microsoft projects). Median change size 44 lines (AMD) and 263 lines (Lucent). Another study (Czerwonka et al.) gives 24 h at Microsoft
Over 80% of changes involve at most one iteration of resolving comments

Derived by the stream, not stated in the paper: 3.2 h/week divided by about 4 changes reviewed/week gives roughly 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change. This is crude because it divides a mean by a median
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: The best large-scale, log-based baseline for reviewer effort on human-written code (rho). About 3 hours per week goes to review, roughly 8% of a 40-hour week (the 40 hours is an assumption). That is at a median change size of 24 lines and one reviewer. Review effort, measured by comments, grows with change size up to about 1,250 lines, which matters because agent PRs are larger. The latency numbers are elapsed calendar time and must not be used directly as rho. Note: if about 45-50 minutes goes to a 24-line change, the implied rate is about 30 lines/hour. Using the 2000 Census 5% PUMS (place-of-work metro areas), they compute a demand-weighted locational Gini for each industry and occupation. An industry or occupation with Gini of 0.1 or more is classed as tradable. The 0.1 cutoff was chosen by checking it against goods-producing industries, which are known to be mostly tradable.
key_numbers: Employment in tradable professional and business service industries (NAICS 51-56): 13.7% of total US employment, more than tradable manufacturing (12.4%)

Share of employment classed as tradable, by occupation group: computer and mathematical 100%, legal 96%, life/physical/social sciences 83%, business and financial operations 68%, architecture and engineering 63%

Across ALL industries, workers in tradable industries earn 6% more, controlling for demographics and industry and region fixed effects. Within professional services, tradable-industry workers earn almost 15% more

Mean tradable service industry employment growth was 7.6%, against 6.7% for non-tradable services. There is some evidence of lower growth at the low-skill end and higher displacement rates in tradable services
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: An objective, outcome-based exposure measure that complements Blinder's judgment-based one. It classes all US computer and mathematical occupations as tradable. It is still an extensive-margin, yes/no classification and says nothing about labor saved. Its useful idea for the project is identifying exposure from revealed behavior rather than judgment. The AI analogue (inferring theta_j from where firms actually send work to AI) is the researcher's suggestion, not something in the paper.
works_verified.limitations: Measures tradability, not labor saved. The 0.1 threshold is a judgment call. Uses US 2000 data. Covers US occupations, so mapping to Indian IT/BPO roles is an inference: BPO roles such as call centre and data entry sit in office/admin support and sales groups, not in computer and mathematical.
works_verified.corrections: The 6% wage premium is for tradable vs. non-tradable industries across ALL industries, not specifically service industries; the 'almost 15%' figure is within professional services. Added the 7.6% vs 6.7% service growth figures. Added published-version details (Brookings Trade Forum 2005, published 2006, pp. 75-116, eds. Collins and Brainard), taken from a reference list and not independently opened; that version's title says 'Outsourcing' where the WP says 'Offshoring'. Removed w_j from params. Toned down the relevance claim that 'essentially the whole Indian IT/BPO workforce' is fully exposed, because BPO occupations are not in the computer and mathematical group. The WP number 05-9 comes from the PDF filename and the September date from the cover; the PIIE landing page was not found (404).
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works_verified.title: Introduction to 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization' (summarizing van Welsum and Reif, 'We Can Work It Out: The Globalization of ICT-enabled Services', chapter 9)
works_verified.authors: Marshall Reinsdorf and Matthew J. Slaughter (introduction); the underlying chapter is by Desirée van Welsum and Xavier Reif
works_verified.venue: NBER volume 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization', eds. Reinsdorf and Slaughter, University of Chicago Press, May 2009 (conference April 28-29, 2006); introduction is chapter c11604, pp. 1-24
works_verified.what_measured: The editors' summary of the volume, including van Welsum and Reif's estimate of the share of employment in OECD countries that is potentially offshorable.
works_verified.method_plain: Per the editors, van Welsum and Reif count employees in detailed occupations with four attributes: (a) intensive use of ICT; (b) output that can be transmitted by ICT; (c) highly codifiable knowledge content; and (d) no need for face-to-face contact.
key_numbers: 18 to 20 percent of total employment is potentially offshorable in the OECD countries with detailed enough data; the editors call this an upper bound
The editors say this is slightly above the US tradable-services employment share found by Jensen and Kletzer
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Its four criteria (codifiable knowledge, output sent digitally, no face-to-face contact) resemble the features used in LLM exposure rubrics. It is extensive-margin only. The link to f_j(h), that codified work comes in short units where p(h,t) is highest, is the researcher's hypothesis and is not in the source.
works_verified.limitations: Only the editors' introduction was read; the van Welsum-Reif chapter itself was not opened, so its details are second-hand. Extensive margin only.
works_verified.corrections: No numeric changes; the four attributes, the 18-20% figure and the Jensen-Kletzer comparison all match the PDF. The introduction refers to the chapter as 'We can Work it Out: The Globalization of IT-enabled Services'. Marked the f_j(h) link as the researcher's speculation.
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works_verified.title: Reputation Effects and the Limits of Contracting: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works_verified.authors: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo
works_verified.what_measured: How ex ante contract terms and ex post outcomes after renegotiation in Indian customized-software projects vary with firm characteristics linked to reputation. The abstract does not mention fixed-price vs. time-and-materials contracts, so that framing is not confirmed here.
works_verified.method_plain: The authors collected their own data on 230 software projects carried out by 125 Indian firms. They relate contract terms and outcomes to reputation-related firm characteristics, controlling for project, client and firm characteristics, and interpret the results with a model in which reputation shapes contracts.
key_numbers: 230 projects
125 Indian software firms
Abstract: both ex ante contract terms and ex post outcomes vary with reputation-related firm characteristics, after controls
No effect sizes confirmed; the full text was not read
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Not about theta_j. It is classic micro evidence on how Indian IT contracts handle risk and reputation, which bears on pass-through phi. The researcher's argument that savings pass to the client under time-and-materials (phi near 1) but stay with the vendor under fixed price until renegotiation is a plausible hypothesis, not a finding of this paper as far as could be checked. Using this kind of data to measure q or rho is speculative.
works_verified.limitations: Late-1990s data. Only the abstract and metadata were read (paywalled), so no coefficients and no fixed-price/T&M results are confirmed.
works_verified.corrections: The citation is correct; added the August 2000 issue date. Removed 'fixed-price vs. time-and-materials' from what_measured as a confirmed feature, because the abstract does not mention it. It may be in the full text, but that was not checked. Marked the phi, q and rho arguments as the researcher's hypotheses. The claim that TCS and Infosys report a fixed-price/T&M revenue split in their annual reports was not checked.
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works_verified.title: Quality Certification and the Economics of Contract Software Development: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works_verified.authors: Ashish Arora and Jai Asundi
works_verified.venue: NBER Working Paper 7260 (July 1999); no published version listed on the NBER page
works_verified.what_measured: Whether ISO 9001 certification is associated with firm growth and with higher revenue for a given firm size (implying higher price or quality) for Indian contract-software firms.
works_verified.method_plain: A simple model of a firm that develops software for others under contract, plus data on 95 Indian software firms and their US clients, plus field interviews.
key_numbers: 95 Indian software firms
ISO certification increases firm growth
Partial evidence that certified firms earn more revenue for a given size, implying higher prices per unit of output and so higher quality
Field interviews: most firms see ISO mainly as a marketing tool, though some adopted more systematic, better-defined development processes
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Shows that Indian IT firms signalled quality to distant clients through certification, a verification problem similar to the one now facing AI delegation (q, rho). The paper does not measure verification cost or task length. The ideas that process-heavy delivery pushes f_j(h) toward short tasks, and that this feeds q, are the researcher's inference.
works_verified.limitations: Old data; a working paper; only the abstract was read, and it gives no coefficients. Interviews suggest certification was often a marketing signal rather than a real process change, which weakens the 'made verifiable' reading.
works_verified.corrections: Citation and abstract claims confirmed. Removed q from params: the paper does not estimate acceptance rates. Noted that the 'pre-specified tasks push f_j(h) short' link is the researcher's inference. The companion Research Policy 2001 paper (Arora, Arunachalam, Asundi, Fernandes) was not verified.
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works_verified.title: The Service Sector as India's Road to Economic Growth
works_verified.authors: Barry Eichengreen and Poonam Gupta
works_verified.venue: NBER Working Paper 16757 (February 2011); published as 'The Service Sector as India's Road to Economic Growth?' in India Policy Forum 7(1): 1-42 (NCAER, 2011), per the NBER page
works_verified.what_measured: India's services growth compared with international norms, the roles of modern services (business services, communications, banking) and of IT in traditional services, and the skill mix of service employment.
works_verified.method_plain: Compares India's services share with cross-country norms, and uses Indian sectoral and household data to see who works in modern services.
key_numbers: India's services growth started about 15 years earlier from unusually low levels, and the services share has roughly converged to international norms

Continued above-norm growth depends on modern services and on applying IT to traditional services (retail and wholesale trade, transport and storage, public administration). The abstract says the latter helps output more than employment
Modern service employment is not simply manufacturing in disguise. The skill mix in manufacturing and services is increasingly similar, so modern services are not only for the highly skilled
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: Macro context for demand d and for why IT/BPO jobs matter for India's growth model. It does not inform theta_j. Its remark that IT in traditional services raises output more than employment loosely echoes the s versus eps*phi question.
works_verified.limitations: Pre-AI and macro-level; only the abstract was read.
works_verified.corrections: The published India Policy Forum title ends with a question mark ('...Road to Economic Growth?'). The other content matches the abstract.
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works_verified.title: Do Labor Market Opportunities Affect Young Women's Work and Family Decisions? Experimental Evidence from India
works_verified.authors: Robert Jensen
works_verified.what_measured: Effects of BPO recruiting services, offered in randomly chosen rural Indian villages, on young women's employment, schooling, marriage and fertility.
works_verified.method_plain: For three years, recruiting services for BPO jobs were provided to young women in randomly selected villages. The industry was new and little known, so this shifted households' perceived job options for women in a way they had not anticipated. Outcomes are compared with control villages.
key_numbers: Young women in treatment villages were less likely to marry or have children during the study period, and more likely to enter the labor market or get more schooling or post-school training
They reported wanting fewer children and expecting to work more continuously over their lives
Sample sizes and coefficients not recorded: paywalled, only the abstract was read
works_verified.relevance_to_theta: No bearing on theta_j. Relevant to who bears losses if BPO employment shrinks, and to the idea that perceived job prospects change human-capital investment. The claims that BPO is the most exposed service line and has the highest AI pass rates are the researcher's speculation, not from this paper.
works_verified.limitations: A recruitment intervention from the 2000s, not a labor-demand shock; only the abstract was read.
works_verified.corrections: Citation confirmed. Marked as speculation the relevance claims about BPO being most exposed and having the highest pass rates.
works_verified.stream: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models (arXiv v5); published as 'GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs', Science, 2024
works.authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
works.year: 2023 (arXiv v1 Mar 2023, v5 Aug 2023); Science 20 Jun 2024
works.venue: arXiv 2303.10130; Science (2024). I could not open the Science page (HTTP 403), so the volume and pages are unverified. The GovAI summary page confirms the Science publication and its headline numbers.
works.what_measured: Whether each O*NET task or Detailed Work Activity (DWA) is 'exposed' to LLMs. The dataset has 19,265 tasks and 2,087 DWAs. Each one gets one of three labels. E0 means no or minimal time saving at equal quality, or a loss of quality. E1 means direct ChatGPT/Playground access cuts task time by at least 50% at equivalent quality. E2 means the LLM alone does not reach 50%, but software built on top of it plausibly would. These labels are rolled up into occupation shares: alpha = E1, beta = E1 + 0.5*E2, zeta = E1 + E2.
works.method_plain: Annotators read task descriptions and applied a rubric. The authors labeled the clearly physical DWAs themselves. Contracted annotators did the rest; they had experience reviewing GPT-3/3.5/4 outputs from OpenAI alignment work, but they were not workers in the occupations. Separately, an early GPT-4 was prompted with a slightly modified rubric, tuned to agree with a sample of the authors' labels, and it labeled every task-occupation pair. 'Equivalent quality' is defined as the recipient of the output would not notice or care that an LLM helped. Tasks are aggregated to occupations with core tasks weighted twice as heavily as supplemental tasks. Time spent per task is not used.
key_numbers: Abstract: ~80% of US workers could have >=10% of their tasks affected; ~19% may have >=50% of their tasks affected. This is beta exposure, i.e. a share of TASKS. It is not a share of time saved.
Abstract: ~15% of all worker tasks could be done 'significantly faster at the same level of quality' with LLM access alone; 47-56% with LLM-powered software.
Mean occupation-level alpha is 0.14-0.15 (human and GPT-4 labels); beta >0.30; zeta >0.50.
Human labels: 2.3% of occupations are alpha-50 exposed, 21.6% beta-50, 47.3% zeta-50.
GPT-4 (Rubric 1) vs human agreement at the occupation level: 80.8% for alpha (Pearson 0.223), 65.6% for beta (0.591), 82.1% for zeta (0.654).

Science version (per GovAI page): ~1.8% of jobs have >half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces; 'just over 46%' when complementary software is counted. People often quote the 80%/19% preprint figures as if they were time savings or job losses. They are neither.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the canonical extensive-margin measure. E1 is a thresholded indicator: 1{believed time saving >= 50% at equal quality}. It does not measure the size of the saving. If you read it as a bound on the per-task saving theta, it only gives: theta >= 0.5 on E1 tasks and theta < 0.5 on E0 tasks. So for a service line with E1 share alpha_j, theta_j lies roughly between 0.5*alpha_j and 0.5 + 0.5*alpha_j. That interval is too wide to be useful. The labels are also GROSS. They are about time to produce output; review cost (rho), rejection of output that passes checks (q) and running cost are not netted out. The authors say they chose a high threshold because they 'guessed that the real-world reduction in task time would likely be slightly or significantly lower than our estimates'. The 0.5 weight on E2 in beta is a discount for the complementary investment needed. It is not a time fraction. 'Equivalent quality' (the recipient would not notice or care) is close in spirit to our q, but it is a labeler's belief, not something measured. Task weights are core/supplemental counts, not hours, so they do not give f_j or w_j. The measure is a snapshot of early GPT-4, so it has no time variation.
works.limitations: Labels are subjective, and the annotators are not occupationally diverse. GPT-4 labels are sensitive to prompt wording. There is no time-use weighting and no task-length dimension (h). Labels are binary/ordinal, not continuous. It is a single snapshot in time. It measures gross time saving, not net of review. It uses US O*NET tasks, which may not match how work is split up in Indian IT services.

works.title: Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses (AIOE); plus follow-up 'How will Language Modelers like ChatGPT Affect Occupations and Industries?'
works.authors: Edward Felten, Manav Raj, Robert Seamans
works.what_measured: The AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) score for each occupation. Industry (AIIE) and county (AIGE) versions are built by aggregating it.
works.method_plain: Ten AI application areas are taken from the Electronic Frontier Foundation's AI Progress Measurement: games, image recognition, visual question answering, image generation, reading comprehension, language modeling, translation, speech recognition, and others. A crowd survey on Mechanical Turk rates how related each application is to each of O*NET's 52 human abilities. Ability-level exposure is the sum of those relatedness scores. Occupation exposure averages ability exposure, weighted by O*NET's prevalence and importance of each ability, and the result is standardized. The 2023 'language modeling' version sets every application weight to zero except language modeling.
key_numbers: 10 AI applications × 52 O*NET abilities × 800+ occupations.
LM-AIOE top exposed occupations: telemarketers and post-secondary teachers (English, foreign languages, history). Top exposed industries: legal services and securities/commodities/investments.
The score is a standardized relative index. It has no natural units such as % of time.
works.relevance_to_theta: Ordinal and relative only. It ranks occupations by how much their abilities overlap with AI capabilities. It says nothing about time saved, review cost or failure rates. The application-weighting step can be updated as capabilities change (shown in the 2023 LM version), so it can in principle vary over time. But the weights are set by hand, not tied to measured capability like METR's p(h,t). It is useful at most as a cross-check on the relative ordering of exposure across IT service lines. It cannot supply a theta level.
works.limitations: Ability-based rather than task-based. Based on crowd relatedness judgments, not observed performance. Units are standardized, so levels cannot be compared over time. It does not separate substitution from augmentation (the authors deliberately call it 'agnostic').

works.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market
works.authors: Michael Webb
works.venue: Working paper (Stanford job market paper; SSRN 3482150; NBER conference draft)
works.what_measured: Exposure of occupations to AI (and, historically, to software and robots), based on how much text overlaps between patents and O*NET task descriptions.
works.method_plain: Verb-noun pairs (e.g. 'diagnose disease') are pulled from AI patent titles and from O*NET task descriptions. Each task is scored by how common its verb-noun pairs are in AI patents. Scores are aggregated to occupations using O*NET's task importance/frequency scores. The method is validated on historical cases: occupations that score as highly exposed to software and robots saw employment and wage declines. Those fitted relationships are then used to project AI's effects.
key_numbers: Headline finding: unlike software and robots, AI is directed at high-skilled tasks.
Projection: AI will reduce 90:10 wage inequality but will not affect the top 1% (under the assumption that historical substitution patterns persist).
Exposure is a relative (percentile-style) score, not a time fraction.
works.relevance_to_theta: It measures where inventive effort is aimed, not how much labor is saved. Its value for our project is methodological: it ties exposure scores to realized employment changes in past technology waves. That is the same kind of check as comparing our bottom-up S(t) against the top-down 2.3 pp/yr. It does not give theta, p, q or rho.
works.limitations: Based on patents from before the LLM era. Verb-noun matching misses semantics. Scores are relative only. Assumes past substitution patterns carry over.

works.title: What Can Machines Learn, and What Does It Mean for Occupations and the Economy? (Suitability for Machine Learning, SML)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Tom Mitchell, Daniel Rock
works.what_measured: A Suitability for Machine Learning (SML) score for 18,156 O*NET tasks, aggregated to occupations.
works.method_plain: A rubric from Brynjolfsson and Mitchell (Science 2017) is applied to task statements; the MIT IDE page describes it as a '21-item' rubric. The items ask about features that make a task learnable by supervised ML, e.g. clear input-output mapping, availability of data, and tolerance for errors. I could not open the full PDF (the DSpace bitstream returned empty), so the rater platform and rating scale are UNVERIFIED. They are commonly described as crowdsourced ratings on a Likert scale.
key_numbers: 18,156 O*NET tasks scored.

Findings: (i) ML affects different occupations than earlier automation waves; (ii) most occupations have at least some SML tasks; (iii) few occupations are fully automatable by ML; (iv) realizing the gains usually requires redesigning jobs.
works.relevance_to_theta: An ordinal suitability score from the pre-LLM era. Its rubric items about error tolerance and verifiability of outputs are conceptually close to our q and rho, so they could inspire extra dimensions to code for each IT task. But the score itself is not a time fraction. Its key point, that partial exposure within occupations is the norm, supports a sum-over-tasks construction like S = sum w_j theta_j.
works.limitations: Built for supervised ML (2017-era), not LLMs or agents. I did not verify the rater details. Ordinal. Not time-weighted.

works.title: Beyond AI Exposure: Which Tasks are Cost-Effective to Automate with Computer Vision?
works.authors: Maja S. Svanberg, Wensu Li, Martin Fleming, Brian C. Goehring, Neil C. Thompson
works.what_measured: For tasks exposed to computer vision: the accuracy required (from surveys of workers on Prolific), the cost of building a system that reaches that accuracy (data, compute, deployment), and whether that system beats the human wage bill at the firm's scale.
works.method_plain: An end-to-end cost-benefit model. Exposed tasks are identified following the exposure literature. Workers who know each task state the accuracy needed (about 9 responses per task on average). Scaling laws convert required accuracy into data and compute cost; 35 case studies supply deployment costs. The model assumes a 5% real discount rate and compute costs falling 22% per year. Automation is called economically attractive only when the deployment exceeds the 'minimum viable scale' at which AI's average cost equals the cost of human labor. A task's share of an occupation's compensation is set by O*NET task-importance scores.
key_numbers: Only 23% of worker compensation paid for vision-exposed tasks would be cost-effective to automate at current costs. This is commonly misquoted as '23% of jobs' or '23% of tasks'. In the source it is a share of compensation within vision tasks.
36% of jobs in US non-farm businesses have at least one vision-exposed task. Only 8% (23% of them) have at least one task that is economically attractive to automate.
Vision tasks are 1.6% of US non-farm compensation, and 0.4% is attractive to automate.
Robustness: different cost assumptions move the 23% to at most 33%. AI-as-a-service scale raises it, in one scenario to 49% (0.79% of compensation).
Example: checking food quality is about 6% of a baker's duties.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the clearest example in this stream of going past exposure to an economic net-benefit test, which is what our net theta tries to do. It nets out AI system cost (our 'AI running cost') and uses required accuracy (a cousin of p and q). It is a binary decision per task, though. It does not measure the fraction of labor time saved. It weights tasks by O*NET 'importance' as a stand-in for time share. That is a known weak point, and it is exactly the w_j/f_j measurement problem we face. The fixed-cost logic matters less for LLMs, which are general-purpose and close to zero fixed cost per task. Large firms like TCS and Infosys sit far above any minimum viable scale anyway.
works.limitations: Computer vision only. Assumes large fixed costs for training custom models, unlike off-the-shelf LLMs. Uses importance scores as a proxy for time. Required accuracy is self-reported by workers. Working paper.

works.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140); updates Gmyrek, Berg & Bescond (2023) ILO WP 96
works.authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kamiński, Filip Konopczyński, Agnieszka Ładna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Rosłaniec, Marek Troszyński
works.what_measured: A CONTINUOUS 0-1 'automation potential by GenAI' score for each task (0 = cannot be automated; 1 = could be done without a human operator). The occupation-level mean and standard deviation of task scores are then mapped to exposure gradients 1-4.
works.method_plain: (1) GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5 score all 29,753 tasks in Poland's 6-digit occupational classification. (2) A worker survey asks 1,640 respondents to rate a sample of 2,861 tasks on a 0-100 slider, producing 52,558 data points. (3) International experts review the scores through a survey and Delphi-style rounds. (4) An AI assistant built on the adjusted scores predicts scores for the ISCO-08 task descriptions. The 2023 version (WP 96) used GPT-4 alone to assign 0-1 scores, with humans reviewing the justifications. Gradient 4 means mean >= 0.6 and mean minus SD >= 0.5.
key_numbers: Globally, 1 in 4 workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment is in Gradient 4 (highest); the 2023 'automation' category was 2.3%.
Gradients 1-3 combined: 20.5% of world employment, versus 29.2% for 2023's 'augmentation' (13%) plus 'big unknown' (16.2%).
Exposed share of employment: 11% in low-income countries vs 34% in high-income countries.

IT occupations (ISCO-08 4-digit, mean / SD of task scores): Web and Multimedia Developers (2513) 0.60 / 0.08, Gradient 4. Applications Programmers (2514) 0.57 / 0.08, Gradient 3. Software Developers (2512) 0.53 / 0.07, Gradient 3. Database Designers and Administrators (2521) 0.55 / 0.04.
Digitized occupations (web/media developers, software, database, finance) had higher mean scores in 2025 than in 2023, which the authors attribute to multimodal and agentic capabilities.
Task-level scores are public: https://pgmyrek.github.io/2025_GenAI_scores_ISCO08/
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the ONLY major exposure index whose task score is continuous and on a 0-1 scale. It is still not time saved. It is perceived 'automatability' (what share of the task GenAI could do without a human), elicited from workers, experts and LLMs, with no definition of quality, review or cost. You could treat it as an upper-bound proxy for gross theta (roughly q*p + kappa with rho = 0). The software developer scores of 0.53-0.60 would then imply that at most about half of the labor in these tasks is automatable 'in principle'. Having 2023 and 2025 vintages gives crude time variation. The ISCO coding fits India: India's PLFS household survey records occupations on the NCO-2015 classification, which maps to ISCO-08. The authors stress the scores are an 'upper threshold' of exposure, not impact.
works.limitations: Measures perceived automatability, not measured time savings. Review and verification are not netted out. The task base is the Polish classification, mapped to ISCO. Survey respondents are not task-specific experts. Labels from LLM scoring are hard to reproduce exactly.

works.title: Generative AI and Firm Values (later drafts titled 'The Labor Impact of Generative AI on Firm Values', with Bledi Taska)
works.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang (later drafts add Bledi Taska)
works.year: 2023 (NBER WP 31222, May 2023; revised Jan 2026 per NBER page)
works.what_measured: Firms' workforce exposure to GenAI: Eloundou-style task labels aggregated by each firm's occupation mix, split into exposure through core tasks and through supplemental tasks. The paper relates this to stock returns, hiring and wages after ChatGPT's release.
works.method_plain: GPT-3.5 Turbo, with few-shot prompts, labels all 19,265 O*NET tasks using Eloundou et al.'s rubric: direct exposure = 1 (ChatGPT cuts time >= half), indirect = 0.5, none = 0. Occupation exposure is aggregated to firms using their occupation employment mix. The authors explicitly treat the LLM as a 'research assistant' applying researcher-defined categories, not as a judge of its own abilities.
key_numbers: On average, 77% of occupations' exposure comes from core tasks and 23% from supplemental tasks.
The 'Artificial-minus-Human' portfolio earned 44 basis points higher daily returns in the two weeks after ChatGPT's release (the NBER abstract says ~5% over the two weeks).
Occupations exposed through core tasks (e.g. proofreaders, web developers) show labor-demand declines. Supplemental-task exposure points to complementarity.
works.relevance_to_theta: It reuses the Eloundou >=50% threshold through GPT-3.5, so it inherits the same extensive-margin limitation. It confirms that LLM labelers can reproduce the rubric at scale. Its useful addition is the core/supplemental split. That is a rough stand-in for whether saved time is substitution-prone, which bears on how theta turns into lower headcount rather than more output per person. The firm-level aggregation template (occupation mix × task labels) is directly portable to TCS/Infosys if their role mix can be found.
works.limitations: Binary/ternary labels from GPT-3.5. No measure of the size of time savings. US public firms. Core/supplemental is O*NET's designation, not a time share.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.what_measured: The 10-year total factor productivity (TFP) gain from AI. TFP is output per unit of all inputs combined. The estimate multiplies (share of tasks exposed) × (share profitably automated) × (cost saving per affected task).
works.method_plain: A task-based model with Hulten's theorem: the aggregate gain is approximately the GDP share of affected tasks times the average cost saving on them. Exposure is the wage-bill-weighted share of exposed occupations, about 20%, from Eloundou et al. and Svanberg et al. The share of those that are profitably automatable within 10 years is 23% (from Svanberg et al.). The labor cost saving per affected task is 27%, the average of experimental studies (Noy and Zhang 2023, Brynjolfsson et al. 2023). With industry labor shares, this gives 14.4% overall cost savings on affected tasks.
key_numbers: About 20% of US labor tasks are exposed (wage-bill weighted).
0.23 × 0.20 = 4.6% of all tasks affected within 10 years.
Average labor cost saving of 27% → 14.4% overall cost saving on affected tasks.
TFP gain of no more than 0.66% over 10 years (about 0.064%/yr), or <0.53% after adjusting for hard-to-learn tasks. An alternative exposure value of 0.193 gives 0.89%.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the clearest published example that exposure measures alone CANNOT give the intensive margin. Acemoglu has to bring in a separate per-task saving (27%, from RCTs) and multiply it onto the exposure share. Structurally that is S = sum w_j × 1{exposed_j} × adoption × theta_intensive, exactly the product our recipe replaces with a capability-based theta_j(t). His 27% is a gross experimental time saving on short, well-defined writing and support tasks, with no netting of review or task length. It does not depend on time or capability.
works.limitations: Assumes static capability. Treats the 23% figure for computer vision as applying to LLMs. The intensive-margin number comes from a few short-task RCTs. US economy-wide, not IT services.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic Economics team)
works.what_measured: Estimated time per task WITHOUT AI vs WITH AI for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks, giving a CONTINUOUS time-saved fraction for each task.
works.method_plain: Claude reads each conversation and estimates how long a professional would take without AI and how long the task took with AI. Results are aggregated to O*NET tasks by medians and valued at BLS wages. Validation: self-consistency across prompt variants, and JIRA software tickets that have developer estimates and actual tracked times. The report then extrapolates to economy-wide productivity assuming universal adoption over 10 years.
key_numbers: Headline: Claude speeds up individual tasks by 'about 80%'. The median conversation shows an estimated 84% time saving; the overall median is 81%. All three figures appear in the source.
The average task would take ~90 minutes (stated elsewhere as 1.4 hours) without AI.
Implied: +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth over the next decade, assuming universal adoption over 10 years and current models.
JIRA validation: Claude Sonnet 4.5's estimates have Spearman correlation 0.44 with actual times, vs 0.50 for developers' own estimates. Claude's estimates are more compressed than the true times.
Stated limitation: it cannot account for time spent outside the conversation, 'including validating the quality or accuracy of Claude's work'.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only large-scale source in this stream that gives a continuous time-saved fraction per task. The 80% figure is GROSS: it is not net of review (rho), of output that is later rejected (q), or of failed attempts (the conversations are conditional on the user choosing to use AI). It suffers from selection: people bring AI the tasks AI is good at. That makes it an upper bound on theta_j for the tasks used, not an average over the whole hours distribution f_j(h). The 'time without AI' estimates give a rough task-length distribution, a possible input for f_j(h) on software tasks.
works.limitations: Times are model-estimated and only weakly validated (Spearman 0.44). Ignores verification time. Selection on the tasks people bring to Claude. Consumer Claude.ai sample only. Not net of AI running cost. Not peer reviewed.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded win/tie rates of frontier models against industry professionals on 1,320 tasks from 44 occupations, plus speed and cost multipliers that INCLUDE the expert's time to review and redo the work.
works.method_plain: Experts with an average of 14 years' experience write realistic tasks and also produce human deliverables. Other experts blind-grade model output against human output. The speed analysis has three scenarios. 'Naive' compares human time to model sampling time. 'Try 1x, then fix it' and 'Try n times, then fix it yourself' add the expert's review time and the cost of doing the task manually when the model fails, using the model's win rate as the success probability.
key_numbers: Gold subset (220 tasks): average human expert completion time H_T = 404 minutes (cost $361). Average expert review time R_T = 109 minutes ($86).
Best model on the gold subset: Claude Opus 4.1, 47.6% wins or ties vs experts.
GPT-5 (39.0% win rate): speed 90x naive → 1.12x try-once → 1.39x try-n. Cost 474x naive → 1.18x → 1.63x.
GPT-4o (12.5% win rate): try-n speed 0.46x, i.e. using the model is SLOWER than doing it yourself. o3 (35.2%): 1.28x.
Authors: 'When incorporating time to review and redo work, the payoff from using a model shrinks.'
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the closest thing in the 2025-26 literature to our NET theta formula, though it sits in the benchmark literature rather than the exposure literature. Review time over human time = 109/404 ≈ 0.27, a direct empirical rho for long (~7-hour) knowledge-work tasks. The win rate is roughly q*p. A try-n speedup of 1.39x means time saved = 1 - 1/1.39 ≈ 28% for GPT-5 on these tasks (gpt-4o's 0.46x means negative savings). The max{..., kappa} floor in our formula would rule out negative savings. Moving from a naive 90x to a net 1.39x is a strong quantitative case that gross exposure and time-saving measures overstate net theta by a wide margin.
works.limitations: Covers 44 US occupations; software and IT services are only partly represented. Tasks are one-shot deliverables, not maintenance of existing codebases. Review time comes from graders, not from production code review. Cost data are missing for non-OpenAI models. Excludes the cost of catastrophic errors. Produced by a model developer.

works.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
works.authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, Siddharth Suri (Microsoft Research)
works.what_measured: An occupation-level 'AI applicability score' built from 200k anonymized Bing Copilot conversations (US, Jan-Sep 2024) mapped to O*NET Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). It separates what the user wanted done (user goal) from what the AI itself did (AI action).
works.method_plain: An LLM pipeline classifies each conversation into IWAs and rates (a) whether the AI completed the user's goal (completion rate) and (b) how much of the activity it covered (impact scope, counted at moderate or higher). For each IWA the term is completion × scope × coverage indicator, where coverage requires activity share > 0.05%. Terms are summed with O*NET importance/relevance weights to the 785 occupations, averaging the user-goal and AI-action sides.
key_numbers: 200k conversations; 785 SOC occupations scored.
The most common and successful AI-assisted work is information work ('creation, processing, and communication of information').
AI applicability rose over the 9-month window, mainly because people used AI for a wider range of tasks.
Released files: iwa_metrics.csv, ai_applicability_scores.csv, soc_metrics.csv and others. The repo says the metrics measure consumer usage and are 'not a measure of job replacement'.
works.relevance_to_theta: Usage-based, not capability-ceiling. The completion rate is a crude observed analog of p (task success), and the user-goal vs AI-action split maps onto kappa (assisting a human) vs delegation. It still does not measure time saved, and 'scope' is an ordinal rating. Mixing in adoption runs against our design, which drops adoption from theta.
works.limitations: Based on consumer Bing chats. Classification and completion are judged by an LLM. Includes adoption. No time units. Reflects pre-agentic (2024) usage.

works.title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations (Anthropic Economic Index)
works.authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, et al. (15 authors)
works.what_measured: Distribution of Claude.ai usage over O*NET tasks and occupations, and the split between automation and augmentation.
works.method_plain: A privacy-preserving pipeline (Clio) classifies more than 4 million conversations into O*NET tasks and into interaction modes. Directive and feedback-loop modes count as automation; learning, iterating and validating count as augmentation.
key_numbers: Software development and writing are together nearly half of all usage.
~36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their associated tasks.
57% of usage is augmentation, 43% automation.
works.relevance_to_theta: Usage-share data, not time saved. The automation/augmentation split is a rough empirical anchor for how much of AI's labor effect comes through the assistant channel (kappa) versus delegation (q*p). It also gives task-mix evidence that software tasks dominate actual use.
works.limitations: Measures usage shares, not labor savings. Consumer platform. Interaction mode is classified by an LLM. Includes adoption.

research.stream_summary:
The working hypothesis largely holds. The classic exposure measures answer 'can AI touch this task?' and not 'how much labor does it remove, net of checking?' None of them gives a measured, continuous fraction of time saved per task.

Eloundou et al. label tasks E0/E1/E2. E1 means the labeler believes ChatGPT cuts task time by at least 50% at quality the recipient would not notice or care about. The labels come from human annotators (OpenAI alignment reviewers, not workers in the occupations) and from GPT-4 with a tuned prompt. Their agreement is 66-82% depending on the measure. Because E1 is a 50% threshold, it only says theta >= 0.5 on E1 tasks and < 0.5 on others. Even that is gross of review cost. Felten-Raj-Seamans (ability-based crowd ratings), Webb (patent text) and Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock (an ML-suitability rubric) are relative or ordinal scores with no time units. Eisfeldt et al. reuse the Eloundou rubric through GPT-3.5.

There are three partial exceptions. The ILO 2025 index gives continuous 0-1 'automatability' scores; software developers average 0.53. But those scores are perceptions with no review netting. Anthropic's Tamkin and McCrory (2025) give continuous per-task time savings (about 80%), but these are model-estimated, selected on tasks people chose to bring to AI, and explicitly exclude verification time. OpenAI's GDPval (2025) is the only source that nets out review. Expert review takes about 27% of human task time (109 of 404 minutes), and GPT-5's speedup falls from 90x naive to 1.39x once review and redo are counted, roughly 28% time saved.

The economics bridge papers show the gap directly. Acemoglu has to multiply exposure (20%) by an externally sourced 27% per-task saving. Svanberg et al. show that only 23% of vision-exposed compensation is worth automating once costs are counted.

For our recipe, exposure measures can at most give the extensive-margin mask and task weights. p, q, rho and kappa must come from benchmark and field evidence.
gaps_noticed: No exposure measure gives a measured, continuous labor-time-saved fraction per task that is net of review, rejection and AI cost. The ILO (perceived 0-1) and Tamkin-McCrory (model-estimated, gross) are the nearest.
No exposure measure has a task-length (h) dimension. They cannot be linked to METR's p(h,t) without new data on how long the tasks in each service line take, i.e. f_j(h).
Task weights everywhere are O*NET importance, frequency or core/supplemental counts, not hours. The time-use weights (w_j) for Indian IT services are unmeasured in this literature.

The measures are almost all single snapshots. The exceptions are ILO 2023 vs 2025, Microsoft's 9-month trend, and Felten's re-weighting. None is indexed to a capability metric, so none gives theta as a function of time t.

Who labels matters. Eloundou's annotators were not workers in the occupations, and GPT-4 labels shift with prompt wording. No one has validated E1 labels against measured time savings on the same tasks.
None is specific to IT services or BPO, or to India. US O*NET tasks may not match how work is divided in TCS/Infosys delivery (maintenance, testing, application management).
Review/verification cost (rho) shows up only in GDPval (one-shot deliverables). There is no estimate of rho for code maintenance or BPO process work.
I could not verify the BMR 2018 rater platform or scale (PDF would not fetch). The Science 2024 volume and pages of Eloundou et al. were also not verified because the page returned 403.

datasets.name: Eloundou et al. GPTs-are-GPTs task and occupation exposure labels (E0/E1/E2; alpha/beta/zeta)
datasets.description: Task-level human and GPT-4 labels on 19,265 O*NET tasks and 2,087 DWAs; released with the paper (I have not independently confirmed the repository link). Gives the extensive-margin mask only.

datasets.name: AIOE / AIIE / AIGE and LM-AIOE data appendix
datasets.description: Occupation (SOC), industry (NAICS) and county exposure scores, plus the AI application × ability relatedness matrix from the MTurk survey; includes language-modeling and image-generation variants.

datasets.name: ILO 2025 GenAI task-level scores (ISCO-08)
datasets.description: Continuous 0-1 automatability scores per ISCO-08 task, plus occupation means and SDs (Appendix Table A1 of WP140). ISCO maps to India's NCO-2015 classification, which PLFS uses.

datasets.name: Microsoft Working with AI: IWA metrics and AI applicability scores
datasets.description: IWA-level completion, scope and share metrics and SOC-level applicability scores from 200k Bing Copilot conversations (2024).

datasets.name: GDPval gold subset (220 tasks) and grading service
datasets.description: Open-sourced expert tasks with human completion times and costs; the paper reports review times and speed/cost multipliers net of review. The full set of 1,320 tasks is not public.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index data releases
datasets.description: Usage shares by O*NET task and automation/augmentation splits from Claude conversations. The Nov 2025 per-task time-saving estimates are summarized on the Anthropic page; I did not verify whether the task-level time estimates were released.

datasets.name: O*NET task statements, task ratings (importance/frequency/relevance), DWAs and IWAs
datasets.description: The common task base used by almost every US exposure measure. Its frequency ratings are the nearest public stand-in for task time shares.

datasets.name: Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock SML replication package
datasets.description: Replication package linked from the AEA page. I did not open it, so its contents are unverified.

datasets.name: Svanberg et al. vision-task survey and cost model
datasets.description: Prolific worker survey of required accuracy for vision tasks plus 35 case studies. I did not find a public data release; it may be available from the authors on request.

works.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models (arXiv); published as 'GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs', Science 2024
works.authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
works.year: 2023 (arXiv v1 17 Mar 2023; v5 21 Aug 2023); Science online 20 Jun 2024, issue 21 Jun 2024
works.what_measured: Whether each O*NET task or Detailed Work Activity (DWA) is 'exposed' to LLMs. The dataset has 19,265 tasks and 2,087 DWAs. Labels: E0 means no or minimal time saving at equivalent quality, or a loss of quality. E1 means ChatGPT/Playground access can cut task time by at least 50%. E2 means the LLM alone does not reach 50%, but software built on top of it could, at equal quality. Labels are rolled up into occupation shares: alpha = E1, beta = E1 + 0.5*E2, zeta = E1 + E2.
works.method_plain: Annotators applied a rubric to task descriptions. The authors labeled the DWAs that clearly need physical work or manual dexterity. Contracted annotators did the rest; they had reviewed GPT-3/3.5/4 outputs for OpenAI's alignment work and were not workers in the occupations. Separately, an early GPT-4 was given a slightly modified rubric, tuned to agree better with a set of human labels, and labeled every task-occupation pair. 'Equivalent quality' means a third party, typically the recipient, would not notice or care that an LLM helped. Tasks are aggregated to occupations with core tasks weighted twice as heavily as supplemental tasks. Time spent per task is not used; a robustness check with O*NET importance weights reportedly changed little.
key_numbers: Abstract/text: 80% of US workers are in occupations with >=10% of tasks exposed, and 19% are in occupations with >50% of tasks exposed. Both use beta exposure, so they are shares of TASKS, not time saved or jobs lost.
Abstract: about 15% of all US worker tasks could be done significantly faster at the same quality with LLM access alone; 47-56% with LLM-powered software.

Table 3, occupation-level means: alpha 0.14 (human and GPT-4); beta 0.30 (human) / 0.34 (GPT-4); zeta 0.46 (human) / 0.55 (GPT-4). The text rounds these to 'over 30%' and 'surpasses 50%'; the human zeta is actually below 0.50.
Human labels: 2.3% of occupations are alpha-50 exposed, 21.6% beta-50, 47.3% zeta-50 (Figure 3 uses equal task weights).
GPT-4 (Rubric 1) vs human agreement (Table 2): 80.8% for alpha (Pearson 0.223), 65.6% for beta (0.591), 82.1% for zeta (0.654).
Science version (per GovAI summary page): about 1.8% of jobs have over half their tasks affected by LLMs with simple interfaces, and 'just over 46%' once complementary software is counted.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the canonical extensive-margin measure. E1 is a threshold indicator: 1{believed potential time saving >= 50%}. It does not measure the size of the saving. If you trust the labels and weight tasks equally, a service line with E1 share alpha_j has theta_j somewhere between 0.5*alpha_j and 0.5 + 0.5*alpha_j, which is too wide to use. Even that bound assumes the labels are accurate, and they are judgments, not measurements. The labels are gross: review cost (rho), rejection of output that passes checks (q) and AI running cost are not netted out. The authors say they chose a high threshold because they guessed the real-world time reduction would be lower than their estimates. The 0.5 weight on E2 is a discount for needed complementary investment, not a time fraction. Task weights are core/supplemental, not hours, so they give neither f_j nor w_j. The labels are a single snapshot of early GPT-4.
works.limitations: Labels are subjective, and the annotators were not workers in the occupations. GPT-4 labels depend on prompt wording (Rubric 1 vs 2 agreement on beta is only 76%). No time-use weighting and no task-length (h) dimension. Labels are ordinal. Single snapshot. Gross of review. Based on US O*NET tasks.
works.corrections: Added the Science volume, issue and pages from the Crossref record of DOI 10.1126/science.adj0998: 384(6702):1306-1308. Corrected the summary statistics. 'beta >0.30; zeta >0.50' repeated the paper's prose, but Table 3 shows human beta = 0.30, human zeta = 0.46 and GPT-4 zeta = 0.55; the key number now gives the table values. Clarified that the 80%/19% figures refer to workers in occupations. Clarified that the authors labeled the DWAs needing physical work or dexterity, and that the human annotators labeled DWAs plus a subset of tasks. All other numbers matched the PDF text.

works.title: Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses (AIOE); follow-up 'How will Language Modelers like ChatGPT Affect Occupations and Industries?'
works.authors: Edward Felten, Manav Raj, Robert Seamans
works.year: 2021 (SMJ, December 2021); follow-up arXiv March 2023 (PDF dated 18 March 2023)
