works.what_measured: An AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) score for each occupation. Industry (AIIE) and county (AIGE) versions aggregate it.
works.method_plain: Ten AI application areas come from the Electronic Frontier Foundation's AI progress statistics: abstract strategy games, real-time video games, image recognition, visual question answering, image generation, reading comprehension, language modeling, translation, speech recognition, and instrumental track recognition. A crowdsourced (mTurk) survey rates how related each application is to each of O*NET's 52 human abilities. Ability-level exposure is the sum of those relatedness scores. Occupation exposure is the average of ability exposure, weighted by O*NET's prevalence and importance of each ability, and is then standardized. The 2023 language-modeling version sets every application weight to zero except language modeling.
key_numbers: 10 AI applications x 52 O*NET abilities, applied to the 800+ occupations O*NET tracks.
The LM-AIOE correlates 0.979 with the original AIOE.

Most exposed occupations under LM-AIOE: telemarketers, then post-secondary teachers of English language and literature, foreign languages, and history. Most exposed industries: legal services, and securities, commodities and investments.
The score is a standardized relative index with no natural units.
works.relevance_to_theta: Ordinal and relative only. It ranks occupations by how much their abilities overlap with AI applications, and says nothing about time saved, review cost or failure rates. The application weights can in principle be updated over time. In practice, the language-modeling reweighting barely changed the ranking (correlation 0.979), so the index has little power to track capability change. It is at most a cross-check on relative exposure across IT occupations. It cannot give a theta level.
works.limitations: Built on abilities, not tasks. Based on crowd judgments of relatedness, not observed performance. Standardized units. Deliberately 'agnostic' about substitution versus augmentation. Reweighting changes rankings very little.
works.corrections: No substantive errors. Filled in the full list of 10 applications and the SMJ DOI. Added the 0.979 correlation from the arXiv paper, which weakens the record's claim that the index can usefully vary over time.

works.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Labor Market
works.authors: Michael Webb
works.venue: Working paper (Stanford; SSRN 3482150; NBER conference draft)
works.what_measured: How exposed occupations are to AI, and historically to software and robots, measured by text overlap between patents and O*NET task descriptions.
works.method_plain: Verb-noun pairs (e.g. 'diagnose disease') are pulled from patent titles and from O*NET task descriptions. Each task is scored by how common its verb-noun pairs are in the relevant patents. Scores are averaged to occupations, with weights that average O*NET task frequency, importance and relevance. The method is validated on historical cases: occupations scored as highly exposed to software and robots saw employment and wage declines. Those fitted relationships are then used to project AI's effects.
key_numbers: Unlike software and robots, AI is directed at high-skilled tasks; exposure peaks around the 90th percentile of the wage distribution.
Assuming historical patterns of long-run substitution continue, AI will reduce 90:10 wage inequality but will not affect the top 1%.
Exposure scores are relative (percentile-style), not time fractions.
works.relevance_to_theta: It measures where inventive effort is aimed, not how much labor is saved. Its use for this project is methodological: it validates exposure scores against realized employment changes, which is the same kind of check as comparing a bottom-up S(t) with the top-down 2.3 pp/yr. It does not give theta, p, q or rho.
works.limitations: Uses pre-LLM patents. Verb-noun matching misses meaning. Scores are relative only. Assumes past substitution patterns carry over.
works.corrections: No errors. The SSRN date (6 Nov 2019) was confirmed by search; the SSRN page itself returned 403. Added that the weights average frequency, importance and relevance, not only importance and frequency.

works.title: What Can Machines Learn, and What Does It Mean for Occupations and the Economy? (Suitability for Machine Learning, SML)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Tom Mitchell, Daniel Rock
works.what_measured: A Suitability for Machine Learning (SML) score, rated at the DWA level and mapped to 18,156 O*NET tasks and on to occupations.
works.method_plain: The rubric from Brynjolfsson and Mitchell (Science 2017) is applied to O*NET Detailed Work Activities. Its items cover features that make a task learnable by supervised ML, such as a clear input-output mapping, available data, and tolerance for errors. Brynjolfsson's 2020 slides describe 2,059 DWAs, a five-point 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree' scale, and 10 different raters per DWA. Scores are mapped to tasks and to occupations weighted by task importance. The replication files (HITRubric.docx, cf_report_DWAS_input.csv, cfProcessor_AEAPnP.py) and a later replication paper point to CrowdFlower as the crowd platform. I could not confirm the platform from the paper text itself, because the PDF would not download.
key_numbers: 18,156 O*NET tasks (paper abstract). The author's slides give 2,059 DWAs and 18,112 occupation-specific tasks, so counts differ slightly across sources.
Ratings on a 5-point Likert scale, 10 raters per DWA (author slides, 2020).

Findings: (i) ML affects different occupations than earlier automation waves; (ii) most occupations have at least some SML tasks; (iii) few occupations are fully automatable by ML; (iv) realizing the gains usually requires redesigning jobs.
works.relevance_to_theta: An ordinal suitability score from before LLMs. Its items on error tolerance and verifiability of outputs are conceptually close to our q and rho, so they could suggest extra dimensions to code for each IT task. The score is not a time fraction. Its central finding, that partial exposure within occupations is the norm, supports building S as a sum over tasks, S = sum w_j theta_j.
works.limitations: Built for supervised ML (circa 2017), not LLMs or agents. Ordinal. Not time-weighted. Rubric item count is unclear: the MIT IDE page says 21 items, a later replication paper says 23 factors.
works.corrections: Added the rating details from the author's own 2020 slides: 5-point scale, 10 raters per DWA, rated on about 2,059 DWAs rather than on task statements directly. Flagged CrowdFlower as likely (from replication file names) but unconfirmed in the paper text. Noted the 21 vs 23 rubric-item discrepancy. Confirmed the replication package (openICPSR 114436) and listed its files. Raised bibliographic confidence to high.

works.title: Beyond AI Exposure: Which Tasks are Cost-Effective to Automate with Computer Vision?
works.authors: Maja S. Svanberg, Wensu Li, Martin Fleming, Brian C. Goehring, Neil C. Thompson
works.venue: MIT FutureTech working paper (also on SSRN); I found no journal version
works.what_measured: For tasks exposed to computer vision: the accuracy required (from a survey of workers on Prolific), the cost of building a system that reaches that accuracy, and whether that system beats the human wage bill at a given deployment scale.
works.method_plain: An end-to-end cost-benefit model. Workers familiar with each task state the accuracy needed (about 9 responses per task on average; 80% of tasks have 5 or more valid responses). Scaling laws turn required accuracy into data and compute cost, and 35 case studies supply further cost data. The model assumes a 5% real discount rate and compute costs falling 22% per year. Automation is called economically attractive only when the deployment exceeds the 'minimum viable scale'. A task's share of an occupation's compensation is set by O*NET task-importance scores.
key_numbers: Only 23% of worker compensation paid for vision tasks would be attractive to automate at today's costs. This is a share of compensation within vision-exposed tasks, not a share of jobs or of tasks.
36% of jobs in US non-farm businesses have at least one vision-exposed task. Only 8% (23% of them) have at least one that is economically attractive to automate.
Vision tasks are 1.6% of US non-farm compensation, and 0.4% is attractive to automate.
Robustness to cost parameters raises the 23% to at most 33%. If AI delivers twice the human worker's value, it rises to 30%.
A 'bare-bones implementation' (free data, free compute, minimal engineering) raises firm-level attractiveness only to 49% (0.79% of compensation).
If one system could serve the whole national economy (AI-as-a-service), AI already has a cost advantage for 88% of vision task compensation.
Example: checking food quality is roughly 6% of a baker's duties.
works.relevance_to_theta: The clearest example in this stream of moving from exposure to a net economic test. It nets out the cost of the AI system and uses required accuracy, a cousin of p and q. But it gives a yes/no decision per task, not the fraction of labor time saved. Its use of O*NET importance as a stand-in for time share is a known weak point, and it is exactly the w_j/f_j measurement problem we face. The fixed-cost scale logic matters less for off-the-shelf LLMs, and for very large firms like TCS and Infosys.
works.limitations: Computer vision only. Assumes large fixed costs for custom models. Uses importance scores as a proxy for time. Required accuracy is self-reported by workers. Working paper.
works.corrections: The record attributed the 49% (0.79% of compensation) to AI-as-a-service scale. In the source, 49% is the firm-level 'bare-bones implementation' scenario (free data and compute). The AI-as-a-service figure is 88% of vision task compensation at national scale. Added the 30% result for AI that doubles the worker's value. All other numbers matched the PDF.

works.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140); updates Gmyrek, Berg & Bescond (2023), ILO WP 96
works.authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kamiński, Filip Konopczyński, Agnieszka Ładna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Rosłaniec, Marek Troszyński
works.what_measured: A continuous 0-1 GenAI automation-potential score for each task: 0 means the task cannot be automated, 1 means it could be done without a human operator. Occupation-level mean and SD of task scores are mapped to exposure gradients 1-4.
works.method_plain: (1) GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5 score the 29,753 tasks in Poland's 6-digit occupational classification. (2) A survey of 1,640 workers in Poland rates a representative sample of 2,861 tasks on a 0-100 slider, giving 52,558 data points. (3) International experts review the scores through a survey and Delphi-style rounds. (4) An LLM assistant built on the adjusted scores predicts scores for ISCO-08 task descriptions. Gradient 4 means mean >= 0.6 and mean minus SD >= 0.5. Gradient 3 means 0.5 <= mean < 0.6 and mean plus SD >= 0.5.
key_numbers: Globally, one in four workers is in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment is in Gradient 4; the 2023 'automation' category was 2.3%.
Gradients 1-3 combined: 20.5% of world employment, versus 29.2% for 2023's 'augmentation' (13%) plus 'big unknown' (16.2%).
Exposed share of total employment: 11% in low-income countries vs 34% in high-income countries.

Appendix Table A1 (ISCO-08 4-digit, mean / SD): Web and Multimedia Developers (2513) 0.60 / 0.08, Gradient 4. Applications Programmers (2514) 0.57 / 0.08, Gradient 3. Database Designers and Administrators (2521) 0.57 / 0.08, Gradient 3. Systems Administrators (2522) 0.57 / 0.05, Gradient 3. Software Developers (2512) 0.53 / 0.07, Gradient 3.

Highly digitized occupations (web and media developers, database specialists, finance and software-related occupations) had higher mean scores in 2025 than in 2023; the authors attribute this to multimodal and agentic capabilities.
The 2025 estimates are described as the 'upper threshold' of exposure.
works.relevance_to_theta: Among the main exposure indices, it is one of the few with a continuous 0-1 task score; the 2023 WP96 version already had one. It is still not time saved. It is perceived automatability, with no definition of quality, review or cost. It could serve as a rough upper-bound proxy for gross theta. With the 2023 and 2025 vintages it gives crude time variation. India's NCO-2015 classification is aligned with ISCO-08, which helps. But public PLFS microdata appear to record occupation at only 3 digits (per microdata.gov.in variable listings seen in search). In that case PLFS cannot separate 2512, 2513 and 2514, which all fall within 251.
works.limitations: Perceived automatability, not measured time savings. Review is not netted out. The task base is the Polish classification. Respondents are not task-specific experts. LLM scoring is hard to reproduce. The scores are an upper threshold of exposure, not impact.
works.corrections: Database Designers and Administrators (2521) is 0.57 / 0.08 in Table A1, not 0.55 / 0.04. Added Systems Administrators (2522). Toned down 'the ONLY major exposure index with a continuous 0-1 task score': the 2023 ILO version also had one. Noted that the pgmyrek.github.io page is an interactive tree visualization, and I could not confirm a downloadable task-level file there. Flagged the 3-digit PLFS coding limit, which I took from search results and did not open directly.

works.title: Generative AI and Firm Values (a March 2024 draft circulated as 'The Labor Impact of Generative AI on Firm Values')
works.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang (NBER cover). Bledi Taska is a co-author on the 2024 drafts and on the Internet Appendix of the January 2026 revision.
works.what_measured: Firms' workforce exposure to GenAI: Eloundou-style task labels aggregated by each firm's occupation mix, split into exposure through core tasks and through supplemental tasks. The paper relates this to stock returns, labor demand and profitability after ChatGPT's release.
works.method_plain: GPT-3.5 Turbo, given few-shot prompts, labels all 19,265 O*NET tasks with an Eloundou-style rubric: direct exposure = 1 (ChatGPT cuts time by at least half), indirect = 0.5, none = 0. Occupation exposure is aggregated to firms by their occupation employment mix. The authors treat the LLM as a 'research assistant' applying categories the researchers defined.
key_numbers: 14% of the 19,265 tasks are classed as directly exposed.
On average, 77% of occupations' exposure comes from core tasks and 23% from supplemental tasks.
The 'Artificial-minus-Human' portfolio earned 44 basis points higher daily returns in the two weeks after ChatGPT's release, about 5% over the two weeks (NBER abstract).
Occupations exposed through core tasks (e.g. proofreaders, web developers) point to substitution; exposure through supplemental tasks points to complementarity.
works.relevance_to_theta: It reuses the Eloundou 50% threshold through GPT-3.5, so it has the same extensive-margin limitation. It shows LLM labelers can apply the rubric at scale. Its useful addition is the core/supplemental split, a rough stand-in for whether saved time turns into lower headcount. The firm-level template (occupation mix x task labels) carries over to TCS/Infosys if their role mix is available.
works.limitations: Ternary labels from GPT-3.5. Nothing on the size of time savings. US public firms. Core/supplemental is O*NET's designation, not a time share.
works.corrections: Title and authorship history clarified. The 'Labor Impact...' title appears on a March 2024 four-author draft (UW Foster copy). The current NBER revision (January 2026) is titled 'Generative AI and Firm Values' with three authors on the cover and Taska on the Internet Appendix, so 'later drafts' is not accurate for the latest version. Added the 14% direct-exposure share. All numbers verified.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.what_measured: The 10-year gain in total factor productivity (TFP), meaning output per unit of all inputs combined. It is computed as (GDP share of tasks affected within 10 years) x (average cost saving on those tasks).
works.method_plain: A task-based model using Hulten's theorem: the aggregate gain is roughly the GDP share of affected tasks times the average cost saving on them. Exposure comes from Eloundou et al.: the wage-bill-weighted share of exposed occupations is 20%. Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate (23% profitably automatable) is applied to all exposed tasks, giving 4.6% of tasks affected within 10 years. The labor cost saving per affected task is 27%, the average of Noy and Zhang (2023) and Brynjolfsson et al. (2023). Multiplying by the exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535 gives an overall cost saving of 14.4%.
key_numbers: 20% of US labor tasks exposed (wage-bill weighted, from Eloundou et al.).
0.23 x 0.20 = 4.6% of tasks affected within 10 years.
27% average labor cost saving x 0.535 labor share = 14.4% overall cost saving on affected tasks.
TFP gain of no more than 0.66% over 10 years (about 0.064% per year), or under 0.53% after adjusting for hard-to-learn tasks.
Adding Peng et al.'s Copilot estimate raises the labor cost saving to 36% and the overall cost saving to 0.193, which gives a TFP gain of 0.89%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Clear evidence that exposure measures alone do not give the intensive margin. Acemoglu has to bring in a separate per-task saving (27%, from experiments) and multiply it onto exposure and the 23% feasibility share. Structurally that is S = sum w_j x 1{exposed_j} x feasibility x saving, the product our recipe replaces with a capability-based theta_j(t). His 27% is a gross experimental saving on short, well-defined tasks. It is not net of review and does not change with capability.
works.limitations: Assumes static capability. Applies a computer-vision feasibility share to LLMs. The intensive-margin number comes from a few short-task experiments. US economy-wide.
works.corrections: The record said 'an alternative exposure value of 0.193 gives 0.89%'. In fact 0.193 is an alternative overall COST SAVING (36% labor cost saving x 0.535, after adding Peng et al.), not an alternative exposure. The 20% exposure comes from Eloundou et al. alone; Svanberg et al. supply only the 23%. Made the 0.535 labor-share step explicit. Economic Policy citation verified on RePEc.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.year: 2025 (November; the page shows 25 Nov 2025 while its suggested citation says 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: Model-estimated time per task WITHOUT AI and WITH AI, for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro and Max tiers) mapped to O*NET tasks. This gives a continuous time-saved fraction for each task.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a professional would take without AI and how long the task took with AI. Estimates are aggregated to O*NET tasks by the median for each task, and valued at May 2024 OEWS wages. Validation uses self-consistency across prompt variants and 1,000 open-source JIRA tickets with tracked times. The report extrapolates to economy-wide productivity using Hulten's theorem (labor share 0.6), assuming universal adoption within 10 years and capabilities fixed at today's level.
key_numbers: Headline: Claude speeds up individual tasks by 'about 80%'. The text gives a median saving of 84%, and a figure caption gives 81%; the report does not reconcile them.
The average task would take about 90 minutes without AI per the overview; the key findings say 1.4 hours on average for complex tasks. These are not reconciled.
Implied: +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth over the next decade (about 1.1% per year in TFP), under universal adoption and current models.
JIRA validation: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 (log Pearson 0.46) vs actual times; developers' own estimates 0.50 (0.67). Claude overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones.
Stated limitation: it cannot account for time outside the conversation, 'including validating the quality or accuracy of Claude's work'.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only large-scale source in this stream with a continuous time-saved fraction per task. The roughly 80% figure is GROSS: it is not net of review (rho), of output later rejected (q), or of failed attempts. It is also selected, because people bring AI the tasks it is good at, so it is closer to an upper bound for the tasks used than an average over f_j(h). The 'time without AI' estimates give a rough task-length distribution. The January 2026 Anthropic follow-up (added below) adjusts these figures for task success.
works.limitations: Times are model-estimated and only moderately validated (Spearman 0.44). Ignores verification time. Selected on tasks people bring to Claude. Consumer Claude.ai sample. Not net of AI running cost. Not peer reviewed. Task-level estimates do not appear to be publicly released.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Added the date discrepancy, OEWS wage source, labor share of 0.6, log-Pearson values, and the direction of Claude's bias. Removed 'more compressed' as a paraphrase and replaced it with what the source says (overestimates short tasks, underestimates long ones).

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded win/tie rates of frontier models against industry professionals on 1,320 tasks from 44 occupations in the top 9 US GDP sectors. It also gives speed and cost multipliers that include an expert's time to review the work and redo it when it fails.
works.method_plain: Experts averaging 14 years of experience write realistic tasks and produce human deliverables. Other experts blind-grade model output against human output. The speed analysis has three scenarios: 'naive' (human time vs model sampling time), 'try 1x, then fix it', and 'try n times, then fix it yourself'. The last two add review time and the cost of doing the task by hand when the model fails. Review time R_T is the observed time each expert took the first time they graded a task, from task-monitoring software. It is grading time, not production code review.
key_numbers: Gold subset (220 tasks, open-sourced): average human completion time H_T = 404 minutes (cost $361); average review time R_T = 109 minutes (about $86).
Best model on the gold subset: Claude Opus 4.1, 47.6% wins or ties vs experts.
GPT-5 (39.0% win rate): speed 90x naive, 1.12x try-once, 1.39x try-n. Cost 474x, 1.18x, 1.63x.
o3 (35.2%): speed 161x, 1.08x, 1.28x. GPT-4o (12.5%): speed 327x, 0.87x, 0.46x, so with GPT-4o, using the model is slower than doing the task yourself.
Authors: 'When incorporating time to review and redo work, the payoff from using a model shrinks.'
No cost estimates for Claude, Gemini or Grok.
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest thing in this stream to our NET theta formula, though it comes from the benchmark literature, not the exposure literature. R_T/H_T = 109/404 ≈ 0.27 is an empirical rho for long (about 7-hour) knowledge-work tasks, but it measures grading time. The win rate is roughly q*p. The paper's appendix defines win rate as 'rated better', while the headline 47.6% counts ties, so the two uses differ. A try-n speedup of 1.39x means about 28% time saved for GPT-5; GPT-4o's 0.46x means negative savings, which our max{..., kappa} floor would rule out. The fall from 90x to 1.39x shows how far gross measures overstate net savings.
works.limitations: 44 US occupations, with software only partly covered; Software Developer tasks were excluded from the automated grader. Tasks are one-shot deliverables, not maintenance of existing code. Review time is grading time. Cost data are missing for non-OpenAI models. Produced by a model developer.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the o3 multipliers, how R_T was measured (grading time from monitoring software), and the ambiguity in how 'win rate' is defined.

works.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
works.authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, Siddharth Suri (Microsoft Research)
works.what_measured: An occupation-level 'AI applicability score' built from about 200k anonymized US Bing Copilot conversations (1 Jan to 30 Sep 2024) mapped to O*NET Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). It separates the user's goal from what the AI itself did.
works.method_plain: An LLM pipeline classifies conversations into IWAs and rates completion (whether the AI completed the user's goal) and impact scope (counted when moderate or higher). An IWA counts only if its activity share exceeds 0.05%. Scores are weighted by O*NET relevance and importance and aggregated to 785 SOC occupations. The final score averages the user-goal side and the AI-action side; the AI-action side counts only nonphysical tasks. The data are two samples of about 100k conversations each (uniform and thumbs-feedback).
key_numbers: About 200k conversations; 785 SOC occupations covering 149.8 million workers.
The most common and successful AI-assisted activities are information work ('the creation, processing, and communication of information').
Occupation-level AI applicability rose over the 9 months, mainly because people used AI for more varied tasks.

Repo files include iwa_metrics.csv, ai_applicability_scores.csv, soc_metrics.csv, soc_iwa_weights.csv and physical_tasks.csv. The repo says the metrics 'should not be misconstrued or misrepresented as measuring the ability of AI to replace jobs'.
works.relevance_to_theta: Based on usage, not a capability ceiling. The completion rate is a crude observed analog of p, and the user-goal vs AI-action split maps roughly onto assisting (kappa) vs delegating. The paper says its metrics do not capture productivity impact, so there is no time-saved measure. Because it mixes in adoption, it runs against our design, which drops adoption.
works.limitations: Consumer Bing chats, US only. Classification and completion judged by an LLM. Includes adoption. No time units. 2024 usage, before agents.
works.corrections: The quoted phrase 'not a measure of job replacement' is not verbatim; replaced it with the repo's actual wording. Added exact dates, US-only scope, the two 100k samples, the 149.8 million worker coverage, and the paper's statement that it does not measure productivity.

works.title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations (Anthropic Economic Index)
works.authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Sarah Heck, et al. (15 authors)
works.what_measured: How Claude.ai usage is spread over O*NET tasks and occupations, and the split between automation and augmentation.
works.method_plain: A privacy-preserving pipeline (Clio) classifies conversations into O*NET tasks and interaction modes; more than 4 million conversations in total. The task and automation analyses use about 1M conversations from 16-23 December 2024. The Directive and Feedback Loop modes count as automation; Task Iteration, Learning and Validation count as augmentation.
key_numbers: Software development and writing together are nearly half of all usage.
About 36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their associated tasks.
57% of usage is augmentation, 43% automation.
works.relevance_to_theta: Usage shares, not time saved. The automation/augmentation split is a rough anchor for how much of AI's effect runs through the assistant channel (kappa) versus delegation (q*p). It also shows that software tasks dominate actual use.
works.limitations: Usage shares, not labor savings. Consumer platform. Interaction mode classified by an LLM. Includes adoption. Short sample windows.
works.corrections: No errors. Added the sixth author, the sample windows (the task analysis uses about 1M conversations from Dec 2024, not the full 4M+), and the mode definitions.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index: New building blocks for understanding AI use ('Economic Primitives' report). ADDED BY FACT-CHECKER: missing from the stream.
works.authors: Anthropic Economics team (no individual authors named on the page)
works.venue: Anthropic research report (web); data on Hugging Face (Anthropic/EconomicIndex, release_2026_01_15)
works.what_measured: Per-conversation 'primitives' estimated by Claude: human time without AI, time with AI, Claude's own assessment of task success, autonomy given to the AI, skill or education level, and purpose. It also gives success rates by task length.
works.method_plain: Claude classifies Claude.ai and first-party API conversations from November 2025 on these dimensions. It then reweights the earlier productivity extrapolation by task success.
key_numbers: After adjusting for task reliability, the earlier +1.8 pp/yr labor productivity estimate falls to about 1.2 pp/yr for Claude.ai tasks and 1.0 pp/yr for API tasks.

Claude reaches 50% success on tasks of about 3.5 human-hours on the API and about 19 hours on Claude.ai; the page contrasts this with METR's roughly 2-hour 50% horizon for Sonnet 4.5 and notes the methods differ.
Success is 66% on tasks needing a college degree vs 70% on tasks needing less than high school. Speedups are about 9x (high-school-level tasks) vs 12x (college-level).
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest observational analog to our p(h,t): success as a function of human task length, from real usage rather than a benchmark. It is a direct test of our 'net of failure' step, because adjusting for success cuts the gross estimate by about a third. Success is self-assessed by the model and selected on tasks users chose, and review time is still not netted out.
works.limitations: Self-assessed success. Consumer and API usage selection. Gross of review. I read only the web summary; I did not confirm which fields are in the Hugging Face release.
works.corrections: Added because it bears directly on the stream's claims that no source nets out failure, and that none ties success to task length. Numbers come from the Anthropic page as read through WebFetch.

summary_flags: Eloundou summary statistics: the record says zeta > 0.50, but Table 3 shows the human zeta at 0.46 (GPT-4: 0.55) and the human beta at exactly 0.30.
Acemoglu: '0.193' is an alternative cost-saving number (after adding Peng et al.), not an alternative exposure value. And '20% from Eloundou and Svanberg' is wrong: the 20% comes from Eloundou alone.

Svanberg: the 49% (0.79% of compensation) comes from the firm-level 'bare-bones implementation' scenario, not from AI-as-a-service. The AI-as-a-service figure is 88% of vision task compensation at national scale.
ILO: the Database Designers and Administrators (2521) score is 0.57 / 0.08, not 0.55 / 0.04.

ILO called 'the ONLY major exposure index with a continuous 0-1 task score': overstated. The 2023 ILO WP96 already had one, and the record's own list includes a continuous usage-based measure (Tamkin-McCrory).

ILO 'ISCO fits India via PLFS': NCO-2015 is aligned with ISCO-08. But public PLFS microdata appear to record occupation at only 3 digits (from search results, not opened), so software developers (2512), web developers (2513) and applications programmers (2514) cannot be told apart in PLFS.

Eloundou bounds ('theta >= 0.5 on E1 tasks'): this holds only if the labels are accurate. The labels are annotator or GPT-4 beliefs about POTENTIAL savings and have never been checked against measured times. Write it as an implied bound, not a fact.
Summary says Acemoglu 'multiplies exposure (20%) by a 27% saving'. That leaves out the 23% feasibility factor and the 0.535 labor-share conversion (0.20 x 0.23 x 0.27 x 0.535).

'GDPval is the only source that nets out review': true only within this stream. GDPval's R_T is the time graders took to grade, not production review time. Also, the January 2026 Anthropic Economic Index report (missing from the stream) nets out task FAILURE, cutting the 1.8 pp/yr estimate to about 1.0-1.2 pp/yr.

Gap claim 'no exposure measure has a task-length (h) dimension': this is accurate for exposure indices, but the January 2026 Anthropic report gives success as a function of human task length (50% at about 3.5h on the API, about 19h on Claude.ai). That is a usage-based analog of METR's p(h) and should be cited.

Eisfeldt et al.: 'later drafts titled The Labor Impact...' is wrong as a description of the latest version. That title was a March 2024 draft; the January 2026 NBER revision is titled 'Generative AI and Firm Values'.
Microsoft: the quotation 'not a measure of job replacement' is not verbatim.
Felten LM-AIOE: the record presents reweighting as a route to time variation, but the LM version correlates 0.979 with the original, so in practice it barely changes rankings.

Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock: the rating platform is still not confirmed from the paper text (likely CrowdFlower, per replication file names). The rubric item count conflicts across sources (21 vs 23). Ratings were made on DWAs, not directly on task statements.

Tamkin-McCrory: the report gives both 84% (text) and 81% (figure caption) as the median saving, and both 90 minutes and 1.4 hours as the average task length, without reconciling them. Cite 'about 80%' and note the inconsistency.
verify.corrected_summary:
The working hypothesis largely holds for the classic exposure literature. Those measures answer 'can AI touch this task?' and not 'how much labor does it remove, net of checking and failure?' None of them gives a measured, continuous fraction of time saved per task.

Eloundou et al. (arXiv 2023; Science 384:1306-1308, 2024) label tasks E0/E1/E2. E1 means the labeler believes ChatGPT could cut task time by at least 50% at quality the recipient would not notice or care about. The labels come from human annotators (OpenAI alignment reviewers, not workers in the occupations) and from early GPT-4 with a tuned rubric. Agreement with humans is 66-82% depending on the measure. Mean occupation-level exposure is alpha 0.14, beta 0.30-0.34 and zeta 0.46-0.55 (human vs GPT-4). If the labels were accurate, E1 would imply theta >= 0.5 on E1 tasks. But they are beliefs about gross potential savings, never checked against measured times. Felten-Raj-Seamans (ability-based crowd ratings), Webb (patent text) and Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock (ML-suitability rubric rated on DWAs) are relative or ordinal scores with no time units. Eisfeldt et al. reuse the Eloundou rubric through GPT-3.5.

Several sources go partway past exposure. The ILO 2025 index gives continuous 0-1 perceived-automatability scores. Software developers (ISCO 2512) average 0.53 and web developers 0.60, with nothing netted out for review. Tamkin and McCrory (Anthropic, Nov 2025) give model-estimated per-task time savings of about 80%. These are selected on tasks people chose to bring to AI and exclude verification time. Anthropic's January 2026 Economic Index report adjusts for task success, cutting the implied productivity gain by about a third. It also reports success as a function of human task length, a usage-based cousin of METR's p(h). OpenAI's GDPval (2025) is the only source here that includes the time to review and redo work. Expert grading time is about 27% of human task time (109 of 404 minutes). GPT-5's speedup falls from 90x naive to 1.39x once review and redo are counted, about 28% time saved.

Two economics papers show the gap directly. Acemoglu (2024/2025) multiplies wage-bill-weighted exposure (20%) by a 23% feasibility share (borrowed from computer vision) and by a separate 27% per-task labor saving taken from experiments. Svanberg et al. show that only 23% of vision-exposed compensation is worth automating once system costs are counted.

For our recipe, exposure measures can at most supply an extensive-margin mask and rough task weights. p, q, rho and kappa have to come from benchmarks (METR, GDPval) and field or usage evidence. The task weights w_j and length distributions f_j(h) for Indian IT services still need new data.
verify.dataset_notes:
Eloundou et al.: a public repo exists at https://github.com/openai/GPTs-are-GPTs (MIT license), with occupation-level scores (occ_level.csv; alpha/beta/gamma variants, human and GPT-4). I could not confirm that task-level labels are included. Use this URL instead of the arXiv page.

ILO 2025: occupation means and SDs are in Appendix Table A1 of WP140 (https://doi.org/10.54394/HETP0387). https://pgmyrek.github.io/2025_GenAI_scores_ISCO08/ is an interactive tree visualization; I found no downloadable task-level file there, so access should read 'public (visualization); task-level download unconfirmed'. Public PLFS microdata appear to code occupation (NCO-2015) at only 3 digits (seen in search results for microdata.gov.in, not opened), so 4-digit ISCO scores would need averaging within NCO 251, 252 and so on.

Anthropic Economic Index: the data live on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex), not on arXiv. Releases: 2025-02-10, 2025-03-27, 2025-09-15, 2026-01-15 ('economic primitives', which may include time-with/without-AI and success fields; unverified), 2026-03-24, 2026-06-26. I found no confirmed public release of the November 2025 Tamkin-McCrory task-level time-saving estimates.

Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock replication package (openICPSR 114436, https://doi.org/10.3886/E114436V1) confirmed public. Files: HITRubric.docx, cf_report_DWAS_input.csv, cf_report_DWAS_physical_input.csv, cfProcessor_AEAPnP.py and a data-appendix readme. These are DWA-level crowd ratings; final SML scores are not confirmed to be included.

AIOE GitHub confirmed, including Language Modeling and Image Generation AIOE/AIIE files and the mTurk application-ability matrix.

Microsoft working-with-ai repo confirmed. Files: iwa_metrics.csv, ai_applicability_scores.csv, soc_metrics.csv, soc_iwa_weights.csv, soc_iwa_nonphysical_weights.csv, soc_to_iwas.csv, physical_tasks.csv.

GDPval: the paper states that a 220-task gold subset is open-sourced and that the full 1,320 tasks are not. I did not open the hosting location.

Svanberg et al.: no public data release found; access 'unknown' is correct.

works.title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence (working paper version of the Science 2023 article 'Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence')
works.authors: Shakked Noy, Whitney Zhang
works.venue: MIT working paper (preregistered, AEARCTR-0010882); later Science
works.what_measured: Time to complete and blind-graded quality of occupation-specific, incentivized professional writing tasks (press releases, short reports, analysis plans, delicate emails) with vs. without ChatGPT.
works.method_plain: Online randomized experiment: 444 college-educated professionals each did two tasks; half were told to use ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 era, early 2023) on the second task. Experienced professionals in the same occupations graded outputs blind. A two-week follow-up asked whether people kept using it at work.
key_numbers: N = 444 professionals; 92% of treated successfully signed up for ChatGPT
Time on second task fell by 10 minutes (37%) vs control average of 27 minutes (WP text); abstract states -0.8 SD in time
Quality rose 0.45 SD (WP text; abstract says 0.4 SD); fixed-15-minute arm: +0.39 SD
68% of treated submitted ChatGPT's first output unedited; treated workers active only ~3 minutes after pasting text; essays did not beat raw ChatGPT output
Correlation between first- and second-task grades: 0.49 in control vs 0.25 in treatment (inequality compressed; low-ability benefit most)
The widely quoted Science headline (roughly 40% time saved, 18% quality gain) is from the published version, which I could not open (403); the WP numbers above are what I verified
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a near-direct theta for short (~27-minute) text-generation tasks: about 0.37 of labor time saved with quality not falling. Because most treated workers pasted AI output with almost no editing, it implies rho near zero and q near 1 for low-stakes writing, i.e. it is the regime where the task is delegated outright. Useful as an upper anchor for short-h tasks in BPO/consulting documentation, not for long tasks.
works.limitations: Short, artificial, self-contained tasks (h ~ 0.5 hour); graders could not check facts against real context, so review cost is understated; GPT-3.5-era model; online sample, not firm workflow; time self-reported/platform-measured.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.year: 2025 (QJE 140(2)); arXiv v2 Nov 2024; NBER WP 31161 April 2023
works.what_measured: Resolutions per hour, average handle time (AHT), chats per hour, resolution rate, customer satisfaction (NPS), sentiment, attrition for chat-based technical support agents.
works.method_plain: Natural experiment: a GPT-family-based assistant that suggests replies was rolled out to agents at different dates (staggered), so the authors compare agents before/after access against not-yet-treated agents (difference-in-differences). Agents could accept or ignore suggestions.
key_numbers: 5,172 agents (NBER WP: 5,179); a Fortune 500 enterprise-software firm's support, mostly outsourced agents in the Philippines; sessions average ~40 minutes
Resolutions per hour +15% on average (NBER 2023 version: +14%)
AHT -8.5% from baseline mean of 43 minutes; chats per hour +0.37 (~15%); resolution rate +1.3 pp on 82% base (not significant); no average effect on NPS
Lowest skill quintile: +0.5 resolutions/hour, i.e. +36%; intro says ~30% for less-skilled/less-experienced; top quintile: no productivity gain and small declines in resolution rate and satisfaction
Agents adopt about 35-38% of AI suggestions on average (IQR 23%-50%)
Treated agents with 2 months tenure perform like untreated agents with 6+ months
works.relevance_to_theta: Closest classic analogue to Indian BPO voice/chat work. Implies theta for chat support of roughly 0.08 (AHT) to 0.13 (1 - 1/1.15 from throughput) with an assist-only tool, which is a kappa-type estimate (AI as assistant, not delegate). The 35-38% suggestion-adoption rate is a measured analogue of q for drafts. Heterogeneity says theta depends on the workforce's skill mix: large for novices, ~0 for experts.
works.limitations: Not randomized (staggered rollout); one firm, one product line; 2020-2021-era model; measures throughput, not labor hours removed; assist-only tool so says nothing about autonomous agents; includes the partial adoption that the theta definition wants to strip out.

works.title: Generative AI in Action: Field Experimental Evidence from Alibaba's Customer Service Operations
works.authors: Xiao Ni, Yiwei Wang, Tianjun Feng, Lauren Xiaoyan Lu, Yitong Wang, Congyi Zhou
works.year: 2026 (arXiv v1 Feb 2026, v2 Jul 2026; WP dated Nov 2025)
works.what_measured: Issue identification time, chat duration, agent response time, shift-away time, customer ratings, dissatisfaction rate, and objective quality (customer retrial) in e-commerce after-sales chat support.
works.method_plain: True randomized field experiment: agents randomized by ID to get a Qwen-based assistant that drafts issue diagnoses and solution proposals at the start of chats (Jan 23 - Feb 19, 2024). Estimates both the effect of access (intent-to-treat) and of actual use (instrumenting use with assignment).
key_numbers: 2,895 treated vs 3,045 control agents (5,940; 15.6% of official agents); after-sales issues = 56.5% of all chats
Baseline: issue identification 35.5 s, chat 465.6 s
Access (ITT): identification time -8.2% (-3.2 s), chat duration -1.1% (-5.7 s); dissatisfaction -3.4%; rating +1.2%
Full usage (usage rate 0 to 1): identification time -32.3%, chat duration -4.2%; agent response time over whole chat -5.7%; dissatisfaction -15.4%
Average usage rate 0.287 at agent-day level; 17.9% of treated agents never used it
Lower-performing agents gain most; top-performers see declines in subjective and objective quality (workflow disruption)
No significant effect on objective quality (retrials)
works.relevance_to_theta: The most BPO-like randomized evidence found. Separates adoption from per-use effect, which is exactly what the theta definition needs: at full use, chat time falls only ~4% even though the targeted sub-step (diagnosis) falls ~32%. This illustrates that theta_j is the targeted sub-step saving times its share of task time (w within the task), and that assistant tools on short (~8 minute) chats yield small kappa.
works.limitations: Assistant touches only the opening stage of chats; Qwen model of early 2024; Chinese e-commerce, not enterprise IT support; 4-week window; working paper.

works.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
works.authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, Hila Lifshitz-Assaf, Katherine C. Kellogg, Saran Rajendran, Lisa Krayer, François Candelon, Karim R. Lakhani
works.year: 2023 (HBS WP 24-013); later Organization Science (DOI 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838; journal page not opened)
works.venue: Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013 / SSRN 4573321
works.what_measured: Tasks completed, speed, and graded quality on 18 consulting tasks inside AI's frontier; correctness on one task chosen to be outside the frontier.
works.method_plain: Preregistered experiment at BCG: consultants did a baseline task, then were randomized to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 plus a prompt-engineering overview.
key_numbers: N = 758 consultants (~7% of BCG individual-contributor consultants); model GPT-4
Inside frontier: 12.2% more tasks completed, 25.1% faster, >40% higher quality vs control
Below-average baseline performers +43%, above-average +17% (vs own baseline scores)
Outside frontier: control correct 84.5%; AI groups 60% and 70%; average -19 percentage points (GPT+overview -24 pp, GPT only -13 pp)
works.relevance_to_theta: Key evidence that theta varies sharply across tasks of similar apparent difficulty, so f_j over 'length' alone may miss a second dimension (in/out of frontier). Inside frontier, time saved ~20% (1 - 1/1.251) with quality gains; outside, using AI lowers correctness, which in the formula means negative net value unless rho is spent detecting failures. Supports modelling q and p as task-specific and adding an explicit error penalty.
works.limitations: Single firm; tasks designed by researchers; time limits shape 'speed' measure; GPT-4 of 2023; outside-frontier result from one task only; the published Organization Science version was not opened.

works.title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise
works.authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Charles Ayoubi, Hila Lifshitz, Raffaella Sadun, Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Yi Han, Jeff Goldman, Hari Nair, Stewart Taub, Karim Lakhani
works.what_measured: Quality of product-innovation solutions (standardized), time spent, top-10% solutions, balance of technical/commercial content, emotions, for individuals vs. two-person teams, with/without AI.
works.method_plain: Preregistered 2x2 field experiment in one-day P&G workshops: professionals randomized to work alone or in an R&D+Commercial pair, with or without GPT-4 (GPT-4o in July workshop), on real business-unit innovation challenges.
key_numbers: N = 776 P&G professionals
Quality: teams without AI +0.24 SD over individuals without AI; individuals with AI +0.37 SD; teams with AI +0.39 SD
Time spent: individuals with AI 16.4% less, teams with AI 12.7% less than control
AI users more likely to produce top-10% solutions; positive emotions +0.457 SD (individuals with AI)
works.relevance_to_theta: For consulting/solutioning-type work (Indian IT 'consulting' service line), shows AI saving ~13-16% of time while raising quality, and one person with AI matching a two-person team, which is a labor-per-output effect (halving headcount at equal quality) larger than the time saving alone. Suggests theta for collaborative tasks should count headcount substitution, not just hours.
works.limitations: One-day workshop tasks; quality judged by experts, not market outcome; GPT-4/4o, chat interface; working paper.

works.title: AI-Powered Lawyering: AI Reasoning Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and the Future of Legal Practice (also covers the earlier Choi, Monahan & Schwarcz GPT-4 RCT)
works.authors: Daniel Schwarcz, Sam Manning, Patrick Barry, David R. Cleveland, J.J. Prescott, Beverly Rich
works.venue: Working paper (Univ. of Minnesota / Michigan law; Berkeley-hosted copy)
works.what_measured: Blind-graded quality, completion time, and 'productivity' (quality points per minute) on six realistic legal tasks; hallucinations.
works.method_plain: RCT: upper-level law students at Minnesota and Michigan randomized to use Vincent AI (retrieval-augmented legal tool), OpenAI o1-preview, or no AI on six assignments.
key_numbers: 127 participants enrolled (114 completed at least some work)

Time saved on tasks with significant speed gains: 14-37% (Vincent) and 12-28% (o1-preview); averages across tasks: Vincent -21% (6 tasks), o1-preview -19%; prior GPT-4 study averaged ~22% across 4 tasks
Commonly quoted 'productivity' gains of 38%-115% (Vincent) and 34%-140% (o1-preview) are quality points PER MINUTE, not time saved
No speed or quality gain on the NDA drafting task (template provided)
o1-preview produced some hallucinations; Vincent about as many as no-AI

Companion study Choi, Monahan & Schwarcz, 109 Minn. L. Rev. 147 (2024): GPT-4 gave large consistent speed gains, small/inconsistent quality gains, biggest quality gains for lowest-skilled (abstract opened at scholarship.law.umn.edu; figures above from this later paper's comparison)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives document-analysis/drafting theta of ~0.2 for assistant-mode use, and shows it barely changed from GPT-4 to o1-preview/RAG (19-21% vs 22%) even as quality rose: capability gains went into quality rather than labor saved. This is a caution against mapping p(h,t) improvements straight into theta. Also a clear example of a misquoted number.
works.limitations: Law students, not practicing lawyers; lab assignments; graders blind but subjective; productivity metric mixes quality and speed; working paper.

works.title: The Uneven Impact of Generative AI on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya
works.authors: Nicholas G. Otis, Rowan Clarke, Solène Delecourt, David Holtz, Rembrand Koning
works.what_measured: Revenues and profits of small businesses after access to a GPT-4 business advisor via WhatsApp.
works.method_plain: Field RCT in Kenya: entrepreneurs randomized to a GPT-4-powered AI business assistant or control; effects split by baseline performance.
key_numbers: ~634 entrepreneurs completed at least one post-treatment survey wave
Average effect on revenue/profit: cannot reject zero
Effect for low baseline performers >0.20 SD lower than for high performers
Subsamples: low performers ~10% worse, high performers possibly >15% better
Differences came from which advice was implemented, not from questions asked or advice given
works.relevance_to_theta: Not a time-saving study; relevant because it shows that the value of AI output depends on the user's ability to judge it (a q/review problem). When the human cannot verify, AI can lower output. Supports keeping the max{.,kappa} floor and modelling q as a function of reviewer skill.
works.limitations: Advice task, not production work; outcomes are business results not labor time; small sample; emerging-market micro-enterprises unlike IT-services firms.

works.title: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation
works.authors: Ali Merali
works.what_measured: Task completion time, grades and earnings per minute for professional translators using one of 13 LLMs of different training compute, or none.
works.method_plain: Randomized experiment: 300 professional translators did 1,800 tasks, each randomly given a model of a different size (or no model); relates productivity to model training compute.
key_numbers: 10x model training compute -> 12.3% faster task completion
10x compute -> +0.18 SD grades; +16.1% earnings per minute
Gains about 4x larger for lower-skilled workers

Follow-up (arXiv 2512.21316, Dec 2025, >500 consultants/analysts/managers, 13 LLMs): each year of model progress cut task time by 8%; gains larger for non-agentic analytical tasks than for agentic tool-use workflows; 56% of gains from compute, 44% algorithmic
works.relevance_to_theta: The only experiments found that directly estimate how theta moves with capability (the t in theta_j(t)): ~12% faster per 10x compute in translation; ~8% less task time per year of progress in consulting/analysis. Gives an empirical slope to check the METR-based p(h,t) extrapolation against, and the agentic-vs-non-agentic finding suggests the delegation channel lags the assistance channel.
works.limitations: Short tasks; mostly older/smaller models; translation is a near-ideal LLM task; the 2025 consulting follow-up was read only at abstract level; single author, not yet peer-reviewed.

works.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice - A Randomized Trial
works.authors: Paul J. Lukac, William Turner, Sitaram Vangala, Aaron T. Chin, Joshua Khalili, Ya-Chen Tina Shih, Eric M. Cheng, John N. Mafi, Catherine Sarkisian
works.venue: NEJM AI (DOI 10.1056/AIoa2501000); journal page returned 403, details from UCLA Health press release
works.what_measured: Time spent writing each clinical note, burnout, workload, note inaccuracies, safety events.
works.method_plain: Three-arm RCT at UCLA, Nov 2024 - Jan 2025: outpatient physicians randomized to Microsoft DAX, Nabla, or usual care; EHR logs measure time-in-note.
key_numbers: 238 physicians, 14 specialties, ~72,000 encounters
Nabla: time per note 4:30 -> 3:49 (-41 s); control 4:22 -> 4:04 (-18 s); reported as ~9.5% reduction vs control, significant
DAX: smaller, non-significant reduction (search snippet: ~1.7%, p = 0.66; not verified on the journal page)
Burnout scores ~7% better in both AI arms vs control
Occasional clinically significant inaccuracies (omissions, pronoun errors); one mild safety event
Related: Goh et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 (opened): 50 physicians, GPT-4 did not improve diagnostic reasoning (76% vs 74%, p = 0.60), time per case -82 s (n.s.), but GPT-4 alone scored 92%
works.relevance_to_theta: Documentation is the closest medical analogue to BPO document processing. Even a purpose-built tool saved only ~10% of note time, because review/correction of AI drafts (rho) eats most of the drafting saving. Goh et al. shows the reverse problem: human+AI did no better than human, while AI alone did much better, i.e. kappa (assist) can be far below the delegation value q*p.
works.limitations: Single center, short duration; journal article not opened directly; time-in-note excludes after-hours review elsewhere; Goh is a vignette study.

works.title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI
works.authors: Eleanor Wiske Dillon, Sonia Jaffe, Nicole Immorlica, Christopher T. Stanton
works.what_measured: Telemetry-measured time on email, documents and meetings for knowledge workers given Microsoft 365 Copilot.
works.method_plain: Randomized field experiment across 66 firms: within each firm, workers randomly given Copilot licenses or not; outcomes from Microsoft usage logs.
key_numbers: 7,137 knowledge workers in 66 firms
Workers who used the tool spent about two fewer hours per week on email (abstract v4)
Earlier v1 and secondary summaries report ~25-31% less email time for regular users and 5-25% faster document completion; I did not verify these against the paper's tables
No reported change in meetings in the abstract
works.relevance_to_theta: Back-office-like evidence with objective time logs at scale; implies theta for email/correspondence work on the order of a quarter of that time, but only a couple of hours out of a 40-hour week, i.e. small w for the affected task. Shows the w_j * theta_j weighting matters more than theta_j alone.
works.limitations: Assistant-mode Copilot; time in apps, not output; heterogeneous firms; only the abstract was verified.

works.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.venue: Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper 2025-56 (also NBER)
works.what_measured: Adoption, self-reported time savings, new tasks, earnings and hours in 11 AI-exposed occupations, including customer support specialists, IT support specialists, software developers, accountants and office clerks.
works.method_plain: Two large surveys (late 2023 and 2024) linked to Danish administrative employer-employee records; difference-in-differences using employer encouragement as variation.
key_numbers: 25,000 workers, 7,000 workplaces, 11 occupations
Average time savings 3% (abstract); users report 2.8% of work hours
On days they use chatbots, time savings 6-7%; adopters actively use chatbots only 5-6% of hours on usage days; typical adopter uses them every third to fourth day
Savings highest in occupations covered by RCTs (customer/IT support, marketing, software); about half as large for teachers, accountants, financial advisors
~7% time savings for marketers and software developers whose employers promote AI
New job tasks created for 8.4% of workers
Earnings/hours effects: precise zeros, CIs rule out effects > 1%
works.relevance_to_theta: The bridge between RCT-style theta (15-40%) and realized economy-wide savings (~3%). It shows the gap comes from adoption intensity and the small share of hours where chatbots apply (w_j), not necessarily from small per-task theta. Useful as a sanity check on S(t): the top-down 2.3 pp/yr from Indian filings is in the same order of magnitude.
works.limitations: Self-reported time savings; 2023-2024 chatbots, pre-agent; Denmark; working paper.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded win rates of model deliverables vs industry experts on 1,320 tasks (220 gold) from 44 occupations; time and cost to complete, review, and redo.
works.method_plain: Not an RCT. Experts (avg 14 years experience) wrote real tasks and deliverables; other experts blindly compared model vs human outputs. The authors then compute expected time saved under 'try the model, review it, and do it yourself if it fails' (once, or n times).
key_numbers: Expert task time HT = 404 minutes on average; expert review time RT = 109 minutes (so review is ~27% of task time)
Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% wins-or-ties vs experts on gold set
Win rate (strictly better) and speed-up: GPT-4o 12.5% (try-1: 0.87x, try-n: 0.46x); o4-mini 29.1% (1.02x, 1.06x); o3 35.2% (1.08x, 1.28x); GPT-5 39.0% (1.12x, 1.39x)
Naive speed ratio (ignoring review) 90x-327x, collapsing to ~1.1-1.4x once review and redo are counted
Implied fraction of time saved for GPT-5: ~11% (try once) and ~28% (try until success)
works.relevance_to_theta: Essentially the draft formula, measured: E[T] = MT + RT + (1-w)HT maps onto theta = q*p - rho with w as the accept probability (q*p) and RT/HT as rho (~0.27 for multi-hour tasks). It provides empirical rho and win rates by occupation/sector, and shows how sensitive theta is to rho: with a 39% win rate, review cost takes the saving from 'infinite' to ~11-28%.
works.limitations: Benchmark, not field experiment; review time is grader time, not workplace review; win rate counts only 'better than expert'; self-reported task hours; US occupations; tasks long (avg ~7 h) and one-shot, so may understate iterative workflows.

research.stream_summary: Experiments outside coding mostly test AI as an assistant, not as a worker you hand a task to. The pattern holds across settings. On short, self-contained text tasks, time savings are large: Noy and Zhang found 37% on 27-minute writing tasks, and BCG consultants were 25% faster on tasks inside the AI's 'frontier'. In real operational settings the savings are much smaller. In chat customer support, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found throughput up 15% and handle time down 8.5%. In Alibaba's randomized trial, chat time fell only about 4% even when the tool was fully used. AI medical scribes cut note time by about 10%, and legal drafting time fell about 20%. Gains are concentrated among less-skilled workers. Experts gain little or lose quality. When the task is outside what the AI can do, or the user cannot judge the output (BCG's out-of-frontier task, Kenyan entrepreneurs), AI makes results worse. Better models have mostly raised quality rather than time saved: the legal time savings barely moved from GPT-4 to o1. Only Merali's experiments estimate how savings change with model capability, at about 12% per 10x compute in translation and about 8% per year in consulting and analysis tasks. GDPval comes closest to the project's formula. Expert review takes about 27% of the task's own time, and with a 39% win rate GPT-5 saves only about 11-28% of time. Danish administrative data show realized savings of about 3% of hours, because AI touches only a small share of work. This supports the working hypothesis, with one nuance: the intensive margin is measured, but only for assistant use, on short tasks, and with 2023-24 models. Almost nothing measures the review cost and acceptance rate of delegated, agent-style work in BPO settings over time.
gaps_noticed: No randomized experiment yet measures delegation to autonomous agents in BPO/back-office work (claims, invoice processing, KYC, ticket triage) with the review time recorded separately; Ju & Aral (arXiv 2503.18238, 2,234 participants, 50% more ads per worker in human-AI teams) is the closest 'agent teammate' RCT but is a marketing task.
Review cost (rho) is almost never measured directly in field studies. GDPval's 109-minute review on 404-minute tasks is the main number, and it is grader time, not workplace QA time.
Few studies vary model capability within one design (only Merali), so the time path of theta_j(t) is largely an extrapolation.
No study is set in Indian IT/BPO firms. The closest settings are Philippine outsourced support (BLR) and Alibaba's after-sales chat.
Studies report per-task time savings but rarely the distribution of task lengths (f_j); Alibaba shows that saving 32% on a sub-step can mean only 4% of the whole chat.
Quality effects are measured inconsistently (SD of grades, NPS, retrials), so it is hard to net out quality-for-time trade-offs into a single labor-saving number.

Remote Labor Index (arXiv 2510.26787): best agent completes only 2.5% of 240 real Upwork projects end to end (mean 28.9 hours each), versus 15-40% assistant-mode savings. This gap between delegation and assistance is not explained in any experiment.

Could not open the published Science (Noy-Zhang), QJE full text, Organization Science (Dell'Acqua), or NEJM AI (Lukac) journal pages (403); numbers are from working-paper or official press versions as noted.

datasets.name: GDPval gold subset (220 tasks with prompts, reference files, expert deliverables)
datasets.description: Open-sourced tasks from 44 occupations with expert completion times; full 1,320-task set and grading data are internal. Can be used to estimate rho and win rates by occupation using one's own graders.

datasets.name: Remote Labor Index public projects
datasets.description: 10 public Upwork projects with briefs, human deliverables, time and cost; the 230-project test set is private. Includes data entry, transcription and translation categories that resemble BPO work.

datasets.name: Noy & Zhang replication data
datasets.description: Preregistered (AEARCTR-0010882) experiment data with times and grades; replication package availability via Science not verified.

datasets.name: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond customer support data
datasets.description: Agent-month and chat-level data from a private AI vendor and its client firm; proprietary.

datasets.name: Alibaba customer service experiment data
datasets.description: Chat-level logs for 5,940 agents, with access and usage measured; proprietary to Alibaba.

datasets.name: AI-Powered Lawyering experiment data
datasets.description: Anonymized data and code for the six-task legal RCT, available on request from the authors per the paper.

datasets.name: Danish AI chatbot adoption surveys linked to registers (Humlum-Vestergaard)
datasets.description: Survey of 25,000 workers in 11 occupations linked to Statistics Denmark registers; register access is restricted to approved researchers.

datasets.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot field experiment telemetry (Dillon et al.)
datasets.description: Work-pattern logs for 7,137 workers in 66 firms; Microsoft internal.

works.title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence (working paper, March 2, 2023); published as 'Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence', Science 381(6654):187-192, July 2023
works.authors: Shakked Noy, Whitney Zhang
works.venue: MIT working paper (preregistered, AEARCTR-0010882); published in Science, DOI 10.1126/science.adh2586
works.what_measured: Time to complete and blind-graded quality of occupation-specific, incentivized professional writing tasks (press releases, short reports, analysis plans, delicate emails), with and without ChatGPT.
works.method_plain: Online randomized experiment. College-educated professionals each did two writing tasks. Half were randomly given ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 era, early 2023) for the second task. Experienced professionals in the same occupations graded the outputs without knowing which group wrote them. A two-week follow-up asked whether people kept using ChatGPT at work.
key_numbers: WP sample: 444 professionals. 92% of treated participants signed up for ChatGPT. (The Science version reports 453 participants per a search snippet; not checked on the journal page.)
WP: time on the second task fell by 10 minutes (37%) against a control average of 27 minutes. The abstract gives this as -0.8 SD (figure shows -0.83 SD).
WP: grades rose 0.45 SD in the text (abstract rounds to 0.4 SD). In the arm where everyone had to spend exactly 15 minutes, grades rose 0.39 SD, but this was imprecise (p = 0.13).
Published Science abstract (seen on Stanford SCALE's listing): average time fell 40% and quality rose 18%.

68% of treated participants SAID they submitted ChatGPT's first output without editing (self-report). Treated participants were active for only about 3 minutes after first pasting in a large block of text. Their essays were not graded higher than raw ChatGPT output.
Correlation between first- and second-task grades was 0.49 in control and 0.25 in treatment (p = 0.004 for the difference in slopes), so the gap between stronger and weaker writers shrank.
works.relevance_to_theta: A near-direct theta for short (about 27-minute), self-contained writing tasks: roughly 0.37-0.40 of labor time saved with no fall in graded quality. Because most treated workers submitted AI output with little editing, it looks like outright delegation with low rho for low-stakes writing. But graders could not check facts against real context, so the implied q near 1 and rho near 0 hold only for tasks where nobody checks deeply. Use it as an upper anchor for short tasks, not for long or high-stakes ones.
works.limitations: Short, artificial tasks (h about 0.5 hour). Graders had no real context to check facts against, so review cost is understated. GPT-3.5-era model. Online sample, not a firm's workflow. The 'unedited' share is self-reported. Humlum and Vestergaard (2025, footnote 18) describe the same study as about 14 minutes of manual editing after pasting, which does not match the WP's 3 minutes. The WP figure is used here.
works.corrections: WP numbers were checked against the PDF text and match. Added the published Science figures (40% time, 18% quality), confirmed on the Stanford SCALE listing; the record said it could not open them. Added the DOI and page range. Noted that the 15-minute-arm result is not significant (p = 0.13) and that the 68% figure is self-reported. The Science sample of 453 comes from a search snippet only and is not verified.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.year: 2025 (QJE 140(2):889-942, May 2025); arXiv v1 April 2023, v2 Nov 6, 2024; NBER WP 31161 April 2023, revised Nov 2023
works.what_measured: Resolutions per hour, average handle time (AHT), chats per hour, resolution rate, customer satisfaction (net promoter score), and adherence to AI suggestions, for chat-based technical support agents.
works.method_plain: Natural experiment. A GPT-family assistant that suggests replies in real time was switched on for agents at different dates (staggered, Fall 2020 to Winter 2021). Agents before and after access are compared with agents not yet given access (difference-in-differences). Agents could accept, edit or ignore suggestions.
key_numbers: 5,172 agents (NBER WP: 5,179). Fortune 500 enterprise-software firm. Most agents work in the Philippines. Support sessions average about 40 minutes.
Resolutions per hour rose 15% on average (0.30 chats, 15.2%, with agent and tenure fixed effects). NBER 2023 version: 14%.

AHT fell 3.7 minutes (8.5% of a 43-minute baseline). Chats per hour rose 0.37 on a 2.4 base (about 15%). Resolution rate rose 1.3 pp on an 82% base (not significant). No meaningful change in net promoter score (-0.12 pp on an 80% mean).

Lowest skill quintile: +0.5 resolutions per hour (+36%). Introduction: about 30% for less-skilled/less-experienced workers (NBER abstract: 34%). Top quintile: no productivity gain, and small significant declines in resolution rate and satisfaction.
Agents follow AI recommendations 35% of the time on average (mechanism text). Average adherence rate is 38% elsewhere in the paper, interquartile range 23-50%.
Treated agents with 2 months of tenure perform like untreated agents with more than 6 months.
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest classic analogue to Indian BPO chat work. Implies theta for chat support of about 0.08 (from AHT) to 0.13 (1 - 1/1.15 from throughput) with an assist-only tool, so it is a kappa-type estimate. The 35-38% adherence rate is a rough measured analogue of q for drafts. Theta depends on the skill mix: large for novices, about zero for top agents.
works.limitations: Not randomized (staggered rollout). One firm, one product line. 2020-21 GPT model. Measures throughput, not labor hours removed. Assist-only, so it says nothing about autonomous agents. Includes partial adoption, which the theta definition wants to strip out.
works.corrections: Numbers match the arXiv v2 PDF. Minor additions only: QJE page range 889-942 and DOI. The NBER abstract gives a 34% gain for novices. Two adherence figures appear in the paper (35% and 38%).

works.title: Generative AI in Action: Field Experimental Evidence from Alibaba's Customer Service Operations
works.authors: Xiao Ni, Yiwei Wang, Tianjun Feng, Lauren Xiaoyuan Lu, Yitong Wang, Congyi Zhou
works.year: 2026 (arXiv v1 Feb 8, 2026; v2 Jul 31, 2026; current PDF dated July 2026)
works.what_measured: Issue identification time, chat duration, agent response time, shift-away time, customer ratings, dissatisfaction rate, and objective quality (customer retrials) in Taobao after-sales chat support.
works.method_plain: Randomized field experiment. New agents (less than one year of tenure) were randomized by agent ID to get a Qwen-based assistant that drafts issue diagnoses and solution proposals in the opening stage of a chat (Jan 23 - Feb 19, 2024). The paper estimates the effect of access (intent-to-treat) and of actual use (using assignment as an instrument for use).
key_numbers: 5,940 new agents: 2,895 treated (48.7%), 3,045 control (51.3%). They were 15.6% of Taobao's official customer service agents. About 2.56 million chats.
After-sales issues are 56.5% of all customer service chats.
Baseline: issue identification 35.53 s, chat 465.62 s.
Access (ITT): identification time -8.2% (-3.2 s), chat duration -1.1% (-5.7 s). Dissatisfaction -0.012 (3.4% of the 0.35 mean). Rating +0.042 points (1.2%).
Usage rate from 0 to 1: identification time -32.3%, chat duration -4.2%. Agent response time over the whole chat -5.7%. Dissatisfaction -0.054 (15.4%).
Average usage rate 0.287 at the agent-day level. 17.9% of treated agents never used it.
Lower performers gain most. Top performers see declines in both subjective and objective quality, consistent with workflow disruption. No significant average effect on objective quality (retrials).
works.relevance_to_theta: The most BPO-like randomized evidence here, and it separates adoption from the effect per use, as the theta definition needs. At full use, chat time falls only about 4% even though the targeted sub-step (diagnosis, about 36 s of a 466 s chat) falls about 32%. So theta for the task is roughly the saving on the targeted sub-step times that sub-step's share of task time, and an assistant on short (about 8-minute) chats gives a small kappa.
works.limitations: Assistant touches only the opening stage. Sample is new agents (tenure under one year), so results may not carry over to experienced staff. Early-2024 Qwen model. Chinese consumer e-commerce, not enterprise IT support. 4-week window. Working paper.
works.corrections: Fixed author name: 'Lauren Xiaoyuan Lu' (not 'Xiaoyan'). The current PDF is dated July 2026. The record's 'WP dated Nov 2025' could not be verified and was removed. Added that the sample is only new agents with under one year of tenure. Submission dates were confirmed on the arXiv page (v1 is dated Feb 8, 2026 even though the ID is 2603). All numbers were checked against the PDF.

works.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
works.authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Edward McFowland III, Ethan Mollick, Hila Lifshitz-Assaf, Katherine C. Kellogg, Saran Rajendran, Lisa Krayer, François Candelon, Karim R. Lakhani
works.year: 2023 (HBS WP 24-013); published in Organization Science, lead article of the March-April 2026 issue
works.venue: Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013 / SSRN 4573321; Organization Science (DOI 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838)
works.what_measured: Share of 18 consulting subtasks completed, time to reach the final question, and graded quality on a task inside AI's frontier; correctness, time and recommendation quality on one task chosen to be outside the frontier.
works.method_plain: Preregistered experiment at BCG. Consultants did a baseline assessment task, then were randomized to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 plus a prompt-engineering overview.
key_numbers: N = 758 consultants (about 7% of BCG's individual-contributor consultants). Model: GPT-4.

Inside the frontier (abstract): 12.2% more tasks completed, 25.1% faster, more than 40% higher quality. Speed is measured as time to reach the last of 18 questions: GPT+overview 22.5% less time (18.8 min), GPT only 27.6% less (23.1 min).
Bottom-half baseline performers +43%, top half +17%.

Outside the frontier: control correct 84.5%, AI groups 60% and 70%, an average drop of 19 pp (GPT+overview -24 pp, GPT only -13 pp). AI users were also faster on this task (30% and 18% less time) and got higher recommendation-quality scores even when wrong.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that theta varies sharply between tasks of similar apparent difficulty, so an f_j over task length alone may miss a second dimension (inside or outside the frontier). Inside the frontier, time saved is about 0.22-0.28 (the paper's numbers are already reductions in time; the record's 1 - 1/1.251 = 20% conversion is wrong). Outside it, AI lowered correctness while making answers look better and arrive faster. Errors become harder to detect, which argues for an explicit error penalty and task-specific q and p.
works.limitations: Single firm. Tasks designed by researchers. Time limits shape the speed measure (subjects had to use the full time, so speed is time to reach the last question). GPT-4 of 2023. The outside-frontier result rests on one task. The published Organization Science text was not opened.
works.corrections: Venue updated: an AOM post confirms it is the lead article in Organization Science's March-April 2026 issue, with that DOI. The journal text itself was not opened. Clarified how speed is measured (22.5% / 27.6% less time to reach the last question). Fixed the record's theta inference: the 25.1% is already a time reduction, so theta is about 0.25, not 0.20. Added the outside-frontier timing and quality results.

works.title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI Reshaping Teamwork and Expertise
works.authors: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Charles Ayoubi, Hila Lifshitz, Raffaella Sadun, Ethan Mollick, Lilach Mollick, Yi Han, Jeff Goldman, Hari Nair, Stewart Taub, Karim Lakhani
works.what_measured: Standardized quality of product-innovation solutions, time spent, top-10% solutions, balance of technical and commercial content, and emotions, for individuals vs. two-person teams, with or without AI.
works.method_plain: Preregistered 2x2 field experiment in P&G workshops (May-July 2024). Professionals were randomized to work alone or in an R&D+Commercial pair, with or without GPT-4 (GPT-4o in the July workshop), on real business-unit innovation challenges.
key_numbers: N = 776 P&G professionals.
Quality vs individuals without AI: teams without AI +0.24 SD, individuals with AI +0.37 SD, teams with AI +0.39 SD.
Time spent: individuals with AI 16.4% less, teams with AI 12.7% less than control.
AI users were more likely to produce top-10% solutions. Positive emotions +0.457 SD for individuals with AI.
works.relevance_to_theta: For consulting or solution-design work, AI saves about 13-16% of time while raising quality. One person with AI matched a two-person team's quality, which suggests a possible labor-per-output effect larger than the time saving. That headcount reading is an inference: the paper did not measure staffing changes.
works.limitations: One-day workshop tasks. Quality judged by experts, not by the market. GPT-4/4o in a chat interface. Working paper.
works.corrections: All numbers match the NBER PDF. Only change: flagged the 'halving headcount' reading as the stream's own inference.

works.title: AI-Powered Lawyering: AI Reasoning Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and the Future of Legal Practice
works.authors: Daniel Schwarcz, Sam Manning, Patrick Barry, David R. Cleveland, J.J. Prescott, Beverly Rich
works.year: 2025 (draft dated about March 2, 2025 per a secondary listing; SSRN page not opened)
works.venue: Working paper (Univ. of Minnesota / Univ. of Michigan law; copy hosted by Berkeley Law)
works.what_measured: Blind-graded quality, completion time, 'productivity' (quality points per minute) and hallucinations on six realistic legal tasks.
