works.method_plain: Preregistered RCT with upper-level law students at Minnesota and Michigan. Each student did all six assignments: two with no AI, two with OpenAI o1-preview, and two with Vincent AI (a retrieval-augmented legal tool). Which tool went with which assignment was randomized across students. Lawyer graders did not know the condition.
key_numbers: 153 students formally enrolled. 127 completed the study. 114 of the 127 completed the post-experiment survey.

On tasks with significant speed gains: 14-37% less time (Vincent), 12-28% (o1-preview). Average time reduction: Vincent 21% across six tasks, o1-preview 19%. The prior GPT-4 study averaged about 22% across four tasks (the authors say a perfect comparison is not possible).
The headline 'productivity' gains (about 38-115% for Vincent, 34-140% for o1-preview, significant in five of six tasks) are quality points per minute, not time saved.
No significant speed or quality gain on the NDA drafting task (a template was provided).
Hallucinations: Vincent 3 in total, o1-preview 11, no AI 4.

Companion study: Choi, Monahan & Schwarcz, 'Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence', 109 Minn. L. Rev. 147 (2024). GPT-4 gave large, consistent speed gains and only slight, inconsistent quality gains. The lowest-skilled gained most on quality where it helped.
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a theta of about 0.2 for legal analysis and writing in assistant mode. Time savings were about the same with GPT-4 (22%) as with o1-preview and RAG (19-21%), while quality rose. That suggests capability gains may go into quality rather than labor saved, though this is a cross-study comparison with different tasks. It is a caution against mapping p(h,t) improvements straight into theta. It is also a clear example of a misquoted number (productivity per minute read as time saved).
works.limitations: Law students, not practicing lawyers. Lab assignments. Self-selected volunteers. Graders blind but subjective. The productivity metric mixes quality and speed. GPT-4 vs o1 is compared across studies, not within one design. Working paper.
works.corrections: Sample fixed: 153 enrolled, 127 completed, 114 answered the survey. The record said '127 enrolled, 114 completed at least some work', which is wrong. Design fixed: within-subject rotation, with each student using each condition on two tasks, not three separate groups. Added hallucination counts and the authors' caveat about the cross-study comparison. The summary's phrase 'legal drafting time' is too narrow: the 19-21% averages cover analysis, letters, emails and complaint tasks, and the one drafting task (NDA) showed no time saving.

works.title: The Uneven Impact of Generative AI on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya
works.authors: Nicholas G. Otis, Rowan Clarke, Solène Delecourt, David Holtz, Rembrand Koning
works.what_measured: Revenues and profits of small businesses after access to a GPT-4 business advisor on WhatsApp.
works.method_plain: Field RCT with 640 Kenyan small-business owners. Half got a GPT-4-powered AI business assistant on WhatsApp; the control group got standard business guides. Effects are split by baseline performance.
key_numbers: 640 entrepreneurs randomized. 634 completed at least one post-treatment survey wave.
Average effect on revenue and profit: zero cannot be ruled out.
Effect for low baseline performers is more than 0.20 SD lower than for high performers.
Subsamples: low performers did nearly 10% worse; high performers may have gained more than 15%.
The difference came from which advice entrepreneurs implemented, not from the questions they asked or the advice they got.
works.relevance_to_theta: Not a time-saving study. It is relevant because the value of AI output depended on which suggestions users picked and implemented (a q/selection problem): weaker users adopted generic advice and did worse. It supports keeping the max{., kappa} floor and modelling q as depending on the reviewer's judgment. That users 'could not judge' the output is the authors' plausible mechanism, not a direct measurement.
works.limitations: Advice task, not production work. Outcomes are business results, not labor time. Modest sample. Emerging-market micro-enterprises, unlike IT-services firms.
works.corrections: Numbers match the eScholarship copy. Added that 640 were randomized and that the control group got business guides.

works.title: Scaling Laws for Economic Productivity: Experimental Evidence in LLM-Assisted Translation
works.authors: Ali Merali
works.what_measured: Task completion speed, grades and earnings per minute for professional translators using one of 13 LLMs of different training compute, or no model.
works.method_plain: Preregistered online experiment. 300 professional translators completed 1,800 tasks, each with one of 13 LLMs (or a control). Productivity is related to the model's training compute.
key_numbers: 10x model training compute: task completion speed improved 12.3%.
10x compute: grades +0.18 SD, earnings per minute +16.1%.
Gains four times larger for lower-skilled workers.

Follow-up (arXiv 2512.21316, Dec 24, 2025; over 500 consultants, data analysts and managers; 13 LLMs; preregistered): each year of model progress cut task time by 8%, with 56% of gains from more compute and 44% from algorithmic progress. Gains were significantly larger for non-agentic analytical tasks than for agentic workflows needing tool use. Only the abstract was read.
works.relevance_to_theta: Among the works checked here, the only experiments that randomize model capability within one design, so they give an empirical slope for theta_j(t): about 12% faster per 10x compute in translation, and about 8% less task time per year of model progress in consulting and analysis. The finding that agentic work gains less suggests the delegation channel may lag the assistance channel. GDPval also shows the speed-up rising across model generations, but it is a benchmark calculation, not an experiment.
works.limitations: Short tasks. Mostly older and smaller models. Translation is close to an ideal LLM task. The 2025 follow-up was read only at abstract level. Single author. Not peer reviewed.
works.corrections: Abstract numbers for both papers were checked on arXiv. Narrowed 'the only experiments' to 'among the works checked here'.

works.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial
works.authors: Paul J. Lukac, William Turner, Sitaram Vangala, Aaron T. Chin, Joshua Khalili, Ya-Chen Tina Shih, Catherine Sarkisian, Eric M. Cheng, John N. Mafi
works.what_measured: Change in EHR-logged writing time-in-note (primary outcome); burnout, task load and work-exhaustion surveys; accuracy and safety.
works.method_plain: Three-arm pragmatic RCT at UCLA, Nov 4, 2024 - Jan 3, 2025. 238 outpatient physicians were assigned 1:1:1 to Microsoft DAX Copilot, Nabla, or usual care. Time-in-note comes from EHR logs.
key_numbers: 238 physicians in 14 specialties. About 72,000 encounters (press release).
Scribes were used in only 33.5% of 24,696 DAX visits and 29.5% of 23,653 Nabla visits.
Nabla: time-in-note fell 9.5% vs control (95% CI -17.2% to -1.8%, p = 0.02). Per note, about 4:30 to 3:49 (-41 s) vs control 4:22 to 4:04 (-18 s) (press release).
DAX: -1.7% vs control (95% CI -9.4% to +5.9%, p = 0.66), not significant.
Burnout, task-load and exhaustion scores suggest improvement in both arms. The press release gives about 7% better burnout scores. Secondary outcomes need confirmation.
Clinically significant inaccuracies were reported 'occasionally'. One grade 1 (mild) adverse event.

Related: Goh et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(10):e2440969. 50 physicians. GPT-4 access did not improve diagnostic reasoning (median 76% vs 74%, p = 0.60). Time per case -82 s (not significant). GPT-4 alone scored 92%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Documentation is the closest medical analogue to BPO document processing. The 9.5% is an intent-to-treat effect with the scribe used in only about 30% of visits, so the saving per use is likely much larger. It must not be read as theta at full adoption. The record's claim that review and correction 'eats most of the drafting saving' is not shown by the trial. Goh et al. shows a different pattern: human plus AI did no better than the human alone, while AI alone did much better, so assist-mode gains (kappa) can be far below the delegation value.
works.limitations: Single center, two months. Low usage rates mix adoption with per-use effect. Time-in-note excludes review done elsewhere. Goh is a vignette study.
works.corrections: Opened the journal abstract via PubMed E-utilities; the record relied on the press release and a search snippet. The DAX -1.7% (p = 0.66) is now verified. Fixed author order: Sarkisian is 7th, Cheng 8th, Mafi last. Added the issue (2(12), Dec 2025) and the trial registration. Added the key missing fact that scribes were used in only about 30% of visits, which undercuts the record's interpretation that review cost eats the saving. Raised confidence to high.

works.title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI
works.authors: Eleanor Wiske Dillon, Sonia Jaffe, Nicole Immorlica, Christopher T. Stanton
works.year: 2025 (arXiv v1 Apr 15, 2025; v4 Nov 13, 2025; NBER WP 33795, May 2025, revised Nov 2025)
works.what_measured: Telemetry-measured time on email, Teams meetings and Word documents, and time outside regular hours, for knowledge workers given Microsoft 365 Copilot.
works.method_plain: Randomized field experiment over 6 months across 66 firms. Within each firm, some workers were randomly given Copilot licenses. Outcomes come from Microsoft usage logs. The effect of actual use (LATE) is estimated by instrumenting use with assignment.
key_numbers: 7,137 knowledge workers in 66 firms.
Baseline: 11.7 hours per week reading and writing email.
Months 4-6: ITT -1.4 hours per week of email (12%). Among the roughly 80% of treated workers who used it (LATE): -2 hours per week (17%).
No significant change in Teams meeting time (mean 5.22 hours per week) or Word time (+0.14 hours, just misses significance). Same number of documents completed and meetings attended.
Time worked outside regular hours fell about 0.25 hours per week (9%).
Weekly use stabilized at just under 40% of treated workers. 20% never used it in months 4-6.
works.relevance_to_theta: Back-office-like evidence with objective time logs at scale. Implies a theta for email work of about 0.17 among users (0.12 at intent-to-treat), and roughly zero for meetings and document writing. Email is about 11.7 of roughly 40 weekly hours (w about 0.29), so the whole-job saving is about 2 hours per week (about 5%). That shows how w_j times theta_j shrinks the aggregate. The record's claim that email is only 'a couple of hours' of the week confused the saving with the base.
works.limitations: Assistant-mode Copilot. Measures time in apps, not output. Heterogeneous firms with very different take-up. Individual-level provision may miss team-level effects.
works.corrections: Read the v4 PDF, not just the abstract. Removed the unverified '25-31% less email time' and '5-25% faster document completion' figures, which v4 does not support. v4 gives 12% (ITT) and 17% (LATE) less email time and no significant change in Word time. Replaced 'no reported change in meetings in the abstract' with the paper's estimate. Corrected the w reasoning (email is about 29% of the week, not 'a couple of hours'). Confirmed NBER WP 33795.

works.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.venue: Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper 2025-56; also NBER Working Paper 33777
works.what_measured: Chatbot adoption, self-reported time savings, new tasks, and register-recorded earnings and hours in 11 AI-exposed occupations: accountants, customer support specialists, financial advisors, HR professionals, IT support specialists, journalists, legal professionals, marketing professionals, office clerks, software developers, teachers.
works.method_plain: Two large surveys (late 2023 and 2024) linked to Danish employer-employee administrative records. Difference-in-differences, using employer encouragement policies as quasi-experimental variation.
key_numbers: About 25,000 workers from 7,000 workplaces in each survey round. 11 occupations.
Average time savings 3% (abstract). Users report savings of 2.8% of total work hours.
On days they use chatbots, savings are 6-7%. Even on those days, adopters actively use chatbots for only 5-6% of work hours. The typical adopter uses them every third to fourth day.
Reported savings are highest in occupations covered by RCTs (customer and IT support, marketing and HR, software development) and about half as large for teachers, accountants and financial advisors.
Marketers and software developers whose employers promote chatbots report about 7% time savings.
Chatbots created new job tasks for 8.4% of workers.
Earnings and recorded hours: precise zeros, with confidence intervals ruling out effects larger than 1%.
works.relevance_to_theta: The bridge between RCT-style theta (15-40%) and realized economy-wide savings (about 3%). The authors attribute the gap to infrequent use, limited applicability within the job (small w_j), and weaker coordination than in RCTs, not necessarily to small per-task theta. Useful as a sanity check on S(t): the top-down 2.3 pp/year from Indian filings is of the same order, though one is cumulative savings in Denmark and the other a yearly labor-intensity decline in India, so the comparison is loose.
works.limitations: Self-reported time savings. 2023-24 chatbots, before agents. Denmark. Working paper.
works.corrections: All numbers match the BFI PDF. Added the NBER working paper number (33777, confirmed via IDEAS/RePEc listing in search). Listed all 11 occupations. Noted that 'savings highest in RCT occupations' includes marketing and HR. Softened the S(t) comparison.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simón Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. Kim, Patrick Chao, Samuel Miserendino, Gildas Chabot, David Li, Michael Sharman, Alexandra Barr, Amelia Glaese, Jerry Tworek (OpenAI; 19 authors)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded win rates of model deliverables against industry experts' deliverables, on 1,320 tasks (220 gold) from 44 occupations in 9 sectors. Also time and cost to complete, review and redo.
works.method_plain: A benchmark, not an RCT. Experts (on average 14 years of experience) wrote real tasks and deliverables, and other experts blindly compared model and human outputs. The authors then compute expected time saved if you try the model, review it, and do the task yourself if it fails (once, or repeatedly n times).
key_numbers: Gold subset averages: expert task time HT = 404 minutes (self-reported, validated). Expert review (grading) time RT = 109 minutes. So review is about 27% of task time.
Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% wins or ties against experts on the gold set.

Win rate (strictly better) and speed-up: GPT-4o 12.5% (naive 327x, try once 0.87x, try n times 0.46x); o4-mini 29.1% (186x, 1.02x, 1.06x); o3 35.2% (161x, 1.08x, 1.28x); GPT-5 39.0% (90x, 1.12x, 1.39x).
Implied share of time saved for GPT-5: about 11% (try once) and about 28% (try n times).
works.relevance_to_theta: Essentially the draft formula, measured. E[T] = MT + RT + (1-w)HT maps onto theta = w - RT/HT - MT/HT, with w (strict win rate) as the accept probability (like q*p) and RT/HT as rho (about 0.27 for multi-hour tasks). For GPT-5 trying once, roughly 61% of HT is spent redoing failed tasks and 27% on review. So the collapse from the naive 90x to 1.12x comes mainly from redoing failures, not from review alone. The rising speed-ups across model generations give a second, non-experimental capability slope.
works.limitations: Benchmark, not a field experiment. RT is graders' time on pairwise comparisons, not workplace review. Win rate counts only 'better than expert'. Task hours self-reported. US occupations. Tasks are long (average about 7 hours) and one-shot. The authors note they ignore review of human work and the cost of catastrophic errors.
works.corrections: All numbers match Table 2 and Appendix A.2.1. Completed the author list. Corrected the interpretation: the drop from the naive ratio is driven mainly by the redo term (1-w)HT, not just review cost.

summary_flags: Scribes '~10%' is misread: the 9.5% (Nabla) is an intent-to-treat effect with scribes used in only 29.5-33.5% of visits. The saving per use is likely much larger. The claim that review 'eats most of the drafting saving' is not supported by the trial.

'Legal drafting time fell about 20%' mislabels the tasks: the 19-21% averages span six legal analysis and writing tasks. The one drafting task (NDA, with a template) showed no time saving. Subjects were law students in a within-subject design.

'Better models have mostly raised quality rather than time saved' generalizes from one cross-study comparison (GPT-4 vs o1/RAG in law) that the authors call imperfect. It also conflicts with Merali (time falls with compute) and GDPval (speed-up rises across model generations).

'Only Merali's experiments estimate how savings change with model capability' is too strong. It is the only within-design randomization of models here, but GDPval and the legal studies also give cross-model comparisons, non-experimental or across studies.
BCG '25% faster': speed was time to reach the last question under a fixed time limit (22.5% / 27.6% less time). The record's theta of about 0.20 (1 - 1/1.251) is miscomputed; about 0.25 is right.

GDPval: the collapse from the naive speed-up to 1.1-1.4x is driven mainly by redoing the roughly 61% of failed tasks, not by review time alone. RT is graders' pairwise-comparison time, not workplace review.

Copilot: the '25-31% less email time / 5-25% faster documents' figures are not supported by v4 (12% ITT, 17% among users, no change in Word or meeting time). The claim that email is only 'a couple of hours' of the week is wrong (baseline 11.7 hours per week).

Danish 3%: the summary says 'because AI touches only a small share of work'. The authors give several reasons (infrequent use, limited applicability, weaker employer coordination), and the savings are self-reported.
'Experts gain little or lose quality' holds for customer support (BLR, Alibaba). In BCG the top half still gained 17%, and in the P&G study gains were broad.
Alibaba's sample is only new agents (tenure under one year). This matters before applying the 4% figure to experienced BPO staff.
Kenya: 'the user cannot judge the output' is the authors' plausible mechanism (differential implementation of advice), not a direct measure of judging ability.
P&G 'one person with AI matches a two-person team' was read as halving headcount. That is an inference: no staffing change was measured.

Noy-Zhang: the summary's 37% is the working-paper figure. The published Science version reports 40% time saved and 18% quality gain, and says N = 453 per a search snippet (not verified on the journal page). Cite the version you use.

'This supports the working hypothesis' is only half tested: this stream checked intensive-margin experiments but did not examine the exposure literature (e.g. Eloundou et al.), so the claim that it covers only the extensive margin is not established here.

Gap claim about the Remote Labor Index (2.5% automation, 240 projects, mean 28.9 hours) checks out (best agent: Manus). Ju & Aral (2,234 participants, 50% more ads per worker) also checks out. The claim that the delegation-vs-assistance gap is 'not explained in any experiment' is an untested generalization.
verify.corrected_summary:
Experiments outside coding mostly test AI as an assistant that helps a worker, not as an agent you hand a whole task to. On short, self-contained writing tasks, time savings are large. Noy and Zhang found 37% (working paper; 40% in the published Science version) on roughly 27-minute writing tasks with no loss in graded quality. BCG consultants took about 22-28% less time on tasks inside the AI's 'frontier' (Dell'Acqua et al.).

In real operations, the measured effects are smaller, partly because of how much the tool is actually used. In chat customer support at a large software firm, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found resolutions per hour up 15% and handle time down 8.5%, with an assist-only tool. In Alibaba's randomized trial with new agents, chat time fell only about 4% even at full use, because the tool sped up only the opening diagnosis step (by about 32%). In a UCLA trial, an AI scribe cut note-writing time by about 10% on average, but doctors used it in only about 30% of visits, so the saving per use is likely larger. In a law-student experiment, time on six legal tasks fell about 19-21%, similar to an earlier GPT-4 study, while quality improved. That cross-study comparison is imperfect, so it is weak evidence that better models raise quality rather than time saved. A Microsoft Copilot experiment cut email time by about 17% for users (about 2 hours a week) but did not change meeting or document time.

Gains are usually largest for less-skilled workers. Top performers in customer support gain little or lose quality. When the task is outside what the AI handles well (BCG's out-of-frontier task), or when users pick poor advice to act on (Kenyan entrepreneurs), outcomes get worse. Among the studies checked, only Merali randomizes model capability within one design: about 12% faster per 10x compute in translation, and about 8% less task time per year of model progress in consulting and analysis tasks, with smaller gains for tool-using, agentic workflows. GDPval, a benchmark rather than an experiment, is closest to the project's formula. Grading a deliverable took about 27% of the expert's task time. With GPT-5 strictly beating experts 39% of the time, the expected time saving is only about 11% (try once) to 28% (retry until success), mostly because failed outputs must be redone. Danish survey and register data show self-reported savings of only about 3% of hours, which the authors attribute to infrequent use and limited applicability within jobs, with no detectable effect on earnings or hours.

Overall: the intensive margin (how much labor AI removes per task) is measured, but almost only for assistant use, on short tasks, with 2023-24 models, and often mixed with partial adoption. Review cost and acceptance rates for delegated, agent-style work in BPO settings are almost unmeasured. This stream did not review the exposure literature, so the other half of the working hypothesis (that exposure studies cover only the extensive margin) is not tested here.
verify.dataset_notes:
GDPval gold subset: the public copy is on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gdpval), not just the arXiv page. It has 220 rows with prompt, reference files, expert deliverable files and grading rubrics. Its listed fields do NOT include expert completion times, so the claim 'with expert completion times' is unverified. Per-task HT and RT are reported only as averages in the paper. The full 1,320-task set and grading data are not public.

Remote Labor Index: 240 projects in total, 10 public and 230 private. Verified on the arXiv HTML (mean 28.9 hours, median 11.5 hours, mean cost $632.6). The claim that the public set includes data entry, transcription and translation categories was not verified.

Noy & Zhang: access status unknown is correct. A Science replication package was not checked.

AI-Powered Lawyering: 'Anonymized data and code ... made available upon request' is confirmed in the paper, so 'on-request' is correct.

Humlum-Vestergaard: the survey data are linked to Statistics Denmark registers, which only approved researchers can access, so 'restricted' is more accurate than 'on-request'.

Dillon et al. (Copilot telemetry), Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond, and Alibaba: proprietary / lab-internal is consistent with the papers.

UCLA scribe trial: registered as NCT06792890. Data access was not stated in what I opened.

Working PDFs are saved in a temporary folder (since deleted).

works.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
works.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
works.what_measured: Time to finish one fixed, greenfield coding task (write an HTTP server in JavaScript that passes 12 hidden-from-editing tests), with vs without Copilot.
works.method_plain: Lab-style RCT run on Upwork in May-June 2022. 95 freelance developers were randomized (45 treated, 50 control); 35 in each group finished. Completion time = repo creation to first commit passing all 12 tests.
key_numbers: Mean completion time 71.17 min (Copilot) vs 160.89 min (control): a 55.8% REDUCTION in time, 95% CI 21% to 89%, p=0.0017. This is often misquoted as '55% more productive'; in speed terms it is about 2.26x.
Success-rate difference +7 pp, not significant (95% CI -0.11 to +0.25).
Participants mostly aged 25-34 from India and Pakistan, median income $10k-19k/yr, about 6 years coding experience.
Self-estimated gain averaged 35%, below the measured 55.8%.
Less experienced developers, older developers (25-44), and those coding more hours per day benefited more.
works.relevance_to_theta: An upper bound for kappa (assistant speedup) on short, self-contained, greenfield 'development' tasks with a clear test oracle. Since time saved = 1 - 71/161 = 0.558, it maps directly to theta for that narrow task type at autocomplete-era capability. It does not measure review cost (rho) or acceptance (q), because passing the tests was the acceptance criterion.
works.limitations: One toy greenfield task (h is about 1-3 hours), no maintenance, no code review, freelancers rather than firm employees, 2022 model. Selective completion (35 of 45 and 35 of 50) could bias the estimate. The population, though, is close to the Indian IT labor pool.

works.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
works.authors: Kevin Zheyuan Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz
works.year: 2025 (working paper Feb 2025; SSRN 4945566; Management Science, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535)
works.what_measured: Weekly completed pull requests (main outcome), commits, builds, and build success rate for developers randomly given Copilot access in their normal jobs.
works.method_plain: Three company-run field RCTs: Microsoft (1,746 devs, Sept 2022-May 2023), Accenture (320 devs in Southeast Asian offices, from July 2023, 61.3% treated), and an anonymous Fortune 100 electronics firm (3,054 devs, staggered rollout). Not everyone offered the tool used it, so the authors use random assignment as an instrument for usage (an IV estimate of the effect on actual users). The three estimates are combined by precision-weighted averaging.
key_numbers: Pooled: +26.08% weekly completed PRs (SE 10.3%), +13.55% commits (SE 10.0%), +38.38% builds (SE 12.55%), build success rate -5.53% (SE 3.64%, not significant).
Microsoft alone: +27.38% PRs (SE 12.88%).
Build success rate was negative at Accenture. The text describes this as weak support for more trial-and-error coding.
A second Accenture experiment was abandoned after a layoff affected 42% of participants. Including it, pooled PRs are +21.34% (SE 9.92%).
Adoption was far from 100%: at Accenture by April 2024, 69.4% of treated developers had adopted. At Microsoft, short-tenure developers adopted at 81.6% vs 72.1% for long-tenure.
Heterogeneity (Microsoft): short-tenure +27% to 39% vs long-tenure +8% to 13%; junior +21% to 40% vs senior +7% to 16% (noisy).
works.relevance_to_theta: The best field evidence on autocomplete-style (kappa) effects in real jobs, including at an IT services firm (Accenture) with offshore delivery staff. The authors note that the gap between the lab's 55.8% and the field's 26% arises partly because coding is only part of the job. That is exactly the w_j vs theta_j distinction: the job-level effect is roughly sum of w_j*theta_j. PRs per week is an output-per-worker measure, so it maps to 1/(1-theta) - 1 only if hours are fixed. A 26% throughput rise implies about 21% labor saved per unit of output.
works.limitations: 2022-23 autocomplete only (no chat or agents). PR counts are an imperfect output measure, and PR size or quality could change. Estimates are imprecise, and the Accenture sample is small (320). There is no task-type breakdown (maintenance vs development).

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth (Beth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: Implementation time on real issues (bug fixes, features, refactors) in mature repositories the developers had worked on for years, with AI allowed vs disallowed.
works.method_plain: Within-developer RCT: each of 246 issues (about 2 hours each on average) was randomly assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. 16 experienced developers on repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code, paid $150/hr, with screen recordings. Tools were mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet.
key_numbers: With AI allowed, issues took 19% LONGER (95% CI +2% to +39%, per METR's Feb 2026 update).
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed in a 20% speedup afterward.
Experts predicted large speedups: economics experts 39% shorter, ML experts 38% shorter completion times.
5 of 20 candidate factors were judged likely to contribute to the slowdown.
METR now labels these results out of date.
works.relevance_to_theta: The key counter-evidence for maintenance on large, mature, familiar codebases. It implies that the assistant term kappa minus review cost rho can be negative for experts in brownfield code, so the max{.,kappa} floor in the formula should allow kappa < 0 (or let users opt out). It is also a strong warning that self-reports overstate gains by about 40 pp, so survey-based theta_j should not be trusted.
works.limitations: Small n (16 developers), an unusual population (top OSS maintainers with deep repo familiarity), and early-2025 tools. Indian IT maintenance work is usually on client codebases that workers know less well, where AI help might be larger.

works.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design (METR uplift update)
works.authors: METR (Joel Becker et al.)
works.what_measured: The same design as the 2025 RCT, repeated with late-2025 tools (including agentic tools) on a larger sample.
works.method_plain: Task-level randomization, as in 2025. 57 developers (10 returning, 47 new; median 10 years' experience), 143 repos, 800+ tasks, pay cut to $50/hr. METR judged the result unreliable because of selection effects.
key_numbers: Sign convention: negative = speedup. Returning developers -18% (CI -38% to +9%); new developers -4% (CI -15% to +9%). Early-2025 comparison: +19% (CI +2% to +39%).
30% to 50% of developers said they withheld some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
Some developers rarely completed AI-disallowed tasks; one completed none.
With concurrent agents, developers did other work while waiting, which made time tracking unreliable.
METR calls the result a likely lower bound on the speedup and 'very weak evidence' on its size.
works.relevance_to_theta: The direct time-varying test of theta for maintenance-type work: the point estimate moved from -19% to roughly +4% to +18% time saved in about a year, but with CIs spanning zero. Methodologically, it shows that per-task time RCTs break down with agents (parallelism, task substitution), so theta_j for delegated work may need to be measured as labor-hours per accepted unit of output, not wall-clock time per task.
works.limitations: Self-acknowledged selection bias. Quality differences between conditions were not measured. Not a peer-reviewed paper.

works.title: How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial
works.authors: Elise Paradis, Kate Grey, Quinn Madison, Daye Nam, Andrew Macvean, Vahid Meimand, Nan Zhang, Ben Ferrari-Church, Satish Chandra (Google)
works.year: 2024 (arXiv Oct 2024; ICSE 2025 Software Engineering in Practice track)
works.what_measured: Time to complete one enterprise-style task: extend an existing change list of 10 files and 474 lines to add a logging service, updating build, data and test files until all tests pass.
works.method_plain: RCT with 96 full-time Google engineers (48 AI, 48 control; 93 finished). AI features were code completion, Smart Paste, and natural-language-to-code. Regression of log time on treatment plus controls.
key_numbers: Mean time 96 min (SE 9.3) with AI vs 114 min (SE 8.1) control.
Best-fit regression gives about 21% faster, but the 95% CI is [-0.51, 0.03] on the log scale, p=0.086. Another model gives 26%. The t-test on log time has p=.038.
Engineers coding 5+ hours per day were about 32% faster overall. The AI x coding-hours interaction (beta=-0.29) was not significant.
AI x seniority interaction not significant (p=0.706).
works.relevance_to_theta: A kappa estimate for an 'extend existing code' task, between Peng's greenfield toy (56%) and METR's mature-repo maintenance (-19%). It suggests theta for assistant-mode modification work is roughly 0.15-0.25 at 2024 capability.
works.limitations: A single task and lab setting with internal Google tools (summer 2024). Wide CI. Engineers are elite, and the codebase was unfamiliar but well-structured.

works.title: Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI
works.authors: Emerson Murphy-Hill, Jenna Butler, Alexandra Savelieva
works.what_measured: Merged pull requests per engineer per day after adopting agentic command-line coding tools, plus adoption and retention patterns.
works.method_plain: Observational. Part 1 is a synthetic control (Bayesian structural time series, CausalImpact) comparing adopters to a counterfactual built from non-adopters. Part 2 is engineer and week fixed-effects Poisson regressions on tool-use intensity. Tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers, Jan-Apr 2026, plus a 609-response survey.
key_numbers: +24.0% PRs per engineer per day over the 115-day post-period, 95% CI +14.5% to +33.7%. Placebo test: -1.1% (CI -10.6% to +8.6%).
No significant decay: February +29.4%, March-April +20.0%.
Single-tool users: Claude Code +11.4% (CI +9.4% to +13.6%); Copilot CLI +24.9% (CI +23.0% to +26.8%).
Dose-response: +15.0% at 3 tool-use days per week, rising to +50.1% at 5+ days.
No quality, revert or review-time outcomes reported.
works.relevance_to_theta: The largest real-firm evidence for the agentic (delegate, p-like) regime. A 24% throughput rise at fixed headcount implies about 19% labor saved per PR. The dose-response hints at the full-adoption ceiling that theta_j is meant to capture (+50% at heavy use corresponds to about 33% labor saved), though heavy-use weeks are self-selected.
works.limitations: Not randomized, and adopters self-select. Single firm. Merged PRs can reward smaller PRs. Quality is not measured. Authors are Microsoft employees, and Microsoft owns GitHub (Copilot CLI's maker). No task-type split.

works.title: Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects
works.authors: Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon)
works.what_measured: Project-level velocity (lines added, commits) and quality (static-analysis warnings, code complexity) after GitHub projects adopted Cursor.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences: 806 Cursor-adopting repos (adoption Jan 2024-Mar 2025) compared with 1,380 matched non-adopting repos. A panel GMM model then links the quality changes to later velocity.
key_numbers: Lines added: +281.3% in month 1, +48.4% in month 2, +28.58% averaged over the whole period. Only the first two months are significant.
Commits: +55.4% in month 1, +2.63% overall (not significant).
Static-analysis warnings: +30.26%, persistent. Code complexity: +41.64%, persistent (Table 2; the Discussion section cites about 25%, an internal inconsistency).
The rise in warnings and complexity predicts the later velocity slowdown; codebase growth absorbs much of the warning increase.
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that gross speedups on development are partly offset by deferred maintenance cost: technical debt raises future maintenance labor. For the model, theta_dev net of downstream costs could be much smaller than the gross figure, and AI-generated code may raise w_maintenance later. This bears on q (the acceptability of passing output) and on review and rework cost.
works.limitations: Open-source projects, not client delivery work. Adoption is detected from config files. Lines added is a poor productivity measure.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: METR
works.what_measured: Whether active maintainers would merge AI-generated PRs that pass SWE-bench Verified tests.
works.method_plain: 4 maintainers from scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest reviewed 296 agent PRs (from agents spanning mid-2024 to late 2025) as if for real, plus 47 human 'golden' PRs as a noise baseline.
key_numbers: The automated grader's pass rate exceeds the maintainer merge rate by 24.2 pp on average (SE 2.7), after normalizing to the golden baseline. The raw gap is 34.9 pp (SE 2.2).
Only about 68% of human golden patches were merged by the same maintainers.
Roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged.
Merge rates improve about 9.6 pp/yr slower than grader scores (SE 5.5; weak evidence, significant only at the 10% level).
Agents were not allowed to iterate on feedback.
works.relevance_to_theta: The direct source for q of about 0.5. It also suggests q may itself be time-varying and improving more slowly than p, which would make q*p(h,t) grow more slowly than benchmark curves imply.
works.limitations: 3 Python repos with high standards. No iteration allowed. Small number of reviewers. Exact rejection-reason shares appear only in a figure.

works.title: DORA State of DevOps 2024 / State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025
works.authors: DORA team, Google Cloud
works.venue: Google Cloud / DORA industry survey reports
works.what_measured: Survey-based links between AI adoption and team delivery metrics (throughput, stability), plus self-reported productivity and trust.
works.method_plain: Large cross-sectional surveys of tech professionals, with statistical modeling of associations. Not causal. 2025 had nearly 5,000 respondents plus over 100 hours of qualitative data.
key_numbers: 2024 (from the Google Cloud 2024 announcement blog, https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report): a 25% increase in AI adoption is associated with +7.5% documentation quality, +3.4% code quality and +3.1% code review speed. As AI adoption rose, delivery throughput was estimated at -1.5% and stability at -7.2% (the blog does not say whether these are also per 25% of adoption). 39% reported little or no trust in AI code; 75%+ rely on AI for at least one daily task.

2025: 90% use AI at work; more than 80% believe it raised their productivity; 30% have little or no trust in AI code. AI adoption is now positively related to throughput but still negatively related to stability.
works.relevance_to_theta: Weak for theta itself (self-report, correlational). Useful for the system-level point: gains on coding tasks do not flow through to delivery when testing and review are bottlenecks. This argues for raising rho or adding a downstream stability cost, and shows that aggregation across stages (w_j weighting) matters.
works.limitations: Self-reported, cross-sectional, and the adoption measure is vague. Secondary sources misquote both sample size and the stability figure (e.g., '14%'). I opened only the Google Cloud blog announcements, not the full PDFs.

works.title: Does AI Actually Boost Developer Productivity? (Stanford SWE Productivity Research, 100k developers)
works.authors: Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford SWE Productivity Research Group)
works.venue: Conference talk, AI Engineer World's Fair, 5 June 2025 (no peer-reviewed paper found)
works.what_measured: Net 'delivered functionality' per developer from git commits, split by greenfield vs brownfield, task complexity, language popularity, and rework.
works.method_plain: A model trained to mimic a 10-15-person expert panel scores each commit (reported r > 0.85 against experts). Applied to git histories from 100k+ engineers at 600+ companies; 136 teams from 27 companies were used for the AI-adoption comparison.
key_numbers: Mean net gains: greenfield low-complexity 31%; greenfield high-complexity 12%; brownfield low-complexity 16%; brownfield high-complexity 7% (the distribution extends to about -20%).
Gross new code up 30-40%, rework offsets 15-25%, net about 15-20%.
Popular languages: +20-25% simple, +10-15% complex. Niche languages (COBOL, Haskell, Elixir): 0-5% simple, -5% to +5% complex.
Self-assessed productivity was off by about 30 percentile points in a 43-developer sample.
The decline of gains with codebase size is presented as a hypothesis, not a measured result.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only large-sample source I found that splits gains by maintenance vs greenfield and by complexity, which is exactly the j-dimension needed. Brownfield/high-complexity at about 7% vs greenfield/low at about 31% gives a prior ordering for theta_maintenance < theta_development. The rework offset is an empirical rho. The legacy and niche-language result matters for Indian IT, which carries much COBOL/mainframe maintenance.
works.limitations: A talk, not a paper. The method is proprietary and not fully validated. Observational adoption comparison. 2024-early 2025 tools. Numbers are described as 'orientative'.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Anthropic Economic Research
works.what_measured: Model-estimated task time with vs without AI for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a professional would take without AI and how long the task took with AI. Time savings = 1 - with/without. Validated against about 1,000 JIRA software tasks with known durations.
key_numbers: Average task length without AI about 90 min (1.4 hr); time savings about 80% (median given as 84% or 81% in different places).
Software developers account for the largest share (19%) of the implied labor productivity gain.
Implied +1.8%/yr US labor productivity growth at universal adoption over 10 years.
Time-estimate validation on JIRA tasks: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 vs 0.50 for human developers. Claude compresses estimates (overestimates short tasks, underestimates long ones).
Excludes time spent validating output outside the chat.
works.relevance_to_theta: An upper bound on gross theta for chat-sized tasks, since it ignores review (rho) and failure (q). The roughly 80% vs 26% (field RCT) gap is a measure of how much rho, q and non-coding time cut gross savings. The JIRA validation dataset is a template for building f_j(h) (task-length distributions) from ticket data.
works.limitations: Model self-estimates, not measurements. A selected sample of tasks people chose to bring to Claude. No review cost. No developer-specific savings figure.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Anthropic
works.what_measured: Survey (132 engineers and researchers), interviews (53), and analysis of about 200,000 internal Claude Code transcripts (Feb vs Aug 2025).
works.method_plain: Descriptive. Self-reported shares of work using Claude, self-reported productivity, and shares of work that can be fully delegated, plus transcript metrics on agent autonomy.
key_numbers: About 59-60% of work uses Claude (vs 28% a year earlier); self-reported productivity +50% (vs +20%).
Most employees can 'fully delegate' only 0-20% of their work.
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done.
Consecutive tool calls per transcript rose from 9.8 to 21.2; human turns fell from 6.2 to 4.1.
New-feature tasks rose from 14.3% to 36.9% of Claude Code use.
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly separates the assistant share (about 60% of work touched) from the delegate share (0-20% fully delegatable). This maps onto the kappa vs q*p split. Falling human turns per transcript is a proxy for falling rho over time. The 27% 'new work' figure warns that throughput gains are not all labor savings, because demand expansion inside the firm mixes with theta.
works.limitations: Self-reported, at a frontier AI lab (an extreme early-adopter population). Self-reports are known to be inflated (METR 2025).

research.stream_summary: The software-engineering experiments give a consistent picture: the measured gain shrinks as studies move from toy tasks to real jobs, and from new code to old code. On a self-contained greenfield task, Copilot cut completion time by 55.8% (Peng et al. 2023; CI 21-89%; mostly Indian and Pakistani freelancers). Large field RCTs at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm find a smaller effect: about 26% more completed pull requests (SE 10%), with juniors gaining most. Google's enterprise RCT found about 21% (wide CI). METR's RCT on experienced maintainers of large, familiar codebases found a 19% slowdown in early 2025. Its late-2025 rerun points to modest speedups (4-18%), but METR says selection bias makes it unreliable. For agentic tools, Microsoft's 2026 rollout of Claude Code and Copilot CLI shows about +24% merged PRs per engineer (not randomized), rising to about +50% in heavy-use weeks. Quality evidence cuts the other way. Cursor adoption raised static-analysis warnings by about 30% and complexity by about 42%, persistently, while velocity gains faded after two months. METR's maintainers would reject about half of SWE-bench-passing PRs (q of about 0.5). Stanford's git-based data show brownfield/high-complexity gains of about 7% vs about 31% for greenfield/low-complexity. For the theta_j recipe, the extensive-margin hypothesis holds up: every study finds AI 'touches' coding, but the intensive margin ranges from -19% to +56% depending on task type, codebase familiarity, review burden and tool generation. Assistant effects (kappa) for maintenance on familiar code are near zero or negative. Development tasks sit around 20-30%. Delegate (p) effects are only now becoming measurable, and per-task time RCTs break down when agents run in parallel. Self-reports overstate gains by 30-40 pp and should not be used for theta.
gaps_noticed: No RCT or field study isolates testing, infrastructure/ops, or BPO-style tasks within IT services. The evidence is almost all 'write or modify code', so theta for testing and infrastructure is extrapolation.
No study reports gains by task length h, so f_j(h)-weighted integration cannot be validated against experiments. The Anthropic JIRA validation set and METR issue data are the closest sources.
No randomized study of agentic (delegate) tools yet. The Microsoft 2026 evidence is a synthetic control with self-selected adopters, and the METR 2026 RCT is compromised by selection.
No direct measurement of review time rho as a share of h for AI-generated code. Only indirect proxies exist (rework share, human turns, merge rates).

Outcomes are throughput (PRs, lines, commits), not labor hours per accepted unit of client output. Converting a throughput gain g into labor saved uses theta = 1 - 1/(1+g) and assumes fixed hours and constant PR size.

Only one study has an Indian/offshore IT services site (Accenture Southeast Asia, n=320, 2023 Copilot). None covers TCS, Infosys or Wipro delivery teams, fixed-price vs time-and-materials contracts, or client codebases unfamiliar to the vendor.
Legacy/niche-language maintenance (COBOL, mainframe), a large part of Indian IT AMS work, appears only in the Stanford talk, with little support.
Downstream costs (tech debt, instability) are documented (CMU Cursor study, DORA) but not quantified in labor-hours, so the net theta for development over a multi-year horizon is unknown.

I could not open the full DORA PDFs or confirm DORA sample sizes, and I did not open the full Qiao et al. brownfield paper (arXiv 2511.02922; 18 grad students, Copilot cut time but comprehension did not improve).

datasets.description: 246 issues by 16 developers with randomized AI condition and implementation times. Public release status not confirmed; the paper is arXiv 2507.09089.

datasets.name: METR SWE-bench maintainer-review labels
datasets.description: 296 agent PRs plus 47 golden PRs with maintainer merge decisions and rejection reasons. The direct input for q. Release status not confirmed.

datasets.name: SWE-bench Verified
datasets.description: Real GitHub issues with test-based grading. The base for p(h) on maintenance-type tasks when paired with human time estimates.

datasets.description: Developer-week PR, commit and build panels from company experiments. Proprietary. AEA RCT registry AEARCTR-0014530 holds the design only.

datasets.name: Cursor-adoption GitHub panel (He et al., MSR'26)
datasets.description: 806 treated and 1,380 control open-source repos, with velocity and SonarQube-style quality metrics. Built from public GitHub; replication package likely available (not verified).

datasets.name: GH Archive / GitHub public events
datasets.description: Raw public GitHub activity. Can be used to detect agent co-authored commits (e.g., Claude Code or Codex trailers) and measure PR throughput and revert rates over time.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index / Claude productivity estimates
datasets.description: Task-level (O*NET) estimates of time with and without AI. The aggregated Economic Index data are released publicly. Includes a JIRA-based time-estimate validation method.
