datasets.description: Annual report PDFs with modeled associations. Respondent-level microdata are not public as far as I could tell.

datasets.name: Stanford SWE Productivity git-commit dataset
datasets.description: Git histories from 100k+ engineers at 600+ companies, scored by an expert-panel-mimicking model, split by greenfield/brownfield and complexity. Private-company data; partnership required.

datasets.name: Microsoft internal Azure DevOps PR telemetry (Murphy-Hill et al. 2026)
datasets.description: Engineer-week merged PRs and Claude Code / Copilot CLI usage for tens of thousands of engineers, Jan-Apr 2026.

works.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
works.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
works.what_measured: Time to finish one fixed greenfield coding task (write an HTTP server in JavaScript) with vs without Copilot. Completion = first commit passing all 12 tests in a provided suite; participants could see the tests but could not alter them.
works.method_plain: Randomized experiment on Upwork, 15 May to 20 June 2022. 166 offers sent, 95 accepted; 45 randomized to Copilot, 50 to control. The paper says 'Thirty-five developers from both the treated and control groups completed the task and survey', which is ambiguous between 35 per group and 35 in total. Five treated participants never finished Copilot sign-up and did the task without it. Completion time = repo creation to first commit passing all 12 tests, conditional on completing.
key_numbers: Mean completion time, among those who finished: 71.17 min (Copilot) vs 160.89 min (control). That is a 55.8% reduction in time, 95% CI 21% to 89%, t-test p = 0.0017. In speed terms that is about 2.26x (160.89/71.17). Four control-group outliers above 300 min; the authors say the result holds without them.
Success rate 7 pp higher with Copilot, not significant (95% CI -0.11 to +0.25).
Participants were mostly aged 25-34 and from India and Pakistan. Median income was $10k-19k/yr, average coding experience 6 years, and they reported about 9 hours of coding per working day.
Self-estimated gain averaged 35% in both the treated and control groups, below the measured 55.8%.

Heterogeneity (Table 1): less experienced developers (p = 0.063), developers coding more hours per day (p = 0.017) and those aged 25-44 (p = 0.030) benefited more. The experience result is significant only at the 10% level.
works.relevance_to_theta: An upper-bound estimate of kappa (the assistant speedup) on a short, self-contained greenfield development task with a clear test oracle. Time saved = 1 - 71.17/160.89 = 0.558, so it maps directly to theta for that narrow task type with 2022 autocomplete. It does not measure review cost (rho) or acceptance (q), because passing the tests was the acceptance criterion.
works.limitations: One toy greenfield task. No maintenance work and no code review. Freelancers, not firm employees. 2022 Copilot model. Time is measured only for those who finished, so selective completion could bias the estimate. The sample (mostly India/Pakistan) is demographically close to the Indian IT labor pool, but the work setting is not.
works.corrections: Number of finishers: the paper's sentence is ambiguous, so do not cite '35 in each group' as fact. Added that self-estimates (35%) came from both groups, that five treated participants did not have Copilot active, and that the experience effect is significant only at the 10% level. All other numbers were confirmed in the PDF text.

works.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
works.authors: Kevin Zheyuan Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng, Tobias Salz
works.year: 2025 (draft dated Feb 2025; SSRN last revised Aug 2025)
works.venue: Management Science, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535 (volume/issue not confirmed: INFORMS page returned 403); SSRN 4945566
works.what_measured: Weekly completed pull requests (main outcome), commits, builds, and build success rate for developers randomly offered Copilot in their normal jobs.
works.method_plain: Three company-run field experiments. Microsoft: 1,746 developers, mostly in the US, 50.4% treated, Sept 2022 to 3 May 2023. Accenture: 320 developers in Southeast Asian offices, 61.3% treated, from late July 2023. Anonymous Fortune 100 electronics firm: 3,054 developers, staggered rollout from Oct 2023. 4,867 developers in total. Not everyone offered the tool used it, so the authors use random assignment as an instrument for usage: a weighted IV (2SLS) estimate of the effect on users. The three estimates are pooled by precision-weighted averaging. Post-registered as AEARCTR-0014530.
key_numbers: Pooled (weighted IV): +26.08% weekly completed PRs (SE 10.3%), +13.55% commits (SE 10.0%), +38.38% builds (SE 12.55%), build success rate -5.53% (SE 3.64%, not significant).
Microsoft alone, weighted IV: +27.38% PRs (SE 12.88%).
Build success rate at Accenture: -17.40% (SE 7.12; DiD -20.72%). The authors say this only weakly supports a 'more trial-and-error coding' interpretation.
A second Accenture experiment (April 2023) was abandoned after a layoff affected 42% of its participants. Including it, pooled PRs are +21.34% (SE 9.92%).

Adoption was well below 100%. At Accenture by April 2024: 69.4% of treated and 24.4% of control developers had adopted. At Microsoft by end of sample: short-tenure 81.6% vs long-tenure 72.1%; junior 79.2% vs senior 74.4%.
Heterogeneity (Microsoft): short-tenure +27% to 39% vs long-tenure +8% to 13%; junior +21% to 40% vs senior +7% to 16%. These are imprecise.
works.relevance_to_theta: The best field evidence on autocomplete-style (kappa) effects in real jobs, including at an IT services firm (Accenture). The conclusion compares the 26% with the lab result (which it cites as a '58% decrease' in time). It explains the gap partly by noting that coding is only part of the job: that is the w_j vs theta_j distinction. PRs per week measure output per worker. Under fixed hours and constant PR size, a 26% rise implies 1 - 1/1.26, about 21% labor saved per PR.
works.limitations: 2022-23 autocomplete only, no chat or agents. PR counts are an imperfect output measure, and PR size or quality could change. Estimates are imprecise, and the Accenture sample is small (320). The Accenture offices are in Southeast Asia, not India. No breakdown by task type (maintenance vs development).
works.corrections: The paper's conclusion cites the Peng et al. lab result as a '58% decrease', not 55.8%. Added Accenture control-group adoption (24.4%), the junior/senior adoption figures, and the Accenture build-success estimate. Venue: the Management Science DOI is confirmed via search index and the Microsoft Research page links the preprint, but I could not open the INFORMS page (403), so final publication details are unconfirmed. All headline numbers were confirmed in the PDF text.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein
works.venue: METR report (blog 10 July 2025); arXiv 2507.09089 (v1 12 July 2025, v2 25 July 2025)
works.what_measured: Implementation time on real issues in mature repositories the developers had worked on for years (about 5 years on average), with AI allowed vs disallowed.
works.method_plain: Within-developer randomized trial. Each of 246 issues (about 2 hours each on average) was randomly assigned to AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. 16 experienced developers on repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code, paid $150/hr. Tools were mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet.
key_numbers: With AI allowed, issues took 19% longer. The 95% CI of +2% to +39% comes from METR's Feb 2026 update; the July 2025 blog said CIs were forthcoming.
Developers expected a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed in a 20% speedup afterward.
Experts predicted large speedups: economics experts 39% shorter and ML experts 38% shorter completion times.
Of 20 candidate factors examined, 5 were judged likely to contribute to the slowdown.
The METR page now says 'These results are out of date' and links to the Feb 2026 update.
works.relevance_to_theta: Key counter-evidence for maintenance on large, mature, familiar codebases with early-2025 tools. It implies that the assistant term net of review cost can be negative for experts in brownfield code. The formula's max{.,kappa} floor should therefore allow kappa < 0, or allow workers to opt out of AI. It also shows that self-reports can be badly wrong: a gap of about 40 pp between believed and measured speedup in this setting.
works.limitations: Small n (16 developers). An unusual population: top OSS maintainers with deep repo familiarity. Early-2025 tools. Indian IT maintenance is usually on client codebases that workers know less well, where AI help might be larger.
works.corrections: No substantive changes. Clarified that the CI is from the Feb 2026 update, not the original release.

works.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
works.what_measured: The same task-level design as the 2025 study, repeated with late-2025 tools (including agents) on a larger sample.
works.method_plain: Task-level randomization, as in 2025. 57 developers (10 returning, 47 new; median 10 years' experience), 143 repos, 800+ tasks, pay cut from $150/hr to $50/hr. METR judges the result unreliable because of selection effects.
key_numbers: Sign convention: negative = AI sped up tasks. Returning developers -18% (95% CI -38% to +9%); new developers -4% (CI -15% to +9%). Early-2025 study restated: +19% (CI +2% to +39%).
Between 30% and 50% of developers said they chose not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
Some developers were less likely to complete AI-disallowed tasks; one completed none.
Developers running several agents at once, or doing unrelated work while waiting, made time tracking unreliable.

METR calls the central estimate likely a lower bound on the true speedup and 'very weak evidence' on the size of the recent increase. It is redesigning the study (considering fixed-task experiments, developer-level randomization, observational data and questionnaires).
works.relevance_to_theta: The only repeated measurement of the same design over time for maintenance-type work. The point estimate moved from about 19% slower to roughly 4-18% faster, but both new CIs include zero and selection biases the estimate. It also shows that per-task time trials break down with agents (parallel work, task withholding). So theta_j for delegated work may need to be measured as labor-hours per accepted unit of output, not wall-clock time per task.
works.limitations: Selection bias that METR itself acknowledges. Quality differences between conditions were not measured. A blog post, not a peer-reviewed paper.
works.corrections: Authors: the post lists Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein and Khalid Mahamud (not 'METR (Joel Becker et al.)'). Corrected 'rarely completed AI-disallowed tasks' to 'were less likely to complete', which is what the page says. Numbers confirmed.

works.title: How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial
works.authors: Elise Paradis, Kate Grey, Quinn Madison, Daye Nam, Andrew Macvean, Vahid Meimand, Nan Zhang, Ben Ferrari-Church, Satish Chandra (Google)
works.venue: arXiv 2410.12944 (v1 16 Oct 2024, v3 11 Nov 2024); ICSE 2025 Software Engineering in Practice (SEIP) track
works.what_measured: Time to complete one enterprise-style task: starting from an existing change list of 10 files and 474 lines, implement a service that logs messages to Google's internal storage, updating build, data-structure and test files until all tests pass. The task was designed to take 30 min to 2.5 hours.
works.method_plain: Randomized trial with 96 full-time Google engineers (48 AI, 48 control); 93 finished (47 AI, 46 control). Run June-July 2024. AI features: code completion, Smart Paste and natural-language-to-code in Google's internal IDE. Regressions of log time on treatment plus controls.
key_numbers: Mean time 96 min (SE 9.3) with AI vs 114 min (SE 8.1) control.

Best-fit model (developer covariates): beta = -0.24 on log time, about 21% faster, 95% CI [-0.51, 0.03], p = 0.086. A task-covariate model gives beta = -0.30 (about 26% faster, p < .05) but is not the authors' preferred model. A t-test on log time gives p = .038.

Developers coding 5+ hours/day were about 32% faster regardless of condition (a main effect of coding hours, not an AI effect). The AI x coding-hours interaction (beta = -0.29, SE 0.29) was not significant.
AI x seniority interaction not significant (p = 0.706).
works.relevance_to_theta: A kappa estimate for an 'extend existing code' task, sitting between Peng's greenfield toy task and METR's mature-repo maintenance. It suggests assistant-mode time saved for modification work of roughly 0.2 at mid-2024 capability, with a CI that includes zero.
works.limitations: One task in a lab setting with internal Google tools (summer 2024). Wide CI. Elite engineers. The codebase was unfamiliar to them but well structured.
works.corrections: Clarified that the '32% faster' figure is a main effect of coding 5+ hours/day, not an AI effect; the record's phrasing could be read as AI making heavy coders 32% faster. Added sample sizes per arm and study dates. Venue confirmed on the ICSE 2025 researchr page (SEIP track, 2 May 2025); that listing omits Vahid Meimand, who is on the arXiv author list.

works.title: Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI
works.authors: Emerson Murphy-Hill, Jenna Butler, Alexandra Savelieva
works.what_measured: Merged pull requests per engineer per day after adopting command-line agentic coding tools, plus adoption and retention patterns (adoption modeled for Copilot CLI).
works.method_plain: Observational, not randomized. Part 1 is a synthetic control using Bayesian structural time series (CausalImpact): adopters are compared with a counterfactual built from non-adopter PR creators. Pre-period Oct 2024 to 4 Jan 2026; post-period 5 Jan to 29 Apr 2026 (115 days). Part 2 uses Poisson regressions with engineer and week fixed effects on tool-use intensity. Tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers, Azure DevOps data only, plus a 609-response survey of attendees of an internal 'Agentic Engineering Day'.
key_numbers: +24.0% PRs per engineer per day over the 115-day post-period (95% CI +14.5% to +33.7%). Placebo at 6 Oct 2025: -1.1% (CI -10.6% to +8.6%).
February +29.4% (CI +17.7% to +44.4%); 1 March to 29 April +20.0% (CI +7.4% to +35.9%). The authors call the gain 'sustained', based on overlapping intervals, not a formal test of decay.
Single-tool users, any-use weeks vs the engineer's own zero-use weeks: Claude Code +11.4% (CI +9.4% to +13.6%); Copilot CLI +24.9% (CI +23.0% to +26.8%).
Dose-response: +15.0% at 3 tool-use days per week, +50.1% at 5+ days (no CIs given). The authors treat this as an association, not a causal effect.
No quality, revert or review-time outcomes reported. The authors say quality is an open question.
works.relevance_to_theta: The largest real-firm evidence for the agentic (delegate) regime. A 24% throughput rise at fixed hours and constant PR size implies about 19% labor saved per PR. The dose-response hints at a full-adoption ceiling (+50% corresponds to about 33% labor saved), but heavy-use weeks are self-selected and the authors call it an association.
works.limitations: Not randomized; adopters self-select. Single firm, Azure DevOps only. Merged-PR counts can reward smaller PRs. Quality not measured. The authors are Microsoft employees, and the paper notes Microsoft sells AI tools and owns GitHub (Copilot CLI's maker). No task-type split.
works.corrections: 'No significant decay' was replaced: the paper reports no formal decay test and argues persistence from overlapping CIs. Added the monthly CIs, and noted that the dose-response is an association with no CIs given, that the data are Azure DevOps only, and where the survey sample came from. Other numbers confirmed.

works.title: Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects
works.authors: Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon)
works.venue: MSR '26 (23rd Int. Conf. on Mining Software Repositories, Rio de Janeiro, April 2026), DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793349; arXiv 2511.04427
works.what_measured: Project-level velocity (lines added, commits) and quality (static-analysis warnings, code complexity, duplication) after GitHub projects adopted Cursor.
works.method_plain: Staggered difference-in-differences (Borusyak et al. imputation estimator). 806 Cursor-adopting repos (adoption Jan 2024 to Mar 2025, mostly Aug 2024 to Mar 2025) are compared with 1,380 propensity-matched non-adopters, observed Jan 2024 to Aug 2025. A panel GMM (Arellano-Bond) model then links quality changes to later velocity.
key_numbers: Lines added: +281.3% in month 1, +48.4% in month 2, +28.58% averaged over the whole period. Significant only in the first two months.
Commits: +55.4% in month 1, +14.5% in month 2, +2.63% overall. The text calls the overall effect not significant, though Table 2's significance markers conflict with the text.
Static-analysis warnings: +30.26%, persistent. Code complexity: +41.64%, persistent (Table 2). The Discussion cites about 25% for complexity, which is inconsistent with the table.
In the GMM model, a 100% increase in complexity is associated with a 64.5% decrease in lines added, and a 100% increase in warnings with a 50.3% decrease.
Codebase growth explains most of the rise in warnings and complexity. After controlling for it, Cursor adoption still has a significant effect on complexity (about 9%).
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that gross speedups on development are partly offset by deferred maintenance cost: technical debt may raise future maintenance labor. For the model, theta_dev net of downstream costs could be smaller than the gross figure, and AI-written code may raise w_maintenance later. Relevant to q (acceptability of passing output) and to rework cost. Because much of the quality decline tracks codebase size, the net quality effect per unit of code is smaller than the headline +30%/+42%.
works.limitations: Open-source projects, not client delivery work. Adoption is detected from Cursor config files. Lines added is a poor productivity measure. Quality metrics are static-analysis proxies, not labor hours.
works.corrections: Year/venue: the arXiv preprint is from Nov 2025; MSR '26 was in April 2026 (DOI added). Added the month-2 commits figure, the text-vs-table conflict on commit significance, the GMM magnitudes, and that codebase growth absorbs most of the variance in both warnings and complexity, not just warnings (complexity still about +9% after controls). Headline numbers confirmed.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether active maintainers would merge AI-generated PRs that pass the SWE-bench Verified automated grader.
works.method_plain: 4 active maintainers (2 scikit-learn, 1 Sphinx, 1 pytest) covering 95 of 500 SWE-bench Verified issues. They reviewed 296 agent PRs as if for real. Agents: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (old), 3.7 Sonnet, 4 Opus, 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-5, released mid-2024 to mid/late 2025. 47 original human ('golden') PRs serve as a noise baseline. Agents got one attempt with no feedback.
key_numbers: Maintainer merge rates are about 24.2 pp below grader pass rates on average (SE 2.7), after normalizing to the golden baseline. The raw gap is 34.9 pp (SE 2.2).
About 68% of human golden patches were merged by the same maintainers.
Roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged, even after adjusting for maintainer noise.

Merge rates improve about 9.6 pp/yr more slowly than grader scores (SE 5.5; significant only at 10%, which the authors call weak and fragile; 15.5 pp/yr on the raw scale; not significant when restricted to state-of-the-art models).
Agents were not allowed to iterate on feedback. The authors say this is not evidence of a fundamental capability limit.
works.relevance_to_theta: The direct source for q of about 0.5. Because agents could not iterate, 0.5 is a pessimistic one-shot value. q may also improve more slowly than p, which would make q*p(h,t) rise more slowly than benchmark curves imply, but that trend evidence is weak.
works.limitations: 3 Python repos with high standards. No iteration allowed. Only 4 reviewers. Rejection-reason shares appear only in a figure.
works.corrections: Authors: the note is by Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker and Nate Rush, not just 'METR'. Added the list of agents, the 95-issue coverage, the raw-scale trend figure, and that the trend result disappears for state-of-the-art models only. Numbers confirmed.

works.title: Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 / 2025 DORA Report: State of AI-assisted Software Development
works.authors: DORA team, Google Cloud (announcement blogs by Nathen Harvey and Derek DeBellis)
works.venue: Google Cloud / DORA industry survey reports (blogs 22 Oct 2024 and 23 Sept 2025)
works.what_measured: Survey-based associations between AI adoption and team delivery metrics (throughput, stability), plus self-reported productivity and trust.
works.method_plain: Large cross-sectional surveys of tech professionals, with statistical modeling of associations. Not causal. The 2025 survey had nearly 5,000 respondents plus over 100 hours of qualitative data. The 2024 blog does not state a sample size.
key_numbers: 2024 (blog): a 25% increase in AI adoption is associated with +7.5% documentation quality, +3.4% code quality and +3.1% code review speed. Delivery throughput is estimated 1.5% lower and stability 7.2% lower as AI adoption rises (the blog does not say whether these are also per 25% of adoption). 39% report little or no trust in AI code; more than 75% rely on AI for at least one daily task.

2025 (blog): 90% use AI at work; more than 80% believe it raised their productivity; 30% have little or no trust in AI code. AI adoption is now positively related to throughput but still negatively related to stability.
works.relevance_to_theta: Weak evidence for theta itself (self-reported, correlational). Useful for the system-level point: gains on coding do not flow through to delivery when testing and review are bottlenecks. That argues for a larger rho or a downstream stability cost, and shows that aggregation across stages (w_j weights) matters.
works.limitations: Self-reported and cross-sectional; the adoption measure is vague. Only the blog announcements were opened, not the full PDFs.
works.corrections: Numbers match both blogs. Added the 2024 report's formal title and the blog authors and dates. The 2024 sample size is not stated in the blog and remains unconfirmed.

works.title: Does AI Actually Boost Developer Productivity? (Stanford / 100k Devs Study)
works.authors: Yegor Denisov-Blanch (Stanford SWE Productivity Research Group)
works.venue: Conference talk, AI Engineer World's Fair, 5 June 2025 (no peer-reviewed paper found)
works.what_measured: Net 'delivered functionality' per developer from git commits, split by greenfield vs brownfield, task complexity, language popularity, and rework.
works.method_plain: Expert panels of 10-15 engineers rated code changes, and a model was trained to reproduce their ratings (slide reports r > 0.85 vs a 15-expert panel; full validation not given). The model scores each commit. Applied to git histories from 100k+ engineers at 600+ companies (about 80% private repos). The AI comparison by task type uses 136 teams from 27 companies. The gross/rework/net split comes from a smaller pilot.
key_numbers: Mean gains (136 teams): greenfield low-complexity 31%, greenfield high-complexity 12%, brownfield low-complexity 16%, brownfield high-complexity 7%. Guideline ranges: 30-40%, 10-15%, 15-20% and 0-10%.
From a pilot (about 120 developers, Aug 2024): new code up about 30-40%, rework about 15-25%, net about 15-20%.
Popular languages: +20-25% on simple tasks, +10-15% on complex. Niche languages (COBOL, Haskell, Elixir): 0-5% simple, -5% to +5% complex.
Self-assessed productivity missed measured productivity by about 30 percentile points in a 43-developer sample; only about 1 in 3 placed themselves in the right quartile.
The decline of gains with codebase size is shown as an illustrative curve, not a measured result.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only large-sample source found that splits gains by maintenance vs greenfield and by complexity, which is the j-dimension the model needs. Brownfield/high-complexity at about 7% vs greenfield/low at about 31% gives a prior ordering theta_maintenance < theta_development. The rework offset is a rough empirical proxy for rho. The niche-language result is suggestive for COBOL/mainframe maintenance in Indian IT but thinly supported.
works.limitations: A talk, not a paper. Proprietary, not fully validated method. Observational adoption comparison. Data from 2023 to early 2025 tools. The speaker calls the numbers guidelines ('orientative'). The 30-percentile-point self-assessment gap is in percentile ranks, not percentage points of productivity.
works.corrections: 'The distribution extends to about -20%' was rewritten: the talk says the violin chart's axis starts at -20%, and that high-complexity work can reduce productivity, without quantifying how far. Specified that the gross/rework/net numbers come from a small pilot (about 120 developers, Aug 2024), not the full sample, and added the guideline ranges.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.venue: Anthropic research note, November 2025 (page dated 25 Nov 2025)
works.what_measured: Model-estimated task time with vs without AI for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro and Max tiers), mapped to O*NET tasks.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a competent professional would need without AI and how long the user took with AI. Time savings = 1 - with/without. The time estimates were validated on about 1,000 open-source JIRA tasks with known durations.
key_numbers: Average task length without AI about 90 min (1.4 hours in the body). Time savings about 80% in the overview; the body gives a median of 84% per conversation, and a figure caption gives 81%.
Software developers account for the largest share (19%) of the implied labor productivity gain.
Implied +1.8%/yr US labor productivity growth over 10 years assuming universal adoption of current models. The authors say this is not a forecast.

JIRA validation: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 vs 0.50 for human estimates (0.39 with ten calibration examples). Claude's estimates are compressed: it overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones.
Excludes time spent validating, refining or iterating outside the chat. The authors say this may overstate current effects.
works.relevance_to_theta: An upper bound on gross time saved for chat-sized tasks, since it ignores review (rho) and failure (q). The JIRA validation is a template for building f_j(h) (task-length distributions) from ticket data. The 80% vs 26% gap with the field RCT is suggestive but not a clean measure of review and failure costs: the two differ in population, tasks, AI generation, and outcome (time per task vs output per worker).
works.limitations: Model self-estimates, not measurements. A selected sample of tasks people chose to bring to Claude. No review cost. No developer-specific savings figure.
works.corrections: Authors are Alex Tamkin and Peter McCrory, not just 'Anthropic Economic Research'. Added the date, the calibrated-model correlation, and the authors' caveat that 1.8% is not a prediction. Softened the claim that the 80% vs 26% gap measures rho and q. Numbers confirmed.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Saffron Huang, Bryan Seethor, Esin Durmus, Kunal Handa, Miles McCain, Michael Stern, Deep Ganguli (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: A survey (132 engineers and researchers), interviews (53), and analysis of about 200,000 internal Claude Code transcripts (Feb vs Aug 2025).
works.method_plain: Descriptive. Self-reported share of work using Claude (now vs 12 months earlier, as recalled), self-reported productivity, and the share of work that can be fully delegated, plus transcript metrics on agent autonomy.
key_numbers: 59% of work uses Claude (rounded to 60% in the key findings) vs 28% a year earlier (recalled); self-reported productivity boost +50% vs +20%.
More than half of respondents said they can fully delegate only 0-20% of their work.
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done.
Consecutive tool calls per transcript rose from 9.8 to 21.2; human turns fell from 6.2 to 4.1 (Feb to Aug 2025).
New-feature implementation rose from 14.3% to 36.9% of Claude Code use.
works.relevance_to_theta: Separates the assistant share (about 60% of work touched) from the delegate share (0-20% fully delegatable for most respondents). That maps loosely onto the kappa vs q*p split. Falling human turns per transcript is a proxy for falling oversight per task, but not a direct measure of rho. The 27% 'new work' figure warns that throughput gains are not all labor savings: demand expansion inside the firm mixes with theta.
works.limitations: Self-reported, at a frontier AI lab (an extreme early-adopter population). The year-earlier figures are recalled. Self-reports can be inflated (METR 2025).
works.corrections: Authors added (the page lists named contributors). 'Most employees' was changed to 'more than half of respondents', the page's wording. Noted that 59% is the exact figure and 60% the rounding, and that year-earlier figures are recalled. Numbers confirmed.

summary_flags: 'Self-reports overstate gains by 30-40 pp' is overgeneralized. METR 2025 shows a gap of about 40 pp (believed 20% faster vs measured 19% slower). Peng et al. show the opposite direction: self-estimates of 35% were BELOW the measured 55.8%. Stanford's figure is about 30 percentile points of rank, not percentage points of gain. A safer claim: self-reports are unreliable and can err in either direction.

'The extensive-margin hypothesis holds up: every study finds AI touches coding' is not a test. These studies were selected because they study coding, so finding that AI touches coding is built into the sample. They say nothing about extensive-margin coverage of testing, infrastructure, BPO or consulting tasks.

'Intensive margin ranges from -19% to +56%' mixes units: Peng, Google and METR measure time per task, while Cui, Microsoft 2026 and Cursor measure output per worker (PRs, lines). Convert with theta = 1 - 1/(1+g) before comparing; 26% more PRs is about 21% labor saved, not 26%.

'Assistant effects (kappa) for maintenance on familiar code are near zero or negative' rests on one 16-developer study with early-2025 tools. METR's own late-2025 rerun points to speedups (point estimates 4-18%, CIs spanning zero, likely biased toward zero). Say 'were negative in early 2025 in one small study; the current sign is uncertain'.

'Development tasks sit around 20-30%' quotes throughput gains (PRs) and a 21% time reduction (Google) with a CI that includes zero. In labor-saved terms it is closer to 15-25%, and the field figures come from 2022-23 autocomplete.

Microsoft 2026 '+24% merged PRs ... rising to about +50% in heavy-use weeks': the +50% is a within-engineer association that the authors themselves say is not causal. 'No significant decay' was asserted without a formal test.

Cursor 'raised warnings ~30% and complexity ~42%': the paper finds that codebase growth explains most of this. The complexity effect net of growth is about 9%, and the paper's own Discussion gives about 25% for complexity, inconsistent with Table 2.
q of about 0.5 from METR is a one-shot, no-iteration value from 3 high-standard Python repos with 4 reviewers. It is likely pessimistic for real workflows where agents or humans revise PRs.

The gaps list says Accenture Southeast Asia is the 'only Indian/offshore IT services site'. Southeast Asia is not India. Peng et al.'s sample (mostly Indian and Pakistani freelancers) is the closest match to the Indian labor pool, though not to firm delivery work.

Gap item on Qiao et al.: v1 (Nov 2025) had 18 grad students under a different title. The current version (v3, Sept 2026, 'Faster but Not Wiser: GitHub Copilot Decouples Programming Performance from Code Comprehension in Brownfield Tasks') reports 15. Its abstract gives no time-savings percentage.

The Anthropic 80% vs field 26% gap is presented as 'a measure of how much rho, q and non-coding time cut gross savings'. The two differ in population, task selection, AI generation and outcome measure, so the gap is not cleanly attributable to rho and q.
Cui et al. compare their result with a '58% decrease' in the lab, not 55.8%. Minor, but quote the paper correctly if citing their comparison.
verify.corrected_summary: The software-engineering experiments mostly show smaller measured gains as studies move from toy tasks to real jobs, and from new code to old code, though the outcome measures differ and are not directly comparable. On one self-contained greenfield task, Copilot cut completion time by 55.8% (Peng et al. 2023; CI 21-89%; mostly Indian and Pakistani freelancers; 2022 Copilot). Field RCTs at Microsoft, Accenture (Southeast Asian offices) and a Fortune 100 firm find about 26% more completed pull requests per week among users (SE 10%). That is roughly 21% labor saved per PR if hours and PR size are fixed, with larger gains for short-tenure and junior developers (2022-23 autocomplete). Google's enterprise RCT found about 21% less time on an 'extend existing code' task, with a CI that includes zero. METR's RCT on experienced maintainers of large, familiar codebases found a 19% slowdown with early-2025 tools. Its late-2025 rerun gives point estimates of 4-18% faster with CIs spanning zero, and METR considers it unreliable (likely understating the speedup) because of selection. For agentic tools, Microsoft's 2026 rollout of Claude Code and Copilot CLI is associated with about 24% more merged PRs per engineer (synthetic control, not randomized, no quality measures). Heavy-use weeks show about +50%, but the authors treat that as an association. Quality evidence cuts the other way. Cursor adoption in open-source projects raised static-analysis warnings (+30%) and complexity (+42%) persistently, much of it tracking codebase growth (about +9% complexity net of growth), while velocity gains faded after two months. METR's maintainers would not merge roughly half of SWE-bench-passing PRs in a one-shot, no-iteration setting (q of about 0.5, likely pessimistic). A Stanford talk (not peer-reviewed) reports mean gains of about 7% for brownfield/high-complexity work vs about 31% for greenfield/low-complexity. For the theta_j recipe, these studies speak only to coding tasks, so they cannot test the extensive-margin hypothesis for testing, infrastructure, BPO or consulting. On the intensive margin, measured effects range from a 19% slowdown to a 56% time saving, depending on task type, codebase familiarity, review burden and tool generation. Mixed outcome units (time per task vs output per worker) must be converted before comparison. The assistant effect for maintenance on familiar code was negative in one small early-2025 study, and its current sign is uncertain. Development-type assistant gains cluster around 15-25% labor saved. Delegate effects are only now becoming measurable, and per-task time RCTs break down when agents run in parallel. Self-reports are unreliable in both directions (METR: overstated by about 40 pp; Peng: understated by about 20 pp) and should not be used for theta.

works.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (original time-horizon paper)
works.authors: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, et al. (26 authors, incl. Lawrence Chan, Elizabeth Barnes)
works.what_measured: For each AI model, the length of task (in skilled-human minutes) the model completes with 50% (and 80%) probability, on 170 software/ML/cyber tasks: HCAST (97 tasks, 46 families), RE-Bench (7) and SWAA (66 short tasks).
works.method_plain: Time skilled humans on each task (task length = geometric mean of SUCCESSFUL baseliners' times). Run agents on the tasks. For each model fit a logistic curve: p(success) = sigmoid(beta * (log h_model - log t_task)). h_model is the 50% horizon; beta is the slope. Track h over model release dates.
key_numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 50% horizon about 50 min (paper abstract; TH1.1 later re-estimates 60 min)
50% horizon doubling time 207 days (95% CI 166-240) over 2019-2025; 80% horizon doubling 204 days
80% horizons are '4-6x shorter' than 50% horizons across models
SWE-bench Verified implied doubling about 70 days vs 143 days on METR suite for 2024 models (attributed partly to annotator underestimates of easy-task time)
Contractors took 5-18x longer than repo maintainers on internal PRs; AI performance looked consistent with contractor time, worse than predicted by maintainer time
148 of 169 tasks have human baselines; 21 HCAST tasks use researcher estimates
Models do worse on 'messier' tasks (16 messiness factors) at fixed length, but the time trend is similar on messy subset
works.relevance_to_theta: Direct source of p(h,t): gives the logistic functional form in log task length, per-model 50%/80% horizons, and a trend for t. The 5-18x maintainer-vs-contractor finding warns that h in the METR fit is 'low-context-contractor time', so applying p(h,t) to Indian IT service lines needs a context adjustment to h (a client-familiar engineer is faster). Says nothing about q, rho, kappa.
works.limitations: Software/ML/cyber only; tasks are well-specified, automatically scored, low-context; success ignores code quality/mergeability; human time excludes failed baselines; few long tasks; slope beta fit per model with regularization later found to matter.

works.title: Time Horizon 1.1 (task-suite update) and benchmark_results_1_1.yaml
works.authors: METR
works.year: 2026 (29 Jan 2026; data file current to Sep 2026)
works.what_measured: Re-estimated time horizons on an expanded suite (228 tasks; 31 tasks of 8h+), with per-model p50 and p80 horizons and CIs.
works.method_plain: Same logistic method; more long tasks; moved from Vivaria to Inspect scaffold.
key_numbers: Suite 170 -> 228 tasks (73 added, 15 removed); 8h+ tasks 14 -> 31, but only 5 long tasks human-baselined
Doubling time since 2023: 130.8 days [107,161] under TH1.1 vs 165.3 under TH1.0; since 2024: 88.6 days
Yaml doubling_time from_2023_on 128.7 days [104.4, 158.0], excluding points with p50 > 16 h

p50/p80 ratios for top models range ~4.3x (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to ~10x (Opus 4.6). My derivation (not METR's): with natural-log slope beta, beta = ln4 / ln(p50/p80), so beta ~0.6-0.95 per natural-log unit of task length
Dashboard: 'Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite'; page no longer actively updated as of Sep 8, 2026
works.relevance_to_theta: Best public calibration of p(h,t) at frontier as of 2026, including the p80 points that pin the slope. The implied shallow slope (beta < 1) means p decays slowly in h: a model with a 12h p50 still fails a meaningful share of 1h tasks, which matters for the max{...} kink in theta_j.
works.limitations: CIs very wide at top (Opus 4.6 p50 upper bound ~5x point estimate); suite saturating; scaffold sensitivity; slope not published per model, must be backed out from p50/p80.

works.title: Impact of modelling assumptions on time horizon results
works.authors: METR
works.what_measured: Sensitivity of 50%/80% horizons to the logistic fit choices: slope regularization, shared vs per-model slope, task weighting.
works.method_plain: Refit the same data under alternative reasonable statistical choices and compare horizons.
key_numbers: Original fit had a beta^2 penalty (C=10) that made curves 'slightly shallower'; fixed 3 Mar 2026; reduced recent models' 50% horizons by up to 20%
Shared (fixed) slope across models had the best leave-one-family-out CV error; Opus 4.6 under fixed slope: p50 7h51m, p80 1h30m (full data)
Reasonable alternatives cut recent 50% horizons by up to 35% and raise 80% horizons by up to 100%
Forcing Opus 4.6 to succeed on all <15-min tasks: p50 12h -> 9h, p80 nearly doubles to >2h
Across reasonable methods Opus 4.6 varies ~1.5x (p50) and ~2x (p80)
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly about the shape of p(h,t). Supports using a single shared slope across models (simplifies the theta_j recipe: one beta, time-varying h50). Shows the 80% horizon (the part of the curve that matters for reliable delegation) is the least well identified.
works.limitations: No numeric beta values published; software tasks only.

works.title: Clarifying limitations of time horizon
works.authors: Thomas Kwa (METR)
works.what_measured: Conceptual note on what time horizons do and do not imply for automation.
works.method_plain: Discussion; no new data.
key_numbers: 'A 50% time horizon of X hours does not mean we can delegate tasks under X hours to AIs'
Reliability-critical tasks may need 98%+ success to be worth automating
99% horizons would need ~300 diverse tasks per time bucket and <=1% label noise
Arithmetic-mean task times would be ~25% higher than geometric mean
Visual computer-use horizons are 40-100x lower than software horizons
Converting horizon to speedup requires measuring human time spent prompting, waiting, checking output
works.relevance_to_theta: METR itself states the conversion from p(h,t) to labor saved requires the review/prompting terms (rho, kappa) the draft formula includes, and that it has not done this. The 40-100x lower horizon for GUI tasks matters for BPO/infra service lines (p is domain-specific).
works.limitations: Non-quantitative for conversion; no estimates of rho.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged into main
works.authors: METR
works.what_measured: Whether repo maintainers would merge AI-written PRs that pass SWE-bench Verified tests.
works.method_plain: 4 maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx, pytest reviewed 296 AI PRs blind, plus 47 original human 'golden' PRs to calibrate maintainer noise.
key_numbers: Golden (human, actually merged) patches re-accepted ~68% of the time
Test-pass rate exceeds maintainer merge rate by 24.2 pp (SE 2.7) after golden normalization; 34.9 pp raw (SE 2.2)
Raw merge rates ~1/3 to 1/2 of grader pass rates ('roughly half' would not be merged)
Merge rate improved ~9.6 pp/yr slower than test pass rate (SE 5.5; weak); SOTA-only 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1, n.s.)
Claude Sonnet 4.5: ~50 min horizon under tests vs ~8 min under maintainer review (~7x overstatement)
works.relevance_to_theta: The origin of q ~0.5. Note the normalized figure (q relative to human golden patches) is closer to (pass - 24pp)/pass, and the horizon-based framing suggests a merge criterion shifts h50 down ~7x rather than scaling p by a constant q. That suggests modeling q as a horizon shift (q(h)) rather than a flat multiplier. Weak evidence the gap is not closing.
works.limitations: 3 Python repos, older models (to GPT-5/Sonnet 4.5), agents got no chance to iterate on feedback; short tasks.

works.title: Research Update: Towards reconciling slowdown with time horizons (algorithmic vs holistic evaluation)
works.authors: METR
works.what_measured: How often agent PRs that pass tests are actually usable, and how long humans take to fix them.
works.method_plain: Claude 3.7 Sonnet agent on 18 real issues from stdlib-js and hypothesis; humans reviewed and timed the fix-up to mergeable.
key_numbers: 38% (+/-19%) of attempts pass maintainer tests (27% on manually reviewed subset)
0% mergeable as-is
Average human fix time 42 min for all reviewed PRs; 26 min (min 15) for test-passing PRs
Original human completion time averaged 1.3 h (~78 min), so fixing a passing PR costs about a third of doing it from scratch
works.relevance_to_theta: The only direct measurement found of rho-like cost: review+fix of a test-passing AI PR ~ 0.33 of h (26/78), vs ~0.54 of h for all PRs (42/78). Implies even 'passing' output is not free; suggests rho of order 0.3 for early-2025 models on real repos.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (15 reviewed tasks), one model, two repos; authors say not to over-read absolute numbers.

works.title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?
works.authors: Samuel Miserendino, Michele Wang, Tejal Patwardhan, Johannes Heidecke
works.what_measured: Dollar value of real Upwork (Expensify) software tasks an AI completes, judged by end-to-end tests or matching the manager's chosen proposal.
works.method_plain: 1,488 tasks with their actual historical bounties; model earns the bounty if it passes triple-verified end-to-end tests (IC tasks) or picks the same proposal the real manager picked (manager tasks).
key_numbers: Full set: 1,488 tasks worth $1,000,000 (764 IC SWE = $414,775; 724 manager = $585,225); payouts $50 to $32,000
Diamond set: 502 tasks worth $500,800
Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 33.7% pass@1, $403k of $1M (40.3%) on full set; IC SWE Diamond 26.2% pass@1, $58k of $236k
Authors note verification of solutions can take over 24 hours
works.relevance_to_theta: Closest benchmark to a 'dollar value of work automated' for software; bounty value is a proxy for h-weighted f_j (bigger bounty ~ longer task). Lets one compute a value-weighted pass rate vs count-weighted pass rate, which is the integral over f_j(h) in the draft formula. Still a gross number: no review cost, no q.
works.limitations: One codebase; bounties are historical market prices, not labor time; pass = tests, not mergeability; manager tasks are multiple-choice; no updated frontier results checked here.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Whether expert graders prefer AI deliverables over expert human deliverables on 1,320 tasks from 44 occupations in the top 9 US GDP sectors; plus a speed/cost scenario including human review.
works.method_plain: Professionals (avg 14 yrs experience) write representative tasks and deliverables; blinded experts compare model vs human output. Task value = expert completion time x occupation median wage. 'Try n times, then fix' scenario: expert reviews model output, resamples, and does it themselves if no output is acceptable.
key_numbers: 1,320 tasks; 220-task open gold subset
Average task length stated as ~7 h in intro; tables give 9.49 h (gold) and 8.63 h (full) - inconsistent in the paper
Claude Opus 4.1 best at release: 47.6% win-or-tie vs experts; GPT-5 win rate 39.0% (wins only)
Naive GPT-5: 90x faster, 474x cheaper; with 'try 1x then fix': 1.12x faster, 1.18x cheaper; 'try n then fix': 1.39x faster, 1.63x cheaper
Review adds an average 109 minutes and $86 per deliverable
Secondary sources (not verified on OpenAI page, which returned 403): GPT-5.2 Thinking 70.9% win/tie, Pro 74.1%
works.relevance_to_theta: The single best existing worked example of converting benchmark success into net labor saved including review: 'try n then fix' speedup of 1.39x implies time saved = 1 - 1/1.39 ~ 28% for GPT-5 on these tasks, versus ~99% naive. This is essentially theta_j-direct with q, rho built in; the 109-min review cost per ~7-9h task gives rho ~0.2. Covers occupations similar to BPO/consulting deliverables.
works.limitations: One-shot, well-specified tasks with full context; preference grading not acceptance; US occupations; review time is a fixed assumption, not measured in deployment; newer-model numbers not verified from primary source.

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work (and live leaderboard)
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika, Alice Gatti, Cristina Menghini, et al. (47 authors incl. Dan Hendrycks; CAIS and Scale AI)
works.what_measured: Share of real, paid Upwork freelance projects where an AI agent's deliverable would be accepted by a reasonable client as the commissioned work.
works.method_plain: 240 end-to-end projects (230 private test) with the real human deliverable, price and hours; three evaluators majority-vote on whether the AI deliverable is at least as good / acceptable.
key_numbers: Projects: >6,000 hours of work, >$140,000 value; mean $632.6 (median $200), mean 28.9 h (median 11.5 h)
Paper (Oct 2025): best agent Manus 2.5% automation rate, earned $1,720 of $143,991; Sonnet 4.5 2.1%; GPT-5 1.7%
Inter-annotator agreement 94.4%
Leaderboard (Oct 2026, as listed): Opus 5.5 21.25%, GPT 6 Astra 20.83%, Fable 5.1 17.92%, Gemini Argon 4 17.08%, Opus 4.8 8.33%, GPT-5.2 2.08-2.50%; no CIs reported
works.relevance_to_theta: A full-delegation (no human in loop) measure on long, messy, multi-modal projects: roughly q*p at large h. The jump from ~2% to ~21% within a year shows p for long, messy work moving fast. Values the q*p term but has no kappa (assistance) or rho.
works.limitations: Mostly creative/design/media work, little IT services or BPO; binary acceptance; small n (230) and no CIs; dollar-weighted earnings vs count-weighted rate differ.

works.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
works.authors: Frank F. Xu, ..., Graham Neubig (21 authors, CMU)
works.what_measured: Agent completion of 175 workplace tasks in a simulated software company (code repo, chat, docs, project tracker), across SWE, PM, HR, admin, data science, finance.
works.method_plain: Tasks graded by checkpoints; partial score = 0.5*(checkpoints passed share) + 0.5*(full success).
key_numbers: 175 tasks; by category SWE 69, HR 29, PM 28, Admin 15, DS 14, Finance 12
Best (Gemini 2.5 Pro): 30.3% full completion, 39.3% partial score, 27.2 steps, $4.2 per task
DS, admin and finance tasks hardest; SWE easiest; RocketChat (colleague chat) and ownCloud platforms hardest
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives p by task category inside an IT firm (rough analog to j: development vs admin/BPO-like tasks). Checkpoint partial credit is a crude handle on kappa (AI does part, human finishes).
works.limitations: No human time baselines, so cannot map to h; simulated colleagues; older models in latest version.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (and 2026 follow-up)
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: Randomized trial of task completion time with vs without AI tools for experienced developers on their own repos.
works.method_plain: Developers list real tasks; each is randomly assigned AI-allowed or not; compare completion times.
key_numbers: 2025: 16 devs, 246 tasks; AI made tasks 19% LONGER (CI +2% to +39%); devs forecast -24% and afterwards believed -20%
Late-2025 follow-up: 57 devs, 143 repos, 800+ tasks; sign convention negative = speedup; returning devs -18% (CI -38% to +9%), new devs -4% (CI -15% to +9%)
METR calls the follow-up 'an unreliable signal' due to selection (devs refusing no-AI condition; 30-50% withheld tasks; pay cut $150 -> $50/h)
Related METR notes (opened): transcript analysis of 7 staff gave a 'soft upper bound' time-savings factor of ~1.5x to ~13x (Jan 2026)
works.relevance_to_theta: The only RCT-grade evidence on kappa (assistant-mode speedup) for high-context engineers: near zero or negative in early 2025, small positive and imprecise in late 2025. Strong warning that benchmark p does not translate to time saved for repo-familiar workers (high context lowers h baseline).
works.limitations: Expert maintainers on large familiar repos (unlike typical IT services staff); small samples; selection bias in follow-up; not task-length-resolved.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: Per-task time savings for 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks and wages.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates time a professional would need without AI and time the user spent with AI; savings = 1 - with/without; aggregated to O*NET tasks and occupations.
key_numbers: Average unassisted task ~90 min; median savings ~80% (body says 84%, figure 81%)
Implied +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth over a decade at full adoption (not a forecast)
Validation on 1,000 JIRA tickets: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 vs human devs 0.50
Excludes time spent validating output outside the chat; estimates compressed (overstate short tasks, understate long)
works.relevance_to_theta: A task-level intensive-margin estimate (theta-like) with an O*NET task-to-occupation aggregation that mirrors w_j. Directly contradicts the hypothesis that nobody measures the intensive margin, but it is self-selected tasks, LLM-estimated, and gross of review (rho omitted), so it is an upper bound.
works.limitations: Model-estimated times, selection into tasks people bring to Claude, no review cost, not benchmark-based.

works.title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
works.authors: David Rein, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, ..., Elizabeth Barnes (22 authors, METR)
works.what_measured: 189 tasks in ML engineering, cyber, SWE and reasoning with 563 human baselines (>1,500 hours).
works.method_plain: Skilled humans attempt tasks under the same conditions as agents; their times calibrate task length.
key_numbers: 189 tasks; 563 baselines; >1,500 human hours
Agents: 70-80% success on tasks under 1 hour for humans; under 20% on tasks over 4 hours
works.relevance_to_theta: The human-time calibration backbone for p(h,t). Its baselining protocol is the template for building f_j(h) and h for Indian IT service tasks.
works.limitations: Low-context baseliners; few long tasks; 2024-25 models.

research.stream_summary:
Benchmarks now give a well-measured version of p(h,t) for software tasks. METR fits a logistic curve in log task length. The 50% horizon roughly doubles every 4-7 months (TH1.1 gives 129-131 days since 2023). Frontier 50% horizons reached about 6-17 hours by spring 2026 (Opus 4.6 about 719 min, Claude Mythos preview about 1,045 min). 80% horizons are much shorter, about 54-186 min. The gap between them implies a shallow slope: by my calculation, about 0.6-0.95 per natural-log unit of task length. That slope is the least robust part of the fit; METR's own March 2026 note says reasonable choices move 80% horizons by up to 2x.

Has anyone converted benchmark results into labor saved? Only partly.
- **Dollar values:** SWE-Lancer and the Remote Labor Index attach real market prices to tasks. Both measure what a fully delegated AI can deliver (roughly q times p), with no allowance for review.
- **Review included:** GDPval is the one benchmark that nets out review. Its 'try n times, then fix' scenario for GPT-5 gives a 1.39x speedup, about 28% of time saved, against 90x naively. Review costs about 109 minutes per task of roughly 7-9 hours.
- **The q and rho parameters:** METR measured them directly in two places. About half of SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged; under merge criteria, one model's horizon was about 7x shorter. Fixing an early-2025 agent PR that passed tests took about 1/3 of the original human time.
- **The kappa parameter:** METR's randomized trials put assistant-mode speedup near zero or below in 2025, and their late-2025 follow-up is imprecise.

So the working hypothesis is mostly supported: no one has combined p(h,t), q, rho and a task-length distribution into theta_j. GDPval comes closest, and Anthropic's conversation study estimates time saved per task but leaves out review time. Remote Labor Index acceptance rates rose from about 2.5% to about 21% within a year.
gaps_noticed: No study integrates p(h,t) over an hours-weighted task-length distribution f_j(h) for any real occupation or firm; METR says the conversion needs prompting/review time data it does not have.

No benchmark covers IT-services maintenance, testing, infrastructure ops or BPO process work with human-time baselines; computer-use (GUI) horizons are 40-100x lower than software horizons (METR Jan 2026 note), so software p(h,t) cannot be reused for BPO.

q is measured only on short Python repo tasks with older models (up to GPT-5/Sonnet 4.5); evidence suggests q acts more like a horizon shift (~7x) than a constant multiplier, which changes the theta formula.
rho measured once (n=15, Claude 3.7) at ~0.33 of h for test-passing PRs; GDPval assumes rather than measures review time.
80%+ horizons (relevant for delegation) are poorly identified; 98-99% horizons are infeasible with current suites.
Task length h in METR uses low-context contractors; repo maintainers are 5-18x faster, so the right h for Indian IT staff (client-context-rich) is unknown.

GDPval post-launch numbers (GPT-5.2 70.9% win/tie) could not be verified from OpenAI's page (403); OpenAI's SWE-bench Verified difficulty split (196 tasks under 15 min, 45 over 1 h, out of 500) also came only from search snippets because the page returned 403.
I did not open RE-Bench (Wijk et al. 2024) or OSWorld-Verified separately beyond the OSWorld abstract (369 tasks; humans 72.36%, best model 12.24% at publication in 2024).

works.title: Time Horizon 1.1 (task-suite update) and benchmark_results_1_1.yaml
works.authors: METR

Doubling time since 2023: 130.8 days [107, 161] under TH1.1 vs 165.3 days [129, 211] under TH1.0; since 2024: 88.6 days (TH1.1, no CI) vs 108.9 days (TH1.0)
YAML doubling_time from_2023_on 128.7 days [104.4, 158.0]; all_time_stitched 187.8 days; excludes points with central p50 > 16 h (so Mythos Preview is excluded)

p50/p80 ratios for top models run from about 4.3x (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to about 10.3x (Opus 4.6). Researcher's own derivation, not METR's: with a natural-log slope beta, beta = ln4 / ln(p50/p80), giving roughly 0.6-0.95 (arithmetic checked)
Dashboard: 'Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite' (added 8 May 2026); the page says it is 'no longer actively updated' (8 Sep 2026 update)
works.relevance_to_theta: Best public calibration of p(h,t) at the frontier in 2026, including the p80 points that pin down the slope. The implied shallow slope (beta < 1) means p falls slowly with h: at beta 0.6-0.95, a model with a 12h p50 still fails roughly 9-18% of 1h tasks. That matters for the max{...} kink in theta_j. Caution: the March 2026 modelling note shows part of the shallowness may come from label noise and fitting choices.
works.limitations: CIs are very wide at the top (Opus 4.6's p50 upper bound is about 5x its point estimate); the suite is saturating, and p50 above 16 h is officially unreliable; the CIs likely understate run-level variance (METR's words); per-model slopes are not published and must be backed out from p50/p80.
works.corrections: Fixed rounding: Gemini 3.1 Pro p50 is 384.1 (not 384.2) and GPT-5.2 p50 is 352.2 (not 352.3), per the raw YAML. The YAML's newest model is Mythos Preview (released 2026-04-07), so 'data file current to Sep 2026' is wrong: the September 2026 change was the dashboard's 'no longer actively updated' notice, not new data. Added the TH1.0 CI for 2023+ [129, 211] and the 'all_time_stitched' 187.8 days. Noted that Mythos (p50 > 16 h) is excluded from the doubling fit.

works.title: Impact of modeling assumptions on time horizon results
works.authors: Alexander Barry (METR)
works.what_measured: How much 50%/80% horizons move under different logistic-fit choices: slope regularization, a shared vs per-model slope, a reliability ceiling, Weibull and LOESS alternatives, and noise adjustment (SIMEX).
works.method_plain: Refit the same data under alternative reasonable statistical choices, compare the horizons, and score the models by leave-one-family-out cross-validation.
key_numbers: The original fit penalized beta^2 with C=10; changed 3 Mar 2026 (now C=100,000, no practical effect); the intro says the fix 'decreased recent models' 50% time horizon results by up to 20%' and generally lowered 80% horizons (the body text says it raised 50% horizons for strong models, which conflicts with the intro)
The fixed (shared) slope logistic model had the best leave-one-family-out CV on both MSE and log-likelihood

In the note's 'Opus 4.6 SIMEX Results' table, the fixed-slope row reads 7h 51m (-6%) and 1h 30m (-6%), with noise-adjusted 5h 36m and 1h 3m; the column labels in the fetched text were ambiguous, so treat these as approximate fixed-slope 50%/80% values
Reasonable alternative fits 'decrease the 50% time horizons by up to 35%' and 'increase the 80% time horizon by up to 100%'
Forcing Opus 4.6 to succeed on all <15-min tasks: 50% horizon falls 'from 12 hours to 9 hours'; 80% horizon 'almost doubles to over 2 hours'
'The variation in the results from reasonable methods is ~1.5x in 50% TH and 2x in 80% TH for Opus 4.6'
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly about the shape of p(h,t). Supports a single slope shared across models, which simplifies the recipe to one beta plus a time-varying h50. Shows that the 80% horizon, the part of the curve that matters for reliable delegation, is the least well identified, and that noise on short tasks makes curves look shallower.
works.limitations: No numeric beta values published; software tasks only; the note's own text is internally inconsistent on the direction of the regularization fix's effect on 50% horizons.
works.corrections: Author is Alexander Barry (the record said only 'METR'). The 7h51m / 1h30m figures come from the SIMEX results table, not a stand-alone fixed-slope fit description; relabelled them. The phrase 'slightly shallower' could not be confirmed and was replaced with what the note does say. Flagged the note's intro-vs-body inconsistency.

works.title: Clarifying limitations of time horizon
works.authors: Thomas Kwa (METR)
works.what_measured: Conceptual note on what time horizons do and do not imply for automation.
works.method_plain: Discussion; no new data.
key_numbers: 'A 50% time horizon of X hours does not mean we can delegate tasks under X hours to AIs'
'Some (reliability-critical and poorly verifiable) tasks require 98%+ success probabilities to be worth automating'
99% horizons would need '~300 highly diverse tasks in each time bucket' and label noise well under 1%
Using the arithmetic instead of the geometric mean of multiple baseline times would raise averages by about 25%
Horizons are 'fairly similar for math, but 40-100x lower for visual computer use tasks'
Converting horizons to speedup requires measuring how much time a human spends 'prompting AIs, waiting for generations, checking AI output' (richer data such as Cursor logs or screen recordings)
works.relevance_to_theta: METR itself says converting p(h,t) into labor saved needs the prompting and review terms (rho, kappa) that the draft formula includes, and that it has not done this. The 40-100x lower horizon for visual computer-use tasks matters for BPO and infrastructure service lines: p is domain-specific.
works.limitations: Gives no numbers for the conversion; no estimates of rho.
works.corrections: Minor: the ~25% arithmetic-vs-geometric figure refers to aggregating multiple baselines per task, not to task times in general.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether repo maintainers would merge AI-written PRs that pass SWE-bench Verified tests.
works.method_plain: 4 active maintainers (2 scikit-learn, 1 Sphinx, 1 pytest) blind-reviewed 296 AI PRs, plus original human 'golden' PRs (47 golden patches; about half were randomly selected for review) to calibrate maintainer noise.
key_numbers: Golden (human, actually merged) patches were re-accepted about 68% of the time
The automated grader's pass rate exceeds the maintainer merge rate by 24.2 pp (SE 2.7) after golden normalization; 34.9 pp raw (SE 2.2); 23.8 pp progress-based (SE 2.0)
Summary claim: 'roughly half of test-passing SWE-bench Verified PRs' would not be merged (no per-model conditional merge rate was found to check this against)

The merge rate improved 9.6 pp/yr more slowly than the test-pass rate (SE 5.5; significant only at 10%; 15.5 pp/yr raw, SE 4.6); SOTA-only 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1, not significant), with a level gap of 20.6 pp (SE 3.0)
Claude Sonnet 4.5: about 50 min horizon under the automated grader vs about 8 min under maintainer review (roughly 7x overstatement)
works.relevance_to_theta: The source of q ~0.5. The normalized figure (relative to human golden patches) is closer to (pass - 24pp)/pass. The horizon framing suggests a merge criterion shifts h50 down about 7x rather than scaling p by a constant q, so q may be better modelled as a horizon shift q(h) than as a flat multiplier. Weak evidence that the gap is not closing.
works.limitations: 3 Python repos; models only up to GPT-5 / Claude Sonnet 4.5; agents got one submission with no chance to iterate on feedback; short tasks.
works.corrections: Authors are Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker and Nate Rush (not just 'METR'). Removed 'raw merge rates ~1/3 to 1/2 of grader pass rates': I could not confirm it and replaced it with the note's own 'roughly half' wording. Added the raw 15.5 pp/yr trend and the 20.6 pp SOTA level gap. Clarified that only about half of the 47 golden patches were reviewed.

works.title: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation (URL slug: towards reconciling slowdown with time horizons)
works.authors: David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: How often agent PRs that pass tests are actually usable, and how long humans would take to fix them.
works.method_plain: A Claude 3.7 Sonnet agent (Inspect ReAct scaffold) ran on 18 real issues (15 stdlib-js, 3 hypothesis); 15 of the resulting PRs were reviewed manually, and the fix-up time to a mergeable state was ESTIMATED by comparison with the reference human PR (not timed).
key_numbers: 38% (+/-19%, 95% CI) of all 18 attempts pass maintainer tests; 27% (+/-20) on the 15 manually reviewed
0 of the reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is
Estimated average fix time 42 min for all 15 reviewed PRs; 26 min (min 15) for the n=4 test-passing PRs
Original human completion time averaged 1.3 h (range 20 min to 4 h) across all 18 tasks; 26/78 is roughly one-third, but the numerator and denominator come from different task sets
works.relevance_to_theta: A rough rho-like data point: fixing a test-passing AI PR was estimated at about a third of the human task time (26/78), and about 0.54 for all reviewed PRs (42/78). Shows even 'passing' output is not free. But the passing-PR figure rests on 4 PRs and subjective estimates, so treat rho ~0.3 as an order-of-magnitude hint only.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (4 passing PRs; 15 reviewed); one model; two mature repos with high standards; fix times are subjective estimates, not measurements; little elicitation, so not an upper bound on agent performance.
works.corrections: The author is David Rein. The page title is 'Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation'. The 26-min figure is based on n=4 test-passing PRs, not n=15. Fix times were estimated, not timed. The 1.3 h average covers all 18 tasks, so the one-third ratio mixes samples.

works.title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?
works.authors: Samuel Miserendino, Michele Wang, Tejal Patwardhan, Johannes Heidecke
works.what_measured: The dollar value of real Upwork (Expensify) software tasks an AI completes, judged by end-to-end tests (IC tasks) or by matching the hiring manager's chosen proposal (manager tasks).
works.method_plain: 1,488 tasks with their actual historical bounties. A model earns the bounty if it passes triple-verified end-to-end Playwright tests (IC tasks) or picks the same proposal the real manager picked (manager tasks).
key_numbers: Full set: 1,488 tasks worth $1,000,000 (764 IC SWE = $414,775; 724 manager = $585,225); payouts from $50 to $32,000
Diamond public split: 502 tasks worth $500,800
Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 33.7% pass@1 and $403k of $1M on the full set; Diamond overall 36.1% pass@1, about $208k of $500.8k; IC SWE Diamond 26.2% pass@1, $58k of $236,300
Model-first-with-freelancer-fallback cuts costs about 9% (GPT-4o) and 13% (o1) at pass@1, and about 19% and 34% at pass@5
Authors: the pass@5 savings analysis 'assumes quick verification of correct solutions, but in practice this can take over 24 hours'
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest benchmark to a 'dollar value of work automated' for software. Bounty value is a proxy for h-weighted f_j (bigger bounty ~ longer task), so it allows a value-weighted vs count-weighted pass rate, which is the integral over f_j(h) in the draft formula. The fallback cost analysis is a crude net-savings calculation, but it assumes verification is free and has no q.
works.limitations: One codebase; bounties are historical market prices, not labor time; pass = tests, not mergeability; manager tasks are multiple choice; models cannot ask clarifying questions; possible contamination; no updated frontier results checked.
works.corrections: Numbers matched. Added the Diamond overall result and the fallback cost-savings analysis. That analysis means the stream summary's claim that SWE-Lancer makes 'no allowance for review' is slightly too strong: it does a fallback calculation, though it assumes verification costs nothing.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Whether expert graders prefer AI deliverables over expert human deliverables on 1,320 tasks from 44 occupations in the 9 sectors that contribute most to US GDP; plus speed/cost scenarios that include expert review.
works.method_plain: Professionals (average 14 years' experience, minimum 4) write representative tasks and deliverables; blinded experts compare model output with human output. Task value = estimated completion time x the occupation's median wage (OEWS). In 'try n times, then fix', an expert reviews the model output, accepts it with probability equal to the model's WIN RATE, resamples on failure, and does the task themselves after n failures.
key_numbers: 1,320 tasks; 220-task open gold subset (5 per occupation)
Average task length: intro says 7 h; Table 3 (gold) mean 9.49 h (median 5.0 h); Table 4 (full) mean 8.63 h (median 4.0 h); Appendix A.2.1 gives 404 min for gold. The paper is internally inconsistent
Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% win-or-tie vs experts (best in the paper); GPT-5 win rate 39.0% (wins only)
GPT-5 vs experts: naive 90x faster and 474x cheaper; 'try 1x then fix' 1.12x faster and 1.18x cheaper; 'try nx then fix' 1.39x faster and 1.63x cheaper
Expert review averaged 109 minutes and $86 per deliverable, MEASURED from task-monitoring software during first grading
Not verified from primary source (OpenAI page returned 403): GPT-5.2 Thinking 70.9% wins-or-ties (seen in search snippet of OpenAI's launch post); GPT-5.2 Pro 74.1% not confirmed at all
works.relevance_to_theta: The best existing worked example of turning benchmark success into net labor saved including review. 'Try n then fix' at 1.39x implies time saved = 1 - 1/1.39 ~ 28% for GPT-5 on these tasks, versus ~99% naively. That is effectively theta_j-direct with an acceptance probability (win rate, a q*p proxy) and review cost built in. 109 min of review on a 6.7-9.5 h task gives rho of about 0.19-0.27. It covers occupations similar to BPO/consulting deliverables.
works.limitations: One-shot, well-specified tasks with full context; acceptance is proxied by preference (win rate), not real acceptance; US occupations; review time is grading time in an evaluation setting, which may differ from deployment review; n in 'try n' is not stated (the paper analyzes the limit); the authors say the scenario over-penalizes the model; newer-model numbers not verified from primary source.
works.corrections: The 109-min review time was MEASURED (task-monitoring software, first grading), not a 'fixed assumption'; fixed the limitations and the related gap. Added that acceptance probability = win rate. Added the 404-min appendix figure, so the rho range is ~0.19-0.27, not ~0.2. GPT-5.2 Pro 74.1% removed as unconfirmed; GPT-5.2 Thinking 70.9% only seen in a search snippet of OpenAI's page (403).

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work (and Scale Labs leaderboard)
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika, Alice Gatti, Cristina Menghini, et al. (47 authors incl. Dan Hendrycks; CAIS and Scale AI)
works.what_measured: Share of real, paid Upwork freelance projects where an AI agent's deliverable would be accepted by a reasonable client as the commissioned work (the 'automation rate').
works.method_plain: 240 end-to-end projects (230 private test, 10 public) with the real human deliverable, price and hours across 23 Upwork subcategories. Human evaluators judge each AI deliverable on a 3-point holistic scale. Sec 3.4 says majority vote over three evaluations; Appendix B.2 says two evaluations with a third to break ties.
key_numbers: Projects: over 6,000 hours of work worth over $140,000; mean $632.6 (median $200); mean 28.9 h (median 11.5 h)
Paper (Oct 2025): best agent Manus 2.5% automation rate, earning $1,720 of $143,991; Grok 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 2.1%; GPT-5 1.7%; ChatGPT agent 1.3%; Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.8%
Inter-annotator agreement on automation rate 94.4%

Leaderboard (checked Oct 2026): Opus 5.5 21.25%, GPT 6 Astra 20.83%, Fable 5.1 17.92%, Gemini Argon 4 17.08%, Fable 5 15.83%, Opus 4.8 8.33%, gpt-5.2 2.08-2.50%; the page states there is no confidence interval for the automation rate
works.relevance_to_theta: A full-delegation (no human in the loop) measure on long, messy, multimedia projects: roughly q*p at large h. The best score rising from ~2.5% to ~21% within a year suggests p for long, messy work is moving fast. It captures the q*p term but not kappa (assistance) or rho.
works.limitations: Mostly creative, design and media work, little IT services or BPO; binary acceptance; small n (230-240), so a 21% rate has a standard error of roughly +/-2.6 pp and no CIs are reported; dollar-weighted earnings differ from the count-weighted rate; the paper's description of evaluator voting is inconsistent.
works.corrections: Numbers matched. Added the other paper-era agents and Fable 5. Noted the paper's inconsistent description of the voting procedure (three-way majority vs two plus a tie-break).

works.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
works.authors: Frank F. Xu, ..., Graham Neubig (21 authors, CMU)
works.what_measured: How well agents complete 175 workplace tasks in a simulated software company (code repo, chat, office docs, project tracker) across SWE, PM, HR, admin, data science and finance roles.
works.method_plain: Tasks are graded by checkpoints; partial score = 0.5*(share of checkpoints passed) + 0.5*(full success indicator).
key_numbers: 175 tasks; by category SWE 69, HR 29, PM 28, Admin 15, DS 14, Finance 12 (these sum to 167; the rest are not itemized in the text read)
Best (Gemini 2.5 Pro, OpenHands 0.28.1): 30.3% full completion, 39.3% partial score, 27.2 steps, $4.2 per task
Data science, admin and finance tasks were hardest; SWE easiest; the RocketChat (colleague chat) and ownCloud (office suite) platforms were hardest
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives p by task category inside an IT-firm-like setting, a rough analogue to j (development vs admin/BPO-like tasks). The checkpoint partial credit is at best a very loose hint of partial automation; it does not measure kappa, which is a speedup when AI assists a human.
works.limitations: No human time baselines, so results cannot be mapped to h; simulated colleagues; older models in the latest version.
works.corrections: Numbers matched. Softened the claim that partial credit is a handle on kappa: it measures partial task completion, not human speedup. Noted the category counts sum to 167.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (and Feb 2026 follow-up 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design')
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025 paper); follow-up post by Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
works.what_measured: A randomized trial of task completion time with vs without AI tools for experienced developers working on their own repos.
works.method_plain: Developers list real tasks; each task is randomly assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed; completion times are compared.
key_numbers: 2025: 16 devs, 246 tasks; AI-allowed tasks took 19% LONGER (CI +2% to +39%); devs forecast a 24% speedup and afterwards believed 20%; economics and ML experts forecast 39% and 38% speedups
Late-2025 follow-up: 57 devs (10 returning, 47 new), 143 repos, 800+ tasks; negative = speedup; returning devs -18% (CI -38% to +9%), new devs -4% (CI -15% to +9%)

METR: the new data give 'an unreliable signal' because of selection: some developers declined to take part because they did not want to work without AI, 30-50% of developers said they chose not to submit some tasks they did not want to do without AI, and pay was cut from $150/h to $50/h
Related METR note (Amy Deng, 17 Feb 2026; 5,305 Claude Code transcripts from 7 staff, Jan 2026): time-savings factor about 1.5x to 13x, called a 'soft upper bound'
works.relevance_to_theta: The only RCT-grade evidence on realized speedup (closest to kappa, though the AI-allowed arm includes agentic use, not only assistant mode) for high-context engineers: negative in early 2025, small positive and imprecise in late 2025. A strong warning that benchmark p does not translate one-for-one into time saved for repo-familiar workers.
works.limitations: Expert maintainers on large familiar repos (unlike typical IT services staff); small samples; selection bias in the follow-up; not resolved by task length; the AI-allowed condition mixes assistant and delegate use.
works.corrections: '30-50% withheld tasks' was wrong: it is 30-50% of DEVELOPERS who said they withheld some tasks. Added the follow-up post's title and its different author list (Tom Cunningham and Khalid Mahamud, no Elizabeth Barnes). The transcript note is dated 17 Feb 2026 (by Amy Deng; it analyzes Jan 2026 transcripts), not Jan 2026.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.year: 2025 (Nov 2025; page shows 25 Nov 2025, citation block shows 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: Per-task time savings for 100,000 anonymized Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks and wages.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a professional would need without AI and how long the user spent with AI; savings = 1 - with/without; results are aggregated to O*NET tasks and occupations.
