key_numbers: Average unassisted task about 90 minutes (another bullet says 1.4 h); median savings about 80% (Results text 84%, density-plot caption 81%)
Implied about 1.8% per year US labor productivity growth over the next decade at universal adoption with current models; explicitly 'not a prediction of the future'
Validation on 1,000 open-source JIRA tickets: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman rho 0.44 vs human developers 0.50
Excludes time spent outside the chat, including validating output; Claude's estimates are compressed (overestimates short tasks, underestimates long ones) and tend to overestimate overall
works.relevance_to_theta: A task-level intensive-margin estimate (theta-like) with an O*NET task-to-occupation aggregation that mirrors w_j. It contradicts the idea that nobody measures the intensive margin, but it covers self-selected tasks, uses LLM-estimated times, and is gross of review (rho omitted), so it is an upper bound.
works.limitations: Model-estimated times; selection into the tasks people bring to Claude; no review cost; not benchmark-based; the Claude.ai sample is not representative of all AI use.
works.corrections: Numbers matched. Noted the page's own date conflict (25 Nov vs 5 Nov 2025) and the 90 min vs 1.4 h discrepancy.

works.title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks
works.authors: David Rein, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, Seraphina Nix, ..., Lawrence Chan, Elizabeth Barnes (22 authors, METR)
works.what_measured: 189 tasks in ML engineering, cybersecurity, software engineering and general reasoning, with 563 human baselines (over 1,500 hours); tasks take humans from about 1 minute to 8+ hours.
works.method_plain: Skilled humans attempt the tasks under the same conditions as the agents; their times calibrate task length.
key_numbers: 189 tasks; 563 baselines; over 1,500 human hours
Agents succeed 70-80% of the time on tasks humans take under 1 hour, and under 20% on tasks over 4 hours
works.relevance_to_theta: The human-time calibration backbone for p(h,t). Its baselining protocol is the template for building f_j(h) and h for Indian IT service tasks.
works.limitations: Low-context baseliners; few long tasks; 2024-25 models; most tasks private.
works.corrections: Numbers matched. Fixed the author list: Elizabeth Barnes is last author and Lawrence Chan is second to last.

summary_flags: 'GDPval is the one benchmark that nets out review' overstates it. METR's Aug 2025 holistic-evaluation post estimates fix-up time, and SWE-Lancer runs a model-first, freelancer-fallback cost analysis (9-34% savings), although that analysis assumes verification is free.

The gap that 'GDPval assumes rather than measures review time' is wrong. The 109 min was measured from task-monitoring software during expert grading. The real caveat is that evaluation grading time may not equal review time in deployment.
GDPval's acceptance probability is the preference WIN RATE, not real client acceptance, so the 28% net time saving rests on a preference proxy for q*p.

Calling METR's fix-up figure a direct measurement of rho ('about 1/3 of the original human time') overstates it. It rests on n=4 test-passing PRs with subjective ESTIMATED fix times, and its denominator is the 1.3 h average over all 18 tasks. The gap's 'n=15' should be n=4 for the passing-PR figure.

Frontier '6-17 hours' horizons need a caveat. METR says measurements above 16 h are unreliable, Mythos Preview (17.4 h) is excluded from METR's own doubling fit, and Opus 4.6's CI runs from 5 h to 61 h.

The shallow slope (beta about 0.6-0.95) is the researcher's own derivation. METR's March 2026 note shows label noise on short tasks and fitting choices flatten the curve, so beta may be steeper than this implies.
'Raw merge rates ~1/3 to 1/2 of grader pass rates' could not be confirmed. Only the note's 'roughly half' wording and the 24.2 pp (normalized) / 34.9 pp (raw) gaps are verified.

'The working hypothesis is mostly supported' is too strong. Several intensive-margin measurements exist (Anthropic conversation study, GDPval try-n-then-fix, METR RCTs, SWE-Lancer fallback). GDPval also combines an acceptance probability, review cost and a task mix into one net-time-saved number. What is missing is integration over a task-LENGTH distribution as a function of capability, for IT-services task types.

Calling the METR RCT 'assistant-mode speedup (kappa)' mislabels it. The AI-allowed arm includes agentic delegation, so it measures realized total speedup, not kappa alone. The follow-up's '30-50% withheld tasks' is actually 30-50% of developers withholding some tasks.

The RLI rise from about 2.5% to about 21% compares the paper with the live leaderboard. There are no CIs (n~240 gives a SE of roughly +/-2.6 pp at 21%), and the work is mostly creative/media, not IT/BPO.
'TH1.1 data file current to Sep 2026' is wrong. The YAML's newest model was released 7 Apr 2026; in Sep 2026 the dashboard was marked no longer actively updated.

Minor numeric errors: Gemini 3.1 Pro p50 is 384.1 (not 384.2) and GPT-5.2 p50 is 352.2 (not 352.3). Several METR notes have named authors that the record gave only as 'METR' (Alexander Barry; Whitfill, Wu, Becker, Rush; David Rein).
GDPval GPT-5.2 Pro 74.1% is unverified and should not be cited. GPT-5.2 Thinking 70.9% appears only in a search snippet of OpenAI's page (403 on fetch).

Checked separately: OpenAI's SWE-bench Verified split (196 tasks under 15 min, 45 over 1 h) is consistent with Epoch's 39% / 52% / 8% / 3 tasks over 4 h, but the OpenAI page itself was not opened. OSWorld abstract numbers (369 tasks, humans 72.36%, best model 12.24%) were verified.
verify.corrected_summary:
Benchmarks give a reasonably well-measured version of p(h,t) for software tasks. METR fits a logistic curve of success against log task length. The 50% horizon doubled about every 7 months over 2019-2025 (207 days), and faster since 2023 (about 129-131 days under Time Horizon 1.1). By spring 2026, METR's point estimates for frontier 50% horizons were about 6-12 hours (Gemini 3.1 Pro 384 min, Opus 4.6 719 min), with Claude Mythos Preview at about 1,045 min. Two caveats apply: METR says measurements above 16 hours are unreliable, and the confidence intervals are very wide (Opus 4.6: about 5 to 61 hours). 80% horizons are much shorter, about 54-186 min. My own back-of-envelope calculation (not METR's) gives an implied slope of about 0.6-0.95 per natural-log unit of task length. METR's March 2026 note says reasonable modelling choices move 80% horizons by up to 2x, and that noise on short tasks flattens the curve. So the slope is the least robust part of the fit.

Has anyone converted benchmark results into labor saved? Partly, in several ways, but never as a function of task length and capability.
- **Dollar values:** SWE-Lancer and the Remote Labor Index attach real market prices to tasks. Both measure what a fully delegated AI delivers (roughly q times p). SWE-Lancer's fallback cost analysis gives savings of 9-34%, but it assumes checking a solution is free.
- **Review included:** GDPval's 'try n times, then fix' scenario for GPT-5 gives a 1.39x speedup, about 28% of time saved, against about 90x naively. It uses the expert preference win rate as the chance an output is accepted, and a measured expert review time of about 109 minutes per task of roughly 7-9 hours (rho about 0.2-0.27).
- **The q and rho parameters:** METR has two data points. In a 2026 study, maintainers would not merge roughly half of SWE-bench-passing PRs; under merge criteria, one model's horizon was about 7x shorter. A 2025 pilot estimated that fixing a test-passing agent PR would take about a third of the original human time, but that rests on only 4 PRs and subjective estimates.
- **Realized speedup:** METR's randomized trials found a 19% slowdown in early 2025. Their late-2025 follow-up is imprecise and selection-biased, by METR's own account. These trials measure total speedup with AI allowed, not purely the assistant-mode parameter kappa.

So the working hypothesis needs refining rather than confirming. Intensive-margin estimates do exist: Anthropic's conversation study (gross of review), GDPval (net of review), and the METR trials. What no one has done is integrate p(h,t), q and rho over an hours-weighted task-length distribution for IT-services task types, or track how that net saving changes as capability rises. The Remote Labor Index's best automation rate rose from 2.5% (paper, Oct 2025) to about 21% (leaderboard, Oct 2026). That leaderboard reports no confidence intervals and covers mostly creative and media work.
verify.dataset_notes:
METR benchmark_results_1_1.yaml: public; confirmed. The newest model in it was released 2026-04-07 (Mythos Preview), so it is not current to Sep 2026. The doubling fit excludes points with p50 > 16 h.

HCAST: access 'on-request' is not confirmed by anything I opened. The abstract page does not state access terms, and the description's 'most tasks private' was not verified. Treat it as 'mostly private / unknown'.

GDPval gold subset: 220 tasks (5 per occupation x 44) are open-sourced per the abstract. The URL given is the paper, not the dataset host; the dataset location was not opened.

Remote Labor Index: 10 public and 230 private projects, confirmed from the paper. Leaderboard URL confirmed.

SWE-Lancer Diamond: 502 tasks worth $500,800, public, confirmed from the paper. The URL is the paper, not the code/data repo.

SWE-bench Verified: the Epoch page (https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-verified) confirms 484 of 500 tasks run and a 5-10% estimated error rate, but it does NOT describe the time-to-fix annotations. The difficulty buckets come from OpenAI's annotation release (https://openai.com/index/introducing-SWE-bench-verified/, not opened here: 196 tasks under 15 min, 45 over 1 h per search snippets). Epoch's analysis (https://epoch.ai/blog/what-skills-does-swe-bench-verified-evaluate, Brand and Denain, 13 Jun 2025) gives 39% under 15 min, 52% 15 min-1 h, 8% 1-4 h, and 3 tasks over 4 h.

METR maintainer-review data: release status unknown; confirmed authors are Whitfill, Wu, Becker, Rush.

TheAgentCompany: public via the paper; URL is the paper.

Anthropic productivity-gains: the research page was opened, but the public data-release location was not checked, so 'public' is unconfirmed for this specific dataset.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests would actually be merged by real maintainers of the repos.
works.method_plain: 4 active maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest (95 of the 500 SWE-bench Verified issues) blind-reviewed 296 agent PRs from Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 3.7 Sonnet, 4 Opus, 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-5, plus 47 original human 'golden' patches that had really been merged. Agent scores are rescaled by the golden-patch merge rate, which corrects for how noisy maintainers are. One attempt per issue, no chance to revise after feedback.
key_numbers: Maintainers re-approved only about 68% of the golden human patches. All agent scores are expressed relative to this baseline.
Normalized: the automated grader scores about 24.2 percentage points higher than maintainer merge decisions (SE 2.7). Roughly half of test-passing patches would not be merged.
Raw (unnormalized) gap: 34.9 pp (SE 2.2). Maintainer merge rates are about one-third to one-half of grader pass rates.
SOTA-models-only gap: 20.6 pp (SE 3.0).

Trend: maintainer-judged scores improve about 9.6 pp/yr slower than grader scores (SE 5.5; significant only at the 10% level). Raw trend gap is 15.5 pp/yr (SE 4.6). SOTA-only trend gap is 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1), not significant.
Time horizon for Claude Sonnet 4.5: about 50 minutes under the automated grader vs about 8 minutes under maintainer review, roughly a 7x overstatement.
Grader false negatives: 1 of 27 issues checked (3.7%).
Golden patches average about 17 lines changed.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the primary source for q. Normalized q is about 0.5 (raw q about 0.33-0.5) for one-shot agent output on small open-source fixes. It also suggests q may be rising more slowly than p: the gap between grader-passing and maintainer-acceptable code may widen over time, although that trend evidence is weak. Its horizon result implies q depends on h: the maintainer-judged horizon is about 7x shorter than the test-judged one. Maintainers also logged review time and time to write the fix from scratch, which would give rho directly, but the text does not report those aggregates.
works.limitations: Only 3 repos, which are mature Python libraries with high standards. The most recent model studied is Sonnet 4.5. Agents could not iterate on feedback, so q is a lower bound for an agent-plus-human loop. No CI, old issues. The review-time data was collected but not published (it may be available from METR on request). Indian IT maintenance on client codebases may have different, likely lower, code-quality bars.

works.title: Research Update: Towards Reconciling Slowdown with Time Horizons (Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation)
works.authors: David Rein (METR)
works.venue: METR blog, 12/13 August 2025 (also cross-posted to LessWrong)
works.what_measured: How agent success on real repo issues compares under test-based (algorithmic) scoring vs a human judgment of mergeability (holistic), and how long it takes to fix agent PRs.
works.method_plain: Claude 3.7 Sonnet in a basic agent scaffold attempted 18 real GitHub issues from stdlib-js and hypothesis. Human time per issue was 20 minutes to 4 hours, with a mean of 1.3 hours. Outputs were scored by hidden tests, then 15 were manually reviewed for mergeability, with an estimate of the time needed to bring each to mergeable state.
key_numbers: Algorithmic (test) success: 38% (±19%, 95% CI) on all 18 tasks. 27% (±20%) on the 15 reviewed tasks.
Holistic: 0 of 15 reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is.
Mean time to fix all reviewed PRs: about 42 minutes.
Mean time to fix test-passing PRs: about 26 minutes (minimum 15 minutes). The author calls this about one-third of the 1.3-hour average task time.
Among test-passing PRs (n=4): test coverage problems in 100%, documentation in 75%, lint/format/typing in 75%, other code quality in 50%, core functionality in 25%.
Every reviewed PR had at least 3 of the 5 problem types.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the best direct number for the cost of fixing passing AI output: about 0.33 of h for test-passing PRs (about 0.5 of h for all PRs), on top of review. It shows that q is not binary. Passing-but-unmergeable output still has partial value, because fixing it (about 26 minutes) is cheaper than doing the task from scratch (about 78 minutes). Consider replacing q*p with p*(1 - fix_share) in the formula. Read 'rho + fix' together as about 0.3-0.5 of h for 2025-era models.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (n=15 reviewed, n=4 passing). The author says not to take the absolute numbers seriously. One model, a weak scaffold and early-2025 capabilities. Fix times are subjective estimates.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: Causal effect of allowing AI tools (mainly Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on how long experienced developers take to complete real issues in their own repos, plus how their time was spent.
works.method_plain: Randomized controlled trial. 16 developers each worked on 246 real issues averaging about 2 hours, and each issue was randomly assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. Screen recordings were labeled by activity.
key_numbers: AI-allowed issues took 19% longer, a slowdown.
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and believed afterward they had sped up about 20%. Economics experts forecast a 39% speedup and ML experts 38%.
Developers accepted less than 44% of Cursor generations (Section C.1.4).
Reviewing and cleaning AI outputs took about 9% of AI-allowed time (44 issues with labeled recordings).
Waiting on AI generations took about 4% of AI-allowed time.
Survey: 75% of developers read every line of AI code, 56% often make major changes to clean it up, and 100% report needing to modify it.
Post-review implementation time averaged 15 minutes with AI vs 9 minutes without, not statistically significant.
works.relevance_to_theta: Main evidence for kappa (assistant mode) and an acceptance share for assistant mode. In this setting, kappa was negative for experts on familiar large repos in early 2025. Review and cleanup of about 9% of total time is an observed rho-like quantity for assistant use. The less-than-44% acceptance of generations is a q analogue for assistant mode.
works.limitations: Experts working in their own repos (high familiarity, high quality bar), which is unlike junior Indian IT staff on client code. Early-2025 tools. The paper reports time-allocation details mostly as figures, so exact numbers beyond those above were not visible to me. METR has marked these results as out of date.

works.title: Uplift update (late-2025 follow-up to the developer productivity RCT)
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
works.what_measured: Updated estimate of AI's effect on developer task time with late-2025 tools.
works.method_plain: Same RCT design. 57 developers, 143 repos and more than 800 tasks, with data collection starting August 2025.
key_numbers: Original developers: -18% time change, i.e. a speedup (CI -38% to +9%).
Newly recruited developers: -4% (CI -15% to +9%).
Early-2025 study for comparison: +19% (CI +2% to +39%).
30-50% of developers said they skipped submitting some tasks because they did not want to work without AI, a selection problem.
METR calls the data 'very weak evidence' for the size of the speedup. The estimate is likely a lower bound.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows kappa moving from negative toward a modest positive value (about 0.04-0.18) between early and late 2025. This gives a time path for kappa(t), but with very wide confidence intervals. It also flags that RCTs are becoming hard to run as AI use becomes the default.
works.limitations: Selection bias is acknowledged. Concurrent multi-agent work breaks time tracking. Confidence intervals include zero. Same expert population as the earlier study.

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika et al. (47 authors; Center for AI Safety and Scale AI)
works.what_measured: Share of real paid freelance projects where an AI agent's deliverable would be accepted by a reasonable client, judged holistically against the human deliverable.
works.method_plain: 240 real freelance projects (230 used for evaluation) with known human time and price. Agents produce deliverables. Trained evaluators judge whether a client would accept each one, with 3 votes per item and 94.4% agreement. The authors say LLM-based automatic grading is not feasible.
key_numbers: Human mean completion time: 28.9 hours (median 11.5). Mean cost: $632.6 (median $200). Total: more than 6,000 hours, worth more than $140,000.
Automation rate: Manus 2.5%, Grok 4 2.1%, Sonnet 4.5 2.1%, GPT-5 (CLI) 1.7%, ChatGPT agent 1.3%, GPT-5 (CUA) 0.8%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.8%.
Dollars earned: at most $1,720 of $143,991 (Manus).
Failure modes among AI deliverables: poor quality 45.6%, incomplete 35.7%, corrupted files 17.6%, inconsistencies 14.8%.
works.relevance_to_theta: A holistic, client-acceptance measure of q*p on long tasks (h from about 10 to 30 hours). Near zero for late-2025 agents in full-delegation mode, which is consistent with the logistic p(h) at large h. Its dollar-weighting is analogous to f_j and w_j weighting. Useful as an upper anchor for the long-task tail of f_j(h) in consulting, design and BPO-adjacent work.
works.limitations: Projects are mostly creative/multimedia freelance work (design, audio, video), not IT maintenance or testing. All-or-nothing acceptance ignores partial value and the assistant mode. Late-2025 agents only.

works.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
works.authors: Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, ..., Graham Neubig (CMU and others)
works.what_measured: Share of tasks in a simulated software company (engineering, project management, HR, admin, finance) that agents complete autonomously.
works.method_plain: A self-hosted company intranet with GitLab, chat, documents and simulated coworkers. Tasks are checked by checkpoints, which gives both full-completion and partial-credit scores.
key_numbers: Abstract: the most competitive agent completes 30% of tasks autonomously.
Secondary coverage, not verified against the paper: Gemini 2.5 Pro 30.3% full / 39.3% partial; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 26.3%; 175 tasks.
works.relevance_to_theta: Closest benchmark to an IT-services task mix: software engineering plus the admin and PM work that resembles BPO and consulting. Its by-category results could provide a per-service-line p_j. Scoring is algorithmic (checkpoints), so it still needs a q correction.
works.limitations: Simulated environment. Per-category numbers were not confirmed from the abstract page. Algorithmic scoring. Models from 2024-25.

works.title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?
works.authors: Samuel Miserendino, Michele Wang, Tejal Patwardhan, Johannes Heidecke (OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Pass rate and dollar value earned on more than 1,400 real Upwork software tasks, worth about $1M in total.
works.method_plain: Individual-contributor (IC) coding tasks are graded with end-to-end tests that experienced engineers triple-verified. Manager tasks, where the model picks the best implementation proposal, are compared with the choice the real hiring manager made.
key_numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, IC SWE full set: 21.1% pass@1; earned $89k of $415k.
IC SWE Diamond set: 26.2%; $58k of $236k.
Manager full set: 47.0%; $314k of $585k.
Manager Diamond set: 44.9%; $150k of $265k.
Total earned: more than $400k of $1M.
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives dollar-weighted p on real outsourced software tasks, the same market Indian IT sells into. Ties task price (a proxy for h) to pass rate, which lets you fit p(h) on outsourcing-like work. The manager tasks are a direct analogue of the review/selection role, a rough capability check for rho.
works.limitations: End-to-end tests are stronger than unit tests but still algorithmic, so a q correction is needed. Single codebase (Expensify). 2024-era models in the paper.

works.title: The Rise of AI Teammates in Software Engineering (SE) 3.0: How Autonomous Coding Agents Are Reshaping Software Engineering (AIDev dataset)
works.authors: Hao Li, Haoxiang Zhang, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.what_measured: Large-scale observational data on agent-authored pull requests in real GitHub repos.
works.method_plain: Collected more than 456,000 PRs by OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code across 61,000 repos and 47,000 developers. Compared agent and human PRs on acceptance, speed and complexity.
key_numbers: More than 456,000 agent PRs across 61,000 repos.
Abstract: agent PRs are 'accepted less frequently' than human PRs and are structurally simpler. No exact rate is given in the abstract.
works.relevance_to_theta: A public dataset from which q (merge share of agent PRs, weighted by task type and size) and review latency can be estimated in deployment, including over time. This is the most promising open input for a q_j(t) series.
works.limitations: Merge is an imperfect proxy for acceptance. Many Codex PRs are probably in the user's own repos and self-merged, which inflates acceptance. There is no measure of reviewer time or of edits after merge. Mostly open-source projects.

works.title: Why Agentic-PRs Get Rejected: A Comparative Study of Coding Agents
works.authors: Sota Nakashima, Yuta Ishimoto, Masanari Kondo, Yasutaka Kamei, Shane McIntosh
works.what_measured: Acceptance rates of agent vs human PRs in repos with at least 100 stars, and coded reasons for rejection.
works.method_plain: Used the AIDev-pop subset. Merged PRs count as accepted and closed-unmerged as rejected. Hand-coded 654 rejected PRs (109 per group).
key_numbers: 67.9% of rejected PRs have no explicit feedback.
Rejection reasons, agent vs human: alternative solution chosen 9.2% vs 15.6%; inactive 7.5% vs 2.8%; too large 1.5% vs 0.0%; 'no confidence in AI-generated code' 0.2%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Deployment-level q relative to a human baseline: agent acceptance divided by human acceptance ranges from about 0.67 (Copilot/Devin) to about 1.04 (Codex). Agent-to-human ratios like these are what q should mean. This is far higher than METR's about 0.5, which shows that q depends on selection: what developers chose to delegate, and whose repo it is.
works.limitations: Acceptance is not conditioned on passing tests and is not linked to task difficulty. Selection into delegation is strong. Most rejections have no stated reason. No review-time data.

works.title: Comparing AI Coding Agents: A Task-Stratified Analysis of Pull Request Acceptance
works.authors: Giovanni Pinna, Jingzhi Gong, David Williams, Federica Sarro
works.what_measured: PR acceptance by agent and task type, and its trend over time.
works.method_plain: 7,156 closed AIDev PRs in permissively licensed repos with at least one outside review, broken down into 9 task categories.
key_numbers: Documentation tasks: 82.1% acceptance. New features: 66.1%.
Codex: 59.6-88.6% across categories. Claude Code: 92.3% on docs, 72.6% on features. Cursor: 80.4% on fixes.
Devin is the only agent with a consistent upward trend (+0.77 pp/week over 32 weeks). The others are flat.
Overall rate in this subset is about 69% (from search summary; not confirmed on the abstract page).
works.relevance_to_theta: Task-type variation in q maps onto the j index: docs and tests vs features vs fixes. A template for estimating q_j.
works.limitations: Open source, externally reviewed PRs only. No difficulty or length (h) control. No review time.

works.title: The AI Productivity Paradox Research Report (2025) and AI Engineering Report 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash
works.authors: Faros AI (Faros Research)
works.what_measured: Correlation between team AI adoption and engineering telemetry: throughput, PR volume, review time, bugs, incidents.
works.method_plain: Telemetry from version control, CI/CD, task trackers and incident systems. 2025: more than 10,000 developers in 1,255 teams. 2026: about 22,000 developers in 4,000 teams. Compares each team's lowest-adoption quarters with its highest-adoption quarters, using Spearman correlations.
key_numbers: 2025, high-adoption teams: +21% tasks completed, +98% PRs merged, +91% PR review time, +154% average PR size, +9% bugs per developer. No significant company-level delivery improvement.

2026 landing page (https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash): median review time up 5x; PR size +51%; task throughput +33.7%; epics +66.2%; bugs per PR +28.7%; incidents per PR +242.7%; code churn +861%; 25% of PRs reviewed by an AI agent.
Search summary, not seen on the pages I opened: review time +199.6% mean / +441.5% median, and 31% more PRs merged without review.
works.relevance_to_theta: Industry evidence that review is the bottleneck. Review time grows roughly in proportion to PR volume, so per-unit rho does not fall much. The gap between team-level task gains and flat company-level delivery is an aggregation warning: summing theta_j over w_j may overstate firm-level s.
works.limitations: Vendor reports. Correlational, not causal. Methods are only partly disclosed. Review time is elapsed time, not effort hours. Not peer reviewed.

works.title: AI-Generated 'Workslop' Is Destroying Productivity
works.authors: Kate Niederhoffer, Gabriella Rosen Kellerman, Angela Lee, Alex Liebscher, Kristina Rapuano, Jeffrey T. Hancock (BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab)
works.what_measured: How often workers receive low-effort AI-generated work ('workslop') and the time it costs recipients.
works.method_plain: Online self-report survey of US full-time desk workers, September 2025.
key_numbers: From BetterUp's page (https://www.betterup.com/workslop): 1,150 US full-time desk workers surveyed; 40% received workslop in the last month; about 2 hours on average to resolve each incident; $186 per employee per month; $9M per year for a 10,000-person company (calculation not shown).
Secondary only, not confirmed in a primary source I opened: about 15% (often quoted as 15.4%) of content received is workslop, and 1 hour 56 minutes per incident.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows review and cleanup cost pushed downstream onto colleagues. Self-reviewing alone understates rho, and firm-level net savings should subtract this cost. Relevant to the BPO and consulting j categories, where output is documents rather than code.
works.limitations: Self-report, not a controlled study. The HBR text I could fetch was truncated, so the core statistics come from BetterUp's own page. The dollar figure is an extrapolation.

works.title: Delegation and Verification under AI
works.authors: Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi
works.what_measured: Theory: a worker chooses how much to delegate to AI and how hard to verify, with convex verification cost, an imperfect detection function and a redo cost.
works.method_plain: Formal optimization model with an illustrative calibration on the Collab-CXR radiology dataset (324 cases, 33 clinicians).
key_numbers: Three regimes: manual work, delegation without verification, and verified delegation. Switches between them are abrupt.
Calibrated clinician: success alone 0.447, AI alone 0.368, with AI 0.395. Model costs: execution 172.5 vs assisted 116.8. Model predicts staying manual.
Weak verifiers rationally over-delegate, and better AI can widen the region where quality degrades ('verification amplification').
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives microfoundations for the max{..., kappa} switch in the formula, and shows that rho should be chosen endogenously, trading off detection against cost. Implies theta_j depends on reviewer skill (alpha), which matters for India's junior-heavy pyramid.
works.limitations: Theory with a single-clinician illustration. Medical, not IT. Its cost units are not measured review time.

works.title: Some Simple Economics of AGI
works.authors: Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui, Jane Wu
works.what_measured: Conceptual model: the cost to automate falls exponentially while the cost to verify is bounded by human time.
works.method_plain: Theory and essay (112 pages). Argues that verification bandwidth becomes the binding constraint, and names 'measurability-biased technical change'.
key_numbers: No quantitative parameters were reported on the abstract page I opened.
works.relevance_to_theta: Supports modeling rho(t) as falling much more slowly than 1-p(t), so theta_j levels off near 1 - rho rather than 1. Also suggests task measurability (how cheaply output can be checked) as a dimension for splitting j.
works.limitations: Not empirical. Only the abstract was read.

research.stream_summary:
The working hypothesis largely holds. Benchmarks and exposure scores say whether AI can touch a task. Holistic-review studies show that only part of 'passing' AI output removes labor, and that checking it costs real time.

Best numbers for q:
- METR's March 2026 note: after correcting for maintainer noise (maintainers re-merged only 68% of real human patches), about half of SWE-bench-passing agent patches would not be merged. Normalized q is about 0.5; the raw ratio is 0.33-0.5.
- Weak evidence that this gap is widening by about 10 pp/yr, so q(t) may not rise as fast as p(t).
- In the field, agent PRs on GitHub are merged at 55-86%, against 83% for human PRs. Relative q is about 0.67-1.0, because people delegate easy tasks and often merge into their own repos.

Best numbers for rho:
- METR's August 2025 holistic study: fixing test-passing agent PRs took about 26 minutes on tasks averaging 1.3 hours, about 0.33 of h. For all PRs it took about 42 minutes, about 0.5 of h. Tiny sample.
- METR's RCT: about 9% of AI-allowed time went to reviewing and cleaning AI output, and fewer than 44% of generations were accepted.
- Faros telemetry: review time up 91% (2025) and a 5x rise in median review time (2026) as PR volume rose. Review grows with output, so per-unit rho does not shrink much.

Kappa, the assistant-mode speedup, went from -19% (early 2025) to about +4-18% (late 2025) for expert developers.

Agent-only acceptance on long real projects is near zero: 2.5% at best on the Remote Labor Index, and 30% of TheAgentCompany tasks.

Recommendation: replace the binary q with a 'fix-up fraction'. Passing-but-unmergeable work still saves time. Treat rho as rising with reviewer inexperience, as the theory papers suggest.
gaps_noticed: No study measures reviewer time as a share of human task time (rho) at scale as a function of task length h. METR collected maintainer review times and from-scratch times in the March 2026 study but did not publish the aggregates. Ask METR.
No holistic review study on client-style enterprise maintenance or testing code, the core of Indian IT. All q estimates come from open-source Python or JS repos with high quality bars.

Nothing measures q and rho for non-code outputs relevant to BPO (tickets, documents, reconciliation). Workslop is self-report only, and its exact percentages could not be confirmed from a primary source.
No study measures q for agents allowed to iterate on reviewer feedback. All of METR's holistic numbers are one-shot, so they are lower bounds for the 'delegate plus revise' mode.
Deployment acceptance data (AIDev) is not conditioned on test-passing or on task length, so it cannot be mapped directly onto q*p(h). Merged PRs are not tracked for later reverts or bugs.
The q trend over time is weakly identified (METR's trend gap is significant only at 10%; Devin is the only agent with a rising trend in AIDev).
Formal delegation and verification models are not calibrated on software or IT data. The only calibration found is radiology.

Could not confirm the oft-cited Copilot acceptance rate (about 27-30%) from the Ziegler et al. 2022 abstract. Also could not confirm SWE-bench Verified human-baseline and TheAgentCompany per-category numbers from primary text.

datasets.name: AIDev (agentic PRs on GitHub)
datasets.description: More than 456k PRs by Codex, Devin, Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code across 61k repos, with merge status, timestamps, review comments and task labels (used by the AIDev-pop studies). Can be used to estimate q_j(t) and review latency.

datasets.name: METR maintainer-review data on SWE-bench-passing PRs
datasets.description: 296 agent PRs and 47 golden patches with merge decisions, progress scores (0-100), maintainer review time and time to write from scratch. The direct input for q and rho. Release status is unclear; contact METR.

datasets.name: METR developer RCT screen-recording labels
datasets.description: Activity-labeled time use (reading generations, AI code cleaning, waiting, prompting) for 246 issues. Gives rho and kappa for assistant mode.

datasets.name: Remote Labor Index
datasets.description: 240 freelance projects with human hours, prices and holistic client-acceptance judgments. 10 projects are public and 230 are private.

datasets.name: SWE-Lancer
datasets.description: More than 1,400 Upwork software tasks with real dollar payouts and end-to-end tests (the Diamond subset is open-sourced). Use it to fit p(h) on outsourcing-like work, with price as a proxy for length.

datasets.name: TheAgentCompany
datasets.description: 175 tasks in a simulated software company across SDE, PM, HR, admin and finance, with checkpoint scoring. Gives per-category p for IT and BPO-like work.

datasets.name: Faros AI engineering telemetry
datasets.description: Aggregated vendor telemetry on review time, PR volume, bugs and incidents vs AI adoption. Only summary statistics are public.

datasets.name: BetterUp/Stanford workslop survey
datasets.description: Survey of 1,150 US desk workers on receiving low-quality AI work and the time to fix it. Microdata does not appear to be public.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests would actually be merged by real maintainers of those repositories.
works.method_plain: 4 active maintainers (2 for scikit-learn, 1 for Sphinx, 1 for pytest) reviewed 296 agent PRs on 95 of the 500 SWE-bench Verified issues (19%). The PRs came from Claude 3.5 Sonnet (old), Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus, Claude 4.5 Sonnet and GPT-5. The maintainers also reviewed 47 original human 'golden' patches that had really been merged, a randomly chosen half of the golden patches. Agent scores are rescaled by the golden-patch merge rate, which corrects for how noisy maintainer decisions are. Agents got one attempt and could not revise after feedback. CI tools were not active, so maintainers had no linting or tests.
key_numbers: Maintainers re-approved about 68% of the golden human patches. Normalized agent scores are expressed relative to this baseline.

Normalized gap: automated-grader pass rates exceed maintainer merge rates by about 24.2 percentage points (SE 2.7). Headline: roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged, even after adjusting for maintainer noise.
Raw (unnormalized) gap: 34.9 pp (SE 2.2). Appendix A4: under this specification, maintainer merge rates are roughly one-third to one-half of grader pass rates.
Gap for state-of-the-art models only: 20.6 pp (SE 3.0).

Trend: maintainer-judged scores improve about 9.6 pp/yr more slowly than grader scores (SE 5.5; weak evidence). Raw trend gap: 15.5 pp/yr (SE 4.6). SOTA-only trend gap: 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1), not significant.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 time horizon: about 50 minutes under the automated grader vs about 8 minutes under maintainer review, roughly 7x.
Grader false negatives (valid patch rejected by the grader): 1 of 27 issues checked (3.7%), from 31 patches.
Golden patches change about 17 lines on average.
works.relevance_to_theta: The primary source for q. Normalized q is about 0.5 for one-shot agent output on small open-source Python fixes. On a raw basis, merge rates are one-third to one-half of pass rates. There is weak evidence that the grader/maintainer gap widens over time (normalized trend about 1.7 SE from zero; the SOTA-only trend is not significant), so q(t) may lag p(t). The horizon result (50 vs 8 minutes) implies acceptance falls with task length, i.e. q depends on h. Maintainers were asked to record review time and the time to write a proper PR from scratch, which would give rho directly, but the note does not report these values.
works.limitations: Only 3 mature Python repos with high standards. The newest model is Sonnet 4.5. One attempt, no iteration on feedback, so q is a lower bound for an agent-plus-human loop. No CI. Old issues. The review-time and from-scratch-time data were collected but are not reported, and the note says nothing about releasing them (any 'on request' availability is unconfirmed). Client codebases in Indian IT may have different quality bars.
works.corrections: Citation and all key numbers match the source. Additions: the 47 golden patches are a randomly chosen half (the note says maintainers reviewed only half, chosen at random). The 'one-third to one-half' statement comes from Appendix A4 using raw rates. The limitation that review-time data 'may be available from METR on request' is not supported by the page, which does not mention any data release, so it is reworded as unconfirmed.

works.title: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation
works.authors: David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: How agent success on real repository issues compares under test-based (algorithmic) scoring and under human judgment of mergeability (holistic), and roughly how long it takes to fix the agent PRs.
works.method_plain: Claude 3.7 Sonnet in an Inspect ReAct agent scaffold, with little elicitation, attempted 18 real GitHub issues: 15 from stdlib-js and 3 from hypothesis. Human time per issue was 20 minutes to 4 hours, mean 1.3 hours. Outputs were scored by hidden tests. 15 were then manually reviewed for mergeability, with a rough estimate of the time needed to make each one mergeable.
key_numbers: Algorithmic (test) success: 38% (±19%, 95% CI) on all 18 issues; 27% (±20%) on the 15 reviewed.
Holistic: 0 of 15 reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is.
Mean estimated time to fix, all reviewed PRs: about 42 minutes.
Mean estimated time to fix, test-passing PRs: about 26 minutes (minimum 15). The author puts this at about one-third of the 1.3-hour mean human task time.
Among test-passing PRs (n=4), share with each problem type: test coverage 100%, documentation 75%, lint/format/typing 75%, other code quality 50%, core functionality 25%.
All 15 reviewed PRs had at least 3 of the 5 problem types; 60% had at least 4 and 20% had all 5.
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a rough direct number for the cost of fixing passing AI output: about one-third of h for test-passing PRs (about 0.5 of h for all reviewed PRs). This is fix time, separate from review time. It shows that acceptance (q) is not binary, because fixing passing-but-unmergeable output (about 26 minutes) is cheaper than doing the task from scratch (about 78 minutes). This supports replacing q*p with p*(1 - fix_share). 'rho + fix' of about 0.3-0.5 of h is a very rough, single-model, early-2025 anchor.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (15 reviewed, 4 passing). The author calls the time-to-fix estimates very rough and high variance. One model with a weakly elicited scaffold, so the results are not an upper bound on agent performance. Large mature repos with strict standards, and a selection toward issues with many explicit tests.
works.corrections: Title corrected: the page's title and H1 are 'Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation', and 'Towards Reconciling Slowdown with Time Horizons' appears only in the URL slug. Date shown is 13 August 2025. The scaffold is Inspect ReAct, not just 'basic'. Repo split added (stdlib-js 15, hypothesis 3). The LessWrong cross-post could not be confirmed and is removed from the venue. 'Author says not to take the absolute numbers seriously' is not a confirmed quote; it is replaced with the page's wording that the fix-time estimates are 'very rough/high variance'. Added that 60% of PRs had at least 4 problem types and 20% had all 5.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth (Beth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.venue: arXiv:2507.09089 (v1 12 July 2025, v2 25 July 2025); METR blog 10 July 2025
works.what_measured: The causal effect of allowing AI tools (mainly Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on how long experienced developers take to complete real issues in mature projects they know well, plus how their time was spent.
works.method_plain: Randomized controlled trial. 16 developers completed 246 tasks averaging 2.0 hours, and each task was randomly assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. A subset of screen recordings was labeled by activity.
key_numbers: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%, a slowdown.
Developers forecast 24% shorter completion times beforehand and estimated 20% shorter afterward. Economics experts forecast 39% shorter, ML experts 38% shorter.
Developers accepted '<44%' of Cursor generations (Appendix C.1.4; the paper writes '<<44%'). No data for 3 developers using their own subscriptions.
About 9% of AI-allowed time was spent reviewing and cleaning AI outputs, measured on 44 issues with valid labeled screen recordings.
About 4% of AI-allowed time was spent waiting on AI generations (Section C.2.9, Table 1).
Survey: 75% read every line of AI-generated code, 56% often need to make major changes to clean it up, and 100% report needing to modify it.
Mean post-review implementation time: 15 minutes AI-allowed vs 9 minutes AI-disallowed, not statistically significant (C.2.7, C.3.4).
works.relevance_to_theta: The main early-2025 evidence on kappa (assistant mode). For experts on familiar large repos, kappa was negative (about -0.19). Review and cleanup take about 9% of total AI-allowed time. This is a rho-like quantity, but it is a share of total task time in assistant mode, not review time per unit of delegated output. The under-44% acceptance of generations is a loose q analogue for assistant mode.
works.limitations: Experts in their own repos (high familiarity, high quality bar), unlike junior Indian IT staff on client code. Early-2025 tools. Time-allocation details are mostly in figures. The 9% figure comes from a 44-issue subset. Superseded in part by METR's February 2026 update.
works.corrections: Every key number was confirmed in the arXiv HTML. The author is listed on arXiv as Elizabeth Barnes (Beth Barnes). arXiv submission dates were added. The claim 'METR has marked these results as out of date' was not checked against a source and is removed; the February 2026 update is noted as superseding it in part. Acceptance is written in the paper as '<<44%'.

works.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
works.what_measured: An updated estimate of AI's effect on developer task time with late-2025 tools, plus why METR is changing its study design.
works.method_plain: The same RCT design, run from August 2025. 57 developers (10 from the original study, 47 new) across 143 repos and more than 800 tasks.
key_numbers: Original developers (the 10 who returned): -18% change in task time, i.e. a speedup (CI -38% to +9%).
Newly recruited developers: -4% (CI -15% to +9%).
Early-2025 study for comparison: +19% (CI +2% to +39%).
30-50% of developers said they skipped submitting some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.
METR calls the data 'only very weak evidence' for the size of the increase and says the estimate is likely a lower bound on the true effect.
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests kappa moved from negative (early 2025) toward a modest positive value (point estimates of about 0.04-0.18 time saved) for tools used from August 2025 on. Every confidence interval includes zero, and the 0.18 comes from only 10 returning developers. It also shows that RCTs are getting hard to run as AI use becomes the default.
works.limitations: Selection bias is acknowledged: task skipping, developers declining to take part, and a pay cut from $150/hr to $50/hr. Time tracking is unreliable with concurrent agents. Some developers did not complete AI-disallowed tasks. Confidence intervals include zero.
works.corrections: Title corrected. The post is titled 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design'; 'Uplift update' is only the URL slug. Added that the -18% estimate covers only the 10 returning developers, plus the composition (10 original, 47 new). Data collection is from August 2025 onward, so 'late 2025' is approximate.

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika et al. (47 authors; Center for AI Safety and Scale AI)
works.what_measured: The share of real paid freelance projects where an AI agent's deliverable would be accepted by a reasonable client, judged holistically against the human deliverable.
works.method_plain: 240 real Upwork-style projects across 23 subcategories with known human time and price. 230 form the private test set and 10 are public. Agents produce deliverables, and trained human evaluators judge whether a client would accept each one. The main text describes majority voting over three evaluations; Appendix B.2 describes two evaluations with a third to break ties. The authors say automating the evaluation with LLMs is not currently feasible.
key_numbers: Human completion time: mean 28.9 hours, median 11.5. Cost: mean $632.6, median $200. In total, more than 6,000 hours and over $140,000 ($143,991 maximum earnable).
Automation rate: Manus 2.5%, Grok 4 2.1%, Sonnet 4.5 2.1%, GPT-5 (CLI) 1.7%, ChatGPT agent 1.3%, GPT-5 (CUA) 0.8%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.8%.
Dollars earned: at most $1,720 of $143,991 (Manus).
Inter-annotator agreement on automation rate: 94.4%.
Failure modes among AI deliverables (not mutually exclusive, about 400 evaluations): poor quality 45.6%, incomplete 35.7%, corrupted files 17.6%, inconsistencies 14.8%.
works.relevance_to_theta: A holistic, client-acceptance measure of the combined q*p on long tasks (median about 11.5 hours, mean about 29). It is near zero for late-2025 agents working alone, which is consistent with a logistic p(h) at large h. Its dollar weighting is analogous to hours-weighting by f_j and w_j. Use it as an anchor for the long-task tail in design, data and consulting-adjacent work.
works.limitations: A broad multi-sector mix. By subcategory name, roughly 13 of 23 subcategories are design, art, audio, video, 3D or game work, but the text does not give shares, so 'mostly creative' is unconfirmed. Few projects are IT maintenance or testing. All-or-nothing acceptance ignores partial value and assistant mode. Late-2025 agents only.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Voting procedure clarified: the main text says three votes, but Appendix B.2 says two plus a tie-breaker. The failure-mode shares are not mutually exclusive. The limitation 'mostly creative/multimedia' is softened, because the paper lists 23 subcategories (including web development, data analysis, data entry, translation and law) without giving shares. Affiliations (CAIS, Scale AI) confirmed on the HTML page.

works.title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
works.authors: Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, et al., Graham Neubig (21 authors; CMU and others)
works.venue: arXiv:2412.14161; NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (poster)
works.what_measured: The share of tasks in a simulated software company (software engineering, project management, data science, HR, admin, finance) that agents complete on their own.
works.method_plain: A self-hosted company intranet with GitLab, chat, documents and simulated coworkers. Checkpoints grade each task, giving a full-completion score and a partial-credit score.
key_numbers: Abstract: the most competitive agent completes 30% of tasks autonomously.
Full evaluation set: 175 tasks. Gemini 2.5 Pro: 30.3% full completion, 39.3% partial score.
Claude 3.7 Sonnet: 26.3% full completion, 36.4% partial score (OpenHands 0.28.1).

Task counts in Appendix B: 69 SDE, 28 PM, 14 DS, 15 Admin, 29 HR, 12 Finance (sums to 167; the remaining 8 were not checked). DS, Admin and Finance have the lowest success rates. Per-category percentages are in Appendix Table 5 and were not confirmed.
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest benchmark to an IT-services task mix: software engineering plus PM and admin work resembling BPO and consulting. Its per-category results could give a per-service-line p_j. Scoring is algorithmic (checkpoints), so it still needs a q correction. The 30% is checkpoint-scored autonomous completion, not client acceptance.
works.limitations: Simulated environment. Per-category percentages not confirmed. Algorithmic scoring. Models from 2024-25.
works.corrections: The numbers listed as 'secondary coverage, not verified' are now confirmed in the arXiv HTML: 175 tasks, Gemini 2.5 Pro 30.3% / 39.3%, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 26.3% (partial 36.4%). The NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks poster was confirmed through the OpenReview API, though the arXiv page itself lists no venue. Author count (21) added. Per-category counts added; they sum to 167, not 175.

works.title: SWE-Lancer: Can Frontier LLMs Earn $1 Million from Real-World Freelance Software Engineering?
works.authors: Samuel Miserendino, Michele Wang, Tejal Patwardhan, Johannes Heidecke (OpenAI)
works.venue: arXiv:2502.12115 (v4 29 May 2025); Proceedings of ICML 2025, PMLR 267:44412-44450
works.what_measured: Pass rate and dollar value earned on 1,488 real Upwork software tasks from the Expensify repository, worth $1M in total payouts.
works.method_plain: Individual-contributor (IC) coding tasks are graded with end-to-end tests that experienced engineers triple-verified. Manager tasks, where the model picks the best implementation proposal, are graded against the proposal the original engineering manager chose.
key_numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, IC SWE full set: 21.1% pass@1; earned $89k of $415k.
IC SWE Diamond: 26.2%; $58k of $236k.
SWE Manager full set: 47.0%; $314k of $585k.
SWE Manager Diamond: 44.9%; $150k of $265k.
Total earned (full set): $403k of $1M (33.7%). Diamond total: $208k of $501k (36.1%).
Task values range from $50 bug fixes to $32,000 feature implementations (abstract).
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives dollar-weighted p on real outsourced software tasks, the same market Indian IT sells into. Task price (a proxy for h) can be tied to pass rate to fit p(h) on outsourcing-like work. Manager tasks are an analogue of the review and selection role.
works.limitations: End-to-end tests are stronger than unit tests but still algorithmic, so a q correction is needed. Single codebase (Expensify). The paper evaluates 2024-era models. The open-source harness may differ from OpenAI's internal scaffold.
works.corrections: Citation and numbers match. Added the exact task count (1,488), the ICML 2025 PMLR entry (confirmed on proceedings.mlr.press), and the total earned of $403k. Only the Diamond split (502 tasks, $500,800) is public; the full set is reportedly available on request.

works.title: The Rise of AI Teammates in Software Engineering (SE) 3.0: How Autonomous Coding Agents Are Reshaping Software Engineering
works.authors: Hao Li, Haoxiang Zhang, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.what_measured: Large-scale observational data on agent-authored pull requests in real GitHub repos (the AIDev dataset).
works.method_plain: Collected more than 456,000 PRs by OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Claude Code across 61,000 repos and 47,000 developers. Compared agent and human PRs on acceptance, speed and complexity.
key_numbers: More than 456,000 agent PRs across 61,000 repos and 47,000 developers (paper version).
Abstract: agents are often faster than humans, but their PRs 'are accepted less frequently'. No rate is given in the abstract.
Current dataset (Hugging Face card, v5): 7,685,281 PRs across 961,168 repos from six agents (adds Google Jules), cutoff 31 March 2026, CC-BY-4.0.
works.relevance_to_theta: A public dataset from which the merge share of agent PRs (a deployment q) and review latency can be estimated, including over time. It includes review, comment and timeline tables. Task-type labels are derived by downstream papers and are not listed on the dataset card.
works.limitations: Merge is an imperfect proxy for acceptance. Acceptance is not conditioned on passing tests or on task size. No measure of reviewer effort or of edits and reverts after merge. The claim that many Codex PRs are self-merged in the user's own repos is the researcher's conjecture, not a finding of the paper.
works.corrections: Citation and abstract numbers match. Added the current dataset version (v5, 7.69M PRs, six agents, CC-BY-4.0 on Hugging Face). The self-merge explanation is labeled as unconfirmed conjecture.

works.title: Why Agentic-PRs Get Rejected: A Comparative Study of Coding Agents
works.authors: Sota Nakashima, Yuta Ishimoto, Masanari Kondo, Shane McIntosh, Yasutaka Kamei
works.what_measured: Acceptance rates of agent and human PRs in repos with at least 100 stars, and hand-coded reasons for rejection.
works.method_plain: Used the AIDev-pop subset (the version as of 20 October 2025). Open PRs were excluded; merged PRs count as accepted and closed-unmerged PRs as rejected. 654 rejected PRs were hand-coded, 109 sampled from each of 6 groups (5 agents plus humans).
key_numbers: 67.9% of rejected PRs have no explicit feedback.
Rejection reasons, agent vs human: alternative solution chosen 9.2% vs 15.6%; inactive 7.5% vs 2.8%; too large 1.5% vs 0.0%; no confidence in AI-generated code 0.2% vs 0.0%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Deployment-level acceptance relative to a human baseline. The ratio of agent to human acceptance ranges from about 0.67 (Copilot, Devin) to about 1.04 (Codex). This differs from METR's q, which is conditioned on passing tests and on fixed tasks. The gap between them most likely reflects selection into delegation and repo ownership, but this paper does not test that.
works.limitations: Acceptance is not conditioned on passing tests and not linked to task difficulty or length. Strong selection into what gets delegated. Most rejections have no stated reason. No review-time data.
works.corrections: Author order corrected: the arXiv lists Shane McIntosh before Yasutaka Kamei. Added the AIDev-pop version date and the exclusion of open PRs. All numbers confirmed.

works.title: Comparing AI Coding Agents: A Task-Stratified Analysis of Pull Request Acceptance
works.authors: Giovanni Pinna, Jingzhi Gong, David Williams, Federica Sarro
works.venue: arXiv:2602.08915 (v1 9 Feb 2026, v2 7 May 2026); accepted to the MSR'26 Mining Challenge Track
works.what_measured: PR acceptance by agent and task type, and how it changes over time.
works.method_plain: 7,156 closed PRs, filtered from 33,596 in AIDev-pop. Kept only repos with MIT or Apache-2.0 licenses and PRs with at least one review or comment from someone other than the creator. Stratified into 9 task categories (chore, docs, ci, build, refactor, feat, fix, test, perf).
key_numbers: Documentation tasks: 82.1% acceptance; new features: 66.1%.
Codex: 59.6-88.6% across the 9 categories. Claude Code: 92.3% on docs, 72.6% on features. Cursor: 80.4% on fixes.
Devin is the only agent with a consistent positive trend: +0.77 percentage points per week (R² = 0.34) over 32 active weeks, from about 60% to about 80%. The others are largely stable.
Overall acceptance in the filtered set: 69.3% (Table 1).
works.relevance_to_theta: Task-type variation in acceptance maps onto the j index (docs and tests vs features vs fixes), which makes this a template for estimating q_j.
works.limitations: Open-source, permissively licensed repos only. No control for difficulty or length (h). No review time. High week-to-week variance in the trends.
works.corrections: Overall acceptance confirmed as 69.3% in the HTML Table 1, no longer a search-summary figure. The filter is 'at least one review or comment from someone other than the creator', not strictly 'one outside review'. Added the v2 date and the category list. The Devin trend is reported in the paper as '+0.77% per week' (percentage points).

works.title: The AI Productivity Paradox Report 2025; AI Engineering Report Q2 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash
works.authors: Faros AI (Faros Research)
works.venue: Industry reports (faros.ai); the 2025 report was published 23 July 2025
works.what_measured: Correlation between team AI adoption and engineering telemetry: throughput, PR volume, review time, bugs and incidents.
works.method_plain: Telemetry from version control, CI/CD, task trackers and incident systems. 2025: more than 10,000 developers in 1,255 teams; within-company standardization; Spearman correlations; each team's two lowest-adoption quarters compared with its two highest; only metrics with at least 6 companies and p < 0.05 reported. 2026: 22,000 developers in 4,000 teams over two years, comparing low and high adoption within the same organizations.
key_numbers: 2025, high-adoption teams: +21% tasks completed, +98% PRs merged, +91% PR review time, +154% PR size, +9% bugs per developer. 'No significant correlation' between AI adoption and company-level improvements.

2026 page (https://www.faros.ai/research/ai-acceleration-whiplash): median review time 5x; PR size +51%; task throughput +33.7%; epics +66.2%; bugs per PR +28.7%; incidents per PR +242.7%; code churn +861%; PR merge rate +16.2%; deployments per week -11.7%; bugs per developer +54%; 25% of PRs reviewed by an AI agent.
works.relevance_to_theta: Industry evidence that review is a bottleneck. Elapsed review time per PR rises with adoption, while PRs grow larger. These are correlational, elapsed-time measures, so they do not directly give review effort per unit of work. Flat company-level outcomes alongside team-level task gains are an aggregation warning: summing w_j*theta_j may overstate firm-level s.
works.limitations: Vendor reports. Correlational, not causal. Methods only partly disclosed. Review time is elapsed time, not effort hours. Not peer reviewed. A newer Q3 2026 report ('The Speed Trap') exists and was not checked.
works.corrections: The 2026 report's name is 'AI Engineering Report Q2 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash'. Removed the unconfirmed search-summary numbers (review time +199.6% mean / +441.5% median; 31% more PRs merged without review), which do not appear on the landing page. Added confirmed 2026 numbers (merge rate +16.2%, deployments per week -11.7%, bugs per developer +54%). The 2025 'no company-level improvement' is stated as 'no significant correlation'.

works.title: AI-Generated 'Workslop' Is Destroying Productivity
works.authors: Kate Niederhoffer, Gabriella Rosen Kellerman, Angela Lee, Alex Liebscher, Kristina Rapuano, Jeffrey T. Hancock (BetterUp Labs and Stanford Social Media Lab)
works.what_measured: How often workers receive low-effort AI-generated work ('workslop') and how much time it costs the people who receive it.
works.method_plain: Online self-report survey of 1,150 US full-time desk workers, September 2025.
key_numbers: From BetterUp's page (https://www.betterup.com/workslop): 1,150 US full-time desk workers; 40% received workslop in the last month; about 2 hours on average to resolve each incident; $186 per employee per month; $9M per year for a 10,000-person company (calculation not shown).
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows review and cleanup costs pushed downstream onto colleagues, so self-review alone understates rho and firm-level net savings should subtract this cost. Relevant to BPO and consulting, where output is documents rather than code.
works.limitations: Self-report, not a controlled study. The fetched HBR text did not show the survey statistics, so the numbers come from BetterUp's own page. The dollar figure is an extrapolation.
works.corrections: Removed the secondary-only figures (15.4% of content is workslop; 1 hour 56 minutes per incident), which appear on neither the HBR text nor the BetterUp page as fetched. Authors and dates confirmed on HBR. Core numbers confirmed on BetterUp's page.

works.title: Delegation and Verification under AI
works.authors: Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao (Nanjing University), Nisheeth K. Vishnoi (Yale University)
works.what_measured: Theory: a worker chooses how much to delegate to AI and how hard to verify, given a convex verification cost, an imperfect (concave) detection function and a redo cost.
works.method_plain: A formal optimization model, with an illustrative calibration on the Collab-CXR radiology dataset (324 cases, 33 clinicians), applied to one clinician with 38 cases.
key_numbers: Three regimes: manual work, pure delegation (no verification), and verified delegation. Boundaries are sharp because utility is affine in the delegation share.

Calibrated clinician: success alone 0.447, AI alone 0.368, with AI 0.395. Execution cost 172.5 vs assisted cost 116.8 (AI cost set to 0). Estimated α = 0.108, β = 0.342. The model places this clinician in the manual regime.
Weak verifiers rationally over-delegate. Better AI can enlarge the quality-degradation region for low-α workers ('verification amplification').
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives microfoundations for the max{..., kappa} switch in the formula, and shows that verification effort (rho) is chosen endogenously by trading off detection against cost. It implies the net saving and quality of theta_j depend on reviewer skill (α), which matters for India's junior-heavy staffing pyramid. In the model, low-skill verifiers verify less and over-delegate. It does not say they spend more review time.
works.limitations: Theory with a single-clinician illustration. Medical, not IT. Cost units are not measured review time. The authors say the calibration shows applicability, not causal identification.
works.corrections: Citation and numbers match. Added affiliations, the v2 date, and the α and β estimates. Clarified that weak verifiers over-delegate (verify less); the model does not say they have higher rho.

works.title: Some Simple Economics of AGI
works.authors: Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui, Jane Wu
works.what_measured: Conceptual model: an exponentially falling cost to automate races against a cost to verify that is bounded by human time.
works.method_plain: Theory and essay (112 pages, 3 figures). Argues that human verification bandwidth becomes the binding constraint. Coins 'measurability-biased technical change' and names related mechanisms ('Missing Junior Loop', 'Codifier's Curse', a 'Trojan Horse' externality from unverified deployment).
key_numbers: The abstract reports no quantitative parameters.
works.relevance_to_theta: Qualitative support for modeling rho(t) as falling more slowly than 1 - p(t). The implication that theta_j levels off near 1 - rho is the researcher's inference, not a result of the paper. It also suggests measurability (how cheaply output can be checked) as a dimension for splitting j. The 'Missing Junior Loop' is relevant to India's pyramid staffing model.
works.limitations: Not empirical. Only the abstract was read.
works.corrections: Citation matches. Added dates and the other named mechanisms. The 'levels off near 1 - rho' implication is flagged as the researcher's inference.

summary_flags: 'The working hypothesis largely holds' is overstated for this stream. It reviewed no exposure-literature papers (e.g. Eloundou et al. 2023), so it can show only that holistic-review studies measure something benchmarks miss, not what the exposure literature does or does not cover.

'Weak evidence that this gap is widening by about 10 pp/yr' needs stronger hedging. The normalized trend is 9.6 pp/yr with SE 5.5 (significant only at 10%), and the state-of-the-art-only trend is 4.1 pp/yr with SE 12.1, which is indistinguishable from zero.

'Relative q is about 0.67-1.0, because people delegate easy tasks and often merge into their own repos' presents a conjecture as fact. Nakashima et al. do not test selection or self-merging. AIDev acceptance is also not conditioned on passing tests, so it is a different quantity from METR's q.
The roughly 0.33-of-h figure from METR's August 2025 update is fix time, not review time (rho). It rests on 4 test-passing PRs, and the author calls the estimates 'very rough/high variance'.

The 9% review-and-cleanup share in the RCT is a share of total AI-allowed time in assistant mode on a 44-issue subset, not review time per unit of delegated output. It should not be read as rho for delegation.

'Review grows with output, so per-unit rho does not shrink much' overreads Faros. The measures are elapsed time and correlational. PR review time per PR rose (+91%) while PR size grew, which says nothing direct about review effort per unit of work.

Kappa 'went from -19% to +4-18%': the -18% covers only the 10 returning developers, every late-period confidence interval includes zero, METR calls it 'very weak evidence', and selection bias is acknowledged. The 'late 2025' period is data collected from August 2025 onward.

'Agent-only acceptance on long real projects is near zero: 2.5% RLI and 30% TheAgentCompany' wrongly groups the two. TheAgentCompany's 30% is checkpoint-scored autonomous completion in a simulated company, not holistic client acceptance, and 30% is not near zero.

'Treat rho as rising with reviewer inexperience, as the theory papers suggest' misreads Huang et al. In their model, weak verifiers rationally verify less and over-delegate, which lowers quality. It does not raise review time. The right takeaway is that the net value of theta_j depends on reviewer skill.

Several records relied on titles or venues that were wrong or unconfirmed: METR's August 2025 post title, the February 2026 post title, the LessWrong cross-post, Faros 2026 search-summary numbers, and workslop's 15.4% and 1h56m. All are corrected or removed.
Dataset access labels were partly speculative. METR's maintainer data is listed as 'on-request', but the note says nothing about release.
Gap 'METR collected review times but did not publish aggregates' is confirmed: the note says maintainers were asked to record review time and from-scratch time but reports no values.
verify.corrected_summary:
The holistic-review studies show that only part of 'test-passing' AI output removes labor, and that checking and fixing it costs real time. Benchmarks and pass rates overstate usable output. This stream did not review the exposure literature directly, so it supports the extensive-versus-intensive hypothesis only indirectly.

Best numbers for q (reviewer acceptance of passing output):
- METR (Whitfill, Wu, Becker, Rush; March 2026): roughly half of SWE-bench-Verified-passing agent PRs would not be merged by maintainers, even after adjusting for maintainer noise (maintainers re-approved only about 68% of real merged human patches). The normalized gap is 24.2 pp (SE 2.7). On a raw basis, merge rates are one-third to one-half of grader pass rates. There is weak evidence that the gap widens over time (9.6 pp/yr, SE 5.5); the SOTA-only trend (4.1 pp/yr, SE 12.1) is not significant. The maintainer-judged time horizon for Sonnet 4.5 is about 8 minutes vs about 50 under the grader, so acceptance likely falls with task length.
- In deployment (AIDev-pop, at least 100 stars), agent PRs are merged at 55-86% vs 82.6% for human PRs, a ratio of about 0.67-1.04. Acceptance varies by task type (docs 82.1%, features 66.1%). These rates are not conditioned on passing tests or on task length. The gap with METR probably reflects what people choose to delegate, but no study here tests that.

Fix and review cost (rho and related):
- METR (Rein, August 2025; n=15 reviewed, 4 test-passing): none were mergeable as-is. The estimated time to fix test-passing PRs is about 26 minutes on tasks averaging 1.3 hours (about one-third of h), and about 42 minutes across all reviewed PRs. The author calls these estimates very rough. This is fix time, separate from review.
- METR RCT (early 2025, assistant mode): about 9% of AI-allowed time went to reviewing and cleaning AI output (44-issue subset), about 4% to waiting, and developers accepted under 44% of Cursor generations.
- Faros telemetry (correlational, elapsed time): PR review time per PR was 91% higher on high-adoption teams in 2025, and median review time was 5x in the Q2 2026 report, alongside larger PRs and more bugs and incidents per PR. There was no significant company-level improvement in 2025, which is a warning about summing task-level savings into firm-level savings.

Kappa (assistant-mode time saving) for expert open-source developers moved from -19% (early 2025, CI +2% to +39% longer) to point estimates of 4-18% faster (from August 2025). All later confidence intervals include zero, and METR calls this very weak evidence affected by selection.

Long tasks under full delegation: the best agent's client-acceptance rate on the Remote Labor Index was 2.5% (projects with median 11.5 hours). TheAgentCompany's best agent completes about 30% of simulated-company tasks under checkpoint scoring, which is algorithmic, not holistic.

Recommendations: replace the binary q with a fix-up fraction, since passing-but-unmergeable work still saves time. Model reviewer skill explicitly, because in delegation-and-verification theory low-skill reviewers verify less and over-delegate, which lowers the net value of AI output.
verify.dataset_notes:
AIDev: public, CC-BY-4.0, on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev). The current v5 has 7.69M PRs across 961k repos from six agents (including Google Jules), with a 31 March 2026 cutoff, and includes review, comment, timeline and commit tables. The 456k figure is the paper's original snapshot. Task-type labels are not listed on the card; downstream papers derive them. Use the HF URL as the primary dataset link.

METR maintainer-review data (March 2026): the note does not mention any data release. Access should be 'unknown (contact METR)', not 'on-request'. The note says review time and from-scratch time were recorded but reports neither.

METR RCT screen-recording labels: release status not confirmed, so access is 'unknown', not 'on-request'.

Remote Labor Index: 10 projects public, 230 private (CAIS/Scale AI). Access is 'partially public', not 'lab-internal'.

SWE-Lancer: only the Diamond split (502 tasks, $500,800) is public, via OpenAI's SWELancer-Benchmark GitHub repo. The full 1,488-task set is reportedly available on request. Access is 'partially public'.

TheAgentCompany: the 175-task count is confirmed; the public release of the tasks and environment was not verified here. Per-category counts (69 SDE, 28 PM, 14 DS, 15 Admin, 29 HR, 12 Finance) sum to 167.

Faros: only summary reports are public and the underlying telemetry is proprietary; that the reports are 'paid' was not confirmed. The 2026 report is the Q2 2026 'Acceleration Whiplash', and a Q3 2026 'Speed Trap' report also exists.

BetterUp/Stanford workslop survey: microdata does not appear to be public; access is 'unknown'.

works.title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations (Anthropic Economic Index, report 1)
works.authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Sarah Heck, Jared Mueller, Jerry Hong, Stuart Ritchie, Tim Belonax, Kevin K. Troy, Dario Amodei, Jared Kaplan, Jack Clark, Deep Ganguli
works.what_measured: Which O*NET tasks Claude.ai conversations correspond to, and whether each conversation is automation (AI does the task) or augmentation (AI helps the human iterate or learn).
works.method_plain: Clio, a privacy-preserving tool, has Claude read about 4 million Claude.ai conversations and match each one to one of the roughly 20,000 O*NET task statements. Tasks are rolled up to occupations. A second classifier labels the interaction style.
key_numbers: Computer and mathematical tasks were 37.2% of queries; arts, design and media was second at 10.3%
About 36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their tasks; about 4% use it for at least 75%
Augmentation 57% (57.4%) vs automation 43% (42.6%) of conversations
Software development and writing together account for nearly half of usage
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive margin. It says which tasks AI touches (usage-weighted coverage), not how much labor is saved. It gives the O*NET-task crosswalk that later reports use, which you can use to map service lines j to tasks. The automation share is a rough proxy for delegation (p-type use) versus assistance (kappa-type use), but it classifies conversations, not labor time.
works.limitations: Consumer Claude.ai only, one week of data, a single model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet era). Coverage reflects demand and who uses Claude, not capability. Automation versus augmentation is about interaction style, not the share of work removed.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index: AI's impact on software development
works.authors: Anthropic (page credits the Societal Impacts team; no individual authors named)
works.what_measured: Automation vs augmentation in coding, Claude Code (agentic) vs Claude.ai (chat). Languages, task types, startup vs enterprise.
works.method_plain: Clio classification of 500,000 coding interactions from Apr 6-13 2025.
key_numbers: Automation: 79% of Claude Code conversations vs 49% of Claude.ai
'Directive' (do it with minimal input): 43.8% on Claude Code vs 27.5% on Claude.ai; 'Feedback loop': 35.8% vs 21.3%
JavaScript+TypeScript 31%, HTML+CSS 28%, Python 14%, SQL 6% of queries
UI/UX component development 12% of conversations; web and mobile app development 8%
Startup work 32.9% of Claude Code conversations; enterprise work 23.8% (Claude Code) vs 25.9% (Claude.ai)
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that agentic tools move usage from kappa-style (assistant) to p-style (delegate) work, which supports splitting theta_j into delegation and assist branches. It is closest to the Indian IT 'development' and 'testing' lines. It does not measure time saved.
works.limitations: No time or quality measures. Skews toward startups and web front-end, not legacy enterprise maintenance, which is a large part of Indian IT. One week of data.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Uneven geographic and enterprise AI adoption
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Peter McCrory, Alex Tamkin (leads), Miles McCain, Tyler Neylon, Michael Stern
works.what_measured: First release of first-party API (enterprise/developer) usage, by O*NET task, plus country and US-state adoption.
works.method_plain: 1 million API transcripts from August 2025, sampled from customers making up about half of first-party API usage, plus 1 million Claude.ai conversations (Aug 4-11 2025), classified with Clio. Regressions relate usage to task cost.
key_numbers: API: 77% of transcripts show automation patterns vs 12% augmentation; Claude.ai is roughly even
97% of tasks are automation-dominant in the API vs 47% on Claude.ai
Computer and math tasks are 44% of API traffic; debugging web apps and resolving technical issues are each about 6%
Claude.ai directive share rose from 27% (late 2024) to 39% (Aug 2025)
Controlling for task characteristics, a 1% rise in task cost is associated with 0.29% lower usage (preliminary)
A 1% longer input is associated with 0.38% longer output; authors argue that access to context limits enterprise deployment
works.relevance_to_theta: Business (API) deployments are the right comparison for IT-services firms. The high automation share suggests delegation (q*p) matters more than assistance (kappa) there. The 'context bottleneck' finding is a reason the realized theta could fall below a benchmark-based theta for legacy-codebase maintenance. Token cost data bears on the AI running-cost deduction.
works.limitations: Covers API customers, not end-to-end firm labor. No time saved or success measure in this release. Cost elasticity is a cross-task correlation, not causal.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research blog (page dated Nov 25 2025; its own citation says Nov 5 2025)
works.what_measured: Per-conversation time a task would take a professional without AI vs with AI. Aggregated to O*NET tasks, occupations and the US economy.
works.method_plain: Claude reads 100,000 Claude.ai conversations and estimates (a) hours a professional would need without AI and (b) the time it actually took with Claude. Medians are taken per task, valued at BLS wages, then weighted by occupation time shares (also Claude-estimated). Tasks not seen get zero gain. The estimates were checked against actual completion times on a JIRA software-task benchmark.
