key_numbers: Average task would take about 1.4 hours (about 90 min) without AI
Time reduction about 80% (body: median 84% per conversation; figure caption: 81%)
Median task value about $54-55 of professional labor
Universal adoption over 10 years with current models implies about +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth (TFP about +1.1%/yr with labor share 0.6). Authors call this an exercise, not a forecast
Software developers contribute about 19% of the implied gain; developers spend about 23% of time writing/maintaining code (Claude-estimated)
Validation on JIRA tasks: Spearman correlation with actual time 0.50 for developers' own estimates vs 0.44 for Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones
Self-consistency across prompt variants: log correlations 0.89-0.93
Examples: hardware issues 56% savings; checking diagnostic images 20%
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest lab product to an intensive-margin theta_j: a per-task fractional time saving, weighted by time shares (w_j). The 80% figure is GROSS, inside the chat. It excludes review, validation and iteration outside the conversation (the paper says so) and does not net out failures. So it is an upper bound on q*p(1-kappa)+kappa, with rho effectively 0. The 'human_only_time' estimates also give an h-distribution per task (an f_j proxy).
works.limitations: Time estimates are model-generated and only validated on software. Selection: users bring tasks where Claude helps. Review time outside the chat is ignored. Task lists simplify real jobs. No firm reorganization. Paper notes METR's RCT found no time savings on end-to-end features.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (leads), Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Jan 15 2026 (data Nov 13-20 2025; Sonnet 4.5 classifiers)
works.what_measured: Five new per-conversation 'primitives': task complexity (human-alone time, time with AI, multitasking), skills (education level, could the human do it alone), use case, AI autonomy (1-5) and task success (Claude-judged). Covers Claude.ai and first-party API, by O*NET task.
works.method_plain: Classifiers (Claude) label sampled conversations. Speedups are measured as the log difference of human-alone vs with-AI time per O*NET task. The productivity exercise multiplies each task's time saving by its success rate before aggregating, and adds a CES aggregator (how easily tasks substitute for each other).
key_numbers: Average human-alone time vs with-AI time: Claude.ai 3.1 h vs 15 min; API 1.7 h vs 5 min. Software development requests about 3.3 h human-alone
Task success: Claude.ai 67%, API 49%; software development 61% on Claude.ai vs personal 78%

API success falls from about 60% (tasks under 1 human-hour) to about 45% (5+ hours). Fitted 50% crossing at about 3.5 h (API) vs about 19 h extrapolated (Claude.ai). METR comparison cited: about 2 h (Sonnet 4.5), about 5 h (Opus 4.5)
Productivity: baseline +1.8 pp/yr; success-adjusted +1.2 pp (Claude.ai), +1.0 pp (API); with complementarity (elasticity 0.5) 0.6-0.9 pp; with elasticity 1.5, 2.2-2.6 pp
Augmentation 52%, automation 45% on Claude.ai (Nov 2025); API about three-quarters automation, directive 64%
Computer/math: 34% of Claude.ai, 46% of API; most common task 'modifying software to correct errors' (6% of Claude.ai, about 10% of API)

Public data includes onet_task::human_only_time, onet_task::human_with_ai_time, onet_task::task_success, ai_autonomy, collaboration, with means, medians, CIs and histogram bins; API data has cost and token indices
works.relevance_to_theta: Most directly usable source in this stream. (1) The API success-by-human-length curve is a field-data p(h) for real enterprise traffic, which can be compared with METR's benchmark p(h,t). (2) Per-O*NET-task histograms of human_only_time give an empirical f_j(h) once tasks are mapped to service lines. (3) Success-weighting is a crude q*p adjustment. (4) The with-AI time over human-alone time gives a gross (1-theta) before review cost. It does NOT measure rho: the report says verification would shrink gains but only proxies it with success rates.
works.limitations: Every primitive is Claude judging Claude: success is self-assessed with limited human validation. Time units are not stated in the data documentation. Success depends on which tasks users choose to bring. One week of data. Success on 'completing the request' is not the same as 'mergeable or shippable' (q).

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Peter McCrory (leads), Ruth Appel, Ryan Heller
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Mar 24 2026 (data Feb 5-12 2026; 1M Claude.ai + 1M API conversations)
works.what_measured: Change in usage after Opus 4.5/4.6. Whether experienced (high-tenure) users succeed more. Model choice by task wage.
works.method_plain: Same primitives pipeline; regressions of task success on user tenure with task fixed effects and other controls.
key_numbers: High-tenure users (6+ months): success about 5 pp higher raw, about 3 pp with task fixed effects, about 4 pp with full controls
Top-10 task share on Claude.ai fell 24% to 19%; API top-10 share rose 28% to 33% since Aug 2025
Computer and math 35% of Claude.ai
49% of jobs have at least a quarter of tasks done using Claude (barely changed)
Opus share among paid users 51%; software-developer tasks 34% Opus; +$10/h task wage raises Opus share 1.5 pp (Claude.ai), 2.8 pp (API)
No per-task time-savings figures; human-only time fell about 2 minutes between samples
works.relevance_to_theta: User skill raises success by a few points, so q and p are not purely model properties; firm training and experience matter. The capability-ceiling theta should assume experienced users or add a learning adjustment. It gives little direct parameter value beyond that.
works.limitations: The tenure effect may reflect selection (early adopters are more technical, survivorship), as the authors note. Success is model-judged.

works.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Mar 5 2026 (with appendix PDF)
works.what_measured: 'Observed exposure': theoretical LLM exposure (Eloundou et al. 2023 beta scores) combined with actual Claude work usage, weighted by task time. Then CPS difference-in-differences on unemployment and job finding.
works.method_plain: A task counts as covered if it shows enough work usage. Automated use gets full weight, augmentative use half weight. Coverage is summed to occupations by O*NET time weights. Top-quartile-exposure workers are compared with zero-exposure workers before and after late 2022.
key_numbers: Claude covers 33% of Computer & Math tasks vs a theoretical 94%
Computer Programmers 75% coverage; Data Entry Keyers 67%; Customer Service Reps second
+10 pp coverage is associated with -0.6 pp BLS projected 2024-34 employment growth
No detectable rise in unemployment for highly exposed workers (minimum detectable effect about 1 pp)
Ages 22-25: job-finding rate in highly exposed occupations down about 14% relative to 2022, barely significant
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly tests the working hypothesis. It moves from 'can AI touch it' to 'is AI used for it', but the measure is still extensive (task covered or not) with an ad hoc 1 vs 0.5 weight for automation vs augmentation. That weight is an implicit, uncalibrated stand-in for the gap between delegation (q*p) and assistance (kappa). The gap between theoretical (94%) and observed (33%) is an adoption gap, which our theta deliberately excludes.
works.limitations: US labor data; occupation-level; the 1/0.5 weights are assumed, not estimated; no time-saved dimension; short post-period.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Szymon Sacher, Zoe Hitzig, Shaoyi Zhang, Ryan Heller, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Jun 26 2026 (data Apr 10-Jun 10 2026, incl. Cowork and Claude Code)
works.what_measured: Daily-sampled usage; artifact (deliverable) types; token use by task wage; autonomy in Claude Code vs chat; first linked user survey (about 9,700 respondents).
works.method_plain: Continuous daily sampling and classifiers; survey answers linked to up to 20 sessions per respondent.
key_numbers: 93% of conversations produce an artifact; code and technical work about one-sixth of conversations
Claude Code autonomy averages 0.37 points higher (1-5 scale) than chat/Cowork; 54% of Claude Code sessions use Opus vs 10% of chat
Survey: self-reported gains in speed 86%, scope 82%, quality 69%, cost savings 27%; 10% rate losing their own job as likely
Survey sample skew: Computer/Math about 30% of respondents vs 4% of US employment
No time-savings, success-rate or verification-effort numbers in this report
works.relevance_to_theta: Mainly infrastructure: the move to continuous sampling allows monthly time series (time-varying t in theta_j(t)). Autonomy differences between agentic and chat tools support the delegate-vs-assist split. There is no new intensive-margin number.
works.limitations: Survey respondents are heavily selected. No success or time primitives reported for this window.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Saffron Huang, Bryan Seethor, Esin Durmus, Kunal Handa, Miles McCain, Michael Stern, Deep Ganguli
works.what_measured: How much in-house engineers use AI, self-reported productivity, the share of work fully delegable, and agent autonomy over time in 200,000 internal Claude Code transcripts.
works.method_plain: Survey of 132 engineers/researchers (Aug 2025), 53 interviews, and comparison of Claude Code transcripts from Feb vs Aug 2025.
key_numbers: Share of work using Claude: about 59-60% (vs 28% a year earlier)
Self-reported productivity +50% (vs +20% a year earlier); about 14% report >100%
Merged PRs per engineer per day +67% after the Claude Code rollout
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done
More than half say they can fully delegate only 0-20% of their work
Max consecutive tool calls 9.8 to 21.2 (+116%); human turns per transcript 6.2 to 4.1 (-33%)
works.relevance_to_theta: A frontier-adopter bound. The '0-20% fully delegable' answer is a direct check on the delegation term q*p for real engineering work. The gap between +50% self-reported output and 27% 'new work' warns that output gains are not the same as labor saved (a demand-expansion effect inside the firm). Supervision comments support a positive rho. The time trend in autonomy supports p rising with t.
works.limitations: Unusual workforce (AI lab), non-anonymous self-reports, 31% response rate in one group, older models (Sonnet 4 / Opus 4). Transcripts measure task mix, not volume.

works.title: How People Use ChatGPT
works.authors: Aaron Chatterji, Thomas Cunningham, David J. Deming, Zoe Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Yan Shan, Kevin Wadman
works.what_measured: Growth and composition of consumer ChatGPT messages (Nov 2022-Jul 2025): work vs non-work, topics, Asking/Doing/Expressing intent, O*NET IWAs and GWAs.
works.method_plain: A privacy-preserving automated classifier labels about 1.1 million sampled conversations (May 15 2024-Jun 26 2025). Messages are mapped to one of 332 O*NET Intermediate Work Activities, then rolled up to Generalized Work Activities.
key_numbers: Non-work messages grew from 53% to more than 70% of usage
Asking 49%, Doing 40%, Expressing 11% of all messages; among work messages, Doing is about 56%, Asking 35%, Expressing 9%
Writing is 40% of work-related messages on average; nearly 35% of work queries are Doing+Writing
Computer programming only 4.2% of messages (paper contrasts this with 33% of work-related Claude conversations)
Work GWAs: Documenting/Recording Information 18.4%, Making Decisions and Solving Problems 14.9%, Thinking Creatively 13.0%, Working with Computers 10.8%
About 10% of world adults had adopted by July 2025
works.relevance_to_theta: Extensive margin and use-type only. 'Doing' vs 'Asking' parallels delegate (p) vs assist/decision support (kappa), suggesting much consumer value is kappa-type. There is no time-saved or success measure, and coding is a small share, so it says little about IT-services theta_j.
works.limitations: Consumer plans only (no Enterprise/Team/API); conversation share is not labor time; OpenAI-affiliated authors; not peer-reviewed.

works.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
works.authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, Siddharth Suri
works.venue: arXiv:2507.07935 (v1 Jul 10 2025; latest v7 Oct 2026, listed as NeurIPS 2026)
works.what_measured: For 200k Bing Copilot conversations (9 months), which O*NET IWAs the user wanted help with (user goal) and which the AI performed (AI action), plus completion rate, scope of impact and thumbs feedback. Combined into an occupation-level 'AI applicability score'.
works.method_plain: An LLM classifies each conversation's IWAs. An IWA is 'covered' if it is at least 0.05% of activity. Score = sum over covered IWAs of (relevance weight to occupation x completion rate x share at moderate-or-higher scope), averaged over the user and AI sides.
key_numbers: Top scores: Interpreters/Translators 0.49 (coverage 0.98, completion 0.88, scope 0.57); Customer Service Reps 0.44 (0.72/0.90/0.59); Web Developers 0.35; Data Scientists 0.36
All programming maps to one IWA ('Program computer systems...')
In 40% of conversations the user-goal and AI-action IWAs are completely disjoint
Score vs wage correlation (employment-weighted) 0.07; Bachelor's-required occupations mean 0.27 vs 0.19
Correlation with Eloundou et al. exposure r = 0.73 (occupation), 0.91 (SOC major group)
Paper states it does not measure productivity or job loss
works.relevance_to_theta: Mostly extensive, with a partial intensive element: completion rate (a success proxy, about 0.84-0.90) and 'scope' (how much of the activity AI addresses) are cousins of q*p and of the fraction of the task done. The authors explicitly deny measuring labor saved. The r = 0.73 with Eloundou suggests usage-based and rubric-based exposure largely agree. Customer-service scores are relevant to BPO lines.
works.limitations: Bing Copilot users (consumer, US); completion is LLM-judged; programming collapses into one IWA, so it is useless for splitting maintenance, testing and development; no time dimension.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simon Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. Kim, Patrick Chao, Samuel Miserendino, Gildas Chabot, David Li, Michael Sharman, Alexandra Barr, Amelia Glaese, Jerry Tworek
works.what_measured: Expert-graded quality of model deliverables on 1,320 real tasks (44 occupations, 9 top-GDP sectors), with recorded expert completion time and review time. Speed and cost ratios under 'naive', 'try once then review/fix', and 'try n times then fix' workflows.
works.method_plain: Industry experts (about 14 years' experience on average) write tasks and deliverables. Other experts blind-compare model vs human outputs. Time and cost savings are computed with expert time, measured review time and the win rate.
key_numbers: Gold subset (220 tasks): expert completion time 404 min avg, cost $361; expert review time 109 min avg, cost $86
Win/tie vs expert: GPT-4o 12.5%, o4-mini 29.1%, o3 35.2%, GPT-5 39.0%; Claude Opus 4.1 47.6% (no Claude speed/cost reported)
Speed ratio, naive vs try-1x-then-fix vs try-nx: GPT-5 90x / 1.12x / 1.39x; o3 161x / 1.08x / 1.28x; GPT-4o 327x / 0.87x / 0.46x
Cost ratio, try-1x: GPT-5 1.18x; try-nx 1.63x
works.relevance_to_theta: The only lab dataset here that nets review cost out of time savings, with the same structure as the draft formula. Review time over task time is about 109/404 = 0.27, a direct rho estimate for multi-hour knowledge tasks. The win rate is a q*p analogue. Moving from roughly 100x naive to about 1.1-1.4x speedup shows that rho and failure rates, not raw capability, dominate theta. It suggests theta_delegate is about 1 - 1/1.12 = 11% for GPT-5 try-1x (my derivation, not the paper's).
works.limitations: Not usage data, it is a benchmark; mostly one-shot, document-type deliverables, few software-engineering tasks; expert times self-reported; excludes catastrophic-error cost; 'try nx' likely over-penalizes models (authors note).

research.stream_summary: The AI labs' usage datasets go further than the working hypothesis expected, but not all the way. Anthropic's Economic Index started (Feb 2025) as a pure extensive-margin measure: which O*NET tasks show up in Claude chats, and whether the chat looks like automation or augmentation. Since November 2025 it has added intensive-margin quantities. Tamkin and McCrory have Claude estimate, for each conversation, how long a professional would need without AI and how long it took with AI. The median time cut is about 80% (84% in the text, 81% in a figure caption), on tasks averaging about 1.4 hours. The January 2026 'economic primitives' report adds a Claude-judged task-success rate. On enterprise API traffic it shows success falling from about 60% for sub-hour tasks to about 45% for tasks of 5+ hours, crossing 50% near 3.5 hours. That is a field-data analogue of METR's p(h). Weighting by success roughly halves the implied productivity gain (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr). Crucially, the public Hugging Face data contains per-O*NET-task human-alone time, with-AI time and success, each with histograms, for both Claude.ai and the API. That is enough to build an empirical f_j(h) and a p(h) cross-check. What the usage data cannot see is review time outside the chat (rho) and whether 'successful' output is actually accepted (q). The best lab source for those is OpenAI's GDPval: expert review takes about 109 minutes on 404-minute tasks (rho about 0.27), and once review-and-fix is included, a 90x 'naive' speedup shrinks to about 1.1-1.4x. OpenAI's ChatGPT paper and Microsoft's applicability scores are mostly extensive-margin. Microsoft explicitly says it does not measure productivity. Anthropic's internal study (more than half of engineers can fully delegate only 0-20% of work) gives a sanity bound on the delegation term. Verdict on the hypothesis: partly right. The literature now has gross intensive-margin estimates, but they are not net of verification, and none are specific to IT services.
gaps_noticed: No lab dataset measures human review/verification time on real usage (rho). Anthropic's time-with-AI covers only time in the chat, and the January 2026 report admits verification is proxied only by success rates.
Task success (the q*p proxy) is self-graded by Claude, with small human validation sets. Nothing measures 'merge/accept' rates in deployed enterprise work.

Time estimates are LLM-generated, validated only against one JIRA software benchmark (Spearman 0.44 vs 0.50 for developers' own estimates), with known compression: short tasks are overestimated and long tasks underestimated, which biases f_j(h).
No India- or IT-services-specific cut: the API data has no geographic split, and O*NET tasks do not separate legacy maintenance, testing, infrastructure ops or BPO work as Indian firms organize them.

The June 2026 'Cadences' report drops time and success primitives, so there is no time series of the intensive margin past Feb 2026 in published reports (need to check whether the HF data continues them).
Microsoft collapses all programming into one IWA, which makes it useless for within-software task splits.
Selection: usage data shows tasks users choose to bring to AI, so success and time savings are conditional on self-selection, not a capability ceiling over the full task distribution.
Could not confirm whether the 2026 releases after January keep publishing onet_task::human_only_time and task_success; not checked file-by-file.

Anthropic Fellows (Economics & Policy) and Economic Futures pages suggest no privileged access to raw internal conversations; fellows use public data and APIs. The $200M fund details came only from secondary sources and are unverified.
GDPval reports speed and cost ratios only for OpenAI models (no Claude), and has few software-engineering tasks.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index (Hugging Face: Anthropic/EconomicIndex)
