works.title: Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations (Anthropic Economic Index, report 1)
works.authors: Kunal Handa, Alex Tamkin, Miles McCain, Saffron Huang, Esin Durmus, Sarah Heck, Jared Mueller, Jerry Hong, Stuart Ritchie, Tim Belonax, Kevin K. Troy, Dario Amodei, Jared Kaplan, Jack Clark, Deep Ganguli
works.venue: arXiv:2503.04761 (v1 submitted Feb 11 2025); companion Anthropic blog post Feb 10 2025
works.what_measured: Which O*NET tasks Claude.ai conversations correspond to, and whether each conversation is automation (AI does the task) or augmentation (AI helps the human iterate or learn).
works.method_plain: Clio, a privacy-preserving tool, has Claude read Claude.ai (Free and Pro) conversations (the abstract says over 4 million in total; individual analyses use samples of 1M or 500K) and match each to one of the nearly 20,000 O*NET task statements (19,530 base-level tasks). Tasks are rolled up to occupations. A second classifier labels the interaction style.
key_numbers: Computer and mathematical tasks were 37.2% of queries; arts, design, sports, entertainment and media (mostly writing and editing) was second at 10.3%
About 36% of occupations use AI for at least 25% of their tasks; about 4% use it for at least 75%
Augmentation 57% vs automation 43% of conversations
Data: 7-day snapshots collected in December 2024 and January 2025; model-type analysis covers Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) and Claude 3 Opus
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive margin. It says which tasks AI touches (usage-weighted coverage), not how much labor is saved. It provides the O*NET-task crosswalk that later reports use, which can map service lines j to tasks. The automation share is a rough proxy for delegation (p-type use) versus assistance (kappa-type use), but it classifies conversations, not labor time.
works.limitations: Consumer Claude.ai only (Free and Pro); a few 7-day snapshots from Dec 2024-Jan 2025; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3 Opus. Coverage reflects demand and who uses Claude, not capability. Automation versus augmentation is about interaction style, not the share of work removed.
works.corrections: Removed '57.4% / 42.6%': the paper and blog give only 57% / 43%. Removed 'software development and writing together account for nearly half of usage': neither source says this (37.2% + 10.3% = 47.5% is our own arithmetic, and the categories are occupational groups, not 'software' and 'writing'). Fixed limitations: data are several 7-day snapshots in Dec 2024 and Jan 2025, not one week, and cover two models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet new and Claude 3 Opus), not one. Noted that the blog says about 1 million conversations while the arXiv abstract says over 4 million (the total across analyses).

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index: AI's impact on software development
works.authors: Anthropic (page credits the Societal Impacts team; no individual authors named)
works.what_measured: Automation vs augmentation in coding, Claude Code (agentic) vs Claude.ai (chat). Languages, task types, startup vs enterprise.
works.method_plain: Clio classification of 500,000 coding interactions across Claude.ai and Claude Code, Apr 6-13 2025.
key_numbers: Automation: 79% of Claude Code conversations vs 49% of Claude.ai
'Directive' (do it with minimal input): 43.8% on Claude Code vs 27.5% on Claude.ai; 'Feedback loop': 35.8% vs 21.3%
JavaScript+TypeScript 31%, HTML+CSS 28%, Python 14%, SQL 6% of queries
UI/UX component development 12% of conversations; web and mobile app development 8%

Startup work 32.9% of Claude Code conversations; enterprise work 23.8% (Claude Code) vs 25.9% (Claude.ai). Note: the page's introduction gives a conflicting preliminary 13% for Claude Code enterprise work
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that agentic tools move usage from kappa-style (assistant) to p-style (delegate) work, which supports splitting theta_j into delegation and assist branches. Closest to the Indian IT 'development' and 'testing' lines. It does not measure time saved.
works.limitations: No time or quality measures. Skews toward startups and web front-end, not legacy enterprise maintenance, which is a large part of Indian IT. One week of data. Internal inconsistency on the enterprise share (13% vs 23.8%).
works.corrections: All numbers match the page. Added a note that the page itself gives two inconsistent figures for Claude Code enterprise share (13% in the intro, 23.8% in the body).

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Uneven geographic and enterprise AI adoption
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Peter McCrory, Alex Tamkin (leads), Miles McCain, Tyler Neylon, Michael Stern
works.what_measured: First release of first-party API (enterprise/developer) usage, by O*NET task, plus country and US-state adoption.
works.method_plain: 1 million API transcripts from August 2025, sampled from customers making up about half of first-party API usage, plus 1 million Claude.ai Free and Pro conversations (Aug 4-11 2025), classified with Clio. Regressions relate usage to task cost.
key_numbers: API: 77% of transcripts show automation patterns vs 12% augmentation; Claude.ai is roughly even
97% of tasks are automation-dominant in the API vs 47% on Claude.ai
Computer and math tasks are 44% of API traffic (figure caption; text says 'a little less than half'); debugging web applications and resolving technical issues each about 6%
Claude.ai directive share rose from 27% (Dec 2024-Jan 2025) to 39% (Aug 2025)
Controlling for task characteristics, a 1% rise in task cost is associated with 0.29% lower usage (the raw correlation is positive)
A 1% longer input is associated with 0.38% longer output; the authors suggest, as a hypothesis, that access to context may be a bottleneck for complex enterprise deployments
works.relevance_to_theta: Business (API) deployments are the right comparison for IT-services firms. The high automation share suggests delegation (q*p) matters more than assistance (kappa) there. The possible 'context bottleneck' is a reason realized theta could fall below a benchmark-based theta for legacy-codebase maintenance. Token cost data bears on the AI running-cost deduction.
works.limitations: Covers API customers, not end-to-end firm labor. No time saved or success measure in this release. Cost elasticity is a cross-task correlation, not causal. The context-bottleneck point is a hypothesis.
works.corrections: Numbers match. Softened 'authors argue that access to context limits enterprise deployment' to a hypothesis: the report calls context a 'potential bottleneck'. Clarified the 27% baseline period (Dec 2024-Jan 2025).

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research blog (byline Nov 25 2025; the page's own citation says 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: Per-conversation time a task would take a professional without AI vs with AI. Aggregated to O*NET tasks, occupations and the US economy.
works.method_plain: Claude reads 100,000 Claude.ai conversations and estimates (a) hours a competent professional would need without AI and (b) the time the user actually spent with Claude. Medians are taken per O*NET task; task cost uses BLS OEWS May 2024 wages. Economy-wide gains use log time differences per task, weighted by Claude-estimated task time shares and occupations' wage-bill shares (Hulten's theorem). Unobserved tasks get zero gain. Estimates were checked against actual completion times on a 1,000-task subset of an open-source JIRA software-task dataset.
key_numbers: Average task would take about 1.4 hours (about 90 min) without AI
Time reduction about 80% (body: median 84% per conversation; figure caption: 81%)
Median task value about $54-55 of professional labor
Universal adoption over 10 years with current models implies about +1.8% per year US labor productivity growth (TFP about +1.1%/yr with labor share 0.6). Authors call this an exercise, not a forecast
Software developers contribute about 19% of the implied gain; developers spend about 23% of time writing/maintaining code (Claude-estimated)

Validation on JIRA tasks: Spearman correlation with actual time 0.50 for developers' own estimates vs 0.44 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 (log-scale Pearson 0.67 vs 0.46). Claude overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones
Self-consistency across prompt variants: log correlations 0.89-0.93
Examples: hardware issues 56% savings; checking diagnostic images 20%
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest lab product to an intensive-margin theta_j: a per-task fractional time saving, weighted by time shares (w_j). The 80% figure is GROSS, inside the chat. It excludes validation and refinement outside the conversation (the page says so) and does not net out failures. So it is an upper bound on q*p(1-kappa)+kappa, with rho effectively 0. The human-time estimates also give a task-length distribution per task (an f_j proxy), but over conversations users chose to bring, not hours of work.
works.limitations: Time estimates are model-generated and validated only on software. Selection: users bring tasks where Claude helps. Review time outside the chat is ignored. Task lists simplify real jobs. No firm reorganization. The page cites METR's RCT, which found no time savings (in fact a slowdown) on end-to-end features.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Refined the method description (median per task; log differences with Hulten weighting by time share and wage-bill share; OEWS May 2024 wages; JIRA subset of 1,000 tasks) and added the Pearson validation figures.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (leads), Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Jan 15 2026 (data Nov 13-20 2025; 1M Claude.ai + 1M first-party API records; Sonnet 4.5 classifiers)
works.what_measured: New per-conversation 'primitives': task complexity (human-alone time, time with AI, multitasking), skills (education level, could the human do it alone), use case, AI autonomy (1-5) and task success (Claude-judged). Covers Claude.ai and first-party API, by O*NET task.
works.method_plain: Claude classifiers label sampled conversations. The productivity exercise reuses the Tamkin-McCrory approach, multiplies each task's time saving by its success rate before aggregating, and adds a CES aggregator (how easily tasks substitute for each other).
key_numbers: Average human-alone time vs with-AI time: Claude.ai about 3.1 h vs about 15 min; API about 1.7 h vs about 5 min. Software development requests about 3.3 h human-alone
Task success: Claude.ai 67%, API 49%; software development 61% vs personal 78%

API success falls from about 60% (sub-hour tasks) to about 45% (5+ hours). Fitted 50% crossing at about 3.5 h (API) vs about 19 h extrapolated (Claude.ai). METR comparison cited: about 2 h (Sonnet 4.5), about 5 h (Opus 4.5)

Productivity: baseline about +1.8 pp/yr; success-adjusted +1.2 pp (Claude.ai), +1.0 pp (API); with elasticity of substitution 0.5, baseline 0.7-0.9 pp and success-adjusted 0.8 (Claude.ai) / 0.6 (API); with elasticity 1.5, baseline 2.2-2.6 pp
Augmentation 52%, automation 45% on Claude.ai (Nov 2025); API about three-quarters automation, directive 64%
Computer/math: 34% of Claude.ai, 46% of API; most common task 'modifying software to correct errors' (6% of Claude.ai, about 1 in 10 API records)

Public data (Jan and Mar 2026 releases) includes per-O*NET-task human_only_time, human_with_ai_time, task_success, ai_autonomy and collaboration, with mean, median, SD, 95% CIs and histogram bins; API data adds cost, prompt-token and completion-token indices; API is global only
works.relevance_to_theta: Most directly usable source in this stream. (1) The API success-by-human-length curve is a field-data p(h) for real enterprise traffic, comparable in spirit (not in selection) with METR's benchmark p(h,t). (2) Per-O*NET-task histograms of human_only_time describe the length distribution of tasks users bring to Claude; turning that into f_j(h) needs hours-weighting and a selection correction. (3) Success-weighting is a crude q*p adjustment. (4) The with-AI time over human-alone time gives a gross (1-theta) before review cost. It does NOT measure rho: the report says validation would shrink gains and handles it only through success rates.
works.limitations: Every primitive is Claude judging Claude: success is model-assessed. Time units are not stated in the Jan 2026 data documentation (the report text uses hours for human-alone and minutes for with-AI; the June 2026 documentation states those units). Success depends on which tasks users bring. One week of data. Success on 'completing the request' is not the same as 'mergeable or shippable' (q).
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Made the elasticity-0.5 figures precise (baseline 0.7-0.9; success-adjusted 0.8 / 0.6) instead of '0.6-0.9'. Softened the claim that the histograms directly give f_j(h). Did not independently confirm the 'log difference' detail within this report (it is confirmed in the Tamkin-McCrory post), so removed it from the method.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Peter McCrory (leads), Ruth Appel, Ryan Heller
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Mar 24 2026 (data Feb 5-12 2026; 1M Claude.ai + 1M API conversations)
works.what_measured: Change in usage after Opus 4.5/4.6. Whether experienced (high-tenure) users succeed more. Model choice by task wage.
works.method_plain: Same primitives pipeline; regressions of task success on user tenure with task fixed effects and other controls (model, use case, country, language).
key_numbers: High-tenure users (6+ months): success about 5 pp higher raw, about 3 pp with task fixed effects, about 4 pp with full controls

Top-10 task share on Claude.ai fell from 24% (Nov 2025) to 19% (Feb 2026); the Discussion says API top-10 share rose from 28% to 33% since Aug 2025, but an earlier chapter says API concentration was 'roughly flat'
Computer and math 35% of Claude.ai
About 49% of jobs have at least a quarter of tasks performed using Claude (barely changed)
Opus share among paid Claude.ai users 51%; software-developer tasks 34% Opus; +$10/h task wage raises Opus share 1.5 pp (Claude.ai), 2.8 pp (API)
No per-task time-savings figures; human-only time fell about 2 minutes between samples (p<0.05)
works.relevance_to_theta: User skill raises success by a few points, so q and p are not purely model properties; firm training and experience matter. A capability-ceiling theta should assume experienced users or add a learning adjustment. Little direct parameter value beyond that. The matching HF release (2026-03-24) keeps task_success, human_only_time and human_with_ai_time for both Claude.ai and API, so it is a second time point for the Jan 2026 primitives.
works.limitations: The tenure effect may reflect selection and survivorship (the authors say so). Success is model-judged. The report is internally inconsistent on API concentration.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Added the report's internal inconsistency on API top-10 concentration, and the fact that the March data release keeps the time and success primitives.

works.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Mar 5 2026 (with appendix PDF)
works.what_measured: 'Observed exposure': theoretical LLM exposure (Eloundou et al. 2023 beta scores) combined with actual Claude work usage, weighted by task time. Then CPS difference-in-differences on unemployment and job finding.
works.method_plain: A task counts as covered if it shows enough work-related usage. Automated use gets full weight, augmentative use half weight. Coverage is averaged to occupations by O*NET time weights. Highly exposed workers are compared with unexposed workers before and after late 2022.
key_numbers: Observed coverage of Computer & Math tasks 33% vs a theoretical (beta-based) 94%
Computer Programmers 75% coverage; Data Entry Keyers 67%; Customer Service Representatives ranked second (no percentage given)
+10 pp coverage is associated with -0.6 pp BLS projected employment growth (authors call it slight)
No detectable rise in unemployment for highly exposed workers (rough minimum detectable effect about 1 pp)
Ages 22-25: job-finding rate in highly exposed occupations about 14% lower than in 2022, barely significant; no similar decline over age 25
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly tests the working hypothesis. It moves from 'can AI touch it' to 'is AI used for it', but the measure is still extensive (task covered or not) with an ad hoc 1 vs 0.5 weight for automation vs augmentation. That weight is an implicit, uncalibrated stand-in for the gap between delegation (q*p) and assistance (kappa). The gap between theoretical (94%) and observed (33%) is mostly an adoption gap, which our theta deliberately excludes.
works.limitations: US labor data; occupation-level; the 1/0.5 weights are assumed, not estimated; no time-saved dimension; short post-period.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Dataset access corrected separately: the HF repo has a labor_market_impacts folder (job_exposure.csv, task_penetration.csv), so the measure appears to be public.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Szymon Sacher, Zoe Hitzig, Shaoyi Zhang, Ryan Heller, Peter McCrory
works.venue: Anthropic research report, Jun 26 2026 (chat/Cowork sampled Apr 10-Jun 10 2026, with Claude Code sessions for autonomy comparisons)
works.what_measured: Daily-sampled usage; artifact (deliverable) types; autonomy in Claude Code vs chat; model choice; first linked user survey (about 9,700 respondents).
works.method_plain: Continuous daily sampling and classifiers; survey answers linked to up to 20 randomly sampled sessions per respondent (respondents with fewer than 5 sessions excluded).
key_numbers: 93% of chat/Cowork conversations produce an artifact; code and technical work about one-sixth of conversations
Claude Code autonomy averages 0.37 points higher (1-5 scale) than chat/Cowork; 54% of Claude Code sessions use Opus vs 10% of chat/Cowork
Survey: self-reported gains in speed 86%, scope 82%, quality 69%, cost savings 27%; 10% rate losing their own job as likely
Survey sample skew: Computer/Math about 30% of respondents vs about 4% of US employment

The report text has no time-savings, success-rate or verification numbers; the matching HF release has monthly human_only_time_mean (hours) and human_with_ai_time_mean (minutes) for April and May 2026, but no task_success
works.relevance_to_theta: Mainly infrastructure: continuous sampling and calendar-month aggregates allow a monthly time series (time-varying t in theta_j(t)). The HF release carries gross time-with-AI vs human-alone means by month, though without success rates. Autonomy differences between agentic and chat tools support the delegate-vs-assist split.
works.limitations: Survey respondents are heavily selected. No success primitive in this window. The HF 1P API data excludes Claude Code, and only means (not full distributions) are confirmed in that release.
works.corrections: Report numbers confirmed. Corrected the implication that there is no time data past Feb 2026: the 2026-06-26 HF data documentation lists monthly human_only_time_mean and human_with_ai_time_mean (April-May 2026, with units of hours and minutes), but drops task_success.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Saffron Huang, Bryan Seethor, Esin Durmus, Kunal Handa, Miles McCain, Michael Stern, Deep Ganguli
works.what_measured: In-house engineers' AI use, self-reported productivity, the share of work fully delegable, and agent autonomy over time in 200,000 internal Claude Code transcripts.
works.method_plain: Survey of 132 engineers/researchers (Aug 2025), 53 interviews, and comparison of Claude Code transcripts from Feb vs Aug 2025.
key_numbers: Share of work using Claude: about 59% (rounded to 60%) vs 28% a year earlier
Self-reported productivity +50% (vs +20% a year earlier); 14% report >100%
Merged PRs per engineer per day +67% after the Claude Code rollout
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done
More than half say they can fully delegate only 0-20% of their work
Max consecutive tool calls 9.8 to 21.2 (+116%); human turns per transcript 6.2 to 4.1 (-33%)
works.relevance_to_theta: A frontier-adopter bound. The '0-20% fully delegable' answer is a check on the delegation term q*p for real engineering work. The gap between +50% self-reported output and 27% 'new work' warns that output gains are not the same as labor saved (demand expansion inside the firm). Supervision comments support a positive rho. The autonomy trend supports p rising with t.
works.limitations: Unusual workforce (AI lab), non-anonymous self-reports, 31% response rate in the direct-outreach group (64 of 207), older models (Sonnet 4 / Opus 4). Transcripts measure task mix, not volume.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Note that the page's contributors section omits McCain and Stern, who appear in the citation.

works.title: How People Use ChatGPT
works.authors: Aaron Chatterji, Thomas Cunningham, David J. Deming, Zoe Hitzig, Christopher Ong, Carl Yan Shan, Kevin Wadman
works.what_measured: Growth and composition of consumer ChatGPT messages (Nov 2022-Jul 2025): work vs non-work, topics, Asking/Doing/Expressing intent, O*NET IWAs and GWAs.
works.method_plain: A privacy-preserving automated classifier labels about 1.1 million sampled conversations (May 15 2024-Jun 26 2025). Messages are mapped to one of 332 O*NET Intermediate Work Activities, then rolled up to Generalized Work Activities.
key_numbers: Non-work messages grew from 53% to more than 70% of usage
Asking 49%, Doing 40%, Expressing 11% of all messages; among work messages, Doing nearly 56%, Asking 35%, Expressing 9%
Writing is 40% of work-related messages; nearly 35% of work queries are Doing+Writing
Computer programming 4.2% of messages (paper contrasts this with 33% of work-related Claude conversations, citing Handa et al. 2025)
Work GWAs: Documenting/Recording Information 18.4%, Making Decisions and Solving Problems 14.9%, Thinking Creatively 13.0%, Working with Computers 10.8%
About 10% of world adults had adopted by July 2025
works.relevance_to_theta: Extensive margin and use-type only. 'Doing' vs 'Asking' parallels delegate (p) vs assist/decision support (kappa), suggesting much consumer value is kappa-type. There is no time-saved or success measure, and coding is a small share, so it says little about IT-services theta_j.
works.limitations: Consumer plans only (no Enterprise/Team/API); message share is not labor time; most authors OpenAI-affiliated; not peer-reviewed.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the PDF text.

works.title: Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations
works.authors: Kiran Tomlinson, Sonia Jaffe, Will Wang, Scott Counts, Siddharth Suri
works.venue: arXiv:2507.07935 (v1 Jul 10 2025; v7 Oct 23 2026; arXiv comments say 'NeurIPS 2026')
works.what_measured: For 200k US Bing Copilot conversations (Jan 1-Sep 30 2024), which O*NET IWAs the user wanted help with (user goal) and which the AI performed (AI action), plus completion rate, scope of impact and thumbs feedback. Combined into an occupation-level 'AI applicability score'.
works.method_plain: An LLM classifies each conversation's IWAs. An IWA is 'covered' if it is at least 0.05% of activity. Score = sum over covered IWAs of (importance weight to occupation x completion rate x share at moderate-or-higher scope), averaged over the user and AI sides.
key_numbers: Top scores: Interpreters/Translators 0.49 (coverage 0.98, completion 0.88, scope 0.57); Customer Service Reps 0.44 (0.72/0.90/0.59); Data Scientists 0.36; Web Developers 0.35
All programming maps to one IWA ('Program computer systems or production equipment')
In about 40% of conversations the user-goal and AI-action IWA sets are completely disjoint
Score vs wage correlation (employment-weighted) 0.07; Bachelor's-required occupations mean 0.27 vs 0.19
Correlation with Eloundou et al. exposure r = 0.73 (occupation), 0.91 (SOC major group)
Paper states it measures usage, not downstream productivity or job outcomes
works.relevance_to_theta: Mostly extensive, with a partial intensive element: completion rate (a success proxy; about 0.86-0.90 for the top occupations, 0.55-0.99 across occupations) and 'scope' (how much of the activity AI addresses) are cousins of q*p and of the fraction of the task done. The authors explicitly do not measure labor saved. The r = 0.73 with Eloundou suggests usage-based and rubric-based exposure largely agree. Customer-service scores are relevant to BPO lines.
works.limitations: US Bing Copilot consumer users, 2024; completion is LLM-judged; programming collapses into one IWA, so it cannot split maintenance, testing and development; no time dimension.
works.corrections: Bibliographic data and numbers confirmed. Fixed the completion-rate range in the relevance note: '0.84-0.90' is not a general range; top occupations sit at 0.86-0.90 and the full occupation range is 0.55-0.99. Added the data window (Jan-Sep 2024, US) from the GitHub README. 'NeurIPS 2026' comes only from the arXiv comments field; no proceedings page was checked.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simón Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. Kim, Patrick Chao, Samuel Miserendino, Gildas Chabot, David Li, Michael Sharman, Alexandra Barr, Amelia Glaese, Jerry Tworek
works.what_measured: Expert-graded quality of model deliverables on 1,320 real tasks (44 occupations, top 9 US-GDP sectors), with expert completion and review times. Speed and cost ratios under 'naive', 'try once then review/fix', and 'try n times then fix' workflows.
works.method_plain: Industry experts (about 14 years' experience on average) write tasks and deliverables. Other experts blind-compare model vs human outputs. Time and cost savings combine expert time, review time and the model's win rate.
key_numbers: Gold subset (220 tasks): expert completion time 404 min avg, cost $361; expert review time 109 min avg, cost $86
Win rate (model strictly better than expert, Table 2): GPT-4o 12.5%, o4-mini 29.1%, o3 35.2%, GPT-5 39.0%. Separately, Claude Opus 4.1 had 47.6% wins-or-ties; these two measures are not comparable
Speed ratio, naive vs try-1x-then-fix vs try-nx: GPT-5 90x / 1.12x / 1.39x; o3 161x / 1.08x / 1.28x; GPT-4o 327x / 0.87x / 0.46x (naive = human time / model sampling time)
Cost ratio for GPT-5: try-1x 1.18x; try-nx 1.63x
works.relevance_to_theta: The only source here that nets review cost out of time savings, with the same structure as the draft formula. Review time over task time is about 109/404 = 0.27 (our derivation), a rho estimate for multi-hour knowledge tasks. The win rate is a q*p analogue. Moving from roughly 100x naive to about 1.1-1.4x speedup shows that rho and failure rates, not raw capability, dominate theta. Implied theta_delegate is about 1 - 1/1.12 = 11% for GPT-5 try-1x (our derivation, not the paper's).
works.limitations: A benchmark, not usage data; mostly document-type deliverables, few software-engineering tasks; expert times self-reported (then checked by reviewers); excludes catastrophic-error cost; the authors say try-nx over-penalizes models.
works.corrections: Fixed 'win/tie': 12.5/29.1/35.2/39.0% are strict win rates, while Opus 4.1's 47.6% is wins-or-ties, so the record mixed two measures. Confirmed ICLR 2026 via the proceedings page (the arXiv page lists no venue). Added the abs page and proceedings URL.

summary_flags: 'Weighting by success roughly halves the implied productivity gain (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr)' is overstated: that is a cut of about 33-45%, not half.

'The public HF data ... is enough to build an empirical f_j(h)' is overstated. The histograms describe the length of tasks users chose to bring to Claude, counted by conversation. f_j(h) needs hours-weighting, a selection correction and an O*NET-to-service-line crosswalk. Time units are also unstated in the Jan and Mar 2026 data documentation.

Calling the API success-by-length curve a 'field-data analogue of METR's p(h)' needs a caveat: success is judged by Claude, and both the task mix and the 'human length' (also Claude-estimated) are user-selected, unlike METR's fixed task suite with human baselines.

The verdict that intensive-margin estimates 'are not net of verification' contradicts the summary's own GDPval point. It should say the usage-based estimates are not net of verification; GDPval is, but it is a benchmark.

Gap 'June 2026 Cadences drops time and success primitives, so no time series past Feb 2026' is wrong for the data. The 2026-06-26 HF release has monthly human_only_time_mean (hours) and human_with_ai_time_mean (minutes) for April-May 2026. It does drop task_success.

Gap 'could not confirm whether post-January releases keep the primitives' is now resolved. The 2026-03-24 release keeps task_success, human_only_time and human_with_ai_time for both Claude.ai and API. The 2026-06-26 release keeps the time means but not task_success.

Report 1: 'software development and writing together account for nearly half of usage' is not stated in the source. '57.4%/42.6%' is not in the source. 'One week, single model' is wrong: there are several 7-day snapshots, Dec 2024-Jan 2025, from Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3 Opus.
GDPval: the record mixed strict win rates (OpenAI models) with Claude Opus 4.1's win-or-tie rate.
September 2025 report: the 'context bottleneck' is offered as a hypothesis, not argued as a finding.
Microsoft completion rate '0.84-0.90' is not a general range; across occupations it runs from 0.55 to 0.99.
Datasets list: the labor-market observed-exposure measure is on Hugging Face (labor_market_impacts/job_exposure.csv and task_penetration.csv), so access is public, not 'unknown'.

The Anthropic Fellows source is a third-party job board (Accel), not a primary Anthropic page. Its banner says it no longer accepts applications, while the body says applications are rolling. The '$200M fund' in the gaps is unverified and should not be cited.
verify.corrected_summary: The AI labs' usage datasets go further than the working hypothesis expected, but not all the way. Anthropic's Economic Index started in February 2025 as a pure extensive-margin measure: which O*NET tasks show up in Claude.ai chats, and whether a chat looks like automation (43%) or augmentation (57%). From late 2025 it added intensive-margin quantities, all estimated by Claude itself. Tamkin and McCrory (Nov 2025) have Claude estimate, for 100,000 conversations, how long a professional would need without AI and how long the task took with AI. The median time cut is about 80% (84% in the text, 81% in a figure caption), on tasks averaging about 1.4 hours. These are gross savings inside the chat: they leave out validation and refinement afterwards, and failures are not netted out. The January 2026 'economic primitives' report adds a Claude-judged task-success rate. On first-party API traffic, success falls from about 60% for sub-hour tasks to about 45% for tasks of 5+ hours, crossing 50% near 3.5 hours. That is a field counterpart to METR's p(h), but with model-judged success and user-selected tasks. Weighting by success cuts the implied productivity gain by about a third or more (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr). The public Hugging Face releases for January and March 2026 contain per-O*NET-task human-alone time, with-AI time and success, with means, medians, confidence intervals and histograms, for both Claude.ai and the API (time units are not stated). The June 2026 release continues monthly time means (April-May 2026) but drops success. These data can feed a draft f_j(h) and a p(h) cross-check, after hours-weighting, a selection correction and an O*NET-to-service-line crosswalk. The usage data cannot see review time outside the chat (rho), or whether 'successful' output is actually accepted (q). The best lab source for those is OpenAI's GDPval, a benchmark rather than usage data. On its 220-task gold subset, expert review averages 109 minutes against 404-minute tasks (rho about 0.27, our calculation). Once review-and-fix is included, GPT-5's 90x 'naive' speedup shrinks to about 1.1-1.4x. OpenAI's ChatGPT usage paper and Microsoft's applicability scores are mostly extensive-margin, and Microsoft says it does not measure downstream productivity. Anthropic's internal study (more than half of engineers can fully delegate only 0-20% of their work) gives a sanity bound on the delegation term. Verdict on the hypothesis: partly right. The usage literature now has gross intensive-margin estimates, but they are not net of verification and are model-judged. The one source that nets out review (GDPval) is a benchmark with few software tasks. None are specific to IT services.
verify.dataset_notes: 1) Anthropic/EconomicIndex on Hugging Face: public. Confirmed releases are 2025-02-10, 2025-03-27, 2025-09-15, 2026-01-15, 2026-03-24 and 2026-06-26, plus folders labor_market_impacts and robot_exposure. The README says data CC-BY and code MIT; the metadata tag says MIT. The 2026-01-15 and 2026-03-24 releases both include task_success, human_only_time and human_with_ai_time per O*NET task for Claude.ai (country/state/global) and the 1P API (global only), with API cost and token indices; time units are not stated. The 2026-06-26 release is restructured as calendar-month aggregates (April and May 2026). It includes human_only_time_mean (hours), human_with_ai_time_mean (minutes), ai_autonomy_mean and artifact shares, but not task_success, and its 1P API source excludes Claude Code. 2) The data documentation URL for release_2026_01_15 is correct; also cite release_2026_03_24/data_documentation.md and release_2026_06_26/data_documentation.md. 3) Anthropic observed-exposure measure: change access from 'unknown' to 'public'. Use https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex/tree/main/labor_market_impacts (job_exposure.csv, task_penetration.csv); its link to the Mar 2026 report is inferred from the folder name and timing, not stated. 4) Microsoft working-with-ai: confirmed CC BY 4.0. Files: iwa_metrics.csv (completion, impact_scope, feedback_positive_fraction for user and AI), soc_metrics.csv, ai_applicability_scores.csv, soc_iwa_weights.csv, a nonphysical weights file (name differs between README and repo), soc_to_iwas.csv and physical_tasks.csv. The data are US Bing Copilot conversations, Jan-Sep 2024. 5) GDPval gold subset: the paper says 220 tasks are open-sourced, with an automated grader at evals.openai.com. The arXiv page is not the data URL, and the dataset host URL was not verified. 6) OpenAI ChatGPT sample: lab-internal is correct. 7) Economic Futures program: confirmed $10k-50k awards plus $5k API credits, 'not currently accepting applications', and consultation on Economic Index data. Raw data access is not mentioned. The Fellows listing is on a third-party job board (jobs.accel.com), posted May 22 2026. It names Massenkoff and McCrory as economics mentors and says fellows mainly use external infrastructure and data. The banner says closed while the body says rolling. The '$200M fund' claim is unverified.

streams.name: Surveys of time saved and adoption

works.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David J. Deming
works.year: 2024 (NBER WP Sept 2024, rev. Feb 2025); published Management Science 2026
works.what_measured: US adult (18-64) generative-AI adoption at work and home, intensity (share of work hours assisted) and self-reported time savings, from the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS).
works.method_plain: Nationally representative online survey. Workers who used genAI last week are asked how many extra hours they would have needed to do the same work without it (answer brackets from under 1 hour to over 4 hours). Non-users count as zero saved. Savings are then expressed as a share of all work hours.
key_numbers: Late 2024: nearly 40% of US adults 18-64 use genAI; 23% of employed used it for work in the previous week; 9% every workday (NBER abstract)
genAI assists 1-5% of all work hours; reported time savings = 1.4% of ALL work hours (users and non-users together)
Implied aggregate labor productivity gain ~1.1% (St. Louis Fed summary, Feb 2025)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives an economy-wide, adoption-weighted analogue of S = sum w_j theta_j, but multiplied by adoption and intensity, which our theta_j removes. The ratio (time saved)/(hours assisted) is a rough self-reported estimate of labor saved per AI-touched hour: an intensive-margin number, but not net of review time done outside the AI session and not tied to task length h.
works.limitations: Self-reported counterfactual hours in coarse brackets; US all-sector, not Indian IT; it cannot separate savings from quality gains; savings are 'gross' as perceived by workers. The METR RCT shows that developers' perceptions can have the wrong sign.

works.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Work Productivity (On the Economy blog)
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming
works.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, On the Economy
works.what_measured: Distribution of self-reported time savings among users, broken down by occupation and industry, and the link between hours using AI and time saved.
works.method_plain: Same RPS survey (November 2024 wave). Question: 'How many additional hours of work would you have needed to complete the same amount of work?' The authors then regress time saved on share of hours using AI, across occupations.
key_numbers: Previous-week users save 5.4% of work hours on average (~2.2 h per 40-h week); across ALL workers 1.4%. The 5.4% figure is often quoted without noting it covers users only.
Among users: 33.0% saved 1 h or less, 26.4% saved 2 h, 20.1% saved 3 h, 20.5% saved 4+ h; 33.5% of every-day users saved 4+ h vs 11.5% of one-day users
Computer & mathematical occupations: ~12% of hours using genAI, 2.5% of hours saved; personal services: 1.3% using, 0.4% saved
Information industry: 14.0% of hours using, 2.6% saved (highest); leisure/accommodation 2.3% using, 0.6% saved
Cross-occupation slope 0.17: +10 pp hours using AI is associated with +1.7 pp time saved
Workers are ~33% more productive in each hour they use genAI; aggregate productivity +1.1%
works.relevance_to_theta: The 0.17 slope and the '33% more productive per assisted hour' figure are self-reported analogues of labor saved per AI-touched hour, closest to kappa (assistant-mode speedup) rather than delegation. The computer/math and information rows are the closest US proxy for the IT-services share of hours touched.
works.limitations: Cross-sectional, self-reported, coarse brackets; occupation categories are broader than IT-services task types; no task-length dimension; no correction for review done outside the AI session.

works.title: The State of Generative AI Adoption in 2025; plus the Generative AI Adoption Tracker (FRED series RPSGENAITSALL)
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming
works.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (On the Economy; FRED)
works.what_measured: A quarterly time series of genAI adoption, share of work hours assisted, and share of work hours saved, with occupation and industry breakdowns.
works.method_plain: RPS repeated each quarter with the same question about counterfactual hours. Savings are averaged over all employed adults, with non-users counted as zero.
key_numbers: FRED blog (Aug 2026), Q3 2024 to Q2 2026: used genAI for work last week 28.2% to 39.2%; work hours assisted 4.1% to 6.3%; hours saved 1.6% to 2.2%
Overall adoption 44.6% (Aug 2024, revised from 39.4%) to 54.6% (Aug 2025); work use 33.3% to 37.4%
Pooled Feb/May/Aug 2025: savings = 1.6% of all work hours; implied productivity gain up to 1.3% since ChatGPT
Industry correlation 0.32 between time savings and detrended productivity growth; 1 pp of savings is associated with 2.7 pp higher productivity growth (authors say this is not causal)
works.relevance_to_theta: The only public quarterly series of self-reported time saved. Dividing hours saved by hours assisted gives roughly 2.2/6.3 ≈ 0.35 in Q2 2026, about the same as in 2024 (1.6/4.1 ≈ 0.39). Saved time per assisted hour has been FLAT while assisted hours grew. So, in self-reports, recent growth is on the extensive margin (more hours touched), not the intensive one. This is a testable contrast with the rising capability ceiling that METR-style p(h,t) implies.
works.limitations: Not net of hours added elsewhere (review, rework); self-report; US; industry and occupation series exist on FRED, but I did not open the computer/math series values; the 2024 adoption figure was revised because of a question-order change.

works.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (revised as 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI')
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.year: 2025 (BFI WP May 2025; NBER w33777 issued May 2025, revised March 2026)
works.venue: Becker Friedman Institute WP 2025-56; NBER Working Paper 33777
works.what_measured: Chatbot adoption, self-reported time savings and other benefits in 11 AI-exposed occupations in Denmark (~25,000 workers, 7,000 workplaces), linked to administrative earnings and hours records.
works.method_plain: Two survey waves (2023-24) are linked to Danish register data. Time saved as a % of hours = frequency of use × reported minutes saved per day of use. A difference-in-differences design compares earnings and hours of adopters versus non-adopters, and of encouraging versus non-encouraging workplaces, before and after ChatGPT.
key_numbers: Average time savings among users = 2.8% of work hours (body text); the abstract rounds this to 'average time savings of 3%'
Average 25 minutes saved per day of use; on usage days savings are only 6-7% of hours, and adopters actively use chatbots 5-6% of hours on those days
Range from 6.8% (marketing professionals at encouraging employers) to 0.6% (teachers at non-encouraging schools); software developers and marketers at encouraging firms report ~7%
Employer encouragement raises take-up from 47% to 83% for a typical worker; benefits are 10-40% larger when employers encourage use
Time savings reported by 64-90% of users depending on occupation; 80% reallocate the saved time to other job tasks, under 10% to breaks/leisure
New job tasks created for 8.4% of workers
Earnings and recorded-hours effects are precise zeros: CIs rule out effects larger than 1% (2025 BFI version); the 2026 NBER revision states 'larger than 2% two years after' launch
Only 3-7% of time savings are passed through to earnings
Compares its numbers with RCTs: Noy & Zhang 37% time saved in writing; Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond ~15%; Peng et al. 2023 +58% (as the paper quotes it); Cui et al. 26%
works.relevance_to_theta: The best direct evidence that realized intensive-margin savings (~3% of hours, ~7% on usage days) are an order of magnitude below RCT task-level effects. The paper explicitly decomposes the gap into: applicability (few tasks touched, low f_j mass on AI-suitable tasks), frequency, and management/complementary investment. Its point that 80% of saved time is reallocated to other tasks matters for whether theta turns into headcount reduction.
works.limitations: Danish chatbot use in 2023-24 (pre-agentic); self-reports; occupations include software developers and IT support but not offshore IT services; the bound changed between versions, so cite the version used.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein
works.what_measured: Measured effect of AI tool access on task completion time compared with forecasts and self-perceptions, for experienced open-source developers in their own large repos.
works.method_plain: RCT at the task level: 246 real issues (~2 h each) were randomly assigned to AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. Developers (n=16) mostly used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. The study compares measured completion time with pre-task forecasts and post-task self-estimates.
key_numbers: AI-allowed tasks took 19% LONGER
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed in a 20% speedup afterwards
Economics experts forecast a 39% reduction in time; ML experts 38%
Repos average 22k+ stars, 1M+ lines; developers averaged 5 years on the project

Follow-up (2026, per METR and secondary coverage, not opened in full): estimated -18% (CI -38% to +9%) for returning devs and -4% (CI -15% to +9%) for new devs. METR calls this weak evidence because of selection (devs refusing no-AI conditions)
works.relevance_to_theta: The key calibration point for the gap between self-report and measurement: perceived savings were about +20% while measured savings were about -19%, a gap of ~40 pp. This directly argues against plugging survey time savings into theta_j without adjustment. It also gives an empirical value for kappa (assistant mode) on maintenance-type tasks in mature codebases that can be ≤0 once review is included.
works.limitations: Small n (16 devs); a specific setting (expert developers, familiar huge repos); early-2025 tools; the follow-up was compromised by selection; I did not open the 2026 follow-up post directly.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic Economic Research)
works.what_measured: Model-estimated time to do each task with and without AI, across 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks and wages.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates (a) hours a competent professional would need without AI and (b) the time the user actually spent with AI. Estimates are aggregated to O*NET tasks and weighted by BLS wages. They are validated against 1,000 open-source JIRA tickets with known times.
key_numbers: Tasks would take ~90 minutes on average without AI; median time saving ~80% (body text says 84%, the figure caption 81%)
Validation on JIRA: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman rho = 0.44 vs developers' 0.50; log Pearson r 0.46 vs 0.67; it overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones
Implied +1.8%/yr US labor productivity growth over 10 years at universal adoption (≈1.08% TFP with labor share 0.6); software developers contribute 19% of the total gain
Excludes time spent validating or refining outputs outside the chat
works.relevance_to_theta: Methodologically closest to the intensive-margin recipe: it estimates task length h (useful for f_j) and the time saved per task. But it is gross of review (rho) and acceptance (q), so it is an upper bound on theta. Comparing its ~80% with survey 5-7% and RCT 15-55% shows how sensitive the result is to netting out review.
works.limitations: Time estimates come from the model, not observed; the sample is selected to tasks people chose to bring to Claude (the extensive margin is already conditioned on); it ignores outside-chat review; it is not a peer-reviewed paper.

works.title: AI and Jobs: This Time Is No Different (a case study of India's IT sector)
works.authors: Deepak Mishra, Mansi Kedia, Aarti Reddy, Cledwyn Fernandez, Agrima Khanduri
works.what_measured: Direction of change after AI adoption in hiring, team size, output, cost and time per unit of work, by business division, across 651 Indian IT firms (IT services, products, BPM, ER&D/GCCs, startups) in 10 cities.
works.method_plain: Primary survey, Nov 2025-Jan 2026, 72% in person and 28% online. Firms pick their most AI-affected divisions and rate the change in team size, output volume and quality, time per unit of work, and cost per unit as increased or decreased, modestly or significantly. The report is explicitly about direction, not magnitude.
key_numbers: 65% of firms report hiring declined after AI introduction, 24% increased, 11% no change
Junior level: 55% of firms report employment declines, 35% increases; mid-level 25% declines / 42% increases; senior 82% no change

Of 1,928 most-affected divisions: 38% had team size down with output up (productivity gain), 11% the opposite, 23% unchanged; gains outnumber declines 3.5:1 (3.7:1 in software development & engineering)
31% of divisions had output up with cost down; gain:decline ratio ~2:1
Most affected divisions (top-3 mentions): software development & engineering 72%, IT infrastructure & cloud 48%, project/program management 37%; QA, R&D and marketing among the least affected
Roles with declining demand (open-text, ~595 responses): data entry/clerical/back-office 32%, manual testing/QA 15%, entry-level programming 13%, customer support 8%, routine IT ops/infrastructure 7%
Expectations: 44% no major change in employment, 28% expansion, 27% contraction; only 4% of firms have trained more than half of staff in AI
works.relevance_to_theta: The only India-IT-specific survey found with a division-level breakdown that maps roughly onto j (development, infrastructure, testing, BPM, support). It asks about 'time spent per unit of work', which is conceptually theta_j, but only directionally. Requesting the microdata, or a follow-up asking for percentage magnitudes by division, could give a direct theta_j check.
works.limitations: No magnitudes; not fully representative (the authors say so); skewed toward small and medium firms; funded by OpenAI; respondents are firm representatives, not workers; cross-section only.

works.title: EY India GenAI IT-industry survey (Feb 2025) and 'The AIdea of India 2025: How much productivity can GenAI unlock in India?'
works.authors: EY India (no individual authors identified)
works.venue: EY India report / press release (coverage in tele.net.in)
works.what_measured: Projected (not measured) productivity potential from GenAI for Indian IT functions, and economy-wide task-level exposure.
works.method_plain: AIdea: consultants scored more than 10,000 tasks on exposure, complementarity (human oversight needed) and intensity (time volume), then aggregated to business processes and industries using RBI KLEMS. The IT survey covers about 500 roles. The underlying sample and method for the IT number are not disclosed in what I opened.
key_numbers: IT industry productivity +43-45% over the next 5 years (projection)
By function: software development ~60%, BPO services 52%, IT consulting 47%; these three are 50-60% of the total gain
89% of top IT firms trialling GenAI; 33% of those in production

AIdea economy-wide: 24% of tasks can be fully automated, 42% significantly augmented; +2.61% productivity by 2030 in the organized sector (up to 2.82% more in the unorganized sector); ~38 million jobs affected
AIdea business-process range: call-centre management ~80% productivity uplift to new product development ~17%; the IT bubble in its sector chart sits near 45% potential
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives consultant priors for the theta_j ordering (dev > BPO > consulting). These are capability-potential ceilings, close in spirit to our theta_j, but they are not net of review/failure in any documented way, and no method is published for the IT figure. Use them as an upper-bound prior only.
works.limitations: Projections, not measurements; opaque method; commercial incentive; I could not open the EY IT-survey release itself (only press coverage), so treat the per-function numbers as medium confidence.

works.title: AI use by businesses (BTOS): 'Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users'
works.authors: US Census Bureau
works.venue: Census.gov America Counts story; Business Trends and Outlook Survey
works.what_measured: Share of US firms using AI, by size and sector; expected use within 6 months.
works.method_plain: Biweekly firm survey (~20,000 responses per round). Yes/no question on AI use; in November 2025 the wording changed from 'producing goods or services' to 'any business function'. A supplement on 15 business functions began 17 Nov 2025 (experimental).
key_numbers: National AI use 17-20% of firms from Dec 2025 to May 2026; 19.8% as of 3 May 2026; 20-23% expect to use within 6 months
Firms with 250+ employees: 37%; 100-249: 32%; firms with 4 or fewer: under 20%
Information sector 39.7% currently use (≈42% expected); Finance & Insurance 33.9%; Retail ~14%
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure adoption (extensive) margin: it confirms that adoption is a separate object from the capability ceiling theta_j, which is why dropping adoption from theta is defensible but requires a separate adoption term to reconcile with realized replacement (~2.3 pp/yr).
works.limitations: Firm-weighted (dominated by small firms); binary use measure, no intensity or time saved; series break in Nov 2025; US only.

works.title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy
works.authors: Jeffrey S. Allen
works.what_measured: Reconciles adoption estimates across BTOS (firms), RPS (workers) and the Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty (executives).
works.method_plain: Side-by-side comparison of surveys, with explanations for gaps: weighting by firm vs employment, question wording, respondent knowledge, shadow AI, social desirability.
key_numbers: BTOS ~18% of firms (end-2025)
SBU Nov 2025: 78% of the labor force is at AI-adopting firms and 54% at LLM-using firms (employment-weighted); 69.4% / 46.4% equal-weighted
RPS Nov 2025: 41% of workers use genAI for work; ~12% daily
SBU intensity: 35% of users use AI up to 1 h/week, 29% use it 1-5 h/week
Gallup mid-2025: 8% of workers use AI daily
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows adoption estimates range from 18% to 78% depending on weighting and wording. Any top-down back-out of theta from realized replacement (theta ≈ realized / adoption) is therefore very sensitive to the adoption measure chosen. Employment-weighted measures are the right ones for large Indian IT firms.
works.limitations: US; adoption only, no time saved; descriptive.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2): 889-942
works.what_measured: Measured productivity (issues resolved per hour) of customer-support agents after staggered rollout of a GPT-based assistant.
works.method_plain: Natural experiment using administrative data on 5,179 agents at one firm; staggered access compared over time.
key_numbers: +14% issues resolved per hour on average (NBER abstract; Humlum & Vestergaard cite 15%, likely the QJE figure, which I did not confirm)
+34% for novice/low-skill agents; minimal effect for experienced/high-skill agents
works.relevance_to_theta: The measured BPO/customer-support benchmark for theta_BPO in assistant mode (kappa) with human-in-the-loop review included. Note that the effect is heterogeneous by experience, which interacts with the junior-heavy pyramid of Indian IT/BPO firms.
works.limitations: One firm, a 2020-21 era model, output-per-hour rather than labor saved at fixed output; US/Philippines agents (offshore BPO-like, which helps relevance).

works.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
works.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
works.what_measured: Time to complete a standardized coding task (implement an HTTP server in JavaScript) with and without Copilot.
works.method_plain: Controlled lab experiment, random assignment of Copilot access.
key_numbers: Treatment group completed the task 55.8% faster (often misquoted as '55%' productivity or '58%' as in Humlum & Vestergaard)
works.relevance_to_theta: Upper end of measured kappa on a short greenfield task; contrasts with METR's -19% on long tasks in mature repos. This is consistent with savings declining in task length h and codebase familiarity, which is exactly what p(h,t) and f_j(h) are meant to capture.
works.limitations: A single small, self-contained task; no review or maintenance burden; 2022 model; sample size not shown on the abstract page.

research.stream_summary: Surveys of AI time savings mostly measure something different from theta_j. The biggest US source (Bick, Blandin and Deming's Real-Time Population Survey) asks workers how many extra hours they would have needed without AI. Averaged over ALL workers, savings rose from 1.4% of work hours (late 2024) to about 2.1-2.2% (mid-2026). Among users only it was 5.4% (Nov 2024). Computer/math occupations save about 2.5% of all hours. A key pattern: hours saved per hour assisted has stayed roughly flat (~0.35-0.4) while the share of hours assisted grew. So, in self-reports, recent growth is on the extensive margin (more work touched) rather than the intensive margin. Denmark (Humlum and Vestergaard) finds users save 2.8% of hours (6-7% on days they use AI) and zero detectable effect on earnings or hours, with 80% of saved time moved to other tasks. Experiments give much bigger task-level effects: +14% in customer support and 56% faster on a small coding task. But METR's RCT found experienced developers were 19% SLOWER while believing they were 20% faster, so self-reports can get the sign wrong. Anthropic's model-estimated ~80% saving per conversation excludes review time and is best read as a gross ceiling. For India, the ICRIER 2026 survey of 651 IT firms says which divisions are affected (software development, infrastructure, project management; declining demand for back-office, manual testing, entry-level coding) but only gives directions, not magnitudes. EY's 43-45% (development ~60%, BPO 52%) is a projection with an undisclosed method. Bottom line: the working hypothesis largely holds. Surveys measure adoption × intensity × perceived (gross) savings. None measures net-of-review labor saved per task as a function of task length. The surveys are useful as lower bounds and for weights, not as estimates of theta_j.
gaps_noticed: No survey measures labor saved NET of review/rework time; all are gross perceived savings or exclude outside-session validation (Anthropic note explicitly).
No source links time saved to task length h; none can identify f_j(h) or the p(h,t) curve.

India: ICRIER 2026 asks 'time spent per unit of work' by division but reports only direction; no magnitudes. Asking ICRIER for division-level microdata, or for a magnitude follow-up, could fill the gap.
EY's India IT function-level numbers (dev ~60%, BPO 52%, consulting 47%) could not be traced to a published method; I could not open the EY IT release itself (only press coverage).

Nasscom: no Nasscom-branded time-savings or productivity survey figure was found; only adoption/revenue statements (e.g., ~25% of tech services firms moving AI to production, USD 10-12bn AI services revenue, per secondary coverage I did not open).
PLFS: I found no evidence of an AI-use module in PLFS (not confirmed by opening PLFS documentation); India has no RPS/BTOS equivalent.
Self-report vs measured gap is quantified only for software (METR); there is no comparable validation for BPO, testing or infrastructure work.
Surveys conflate time saved with quality improvement and with time reallocated to new tasks (Humlum: 80% reallocated), so translating them into headcount needs the demand side (eps, phi).
The BBD tracker has occupation/industry time-savings series on FRED; I did not open the computer/math or information series values.
METR 2026 follow-up figures come from METR plus secondary coverage; the primary post was not opened in full.
