works.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David J. Deming
works.year: 2024 (NBER WP Sept 2024, revised Feb 2025); published Management Science 2026
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 32966; Management Science 72(10): 8440-8456 (2026), doi:10.1287/mnsc.2025.02523
works.what_measured: US adult (18-64) generative-AI adoption at work and at home, its intensity (share of work hours assisted) and self-reported time savings, from the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS).
works.method_plain: A nationally representative online survey. Workers who used genAI in the previous week are asked how many extra hours they would have needed to do the same work without it, with bracketed answers (1 hour or less, 2, 3, 4 or more). Non-users count as zero saved. Savings are then expressed as a share of all work hours.
key_numbers: Late 2024: nearly 40% of US adults aged 18-64 used genAI; 23% of employed people used it for work in the previous week; 9% used it every workday (NBER abstract). Note: the authors later revised the 2024 adoption level upward to 44.6% (Aug 2024) after fixing a question-order problem (St. Louis Fed, Nov 2025).
GenAI assisted an estimated 1-5% of all work hours. Reported time savings equal 1.4% of ALL work hours (users and non-users together; NBER abstract).
Implied aggregate labor productivity gain of about 1.1% (St. Louis Fed On the Economy, Feb 2025)
works.relevance_to_theta: An economy-wide analogue of S = sum w_j theta_j, but multiplied by adoption and intensity, both of which our theta_j removes. Time saved divided by hours assisted is a rough self-reported measure of labor saved per AI-touched hour. That is an intensive-margin number, but it is gross: it does not net out review done outside the AI session, and it is not tied to task length h.
works.limitations: Self-reported counterfactual hours in coarse, top-coded brackets (4+ hours); US, all sectors, not Indian IT; cannot separate time savings from quality gains; savings are gross as workers perceive them. METR's RCT shows developers' perceptions can have the wrong sign. The 2024 adoption levels in the NBER abstract were later revised upward.
works.corrections: Added the full Management Science citation (vol. 72(10), pp. 8440-8456) shown on the NBER page. Added a note that the 2024 adoption level was later revised (39.4% to 44.6%). No numeric errors found.

works.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Work Productivity (On the Economy blog)
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming
works.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, On the Economy
works.what_measured: Distribution of self-reported time savings among users, broken down by occupation and industry, and the link between hours spent using AI and time saved.
works.method_plain: Same RPS survey (November 2024 wave for time savings). Previous-week users are asked how many additional hours they would have needed to do the same work without AI. Across occupations, the authors relate time saved to the share of hours spent using AI (a fitted slope).
key_numbers: Previous-week users save 5.4% of work hours on average (about 2.2 h of a 40-h week). Across ALL workers, including non-users, savings are 1.4% of hours. The 5.4% figure covers users only.
Among users (Nov 2024): 33.0% saved 1 h or less, 26.4% saved 2 h, 20.1% saved 3 h, 20.5% saved 4+ h. 33.5% of every-day users saved 4+ h, against 11.5% of users who used it on one day.
Computer & mathematical occupations: genAI used in nearly 12% of work hours, 2.5% of work time saved. Personal services: 1.3% used, 0.4% saved.
Information industry: 14.0% of hours using AI, 2.6% saved (the highest). Leisure, accommodation and other services: 2.3% using, 0.6% saved (the lowest).
Slope 0.17: each 10 pp rise in the share of hours using AI is associated with a 1.7 pp rise in time saved.
Implied productivity gain of 33% per hour of genAI use; aggregate productivity gain about 1.1%.
Share of work hours assisted: 1.3%-5.4% for all workers; 6.0%-24.9% for weekly users.
works.relevance_to_theta: The 0.17 slope and the '33% more productive per hour of use' figure are self-reported analogues of labor saved per AI-touched hour. They are closest to kappa (speedup in assistant mode) rather than to delegation. The computer/math and information rows are the closest US proxy for the share of IT-services hours that AI touches.
works.limitations: Cross-sectional, self-reported, coarse top-coded brackets. Occupation categories are broader than IT-services task types. No task-length dimension. No correction for review done outside the AI session. The authors note that saved time may go to leisure rather than output.
works.corrections: All numbers matched the page. Added the hours-assisted ranges stated on the page.

works.title: The State of Generative AI Adoption in 2025; plus the Generative AI Adoption Tracker (FRED series RPSGENAITSALL, RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL) and FRED Blog 'Does generative AI save time at work?'
works.authors: Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming (tracker and Nov 2025 post); the FRED Blog post (Aug 27, 2026) describes their tracker
works.year: 2025 (Nov 13 post); FRED Blog Aug 27, 2026; FRED data through 2026Q3
works.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (On the Economy; FRED; FRED Blog)
works.what_measured: A quarterly time series of genAI adoption, the share of work hours assisted and the share of work hours saved, with occupation and industry breakdowns.
works.method_plain: The RPS is repeated each quarter with the same counterfactual-hours question. Savings are averaged over all employed adults, with non-users counted as zero. Assisted hours are the midpoint of bracketed days and hours of use, zero for non-users.
key_numbers: Time saved as % of ALL work hours (FRED RPSGENAITSALL, quarterly): 2024Q4 1.41; 2025Q1 1.62; 2025Q2 1.82; 2025Q3 1.76; 2025Q4 1.99; 2026Q1 2.07; 2026Q2 2.17; 2026Q3 2.08
Work hours assisted as % of ALL work hours (FRED RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL): 2024Q4 4.10; 2025Q1 4.68; 2025Q2 4.91; 2025Q3 5.73; 2025Q4 5.59; 2026Q1 5.97; 2026Q2 6.27; 2026Q3 5.31

FRED Blog (Aug 2026): genAI used for work in the previous week rose from 28.2% (Q3 2024) to 39.2% (Q2 2026). Hours assisted rose from 4.1% to 6.3% and hours saved from 1.6% to 2.2% over 'roughly the same stretch' (exact quarters not stated; FRED's own series start in 2024Q4 at 4.10 and 1.41).
Overall adoption 44.6% (Aug 2024, revised from 39.4%) to 54.6% (Aug 2025); work use 33.3% to 37.4%
Pooled Feb/May/Aug 2025: savings equal 1.6% of all work hours; implied productivity gain of 'up to 1.3%' since ChatGPT (an upper bound)

Across industries, the correlation between time savings and detrended productivity growth is 0.32. Industries with 1 pp higher savings had 2.7 pp higher productivity growth relative to the prepandemic trend; the authors say this is not causal.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only public quarterly series of self-reported time saved. Using matched FRED quarters, hours saved per hour assisted is about 0.34 in 2024Q4 (1.41/4.10), 0.35 in 2025Q1, 0.37 in 2025Q2, 0.31 in 2025Q3, 0.36 in 2025Q4, 0.35 in 2026Q1 and 2026Q2 (2.17/6.27), and 0.39 in 2026Q3 (hours assisted fell that quarter). So self-reported saving per assisted hour has been roughly flat at about 0.35 while assisted hours grew. That points to growth in hours touched rather than in saving per touched hour. Two caveats apply. Both series are built from brackets, and the time-saved question is top-coded at 4+ hours, which mechanically limits how far measured intensive savings can rise. The series is also gross of review done outside the AI session. This is a testable contrast with the rising capability ceiling that METR-style p(h,t) implies, but it is not clean evidence against it.
works.limitations: Not net of hours added elsewhere (review, rework); self-reported; US only. Bracketed and top-coded answers. Occupation and industry series exist on FRED, but their values were not opened here. The 2024 and early-2025 figures were reweighted after a question-order problem was found. The FRED Blog's start-period labels (Q3 2024) do not line up exactly with the FRED series, which begin in 2024Q4.
works.corrections: Fixed the ratio calculation. The original paired 1.6% saved (roughly the 2025Q1 level) with 4.1% assisted (the 2024Q4 level) and got 0.39 for '2024'. The matched-quarter ratio from FRED is 0.34 in 2024Q4. Added the FRED hours-assisted series and its values, including the 2026Q3 drop to 5.31. Removed 'tracker updated through 2026-10-20', which I could not confirm; the FRED data run through 2026Q3. Noted the top-coding caveat. All other numbers were confirmed.

works.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (revised as 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI')
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.year: 2025 (BFI WP dated May 9, 2025; NBER w33777 issued May 2025, revised March 2026)
works.venue: Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper 2025-56; NBER Working Paper 33777
works.what_measured: Chatbot adoption, self-reported time savings and other benefits in 11 AI-exposed occupations in Denmark (25,000 workers, 7,000 workplaces), linked to administrative earnings and hours records.
works.method_plain: Two survey waves (late 2023 and 2024) are linked to Danish employer-employee register data. Time saved as a % of hours is the frequency of use times the reported minutes saved per day of use. A difference-in-differences design, using employer encouragement as quasi-experimental variation, compares earnings and recorded hours before and after ChatGPT.
key_numbers: Average time savings among users = 2.8% of work hours (body text); the abstract rounds this to 'average time savings of 3%'

Average of 25 minutes saved per day of use. On usage days, savings are still only 6-7% of hours, and adopters actively use chatbots for 5-6% of their hours on those days. The typical adopter uses chatbots every third to fourth day.

Average time savings range from 6.8% (marketing professionals whose employers encourage use) to 0.6% (teachers at schools that do not). Software developers and marketers at encouraging employers report about 7%.
Employer initiatives nearly double take-up for a typical worker, from 47% to 83%. Reported benefits are 10%-40% greater when employers encourage use.
Time savings are reported by 64%-90% of users, depending on occupation. 80% reallocate saved time to other job tasks; fewer than 10% use it for breaks or leisure.
AI chatbots created new job tasks for 8.4% of workers

Earnings and recorded-hours effects are precise zeros. The 2025 BFI version's confidence intervals rule out effects larger than 1%; the 2026 NBER revision's abstract rules out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's launch.
Only 3-7% of time savings are passed through to earnings (2025 BFI version)

For comparison the paper cites: Noy & Zhang 37% time saved in writing; Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond 15%; Peng et al. 2023 'a 58% increase' (as the paper quotes it; the Peng abstract says 55.8% faster); Cui et al. 26%
works.relevance_to_theta: Strong direct evidence that realized intensive-margin savings (about 3% of hours, 6-7% on usage days) are far below task-level RCT effects. The paper explains the gap through limited applicability (few tasks touched), infrequent use, and employer complementary investment. That maps loosely onto f_j mass and adoption. Its finding that 80% of saved time is reallocated to other tasks matters for whether theta turns into headcount reduction.
works.limitations: Danish chatbot use in 2023-24, before agentic tools; self-reported. The occupations include software developers and IT support, but not offshore IT services. The bound on earnings effects changed between versions, so cite the version used. The 2026 NBER revision's abstract does not restate the time-savings figures, so those come from the 2025 BFI version.
works.corrections: All numbers were checked against the BFI PDF text and the NBER page. I clarified that the 3-7% pass-through and the 2.8% figure come from the 2025 BFI version; the NBER 2026 abstract does not report them.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein
works.what_measured: The measured effect of access to AI tools on task completion time, compared with forecasts and self-perceptions, for experienced open-source developers working in their own large repositories.
works.method_plain: A task-level RCT: 246 real issues (averaging about 2 h each) were randomly assigned to AI-allowed or AI-disallowed. The 16 developers mostly used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. Measured completion time is compared with pre-task forecasts and post-study self-estimates.
key_numbers: AI-allowed tasks took 19% LONGER (CI +2% to +39%, per METR's 2026 update)
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed in a 20% speedup afterwards
Economics experts forecast a 39% reduction in time; ML experts forecast 38% (arXiv abstract)
Repositories average 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code; developers averaged about 5 years on their projects

Follow-up (METR, Feb 24, 2026; 57 developers, 143 repos, 800+ tasks), with change in completion time where negative means FASTER with AI: returning developers -18% (CI -38% to +9%), i.e. an 18% speedup point estimate; new developers -4% (CI -15% to +9%). METR calls this very weak evidence, likely a lower bound on the speedup, because of selection (developers and tasks withheld from no-AI conditions), a pay cut from $150 to $50/hr, and unreliable timing with concurrent agents. The original 2025 page is now labelled out of date.
works.relevance_to_theta: The key calibration point for the gap between self-report and measurement: perceived savings were about +20% while measured time rose by 19%, a gap of roughly 40 pp. This argues against plugging survey time savings into theta_j without adjustment. For early-2025 tools it gives an empirical kappa (assistant mode, review included) on maintenance-type tasks in mature codebases that can be at or below zero. METR's 2026 update suggests this has moved toward positive speedups, though the evidence is weak.
works.limitations: Small sample (16 developers); a specific setting (expert developers in familiar, very large repositories); early-2025 tools that METR now says no longer reflect current AI impact. The follow-up was compromised by selection.
works.corrections: Opened the 2026 follow-up post directly (metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/). The record's '-18%' and '-4%' were ambiguous. METR's convention is change in completion time, so negative values are SPEEDUPS (18% and 4% less time), not slowdowns. Added the sample size, the original CI, METR's 'likely a lower bound' caveat, and the fact that the 2025 page is now labelled out of date. The 2025 numbers were confirmed.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic Economics team)
works.year: 2025 (Nov; the page shows Nov 25, 2025, while its suggested citation says 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: Model-estimated time to do each task with and without AI, across 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks and wages.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates (a) the hours a competent professional would need without AI and (b) the time the user actually spent with AI. The estimates are aggregated to O*NET tasks and weighted by BLS wages. They are validated against 1,000 open-source JIRA tickets with known times.
key_numbers: Tasks would take about 90 minutes on average without AI (the key findings say 1.4 hours). The headline time saving is about 80%; the body text gives a median of 84% and the figure caption 81%.
JIRA validation: Claude Sonnet 4.5 has Spearman rho = 0.44 against developers' 0.50, and log-scale Pearson r = 0.46 against 0.67. It overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones.

Implied +1.8%/yr US labor productivity growth over the next decade, assuming 10 years to universal adoption (about 1.08% TFP with a labor share of 0.6). Software developers contribute about 19% of the total gain.
Cannot account for time spent outside the chat, such as checking the quality or accuracy of Claude's work
works.relevance_to_theta: Methodologically the closest to an intensive-margin recipe: it estimates task length h (useful for f_j) and the time saved per task. But it is gross of review (rho) and acceptance (q), so it is an upper bound on theta. Comparing its ~80% with survey figures (3-7% of hours) and RCT figures (about -19% to +56%) shows how sensitive the result is to what is netted out and to the unit of measurement.
works.limitations: Time estimates come from the model, not from observation. The sample is limited to tasks people chose to bring to Claude, so the extensive margin is already conditioned on. It ignores review outside the chat. Not peer-reviewed. Internal inconsistencies (90 min vs 1.4 h; 84% vs 81%).
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Noted the date discrepancy on the page (Nov 25 vs Nov 5) and the 90-minute vs 1.4-hour inconsistency.

works.title: AI and Jobs: This Time Is No Different (A Case Study of India's IT Sector)
works.authors: Deepak Mishra, Mansi Kedia, Aarti Reddy, Cledwyn Fernandez, Agrima Khanduri
works.venue: ICRIER report (ISBN 978-81-998893-4-7); acknowledges support from OpenAI
works.what_measured: Direction of change after AI adoption in hiring, team size, output, cost and time per unit of work, by business division, from 651 respondents (620 unique firms) in Indian IT: services, products, BPM, ER&D, GCCs and startups, across 10 cities.
works.method_plain: Primary survey, Nov 2025-Jan 2026, 72% in person and 28% online. About 6,500 people were approached, giving a response rate of about 10%. Firms pick their most AI-affected divisions and report changes in team size, output volume and quality, scope, time per unit of work, and cost per unit. The report says it focuses on the direction of change rather than precise magnitudes.
key_numbers: 65% of firms report that hiring declined after AI was introduced, 24% that it increased, 11% no significant change
Entry level: 55% of firms report employment declines, 35% increases. Mid-level: 25% declines, 33% no change, 42% increases. Senior: 82% no change.

Of 1,928 most-affected divisions: 731 (38%) had team size down with output up, 208 (11%) the opposite, 446 (23%) unchanged productivity. Gains outnumber declines 3.5:1 overall, 3.7:1 in software development & engineering, and 7.0:1 in marketing.
591 divisions (31%) had output up and cost down; the gain:decline ratio is about 2:1, both overall and in software development
Most affected divisions (top-3 mentions): software development & engineering 72%, IT infrastructure & cloud 48%, project/program management 37%. QA, R&D and marketing are among the least affected.

Roles with declining demand in the INDUSTRY, not necessarily the respondent's own organization (open text, about 595 of 650 responses classified): data entry/clerical/back-office 32%, manual testing/QA 15%, entry-level programming 13%, creative production 10%, customer support/telecalling 8%, routine IT operations/infrastructure support 7%
Expectations: 44% expect no major change in employment, 28% expansion, 27% decline. Only 4% of firms have trained more than half of their staff in AI-related skills.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only India-IT-specific survey found with a division-level breakdown that roughly maps onto j (development, infrastructure, testing, BPM, support). It asks about 'time spent per unit of work', which is conceptually close to theta_j, but reports only direction. Requesting the microdata, or a follow-up asking for percentage magnitudes by division, could give a direct check on theta_j.
works.limitations: No magnitudes. The authors say it is not fully representative of the sector, though they call it broadly representative. By revenue it is 34% medium, 31% small, 16% micro and 16% very large firms. Response rate about 10%. Supported by OpenAI (per the acknowledgements). Respondents are firm representatives, not workers. Cross-section only. The declining-roles question is about the industry, not the respondent's own firm.
works.corrections: '651 IT firms' is 651 respondents from 620 unique firms (some large firms had multiple respondents). Added the mid-level no-change figure (33%), the counts, and the 7.0:1 marketing ratio. Clarified that the declining-roles question refers to the industry, not necessarily the respondent's organization. Changed 'funded by OpenAI' to 'acknowledges OpenAI support', which is what the report says. Softened 'skewed toward small and medium firms' and added the size shares.

works.title: EY India GenAI IT-industry survey (Feb 2025) and 'The AIdea of India 2025: How much productivity can GenAI unlock in India?'
works.authors: EY India (no individual authors identified)
works.year: 2025 (AIdea report Jan 2025; IT survey reported Feb 11, 2025)
works.venue: EY India report; IT-survey findings known only through press coverage (tele.net.in, YourStory, Reuters syndication)
works.what_measured: Projected (not measured) productivity potential from GenAI for Indian IT functions, and economy-wide task-level exposure.
works.method_plain: AIdea: EY scored more than 10,000 tasks on exposure, complementarity (human oversight needed) and intensity (frequency of tasks in time units), then aggregated them to business processes and industries, using RBI KLEMS to translate labor productivity into output. For the IT survey, the press coverage gives no sample, respondent profile or method.
key_numbers: IT industry productivity +43-45% over the next 5 years (a projection; press coverage of the EY India survey)
By function: software development about 60%, BPO services 52%, IT consulting 47%. Together these three account for 50-60% of the overall gain in tech services (press coverage).
89% of top IT companies have started trialling GenAI; 33% of those projects are already in production (press coverage)

AIdea economy-wide: 24% of tasks can be fully automated and time on another 42% significantly reduced, freeing 8-10 hours per week for corporate workers. Productivity rises 2.61% by 2030 in the organized sector, affecting 38 million employees, plus up to 2.82% in the unorganized sector (5.44% combined).
AIdea business-process uplift: call-centre management 80%, software development 61%, content development 45%, customer service 44%, down to new product development 17%
works.relevance_to_theta: Consultant priors for the ordering of theta_j (development > BPO > consulting; call centre ~80% and software development 61% in AIdea). These are capability-potential ceilings, close in spirit to our theta_j, but they are not net of review or failure in any documented way. No method is published for the IT-survey figures. Use them only as an upper-bound prior.
works.limitations: Projections, not measurements. Opaque method for the IT survey. Commercial incentive. The EY IT-survey release itself was not found on ey.com; the per-function numbers rest on press coverage.
works.corrections: 'The IT survey covers about 500 roles' is a misreading: the coverage says the gains 'will span 500 roles', not that 500 roles were surveyed. Removed 'the IT bubble sits near 45%'. The PDF chart text could not confirm the IT bubble's position; the only nearby label reads 'IT | 19%', whose axis meaning is unclear. Added AIdea's software-development business-process figure (61%), the 8-10 hours/week, and the 5.44% combined figure. Dates are AIdea PDF Jan 15, 2025 and the IT survey press Feb 11, 2025.

works.title: Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users
works.authors: Adam Grundy, Cory Breaux, Dhanapati Khatiwoda (U.S. Census Bureau)
works.venue: Census.gov America Counts story; Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS)
works.what_measured: Share of US firms using AI, by size and sector, and expected use within the next 6 months.
works.method_plain: A recurring firm survey with a yes/no question on AI use. In November 2025 the wording changed from use 'in producing goods or services' to use 'in any business function'. A second AI supplement, covering 15 business functions and reasons for non-use, began on 17 Nov 2025.
key_numbers: National AI use hovered between 17% and 20% of firms from Dec 14, 2025 to May 3, 2026; 19.8% as of 3 May 2026. 20-23% expect to use AI within 6 months.
Firms with 250+ employees: 37%; 100-249 employees: 32%; firms with 4 or fewer: under 20%
Information sector: 39.7% currently use AI (about 42% expected); Finance & Insurance 33.9% (about 39% expected); Retail Trade about 14% (about 17% expected)
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure adoption (extensive margin). It confirms that adoption is a separate object from the capability ceiling theta_j. That is why dropping adoption from theta is defensible, but a separate adoption term is then needed to reconcile theta with realized replacement (~2.3 pp/yr).
works.limitations: Firm-weighted, so dominated by small firms. Binary measure of use, with no intensity or time saved. Series break in Nov 2025. US only.
works.corrections: The authors are named Census staff (Adam Grundy, Cory Breaux, Dhanapati Khatiwoda), not just 'US Census Bureau'. Removed '~20,000 responses per round', which is not stated on the page. Called the survey recurring rather than biweekly, since the page I opened does not state the frequency. The other numbers were confirmed.

works.title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy
works.authors: Jeffrey S. Allen
works.venue: FEDS Notes, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
works.what_measured: Reconciles adoption estimates across BTOS (firms), RPS (workers) and the Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty (SBU, executives).
works.method_plain: A side-by-side comparison of the surveys, with explanations for the gaps: weighting by firms versus employment, question wording, respondent knowledge, shadow AI, and social desirability.
key_numbers: BTOS: about 18% of firms (end-2025, 4-period moving average)
SBU Nov 2025: 78% of the labor force works at AI-adopting firms and 54% at LLM-using firms (employment-weighted); 69.4% and 46.4% equal-weighted
RPS Nov 2025: about 41% (40.7) of workers use genAI for work; 12% used it daily in the previous week
SBU intensity: a plurality (35%) use AI up to 1 h/week; 29% use it 1-5 h/week (the population base is as defined in the note; I did not confirm whether it is users or all employees)
Gallup mid-2025: 8% of workers use AI daily
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows adoption estimates range from about 18% to 78% depending on weighting and wording. Any top-down back-out of theta from realized replacement (theta ≈ realized / adoption) is therefore very sensitive to which adoption measure is chosen. For large Indian IT firms, employment-weighted measures are the relevant ones.
works.limitations: US only; adoption only, with no time saved; descriptive.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Flagged that I did not confirm the population base of the SBU hours-of-use split, so the record's 'of users' wording may not be exact.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2): 889-942 (2025), doi:10.1093/qje/qjae044
works.what_measured: Measured productivity (issues resolved per hour) of customer-support agents after a staggered rollout of a GPT-based conversational assistant.
works.method_plain: A natural experiment using administrative data on agents at one firm. Access was rolled out at different times, so similar agents with and without access can be compared over time.
key_numbers: QJE (2025) abstract: 5,172 agents; AI assistance raised issues resolved per hour by about 15% on average. NBER WP abstract: 5,179 agents and about 14%.

NBER WP: +34% for novice and low-skilled workers, minimal impact for experienced and highly skilled workers. The QJE abstract says the most experienced, highest-skilled workers saw small speed gains and small declines in quality.
works.relevance_to_theta: The measured BPO/customer-support benchmark for theta_BPO in assistant mode (kappa), with the human in the loop included. The effect is heterogeneous by experience, which interacts with the junior-heavy pyramid of Indian IT and BPO firms. Note that it is output per hour, not labor saved at fixed output; a 15% gain in output per hour corresponds to about 13% less labor for the same output.
works.limitations: One firm; an older GPT-3-era model (the exact rollout years were not re-checked here); output per hour rather than labor saved at fixed output.
works.corrections: The published QJE figure is 15% with 5,172 agents (confirmed on the OUP page). 14% with 5,179 agents is the NBER WP figure. That resolves the record's open question; Humlum & Vestergaard cite the QJE 15%. Removed the unverified 'US/Philippines agents' and the '2020-21 era model' specifics. Added the NBER WP dates (Apr 2023, rev. Nov 2023) and the DOI.

works.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
works.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
works.what_measured: Time to complete a standardized coding task (implement an HTTP server in JavaScript) with and without Copilot.
works.method_plain: A controlled experiment with recruited developers randomly given or denied access to Copilot.
key_numbers: The treatment group completed the task 55.8% faster than the control group (abstract). It is often quoted as '55%', and Humlum & Vestergaard quote it as a '58% increase'.
works.relevance_to_theta: The upper end of measured kappa, on a short greenfield task. It contrasts with METR's -19% on long tasks in mature repositories. That pattern fits savings that decline with task length h and codebase familiarity, which is what p(h,t) and f_j(h) are meant to capture, though the two studies differ in many other ways too.
works.limitations: A single small, self-contained task; no review or maintenance burden; 2022-era model; sample size not shown on the abstract page.
works.corrections: Confirmed. Added the submission month (Feb 13, 2023).

summary_flags: The flat 'saved per assisted hour' ratio was computed from mismatched periods. 1.6/4.1 pairs roughly 2025Q1 savings with 2024Q4 assisted hours. The matched FRED ratio is 0.34 (2024Q4) to 0.35 (2026Q2), and 0.39 in 2026Q3 because assisted hours fell to 5.31%. The 'flat' conclusion survives, but the stated '0.35-0.4' range and the 2024 value were wrong.

The inference that 'recent growth is on the extensive margin, not the intensive one' is overstated. The time-saved question is top-coded at 4+ hours and both series are built from brackets, which mechanically limits measured gains per assisted hour. The ratio is also gross of outside review. Treat it as suggestive, not as a test of the capability ceiling.
'+14% in customer support': the published QJE figure is 15%; 14% is the NBER working-paper figure. It is also issues resolved per hour, not fraction of time saved.

METR's 'experienced developers 19% SLOWER' is cited with no time stamp. METR now labels the 2025 result out of date. Its Feb 2026 update gives speedup point estimates (18% less time for returning developers, 4% for new ones), which METR calls very weak evidence and likely a lower bound. The record's '-18%/-4%' was ambiguous about sign: negative means faster.

'Surveys are useful as lower bounds' holds only along the adoption dimension. Per-user perceived savings can overstate measured savings (METR's perception gap), so survey numbers are not a clean lower bound on theta_j.

'None measures net-of-review labor saved per task as a function of task length' is true of the surveys but not of the whole stream. The METR RCT measures realized time net of review on tasks of roughly known length (~2 h), and Anthropic estimates task length per conversation. Keep the claim scoped to surveys.

The working hypothesis 'largely holds' is phrased too strongly. Surveys (RPS, Humlum & Vestergaard) do give an intensive-margin quantity: saved time per assisted hour, and minutes saved per usage day. What they lack is a quantity that is net of review, tied to task length, and indexed to capability. The gap is narrower than 'exposure covers only the extensive margin'.
Humlum & Vestergaard's 'zero detectable effect' should state the bound and the version: CIs rule out effects above 1% (BFI 2025) or above 2% two years after launch (NBER 2026 revision).

ICRIER: '651 IT firms' is 651 respondents from 620 unique firms, with a response rate of about 10%. 'Funded by OpenAI' should read 'acknowledges OpenAI support'. The declining-roles question asks about the industry, not the respondent's own firm.
EY: '500 roles' is how many roles the gains will span, not the survey sample. The 'IT bubble near 45%' could not be confirmed. The per-function IT numbers rest on press coverage only.
Bick et al.'s 2024 adoption levels (nearly 40% of adults) were later revised upward (44.6% for Aug 2024) after a question-order fix. Any time comparison should use the revised tracker series.
'Computer/math occupations save about 2.5% of all hours' is a November 2024 figure and should be dated as such.
Census BTOS: '~20,000 responses per round' is not on the page opened and was removed.
verify.corrected_summary: Surveys of AI time savings mostly measure something different from theta_j. The largest US source is Bick, Blandin and Deming's Real-Time Population Survey, which asks workers how many extra hours they would have needed without AI. Averaged over ALL employed adults (non-users count as zero), time saved rose from 1.41% of work hours in 2024Q4 to 2.17% in 2026Q2, and was 2.08% in 2026Q3 (FRED RPSGENAITSALL). Among previous-week users it was 5.4% in November 2024. Computer/math occupations saved about 2.5% of their hours in November 2024. Using matched FRED quarters, hours saved per hour assisted stayed around 0.35 (0.34 in 2024Q4, 0.35 in 2026Q2) while the share of hours assisted grew from 4.1% to 6.3% (it then fell to 5.3% in 2026Q3). So, in self-reports, most recent growth comes from more work being touched rather than more saving per touched hour. This is suggestive only: the answers are bracketed, the time-saved question is top-coded at 4+ hours, and review done outside the AI session is not netted out. In Denmark (Humlum and Vestergaard, 2023-24 chatbot use), users save 2.8% of work hours (6-7% on days they use AI). Effects on earnings and recorded hours are precise zeros, ruling out effects above 1% (2025 version) or 2% (2026 revision). Only 3-7% of time savings pass through to earnings, and 80% of saved time is reallocated to other tasks. Experiments give much larger task-level effects: issues resolved per hour rose 15% in customer support (QJE version; 14% in the working paper), and a small greenfield coding task was done 55.8% faster with Copilot. METR's early-2025 RCT found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with AI while believing they were 20% faster, so self-reports can get even the sign wrong. METR now labels that result out of date, and its February 2026 update gives point estimates of 4-18% less time, which METR calls very weak evidence. Anthropic's model-estimated ~80% saving per conversation excludes review outside the chat and is best read as a gross ceiling. For India, the ICRIER February 2026 survey (651 respondents from 620 IT firms, Nov 2025-Jan 2026) shows which divisions are most affected (software development 72%, infrastructure/cloud 48%, project management 37%). It also reports where respondents see declining industry demand (data entry/back-office, manual testing, entry-level programming), but it gives directions only, not magnitudes. EY's 43-45% IT productivity projection (development ~60%, BPO 52%, consulting 47%) is a press-reported projection with an undisclosed method. Bottom line: surveys do capture a gross, self-reported intensive margin (saving per assisted hour, minutes saved per usage day), so the hypothesis that the literature covers only the extensive margin is too strong. What no survey measures is labor saved net of review and acceptance, as a function of task length and model capability. The closest measured evidence is METR's RCTs, which cover narrow settings. The surveys are useful as adoption-weighted benchmarks and for weights w_j. They are not lower bounds on theta_j per se, because perceived savings can overstate realized savings.
verify.dataset_notes: RPS / Generative AI Adoption Tracker: public on FRED. The time-saved series is RPSGENAITSALL (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/RPSGENAITSALL) and the hours-assisted series is RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL). Both are quarterly from 2024Q4 to 2026Q3, with occupation-level versions also on FRED. FRED asks users to cite Bick, Blandin and Deming (Management Science 2026). Census BTOS: public, but the URL given is a news story, not the data. The data are on the Census BTOS experimental data product page (https://www.census.gov/data/experimental-data-products/business-trends-and-outlook-survey.html; I did not open it). I did not confirm the survey frequency or the per-round response count from the story. Danish survey-register data (Humlum & Vestergaard): access is restricted, presumably through Statistics Denmark research servers, but I did not confirm the access route. Label it 'restricted' rather than 'lab-internal'. ICRIER: the report does not say whether microdata are available, so 'on-request' is an assumption; mark it 'unknown, contact authors'. METR RCT data: release status unconfirmed ('unknown' is correct). METR's Feb 2026 update (https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/) should be listed with the original. Anthropic Economic Index: 'unknown' is correct for this note's per-task time estimates. Atlanta Fed SBU: the FEDS Note gives only summary figures; microdata access is unknown.

works.title: Growth Accounting with Intermediate Inputs (source of 'Hulten's theorem')
works.authors: Charles R. Hulten
works.what_measured: A theory result, not a measurement. In an efficient economy, the aggregate productivity effect of a small productivity gain in one sector or task equals that unit's sales share of GDP times its own productivity gain.
works.method_plain: An accounting identity built on the envelope theorem. To first order, aggregate TFP change = sum over tasks of (GDP share of task) x (cost saving on task). Every AI macro paper below uses this formula, applied to tasks.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers. The formula as Acemoglu (2024) writes it: d ln TFP = (average cost saving pi) x (GDP share of tasks impacted).
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the aggregation step S = sum_j w_j theta_j. Hulten weights by GDP or cost share; the project weights by labor time share, which is the labor-only analogue. It says nothing about where theta_j comes from: it takes the task-level saving as an input.
works.limitations: Valid only to first order, for small shocks in an efficient economy. AI savings of 30-80% on a task are not small. The RePEc page I opened confirms title, journal, volume and pages but did not display the author; Hulten's authorship is confirmed by the Baqaee-Farhi abstract and by search results.

works.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Microeconomic Shocks: Beyond Hulten's Theorem
works.authors: David Rezza Baqaee, Emmanuel Farhi
works.what_measured: Second-order (nonlinear) corrections to Hulten. These come from elasticities of substitution, network linkages, returns to scale and factor reallocation.
works.method_plain: Theory plus calibration. When a sector or task gets much cheaper, its share of spending can shrink (Baumol's cost disease) when goods are complements. So large positive shocks add less to GDP than the first-order Hulten formula predicts.
key_numbers: Baumol-type nonlinearities account for a 20 percentage point reduction in aggregate US TFP growth over 1948-2014 (abstract).
In the paper's business-cycle calibration, nonlinearities nearly triple the estimated effect of the 1970s oil shocks on world output.
works.relevance_to_theta: Warns that the weights w_j are not fixed. If AI makes testing nearly free, testing's share of labor time falls, so S(t) computed with today's w_j overstates later replacement. At firm level this is the eps*phi demand channel. Recommendation: recompute w_j over time, or report a first-order and a reweighted version.
works.limitations: Macro-sector focus, with no AI-specific numbers. The full text is behind a login; I opened only the abstract page.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.year: 2024 (NBER WP 32487, May 2024); published in Economic Policy 40(121), 2025
works.what_measured: Ten-year TFP and GDP effect of generative AI and computer vision in the US.
works.method_plain: Hulten-style formula: TFP gain = (GDP share of tasks impacted) x (average overall cost saving). The impacted share is exposure x cost-effective share: Eloundou et al. wage-bill-weighted exposure (20%) times Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate, giving 4.6%. The cost saving is the average labor saving from two RCTs (Noy & Zhang writing at about 40%, Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond customer service at 14%), giving 27%. This is multiplied by an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535, giving 14.4%. Tasks are then split into easy and hard (hard tasks get a 7% labor saving).
key_numbers: 20% of US labor tasks exposed (wage-bill-weighted Eloundou et al.)
23% of exposed tasks cost-effective to automate (from Svanberg et al., computer vision only)
0.23 x 0.20 = 4.6% of tasks impacted within 10 years
Average labor cost saving 27% (mean of Noy-Zhang and Brynjolfsson et al.; Peng et al.'s 55.8% coding speedup excluded as too narrow)
Overall cost saving 0.27 x 0.535 = 14.4%
TFP gain of no more than 0.66% TOTAL over 10 years (about 0.064-0.07 pp per year). This is often misquoted as 0.66% per year. The April 2024 draft said 0.71%.
With the easy/hard split: under 0.53% TFP over 10 years. Easy exposed tasks are 3.3% of GDP and hard ones 1.3%. Hard tasks get a 7% labor saving, half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s 14%.
GDP: TFP x 1/(1-0.43), about 1.75. That gives 1.16% over 10 years, or 0.93% with hard tasks; up to 1.4-1.56% with the investment response.
works.relevance_to_theta: The canonical 'exposure x cost-effective share x savings' decomposition. The 27% is an intensive-margin number: RCT speedups on easy, well-defined tasks with 2023-era models, taken as given and constant over time. It is not modeled from capability, and is net of review only to the extent that the experiments' measured time included review. The 7% hard-task value is a judgment call. For theta_j, this is a template to beat: the project replaces the static 27% with a capability-driven, review-netted integral. The 23% cost-effectiveness share comes from computer vision, not LLMs.
works.limitations: Savings are frozen at 2023 levels. Two or three RCTs stand in for the whole economy. The cost-effectiveness share is borrowed from a different technology. Displacement cannot be observed in the experiments, as the paper notes in a footnote.

works.title: AI and Growth: Where Do We Stand?
works.authors: Philippe Aghion, Simon Bunel
works.venue: Working note (hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco)
works.what_measured: Annual productivity growth boost from AI over the next decade, estimated two ways.
works.method_plain: (1) Historical analogy to the electricity and IT waves. (2) A re-run of Acemoglu's 4-term formula with wider inputs: exposure from 18.5% (ILO, Gmyrek et al.) to 68% (IMF, Pizzinelli et al.); cost-effective share 0.23-0.8 (Svanberg scenarios with falling compute costs); labor savings 0.27-0.40 (adding back Peng et al.); labor share 0.57.
key_numbers: Historical-analogy estimate: +0.8 to +1.3 pp per year to aggregate productivity growth
Task-based range: 0.07 to 1.24 pp per year; median 0.68 pp per year of additional TFP growth
Median inputs: 60% exposed (Pizzinelli et al.) x 50% profitable (22%/yr compute-cost decline, Besiroglu & Hobbhahn) x 40% labor saving x 0.57 labor share
Micro inputs: Peng et al. +55.8% (programmers), Noy & Zhang +40%, Brynjolfsson et al. +14% in month 1 rising to 25-30%
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the macro answer swings by more than 10x with the inputs. Most of the swing comes from the extensive margin (exposure, profitability). The intensive input (0.27 to 0.40) moves it by under 1.5x. The intensive margin again comes from the same three RCTs and is not tied to capability growth. Only the cost-effectiveness share is made time-varying.
works.limitations: Note that 0.68 pp is PER YEAR, roughly 10x Acemoglu's annual figure; the two are often compared without converting units. Same three RCTs. Labor share copied from Acemoglu: the note says 0.57, while Acemoglu's text uses 0.535 exposure-adjusted and 0.576 unadjusted.

works.title: Miracle or Myth? Assessing the macroeconomic productivity gains from AI (IPM version); builds on Filippucci, Gal, Jona-Lasinio, Leandro & Nicoletti (2024) 'The impact of AI on productivity, distribution and growth' (OECD) and the G7 paper (OECD AI Paper No. 41)
works.authors: Francesco Filippucci, Peter Gal, Katharina Laengle, Matthias Schief, Filiz Unsal
works.venue: International Productivity Monitor No. 48 (CSLS); companion OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers
works.what_measured: Ten-year AI contribution to annual TFP and labor-productivity growth in the US and G7, with cross-country exposure and adoption scenarios and a multi-sector model that has Baumol effects.
works.method_plain: Micro-to-macro chain: (task-level performance gain) x (exposure, value-added-weighted share of tasks AI can do at least 50% faster, from Eloundou et al.) x (adoption, which rises 23 or 40 pp over 10 years following electricity-like or computer/internet-like S-curves). This feeds a sectoral model in which slowly improving sectors drag down growth.
key_numbers: Assumed micro-level gain: 30% (described as 'conservative', near the average of the three most precise estimates, and excluding coding studies)
Exposure: 30-35% of value added with baseline (2023) LLM capabilities; about 50% with expanded capabilities
Adoption increase over 10 years: +23 pp (slow) or +40 pp (rapid)

US: +0.3 to +0.7 pp per year in TFP growth (IPM abstract). The 2024 OECD paper gave +0.25 to 0.6 pp TFP or +0.4 to 0.9 pp labor productivity (search snippet; I could not open the 2024 page, OECD returned 403).
G7 paper: 0.4-1.3 pp per year labor productivity for high-exposure countries, 0.2-0.8 pp for others such as Italy and Japan (search snippet; OECD page returned 403)
works.relevance_to_theta: Again a single flat intensive-margin number (30%) applied to all exposed tasks, from RCTs. Two points matter here. First, the paper notes the Eloundou '50% faster' threshold makes exposure a binned intensive-margin concept. Second, the 'automation index' variant (LLM completes at least 90% of the task) is what Acemoglu used, which partly explains the gap between the two. The OECD is explicit that it is choosing the average gain in exposed tasks: that is exactly a population-level theta, and they pick it by assumption.
works.limitations: Flat 30% across tasks and time, with no link to capability. Coding is excluded from the micro average, which matters for IT services. I could not open the 2024 OECD and G7 landing pages (403), so the numbers from those papers come from search snippets and are flagged.

works.title: The Potentially Large Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Economic Growth (plus 2025-26 updates by Briggs & Dong)
works.authors: Joseph Briggs, Devesh Kodnani (Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research)
works.venue: Goldman Sachs Global Economics Analyst (client research note)
works.what_measured: Share of work exposed to generative AI automation; the implied productivity and GDP effects.
works.method_plain: O*NET/ESCO task-content mapping of which work activities generative AI could do, aggregated by employment. Exposed work is split into the share that could be substituted and the share complemented; displaced workers are assumed mostly reemployed; labor savings then feed a productivity estimate.
key_numbers: About two-thirds of current US/EU jobs exposed to some degree of AI automation (press coverage)
Generative AI could substitute up to one-quarter of current work; up to 35% of work exposed (generative AI only, excluding robotics) (press coverage)
300 million full-time-job equivalents exposed globally. This is an exposure figure, often misreported as '300M jobs lost'.
Up to 7% increase in annual global GDP over about 10 years; US labor productivity growth up by just under 1.5 pp per year over 10 years after widespread adoption (press coverage)

2025-26 updates (Briggs & Dong, press coverage only): about 15% labor-productivity LEVEL boost at full adoption; 6-7% of US jobs displaced in baseline (range 3-14%); about 2.5% of jobs at risk if current use cases are fully scaled
works.relevance_to_theta: The '25-50% of workload' style number is a judgmental intensive-margin assumption for exposed occupations. It is not measured, net of review or capability-indexed. Useful mainly as a high-end benchmark for S at full adoption: the 15% level effect and 6-7% displacement compare with the project's top-down 2.3 pp/yr.
works.limitations: I COULD NOT OPEN THE PRIMARY REPORT: goldmansachs.com and gspublishing.com returned 403. All numbers come from press coverage that quotes the report. The '25-50% of workload' phrasing appears only in secondary sources and is unverified. Proprietary methodology.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: Per-task time without AI vs with AI for 100,000 real Claude.ai conversations, mapped to O*NET tasks, then aggregated to a US labor-productivity effect.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a competent professional would take with and without AI for each conversation. These estimates are aggregated by median to O*NET tasks, weighted by time share within the occupation and by the occupation's wage-bill share. A Hulten aggregation assumes universal adoption within 10 years.
key_numbers: Average task about 1.4 hours without AI; median labor cost about $54
Median time saving about 80% (84% in text, 81% in density plot)
Validation: Spearman rho = 0.44 for Claude vs 0.50 for developers' own estimates on JIRA software-task durations
Implied +1.8 pp per year US labor productivity growth over the decade (about 1.1 pp TFP at labor share 0.6); software developers contribute 19% of the gain
Explicitly excludes time spent validating and iterating on outputs; RCTs found smaller savings (14-56%)
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing analog to a bottom-up theta_j: task-level time saved, weighted by within-occupation time shares (f_j/w_j analogs). Crucially, it is GROSS of review time (rho) and of acceptance (q), and initially of failure (p). It conditions on tasks users chose to bring, a selection effect.
works.limitations: Model-estimated times, not observed; selection bias; no review cost; Claude.ai users only. The authors call it an exercise, not a forecast.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives (January 2026)
works.authors: Anthropic Economic Research team
works.what_measured: Task success rates, task horizons and complexity in real Claude usage (November 2025), and a success-adjusted revision of the macro productivity estimate.
works.method_plain: Classify each conversation for success, complexity, human-time length and autonomy; multiply the time savings by the success probability; re-aggregate, with CES variants that allow tasks to be complements or substitutes.
key_numbers: Task success: 67% on Claude.ai, 49% on the first-party API
API success falls from about 60% (sub-hour tasks) to about 45% (5+ human-hour tasks); 50% crossing at about 3.5 human hours (API); extrapolated about 19 hours on Claude.ai (multi-turn correction)
Macro estimate: 1.8 pp per year baseline falls to about 1.2 pp (Claude.ai) and 1.0 pp (API) after success adjustment
With complementary tasks (elasticity 0.5): 0.7-0.9 pp before adjustment, 0.6-0.8 pp after; with substitutes (elasticity 1.5): 2.2-2.6 pp before adjustment
works.relevance_to_theta: Operationalizes the project's p(h) term on real-world rather than benchmark tasks. It confirms that p declines with task length h, and that multi-turn use (kappa-like assistance) extends the horizon. It multiplies savings by p but still has no explicit rho (review) or q (acceptance) term. The closest published template for the theta_j integral; its 'success x time-saving' is roughly q*p*(saving) with q=1 and rho=0.
works.limitations: Success is judged by a model and is selection-biased; usage predates Opus 4.5; no review-time netting; not industry-specific.

works.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
works.authors: Alexander Arnon (Penn Wharton Budget Model; directed by Kent Smetters)
works.what_measured: Long-run TFP/GDP level effect of generative AI in the US, with an adoption path.
works.method_plain: Acemoglu's formula with three terms. Exposure comes from Eloundou et al. categories T2/T3/T4, weighted 70/95/100% and wage-weighted to about 40% of labor income, times 23% automated (Svanberg); the cost saving is the labor saving times labor share; both are multiplied by an adoption curve fitted to the PC, internet, smartphone and cloud.
key_numbers: About 40% of labor income exposed; about 9-10% of GDP impacted (rising to about 15% over two decades)
Average labor cost saving 25% from seven studies (range about 10-55%), assumed to rise from 25% to 40% over coming decades
TFP/GDP level +1.5% by 2035, about 3% by 2055, 3.7% by 2075; annual growth boost peaks at 0.2 pp in 2032
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few macro estimates that makes the intensive margin time-varying (25% rising to 40%). But the path is an assumption, not derived from capability metrics like METR horizons. A direct foil for the project's theta_j(t) built from p(h,t).
works.limitations: The savings path is ad hoc; reuses the computer-vision 23%; US only; not industry-specific.

works.title: GATE: An Integrated Assessment Model for AI Automation (plus 'AI and explosive growth redux')
works.authors: Epoch AI team (arXiv 2503.04941); redux essay by Andrei Potlogea and Anson Ho
works.venue: arXiv preprint / Epoch AI Gradient Updates
works.what_measured: Simulated paths of the automated share of tasks, compute investment and output growth.
works.method_plain: Tasks lie on a continuum ordered by difficulty. The fraction automated, f, is a log-linear function of effective training compute between thresholds (the 'FLOP gap'). Each task is either automated or not. Automated tasks get 'digital worker equivalents' = runtime compute allocated / runtime compute required. A CES across tasks (rho = -0.65 default) creates bottlenecks, inside a semi-endogenous growth model with investment.
key_numbers: Default rho (task substitution) = -0.65
Default simulation: about 23% per year world output growth in 2027, which the authors call unlikely
Growth outcomes against the automated share: about 20%+ growth at 30% automation; explosive (>30%/yr) at about 50-70% (redux essay)
Announcement: compute investment may exceed 10% of world GDP; growth 2-20x the historical ~3%/yr over about a decade
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive margin: a task is automated or not, with no partial labor savings per task, no review cost and no failure rate. The inference-compute requirement is a cost-of-running term (part of the project's 'net of AI running cost'). The mentor co-wrote the redux essay. GATE's f(compute) is the macro analog of 'which h-bins have p(h) high enough', so the project's integral could supply a partial-automation version.
works.limitations: Designed for qualitative insight, not forecasts; assumes disembodied AI substitutes perfectly for labor; no industry detail.

works.title: Explosive growth from AI automation: A review of the arguments
works.authors: Ege Erdil, Tamay Besiroglu
works.what_measured: Whether AI automation could raise world output growth roughly tenfold (above 30% per year); a review of nine objections.
works.method_plain: Task-based CES: a fraction of tasks is automated (approximated as receiving unlimited input); the remainder bottlenecks output. Growth models with scalable AI labor deliver increasing returns.
key_numbers: Explosive growth defined as world output growth above 30% per year
Example: with 10% of tasks unautomated and rho = -1, output rises about 100-fold
Human brain about 1e15 FLOP/s; if AI adds only about 9x input intensity per task, the maximum gain is about one order of magnitude
25% of tasks unautomatable with elasticity of about 1/3 could block explosive growth
works.relevance_to_theta: Binary automation; tasks needing human oversight are counted as unautomated. Their remark that finite per-task input intensity caps gains is the macro version of the project's point: theta_j < 1 because of review and failure. No intensive-margin estimate.
works.limitations: Theoretical review; no measured task-level savings; review costs not modeled separately.

works.title: Scenarios for the Transition to AGI
works.authors: Anton Korinek, Donghyun Suh
works.what_measured: Output and wage paths under different speeds of automation toward AGI.
works.method_plain: Work is a set of tasks of varying complexity; automation advances to ever more complex tasks; wages depend on a race between automation and capital accumulation. Whether the complexity distribution is bounded determines whether wages eventually collapse.
key_numbers: The abstract page shows no quantitative results. Acemoglu (2024) reports that Korinek & Suh's 'baseline' implies about 100% GDP growth over 10 years, with an 'aggressive' case near 300%; that figure is second-hand, from Acemoglu's paper.
works.relevance_to_theta: Its complexity distribution of tasks is the analogue of f_j(h), task-length distributions, with an automation frontier moving through it. That frontier is like the METR horizon moving along h. Binary per task (extensive), so no review netting. Conceptually supports building theta_j by integrating over a length/complexity distribution.
works.limitations: Scenario theory, not estimation; I opened only the abstract, so details of the model specification are inferred from the abstract.

research.stream_summary:
Every macro estimate in this stream uses the same skeleton: Hulten's theorem. To a first approximation, AI's productivity effect = (share of the economy's tasks AI touches) x (average cost saved on those tasks). The papers differ mainly in the first factor, the extensive margin: exposure from Eloundou et al. (20-60%) and a 'cost-effective to automate' share (23%) borrowed from a computer-vision study. These choices drive results from 0.07 pp/yr (Acemoglu) to 0.68 pp/yr (Aghion-Bunel) to about 1.5 pp/yr (Goldman Sachs). Watch the units: Acemoglu's famous 0.66% is TOTAL over ten years, not per year.

The second factor, the intensive margin, is almost never estimated. Acemoglu's 27%, the OECD's 30%, Aghion-Bunel's 27-40% and Penn Wharton's 25% (assumed to rise to 40%) all come from two to seven early RCTs: customer service at 14%, writing at about 40%, Copilot at 56%. These are applied flat across tasks and frozen at 2023 capability. None is netted explicitly for review time or acceptance rates, and none is tied to a capability metric. The growth models (Epoch GATE, Erdil-Besiroglu, Korinek-Suh) treat automation as binary per task, with no partial savings at all.

The exception is Anthropic's 2025-26 work. It estimates per-task time savings from real usage (median about 80%) and in January 2026 multiplied them by observed task success. Success falls with task length; the 50% point is about 3.5 hours on the API. That cuts the macro estimate from 1.8 to about 1.0-1.2 pp/yr. This is the closest published analog of the project's q*p(h) term, but it still has no review-cost (rho) or acceptance (q) term.

Verdict on the working hypothesis: largely confirmed. The literature measures the extensive margin carefully and plugs in the intensive margin as an assumption. Baqaee-Farhi adds a caveat: with large savings, the weights w_j themselves shift.
gaps_noticed: No macro paper derives the task-level saving from a capability curve (for example METR horizons). All use static RCT speedups or assumed paths (PWBM's 25% to 40%).
No paper nets savings explicitly for review/verification time (rho) or for the acceptance rate of passing output (q); Anthropic adjusts for success probability (p) only.

The 'cost-effective share' (23%) used by Acemoglu, PWBM and Aghion-Bunel comes from Svanberg et al. on computer vision, not LLMs. There is no LLM-specific cost-effectiveness estimate, which matters for the 'net of AI running cost' part of theta_j.

The OECD micro average explicitly EXCLUDES coding studies. So the IT-services intensive margin is the least covered by the macro literature, even though software accounts for 19% of Anthropic's projected gain.
No industry-specific (IT services/BPO) or India-specific macro aggregation; G7/US only.
Hulten first-order aggregation is used with large shocks (30-80% savings) despite Baqaee-Farhi; only Anthropic (CES variants) and GATE/OECD (Baumol) address reweighting.
Could not open the primary Goldman Sachs reports (403); the 2023 workload-share assumption ('25-50%') and 2025-26 updates are verified only through press coverage.
Could not open the 2024 OECD (Filippucci, Gal, Jona-Lasinio, Leandro, Nicoletti) or G7 landing pages (403); used the IPM 2025 version instead.
Did not open Korinek-Suh full text; its numerical scenarios are cited second-hand via Acemoglu.
Did not find a 2025-26 Acemoglu update or a published Korinek 2025-26 macro estimate in this pass.

datasets.description: Task-level exposure rubric (exposed = at least 50% time reduction at equal quality) used by Acemoglu, the OECD and PWBM. Gives the extensive-margin mask and a binned intensive threshold. I did not open this URL in this stream; verify before use.
