works.title: Growth Accounting with Intermediate Inputs (source of 'Hulten's theorem')
works.authors: Charles R. Hulten
works.what_measured: A theory result, not a measurement. In an efficient economy, to first order, the aggregate productivity effect of a small productivity gain in one sector equals that sector's sales share of GDP times its own productivity gain.
works.method_plain: An accounting result based on the envelope theorem. To first order: aggregate TFP change = sum over sectors (or tasks) of (sales/GDP share) x (cost saving). Acemoglu (2024), Aghion-Bunel (2024), the OECD work, PWBM and Anthropic's Nov 2025 estimate all apply a version of it to tasks. The growth models in this stream (GATE, Erdil-Besiroglu, Korinek-Suh) use CES/growth models instead.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers. As Acemoglu (2024) writes it: TFP gain over 10 years = GDP share of tasks impacted by AI x average cost saving on those tasks (e.g. 0.046 x 0.144 = about 0.0066).
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the aggregation step S = sum_j w_j theta_j. Hulten weights by sales or GDP share. The project weights by labor-time share, the labor-only analogue. It says nothing about where theta_j comes from; it takes the task-level saving as given.
works.limitations: Valid only to first order, for small shocks in an efficient economy. AI savings of 30-80% on a task are not small (see Baqaee-Farhi).
works.corrections: Fixed the URL: the record's '/r/' URL is the RePEc 'cited by' page, and the article page is '/a/'. The article page I opened lists Charles R. Hulten as author, with the same journal, volume, issue, pages and year. Removed the claim that 'every AI macro paper below uses this formula': the growth models in this stream do not.

works.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Microeconomic Shocks: Beyond Hulten's Theorem
works.authors: David Rezza Baqaee, Emmanuel Farhi
works.what_measured: Second-order (nonlinear) corrections to Hulten's theorem. These come from elasticities of substitution, network linkages, returns to scale and factor reallocation.
works.method_plain: Theory plus calibration. When goods are complements, a sector whose costs fall sees its share of spending shrink over time, while low-growth bottleneck sectors gain share (Baumol's cost disease). So nonlinearities shrink the effect of positive shocks and magnify negative ones relative to the first-order Hulten formula.
key_numbers: Nonlinearities that underpin Baumol's cost disease account for a 20 percentage point reduction in aggregate US TFP growth over 1948-2014 (abstract; this is a cumulative figure over the period, not per year).
In a business-cycle calibration, nonlinearities almost triple the estimated impact of the 1970s oil shocks on world aggregate output (abstract).
Average output losses from short-run sectoral shocks are an order of magnitude larger than Lucas's (1987) welfare cost of business cycles (abstract).
works.relevance_to_theta: Warns that the weights w_j are not fixed. If AI makes one task type much cheaper, its share of labor time changes, so S(t) computed with today's w_j can misstate later replacement. At firm level this is tied to the eps*phi demand channel. Suggestion: report both a first-order version and a reweighted version of S.
works.limitations: Macro and sectoral focus, with no AI-specific numbers. Only the abstract page is open; the full text needs a login.
works.corrections: None to the citation. Added the DOI and a third abstract number. Clarified that the 20 pp figure is cumulative over 1948-2014.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 32487; Economic Policy 40(121): 13-58 (2025), doi 10.1093/epolic/eiae042
works.what_measured: Ten-year TFP and GDP effect of generative AI and computer vision in the US.
works.method_plain: Hulten-style formula: TFP gain = (GDP share of tasks impacted) x (average overall cost saving). The impacted share = wage-bill-weighted exposure from Eloundou et al. (20%) x Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate = 4.6%. The labor cost saving is the average of two experiments: Noy & Zhang writing at about 40% and Brynjolfsson et al. customer service at 14%, giving 27%. Peng et al.'s 55.8% Copilot result is used only as a robustness check. Multiplying by an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535 gives an overall cost saving of 14.4%. Tasks are then split into easy and hard, with hard tasks given a 7% labor saving.
key_numbers: 20% of US labor tasks exposed (wage-bill-weighted, from Eloundou et al.)
23% of exposed tasks profitably automatable (Svanberg et al., computer vision)
0.23 x 0.20 = 4.6% of tasks impacted within 10 years
Average labor cost saving 27% (average of Noy-Zhang and Brynjolfsson et al.); adding Peng et al. gives 36% and an overall cost saving of 0.193, i.e. a TFP gain of 0.89%
Overall cost saving 0.27 x 0.535 = 0.144 (unadjusted labor share 0.576)
TFP gain no more than 0.66% in TOTAL over 10 years, about 0.064% per year

Easy/hard split: 72.6% of wage-bill-weighted exposed tasks are easy; easy exposed tasks are 3.3% of GDP and hard ones 1.3%; hard tasks get a 7% labor saving (half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s 14%), giving a TFP gain of about 0.53% over 10 years

GDP = TFP x about 1.75 (= 1/(1-0.43), capital share 0.43): 1.16% over 10 years, or 0.93% with hard tasks; with the Acemoglu-Restrepo investment response, up to 1.56% (no easy/hard split) or 1.4% (with the split)
works.relevance_to_theta: The standard 'exposure x cost-effective share x saving' decomposition. The 27% is an intensive-margin number: experimental speedups on easy, well-defined tasks with 2023-era models, taken as given and held constant. It is not modeled from capability. It is net of review only to the extent that the experiments' measured time included checking. The 7% hard-task value is a judgment call. For theta_j, this is the template to beat. The 23% cost-effectiveness share comes from computer vision, not LLMs, a point the paper itself flags.
works.limitations: Savings are frozen at early-2023 levels. Two or three experiments stand in for the whole economy. The cost-effectiveness share is borrowed from a different technology.
works.corrections: Added Economic Policy pages 13-58 and the DOI (from the NBER page). Removed the claim that 'the April 2024 draft said 0.71%': I could not confirm it (search budget exhausted). Removed the claim that a footnote says displacement cannot be observed in experiments: not checked. Split the 1.4%-1.56% GDP range correctly: 1.56% without and 1.4% with the easy/hard split. All other numbers were checked against the May 12, 2024 PDF.

works.title: AI and Growth: Where Do We Stand?
works.authors: Philippe Aghion, Simon Bunel
works.venue: Working note (PDF hosted on the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco website; authors affiliated with Collège de France/INSEAD/LSE and Banque de France/ENS)
works.what_measured: The boost to annual productivity growth from AI over the next decade, estimated two ways.
works.method_plain: (1) An analogy to the electricity and IT waves. (2) Acemoglu's four-term formula with wider inputs: exposure from 18.5% (Gmyrek et al., ILO) to 68% (Pizzinelli et al., IMF); profitable share 0.23-0.8 (Svanberg et al., with falling compute costs); labor cost saving 0.27-0.40; labor share 0.57 (attributed to Acemoglu).
key_numbers: Historical analogy: +0.8 to +1.3 pp per year in aggregate productivity growth over the next decade
Task-based range: 0.07 to 1.24 pp per year; median estimate 0.68 pp of additional annual TFP growth

Baseline/median inputs: 60% exposed (Pizzinelli et al.) x 50% profitable (from a 22% annual decline in compute costs, Besiroglu & Hobbhahn 2022) x 40% labor saving x 0.57 labor share, multiplied by 10, gives 0.68

Micro inputs: Peng et al. +55.8% (programmers); Noy & Zhang +40%; Brynjolfsson et al. +14% in month 1, +25% in month 2, stabilizing at 25-30%. The 40% average of the three uses about 25% for Brynjolfsson.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the macro answer swings by more than 10x with the inputs. Most of the swing comes from exposure and profitability; the intensive input (0.27 to 0.40) moves it by under 1.5x. The intensive margin again comes from the same three experiments, not from capability growth. Only the profitable share is tied to a time trend (compute cost decline).
works.limitations: 0.68 pp is PER YEAR, roughly 10x Acemoglu's annual 0.064-0.07 pp, so the two must be compared in the same units. Same three experiments. The note says it retains 'Acemoglu's value of 0.57', while Acemoglu's text uses 0.535 exposure-adjusted and 0.576 unadjusted.
works.corrections: Numbers checked against the PDF text. Clarified that the 40% three-study average uses about 25% for Brynjolfsson et al., not 14%. The venue is described only as a note hosted on frbsf.org; I did not confirm any FRBSF conference or series affiliation.

works.title: Opportunities and Risks of Artificial Intelligence for Productivity (IPM article). Builds on: Filippucci, Gal & Schief (2024) 'Miracle or Myth? Assessing the macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence' (OECD AI Papers No. 29); and Filippucci, Gal, Laengle & Schief (2025) 'Macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence in G7 economies' (OECD AI Papers No. 41)
works.authors: Francesco Filippucci, Peter Gal, Katharina Laengle, Matthias Schief, Filiz Unsal (IPM article)
works.venue: International Productivity Monitor No. 48 (CSLS), pp. 3-28; companion OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 29 (2024) and No. 41 (2025)
works.what_measured: Ten-year AI contribution to annual TFP and labor-productivity growth in the US and other G7 countries, with cross-country exposure and adoption scenarios. It also discusses risks, including Baumol effects.
works.method_plain: A micro-to-macro chain: (task-level gain) x (exposure: value-added-weighted share of tasks AI can do at least 50% faster, from Eloundou et al.) x (adoption: rises by 23 or 40 pp over 10 years, following electricity-like or computer/internet-like paths). This feeds a sectoral aggregation in which Baumol effects can drag down growth.
key_numbers: Assumed micro-level gain: 30%, described as conservative, close to the average of the three most precise estimates, and excluding coding studies
Exposure: 30-35% of value added with baseline (2023) LLM capabilities; about 50% with expanded capabilities; the most exposed G7 country is about 15% above the least exposed
Adoption over 10 years: +23 pp (slow, electricity-like) or +40 pp (rapid, computers/internet-like)
US: about +0.3 to +0.7 pp per year in TFP growth over the next decade (IPM abstract); other G7 economies up to 50% smaller
Miracle or Myth (OECD AI Paper No. 29, 2024), via the OECD ECOSCOPE blog: US +0.25 to 0.6 pp per year TFP, or +0.4 to 0.9 pp labor productivity
G7 paper (OECD AI Paper No. 41, 2025; RePEc abstract and SUERF Policy Brief 1283): 0.4-1.3 pp per year labor productivity in high-exposure countries (US, UK); 0.2-0.8 pp in Italy and Japan
works.relevance_to_theta: A single flat intensive-margin number (30%) applied to all exposed tasks, taken from experiments. The authors say they need the average gain in exposed tasks, which is a population-level theta, and they pick it by assumption. The exposure definition (at least 50% faster) is itself a binned intensive-margin threshold. The paper also attributes part of Acemoglu's lower estimate to his use of the stricter 'automation index' (LLM completes at least 90% of the task autonomously).
works.limitations: A flat 30% across tasks and time, with no link to capability. Coding is excluded from the micro average, which matters for IT services.
works.corrections: Title was wrong. The IPM No. 48 article is titled 'Opportunities and Risks of Artificial Intelligence for Productivity' (pp. 3-28). 'Miracle or Myth?' is the separate OECD AI Paper No. 29 (Nov 2024) by Filippucci, Gal and Schief only. The 2024 numbers (+0.25-0.6 pp TFP, +0.4-0.9 pp labor productivity) come from that paper, not from Filippucci, Gal, Jona-Lasinio, Leandro & Nicoletti (2024), which is a different OECD paper. The G7 paper (No. 41) and its 0.4-1.3 pp and 0.2-0.8 pp ranges are now confirmed from RePEc and the SUERF brief, not only from search snippets. All IPM numbers were checked in the PDF text.

works.title: The Potentially Large Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Economic Growth (plus 2025-26 updates)
works.authors: Joseph Briggs, Devesh Kodnani (2023); 2025-26 updates by Joseph Briggs and Sarah Dong (Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research)
works.venue: Goldman Sachs client research note (proprietary); the January 2026 note is reported as 'How Concerned Should We Be About a Job Apocalypse?'
works.what_measured: Share of work exposed to generative-AI automation, and the implied productivity, GDP and job-displacement effects.
works.method_plain: Maps occupational task content (US and European data) to the work activities generative AI could do, aggregates by employment, and splits exposed work into substitution and complementarity. Displaced workers are assumed mostly reemployed. Proprietary details.
key_numbers: About two-thirds of current US/European jobs exposed to some degree of AI automation (press coverage: Yahoo/Independent, People Matters)
Up to one-quarter of current work could be substituted; the share exposed could be as much as 35% based only on generative AI (Yahoo/Independent coverage)
300 million full-time-job equivalents exposed. This is an exposure figure, often misreported as '300M jobs lost' (press coverage)

Up to a 7% rise in annual global GDP over 10 years (press coverage); about 1.5 pp per year US productivity growth over 10 years (as cited by Acemoglu 2024). The IPM article converts this to about 1 pp per year of TFP.

2025 update (eWeek, Aug 25, 2025): about 15% labor-productivity LEVEL boost at full adoption; 6-7% of the US workforce displaced; about 2.5% of jobs at risk if current use cases were scaled; unemployment temporarily up about 0.5 pp
Jan 2026 note (Fortune, Jan 13, 2026): 25% of work hours automatable; 15% productivity uplift; 6-7% displaced; peak unemployment up about 0.6 pp
works.relevance_to_theta: The workload-replaced share for exposed occupations is a judgmental intensive-margin assumption. It is not measured, not netted for review and not tied to capability. Mainly useful as a high-end benchmark: the 15% level effect and 6-7% displacement over the adoption period can be set against the project's top-down 2.3 pp per year.
works.limitations: Primary reports not opened (goldmansachs.com and marcus.com returned 403). All numbers come from press coverage or from Acemoglu's and the OECD's citations. The '25-50% of workload' phrasing is unconfirmed: People Matters says 'nearly a quarter of work tasks' and that most workers would see less than half their workload automated. Proprietary method. The 1.5 pp figure is labor productivity, not TFP.
works.corrections: Added Sarah Dong as co-author of the 2025-26 updates (confirmed by eWeek and Fortune). Removed the '3-14%' displacement range: no source I opened contains it. Added the Jan 2026 note's title and its 25%-of-work-hours figure. Sourced the 1.5 pp figure to Acemoglu (2024), which cites Goldman Sachs 2023, because the press pieces I opened did not contain it. The 'Global Economics Analyst' series name and the exact March 26 date are unconfirmed; the Yahoo coverage is dated March 28, 2023. Status is effectively unverifiable for the primary report.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.year: 2025 (November; the page shows Nov 25, 2025, its citation block says 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: Per-task time without AI vs with AI for 100,000 real Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro, Max), mapped to O*NET tasks, then aggregated to a US labor-productivity effect.
works.method_plain: Claude estimates how long a competent professional would take on each conversation's task with and without AI. These estimates are mapped to O*NET tasks, weighted within occupations and by occupational wage bill, and aggregated Hulten-style, assuming universal adoption over 10 years and no change in capabilities.
key_numbers: Average task about 1.4 hours (about 90 minutes) without AI; median labor cost about $54 per task
Median time saving about 80% (84% in text, 81% in the figure caption)
Validation on 1,000 JIRA software tasks: Spearman rho = 0.44 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 vs 0.50 for human developers
Implied +1.8 pp per year US labor productivity growth over the decade (about 1.1 pp TFP at labor share 0.6); software developers are the largest contributor at 19% of the gain
Excludes time spent outside the chat validating, refining and iterating; the RCTs it cites found 14-56% savings (one found negative)
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing analog to a bottom-up theta_j: task-level time saved, weighted by within-occupation time shares (analogs of f_j and w_j). It is GROSS of review time (rho), acceptance (q) and failure (p). It also only covers tasks users chose to bring, a selection effect.
works.limitations: Model-estimated times, not observed. Selection bias. No review cost. Claude.ai users only. The authors say it is not a prediction of the future.
works.corrections: Numbers match the page. Noted the date discrepancy on the page (Nov 25 vs Nov 5, 2025) and the validation sample size.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (lead authors), Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: Task success rates, task horizons and complexity in real Claude usage (about 1M Claude.ai and 1M first-party API transcripts, Nov 13-20, 2025), and a success-adjusted revision of the macro productivity estimate.
works.method_plain: Classify each conversation for success, complexity, human-time length and autonomy. Multiply the time savings by the success probability, then re-aggregate, with CES variants in which tasks are complements or substitutes.
key_numbers: Task success: 67% on Claude.ai, 49% on the first-party API
API success falls from about 60% (sub-hour tasks) to about 45% (5+ human-hour tasks); 50% crossing about 3.5 human hours on the API; about 19 hours on Claude.ai (an extrapolation)
Macro estimate: 1.8 pp per year labor productivity baseline falls to about 1.2 pp (Claude.ai) and 1.0 pp (API) after success adjustment
CES variants: elasticity 0.5 (complements) gives 0.7-0.9 pp unadjusted and 0.6-0.8 pp success-adjusted; elasticity 1.5 (substitutes) gives 2.2-2.6 pp; elasticity 1 reproduces 1.8 pp
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures the project's p(h) term on real-world rather than benchmark tasks, and shows p falling with task length h. Multi-turn use on Claude.ai extends the horizon, which resembles kappa-type assistance. Savings are multiplied by p, but there is no explicit rho (review) or q (acceptance) term; roughly q*p*saving with q=1 and rho=0.
works.limitations: Success is judged by a model and depends on which tasks users chose to bring. The data (Nov 13-20, 2025) predate Opus 4.5. No review-time netting. Not industry-specific.
works.corrections: Authors were given as 'Anthropic Economic Research team'; the page names Appel, Massenkoff, McCrory (leads), McCain, Heller, Neylon and Tamkin. Added the sample size and dates. The numbers match.

works.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
works.authors: Alexander Arnon (Penn Wharton Budget Model), under the direction of Kent Smetters
works.what_measured: Long-run TFP/GDP level effect of generative AI in the US, along an adoption path.
works.method_plain: Acemoglu's formula. Exposure uses Eloundou et al. categories T2/T3/T4, weighted 70/95/100% and wage-weighted to about 40% of labor income. This is multiplied by 23% automated (Svanberg et al.). The cost saving is the labor saving times the labor share. Both are scaled by an adoption curve informed by the PC, internet, smartphone and cloud.
key_numbers: About 40% of labor income exposed; just under 10% of GDP affected, rising to about 15% over two decades
Average labor cost saving about 25% from seven studies (range roughly 10-55%), assumed to rise from 25% to 40% over coming decades
TFP/GDP level about +1.5% by 2035, nearly 3% by 2055, 3.7% by 2075; annual growth boost peaks at about 0.2 pp around 2032; permanent growth effect under 0.04 pp
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few macro estimates in which the intensive margin changes over time (25% rising to 40%). But the path is assumed, not derived from capability measures such as METR horizons. A direct foil for the project's theta_j(t) built from p(h,t).
works.limitations: The savings path is ad hoc. Reuses the computer-vision 23%. US only; not industry-specific. The seven studies measure different outcomes, so mapping them to cost savings is approximate.
works.corrections: None; the numbers match the page. Added the 0.04 pp permanent effect and the caveat about the studies.

works.title: GATE: An Integrated Assessment Model for AI Automation (plus 'AI and explosive growth redux')
works.authors: Ege Erdil, Andrei Potlogea, Tamay Besiroglu, Edu Roldan, Anson Ho, Jaime Sevilla, Matthew Barnett, Matej Vrzla, Robert Sandler (arXiv 2503.04941); redux essay by Andrei Potlogea and Anson Ho
works.year: 2025 (arXiv v1 March 6, v2 March 12; announcement March 21; essay June 20, 2025)
works.venue: arXiv preprint (2503.04941); Epoch AI blog and Gradient Updates
works.what_measured: Simulated paths of the automated share of tasks, compute investment and output growth.
works.method_plain: Tasks lie on a continuum. The automated share f(C) stays at an initial level, then rises log-linearly in effective compute between a lower threshold and the full-automation threshold (the gap is the 'FLOP gap'), then equals 1. Tasks below the cutoff are automated; tasks above it are not. Automated tasks get digital workers = runtime compute allocated / runtime compute required. A CES across tasks (default rho = -0.65) creates bottlenecks, inside a semi-endogenous growth model with investment and adjustment costs.
key_numbers: Default task substitution parameter rho = -0.65 (range -5 to -0.2; paper appendix and redux essay)
Default simulation: 23% per year world output growth in 2027, which the redux essay calls 'extremely unlikely'

Redux essay: growth may exceed 20% per year at about 30% task automation; explosive growth (>30% per year) needs about 50-70% automation; with three dampening factors, about 12% growth at 40% automation
Epoch announcement: compute investment may exceed 10% of world GDP; growth elevated 2-20x relative to the historical ~3% per year, over roughly a decade
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive margin: a task is automated or not, with no partial labor saving per task, no review cost and no failure rate. The runtime-compute requirement is a cost-of-running term (part of the project's 'net of AI running cost'). The mentor, Andrei Potlogea, co-wrote both the GATE paper and the redux essay. GATE's f(compute) is the macro analog of 'which h-bins have p(h) high enough', so the project's integral could supply a partial-automation version.
works.limitations: Built for qualitative insight, not forecasts (Epoch's own caveat). Assumes AI can substitute for human labor across all tasks. No industry detail.
works.corrections: Authors were given as 'Epoch AI team'. The arXiv abstract lists nine named authors, including Andrei Potlogea (the mentor), so he co-wrote GATE itself, not only the redux essay. The 23%-in-2027 figure comes from the redux essay, not the GATE paper; I did not find it in the arXiv PDF. rho = -0.65 is confirmed in the paper's appendix. Added the essay's 12%-at-40% figure.

works.title: Explosive growth from AI automation: A review of the arguments
works.authors: Ege Erdil, Tamay Besiroglu
works.what_measured: Whether AI automation could speed up world output growth by about an order of magnitude (above 30% per year), and an assessment of nine counterarguments.
works.method_plain: A task-based CES model: a fraction of tasks is automated (approximated as receiving unlimited input) and the remaining fraction f bottlenecks output. Growth models in which AI labor can be accumulated deliver increasing returns.
key_numbers: Explosive growth: growth an order of magnitude above today's frontier economies, operationalized as gross world product growth above 30% per year
With f = 10% of tasks unautomated and rho = -1, output rises 100-fold

Human brain about 1e15 FLOP/s (best guess from Carlsmith 2020, used to cost digital workers); if AI only ever adds nine times the input intensity on automated tasks, the maximum gain is about one order of magnitude in gross world product
f = 25% of tasks unautomated with an elasticity of substitution of about 1/3 could plausibly block explosive growth
works.relevance_to_theta: Automation is binary; tasks that need human oversight count as effectively unautomated. Their point that finite per-task input intensity caps the gains is the macro version of the project's point that theta_j < 1 because of review and failure. No intensive-margin estimate.
works.limitations: A theoretical review; no measured task-level savings; review costs are not modeled separately.
works.corrections: Added version dates and attributed the 1e15 FLOP/s figure to Carlsmith (2020). The numbers match the v3 PDF.

works.title: Scenarios for the Transition to AGI
works.authors: Anton Korinek, Donghyun Suh
works.what_measured: Output and wage paths under different speeds of automation toward AGI.
works.method_plain: Work is a set of atomistic tasks of varying complexity, and automation moves to ever more complex tasks. Wages depend on a race between automation and capital accumulation. If the complexity distribution has a heavy enough infinite tail, wages can rise indefinitely; if it is bounded and full automation occurs, wages collapse.
key_numbers: Paper (Section 3.3): business-as-usual scenario, output grows about 2% per year
Paper: 'baseline AGI' (full automation in 20 years) reaches steady-state growth of about 18% per year after wages collapse
Paper: 'aggressive AGI' (full automation in 5 years), with wage collapse after about 3 years and an earlier growth take-off

Acemoglu (2024, footnote 1) characterizes the paper as predicting 'baseline' GDP growth of 100% over 10 years and an 'aggressive' 300% increase. This is second-hand, and I did not find these exact figures in the paper's text.
works.relevance_to_theta: Its distribution of task complexity is the analogue of f_j(h), the task-length distribution, with an automation frontier moving through it, like the METR horizon moving along h. Automation is binary per task, so there is no review netting. Conceptually supports building theta_j by integrating over a length or complexity distribution.
works.limitations: Scenario theory, not estimation. Growth figures are from calibrated simulations.
works.corrections: Opened the arXiv HTML full text and added the paper's own scenario numbers (2%/yr business-as-usual; about 18%/yr steady state under baseline AGI). Acemoglu's '100% over 10 years / 300%' description is not stated in the paper text I read, so it should not be cited as the paper's result. Confirmed NBER WP 32255 and CEPR DP 18928 via RePEc. Raised citation confidence to high.

summary_flags: 'Every macro estimate in this stream uses the same skeleton: Hulten's theorem' is overstated. GATE, Erdil-Besiroglu and Korinek-Suh are CES/growth models, not Hulten aggregations; Anthropic's January 2026 report adds CES variants; the OECD adds a sectoral model with Baumol effects.

'Exposure from Eloundou et al. (20-60%)' is wrong: 60% (and 68%) is Pizzinelli et al. (IMF), used by Aghion-Bunel. Eloundou-based exposure is 20% (Acemoglu), about 40% of labor income (PWBM), and 30-35% / about 50% of value added (OECD).

Unit mixing: the range '0.07 pp/yr (Acemoglu) to 0.68 (Aghion-Bunel) to about 1.5 pp/yr (Goldman Sachs)' puts TFP figures beside a labor-productivity figure. The OECD converts Goldman Sachs to about 1 pp per year of TFP. Anthropic's 1.8 pp is also labor productivity (about 1.1 pp TFP).

Goldman Sachs does not use Eloundou exposure or the Svanberg 23%; it uses its own proprietary task mapping. So it does not fit 'the papers differ mainly in exposure from Eloundou et al. and a borrowed 23% cost-effective share'.

The record's OECD title was wrong ('Miracle or Myth' is the 2024 OECD AI Paper No. 29; the IPM 2025 article is 'Opportunities and Risks of Artificial Intelligence for Productivity'). The 2024 OECD TFP numbers were attributed to the wrong OECD paper.

GATE is attributed to the 'Epoch AI team', but the mentor, Andrei Potlogea, is a named co-author of the GATE paper itself, not only of the redux essay. The 23%-in-2027 figure comes from the redux essay.
The Goldman Sachs '3-14%' displacement range and the '25-50% of workload' phrasing are unconfirmed. Acemoglu's 'April 2024 draft said 0.71%' is unconfirmed. All were removed or flagged.

Korinek-Suh's '100% over 10 years / 300%' figures come from Acemoglu's description, not the paper. The paper itself reports about 2%/yr business-as-usual and about 18%/yr steady-state growth under baseline AGI.

'None is netted explicitly for review time or acceptance rates' and 'no paper derives the saving from a capability curve' hold only for the papers reviewed here. With a 12-paper sample, they are not established for the whole literature. Also, the experimental speedups (Noy-Zhang, Brynjolfsson, Peng) implicitly include whatever checking the participants did within the measured time.

'Frozen at 2023 capability' does not describe every paper: PWBM assumes savings rise from 25% to 40%, and Aghion-Bunel let the profitable share rise with compute-cost declines. The summary partly acknowledges this.

The verdict 'largely confirmed' is reasonable for this macro stream. But the stream looked only at macro aggregation papers, so it cannot by itself show that no task-level or micro study measures the intensive margin as capability rises.
verify.corrected_summary:
Most of the task-based macro estimates in this stream (Acemoglu 2024; Aghion-Bunel 2024; the OECD's Filippucci et al.; Penn Wharton 2025; Anthropic Nov 2025) use a version of Hulten's (1978) theorem. To a first approximation, AI's productivity effect = (share of the economy's tasks AI affects) x (average cost saved on those tasks). The growth models (Epoch's GATE, Erdil-Besiroglu, Korinek-Suh) use a different setup: CES task models in which each task is either automated or not.

In the Hulten-style papers, most of the spread comes from the first factor, the extensive margin. Exposure ranges from about 20% of the wage bill (Acemoglu, from Eloundou et al.) through 30-35% of value added (OECD) and about 40% of labor income (PWBM) to 60-68% (Pizzinelli et al., used by Aghion-Bunel). Acemoglu, PWBM and Aghion-Bunel also use a 'profitable to automate' share (23%) borrowed from a computer-vision study (Svanberg et al.). TFP results run from about 0.064-0.07 pp per year (Acemoglu: 0.66% TOTAL over ten years) to 0.3-0.7 pp per year (OECD, US) and 0.68 pp per year (Aghion-Bunel median). Goldman Sachs's 'just under 1.5 pp per year' and Anthropic's 1.8 pp per year are labor-productivity figures, roughly 1-1.1 pp of TFP, so check units before comparing.

The second factor, the intensive margin, is taken from outside rather than estimated in these papers. Acemoglu's 27%, the OECD's 30% (which explicitly excludes coding studies), Aghion-Bunel's 27-40% and PWBM's 25% (assumed to rise to 40%) all rest on a handful of early experiments: customer service 14% (rising to about 25-30%), writing about 40%, Copilot about 56%. They are applied flat across exposed tasks. Among the papers reviewed, none explicitly nets savings for separate review time or acceptance rates, and none ties the saving to a capability measure such as METR time horizons. The experiments' measured times do include whatever checking participants did.

Anthropic's 2025-26 reports are the partial exception. They estimate per-task time savings from real usage (median about 80%, gross of validation time outside the chat). In January 2026 they multiplied these by observed task success, which falls with task length; the 50% point is about 3.5 human-hours on the API. That cuts the labor-productivity estimate from 1.8 to about 1.0-1.2 pp per year. This is the closest published analog of the project's p(h) term, but it still has no explicit review-cost (rho) or acceptance (q) term, and the tasks are chosen by users.

On the working hypothesis: within this macro-aggregation literature, it is largely supported. These papers measure or model the extensive margin and plug in the intensive margin as an assumption. This stream alone does not show that the wider micro literature lacks capability-indexed intensive-margin estimates. Baqaee-Farhi (2019) adds a caveat: when savings are large, the weights w_j themselves shift (Baumol effects), so a first-order sum with fixed weights can mislead. Note also that the mentor, Andrei Potlogea, co-wrote the GATE model.
verify.dataset_notes: Anthropic Economic Index (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/EconomicIndex): opened. It is publicly viewable, about 763 MB. Releases listed run from 2025-02-10 (initial O*NET task mappings) to 2026-01-15 (economic primitives) and later (2026-03-24, 2026-06-26). The license is inconsistent: the metadata tag says MIT, while the text says data CC-BY and code MIT. Access 'public' is confirmed. GPTs-are-GPTs (https://github.com/openai/GPTs-are-GPTs): opened. The repo exists, is public, MIT licensed, and includes occ_level.csv plus GPT-4 and human ratings, with README definitions alpha=E1, beta=E1+0.5*E2, gamma=E1+E2. I could not confirm from the README that task-level T0-T4 automation labels are included, so check before relying on them. Epoch GATE (https://epoch.ai/gate): opened; it is the 'GATE Model Playground', public. Goldman Sachs insights page: still 403; 'paid/client-only' is correct for the full reports. O*NET (https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html) and BLS OEWS (https://www.bls.gov/oes/) were not opened in this check, but are standard public sources. Add: OECD AI Papers No. 29 (doi 10.1787/b524a072-en) and No. 41 (doi 10.1787/a5319ab5-en) as sources of OECD exposure and adoption inputs. Search budget ran out before I could check the Acemoglu 0.71% draft claim; a follow-up could check it.

works.title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works.what_measured: Theory, not measurement. A task-based growth model. Automation moves a range of tasks from labor to capital (the 'displacement effect'). Creating new labor-intensive tasks moves work back to labor (the 'reinstatement effect'). Both are pinned down in equilibrium by relative factor prices and endogenous research effort.
works.method_plain: There is a continuum of tasks indexed on a line. Tasks below a threshold I are done by machines, and labor does tasks between I and the newest task N. Automation pushes I up; new tasks push N up. In the static version, automation lowers employment and the labor share and can lower wages. New tasks do the reverse. In the dynamic version, cheap labor slows further automation, which can produce a balanced path. The companion JEP 2019 paper (Acemoglu-Restrepo, 'Automation and New Tasks', JEP 33(2):3-30, abstract opened at https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.33.2.3) splits labor-demand effects into displacement, productivity and reinstatement. Its abstract says automation 'always reduces the labor share in value added'.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers; a theory paper
JEP 2019 companion: abstract gives no figures and attributes slower US employment growth over 'the last three decades' to faster displacement, weaker reinstatement and slow productivity growth
works.relevance_to_theta: Here theta is binary at the task level. A task is either fully automated (labor input 0) or not, so the 'replacement rate' of a task bundle j is the measure of its tasks below the threshold I. That is pure extensive margin. Our theta_j, a continuous fraction of time saved, would correspond to the hours-weighted share of j's subtasks crossing the threshold, which is what the integral over f_j(h) does if each h-slice is a 'task'. The model's productivity and reinstatement effects sit outside theta, in d and eps*phi or in new-task creation. Speaks mainly to w_j (task composition shifting over time) and theta_j-direct.
works.limitations: Labor is perfectly substitutable by capital within an automated task and useless there afterwards, with no partial or assisted mode (no kappa) and no verification cost (no rho or q). Tasks are exogenously ordered. No calibration to AI or to services.

works.title: Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works.what_measured: How much of the change in the US wage structure from 1980 to 2016 is explained by 'task displacement', meaning the loss of tasks in which a worker group specialized, in industries that automated.
works.method_plain: They build a task-displacement measure for each demographic group by combining the group's initial routine-task specialization with industry-level automation signals (labor-share declines, automation capital). They regress changes in group wages on this measure, then use a general-equilibrium model to compute the aggregate effects.
key_numbers: Between 50% and 70% of changes in the US wage structure over the last four decades are accounted for by relative wage declines of groups specialized in routine tasks in rapidly automating industries (abstract, as stated)
GE analysis: large inequality changes can coexist with only modest productivity gains (qualitative in abstract)
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows how to aggregate a task-level displacement measure using group-by-industry task shares. That is structurally the same as S = sum_j w_j theta_j, with w_j being a group's wage-bill share in task j. Also shows that the realized displacement was measured top-down from labor-share declines rather than bottom-up from capability, which is the same top-down vs bottom-up split as the project's 2.3 pp/yr filing-based estimate.
works.limitations: US data and pre-generative-AI automation (robots, software). Displacement is inferred from labor-share declines, which can reflect markups or offshoring (they argue offshoring plays a smaller role). No intensive margin or review cost. Details beyond the abstract not verified by me.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.what_measured: An upper bound on the 10-year TFP and GDP gains from generative AI, built as (share of tasks impacted) x (average cost saving per impacted task).
works.method_plain: By a Hulten's-theorem argument (to first order, aggregate productivity gain = sum over tasks of the task's GDP share times its cost saving), d ln TFP = integral of chi(z)*pi_L(z). He takes Eloundou et al. exposure, weights occupations by their wage bill, and gets 19.9% of tasks exposed. Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision result says 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate, giving 0.23 x 0.199 = 4.6% of tasks impacted. He uses 27% labor cost savings (the average of the Noy-Zhang and Brynjolfsson et al. experiments) and multiplies by a labor share of about 0.57, giving 15.4% total cost savings. TFP gain = 0.046 x 0.154 = 0.71%. He then adds 'hard tasks', which get only 7% savings.
key_numbers: 19.9% of US labor tasks (wage-bill weighted) exposed to AI, from Eloundou et al.
23% of exposed tasks profitably automatable within 10 years (Svanberg et al., computer vision), so 4.6% of tasks impacted
Average labor cost savings 27%; total cost savings 0.27 x 0.57 = 15.4% (20.5% if Peng et al. Copilot results are added, labor savings 36%)
April 2024 text: 10-year TFP gain about 0.71% (about 0.07%/yr); GDP about 1.1%; upper bound 1.6-1.8% with automation-style investment

NBER/published abstract: TFP gain 'no more than 0.66%' over 10 years, and 'less than 0.53%' after the hard-task adjustment. The 0.71% vs 0.66% difference reflects version revisions; quote the version you cite
Hard tasks: cost savings assumed 7% (half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s customer-service effect), giving 0.040 total savings
Faster GPU cost declines (10%/yr) could raise the profitable share from 23% to about 30%, giving about 6% of tasks impacted and about 1% TFP
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing analog to S(t) = sum_j w_j theta_j. In his decomposition theta_j is explicitly a product: (share of j's tasks impacted) x (labor cost saving on impacted tasks). The intensive margin (27%) is borrowed from RCTs on small tasks rather than derived from capability, and it does not rise with capability. His 'easy vs hard task' split is a crude two-point version of f_j(h). He states that the cost savings could come from either automation or task complementarities and that for productivity the distinction matters less. That is the claim to test for employment, where it does matter.
works.limitations: Intensive-margin numbers come from 2023 RCTs (writing tasks, call centres) with pre-agent models. There is no review-cost term, and no link to capability growth beyond the GPU-cost scenario. Svanberg's computer-vision profitability share is extrapolated to all AI. Cost shares rather than hours shares are used.

works.title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018
works.authors: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna M. Salomons, Bryan Seegmiller
works.what_measured: Where new job titles ('new work') come from, linked to patent-based measures of augmenting vs automating innovation, over 1940-2018.
works.method_plain: They digitize Census job-title indexes across decades to detect newly added titles. They link these to Census microdata and to patents matched by text to occupations' outputs (augmentation) or tasks (automation). Shocks from breakthrough patents two decades earlier give causal estimates.
key_numbers: Abstract (as stated): 'The majority of current employment is in new job specialties introduced since 1940'

The commonly quoted '~60% of 2018 employment is in jobs that did not exist in 1940' comes from Autor's talks and press coverage. I did not confirm the exact percentage in the QJE text, so cite the abstract's 'majority' unless you check the paper

Augmentation innovations raise occupational labor demand and automation innovations depress it; demand-eroding effects of automation intensified over the past four decades while augmentation's demand-raising effects did not (qualitative)
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures reinstatement, the term the theta-only decomposition leaves out. It also separates augmentation (raises demand for an occupation's output, closer to kappa-type productivity plus demand response eps*phi) from automation (closer to theta). This means w_j cannot be held fixed over long horizons: new task types j appear.
works.limitations: US and long-run (decades), so too slow to show up in a short window like FY24-26. Patent text is only a proxy for technology. Nothing on review cost or the intensive margin.

works.title: Trading Tasks: A Simple Theory of Offshoring
works.authors: Gene M. Grossman, Esteban Rossi-Hansberg
works.what_measured: Theory of how a falling cost of offshoring tasks affects home factor prices. Identifies a 'productivity effect' that benefits the factor whose tasks are offshored.
works.method_plain: Low-skill tasks i in [0,1] are ordered by how costly they are to do remotely: doing task i abroad needs t(i) times as much foreign labor, with t rising in i. Firms offshore all tasks below a threshold I where the wage gap just equals the remote-work penalty: w = t(I) w*. The unit cost of the L-task bundle becomes w * a_L * Omega(I), where Omega(I) = 1 - I + (integral from 0 to I of t(i) di)/t(I), which is below 1. Cheaper offshoring raises I and lowers Omega, which works like labor-augmenting technical progress for the workers who stay at home.
key_numbers: Threshold condition: w = t(I) w* (eq. 1, Feb 2008 version)
Cost-saving factor Omega(I) = 1 - I + [integral_0^I t(i) di]/t(I) (eq. 3); 1 - Omega(I) is the share of L-task cost saved
No empirical calibration in the paper
works.relevance_to_theta: Mathematically the closest template for theta_j as an integral. Tasks are ordered by a single 'difficulty to hand off' index, a threshold separates delegated from in-house tasks, and the saving 1 - Omega(I) integrates the per-task penalty t(i) over the delegated range. Swap 'offshore worker' for 'AI agent', t(i) for (review + failure-redo cost)/(human cost) at task length h, and I for the h where delegation stops paying, and you get the max{.} integral over f_j(h). The productivity effect is the warning: cost savings raise the remaining domestic workers' effective productivity, so theta does not translate one-for-one into job loss. The model also describes Indian IT services itself, the destination of US task trade.
works.limitations: Task characteristics are invariant to location (perfect substitutes). One-dimensional ordering. Small-country/price-taking assumptions drive the shared-gains result. No quality or error dimension.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence: The Ambiguous Labor Market Impact of Automating Prediction
works.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works.url_opened: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.33.2.31 ; companion NBER WP 24626 'Exploring the Impact of Artificial Intelligence: Prediction versus Judgment' (Information Economics and Policy 2019) at https://www.nber.org/papers/w24626
works.what_measured: Conceptual framework. AI as a fall in the cost of prediction, and how that interacts with human judgment (knowing the payoffs) and decisions.
works.method_plain: A decision combines a prediction about the state of the world with judgment about payoffs. Cheaper prediction can substitute for humans in prediction tasks, let whole decisions be delegated to machines, or raise the value of complementary human judgment. The WP 24626 abstract adds that better prediction enables riskier decisions and more variance, that not all judgment complements AI, and that humans may delegate to machines even when human input would do better.
key_numbers: No quantitative estimates

JEP abstract emphasizes the difference between automating decisions and enhancing human decision-making (I could open only the abstract; the full PDF returned 403, so I have not verified the exact list of channels in the body)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives the economic vocabulary for the delegate-vs-assist split in the theta formula. q*p(h) is the share of decisions fully delegated, and kappa is AI 'enhancing' the human who keeps judgment. Judgment (knowing the client's payoff function) is what review (rho) is for, so tasks where judgment cannot be codified should have high rho or low q. Conceptual only.
works.limitations: Pre-LLM 'prediction machine' framing; no agents, no task-length dimension, no numbers. Body text not verified by me.

works.title: Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production
works.authors: Luis Garicano
works.what_measured: Theory of why knowledge-based hierarchies form. Front-line workers learn common or easy problems, and specialist problem-solvers handle the rarer or harder exceptions, because matching problems to solvers is costly.
works.method_plain: Problems arrive with varying difficulty. Each agent knows how to solve problems up to some knowledge level. Unsolved problems are passed up, and each referral costs the solver communication time. The optimal organization trades off learning costs against helping costs, which gives a pyramid with a span of control.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers in the abstract I opened (full text paywalled)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives the structure of Indian IT delivery pyramids (many juniors, few leads who handle escalations and review). The helping time per referral is the economic analog of the review cost rho. Whose time is saved matters: if AI removes junior work but leads must review it, saved hours are cheap junior hours and added hours are expensive senior hours. So an hours-weighted theta_j and a cost-weighted theta_j can differ.
works.limitations: I only verified the abstract and bibliographic details. Stylized: one-dimensional difficulty, homogeneous time cost of help.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy
works.authors: Enrique Ide, Eduard Talamas
works.venue: Journal of Political Economy (DOI 10.1086/737233; final issue/year not verified by me); also CEPR DP19135
works.what_measured: Theory. How AI with a given knowledge level changes occupational sorting (workers vs solvers), wages and output in a Garicano hierarchy, with 'autonomous' AI (can do work itself) versus 'non-autonomous' AI (copilot only).
works.method_plain: Humans have knowledge z in [0,1], the fraction of problems they can solve. Problem difficulty is Uniform[0,1]. Each referral costs the solver h units of time, so a solver supervises n = 1/(h(1-z)) workers of knowledge z. AI turns compute into agents with fixed knowledge z_AI, which are perfect substitutes for a human of that knowledge. Autonomous AI can act as worker or solver. Non-autonomous AI acts only as solver/copilot.
key_numbers: Team size condition: h * n(z) * (1 - z) = 1
Prop. 2: compute rental rate r* = z_AI; AI is used as a worker if z_AI is in the pre-AI worker range and as a solver if it is in the solver range
Prop. 3: 'basic' AI pushes marginal humans from routine work into solving; 'advanced' AI pushes solvers down into routine work
Prop. 5: wage effects are non-monotone in z_AI, and the human with knowledge z_AI always loses
Prop. 6: non-autonomous (copilot) AI helps the least knowledgeable more but gives strictly lower output than autonomous AI
works.relevance_to_theta: The most direct theory of the delegate-vs-assist distinction in the theta formula. Autonomous AI corresponds to the q*p(h) branch and copilot AI to the kappa branch. z_AI plays the role of p(h,t), the fraction of problems AI solves alone, and h (helping time) plays the role of rho. Key implication: as capability rises, who is displaced changes (juniors first, then seniors), so theta_j differs by job level, and a single theta_j per service line hides which pyramid layer shrinks.
works.limitations: AI is a perfect substitute for a human of equal knowledge (no q < 1 acceptance problem). Compute is abundant. Problem difficulty is uniform and one-dimensional. No calibration.

works.title: Expertise
works.authors: David Autor, Neil Thompson
works.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 23(4): 1203-1271 (NBER WP 33941, June 2025)
works.what_measured: Whether automating some tasks in an occupation raises or lowers the expertise needed for the tasks that remain, and the effect on occupational wages and employment over four decades.
works.method_plain: Model: removing inexpert tasks raises the expertise required for the job (wages up, fewer qualified workers, so employment down). Removing expert tasks does the reverse. Empirics: a content-agnostic measure of task expertise applied to changes in occupational task descriptions over four decades.
key_numbers: Abstract gives no point estimates; finding (qualitative): automation that removed inexpert tasks raised wages and reduced employment; automation that removed expert tasks lowered wages and raised employment
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the same theta_j can have opposite employment effects depending on WHICH tasks inside j are removed. If AI handles short, easy tickets (low h, where p is high), the remaining work is harder, and both w_j and the skill mix shift. The hours-weighted f_j(h) integral captures how much time is saved, not which expertise level it comes from.
works.limitations: US occupations, pre-generative-AI automation. Abstract has no numbers. The expertise measure is built from text.

works.title: O-Ring Automation
works.authors: Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works.what_measured: Theory of automation when tasks are quality complements: output quality multiplies across tasks, and the worker reallocates a fixed time budget among the tasks that remain manual.
works.method_plain: O-ring production: one weak link ruins the product. Machines can do some tasks at a given quality. Because quality multiplies, automating one task changes the value of automating others, and the worker shifts freed time to bottleneck tasks.
key_numbers: No numbers in the abstract

Claims (as stated): task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete; adoption is discrete and may need bundling even when automation quality improves smoothly; labor income can rise under partial automation; linear exposure indices overstate displacement when tasks are complements
works.relevance_to_theta: A direct critique of the additive form S = sum_j w_j theta_j and of 'time saved' = 'labor removed'. Freed time is reallocated to raise quality on bottleneck tasks, so saved hours need not become fewer workers, and theta_j depends on what else is automated.
works.limitations: Theory only; I read only the abstract. Complementarity strength is not measured. In outsourced IT the client may pay for hours rather than quality, which weakens the quality-reallocation channel.

works.title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation
works.authors: Mert Demirer, John J. Horton, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier, Peyman Shahidi
works.venue: NBER WP 34859 (Feb 2026, rev. Sep 2026); arXiv 2606.15960 (v2 Oct 2026); accepted at EC '26
works.what_measured: Theory plus empirical tests of how AI is assigned to sequential workflow steps: manual, augmented (human prompts and verifies), or automated in contiguous 'chains' verified only at the end.
works.method_plain: Production is a Leontief sequence of steps. AI succeeds on step i with probability q_i = alpha^{d_i} (alpha = AI quality, d_i = step difficulty). A chain from step l to r succeeds with probability alpha^{sum d_i}, and a human verifies once at the end, retrying until success. Expected time = t_r^A / product(q_i). The firm picks the partition with the lowest expected time. Empirically they use O*NET tasks with Eloundou et al. exposure and Anthropic Economic Index usage, task orderings generated by GPT-5-mini, and checks against the APQC Process Classification Framework and 4TU.ResearchData process event logs.
key_numbers: Augmented single step expected time = t^A / q (retry until success)
Chain expected time = t_r^A / product of q_i; verification is a fixed cost per chain, not growing with chain length
Worked example: three-step workflow costs 15.6 under optimal chaining vs 35.4 under comparative-advantage assignment (model time units)
Two-step example: optimal strategy switches near alpha = 0.5 and alpha ~ 0.92, so returns to AI quality jump (non-monotone, J-curve-like)
Fragmentation index approximates optimal cost within constant factors (OPT/8 <= FI <= 5*OPT/4)
The portion I read did not report sample sizes or coefficient estimates for the empirical tests
works.relevance_to_theta: The most directly usable 2026 model for the theta formula. q_i = alpha^{d} with additive difficulty is the same logic as METR's logistic-in-log(h) p(h,t), since a longer task means more compounded difficulty. It treats failure as 'retry and re-verify' (expected time t^A/q), whereas the draft formula treats failure as 'human redoes it with kappa assistance'. These give different theta. It also shows that review cost is per verified chunk, not proportional to h, which challenges rho as a constant share of h, and that theta_j depends on how AI-able steps cluster within j, not only on f_j.
works.limitations: Independent step failures; perfect verification at chain end (no undetected errors). Task ordering for O*NET is LLM-generated. Empirical magnitudes not visible in the portion I read. Horton discloses a paid advisory role with Anthropic.

works.title: Delegation and Verification Under AI
works.authors: Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi
works.venue: arXiv 2603.02961 (Mar 2026); Proceedings of ICML 2026 (PMLR 306); also Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper 2500
works.what_measured: Theory of a rational worker choosing how much to delegate to AI (d) and how hard to verify (s), and how this affects quality as judged by the employing institution.
works.method_plain: Success probability p(d,s) = (1-d)p_w + d*p_a + d(1-p_a)phi(s)p_w, where p_a = AI success, p_w = worker success, and phi(s) = chance of catching an AI error at verification effort s (e.g. 1 - e^{-alpha s}). Expected cost = (1-d)C_w + d[C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]: delegate, pay to verify, and redo the caught failures by hand. Because the objective is linear in d, the worker jumps between manual work, pure delegation (no checking) and verified delegation.
key_numbers: Cost of verified delegation = C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)*phi(s)*C_w versus manual cost C_w
Theorem 3.1: three regimes with sharp boundaries in (verification reliability alpha, execution efficiency beta), i.e. phase transitions
Theorem 3.5: quality improves only when verification reliability exceeds a threshold; low-verification workers over-delegate and lower institutional quality
C_w and C_v are calibrated from observed task times (values not extracted)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a micro-foundation for the theta integrand. Time saved per task = 1 - [C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]/C_w, so rho = C_v/C_w, p = p_a, and AI running cost is C_a/C_w. The difference from the draft is that missed errors (1-phi) are accepted silently. The draft's q captures 'passes tests but would not be merged', while this model adds undetected failures that cost quality rather than time. That suggests adding a quality-loss term, or treating verification effort as chosen jointly with rho.
works.limitations: Single task, binary success, worker and AI failures treated simply. Calibration details not extracted. Institution-vs-worker objective is stylized.

research.stream_summary: Task-based economics models a job as a bundle of tasks and asks which tasks move from people to machines. In the classic Acemoglu-Restrepo model (2018, 2019, 2022), a task is either fully automated or not, so their version of a replacement rate is the share of tasks crossing a threshold. That is the extensive margin. Three forces then act on employment: displacement, productivity (cheaper output raises demand), and reinstatement (new tasks). Autor et al. (2024 QJE) measure reinstatement directly: most current US employment is in job types created after 1940. Acemoglu's 'Simple Macroeconomics of AI' is the closest analog to S = sum w_j theta_j. He multiplies the share of tasks impacted (4.6%) by the cost saving per impacted task (27% of labor cost, taken from 2023 experiments). So he does use an intensive margin, but he borrows it from small RCTs rather than deriving it from capability, and it does not grow as models improve. That partly supports the working hypothesis: the intensive margin exists in the theory but is badly measured. Grossman-Rossi-Hansberg's offshoring model is mathematically almost the draft integral. Tasks are ordered by handoff cost, a threshold splits delegated from in-house tasks, and the saving integrates the penalty over the delegated range. Its 'productivity effect' warns that savings can raise, rather than cut, demand for the workers who remain. Garicano and Ide-Talamas map onto Indian IT pyramids: review time is the solver's 'helping time', and autonomous versus copilot AI is delegate versus kappa. Displacement moves from juniors to seniors as AI knowledge rises. The 2026 work (Demirer et al.; Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi; Gans-Goldfarb) supplies verification-cost micro-foundations, and it also shows that theta is not additive across tasks: chaining, quality complementarity and fixed per-chunk verification all break the sum w_j theta_j.
gaps_noticed: No theory paper derives task-level labor saving as a continuous function of a capability index (like METR time horizon) net of review. Acemoglu's 27% is a static number borrowed from RCTs; Demirer et al.'s q = alpha^d is the closest.

The draft formula assumes failed AI output is redone by a human with kappa speedup. Demirer et al. assume retry-and-reverify (t^A/q), and Huang et al. assume caught errors are redone manually while uncaught errors are silently accepted. These give different theta for the same p, so the choice should be explicit and ideally tested.

The draft models review cost rho as proportional to task length h. Theory offers alternatives: a fixed cost per verified chunk (Demirer et al.), a cost convex in effort with detection probability phi(s) (Huang et al.), or a cost driven by feedback latency (Catalini-Hui-Wu 2026, arXiv 2602.20946, opened but not included as a main entry).

Hidden assumption: time saved = labor removed. O-Ring (Gans-Goldfarb) and the GRH productivity effect show freed time can go to bottleneck or quality work, or can raise output demand. For Indian IT, time-and-materials and fixed-price contracts would behave differently here, and no paper models this.

Hidden assumption: additivity across task types (sum w_j theta_j). Chaining and O-ring complementarity make theta_j depend on which neighboring tasks are automated, so workflow-ordered task data is needed, not just f_j(h).

Hours-weighted vs cost-weighted aggregation: Hulten/Acemoglu use cost shares, and Garicano/Ide-Talamas imply that saved junior hours and added senior review hours carry different prices. The Indian IT pyramid makes this a first-order issue.

Hidden assumption: fixed task boundaries and fixed w_j. Autor-Thompson (expertise) and Autor et al. (new work) show that task content changes and new tasks appear, and no paper estimates how fast reinstatement happens in IT services.
No task-based paper is specific to offshored IT/BPO services or India; the GRH offshoring literature and the AI-automation literature have not been joined.

Undetected-error or quality cost is absent from theta, which is a time measure. Huang et al. show over-delegation lowers quality, which may show up as client rework or as price cuts (phi) rather than as time.

Could not verify the body of Agrawal-Gans-Goldfarb JEP 2019 (PDF 403; automated download blocked) or the Garicano 2000 full text (paywalled), so claims about them rest on abstracts. Could not confirm the exact '~60%' new-work figure in the QJE text; the abstract says 'majority'.
