works.title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works.what_measured: Theory, not measurement. A task-based growth model. Automation moves a range of tasks from labor to capital (the 'displacement effect'). Creating new labor-intensive tasks moves work back to labor (the 'reinstatement effect'). In the full model, capital accumulation and the direction of research are endogenous.
works.method_plain: Tasks lie on a line. Tasks below a threshold I can be done by machines, and labor does the remaining tasks up to the newest task N. Automation pushes I up; new tasks push N up. In the static version (fixed capital), automation lowers employment and the labor share and can lower wages, while new tasks do the reverse. In the dynamic version, automation makes labor relatively cheap, which discourages further automation and encourages new tasks, so a stable balanced growth path can exist (unless the long-run rental rate of capital relative to wages is low enough, in which case all tasks are automated). Companion paper: Acemoglu and Restrepo, 'Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor', JEP 33(2): 3-30, Spring 2019 (abstract opened). It splits labor-demand effects into displacement, productivity and reinstatement, and its abstract says automation always reduces the labor share in value added.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers; a theory paper

JEP 2019 companion: abstract gives no figures; it attributes slower US employment growth over the last three decades mainly to faster displacement (especially in manufacturing), weaker reinstatement and slow productivity growth
works.relevance_to_theta: Here theta is binary at the task level: a task is either automated or not, so the 'replacement rate' of a task bundle j is the share of its tasks below the threshold I. That is a pure extensive margin. A continuous theta_j (fraction of time saved) would correspond to the hours-weighted share of j's subtasks crossing the threshold, which is what the integral over f_j(h) does if each h-slice is treated as a 'task'. The productivity and reinstatement effects sit outside theta, in d and eps*phi or in new-task creation. Speaks mainly to w_j (task composition shifting over time) and theta_j-direct.
works.limitations: In an automated task, capital is assumed cheaper than labor, so labor stops doing it. There is no partial or assisted mode (no kappa) and no verification cost (no rho or q). Tasks are ordered exogenously. No calibration to AI or to services.
works.corrections: None of substance. Bibliographic details and abstract claims for both the AER 2018 and JEP 2019 papers match the AEA pages. Small wording fix: the record said labor is 'useless' in automated tasks. In the model labor could still do them, but capital is cheaper, so it does not.

works.title: Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo
works.what_measured: How much of the change in the US wage structure from 1980 to 2016 is explained by 'task displacement', meaning the loss of tasks in which a worker group specialized, in industries that automated.
works.method_plain: They build a task-displacement measure for each demographic group from the group's initial specialization in routine tasks combined with industry-level automation signals. They then relate changes in group wages to this measure and use a general-equilibrium model to compute aggregate effects. Construction details are beyond the abstract and were not checked.
key_numbers: Between 50% and 70% of changes in the US wage structure over the last four decades are accounted for by relative wage declines of worker groups specialized in routine tasks in industries that automated rapidly (abstract)
Automation accounts for most of the task-displacement effect, with offshoring playing a smaller role (abstract, qualitative)
Large changes in inequality can coexist with only modest productivity gains (abstract, qualitative)
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows how to aggregate a task-level displacement measure using group-by-industry task shares. That has the same structure as S = sum_j w_j theta_j, with w_j as a group's wage-bill share in task j. Realized displacement is measured top-down from industry signals, not bottom-up from capability, which matches the project's split between the filing-based 2.3 pp/yr and a capability-based theta.
works.limitations: US data and pre-generative-AI automation (robots, software). Industry automation signals such as labor-share declines can also reflect other forces. The abstract says market power, markups and deunionization do not appear to be major drivers. No intensive margin or review cost. Details beyond the abstract were not verified.
works.corrections: None. Venue, year and the 50-70% figure match the NBER page, which also lists the published Econometrica 90(5): 1973-2016 version.

works.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu
works.url_opened: https://www.nber.org/papers/w32487 ; full text of the April 5, 2024 version read from https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2024-04/The%20Simple%20Macroeconomics%20of%20AI.pdf
works.what_measured: An upper bound on the 10-year TFP and GDP gains from AI, built as (share of tasks impacted) x (average cost saving per impacted task).
works.method_plain: A Hulten's-theorem argument: to first order, the aggregate productivity gain equals the sum over tasks of each task's GDP share times its cost saving. He takes Eloundou et al.'s task exposure (which does not separate automation from task complementarity), weights occupations by wage bill, and gets 19.9% of tasks exposed. He extrapolates Svanberg et al.'s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks are profitable to automate within 10 years, giving 0.23 x 0.199 = 4.6% of tasks impacted. He takes 27% labor cost savings (the average of Noy-Zhang 2023 and Brynjolfsson et al. 2023) and multiplies by an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.57, giving total cost savings of 0.154. TFP gain = 0.046 x 0.154 = 0.71%. He then treats 'hard' tasks separately, with 7% labor savings (0.040 total cost savings).
key_numbers: 19.9% of US labor tasks exposed to AI (Eloundou et al., aggregated to occupations and weighted by wage-bill share)
23% of exposed tasks feasibly and profitably automatable within 10 years (Svanberg et al., computer vision, extrapolated), so 0.23 x 0.199 = 4.6% of tasks impacted

Average labor cost savings 27%; total cost savings 0.27 x 0.57 = 0.154 (15.4%). Adding Peng et al. (GitHub Copilot) raises labor savings to 0.36 and total savings to 0.205, giving 10-year TFP of 0.94%
April 2024 text: 10-year TFP gain at most about 0.71% (about 0.07%/yr); GDP about 1.1% (0.92% with hard tasks); 1.6-1.8% if there is a large investment boom

NBER/published abstract: TFP gain 'no more than 0.66%' over 10 years, and 'less than 0.53%' after the hard-task adjustment. The April 2024 abstract instead says 0.71% and 'less than 0.55%'. Quote the version you cite
Hard tasks: labor cost savings assumed 7% (half of Brynjolfsson et al.'s 14% customer-service effect), giving 0.040 total cost savings
If computer-vision costs fall 10%/yr (Svanberg scenario), the profitable share rises from 23% to about 30%, about 6% of GDP impacted and about 1% TFP over 10 years
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing analog to S(t) = sum_j w_j theta_j. In effect, theta is a product: (share of tasks impacted) x (cost saving on impacted tasks). The intensive margin (27%) is borrowed from 2023 RCTs rather than derived from capability, and it does not rise with capability; only the extensive share responds, in the GPU-cost scenario. His easy/hard task split is a crude two-point version of f_j. He says explicitly that it is unclear whether the RCT savings come from extensive-margin automation or task complementarities, and that the distinction matters less for productivity. That is the claim to test for employment, where it does matter.
works.limitations: Intensive-margin numbers come from 2023 RCTs (writing tasks, call centres, Copilot) with pre-agent models and only measure speed, ignoring quality. No review-cost term. No link to capability growth beyond the GPU-cost scenario. Svanberg's computer-vision profitability share is extrapolated to all AI. Uses cost shares rather than hours shares.
works.corrections: All numbers checked against the April 2024 full text and the NBER abstract. Added the April version's hard-task bound (0.55%), its hard-task GDP figure (0.92%) and the Peng-inclusive TFP figure (0.94%). Clarified that 15.4% is total cost savings and 27% is labor cost savings.

works.title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018
works.authors: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna M. Salomons, Bryan Seegmiller
works.venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(3): 1399-1465 (NBER WP 30389, August 2022)
works.what_measured: Where new job titles ('new work') come from, linked to patent-based measures of augmenting versus automating innovation, 1940-2018.
works.method_plain: They build a database of new job titles across eight decades, link it to Census microdata, and link it to patent-based measures of automation and augmentation. Shocks from breakthrough innovations two decades earlier are used to argue the effects are causal.
key_numbers: Abstract: the majority of current employment is in new job specialties introduced after 1940 (no percentage in the abstract)
New work shifted from middle-paid production and clerical jobs (1940-1980) to high-paid professional jobs and, secondarily, low-paid service jobs (since 1980) (abstract, qualitative)

Augmentation innovations raise occupational labor demand and new work; automation innovations reduce them. The demand-reducing effects of automation intensified over the past four decades, while augmentation's demand-raising effects did not (abstract, qualitative)
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures new work, a proxy for the reinstatement term that a theta-only decomposition leaves out. It also separates augmentation (raises demand for an occupation's output, closer to kappa-type productivity plus demand response eps*phi) from automation (closer to theta). Over long horizons w_j cannot be held fixed, because new task types j appear.
works.limitations: US and long-run (decades), so too slow to show up in a short window like FY24-26. Patent text is only a proxy for technology. Nothing on review cost or the intensive margin.
works.corrections: Bibliographic details and abstract claims match the NBER page. The QJE page was not reopened here, and the record's QJE URL was not independently confirmed to load. Removed the '~60% of 2018 employment' figure from key numbers: I could not confirm it in the paper text, so cite the abstract's 'majority'.

works.title: Trading Tasks: A Simple Theory of Offshoring
works.authors: Gene M. Grossman, Esteban Rossi-Hansberg
works.what_measured: Theory of how a falling cost of offshoring tasks affects home factor prices. Identifies a 'productivity effect' that benefits the factor whose tasks are easier to offshore.
works.method_plain: Low-skill tasks i in [0,1] are ordered by how costly they are to do remotely. Doing task i abroad takes t(i) times as much foreign labor, with t rising in i. Firms offshore every task below a threshold I, where the wage gap just equals the remote-work penalty: w = t(I) w*. The unit cost of the low-skill tasks becomes w * a_L * Omega(I), with Omega(I) = 1 - I + [integral from 0 to I of t(i) di]/t(I). Omega(I) is below 1 when I > 0. Cheaper offshoring works like labor-augmenting technical progress for the low-skill workers who stay at home.
key_numbers: Threshold condition: w = t(I) w* (eq. 1, February 2008 version)
Cost factor Omega(I) = 1 - I + [integral_0^I t(i) di]/t(I) (eq. 3); Omega(I) < 1 for I > 0, so 1 - Omega(I) is the share of low-skill task cost saved
No empirical calibration in the paper
works.relevance_to_theta: A useful structural template, not an identical model. Tasks are ordered by a single 'hard to hand off' index, a threshold separates delegated from in-house tasks, and the saving integrates a per-task penalty t(i) over the delegated range. Replacing the offshore worker with an AI agent, t(i) with (review + redo cost)/(human cost) at task length h, and I with the h at which delegation stops paying gives something close to the max{.} integral over f_j(h). Unlike the draft, though, GRH's penalty is deterministic, with no failure probability. The productivity effect is the warning: savings raise the effective productivity of the workers who remain, so theta need not translate one-for-one into job loss. The model also describes Indian IT services itself, as a destination of offshored tasks.
works.limitations: Task characteristics do not depend on location (foreign and home tasks are perfect substitutes, per the paper's footnote). One-dimensional ordering. The small-country, price-taking assumptions drive the shared-gains result. No quality or error dimension. Equation numbering is from the February 2008 version; the AER version's notation was not checked.
works.corrections: None of substance. Equations 1 and 3 match the February 2008 PDF, and the AER page confirms 98(5): 1978-97, December 2008. The 'mathematically the closest template' language is softened in the relevance note.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence: The Ambiguous Labor Market Impact of Automating Prediction
works.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works.url_opened: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.33.2.31 ; companion NBER WP 24626, 'Exploring the Impact of Artificial Intelligence: Prediction versus Judgment' (May 2018; published in Information Economics and Policy, 2019), https://www.nber.org/papers/w24626
works.what_measured: Conceptual framework. AI is a fall in the cost of prediction, and the paper asks how that interacts with human judgment (knowing the payoffs) and with decisions.
works.method_plain: A decision combines a prediction about the state of the world with judgment about payoffs. The JEP abstract gives examples where automating prediction ends up automating whole decisions and examples where it instead helps humans decide better. The WP 24626 abstract adds three points: cheaper prediction enables riskier decisions, which raises observed productivity and may raise variance; better prediction moves the returns to different kinds of judgment in opposite directions, so not all judgment complements AI; and humans may delegate decisions to machines even when human input would do better.
key_numbers: No quantitative estimates
Only abstracts were verified; the body text (exact list of channels) was not opened
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives economic vocabulary for the delegate-vs-assist split in the theta formula. Fully delegated decisions correspond to the q*p(h) branch, and AI 'enhancing' a human who keeps judgment corresponds to kappa. Judgment (knowing the client's payoff function) is what review (rho) is for, so tasks where judgment cannot be codified should have high rho or low q. Conceptual only.
works.limitations: Pre-LLM 'prediction machine' framing: no agents, no task-length dimension, no numbers. Body text was not verified (the JEP PDF could not be fetched).
works.corrections: Bibliographic details for both papers and the abstract-level claims match the AEA and NBER pages. Raised confidence on the citation itself to high. Claims about the body text remain unverified.

works.title: Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production
works.authors: Luis Garicano
works.what_measured: Theory of why knowledge-based hierarchies form. Front-line workers learn the common or easy problems, and specialist problem-solvers handle the rarer or harder ones, because matching problems to solvers is costly.
works.method_plain: Problems vary in difficulty. Each agent can solve problems up to some knowledge level, and unsolved problems are passed up the hierarchy, costing the solver time to help. The optimal organization trades learning costs against helping costs, which produces a pyramid. The abstract confirms the common/easy versus rare/hard division. The helping-time mechanics are standard in this literature (Ide-Talamas restate them) but were not read in Garicano's own text.
key_numbers: No empirical numbers in the abstract (full text paywalled)
works.relevance_to_theta: Describes the structure of Indian IT delivery pyramids: many juniors, and a few leads who handle escalations and review. Helping time per referral is the economic analog of the review cost rho. Whose time is saved matters: if AI removes junior work but leads must review it, the saved hours are cheap junior hours and the added hours are expensive senior hours, so an hours-weighted theta_j and a cost-weighted theta_j can differ. This application to IT services is the stream's own interpretation, not something the paper does.
works.limitations: Only the abstract and bibliographic details were verified. Stylized: one-dimensional difficulty and a homogeneous time cost of help.
works.corrections: Added the DOI and month. Noted that the helping-time mechanism was not read in the full text.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Knowledge Economy
works.authors: Enrique Ide, Eduard Talamas (also spelled Talamàs)
works.venue: Journal of Political Economy (DOI 10.1086/737233; volume, issue and pages not verified); earlier CEPR Discussion Paper DP19135 (2024)
works.what_measured: Theory. How AI with a given knowledge level changes occupational sorting (workers vs solvers), wages and output in a Garicano-style hierarchy, comparing 'autonomous' AI (can do the work itself) with 'non-autonomous' AI (copilot only).
works.method_plain: Humans have knowledge z in [0,1], the fraction of problems they can solve. Problem difficulty is Uniform[0,1] and independent across problems. Each referral costs the solver h units of time, so a two-layer team satisfies h * n(z) * (1 - z) = 1. AI turns compute into agents with fixed knowledge z_AI. Autonomous AI can act as worker or solver; non-autonomous AI acts only as a copilot.
key_numbers: Team time constraint: h * n(z) * (1 - z) = 1 (Section 3.1)

Prop. 2: AI is always used for independent production; the compute rental rate r* = z_AI; if z_AI is in the pre-AI worker range, AI is used as a worker. The post-AI wage function is continuous, strictly increasing and convex
Prop. 3: 'basic' AI (z_AI in the worker range) displaces humans from routine work into specialized problem solving; 'advanced' AI (z_AI in the solver range) displaces in the opposite direction

Prop. 5: there are always winners at the top, and winners at the bottom exist only if z_AI exceeds a threshold. Section 5.2 text: the individual with knowledge z_AI always loses, and gains are concentrated at the extremes of the knowledge distribution

Prop. 6: with non-autonomous AI the compute rental rate is 0, and overall output is strictly higher with autonomous than with non-autonomous AI. The abstract says autonomous AI primarily benefits the most knowledgeable and non-autonomous AI the least knowledgeable
works.relevance_to_theta: The most direct theory of the delegate-vs-assist distinction in the theta formula. Autonomous AI corresponds to the q*p(h) branch and copilot AI to the kappa branch. z_AI plays the role of p(h,t), the fraction of problems AI solves alone, and h (helping time) plays the role of rho. Implication: as capability rises, which pyramid layer is displaced changes. Basic AI pushes humans out of routine work; advanced AI pushes solvers down into routine work. A single theta_j per service line therefore hides which layer shrinks.
works.limitations: AI is a perfect substitute for a human of equal knowledge (no q < 1 acceptance problem). Compute is abundant. Problem difficulty is uniform and one-dimensional. No calibration.
works.corrections: Prop. 5 was mischaracterized. The record said Prop. 5 shows wage effects are non-monotone in z_AI and that the z_AI human always loses. In fact Prop. 5 states winners at the top always exist and winners at the bottom exist only above a z_AI threshold. The z_AI-human-always-loses statement is in the Section 5.2 text, and the winners-at-the-extremes pattern is across the knowledge distribution, not 'non-monotone in z_AI'. Added Prop. 2's wage-function properties and Prop. 6's r* = 0. The JPE venue is confirmed only through the DOI linked on arXiv and a Nature Index listing (the journal page returned 403), so volume and issue are unverified.

works.title: Expertise
works.authors: David Autor, Neil Thompson
works.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 23(4): 1203-1271 (DOI 10.1093/jeea/jvaf023); NBER WP 33941 (June 2025)
works.what_measured: Whether automating some tasks in an occupation raises or lowers the expertise needed for the remaining tasks, and the effects on occupational wages and employment over four decades.
works.method_plain: Model: removing inexpert tasks raises the expertise required (wages up, fewer qualified workers, so employment down); removing expert tasks does the reverse. Empirics: a new content-agnostic measure of task expertise, applied to changes in occupational task content over four decades.
key_numbers: The abstract gives no point estimates. Qualitative finding: where automation removed inexpert tasks, wages rose and employment fell; where it removed expert tasks, wages fell and employment rose
The abstract says these effects differ from those of changes in task quantity, and for employment they run in the opposite direction
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the same theta_j can have opposite employment effects depending on WHICH tasks inside j are removed. If AI takes short, easy tickets (low h, where p is high), the remaining work is harder, and both w_j and the skill mix shift. The hours-weighted f_j(h) integral captures how much time is saved, not which expertise level it comes from.
works.limitations: US occupations, pre-generative-AI automation. The abstract has no numbers. The expertise measure is built from text.
works.corrections: None. The NBER page confirms JEEA 23(4): 1203-1271 and gives the DOI, which was added.

works.title: O-Ring Automation
works.authors: Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
works.what_measured: Theory of automation when tasks are quality complements: output depends on the product of task qualities, and the worker splits a fixed time budget among the tasks that remain manual.
works.method_plain: O-ring production: one weak link ruins the product. Machines can take over some tasks at a given quality. Because qualities multiply, automating one task changes the value of automating others, and the worker shifts freed time to bottleneck tasks (the 'focus' mechanism).
key_numbers: No numbers in the abstract

Abstract claims: task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete; adoption is discrete and may need bundling even when automation quality improves smoothly; labor income can rise under partial automation; exposure indices that add task-level risk linearly overstate displacement when tasks are complements
works.relevance_to_theta: A direct critique of the additive form S = sum_j w_j theta_j and of treating 'time saved' as 'labor removed'. Freed time is reallocated to raise quality on bottleneck tasks, so saved hours need not become fewer workers, and theta_j depends on what else is automated.
works.limitations: Theory only; only the abstract was read. Complementarity strength is not measured. In outsourced IT the client may pay for hours rather than quality, which weakens the quality-reallocation channel.
works.corrections: None. Title, authors, date, WP number and abstract claims match the NBER page.

works.title: Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work: A Theory of AI Automation
works.authors: Mert Demirer, John J. Horton, Nicole Immorlica, Brendan Lucier, Peyman Shahidi
works.venue: NBER WP 34859 (February 2026, revised September 2026); arXiv 2606.15960 (v1 14 June 2026, v2 2 October 2026); accepted to the 27th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation (EC '26)
works.what_measured: Theory plus empirical tests of how AI is assigned to sequential workflow steps: manual, augmented (human prompts and verifies each step), or automated in contiguous 'chains' verified only at the end.
works.method_plain: Production is a Leontief sequence of steps. AI succeeds on step i with probability q_i = alpha^{d_i} (alpha = AI quality, d_i = step difficulty), independently across steps. A chain succeeds with probability alpha raised to the sum of its steps' difficulties, and a human verifies once at the end, retrying until it succeeds. The firm picks the cost-minimizing split of steps. Empirically they use O*NET tasks (ordered by GPT-5-mini via Expected Parrot) with Eloundou et al. exposure labels and Anthropic Economic Index execution labels. They validate the ordering with the APQC Process Classification Framework and eight 4TU.ResearchData process-mining logs.
key_numbers: Augmented step expected time = t^A / q (retry until success)
Chain expected time = t_r^A / product of q_i; verification happens once per chain
Three-step worked example (Section 4.1): optimal chaining costs 15.6 vs 35.4 under comparative-advantage assignment (model time units)
Two-step example (Section 4.3): below alpha = 0.5 no AI is used; between about 0.5 and about 0.92 only the easy step is augmented; above about 0.92 the two steps are chained
Fragmentation index: (1/8)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT in general; (1/4)OPT <= FI <= (5/4)OPT if every manual time is at least 1

Empirical samples: about 18,000 O*NET tasks in 850+ occupations; 10,708 tasks across 1,748 Detailed Work Activities (Prediction 2); 872 occupations (Prediction 3); APQC PCF 13,482 steps in 525 process groups

Results: mean AI chain length 1.45 (O*NET) and 1.16 (PCF), above randomized placebos; an AI-executed adjacent step raises a step's execution probability by about 0.04-0.11; fragmentation coefficient negative and significant in PCF (about -0.26 to -0.35), small and insignificant in O*NET
works.relevance_to_theta: The most directly usable 2026 model for the theta formula, and it does derive expected labor time as a function of a capability index alpha, net of verification. q_i = alpha^{d} with additive difficulty has the same compounding logic as METR's logistic-in-log(h) p(h,t). It treats failure as 'retry and re-verify' (expected time t^A/q), whereas the draft treats failure as 'a human redoes it with kappa assistance', and these give different theta. Review cost is per verified chunk, not proportional to h, which challenges rho as a constant share of h. theta_j depends on how AI-able steps cluster within j, not only on f_j.
works.limitations: Step failures are independent, and verification at the end of a chain is perfect (no undetected errors). The O*NET task ordering is LLM-generated. The validation event logs are traffic fines, sepsis, loan applications and travel reimbursement, not IT services. Horton discloses on the NBER page that he is a paid advisor to Anthropic, whose Economic Index the paper uses.
works.corrections: All theory numbers confirmed in the arXiv v2 HTML. Replaced 'portion I read did not report sample sizes' with the empirical sample sizes and coefficients from the paper's empirical section. Horton's Anthropic advisory disclosure was confirmed on the NBER page.

works.title: Delegation and Verification Under AI
works.authors: Lingxiao Huang, Wenyang Xiao, Nisheeth K. Vishnoi
works.venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306: 48039-48071; arXiv 2603.02961 (v1 3 March 2026, v2 25 June 2026); Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper 2500
works.what_measured: Theory of a rational worker choosing how much to delegate to AI (d) and how hard to verify (s), and how this affects quality as judged by the employing institution.
works.method_plain: Success probability p(d,s) = (1-d)p_w + d*p_a + d(1-p_a)phi(s)p_w, where p_a = AI success, p_w = worker success, and phi(s) = chance of catching an AI error at verification effort s (e.g. 1 - e^{-alpha s}, or 1 - 1/(1+alpha s)). Expected cost = (1-d)C_w + d[C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]: delegate, pay to verify, and redo the caught failures by hand. The worker's choice jumps between manual work, pure delegation (no checking) and verified delegation.
key_numbers: Cost of verified delegation = C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)*phi(s)*C_w versus manual cost C_w

Theorem 3.1: three regimes (manual; pure delegation; verified delegation) with sharp boundaries in verification reliability alpha and execution efficiency beta, which the authors call phase transitions
Theorem 3.5: quality improves over the no-AI baseline if and only if alpha exceeds a threshold psi(beta); low-verification workers over-delegate and lower institutional quality

Calibration on Collab-CXR clinician data: C_v(s) = 118.1*s and C_w(beta) = 262.3*(1-beta) (maximum observed verification and execution times), giving p_w = 0.447, p_a = 0.368, C_w = 172.5 and cost of verified delegation 116.8
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a micro-foundation for the theta integrand. Time saved per task = 1 - [C_a + C_v(s) + (1-p_a)phi(s)C_w]/C_w, so rho = C_v/C_w, p = p_a, and AI running cost is C_a/C_w. The difference from the draft is that missed errors (1-phi) are silently accepted: they cost quality, not time. The draft's q captures 'passes tests but would not be merged'. This model adds undetected failures, which suggests adding a quality-loss term or treating verification effort as chosen jointly with rho.
works.limitations: A single task with binary success, and failures of worker and AI treated simply. The calibration comes from a radiology (chest X-ray) setting, not software or BPO. The institution-vs-worker objective is stylized.
works.corrections: Venue details confirmed: PMLR 306 pages 48039-48071 (43rd ICML) and Cowles DP 2500 (the Yale repository's own sequence number is 2924; the CFDP number is 2500). Added the v2 date and the calibration values that the record said were 'not extracted'.

summary_flags: 'Grossman-Rossi-Hansberg's offshoring model is mathematically almost the draft integral' is overstated. GRH has a deterministic per-task cost penalty and a single cutoff. The draft has a failure probability, an acceptance rate, review cost and a max{} over delegate vs assist. It is a structural analogy, not a near-identity.

'The 2026 work (Demirer et al.; Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi; Gans-Goldfarb) ... shows that theta is not additive across tasks' over-attributes. Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi is a single-task model and says nothing about additivity. Non-additivity comes from Demirer et al. (chaining, neighbor effects) and Gans-Goldfarb (O-ring complementarity). Per-chunk verification breaks linearity within a task type (in h), not necessarily the sum across j.

'Displacement moves from juniors to seniors as AI knowledge rises' simplifies Ide-Talamas. Basic AI moves humans out of routine work into problem solving; advanced AI moves solvers down into routine work. On wages, gains go to the extremes of the knowledge distribution and the human whose knowledge equals AI's always loses. The record also mislabeled Prop. 5 as 'non-monotone wage effects in z_AI'.
'Autor et al. measure reinstatement directly' is too strong. They measure new job titles linked to patents, which is a proxy for reinstatement, not a direct measure of the reinstatement term.
'Garicano and Ide-Talamas map onto Indian IT pyramids' is the stream's interpretation. Neither paper studies IT services or India.

Gap 1, 'no theory paper derives task-level labor saving as a continuous function of a capability index net of review', is partly contradicted by the stream's own sources. Demirer et al. derive expected labor time as a function of AI quality alpha net of verification, and Huang et al. do so as a function of p_a and verification effort. The real gap is that none is calibrated to a measured capability index like METR time horizons, or to IT/BPO task data.

Gap claiming 4TU logs 'include IT service desk and incident logs' as used by Demirer et al. is wrong for that paper. Demirer et al.'s eight logs are road traffic fines, sepsis cases, BPI 2017 (loan applications) and BPI 2020 (travel reimbursement). IT service-desk logs (e.g. BPI Challenge 2013/2014) may exist on 4TU, but I could not confirm this (data.4tu.nl refused connection).
The Catalini-Hui-Wu 2026 citation in the gaps (arXiv 2602.20946, 'Some Simple Economics of AGI') checks out: its verification cost depends on feedback latency.
'No task-based paper is specific to offshored IT/BPO services or India' is an absence claim based on a limited search. It should be stated as 'none found in this stream'.
The ~60% new-work figure remains unconfirmed and should not be cited; use the abstract's 'majority'.

For Acemoglu, cite the version consistently: 0.71% / <0.55% (April 2024 MIT draft) vs 0.66% / <0.53% (NBER and Economic Policy). The '27% labor saving' converts to 15.4% total cost saving, and the summary's '4.6% x 27%' shorthand should be '4.6% x 15.4%' for the TFP calculation.
verify.corrected_summary:
Task-based economics models a job as a bundle of tasks and asks which tasks move from people to machines. In the classic Acemoglu-Restrepo model (AER 2018; JEP 2019; Econometrica 2022 for the empirical counterpart), a task is either automated or not, so their version of a replacement rate is the share of tasks crossing a threshold. That is the extensive margin. Three forces then act on employment: displacement, productivity (cheaper output raises demand), and reinstatement (new tasks). Autor, Chin, Salomons and Seegmiller (QJE 2024) measure new work, a proxy for reinstatement, using new job titles. They find that the majority of current US employment is in job specialties introduced after 1940.

Acemoglu's 'Simple Macroeconomics of AI' (Economic Policy 2025) is the closest analog to S = sum w_j theta_j. He multiplies the share of tasks impacted (4.6% = 23% profitable x 19.9% exposed) by the total cost saving per impacted task (15.4% = 27% labor cost saving from 2023 experiments x a 0.57 labor share), getting about 0.7% TFP over 10 years (0.66% in the published version). He does use an intensive margin. But he borrows it from small RCTs, says he cannot tell whether it reflects automation or complementarity, and holds it fixed as models improve. That is consistent with the working hypothesis: the intensive margin exists in the theory but is weakly measured and not tied to capability.

Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg's offshoring model gives a structural template: tasks are ordered by handoff cost, a threshold splits delegated from in-house tasks, and the saving integrates a per-task penalty over the delegated range. It has no failure probability or review. Its 'productivity effect' warns that savings can raise, rather than cut, demand for the workers who remain.

Garicano's knowledge hierarchies and Ide-Talamas's extension to AI give a vocabulary that plausibly fits IT delivery pyramids, though neither studies IT services. Review time resembles the solver's 'helping time', and autonomous versus copilot AI resembles delegate versus kappa. In Ide-Talamas, basic AI pushes humans out of routine work, advanced AI pushes solvers down into routine work, and wage gains go to the extremes of the knowledge distribution.

Recent theory adds verification micro-foundations. Demirer et al. (2026) derive expected labor time as a function of an AI-quality index with fixed per-chain verification. Huang, Xiao and Vishnoi (ICML 2026) model delegation and verification effort for a single task, with undetected errors costing quality rather than time. Demirer et al.'s chaining and Gans-Goldfarb's O-ring complementarity show that savings are not additive across neighboring tasks, which challenges a simple sum of w_j theta_j. What is still missing is a calibration of these models to a measured capability index (such as METR time horizons) and to IT/BPO workflow data.
verify.dataset_notes: O*NET (onetcenter.org/database.html): URL not opened by me; access public per general knowledge, unverified here. Eloundou et al. exposure data: https://github.com/openai/GPTs-are-GPTs exists (MIT license, code and data folders, GPT-4 and human ratings, E1/E2-based alpha/beta/gamma measures). I could not see the data files themselves. Anthropic Economic Index: not opened; Demirer et al. confirm they use it (Handa et al. 2025) for AI-execution labels. APQC PCF: not opened; the 'on-request / free with registration' access level is unverified. Demirer et al. use 13,482 PCF steps in 525 process groups. 4TU.ResearchData: Demirer et al.'s eight logs are Road Traffic Fine Management, Sepsis Cases, BPI Challenge 2017 (loan applications) and BPI Challenge 2020 (five travel-reimbursement logs). None is an IT service-desk log, so the description's suggestion that the cited logs cover IT service desks is incorrect. Whether 4TU hosts IT incident logs (e.g. BPI 2013/2014) is unverified: data.4tu.nl refused the connection. Acemoglu-Restrepo 2022 replication package: access still unknown. Autor et al. new-titles database: access still unknown.

works.title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade (Chapter 2: Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact)
works.authors: World Bank, Office of the Chief Economist for South Asia
works.venue: World Bank flagship regional report (CC BY 3.0 IGO), released Oct 7, 2025
works.what_measured: How exposed South Asian jobs are to AI, whether the exposure is 'complementary' (AI helps the worker) or 'substitutable', and how online job postings and posted wages changed after ChatGPT, with a section on business services/IT.
works.method_plain: Occupation exposure scores (Felten-Raj-Seamans; complementarity-adjusted per Pizzinelli et al. 2023) matched to labour-force surveys. Then a difference-in-differences / event study on Lightcast job postings at the 4-digit occupation by month level: compare postings for more versus less exposed occupations, before and after Nov 2022. ChatGPT-4o was used to classify which occupations belong to 'business services'.
key_numbers: 15% of South Asian jobs are highly exposed AND highly complementary; only 7% are highly exposed without complementarity (vs 15% in other emerging markets) (ch. 2 summary, p.27)
GenAI cut monthly job listings by about 20% for the most exposed, least complementary white-collar occupations (p.27)
Call-centre agent postings (top quartile of exposure) fell 24% relative to machine operators (bottom quartile) (p.38)
Business services jobs grew 35% slower and posted wages fell 8% relative to other jobs after ChatGPT (p.38, Fig 2.11, annex A2.10)
By March 2025, 12% of business-services postings required AI skills vs 4% for other jobs, double the pre-ChatGPT level (p.38)
Entry-level postings with software-developer-level exposure grew 21% more slowly than those with electrician-level exposure; senior roles unchanged (p.38)
AI-skill postings carry a wage premium of nearly 30% (28% for AI-focused roles) (p.27, p.37)
works.relevance_to_theta: Pure extensive-margin and labour-demand evidence: it says which occupations AI touches and that postings fell, but gives no time-saved-per-task, review cost or failure rate. It cannot identify theta_j. It is a useful outside check on the sign and rough size of S (fewer postings in exposed IT/BPO roles), and on the claim that BPO/call-centre and software tasks carry the highest exposure.
works.limitations: Postings are not employment or hours, and Lightcast covers formal online postings only. Exposure indices are capability ratings that do not measure labour saved. The DiD effects are relative (exposed vs less exposed), not absolute. The report itself says it cannot tell whether falling listings reflect domestic automation or foreign firms in-sourcing. Not reproducible without a Lightcast licence.

works.title: Automation without Borders: Generative AI and Cross-Border Service Outsourcing (conference slides)
works.authors: Neha Betai and Maggie Chen (George Washington University)
works.venue: Slides, Fourth Annual AI in Action Conference, Georgetown-World Bank, Jan 26, 2026
works.what_measured: Change in cross-border outsourcing contracts, contract value, buyers and active workers on a large global online labour marketplace after ChatGPT, by skill-level GenAI exposure (2,700+ skills, Jan 2022-Dec 2024).
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences: post-ChatGPT x skill exposure, with skill and week fixed effects. Exposure for each skill was elicited by asking GPT 100 times how well generative AI can perform that skill's tasks 'with minimal human input' and averaging the answers. 91% of the platform's transactions cross borders, and supply is concentrated in developing countries, including South Asia.
key_numbers: Coefficient on log(value) -0.820 (SE 0.147); log(contracts) -0.608; log(workers) -0.612 (88,800-90,045 obs)
At mean exposure (6.5 on the score scale): outsourcing value -53%, contracts -34%, buyers -34%, workers -35% (results table slide)
The 'preview' slide instead says value -43%: an internal inconsistency in the deck
Continuing workers: 37% fewer jobs per worker but 41% higher value per remaining contract; net effect on continuing workers insignificant
Top 1% of workers capture a 17-20 pp larger share of jobs/earnings
The skills scored most automatable include Software Engineering (9.434), Programming (9.290) and Coding (9.250); COBOL is among the least (2.820)
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest thing in this stream to a market-level, quasi-causal estimate of how much offshore digital-task demand falls with AI capability. Contracts falling about 34% at mean exposure in two years is an upper-envelope reference for theta_j in freelance-style, well-specified tasks (coding, writing, translation). It also shows task upgrading (higher value per contract), which matters for the eps*phi term. The LLM-elicited 'how well can AI do it with minimal human input' score resembles a crude p, but with no review cost (rho) or acceptance rate (q).
works.limitations: Only conference slides; no paper text, so standard errors on the % conversions and the exact functional form are unverified. Freelance gig work is not IT-services firm work: tasks are smaller and less embedded in client systems. The platform is not named. The value figure differs between the preview (-43%) and the table (-53%). WDR 2026 cites this paper (note 65) for a '39%' fall in jobs outsourced to developing countries in 2025, a number that does not appear in these slides.

works.title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence (Chapter 4: AI's Economic Impact: Transforming Jobs, Productivity, and Growth)
works.authors: World Bank (WDR 2026 team)
works.venue: World Bank flagship report, published Aug 4, 2026 (hdl 10986/45296)
works.what_measured: A synthesis of AI's labour-market effects in developing countries: automation-risk shares, a table of white-collar productivity experiments, a Philippine BPO vignette, and a World Bank Enterprise Survey AI-adoption module (India n=1,355 firms).
works.method_plain: A literature synthesis plus new firm-survey analysis. Table 4.1 compiles micro studies of the percent increase in output or percent of time saved. Freelance-platform evidence is cited from Betai and Chen (2026).
key_numbers: 'Jobs outsourced to developing countries fell by 39 percent in 2025', attributed to a freelance platform (note 65 = Betai and Chen 2026)
Table 4.1: customer care +15% output (Brynjolfsson, Li et al. 2025); consultants +39% (Dell'Acqua et al. 2023); M365 Copilot 12% time saved on email (Dillon et al. 2025); Noy and Zhang 40% time
Philippine BPO employs about 1.3 million workers (ch. 4 vignette)
Enterprise Survey AI module sample: India 1,355 firms; microdata at enterprisesurveys.org
Press coverage attributes to the report 4.5% of LMIC jobs at high automation risk vs 14.2% in high-income economies (not located in the extracted text in this pass)
works.relevance_to_theta: Table 4.1 is a ready-made list of kappa-type estimates (speedup when AI assists a human). For BPO the relevant entry is Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond. The Enterprise Survey AI module is a public, India-specific adoption dataset. It matters for realized S, not for the capability ceiling theta_j.
works.limitations: Secondary synthesis. Table 4.1 labels Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond a 'randomized trial', but the paper uses a staggered rollout, not randomization: a mislabel worth not repeating. The 39% figure is from a freelance platform, not from IT/BPO firms. The 4.5%/14.2% shares were seen only in press coverage in this pass.

works.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140)
works.authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kaminski, Filip Konopczynski, Agnieszka Ladna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Roslaniec, Marek Troszynski
works.venue: ILO Working Paper 140 (with Poland's NASK), May 20, 2025
works.what_measured: Task-level GenAI exposure scores for all ISCO-08 occupations, grouped into four exposure gradients, mapped to global employment.
works.method_plain: A survey of 1,640 Polish workers gave 52,558 ratings of automation potential for 2,861 tasks. Delphi rounds with international experts followed. An AI assistant trained on this knowledge base then scored all ISCO-08 task descriptions. Occupations are placed in gradients by mean task score and by how much scores vary across the occupation's tasks.
key_numbers: About 1 in 4 workers globally is in an occupation with some GenAI exposure
3.3% of global employment is in the highest exposure gradient (Gradient 4)
Gradient 4: 4.7% of female vs 2.4% of male employment; in high-income countries 9.6% vs 3.5%
Total exposure about 11% of employment in low-income vs 34% in high-income countries
Clerical occupations are the most exposed
works.relevance_to_theta: The canonical international 'can AI touch it' measure, and the one World Bank and ING analyses of India and the Philippines build on. It confirms the working hypothesis: the scores are about potential, with no time-saved, review-cost or failure-rate dimension. Task-level scores could still serve as a prior over which tasks inside a service line j are candidates, helping to build f_j.
works.limitations: Exposure is not labour saved. The task taxonomy is Polish/ISCO, not IT-services tasks such as 'L2 ticket resolution'. Scores come from perceptions plus model prediction, not observed performance. No BPO, Philippines or India-specific results on the landing page.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Philippine Labor Market: Mapping Occupational Exposure and Complementarity (IMF WP/25/43)
works.authors: Micholo Cucio and Tristan Hennig
works.what_measured: Share of Philippine workers in occupations highly exposed to AI, split by complementarity, by sector and worker characteristics.
works.method_plain: Philippine labour-force-survey microdata matched to occupation-level AI exposure and complementarity indices (the IMF C-AIOE approach).
key_numbers: About one third of Philippine workers are highly exposed to AI
About 60% of the highly exposed are also highly complementary
BPO is the sector with the highest share of jobs at risk of displacement (no BPO % on the landing page)
works.relevance_to_theta: Philippines analogue to the World Bank India numbers. Extensive margin only. Useful for the claim that BPO is the most substitutable service line, i.e. the prior that theta_BPO is the highest among the j.
works.limitations: Only the abstract page was read; the BPO-specific percentage was not confirmed. Exposure indices do not measure time saved or review cost.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.what_measured: Productivity of 5,172 chat-based technical-support agents (majority in Philippine offices, many via third-party outsourcers) before and after access to a GPT-based assistant that suggests replies.
works.method_plain: Staggered rollout across agents (not a randomized trial), estimated with agent, tenure, location and month fixed effects and Sun-Abraham event studies. The tool suggests text and the human decides whether to use it, so it measures AI as assistant (kappa), not delegation.
key_numbers: Resolutions per hour +0.30 chats, or +15.2%, with agent and tenure fixed effects (abstract: 15%; the NBER page says 14%)
Average handle time -3.7 minutes, an 8.5% decline from a 43-minute baseline
Chats per hour +0.37, about +15% from a 2.4 baseline (agents multitask more)
Resolution rate +1.3 pp, insignificant, from an 82% baseline
Gains concentrated among novice/low-skill agents (NBER summary: about 34%); top-skill agents see small speed gains and small quality declines
Agents with 2 months' tenure and AI perform like untreated agents with over 6 months' tenure
works.relevance_to_theta: The best measured estimate of kappa for BPO/customer support. Converting a 15% throughput gain to labour time saved per unit of work gives about 1 - 1/1.15, roughly 13% (theta_BPO under assistant mode, 2020-21 GPT-3-era tool). The adherence data hint at verification behaviour: agents discard bad suggestions, an implicit q < 1. It does not cover full delegation to voice/chat agents, which is what drives p at high capability.
works.limitations: One firm, one product, a 2020-21 model generation (pre-ChatGPT). Assistant mode only. Throughput is not labour demand: the firm's staffing response is not studied. The heterogeneity means the gain depends on the workforce's skill mix, so the average theta depends on the experience distribution in Indian/Philippine delivery centres.

works.title: HCLTech Q4 FY26 Earnings Conference Call Transcript (Apr 21, 2026)
works.authors: HCL Technologies Ltd (C. Vijayakumar, CEO; analysts incl. Rushabh Jain)
works.what_measured: Management's segmentation of IT-services spend into AI-disrupted, AI-amplified and AI-native, with expected revenue shrink rates.
works.method_plain: Management estimate stated on the earnings call, not a model with disclosed inputs.
key_numbers: 40% of the industry is 'AI disrupted' (application development/support, traditional infrastructure operations, customer support) and 'can shrink 3% to 5% CAGR for a few years', eventually to 25% of enterprise spend
55% is 'AI amplified' (data, cybersecurity, cloud), growing about 10%+; 5% is 'AI native', growing about 30%, to 20%+ of the market in five years
For HCLTech's mix the 3-5% translates to 2-3% of its portfolio
CEO: model improvements mainly speed up the SDLC, which 'could go through a little higher deflation'; production fixes without a human in the loop are 'very limited'
Analyst: pre-AI renewals already carried 10-15% price cuts over deal life (about 3-5%/yr); CEO says the AI figure is incremental to traditional productivity commitments
CEO: 'very little has really played out in already reported numbers'; expected from FY27 onward
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a management-implied split of the w_j (about 40% of spend in high-theta lines) and a revenue shrink rate, which in the model is roughly s*phi for those lines net of demand response. It says theta rises fastest in development/SDLC and stays low for production operations because humans remain in the loop (high rho, low q for unattended fixes). Important caveat for the 2.3 pp/yr top-down estimate: management says FY24-26 weakness was mostly demand, not AI.
works.limitations: A forward-looking, self-interested management estimate. Revenue shrink mixes theta, pass-through (phi) and elasticity (eps). Shares are of spend, not labour hours. Not reproducible.

works.title: Infosys Q4 FY26 Earnings Conference Call Transcript (Apr 23, 2026) and Q1 FY27 Media Call Transcript (Jul 23, 2026)
works.authors: Infosys Ltd (Salil Parekh, CEO; Jayesh Sanghrajka, CFO)
works.venue: SEC Form 6-K exhibits 99.5 (Q4 FY26) and 99.3 (Q1 FY27)
works.what_measured: Client-level AI effort and cost savings, AI tool deployment, volume vs price growth, and statements on productivity pass-through.
works.method_plain: Management statements and case examples, not a systematic measurement.
key_numbers: Hertz COBOL migration (3 mn lines): cost 60% lower and timeline 60% quicker than without AI (Q4 FY26)
BP: 18% improvement in IT operations efficiency, 50% faster contract validation, 95% payment accuracy (Q4 FY26)
30,000+ developers on GitHub Copilot (Q4 FY26); 80,000+ employees using coding tools such as Claude Code or Codex (Q1 FY27)
FY26 volumes roughly flat, growth from realization; FY27 volumes 'flatter or marginally positive'; FY27 guidance 1.5-3.5% cc
CFO: productivity gains largely passed back to clients due to competitive intensity; deflation in existing services not quantified
AI services revenue 8.2% of revenue in Q1 FY27 (5.5% in Q3 FY26)
Headcount above 328,000 at FY26 end; about 20,000 freshers hired in FY26 and planned for FY27
works.relevance_to_theta: Case examples give upper-end, per-project theta for specific task types: legacy code migration (about 60% effort and cost reduction) and IT operations (18%). These are cherry-picked showcase numbers, but they are the only firm-disclosed effort figures by task type and can bound theta_dev/modernization and theta_infra. The statement that gains are 'largely passed back' supports phi close to 1.
works.limitations: Selected success stories, not averages. Cost reduction mixes labour and other inputs. No company-wide effort-reduction figure. Infosys explicitly declined to quantify compression. The Infosys-hosted transcript returned 403; the SEC copy was used.

works.title: TCS Q2 FY27 Earnings Conference Call Transcript (Oct 8, 2026; filed Oct 14, 2026)
works.authors: Tata Consultancy Services (K. Krithivasan, CEO; Samir Seksaria, CFO; Aarthi Subramanian, COO)
works.what_measured: AI revenue, pricing and deflation commentary, and client-level AI efficiency targets.
works.method_plain: Management statements on the earnings call.
key_numbers: Annualized AI revenue $3.1 bn, crossing 10% of revenue
S/4HANA transformation (27 sites, 70+ legal entities): agentic platform 'targets 25% to 30% faster implementation'
HR operations client: target to 'double operational efficiency' and raise self-serve from under 10% to 30%

CEO: 'there is a deflation because of the productivity benefit' in BFSI/Hi-Tech, not yet offset; CFO: 'some frontloading of productivity benefits', revenue per employee shows 'a slight reduction', portfolio pricing 'broadly stable'
Revenue +0.5% QoQ cc, +2.8% YoY cc

The admission of AI deflation with roughly stable pricing implies pass-through through scope/volume rather than rate cards: phi operates on effort, not price per FTE.

works.title: Kotak Institutional Equities sector notes on AI-led deflation (Apr 29, 2026 and Sep 30, 2026)
works.authors: Kotak Institutional Equities (reported by ANI)
works.venue: Broker notes, via press (The Tribune/ANI Apr 29, 2026; NewKerala/ANI Sep 30, 2026)

works.method_plain: Proprietary broker model; inputs not disclosed in coverage.
key_numbers: Apr 2026: base-case industry pricing erosion 3.5%, appearing first in renewals of large multi-year contracts; GenAI deflation 'cyclical, not secular', a 2-3 year phase (Tribune/ANI)
Sep 2026: gross AI-led deflation about 7%, net deflation 3.5% (after new AI work), now visible in base business (NewKerala/ANI)
Tier-1 FY27 growth clustered at 1-4%; global IT services 5% cc 10-year average, slowing to 3% in CY2025

If phi is near 1 and the affected share is about 30-40%, it implies a theta of about 15-25% on the affected lines realized per year. That is a back-of-envelope cross-check, not an estimate. The gross/net split maps onto the d term (new AI work) vs s*phi.
works.limitations: Press-only; the underlying notes are paid. Methodology not disclosed. Revenue deflation mixes theta, phi, adoption and contract timing.

works.title: Indian IT Sector Analysis 2026: Valuation, Growth, AI Risks and Top Picks
works.authors: ICICI Securities research team (ICICIdirect)
works.what_measured: Share of IT services at risk of GenAI deflation, annual deflation rate, revenue-at-risk scenarios.
works.method_plain: Broker scenario analysis with explicit assumptions: at-risk share x deflation rate.
key_numbers: Nearly 30% of the IT services industry at risk of GenAI-led deflation (coding, ADM and testing most visible)
About 2-3% annual deflation of traditional IT services revenue, peaking FY26-FY28, recovery from FY28-end/FY29
Base case applies 50% deflation to the at-risk segment, about USD 40 bn hit for India; worst case (100% loss) USD 80-85 bn, on a USD 280-285 bn industry
Estimate cuts: e.g. TCS -1% FY27, -3% FY28; Mphasis -3%/-5%
works.relevance_to_theta: Its structure (at-risk share x deflation on that share) is exactly sum_j w_j*theta_j with two buckets: w_at-risk = 0.30 and an implied end-state theta = 0.5. Over 3-4 years that is about 15% of revenue, close in spirit to the bottom-up S. Useful as an explicit analyst prior to compare against the recipe.
works.limitations: The 50% is an assumption, not an estimate. Revenue-based, not labour hours. No per-line split.

works.title: Cognizant CEO statements on AI-written code and developer productivity
works.authors: Ravi Kumar S (Cognizant CEO), reported by Outlook Business Desk (from an Economic Times Q&A)
works.what_measured: Share of code written with AI help and developer productivity change by quartile at Cognizant.
works.method_plain: CEO statement in an interview; internal measurement method not described.
key_numbers: About 20% of Cognizant's code written with AI assistance (Feb 2025)
Bottom-quartile developers +34% productivity; top 50% of developers +17%; the '34%' headline applies only to the bottom quartile and is commonly misquoted as firm-wide
Secondary coverage (not verified at primary source in this pass) reports about 30% of developer effort AI-assisted (Q4 2025 call) and nearly 40% of code AI-assisted (Q1 2026 call)
works.relevance_to_theta: A firm-reported assistant-mode speedup for development: 17-34% productivity, roughly 15-25% time saved per unit. Its skill gradient mirrors Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond. Share of code AI-written is an adoption/coverage metric, not theta, and should not be read as labour saved.
works.limitations: Interview claim with an undisclosed metric (likely output-based). Self-interested. The 2026 figures were seen only in search snippets.

research.stream_summary:
Evidence on Indian IT services and BPO falls into three groups, and none of them measures theta_j, the share of labour time saved on a task, directly.

(1) Exposure and job-postings studies: World Bank SADU 2025, ILO WP140, IMF on the Philippines, WDR 2026. They show that AI touches IT and BPO tasks more than most work. After ChatGPT, postings for the most exposed, least complementary jobs fell about 20%, and call-centre postings fell 24% relative to machine operators. Business-services postings grew 35% slower and wages 8% slower. This is the extensive margin plus labour demand, which supports the working hypothesis: these studies say what AI can touch, not how much labour it removes after review.

(2) Micro productivity evidence. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond, a mostly Philippine call centre, is the best measured kappa for BPO: +15% resolutions per hour and -8.5% handle time, so roughly 13% time saved in assistant mode, larger for novices. Betai and Chen's freelance-platform DiD shows the strongest market effect: at mean exposure, contracts -34% and workers -35%, with higher value per surviving contract.

(3) Firm and broker numbers. HCLTech says 40% of industry spend (app dev/support, infra ops, customer support) can shrink 3-5% a year. ICICI assumes 30% of revenue is at risk with 50% eventual deflation. Kotak estimates about 7% gross and 3.5% net deflation. Jefferies assumes 5-35% productivity. Infosys and TCS give showcase cases: 60% on a COBOL migration, 18% in IT ops, 25-30% faster ERP implementation. These figures mix theta with pass-through (phi), demand and contract timing, and management says little has yet shown up in reported numbers.

Net: the stream gives priors on w_j (revenue shares of AMS and at-risk lines), kappa for BPO and coding, and outside checks on s*phi. No source measures review cost (rho), acceptance rate (q) or task-length distributions (f_j) for Indian delivery work.
gaps_noticed: No source measures review/verification time (rho) or acceptance of AI output (q) in IT-services delivery; firm disclosures report gross speedups or showcase cost cuts only.

No hours-weighted task-length distribution (f_j) for Indian IT service lines (e.g. ticket resolution times in AMS, test-case durations); ITSM ticket data would be needed and is held by firms or clients.

No published labour-hours split by service line (w_j); analysts use revenue shares (AMS 22-45% of revenue per Jefferies; 30-40% 'at-risk' per ICICI/HCLTech), which differ from hours shares because of pricing and onsite/offshore mix.

Firm effort-reduction claims are selected case studies (Infosys Hertz 60%, BP 18%; TCS 25-30%); no firm reports an audited portfolio-wide effort reduction. Infosys explicitly declined to quantify compression.

Broker deflation estimates (Kotak, Jefferies, JP Morgan, HFS, Everest, Gartner) are paywalled; only press summaries were accessible, and HFS, Everest and Gartner gave no verifiable deflation or effort-reduction number in this pass. Everest's CEO quote (10% early, 30%+ eventual) was seen only in search snippets.
Nasscom Strategic Review 2026 page returned HTTP 406; its headcount and revenue numbers were not re-verified here.
The '10-15%' TCS savings handback attributed to Krithivasan in secondary coverage was not found in the Q2 FY27 transcript and is unverified.

WDR 2026's '39% fall in outsourced jobs in 2025' cites Betai and Chen (2026), whose slides report -34% contracts and -53% value (preview says -43%) at mean exposure; the 39% number cannot be traced to a primary table.
No India-based call-centre field experiment was found; the Philippine Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond study uses a 2020-21 assistant model, not current voice or chat agents (full delegation).
No study links METR-style capability (p by task length) to realized effort reduction inside an IT-services firm; that bridge would be the novel contribution of the recipe.
Management attributes FY24-26 weakness mostly to demand, not AI (HCLTech), so the top-down 2.3 pp/yr may not be AI-driven, which complicates validating bottom-up theta against it.

works.title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade (Chapter 2: Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact: Labor Market Implications of AI Adoption in South Asia)
works.authors: World Bank, Office of the Chief Economist for South Asia
works.venue: World Bank regional flagship report (CC BY 3.0 IGO; doi:10.1596/978-1-4648-2291-9), embargoed until Oct 7, 2025
works.what_measured: How exposed South Asian jobs are to AI, and whether that exposure is 'complementary' (AI helps the worker) or 'substitutable'. Also how online job postings and posted wages changed after ChatGPT, with a section on business services and IT.
works.method_plain: Occupation-level AI exposure (Felten, Raj and Seamans) and complementarity adjustment (Pizzinelli et al. 2023) are matched to labour-force surveys from the Global Labor Database. Lightcast online job postings then feed event-study and difference-in-differences regressions at the 4-digit occupation-sector by month level: log listings are regressed on post-ChatGPT x exposure, with occupation and month fixed effects. Effects are per 1 standard deviation of exposure. ChatGPT-4o was used in June-July 2025 to classify which occupations belong to business services.
key_numbers: 15% of South Asian jobs are highly exposed and highly complementary (about 70% of AI-exposed jobs). Only 7% are highly exposed without complementarity, vs 15% in other emerging markets (ch. 2 summary, p.27)
GenAI cut monthly job listings by about 20% for the most exposed, least complementary white-collar occupations (p.27)
Postings for call-centre agents (top exposure quartile) fell 24% relative to machine operators (bottom quartile), among less-complementary jobs (p.37)
Business services jobs grew 35% slower and wages fell by 8% relative to other jobs after ChatGPT (p.38; Fig 2.11; annex table A2.10)
By March 2025, 12% of business-services jobs required AI skills vs 4% for other jobs, double the pre-ChatGPT level (p.38)
Entry-level jobs with software-developer-level exposure grew 21% more slowly than those with electrician-level exposure; senior roles unchanged (p.38)
Jobs requiring AI skills carry a wage premium of nearly 30% over other white-collar jobs (p.27). AI-focused roles carry 28% and digital skills 12% (p.37)
works.relevance_to_theta: Extensive-margin and labour-demand evidence only. It says which occupations AI touches and that their postings fell. It gives no time saved per task, review cost or failure rate, so it cannot identify theta_j. It is a useful outside check on the sign of S and on the claim that call-centre and software occupations are among the most exposed and least complementary.
works.limitations: Postings are not employment or hours, and Lightcast covers formal online postings only. Exposure indices rate capability; they do not measure labour saved. The difference-in-differences effects are relative (more vs less exposed, per standard deviation of exposure), not absolute. The report says it cannot tell whether falling listings reflect automation by domestic firms or by foreign firms, which would displace South Asia in global value chains. Online freelancing is outside the data. Not reproducible without a Lightcast licence.
works.corrections: Page fix: the call-centre -24% passage is on p.37, not p.38. Added the 12% digital-skill premium and the 70%-of-exposed detail for context. Release date and licence were confirmed from the PDF's embargo line and copyright page. All other numbers match the text.

works.title: Automation without Borders: Generative AI and Cross-Border Service Outsourcing (conference slides)
works.authors: Neha Betai and Maggie Chen (George Washington University). WDR 2026 lists the first author as 'Nehai Betai'.
works.venue: Slides, Fourth Annual AI in Action (AIA) Conference 'Making AI Work: What Firms and Workers Need', Georgetown-World Bank, Jan 26, 2026
works.what_measured: Change in cross-border outsourcing on a leading global online labour marketplace after ChatGPT: value, contracts, buyers and active workers, by skill-level GenAI exposure. Covers 2,700+ skills, Jan 2022-Dec 2024. The main table is labelled 'Aggregate Effects on Developing Countries'.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences: Post-GPT x skill exposure, with skill and week fixed effects. Exposure comes from prompting GPT, for each skill, 'On a scale from 0 to 1, how well can generative AI perform the tasks requiring skill [ ] relative to a human, with minimal human input?' The question is repeated 100 times and averaged; the reported scores sit on a roughly 0-10 scale, so some rescaling is applied. On this platform, 91% of transactions cross borders, demand comes mainly from the US, Australia and UK, and supply comes mainly from developing countries, including South Asia.
key_numbers: Post-GPT x Exposure coefficients: log(value) -0.820 (SE 0.147); log(contracts) -0.608 (0.089); log(buyers) -0.601 (0.085); log(workers) -0.612 (0.079); 88,800-90,045 observations
At mean exposure (6.5): outsourcing value -53%, contracts -34%, buyers -34%, workers -35% (results table slide)
The preview slide says value -43%, and the summary slide says '34-43% decline in contracts and value': inconsistent with the -53% in the results slide
Continuing workers at mean exposure: 37% fewer jobs per worker and 41% higher value per remaining contract; net effect on continuing workers insignificant
Top 1% of workers capture a 17-20 percentage point larger share of jobs/earnings
Most automatable skills include Software Engineering (9.434), Programming (9.290) and Coding (9.250); COBOL is among the least automatable (2.820, rank 2728 of 2742)
works.relevance_to_theta: A quasi-causal, market-level estimate of how demand for outsourced digital tasks on a gig platform responds to GenAI exposure. It is not a measure of theta_j. The effect combines labour saved per task, buyers doing the work in-house with AI, and demand response, and it is relative across skills (per unit of exposure), not absolute. At most it indicates the direction and rough scale for small, well-specified freelance tasks. The finding of higher value per contract (task upgrading) bears on the demand side (eps*phi, d). The LLM-elicited 'minimal human input' score is a crude capability rating with no review cost (rho) or acceptance rate (q).
works.limitations: Conference slides only, with no paper text, so the functional form behind the % conversions is unverified. Applying the coefficients naively to mean exposure 6.5 does not reproduce the %s, which suggests the exposure was rescaled. Gig-platform work is not IT-services firm work. The platform is not named. Value figures conflict (-43% vs -53%). WDR 2026 cites this work (Overview, note 65) for a '39%' fall in jobs outsourced to developing countries in 2025. That number does not appear in the slides, and the slides' data end in Dec 2024.
works.corrections: Added that the main table is the developing-country sample, plus the exact exposure prompt wording and the summary slide's '34-43%' range. Removed 'theta_j-direct' from params: a platform demand effect is not labour time saved per task. Noted that the slides' data end in Dec 2024, so a '2025' figure cannot come from them. Noted the 'Nehai' spelling in WDR.

works.title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence (Overview and Chapter 4: AI's Economic Impact: Transforming Jobs, Productivity, and Growth)
works.authors: World Bank (WDR 2026 team)
works.venue: World Bank flagship report, doi:10.1596/978-1-4648-2331-2, hdl 10986/45296. The PDF metadata shows it was created Aug 3, 2026; the exact launch date was not confirmed.
works.what_measured: A synthesis of AI's labour-market effects in developing countries. It includes automation and complementarity shares, a table of white-collar productivity studies (Table 4.1), a Philippine BPO vignette, and the World Bank Enterprise Survey on AI Adoption (India n=1,355 firms).
works.method_plain: A literature synthesis plus new firm-survey analysis. Table 4.1 compiles micro studies reporting percent increases in output or percent of time saved. Freelance-platform evidence is cited from Betai and Chen (2026).
key_numbers: Overview (p.16, note 65 = Betai and Chen 2026): a freelance platform 'reported that jobs outsourced to developing countries fell by 39 percent in 2025'. In ch. 4, Betai and Chen is cited (note 59) only qualitatively, for negative displacement effects on platform outsourcing
Overview: about 4.5% of existing jobs in low- and middle-income countries are amenable to automation by GenAI, vs 14.2% in high-income countries; 16.2% are amenable to complementation

Table 4.1 (ch. 4, p.121): customer care +15% output (Brynjolfsson, Li et al. 2025); consultants +39% output (Dell'Acqua et al. 2023); M365 Copilot 12% time saved on email (Dillon et al. 2025); Noy and Zhang 40% time saved per task; Peng et al. GitHub Copilot 56% time saved
Ch. 4 opening vignette: Philippine BPO employs about 1.3 million workers
Enterprise Survey on AI Adoption sample: India 1,355 firms (plus Jordan, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria, Thailand, US); microdata at enterprisesurveys.org
works.relevance_to_theta: Table 4.1 is a ready-made list of kappa-type estimates (speedup when AI assists a human), including the 56% Copilot time saving that matters for development tasks. For BPO the relevant entry is Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond. The Enterprise Survey AI module is an India-specific adoption dataset. It matters for realized S, not for the capability ceiling theta_j.
works.limitations: Secondary synthesis. Table 4.1 labels Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond a 'randomized trial'. The main estimates in that paper come from a staggered rollout; only a small pilot (~50 workers, about half randomized) was randomized. The 39% figure comes from a freelance platform, its source slides contain no 2025 data, and it cannot be traced to a primary table. The donorplatform.org URL is a mirror; cite the hdl/DOI.
works.corrections: The 39% claim and note 65 are in the Overview (p.16), not ch. 4. The 4.5%/14.2% shares ARE in the report (Overview), so they are confirmed, not press-only. Added the 16.2% complementation share and the Peng et al. 56% row. The publication date 'Aug 4, 2026' could not be confirmed (the OKR page returned 403; PDF created Aug 3, 2026). Use the primary handle instead of the mirror.

works.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO Working Paper 140)
works.authors: Pawel Gmyrek, Janine Berg, Karol Kaminski, Filip Konopczynski, Agnieszka Ladna, Balint Nafradi, Konrad Roslaniec, Marek Troszynski
works.what_measured: Task-level GenAI exposure scores for ISCO-08 occupations, grouped into four exposure gradients and mapped to global employment.
works.method_plain: Starts from Poland's occupational task list (29,753 tasks). A survey of 1,640 workers gave 52,558 ratings of perceived automation potential for 2,861 tasks. These were compared with an expert survey and Delphi-style rounds with international experts. An AI assistant built on this knowledge base then predicted scores for ISCO-08 task descriptions, and occupations were grouped into four gradients.
key_numbers: About 1 in 4 workers globally is in an occupation with some GenAI exposure
3.3% of global employment is in the highest exposure gradient (Gradient 4)
Gradient 4: 4.7% of female vs 2.4% of male employment; in high-income countries 9.6% vs 3.5%
Total exposure is about 11% of employment in low-income countries vs 34% in high-income countries
Clerical occupations have the highest exposure
works.relevance_to_theta: The canonical international 'can AI touch it' measure. Its scores are about potential, with no time-saved, review-cost or failure-rate dimension, which is consistent with the working hypothesis. Task-level scores could serve as a prior over which tasks within service line j are candidates, which helps in building f_j.
works.limitations: Exposure is not labour saved. The task taxonomy is Polish/ISCO, not IT-services tasks. Scores are perceptions plus model prediction, not observed performance. The landing page has no BPO-, Philippines- or India-specific results.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Philippine Labor Market: Mapping Occupational Exposure and Complementarity
works.authors: Micholo Cucio and Tristan Hennig
works.venue: IMF Working Paper (file id wpiea2025043, i.e. WP/25/43), Feb 21, 2025, doi:10.5089/9798229001977.001
works.what_measured: Share of Philippine workers in occupations highly exposed to AI, split by complementarity, by sector and worker characteristics.
works.method_plain: Philippine labour-force-survey microdata matched to occupation-level AI exposure and complementarity measures.
key_numbers: About one third of Philippine workers are highly exposed to AI
About 60% of the highly exposed are also highly complementary
Business process outsourcing has the highest share of jobs at risk of displacement (no BPO percentage on the landing page)
The most exposed are college-educated, young, urban, female, well-paid services workers
works.relevance_to_theta: Philippines analogue to the World Bank South Asia numbers. Extensive margin only. Supports the prior that BPO is the most substitutable service line (theta_BPO highest among the j), but gives no magnitude.
works.limitations: Only the landing page was read; the BPO-specific percentage was not confirmed. The WP number is inferred from the file identifier. Exposure indices do not measure time saved or review cost.
works.corrections: Landing page confirms the authors, date and findings. The WP/25/43 number is inferred from the file id 'wpiea2025043', not stated on the page. DOI added.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.what_measured: Productivity of 5,172 chat-based technical-support agents (NBER version: 5,179) before and after access to a GPT-based assistant that suggests replies. Most agents work in Philippine offices, many through third-party outsourcers.
works.method_plain: Staggered rollout across agents (Fall 2020-Winter 2021), estimated with year-month, agent, location and tenure fixed effects and Sun-Abraham event studies. A small pilot of about 50 workers, about half randomized, gives similar results. The tool suggests text and the human decides whether to use it, so this measures AI as an assistant (kappa), not delegation.
key_numbers: Resolutions per hour +0.30 chats, or +15.2%, with agent and tenure fixed effects (abstract: 15%; NBER abstract: 14%)
Average handle time -3.7 minutes, an 8.5% decline from a 43-minute baseline
Chats per hour +0.37, roughly +15% from a 2.4 baseline (agents multitask more)
Resolution rate +1.3 percentage points, insignificant, from an 82% baseline
Gains concentrated among less experienced and lower-skilled agents (NBER abstract: 34% for novice and low-skilled workers); minimal speed gains and small quality declines for the most skilled
Agents with 2 months' tenure and AI perform as well as untreated agents with more than 6 months' tenure
works.relevance_to_theta: The best measured kappa for BPO/customer support. Time saved per chat is about 8.5% (handle time). Converting the 15% throughput gain gives about 1 - 1/1.15, roughly 13%, but part of that throughput gain comes from multitasking rather than less time per chat. So assistant-mode theta_BPO for a 2020-21 GPT-based tool is roughly 8-13%. Agents follow only some suggestions, which implies q < 1. The paper does not cover full delegation to voice or chat agents.
works.limitations: One firm, one product, a 2020-21 model generation (pre-ChatGPT). Assistant mode only. Throughput is not labour demand: the firm's staffing response is not studied. Because the gain depends on the experience mix, the average depends on the tenure distribution in delivery centres.
works.corrections: Numbers match the arXiv v2 text. Added the small randomized pilot, the NBER agent count (5,179), and a note that the 13% conversion overstates time saved per chat because of multitasking. Dropped 'theta_j-direct' from params (it is kappa). The QJE volume and pages were confirmed via the WDR 2026 reference list, not the journal page.

works.title: HCLTech Q4 FY26 Earnings Conference Call Transcript (call held Apr 21, 2026)

works.title: Cognizant CEO says AI now writes 20% of code, boosts developer productivity (Outlook Business report of Economic Times Q&A)
works.authors: Ravi Kumar S (Cognizant CEO), reported by Outlook Business Desk

Bottom-quartile developers: +34% productivity; top 50% of developers: +17% (the 34% applies only to the bottom quartile)

summary_flags: Summary says business-services 'wages 8% slower'; SADU says wages 'fell by 8 percent relative to other jobs'. Also, the call-centre -24% is on p.37, not p.38.

Calling Betai-Chen 'the strongest market effect' and the record's 'upper-envelope reference for theta_j' overstates it.
