The estimates are relative difference-in-differences effects per unit of LLM-rated exposure on one gig platform, for a developing-country sample, and they mix labour saved, buyers doing the work in-house and demand response. They are not labour time saved.
Betai-Chen value effect: the record notes -43% (preview) vs -53% (table); the summary slide also says '34-43%'. Do not cite a single value figure without the caveat.

The '13% time saved' from Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond overstates time saved per chat. The direct time measure is the -8.5% handle time; the 15% throughput gain partly reflects multitasking. Use about 8-13%.

WDR 2026's 39% figure is in the Overview (p.16, note 65), not ch. 4, and cannot come from the Betai-Chen slides, whose data end Dec 2024. The 4.5%/14.2% shares ARE in the WDR Overview; the record wrongly treated them as press-only.
WDR publication date 'Aug 4, 2026' is unconfirmed (PDF metadata: created Aug 3, 2026).
HCLTech: the CEO said 'very little has really played out in already reported numbers'. He did not say FY24-26 weakness was 'mostly demand'; that is an inference.
Kotak 7% gross deflation: the coverage does not give the period, so 'in one year' and the implied theta of 15-25%/yr are unsupported.
ICICI's 50% is assumed revenue deflation, which includes pass-through and demand; reading it as 'end-state theta = 0.5' conflates s*phi with theta.
Jefferies: the 22-45% AMS share is 5paisa narration, not explicitly attributed to Jefferies.
Cognizant 2026 figures (30% of effort, 40% of code) are unverified and were removed.
Gaps cite JP Morgan, HFS, Everest and Gartner, but none is among the works; the Everest CEO quote was seen only in snippets and should not be used.

The extensive-vs-intensive working hypothesis is 'supported' only in the weak sense that the exposure studies in this stream do not measure time saved net of review; this stream does not directly test Eloundou et al.
Searches were capped in this pass (session web-search budget exhausted), so the WDR launch date and the Cognizant 2026 claims could not be re-searched.
verify.corrected_summary:
Evidence on Indian IT services and BPO falls into three groups, and none of them measures theta_j (the share of labour time saved on a task net of review) directly.

(1) Exposure and job-postings studies: World Bank SADU Oct 2025, ILO WP140, IMF on the Philippines, and WDR 2026. They show AI exposure is concentrated in clerical, IT and BPO-type occupations. SADU finds that after ChatGPT, postings for the most exposed, least complementary white-collar occupations fell about 20%, call-centre postings fell 24% relative to machine operators, and business-services postings grew 35% slower while posted wages fell 8% relative to other jobs. These are relative effects on postings, not hours, and they measure what AI can touch plus labour demand. They do not measure how much labour AI removes after review.

(2) Micro and market evidence. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (QJE 2025; mostly Philippine call-centre agents, 2020-21 GPT-based assistant, staggered rollout) is the best measured kappa for BPO: +15% resolutions per hour and -8.5% handle time. That means roughly 8-13% time saved per unit in assistant mode, with larger gains for novices. Betai and Chen's conference slides (Jan 2026) on a gig platform find, for developing-country sellers at mean LLM-rated exposure, contracts -34%, workers -35% and value -43% to -53% (the slides disagree), with higher value per surviving contract. These are relative, platform-level demand effects, not labour saved per task. WDR 2026's '39%' figure, attributed to this work, cannot be traced to the slides.

(3) Firm and broker figures. HCLTech says about 40% of industry spend (app dev/support, infra ops, customer support) could shrink 3-5% a year, and that very little has yet shown up in reported numbers. ICICI assumes 30% of revenue is at risk, with 50% revenue deflation in its base case. Kotak estimates about 7% gross and 3.5% net AI-led deflation (period unstated). Jefferies assumes a 5-35% productivity boost. Infosys and TCS give showcase cases and targets: 60% lower cost on a COBOL migration, 18% better IT-ops efficiency, and a target of 25-30% faster ERP implementation. All of these mix theta with pass-through (phi), demand and contract timing.

Net: the stream gives priors on w_j (revenue shares, not hours), kappa for BPO and coding, and outside checks on s*phi. No source measures review cost (rho), acceptance rate (q) or task-length distributions (f_j) for Indian delivery work.
verify.dataset_notes: Lightcast: paid, correct. World Bank Enterprise Survey on AI Adoption: WDR confirms an India sample of 1,355 firms and that microdata are at enterprisesurveys.org/en/data. 'on-request' (free with registration) is plausible but the access terms were not checked in this pass. ILO WP140 scores: the landing page was confirmed, but whether the task-level score file is downloadable there was not checked, so 'public' is unverified. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond panel: proprietary firm data, not public. The label 'lab-internal' is misleading; call it 'proprietary/not available'. Betai-Chen platform data: the platform is unnamed and the data are not public ('proprietary', not 'lab-internal'). Broker research: ICICI's page is public. Kotak and Jefferies are paid and available only via press. 5paisa's AMS 22-45% figure is not explicitly attributed to Jefferies. Nasscom Strategic Review 2026: not accessed, so its access level is unverified. PLFS microdata (microdata.gov.in): free with registration under a MoSPI agreement requiring aggregate-only use; 'public' should read 'public with registration/agreement'. WDR 2026: cite hdl.handle.net/10986/45296 or doi:10.1596/978-1-4648-2331-2 rather than the donorplatform.org mirror. Local copies of the extracted PDFs used for checking are in a temporary folder (since deleted).

streams.name: Inference from firm and labor-market data

works.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 revision)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
works.what_measured: US employment by age group and occupational AI exposure from ADP payroll records (3.5-5 million workers a month in the analysis sample), November 2022 to June 2026.
works.method_plain: Descriptive comparisons, not causal. Occupations are sorted into five exposure groups (quintiles) using the Eloundou et al. GPT-4 'beta' scores. Separately, the Anthropic Economic Index splits AI use into 'automative' use (AI does the work) and 'augmentative' use (AI helps a person). Employment changes are compared across age by exposure cells, and the percent change in employment by occupation is regressed on the exposure measures.
key_numbers: Workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations: employment 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers (Nov 2022-Jun 2026). The same measure was 15% at the July 2025 data vintage.
In levels, ages 22-25: the two most-exposed quintiles fell about 11% while the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%, a 21 pp divergence. Total 22-25 employment fell about 1.9%.

All ages: ADP sample employment rose about 6% from Nov 2022 to Jun 2026, against about 4% for the most-exposed quintile. That is roughly a 2 pp gap over 3.6 years, or about 0.6 pp a year (my arithmetic).

Table 3, Panel A: the automation-share coefficient for ages 22-25 is -0.098 (s.e. 0.018) per standard deviation in a percent-change regression. It shrinks with age to -0.006 for 50+. The complementarity coefficient is +0.024 for ages 41-49.
Earlier headline regression estimates were a 13% decline (July 2025 data) and 16% (September 2025 data). These are a different metric from the 19%.
The most-exposed coefficient for ages 22-25 roughly halves, from -0.18 to -0.09 (significant only at 10%), when occupational college share is controlled (catalogue entry ACA-01e).
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives realized, net-of-demand employment gaps by exposure, not labor time saved. The gap identifies s(1 - eps*phi) for exposed versus unexposed occupations, scaled by the difference in exposure. Inverting it would need: (a) the theta gap between exposure quintiles; (b) an assumption that demand shocks d are common across quintiles; (c) an eps*phi correction. The automation-versus-augmentation split is a rough way to separate delegation (the q*p term) from assistance (kappa). The all-ages gap of about 0.6 pp a year is a US lower-bound comparison for the 2.3 pp/yr top-down estimate.
works.limitations: US only; ADP data are proprietary. The authors call it descriptive rather than causal, with some pre-trends, sensitivity to the education control, and a larger gap in ADP than in national surveys. Exposure is measured at the occupation level, so it cannot separate tasks within an occupation. Hiring is the main margin of adjustment, which mixes AI with the business cycle for new entrants.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
works.authors: Menaka Hampole, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Lawrence D.W. Schmidt, Bryan Seegmiller
works.what_measured: Labor demand at the task, occupation-by-firm and firm level as a function of the firm's task-level exposure to AI applications, 2010-2023, using Revelio worker profiles and job postings.
works.method_plain: Text-similarity matching between AI applications and job tasks gives each firm-occupation-year a 'mean exposure' (how much of the job AI covers) and a 'concentration' (whether exposure is bunched in a few tasks). The paper regresses employment growth on both, and uses university-hiring networks as an instrument for AI adoption. A task-based model separates direct substitution, reallocation of worker effort to unexposed tasks, and firm growth.
key_numbers: One SD more task-level exposure reduces relative demand for that task's skills by about 2% (within firm-occupation-year).
IV, preferred specification: one SD more mean task exposure reduces the occupation's within-firm employment share by about 14.5% over 5 years. One SD more concentration raises it by about 7.5%.
OLS: one SD of exposure gives a 5.7-8.7% employment decline; IV gives 10.4-15.6%.
Net: within firms, employment in highly exposed occupations (90th percentile of pay) falls about 3.1% relative to the least exposed. This is mildly reversed after firm growth is counted.
Most affected groups (business, financial, engineering): nearly 2% fall in employment share over five years.
One SD more AI adoption leads to 9.7 pp higher revenue growth and 7.5 pp higher TFP over five years. Firm employment +6.8 pp.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the closest published analogue to S = sum_j w_j * theta_j. It is task-based, separates the direct substitution term from reallocation, and has a firm-growth (demand) channel that maps to eps*phi. The concentration result means theta_j is not simply additive: when exposure is concentrated, freed time is reallocated, so realized s is below sum w_j*theta_j. Its exposure is a text-similarity index, not hours saved, so a calibration is needed to convert 'per SD of exposure' into theta.
works.limitations: The data end in 2023, so it mostly measures pre-generative-AI machine learning. Exposure is semantic similarity, not measured capability or net-of-review savings. The data are US-centric. Revelio data are proprietary. Fixed effects absorb the aggregate effects.

works.title: Generative AI and Firm Values (later version titled 'The Labor Impact of Generative AI on Firm Values')
works.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang (a later version adds Bledi Taska, per search results; not verified in the PDF I opened)
works.what_measured: Stock-price reaction to ChatGPT's release by firm workforce exposure to generative AI, plus later analyst EPS forecasts, realized profitability, job postings and wages.
works.method_plain: Each firm's exposure is the employment-weighted share of its workers' tasks that GPT can do faster. The paper builds an 'Artificial-Minus-Human' long-short portfolio (long high-exposure firms, short low-exposure firms) and runs an event study over the two weeks after 30 Nov 2022. It separates core-task exposure (likely substitution) from supplemental-task exposure (likely complementarity).
key_numbers: Artificial-Minus-Human portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks after ChatGPT's release, about 0.45% a day (t = 3.53), or 0.44% with market controls.
One SD more firm exposure: 1.7% higher stock return and a 1.8% larger upward revision to year-end EPS forecasts.
Gross profitability up 0.13% per SD of exposure (2022Q1-2024Q3).
Occupation level: one SD more exposure is associated with 8% fewer job postings and a 0.6% lower hourly wage after ChatGPT. Effects are 66% and 97% larger when exposure comes from core tasks.
Mean occupational exposure is 23% of tasks. White-collar occupations average 40%, blue-collar and service 9%. Firm-level exposure: mean 35%, 10th-90th percentile 27-44%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Markets price the expected present value of labor cost savings. In principle, the abnormal return divided by (wage bill / market value), with a discount rate and adoption path, gives the market-implied s for a firm. The paper's cash-flow decomposition supports reading the return as a cash-flow effect. For Indian IT firms, with a wage bill of roughly half of revenue (a project fact, not from this paper), this could be inverted around model releases. Exposure here is the share of tasks, an extensive-margin w_j*1{theta_j>0} measure, not theta.
works.limitations: Expected, not realized, savings. Mixes labor savings with product-market gains. The sample is US-listed firms. Markets do not separate pass-through: a services firm whose clients capture the savings should fall, not rise, which makes the sign ambiguous for Indian IT.

works.title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data
works.authors: Seyed M. Hosseini, Guy Lichtinger
works.what_measured: Firm-level junior and senior employment at generative-AI-adopting firms versus non-adopters, from Revelio résumés covering 65 million workers at more than 280,000 firms, 2015-2025.
works.method_plain: A firm counts as an adopter when it posts 'GenAI integrator' jobs. The paper uses difference-in-differences and a staggered event study around adoption, and splits outcomes into hiring, separations and promotions. It also tracks whether exposed tasks are removed from junior job postings.
key_numbers: Junior employment at adopters falls about 9% relative to non-adopters after six quarters from 2023Q1. Senior employment shows no break.
Staggered event study (catalogue ACA-02b): junior employment about 8% lower after eight quarters, with no pre-trends.
Decline driven mainly by slower hiring, not more separations.
Junior employment in high-exposure occupations falls about 7% relative to low-exposure occupations (catalogue ACA-02c).
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a realized labor reduction conditional on adoption, which is the right conditioning for a full-adoption ceiling. Adopters are about 16% of employment. A 9% junior decline over 1.5 years is about 6% a year for juniors, net of demand. Weighted by the junior share of headcount it becomes a firm-level s(1-eps*phi). It is the most directly invertible design for Indian IT, if Revelio or LinkedIn coverage of TCS, Infosys and others is adequate. The removal of exposed tasks from junior postings is direct evidence on which j's theta is high.
works.limitations: US firms. The adoption proxy (integrator postings) selects tech-forward firms. Revelio data are proprietary. Adopters may differ in unobserved demand shocks. Gives no hours saved.

works.title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
works.authors: Bharat Chandar, Bouke Klein Teeselink
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
works.what_measured: Employment by seniority and occupation at foreign affiliates of generative-AI-adopting multinationals, using 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records (Revelio/LinkedIn-type data) across 41 countries including India.
works.method_plain: Adoption is inferred from LLM-verified generative-AI job ads. An instrumented event study compares foreign affiliates of adopting companies with matched control affiliates. A structural model splits the employment response into a firm-wide scale effect (cheaper production, more output) and worker-type-specific task-content changes.
key_numbers: Junior share of employment at treated affiliates is 1.9 pp lower than controls by March 2026. Juniors are 57.1% of employment.
Senior employment +6.7%; junior employment -2.5% (not significant); total employment +3.3% (marginally significant).
Model-implied scale terms: +4.3% for seniors, -1.8% for juniors, +2.5% for all workers. The 6.1 pp senior-junior difference is significant.
Country meta-analysis (31 countries): junior share falls in 23 of 31, with a mean decline of 1.1 pp. No country shows a significant fall in total employment.

India ranks first of 41 countries in the AI share of postings. The authors attribute this partly to India's IT-heavy LinkedIn posting mix. LinkedIn coverage of India is about 8% of official employment.
works.relevance_to_theta: Its model explicitly separates per-task productivity gains (our theta) from the scale effect (our eps*phi channel). It is therefore the closest existing attempt to recover a labor-saving parameter net of demand, and it covers India. The modest net effects mean realized s(1-eps*phi) is near zero or positive at multinational affiliates so far, which is in tension with 2.3 pp/yr unless Indian IT pass-through is high or demand is weak.
works.limitations: Multinational affiliates only; Indian IT vendors are not the focus. LinkedIn under-covers India, at about 8% of employment. Adoption is a posting proxy. Productivity estimates are 'suggestive'. Effects are relative to controls, so common shocks drop out.

works.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (previously 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects')
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.what_measured: AI chatbot adoption surveys linked to Danish administrative earnings and hours records for 11 exposed occupations, with self-reported time savings and new tasks.
works.method_plain: Worker- and workplace-level difference-in-differences comparing adopters with non-adopters, and workplaces that encourage chatbot use with those that do not, before and after ChatGPT. Survey questions on time saved per day, coded from bins (0-15 minutes coded as 7.5, and so on), and on new tasks.
key_numbers: Precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours. The design rules out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's launch.
Adopters report average time savings of about 3% of work hours (appendix).
85% of users say they reallocate time saved to other job tasks.
Self-reported earnings impact among adopters is 0-0.5%, an order of magnitude below the time savings.
Early-career employment share: rules out effects larger than about 1/3 pp at encouraging workplaces (catalogue ACA-03b).
works.relevance_to_theta: The only study here that directly measures realized fraction of time saved, about 3% of hours for adopters in 2023-24, with chatbots rather than agents. This is a realized-at-actual-use analogue of theta, and it bounds kappa from above for the chatbot era. It also documents that freed time is absorbed by new tasks, such as AI oversight, which is a review-cost (rho) and reallocation channel that keeps theta from turning into fewer jobs.
works.limitations: Denmark, not IT services. 2023-24 chatbots, before agentic coding. Self-reported time savings coded from bins. Rigid wage setting.

works.title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
works.authors: Xiang Hui, Oren Reshef, Luofeng Zhou
works.what_measured: Monthly jobs and earnings of about 92,500 freelancers on Upwork in occupations more versus less affected by ChatGPT, and by image models in the published version.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences around ChatGPT's release, comparing freelancers in writing-type occupations with other freelancers.
key_numbers: ChatGPT: -2% monthly jobs (s.e. 0.004) and -5.2% monthly earnings (s.e. 0.016) for freelancers in more affected occupations.
Probability of any job in a month -1.2 pp (about a 10% drop). Conditional on working, jobs -4.7%.
Above-median prior earners: reductions of 7% (jobs) and 14% (earnings).
works.relevance_to_theta: Freelance markets are spot markets with near-full pass-through and fast adjustment, so the demand fall approximates labor substituted net of a market-level eps*phi response. It is a lower bound on early theta for writing tasks. Because the market is outsourced, it is a close structural analogue to clients substituting AI for Indian vendors.
works.limitations: Covers 2023 only. Effects are relative between occupations. Freelance tasks are short and well specified, so f_j(h) is very different from enterprise IT. Not task hours.

works.title: Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms
works.authors: Ozge Demirci, Jonas Hannane, Xinrong Zhu
works.what_measured: Job posts on a leading global freelancing platform (not named in the abstract) for automation-prone writing and coding jobs versus manual-intensive jobs.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences around ChatGPT and image-generator releases, with Google Trends awareness as an intensity measure.
key_numbers: Job posts for automation-prone writing and coding jobs fell 21% relative to manual-intensive jobs within 8 months of ChatGPT.
Image-generating AI was associated with a 17% fall in image-creation posts.
The remaining automation-prone jobs are more complex and higher paid.
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures demand for outsourced coding and writing, which bears on client-side substitution of AI for vendors. The finding that remaining jobs are more complex is evidence that substitution removes the short-h part of f_j(h) first, as the p(h) logistic predicts.
works.limitations: Postings, not hours or hires. Covers only 8 months after release. I read only the abstract via the repository page; the full text was not opened. A widely circulated 30% figure for writing jobs could not be confirmed.

works.title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade, Chapter 2 'Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact'
works.authors: World Bank (chapter authors P. Kirby, J. Rexer, S. Sharma per repo catalogue)
works.what_measured: Lightcast job postings in South Asia (mostly India) by occupational AI exposure and complementarity, Aug 2020-Mar 2025, with a business-services sector focus.
works.method_plain: Event study and difference-in-differences at the occupation-by-month level around ChatGPT, using Felten-Raj-Seamans exposure and Pizzinelli et al. complementarity.
key_numbers: Listings growth from 2020 to 2025 averaged 41% for the most-exposed, least-complementary occupations versus 96% for the least exposed.
Call-centre agents (top exposure quartile) saw postings fall 24% relative to machine operators.
Business-services occupations: postings about 35% lower relative to other occupations after ChatGPT (log points -0.349; catalogue WB-01a). Posted wages about -8%.
Entry-level (0-5 years) postings fall most: -11.9% per SD of exposure (catalogue, from the chart workbook).
works.relevance_to_theta: The only study of this kind on Indian business-services postings. It gives a relative demand drop that is much larger than US estimates. Postings are flows, not stocks, so a 35% fall in postings maps to a much smaller fall in the stock of employment, and inverting it needs attrition and hiring rates. It does not identify theta without a demand model.
works.limitations: Lightcast data, which are licensed and skew professional in South Asia. Postings, not hires. Ends March 2025. Occupation-level, not task-level.

works.title: Who Takes the Hit? The Uneven Impacts of Generative AI on Labor Demand Across Countries
works.authors: Shu Yu, Xianguo (Jerry) Huang per the AMRO seminar page. A search result lists Jingyun Huang, Yan Liu, He Wang, Shu Yu instead, so the author list is unconfirmed. Probably the 'Huang et al. (2026)' cited by Chandar & Klein Teeselink.
works.venue: Seminar paper (AMRO Cafe Seminar, July 31, 2026); paper not found online
works.what_measured: Lightcast postings in 84 countries (555 million postings, 2021Q1-2025Q2) for occupations more versus less vulnerable to AI substitution.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences and event study around ChatGPT, controlling for generative-AI exposure and sensitivity to monetary policy.
key_numbers: High-income countries: postings for above-median-vulnerability occupations fell 5.8% on average relative to less substitutable occupations, and the effect grew over time.
Middle- and low-income countries: 'much smaller and statistically insignificant' (no number given).
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests realized substitution in developing countries lags the capability ceiling, because of an adoption gap. That supports treating theta as a ceiling and S as adoption-weighted for India's domestic market. Indian IT exports, however, serve rich-country clients, so the high-income estimate may be the relevant one for client-side substitution.
works.limitations: Only the seminar abstract is available. No coefficients for India. Postings, not employment.

works.title: AI and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Jonathon Hazell, Pascual Restrepo
works.year: 2022 (NBER WP Dec 2020, revised Feb 2022; published Journal of Labor Economics 2022, publication details not checked)
works.what_measured: US establishment-level Burning Glass (now Lightcast) vacancies, 2010-2018: AI hiring, and non-AI hiring at AI-exposed establishments.
works.method_plain: Establishment-level regressions of AI vacancy growth and non-AI hiring on task-based AI exposure measures (Felten et al., Webb, Brynjolfsson-Mitchell SML).
key_numbers: AI-exposed establishments reduce hiring in non-AI positions.
'No discernible relationship between AI exposure and employment or wage growth' at occupation or industry level (abstract). The abstract gives no numeric coefficients; I did not open the full PDF.
works.relevance_to_theta: The classic template for this whole stream. Substitution shows up in establishment hiring but washes out in aggregates, so firm-level designs are needed to see theta. It is the methodological ancestor of Hampole et al. and Hosseini-Lichtinger.
works.limitations: Pre-generative AI (machine learning, 2010-2018). Vacancies only. I opened only the abstract page.

works.title: The Cross-Section of Stock Returns and AI Exposure (previously 'AI Premium')
works.authors: Nicola Borri, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski
works.what_measured: Firms' stock-return sensitivity to a high-frequency factor built from OpenRouter token consumption (380 trillion tokens, more than 400 LLMs, Jan 2024-Apr 2026), and returns around frontier model releases.
works.method_plain: Build an 'AI factor' from token growth. Estimate each firm's AI beta. Sort firms into long-short portfolios. Check returns with and without frontier model-release weeks, and map occupational exposure.
key_numbers: Value-weighted long-short AI-exposure strategy: 60.4 basis points per week.
Excluding frontier model-release weeks: 34.3 bp per week.
The spread is significant in developed markets but insignificant in emerging markets.
Agentic tokens grew from negligible to more than half of total AI consumption.
works.relevance_to_theta: Supplies a model-release calendar and a token-based adoption series that could date shocks to p(h,t) in an event study of Indian IT stocks. The agentic share of tokens is a usage proxy for the shift from assistant (kappa) to delegate (q*p).
works.limitations: Measures returns, not labor. OpenRouter covers about 2% of global tokens and skews to developers. No Indian-IT-specific results found.

research.stream_summary:
No firm or labor-market study measures theta directly. What these studies estimate is a realized gap: exposed workers, firms or occupations compared with less-exposed ones. In our notation that gap is roughly s(1 - eps*phi) multiplied by the difference in exposure. It is net of demand responses, net of adoption, and usually net of time reallocated to new tasks. To turn it back into theta you need three things: (1) the theta gap between treated and control groups, in hours saved rather than an exposure index; (2) an assumption that demand shocks are common to both groups; (3) a correction for eps*phi.

The realized magnitudes are smaller than headline numbers suggest:
- **Canaries (US, all ages):** the most-exposed quintile grew only about 2 pp less than average over 3.6 years, roughly 0.6 pp a year. The well-known 19% figure applies only to workers aged 22-25.
- **Hampole et al.:** about 14.5% within-firm employment-share loss per SD of exposure over five years, mostly offset by reallocation and firm growth.
- **Hosseini-Lichtinger:** junior employment about 9% lower at adopters after six quarters.
- **Chandar & Klein Teeselink (41 countries, including India):** junior share -1.9 pp, but total employment +3.3%.
- **Humlum-Vestergaard:** adopters save about 3% of hours, with no effect on hours or earnings.

Against these, the top-down 2.3 pp/yr for Indian IT is at the high end. That fits an outsourced, pass-through-heavy industry, or demand weakness being blamed on AI.

The most invertible designs for our purpose:
- Hosseini-Lichtinger-style adopter event studies on Indian IT firms using Revelio or LinkedIn.
- Eisfeldt-style stock event studies around model releases, where the abnormal return divided by the wage-bill-to-value ratio gives a market-implied expected s.
- Freelance-platform designs, which are close to full pass-through.

On the working hypothesis: confirmed. These studies measure the extensive margin (exposure) and realized net outcomes, not the intensive, net-of-review margin. Only Humlum-Vestergaard measures hours saved, and only Hampole et al. separate substitution from reallocation.
gaps_noticed: No study estimates labor time saved per task net of review. Firm and labor studies give net employment after demand responses, so theta cannot be recovered without separate eps*phi and exposure-to-hours calibrations.

No firm-level event study on Indian IT vendors (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech). Chandar & Klein Teeselink cover affiliates in India, and the World Bank covers occupations, but nobody runs a Hosseini-Lichtinger design on the vendors themselves.

No published abnormal-return event study of Indian IT stocks around frontier model releases. Press reports say the Nifty IT index fell about 6% in one February 2026 session after an Anthropic launch; this was not verified from a primary source. A market-implied s could be backed out from such a study.

Hanney and Kim (2026, India) and Mishra et al. (2026, survey of 651 Indian IT firms: 55% report lower entry-level hiring) are cited, by Chandar & Klein Teeselink and the World Bank India Development Update Oct 2026 respectively, but I could not locate either paper.
The 'Huang et al. (2026)' developing-country paper is known only from a seminar abstract. Its author list is inconsistent and it has no India coefficients.

Exposure measures used across this stream (Eloundou beta, Felten AIOE, Anthropic Economic Index, text similarity) are occupation-level and static. None varies with capability over time the way p(h,t) does, so the time-varying part of theta is not identified.

Most designs measure postings or hiring flows, not employment stocks or hours. Converting a postings drop into a stock change needs attrition and hiring rates. For Indian IT these come from filings (attrition about 12-20%).
Nearly all evidence is US/European data with chatbot-era AI (2023-2025). There is little evidence on agentic coding tools from 2025-26, which is when theta should jump.
Pass-through phi is not measured anywhere in this stream. Freelance studies implicitly assume full pass-through. Firm studies conflate cost savings with demand expansion.

datasets.name: ADP payroll microdata (via Stanford Digital Economy Lab) and public AI Economic Indicators
datasets.description: US monthly payroll records, 3.5-5 million workers a month, with job titles. The microdata are not public. The authors say they release a public set of AI Economic Indicators for tracking.

datasets.name: Revelio Labs workforce and postings data
datasets.description: LinkedIn-derived résumés and postings, with firm-level employment by seniority. Used by Hampole et al., Hosseini-Lichtinger and Chandar-Klein Teeselink. India coverage is about 8% of official employment, but likely much higher for IT firms.

datasets.name: Lightcast (formerly Burning Glass/EMSI) job postings
datasets.description: Global postings with occupation and skill coding. The World Bank's South Asia analysis and Huang/Yu's 84-country study use it. India coverage is skewed toward professional jobs.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index
datasets.description: Task-level Claude usage with the split between automation ('automative') and assistance ('augmentative'). Used in Canaries Table 3. A possible proxy for the delegate-versus-assistant mix (q*p versus kappa) by task.

datasets.name: Eloundou et al. (2024) GPT exposure scores
datasets.description: O*NET task and occupation exposure ratings (alpha/beta/zeta). Extensive-margin measure used across this stream. URL not opened in this session.

datasets.name: Danish administrative registers linked to adoption surveys (Humlum-Vestergaard)
datasets.description: Survey time savings linked to register earnings and hours. Access through Statistics Denmark is restricted.

datasets.name: Compustat/CRSP, plus NSE/BSE daily prices for an Indian IT event study
datasets.description: Inputs for an Eisfeldt-style event study. NSE/BSE daily prices for Indian IT firms are freely available, and wage-bill data come from the firms' annual reports, which the project already holds.

datasets.name: OpenRouter token consumption data
datasets.description: Token-level LLM consumption, Jan 2024-Apr 2026, about 2% of global tokens. Licensed to the authors. A high-frequency adoption and capability-shock series.

datasets.name: Naukri JobSpeak, foundit, Xpheno (India postings indices)
datasets.description: Monthly Indian postings indices by sector and experience band, already in the repo. Aggregates only; posting flows, not hires.

works.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 version)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
works.what_measured: US employment by age group and occupational AI exposure, from ADP payroll records. The analysis sample is a balanced panel of firms with 3.5 to 5 million workers a month; outcomes run from November 2022 to June 2026.
works.method_plain: Descriptive, not causal. Occupations are split into five exposure groups (quintiles) using the Eloundou et al. GPT-4 beta scores. Separately, Anthropic Economic Index measures split AI use into 'automative' use (AI does the task) and 'augmentative' use (AI helps a person). The paper compares employment changes across age-by-exposure cells, and runs occupation-level long-difference regressions of percent employment change on the exposure measures.
key_numbers: Ages 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations: employment is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers (Nov 2022 to Jun 2026). The same measure was 15% at the July 2025 data vintage.
In levels, ages 22-25: the two most-exposed quintiles fell about 11% and the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%, a 21 pp divergence. Total employment for ages 22-25 fell 1.9%.

All ages: ADP sample employment rose about 6% from Nov 2022 to Jun 2026; the most-exposed quintile grew about 4%. Roughly 2 pp over 3.6 years, about 0.6 pp a year. This is the researcher's arithmetic, against an average that includes the top quintile itself.

Table 3, Panel A (March 2025 AEI release): automation coefficient for ages 22-25 is -0.098 (s.e. 0.018), as a fractional percent change in employment per SD. It shrinks with age to -0.006 for 50+. The complementarity coefficient is +0.024 (s.e. 0.010) for ages 41-49. Panel B (pooled later releases): -0.084 for ages 22-25.
Earlier versions headlined regression estimates of a 13% relative decline (July 2025 data) and 16% (September 2025 data). The 19%/15% figures are a different, purely descriptive metric.

Quintile regression, ages 22-25: most-exposed quintile vs quintile 1 is -0.179 with no controls. With a college-share control it is -0.091, significant only at the 10% level. With all controls it is -0.080 and not significant.
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives realized employment gaps by exposure, net of demand and adoption, not labor time saved. The gap is a reduced form of roughly s(1 - eps*phi) times the exposure difference. Inverting it would need the theta gap between quintiles in hours, an assumption that demand shocks are common across quintiles, and an eps*phi correction. The automation-versus-augmentation split is only a rough occupation-level proxy for delegation (q*p) versus assistance (kappa). It is not a direct measure of theta or kappa.
works.limitations: US only; ADP microdata are proprietary. The authors call the results descriptive, not causal. They note some pre-existing divergent trends, strong attenuation when education is controlled, and larger gaps in ADP than in national surveys. Exposure is occupation-level and static. Hiring is the main margin of adjustment, which mixes AI with business-cycle effects for new entrants.
works.corrections: No errors in the citation or numbers. Clarified the following: the 0.6 pp/yr all-ages figure is the researcher's own arithmetic against the sample average; the Table 3 coefficient units; the full sequence for the college-share control (-0.179 to -0.091*, and -0.080 with all controls). The params tags theta_j-direct and kappa are generous, because the paper measures neither directly.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
works.authors: Menaka Hampole, Dimitris Papanikolaou, Lawrence D.W. Schmidt, Bryan Seegmiller
works.what_measured: Labor demand at the task, occupation-by-firm and firm level as a function of each firm's task-level exposure to its AI applications, 2010-2023. Uses Revelio Labs résumé and job-posting data.
works.method_plain: NLP similarity between AI applications and occupational tasks gives each occupation in a firm two measures: mean exposure (how much of the job AI covers) and concentration (whether exposure is bunched in a few tasks). Employment growth is regressed on both. A shift-share instrument based on historical university hiring networks is used for AI adoption. A task-based model separates direct substitution, reallocation of worker effort and firm growth.
key_numbers: One SD more task-level AI exposure within a firm reduces relative demand for that task's skills by about 2% over five years.
IV, preferred specification: one SD more mean task exposure reduces the occupation's within-firm employment share by about 14.5% over five years. One SD more concentration raises it by about 7.5%.
Range across specifications for one SD of mean exposure: 5.7-8.7% employment decline (OLS) and 10.4-15.6% (IV).
Within firms, employment in highly exposed occupations (90th percentile of pay) falls about 3.1% relative to the least exposed. This is mildly reversed once firm growth is counted.
Most adversely affected occupations (business, financial, engineering): declines of nearly 2% in employment share over five years.
IV: one SD more AI adoption leads to 9.7 pp higher revenue growth, 7.5 pp higher TFP and 6.8 pp higher firm employment over five years.
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest published structural analogue to S = sum_j w_j * theta_j. It is task-based and separates direct substitution from within-occupation reallocation and firm-growth (demand) effects; the last maps loosely to eps*phi. The concentration result implies that realized s can be below a simple sum of w_j*theta_j, because freed time is reallocated. Exposure is a text-similarity index, not hours saved, so an exposure-to-theta calibration would be needed.
works.limitations: Data end in 2023, so this is mostly pre-generative-AI machine learning. Exposure is semantic similarity, not measured capability or savings net of review. US-centric, Revelio data are proprietary, and fixed effects absorb aggregate effects.
works.corrections: No errors. Added 'over five years' to the 2% task-level figure and confirmed that the data source is Revelio Labs. 'Firm employment +6.8 pp' is from the IV specification.

works.title: Generative AI and Firm Values
works.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang. The Internet Appendix of the same January 2026 NBER PDF lists Bledi Taska as an additional author.
works.what_measured: Stock returns after ChatGPT's release by firm workforce exposure to generative AI. Also analyst EPS-forecast revisions, realized profitability, Lightcast job postings, CPS wages, and firm employment of highly exposed occupations.
works.method_plain: An LLM classifies each of 19,265 O*NET tasks by whether it can be done more effectively with ChatGPT. This is aggregated to occupations and then to firms using Revelio occupational shares. An 'Artificial-Minus-Human' long-short portfolio is tracked over the two weeks after 30 Nov 2022. Exposure from core tasks (likely substitution) is separated from exposure from supplemental tasks (likely complementarity).
key_numbers: The AMH portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks after ChatGPT's release: 0.45% a day (t = 3.53), or 0.44% a day with market controls (t = 4.70).
One SD more firm exposure: 1.7% higher stock return, and a 1.8% larger upward revision to year-end EPS forecasts.
One SD more exposure: 0.13% higher gross profitability rate (firm-quarters 2022Q1-2024Q3).

Occupation level: one SD more exposure is associated with 8% fewer job postings and a 0.6% lower hourly wage after ChatGPT. Effects are 66% and 97% larger when exposure comes entirely from core tasks.
Firm level: one SD more exposure is associated with a 0.6% decline in employment of highly exposed occupations.
Mean occupational exposure is 23% of tasks; white-collar occupations 40%, blue-collar and service 9%. Firm-level exposure has mean and median 35% (SD 8%) and a 10th-90th percentile range of 27-44%.
works.relevance_to_theta: Markets price the expected present value of cost savings. The researcher proposes inverting the abnormal return, divided by wage bill over market value, into a market-implied expected s around model releases. That inversion is the researcher's proposal, not something the paper does. Exposure is the share of tasks exposed (roughly w_j * 1{theta_j > 0}), an extensive-margin measure, not theta.
works.limitations: Measures expected, not realized, savings. Mixes labor savings with product-market gains. US-listed firms only. For a services vendor whose clients capture the savings, the sign of the stock response is ambiguous.
works.corrections: The January 2026 NBER revision is still titled 'Generative AI and Firm Values'. The alternative title 'The Labor Impact of Generative AI on Firm Values' could not be confirmed in this session (SSRN returned 403, and the search budget ran out), so it is removed from the main title. Bledi Taska is listed as an author on the Internet Appendix title page inside the PDF the researcher opened, so the 'not verified in the PDF' note was wrong. Added the 0.6% firm-level employment result and the t = 4.70 for the market-controlled return. All other numbers match.

works.title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data
works.authors: Seyed M. Hosseini (cited elsewhere as Hosseini Maasoum), Guy Lichtinger
works.what_measured: Firm-level junior and senior employment at firms that adopt generative AI versus non-adopters. Uses Revelio Labs LinkedIn résumé and posting data covering 65 million workers at more than 280,000 US firms, 2015-2025.
works.method_plain: A firm counts as an adopter when it posts 'GenAI integrator' jobs. The paper uses difference-in-differences, a triple difference (junior versus senior, with firm-by-time fixed effects) and a staggered event study. It decomposes the change into hiring, separations and promotions, and checks whether GenAI-exposed tasks are removed from junior job postings.
key_numbers: Junior employment at adopters falls about 9% relative to non-adopters six quarters after 2023Q1. Senior employment shows no break.
Staggered event study: junior employment about 8% lower eight quarters after adoption, with no significant pre-trends.
The decline is driven mainly by slower hiring. Junior separations also fell, and promotions rose slightly.
Junior employment in high-exposure occupations falls about 7% relative to low-exposure occupations between 2022Q4 and 2025Q1.
Adopters account for about 16% of employment in the dataset.
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a realized junior labor reduction conditional on adoption, net of demand. 9% over 1.5 years is about 6% a year for juniors (researcher's arithmetic); weighted by the junior headcount share it gives a firm-level reduced form for s(1 - eps*phi). The design could in principle be replicated on Indian IT vendors with Revelio data. The removal of exposed tasks from junior postings is suggestive evidence on which tasks have high theta.
works.limitations: US firms only. The adoption proxy (integrator postings) selects tech-forward firms, and the adoption date may be measured with error. Revelio data are proprietary. No hours-saved measure.
works.corrections: Numbers match the May 6, 2026 PDF. The URL is a CDN mirror of the author's GitHub site. The PDF names SSRN 5425555 as the latest version (SSRN returned 403 here), so prefer that as the citation URL. Added that adopters are about 16% of employment and that the high-versus-low-exposure 7% covers 2022Q4-2025Q1.

works.title: How Does AI Change Labor Demand? Evidence from 41 Countries
works.authors: Bharat Chandar, Bouke Klein Teeselink
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
works.what_measured: Employment by seniority and occupation at foreign affiliates of multinationals that adopt generative AI. Uses 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records from Revelio Labs (mainly LinkedIn profiles), across 41 countries including India.
works.method_plain: Adoption is inferred from job ads involving generative-AI use. An instrumented, matched event study compares foreign affiliates of adopting companies with control affiliates. A model splits the employment response into a firm-wide scale (productivity) effect and worker-type-specific changes in task content.
key_numbers: Junior share of employment at treated affiliates is 1.9 pp lower than at controls by March 2026, against a baseline junior share of 57.1%.
Senior employment +6.7%. Junior employment -2.5% (not significant). Total employment +3.3% (marginally significant).
Model-implied scale terms: +4.3% for seniors, -1.8% for juniors, +2.5% for all workers, none individually significant. The 6.1 pp senior-junior difference is significant.

Country meta-analysis (31 countries with strong instruments): junior share falls in 23 of 31, significantly in 7, with an average decline of 1.1 pp. No country shows a significant fall in total employment.

India ranks first of 41 countries in the AI share of LinkedIn postings, which the authors attribute partly to India's IT-heavy posting mix. Active Revelio positions are about 8% of official employment in India.
works.relevance_to_theta: The model explicitly separates a productivity or scale effect (related to eps*phi) from task-content shifts by worker type, so it is the closest attempt to recover a labor-saving parameter net of demand, and it covers India. All effects are relative to matched controls, and the productivity evidence is described as suggestive. They are therefore not directly comparable to an aggregate 2.3 pp/yr replacement rate.
works.limitations: Multinational affiliates only; Indian IT vendors are not the focus. LinkedIn covers India poorly (about 8% of employment). Adoption is a posting proxy. Effects are relative to controls, so common shocks drop out.
works.corrections: Numbers match. Clarified the data source (Revelio Labs, built mainly from LinkedIn profiles and postings, rather than 'LinkedIn-type'). Added that no scale term is individually significant, and that 7 of the 23 country declines are significant.

works.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (previously circulated as 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects')
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.what_measured: AI chatbot adoption surveys in 11 exposed occupations, linked to Danish administrative earnings and hours records. Includes self-reported time savings and new tasks.
works.method_plain: Worker-level and workplace-level difference-in-differences: adopters versus non-adopters, and workplaces that encourage chatbot use versus those that do not, before and after ChatGPT. Survey-binned time savings (0-15 minutes a day coded as 7.5 minutes, and so on) are combined with frequency of use to get time saved as a share of hours.
key_numbers: Precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT's launch.
Adopters report average time savings of about 3% of work hours (appendix).
85% of chatbot users report reallocating saved time to other job tasks. Fewer than 10% take more breaks or leisure, and about 30% spend more time on the same tasks.
Self-reported earnings impacts among adopters range from 0% to 0.5%, an order of magnitude below the time savings.
Early-career employment share at adopting or encouraging workplaces: rules out effects larger than about one third of a percentage point.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only study in this stream that measures the fraction of hours saved, about 3% for adopters in 2023-24, with chatbots, at actual usage intensity. It is a realized, adoption-weighted analogue of theta. It is not a capability ceiling, so it does not bound kappa from above. It documents that freed time goes to new tasks, including AI oversight. That is a reallocation and review (rho) channel that keeps time savings from turning into fewer jobs.
works.limitations: Denmark, not IT services. 2023-24 chatbots, before agentic coding. Time savings are self-reported and coded from bins. Wage setting is rigid.
works.corrections: Numbers match. Rewrote the relevance claim that the 3% figure 'bounds kappa from above': it is an average realized saving at actual usage intensity, not a capability ceiling, so the ceiling could be higher.

works.title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
works.authors: Xiang Hui, Oren Reshef, Luofeng Zhou
works.what_measured: Monthly jobs and earnings of about 92,500 Upwork freelancers in occupations more versus less affected by ChatGPT. Also covers image models (DALL-E 2, Midjourney) for design and image occupations, already in the 2023 working paper.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences around ChatGPT's release, comparing freelancers in writing-related (more affected) occupations with other freelancers. A parallel design around the image-model releases.
key_numbers: ChatGPT: -2% monthly jobs (s.e. 0.004) and -5.2% monthly earnings (s.e. 0.016) for freelancers in more affected occupations.
Probability of any job in a month falls 1.2 pp (about a 10% drop). Conditional on working, jobs fall 4.7% (s.e. 0.011).

Above-median prior earners, ChatGPT: an additional 1.2% fall in jobs (s.e. 0.007) and 2.9% in income (not significant). Image-based AI: reductions of 7% (jobs) and 14% (earnings) for above-median earners, both significant at 1%.
works.relevance_to_theta: A freelance spot market adjusts quickly, so the demand fall is a reduced form of labor substituted net of the market's demand response. The claim of 'near-full pass-through' is the researcher's assumption, not shown in the paper. Covers short, well-specified writing tasks, so the task-length distribution f_j(h) differs greatly from enterprise IT.
works.limitations: 2023 only, so it is a short-run effect. Effects are relative between occupations. Freelance tasks are short and well specified. Not task hours.
works.corrections: Added the volume, issue and pages (35(6): 1977-1989, Nov 2024; confirmed via Crossref and the WashU profile). The CESifo URL now redirects to ifo.de. Fixed a misattribution: the 7% (jobs) and 14% (earnings) reductions for above-median earners are for image-based AI, not ChatGPT. For ChatGPT the above-median effects are an extra 1.2% (jobs) and 2.9% (income), not significant. Image models are already in the 2023 working paper, not only the published version.

works.title: Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms
works.authors: Ozge Demirci, Jonas Hannane, Xinrong Zhu
works.what_measured: Job posts on a leading global freelancing platform (not named in the abstract) for automation-prone writing and coding jobs versus manual-intensive jobs.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences around the releases of ChatGPT and image-generating AI, with Google Trends awareness of ChatGPT as an intensity measure.
key_numbers: Job posts for automation-prone writing and coding jobs fell 21% relative to manual-intensive jobs within eight months of ChatGPT's release.
Image-generating AI was associated with a 17% fall in image-creation posts.
The remaining automation-prone jobs are more complex and higher paid, and competition among freelancers increased.
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures client demand for outsourced coding and writing, which bears on clients substituting AI for vendors. The finding that the remaining jobs are more complex is consistent with AI removing the short, simple tasks first, as a p(h) logistic would predict. That link is the researcher's interpretation, not something the paper tests.
works.limitations: Postings, not hours or hires. Covers only eight months after release. Only the abstract was read through the repository page. A widely circulated 30% figure for writing jobs could not be confirmed.
works.corrections: The citation (authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI) and the abstract numbers (21%, 17%) match the Imperial repository record. Raised citation confidence to high for the citation itself; key numbers are limited to the abstract. The 30% writing-jobs figure remains unconfirmed and should not be cited.

works.title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade. Chapter 2: 'Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact: Labor Market...'
works.authors: World Bank. Chapter 2 prepared by Patrick Kirby, Jonah M. Rexer, Siddharth Sharma.
works.what_measured: Lightcast job postings in South Asia by occupational AI exposure (Felten-Raj-Seamans AIOE) and complementarity (Pizzinelli et al.), August 2020 to February/March 2025. Includes a focus on the business-services sector.
works.method_plain: Event study and difference-in-differences at the occupation-by-month level around ChatGPT's release (Post-ChatGPT x AIOE, Post-ChatGPT x business-services indicator), with occupation and month fixed effects.
key_numbers: Listings growth from 2020 to 2025 averaged 41% for the most-exposed occupations without human-AI complementarity, versus 96% for the least-exposed jobs.
Postings for call-centre agents (top exposure quartile) fell 24% relative to machine operators (bottom quartile).

Business-services occupations after ChatGPT (Annex Table A2.10): log postings coefficient -0.349 (s.e. 0.059), which is about 30% lower in percent terms; the report's text says '35 percent slower'. Log posted salary coefficient -0.080, about 8% lower.
By March 2025, 12% of business-services jobs required AI skills, against 4% for other jobs.

Entry-level (0-5 years' experience) postings, Annex Table A2.12: log-postings coefficient on Post-ChatGPT x AIOE is -0.290 (s.e. 0.058); share coefficient -0.025. In the text, entry-level jobs with a software developer's exposure grew 21% more slowly than those with an electrician's exposure; senior roles saw no change.
works.relevance_to_theta: The only study in this stream on South Asian (largely Indian) business-services postings. Postings are flows, not stocks, so a 30-35% fall in postings maps to a much smaller fall in the stock of employment. Inverting it needs hiring and attrition rates and a demand model. It does not identify theta directly.
works.limitations: Lightcast data are licensed and skew professional in South Asia; the India share of the sample was not checked here. Postings, not hires. Data end in early 2025. Occupation-level, not task-level.
works.corrections: Chapter authors confirmed from the acknowledgments: Patrick Kirby, Jonah M. Rexer, Siddharth Sharma. The -0.349 log points is about a 29.5% decline, not '35% lower'; the 35% wording comes from the report's own text ('grew 35 percent slower'). Removed the claim 'Entry-level (0-5 years) postings fall most: -11.9% per SD of exposure'. That number does not appear in the report. The -0.119 coefficient in the report is the share of postings requiring only secondary education (Annex Table A2.11, column 4). The entry-level coefficient is -0.290 log points per unit of AIOE (Table A2.12). Data window corrected to August 2020 to February/March 2025.

works.title: Who Takes the Hit? The Uneven Impacts of Generative AI on Labor Demand Across Countries
works.authors: Huang, J., Liu, Y., Wang, H. and Yu, S., per the reference list of Chandar & Klein Teeselink (2026). The AMRO seminar page names the speakers as Shu Yu (World Bank) and Xianguo (Jerry) Huang (AMRO); speakers are not necessarily the full author list. Full first names are not confirmed.
works.venue: World Bank working paper; background paper for the World Development Report 2026 (per Chandar & Klein Teeselink). Presented at the AMRO Cafe Seminar, July 31, 2026. Full text not found online.
works.what_measured: 555 million Lightcast job postings in 84 countries, 2021Q1-2025Q2, for occupations more versus less vulnerable to AI substitution.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences and event study around ChatGPT's release, controlling for generative-AI exposure and sensitivity to monetary policy. Cross-country analysis of what predicts larger displacement.
key_numbers: High-income countries: postings for above-median-vulnerability occupations fell 5.8% on average relative to less substitutable occupations, and the effect grew over time.
Middle- and low-income countries: 'much smaller and statistically insignificant' (no number given in the abstract).
Conditional on GDP per capita, displacement is larger where generative-AI adoption, schooling, English proficiency and specialization in digital-services trade are higher.
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests realized substitution in developing countries lags the capability ceiling, because of adoption gaps and missing complements. That supports treating theta as a ceiling and realized S as adoption-weighted. Indian IT exports serve rich-country clients, so the high-income estimate may be more relevant for client-side substitution.
works.limitations: Only the seminar abstract was read; the paper was not opened. No India-specific coefficients are available. Postings, not employment.
works.corrections: Author list resolved using the bibliography of Chandar & Klein Teeselink (2026), which cites Huang, J., Liu, Y., Wang, H. and Yu, S. (2026), a World Bank working paper and WDR 2026 background paper (July 27, 2026 version). The 'Xianguo (Jerry) Huang' attribution rests only on the AMRO speaker list. Abstract numbers (84 countries, 555 million postings, 2021Q1-2025Q2, 5.8%) match the AMRO page. Raised confidence to medium for existence; the full text is still unverified.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies (NBER WP title: 'AI and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies')
works.authors: Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Jonathon Hazell, Pascual Restrepo
works.venue: Journal of Labor Economics 40(S1): S293-S340 (April 2022); NBER Working Paper 28257
works.what_measured: US establishment-level Burning Glass (now Lightcast) vacancies, 2010-2018: AI hiring, and non-AI hiring at AI-exposed establishments. Also occupation- and industry-level employment and wage growth.
works.method_plain: Establishment-level regressions of AI vacancy growth and non-AI hiring on baseline task-based AI exposure measures (Felten et al., Webb, and Brynjolfsson-Mitchell-Rock SML).
key_numbers: One SD more Felten et al. exposure (about the gap between finance and mining/oil extraction) is associated with 15% more AI vacancy posting.
One SD more Felten et al. exposure is associated with roughly 14% fewer non-AI vacancies (coefficient -13.80, s.e. 4.22). For 2014-18 the figure is about 12% (-11.94, s.e. 3.80).
Abstract: 'no discernible relationship between AI exposure and employment or wage growth at the occupation or industry level'.
works.relevance_to_theta: The classic template for this stream. Substitution shows up in establishment hiring but washes out in aggregates, so firm-level designs are needed to see theta. A methodological ancestor of Hampole et al. and Hosseini-Lichtinger. The non-AI hiring regressions drop professional and business services and IT (NAICS 51 and 54), so the paper says nothing directly about IT services.
works.limitations: Pre-generative AI (machine learning, 2010-2018). Vacancies only. The main hiring regressions exclude the IT and professional-services sectors.
works.corrections: Added the published version, Journal of Labor Economics 40(S1): S293-S340, 2022 (confirmed via Crossref); the journal title spells out 'Artificial Intelligence'. Opened the full NBER PDF and added numeric magnitudes (15% more AI vacancies; about 12-14% fewer non-AI vacancies per SD). Noted that NAICS 51 and 54 are excluded.

works.title: The Cross-Section of Stock Returns and AI Exposure (previously circulated as 'AI Premium')
works.authors: Nicola Borri, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski
works.what_measured: Firms' stock-return sensitivity (AI beta) to a weekly AI factor built from OpenRouter consumption data: 380 trillion tokens across more than 400 LLMs, January 2024 to April 2026. Also returns excluding frontier model-release weeks, international spreads, and market-implied occupational exposure.
works.method_plain: The AI factor is the first principal component of weekly growth in tokens, dollars spent and active users. The paper estimates each firm's beta to this factor, sorts firms into long-short portfolios, tests robustness (factor models, excluding release weeks, tech controls) and maps loadings to occupational tasks and skills.
key_numbers: Value-weighted high-minus-low AI-exposure strategy: 60.4 basis points per week (significant at 1%); about 53 bp after Fama-French five-factor plus momentum adjustment.
Excluding frontier model-release weeks: 34.3 bp per week.
About 10 bp per week across developed markets; small and insignificant in emerging markets, including China.
Agentic tokens grew from negligible to more than half of total AI consumption.
OpenRouter is about 2% of global monthly token consumption (authors' estimate).
works.relevance_to_theta: Supplies a token-based adoption and usage series and a model-release calendar, which could date capability shocks to p(h,t) in an event study of Indian IT stocks. The agentic share of tokens is a rough usage proxy for a shift from assistant (kappa) toward delegate (q*p).
works.limitations: Measures returns, not labor. OpenRouter is about 2% of global tokens and overrepresents developers. Data are licensed and not redistributed. No Indian-IT-specific results.
works.corrections: Numbers match the v3 PDF. Added the factor-adjusted figure (about 53 bp) and the developed-market spread (about 10 bp/week).

summary_flags: The working hypothesis is marked 'confirmed', which is overstated. This stream studies realized outcomes, not the exposure literature itself. Several studies touch the intensive margin: Humlum-Vestergaard (self-reported share of hours saved), Hampole et al. (mean exposure as share of tasks covered, plus concentration), Eisfeldt et al. (core versus supplemental tasks) and Chandar-Klein Teeselink (scale versus task-content decomposition). 'Supported for this stream, with caveats' is fairer.

'Only Hampole et al. separate substitution from reallocation' is false. Chandar & Klein Teeselink decompose scale versus task-content effects. Eisfeldt et al. separate core (substitution) from supplemental (complement) exposure. Humlum-Vestergaard document time reallocated to new tasks.

'The top-down 2.3 pp/yr is at the high end' compares unlike quantities. The studies report relative gaps (treated versus control, or exposed versus less exposed) over different horizons, populations and units. 2.3 pp/yr is an aggregate labor-per-unit-of-work replacement rate. Hosseini-Lichtinger's junior decline (about 6%/yr for juniors at adopters) is larger than 2.3 pp/yr, not smaller.

The Canaries all-ages 0.6 pp/yr is the researcher's arithmetic: the top quintile against a sample average that includes it, US, descriptive. Calling it a 'US lower bound' for the 2.3 pp/yr Indian IT estimate is not supported.

Chandar & Klein Teeselink: total employment +3.3% is only marginally significant, and the model's scale terms are not individually significant. Effects are relative to matched controls, so they cannot be read as aggregate s(1 - eps*phi) near zero.

Freelance designs being 'close to full pass-through', and the Eisfeldt-style inversion (abnormal return divided by wage bill over value giving s), are the researcher's proposals and assumptions, not results from these papers.
Humlum-Vestergaard's 3% of hours is a realized, usage-weighted average for adopters. It does not bound kappa from above as a capability ceiling.

World Bank SADU: the '35% lower' business-services postings figure is -0.349 log points, about 30% lower. The '-11.9% per SD for entry-level postings' is not in the report; -0.119 is the secondary-education share coefficient.
Hui et al.: the 7%/14% above-median-earner reductions were attributed to ChatGPT but are for image-based AI.

Gap list: 'could not locate' Hanney and Kim (2026) and Mishra et al. (2026). Both references can be identified. Hanney and Kim (2026) is a magazine article ('Tomorrow's AI Won't Meet Today's World', In Development), per the Chandar-Klein Teeselink bibliography, not a research paper. Mishra, Kedia, Reddy, Fernandez and Khanduri (2026), 'AI and Jobs: This Time Is No Different', is an ICRIER report. Per the World Bank India Development Update (data as of Sep 15, 2026), it surveyed 651 IT firms across 10 cities and found no aggregate employment decline, with 55% of firms reporting lower entry-level hiring against 25% mid-level and 14% senior. Neither primary document was opened.
Gap list: the Nifty IT '6% fall in one session' press claim remains unverified. The '12-20% attrition from filings' is a project fact not checked here.
Acemoglu et al.'s non-AI hiring regressions exclude NAICS 51 and 54 (professional and business services, IT), so the classic template tells us nothing directly about IT services.
Several params tags are generous. Canaries is tagged theta_j-direct and kappa, but it measures neither. Most firm and labor studies identify only reduced forms.
verify.corrected_summary:
No firm or labor-market study in this stream measures theta, the share of labor time saved net of review, directly. What they estimate is a realized relative gap: exposed or adopting workers, firms or occupations compared with less-exposed ones. In our notation that gap is a reduced form of roughly s(1 - eps*phi) times the exposure difference. It is net of demand responses, of actual (not full) adoption, and often of time reallocated to new tasks. Recovering theta would need three things: (1) the theta gap between treated and control groups, in hours rather than an exposure index; (2) an assumption that demand shocks are common to both groups; (3) a correction for eps*phi.

Magnitudes, none directly comparable to an aggregate replacement rate:
- **Canaries (US, ADP):** ages 22-25 in exposed occupations are 19% below the kept-pace path (Nov 2022-Jun 2026). For all ages, the most-exposed quintile grew about 4% against a 6% sample average, roughly 0.6 pp/yr (our arithmetic). The authors call this descriptive, and it attenuates with an education control.
- **Hampole et al. (US, 2010-2023, pre-generative AI):** one SD of mean task exposure cuts an occupation's within-firm employment share by about 14.5% over five years (IV). Concentrated exposure and firm growth largely offset this, so net within-firm effects are about 3% or less.
- **Hosseini-Lichtinger (US):** junior employment about 9% lower at adopters after six quarters, with no break for seniors.
- **Chandar & Klein Teeselink (41 countries, including India):** junior share -1.9 pp at affiliates of adopters, with senior employment +6.7% and total employment +3.3% (marginally significant).
- **Humlum-Vestergaard (Denmark):** adopters self-report saving about 3% of hours, with precise null effects on earnings and hours.
- **World Bank South Asia:** business-services postings about 30% lower (-0.35 log points) after ChatGPT.

Because these are relative gaps measured over different units and horizons, they cannot be ranked against the top-down 2.3 pp/yr for Indian IT without a mapping. Junior-specific effects at US adopters (about 6%/yr) exceed it; aggregate US gaps fall below it.

Candidate designs for inverting theta:
- Hosseini-Lichtinger-style adopter event studies on Indian IT vendors using Revelio data (coverage of India is thin overall, about 8% of employment).
- Stock-price event studies around model releases, in the spirit of Eisfeldt et al. and Borri et al. Converting a return into an implied s is our proposal, and the sign is ambiguous for vendors whose clients capture the savings.
- Freelance-platform designs, if pass-through can be argued.

On the working hypothesis: largely supported for this stream, with caveats. Most studies use static occupation-level exposure and realized net outcomes rather than labor saved net of review as capability rises. Some partial intensive-margin evidence exists: self-reported hours saved (Humlum-Vestergaard), substitution versus reallocation (Hampole et al.), scale versus task-content decomposition (Chandar & Klein Teeselink), and core versus supplemental tasks (Eisfeldt et al.).
verify.dataset_notes: ADP payroll microdata: not public. 'Lab-internal' is right for access. The listed URL is the paper, not a data portal. The paper's abstract confirms a public set of AI Economic Indicators, but its URL was not checked. Revelio Labs: paid, correct. The '8% of official employment in India' is active Revelio positions per Chandar & Klein Teeselink. 'Likely much higher for IT firms' is speculation and was not verified. Lightcast: paid, correct. It is used by the World Bank SADU, by Huang/Liu/Wang/Yu (84 countries) and by Eisfeldt et al. for postings. Anthropic Economic Index: the public access label was not opened this session; the 'automative' and 'augmentative' terms do appear in Canaries Table 3. Eloundou et al. exposure scores (Science 2024, doi 10.1126/science.adj0998): not opened this session, so treat the citation as unverified here. Danish registers: restricted access via Statistics Denmark, so 'on-request' is roughly right. Compustat/CRSP: the URL points to the Eisfeldt paper, not a data source. These are paid (WRDS). NSE/BSE prices and annual-report wage bills are a project assumption, not checked. OpenRouter: the paper says the data are licensed ('used under license; original data not redistributed'), so 'licensed/proprietary' is more accurate than 'on-request'. About 2% of global tokens is the authors' own estimate. Naukri JobSpeak URL: not opened in this check. Additional source located: the World Bank India Development Update, 2026 edition (data as of Sep 15, 2026), at https://documents.worldbank.org/curated/en/099455510022634209/pdf/IDU-26df18db-fc2b-4e0b-91ed-be8ced3d9bce.pdf. It cites the ICRIER survey of 651 Indian IT firms (Mishra et al. 2026).

works.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (originally 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks')
works.authors: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, ... Elizabeth Barnes, Lawrence Chan (METR)
works.what_measured: The '50% time horizon': the length of task (measured by how long skilled humans take) that an AI agent finishes with 50% probability, on software, ML research-engineering and cyber tasks (HCAST, RE-Bench, 66 short SWAA tasks).
works.method_plain: Time humans with domain expertise on each task. Run each AI agent many times on each task. For each model, fit a logistic curve of success against log(human time). Read off the task length where predicted success is 50% (and 80%). Plot that length against model release date.
key_numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 50% horizon about 50 min (abstract); about 59 min with an 80% horizon of about 15 min, as quoted in Ord 2025
Frontier 50% horizon doubled about every 7 months, 2019-2025; the paper says the trend may have accelerated in 2024 (about every 4 months)
Benchmark tasks range from about 1 second to 16 hours of human time
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the source of p(h,t): success probability as a function of task length h and date t. The logistic form, the per-model slope and the doubling time all feed straight into the theta_j integral. It says nothing directly about q, rho, kappa or f_j.
works.limitations: Tasks are clean, self-contained, and scored automatically, with little context. Human baseliners had less context than professionals who work in the codebase, so h is likely overstated for in-house work. Only about 2 tasks per model-run family at long lengths. Success means 'passes the automated checks', not 'mergeable'.

works.title: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (Time Horizon 1.1 page and raw data file benchmark_results_1_1.yaml)
works.authors: METR
works.year: 2026 (TH1.1 introduced Jan 2026; page last updated 8 Sep 2026)
works.what_measured: Updated 50% and 80% horizons, with confidence intervals, for about 26 models on a larger task suite, plus fitted doubling times.
works.method_plain: Same method as Kwa et al., with more long tasks. I downloaded the YAML and tabulated the per-model p50 and p80 estimates myself.
key_numbers: Doubling time from 2023 on: 128.7 days (95% CI 104.4-158.0); all-time stitched: 187.8 days. Both exclude points with p50 > 16 h
Claude Opus 4.6 (Feb 2026): p50 718.8 min (about 12 h), p80 69.9 min
GPT-5.2 (Dec 2025): p50 352 min, p80 66 min
Claude Mythos Preview early (Apr 2026): p50 1044.8 min (about 17.4 h, above the 16 h reliability ceiling), p80 185.9 min
Ratio p50/p80 across models is mostly 4-6x (my calculation from the file); outlier Opus 4.6 at 10.3x
Claude 3.7 Sonnet under TH1.1: p50 60.4 min, p80 12.1 min
METR says measurements above 16 h are unreliable with the current suite. It does not report 99% horizons, and the page is no longer actively updated
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the most current machine-readable input for p(h,t). The p80 figures are about 5x shorter than p50, which shows how strongly theta_j depends on the slope. A task-level file (task_results_1_1.yaml) also exists, so p(h) can be refit with a slope shared across models.
works.limitations: The p50 estimates of recent models are fragile; see the Barry 2026 note. Long-task coverage is thin (about 31 long tasks), and the page is frozen as of Sep 2026.

works.title: Impact of modelling assumptions on time horizon results
works.authors: Alexander Barry (METR)
works.what_measured: How sensitive 50% and 80% horizons are to the choice of curve (logistic, fixed-slope logistic, logistic with a reliability ceiling, Weibull, Cauchy, nonparametric), the regularization, the task weighting, and noise in task lengths.
works.method_plain: Refit the same success data under many different curve shapes and data choices, then compare horizons and out-of-sample fit.
key_numbers: Alternative curve shapes cut recent models' 50% horizons by up to 35% and raised 80% horizons by up to 100%
Spread for Opus 4.6 across reasonable methods: about 1.5x at 50% and about 2x at 80%
Correcting for noisy task lengths (SIMEX) cuts frontier 50% horizons by about 30% (plausible range 0-60%) and raises 80% horizons by about 20%
Opus 4.6 on private-only tasks: 50% horizon fell 40% (11h59m to 7h11m)
A single slope shared by all models gave the best leave-one-family-out cross-validation
Per-model logistic fits produce shallow slopes when easy tasks fail, which inflates the 50% horizon and depresses the 80% horizon
works.relevance_to_theta: theta_j integrates p over the whole task-length distribution, so it depends on the slope and the curve shape, not only the 50% point. This note shows that the curve choice moves the high-reliability region by up to 2x. Recipe implication: fit one shared slope and report theta_j under at least the logistic and constant-hazard curves.
works.limitations: Less-reviewed note. It covers software tasks only and gives no doubling-time estimates.

works.title: Is there a half-life for the success rates of AI agents?
works.authors: Toby Ord
works.what_measured: Whether METR's success-versus-length data fit a constant-hazard (exponential survival) model, in which each minute of human-equivalent work carries a fixed chance of a fatal error.
works.method_plain: Fit a one-parameter exponential decay p(h) = 0.5^(h/T50) to Kwa et al.'s success curves and compare it with their two-parameter log-logistic fit. Then work out the implied high-reliability horizons.
key_numbers: T80 ≈ 1/3 T50; T90 ≈ 1/7 T50; T99 ≈ 1/70 T50; T99.9 ≈ 1/700 T50 (each additional nine divides the horizon by 10)
With a 7-month doubling time, T80 reaches a given length about 1 year after T50, T90 about 2 years after, T99 about 4 years after, and T99.9 about 6 years after
Kwa et al.'s 80% horizon for Claude 3.7 Sonnet was 0.25 of the 50% horizon, close to the 0.322 the constant-hazard model predicts
Human success decays more slowly than constant hazard (above 20% at 12 h, where the model predicts about 6%)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a one-parameter, interpretable alternative form for p(h,t) and makes the reliability tails explicit. My own derivation: with a logistic slope where T80 is about T50/5 (TH1.1 typical), T99 is about T50/200, against T50/70 under constant hazard. The tails therefore differ by about 3x, which matters for long-tailed f_j.
works.limitations: A short, unreviewed note. It covers one task suite only, and the author leaves generalization open.

works.title: How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?
works.authors: Thomas Kwa, Vincent Cheng (METR)
