works.what_measured: Time horizons and their growth rates across 9 benchmarks: software (HRS, SWE-bench Verified), computer use (OSWorld, WebArena), math, competitive programming, science QA, video QA, self-driving, and robotics.
works.method_plain: Estimate human task lengths for each benchmark, fit success-versus-length curves (or assume a slope when only overall scores are available), and compare levels and doubling times.
key_numbers: Software and reasoning cluster: horizons of about 50-200+ min, doubling every about 2-6 months; METR-HRS doubles in about 4 months since 2024
Visual computer use (OSWorld, WebArena): horizons about 40-100x shorter than software, with similar doubling times, about 2 years behind
Tesla FSD: about 0.6 doublings/yr (about 20 months per doubling)
Default slope when only overall scores are available: beta ≈ 0.6 (the METR-HRS average); benchmarks with beta < 0.25 were excluded
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that p(h,t) depends on the domain. BPO and infrastructure work done through GUIs and ticketing tools resembles computer use (horizons about 50x shorter) more than coding, so theta_BPO needs its own, lower horizon curve rather than the METR-HRS coding curve.
works.limitations: Mapping benchmarks onto human time is rough, and many slopes are assumed rather than fitted. No BPO or IT-operations benchmark is included.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: How often AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests would be merged by the real repository maintainers.
works.method_plain: Four maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest reviewed 296 test-passing agent PRs (from Claude 3.5 Sonnet through Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5) without knowing whether a human or an AI wrote them. 47 human 'golden' patches served as the noise baseline. Scores are normalized so that the golden patches score 100%.
key_numbers: Grader score exceeds maintainer merge rate by 24.2 pp (SE 2.7) after normalization; 34.9 pp (SE 2.2) unnormalized
Only about 68% of the human golden patches were merged by the maintainers
Maintainer-judged scores improve about 9.6 pp/yr more slowly than grader scores (SE 5.5; significant only at 10%; fragile)
Claude Sonnet 4.5: about a 50-min time horizon under the grader versus about 8 min under maintainer review
Roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged
works.relevance_to_theta: The direct source for q ≈ 0.5. It also implies q is not constant: the 9.6 pp/yr slower trend suggests q may fall or stay flat as p rises. The horizon shrinks about 6x (50 to 8 min) under the maintainer standard, so 'q*p' can alternatively be modelled as a shifted p(h) curve.
works.limitations: 3 of 12 repos and 95 of 500 issues. Static review with no chance for the agent to iterate. Old issues. The latest model tested is Sonnet 4.5. The authors do not claim a fundamental capability limit.

works.title: Research Update: Towards Reconciling Slowdown with Time Horizons (Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation)
works.authors: David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: On 18 real issues from the RCT repositories, the agent's test-pass rate versus whether its PR was mergeable as-is, plus the estimated human time needed to fix the agent PRs.
works.method_plain: Run Claude 3.7 Sonnet on real issues, score each patch against the original human PR's tests, then manually review 15 PRs against five failure modes and estimate the time a human would need to bring each to mergeable quality.
key_numbers: Test pass rate 38% (±19%, 95% CI); 0 of 15 reviewed PRs mergeable as-is
Estimated fix time averages about 42 min across all reviewed PRs and about 26 min for test-passing PRs (minimum 15 min)
Average human task length 1.3 h (range 20 min-4 h), so fixing a passing PR costs about one-third of the task
Every reviewed PR had at least 3 of the 5 failure modes
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives an empirical anchor for rho, or more precisely the review-plus-fix cost: about 0.33 of h for passing PRs on mature repositories. In the draft formula, 'rejected but fixable' output is not worth zero, so a fix-cost term may be better than a binary q.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (n=15). One older model with a basic scaffold. Two very high-standard repositories (stdlib-js, hypothesis). Fix times are estimates, not measurements.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (plus the Feb 2026 update 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design')
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025); Becker, Rush, Tom Cunningham, Rein, Khalid Mahamud (2026 update)
works.what_measured: Causal effect on task completion time of allowing AI tools (Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) for experienced developers working in their own mature repositories.
works.method_plain: Randomized controlled trial: 246 real issues were each randomly assigned 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed', and completion times were compared.
key_numbers: AI increased completion time by 19% (slowdown); developers forecast a 24% reduction and believed afterward it gave a 20% reduction
Economics experts predicted 39% and ML experts 38% shorter times
16 developers, 246 tasks

2026 follow-up (as reported by METR; full post only partly read): newly recruited developers show an estimated speedup of -4% (CI -15% to +9%). METR calls the data unreliable because developers who refuse to work without AI select out of the study, and it believes early-2026 speedups are likely higher
works.relevance_to_theta: The best causal evidence on kappa, the assistant-mode speedup, for expert maintenance-type work: about zero or negative in early 2025. Combined with the self-report gap, it warns against taking kappa from surveys or from AI-estimated time savings.
works.limitations: Expert developers in their own large, familiar repositories, which is unlike Indian IT services teams on client code. Early-2025 tools. The 2026 redesign shows selection problems now dominate RCTs.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: For 100,000 Claude.ai conversations: Claude's estimate of how long the task would take a professional without AI, and how long it took with AI. These are aggregated to O*NET tasks and occupations.
works.method_plain: An LLM estimates time-without-AI and time-with-AI for each conversation; time saved = 1 - ratio. The duration estimates were validated against JOSSE, a public dataset of Jira tickets with developer estimates and actual tracked time.
key_numbers: Average task length without AI about 1.4 h (about 90 min)
Median time savings about 80% (84% in the text, 81% in a figure caption)
Implied US labor productivity growth +1.8%/yr over 10 years at universal adoption (exercise, not forecast)

Validation on 1,000 JOSSE tickets: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 (r_log 0.46) versus human developer estimates 0.50 (r_log 0.67); Claude compresses estimates (overestimates short tasks, underestimates long ones)
Software developers account for 19% of the aggregate gain; customer service reps about 4%
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing attempt at an intensive-margin, task-level 'fraction of time saved'. It is a ready-made template for theta_j, but it leaves out review and validation time (rho) and acceptance failures (q), so 80% is an upper bound. Its JOSSE validation shows that LLM-estimated h is noisy (rank correlation about 0.44), which matters if f_j is built from LLM estimates.
works.limitations: Excludes time spent outside the chat, such as review and iteration. Claude.ai users only. No ground truth for the savings estimates. The authors note that RCTs find smaller gains.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, et al. (OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded head-to-head comparisons of model versus human deliverables on 1,320 real work tasks from 44 occupations, plus a speed and cost model that includes expert review and fixing.
works.method_plain: Experts with about 14 years of experience wrote tasks from their own work and recorded how long they took. Other experts blindly compared AI and human outputs. A 'try the model, review, fix or resample' workflow converts win rates into net time savings.
key_numbers: Gold subset average expert time 404 min (about 6.7 h); the paper also reports 9.49 h (gold) and 8.63 h (full) means, which are internally inconsistent
Average task value about $398 (gold)
Best win-plus-tie rate versus experts: Claude Opus 4.1, 47.6%; GPT-5, 39.0% wins
Expert review is assumed to take about 109 min (about $86) per task
GPT-5 speed factors: naive (no review) 90x; try once then fix 1.12x; try n times then fix 1.39x. Cost factors 474x / 1.18x / 1.63x
About 29% of GPT-5 failures were rated bad or catastrophic, about 3% catastrophic
works.relevance_to_theta: The only published workflow model that turns raw quality into net time saved once review and fix costs are included, and it is structurally almost identical to the draft max{q p(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa}. It shows that a 90x raw speedup collapses to 1.1-1.4x (about 11-28% time saved) once review is counted, so rho dominates at current q. Review at 109 min against a 404-min task gives rho ≈ 0.27.
works.limitations: US occupations with one-shot deliverables, not maintenance tickets. Review and fix times are assumptions. Cost figures are available for OpenAI models only.

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika, Alice Gatti, Cristina Menghini, ... Dan Hendrycks (CAIS and Scale AI; 47 authors)
works.what_measured: End-to-end completion of 240 real Upwork freelance projects by AI agents, judged by whether the AI deliverable is at least as good as the human one.
works.method_plain: Collect paid freelance projects together with their actual human time and cost, have agents attempt them, and have trained evaluators judge acceptability.
key_numbers: Project human time: mean 28.9 h, median 11.5 h; cost: mean $632.6, median $200
Over 6,000 hours of work worth over $140,000
Best automation rate 2.5% (Manus); Grok 4 and Sonnet 4.5 2.1%; GPT-5 (CLI) 1.7%
Failure reasons: poor quality 45.6%, incomplete 35.7%, corrupted files 17.6%, inconsistencies 14.8%
Inter-annotator agreement 94.4%
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a client-acceptance standard on projects with long, real durations (median 11.5 h), which is the q*p product for long h. Near-zero rates at about 12-29 h are consistent with p(h) falling to near zero at the long end of f_j. The project-duration data are a rare real distribution of outsourced-work lengths.
works.limitations: Late-2025 models only. Dominated by design, multimedia and creative work, with little software maintenance or BPO. Private test set.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2)
works.what_measured: Productivity of 5,179 chat-based technical-support agents (89% outside the US, mostly in the Philippines) before and after a staggered rollout of a GPT-based suggestion tool.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences and event-study comparison of agents who got the tool at different times. Outcomes are resolutions per hour, average handle time, chats per hour, and resolution rate.
key_numbers: Resolutions per hour +14% on average; about +34% for novice and low-skilled agents; about zero for the most skilled
Support chats average about 40 min (average handle time); post-treatment raw average 35 min
Average handle time falls 3.8 min (-9%); chats per hour +0.37 (+14% from 2.6)
Agents with under 1 month of tenure: +0.38 log points (about +46%) resolutions per hour
works.relevance_to_theta: The canonical offshore-BPO estimate of kappa (assistant mode): about 9-14% time saved per transaction with 2020-21 era models. Its handle-time distribution of about 40 min per chat is a concrete f_BPO anchor: BPO tasks are short (minutes to an hour), so the BPO term of theta is driven by p at short h, where it is already high, if the computer-use p curve is used.
works.limitations: Old model, assistant mode only (no full automation). One firm. US clients with Philippine agents, not Indian IT-BPO. Handle-time distribution not published at the transaction level.

works.title: AI 2027 Timelines Forecast, and the AI Futures Model: Dec 2025 Update
works.authors: Eli Lifland, Nikola Jurkovic (with FutureSearch) (2025); Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, Brendan Halstead, Alex Kastner (Dec 2025 update)
works.what_measured: Forecasts of when AI reaches a 'superhuman coder' or 'automated coder', obtained by extrapolating METR 80% time horizons and adding gap adjustments.
works.method_plain: Monte Carlo over subjective parameter distributions: current horizon, doubling time, probability of super-exponential growth, horizon required for full automation, and gaps between benchmarks and real work.
key_numbers: AI 2027 inputs: 80% horizon 15 min (Claude 3.7 Sonnet); doubling time 4.5 months (80% CI 2.5-9); P(superexponential) 0.45 (Eli) / 0.4 (Nikola)
Required 80% horizon for a superhuman coder: Eli 10 years (80% CI 1 month-1,200 years); Nikola 1.5 months (16 h-2 work-years)
Gap medians (months): engineering complexity 3 (FutureSearch 11), feedback loops 6/3 (FutureSearch 18.3)
Dec 2025 model: superhuman coder median Dec 2031 at median parameters; Eli all-things-considered about 2032.5 (10th pct 2027.5, 90th pct 2085); about 3-5 years later than AI 2027
Kokotajlo: about 4-month 'RL-era' doubling, extrapolated exponentially, reaches the automated-coder milestone about 2030; pure exponential with other parameters fixed about 2034
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows how to put a probability distribution over the future path of p(h,t), including a super-exponential branch and explicit 'benchmark-to-real-work' gap adjustments. These are analogous to the q and domain discounts in the theta recipe. Useful for building scenario bands for theta_j(t).
works.limitations: Mostly subjective parameters (the authors say so). Aimed at AI R&D automation, not services labor. A Dec 2025 bug-fix note shifted a median by about 9 months.

works.title: What skills does SWE-bench Verified evaluate?
works.authors: Florian Brand, Jean-Stanislas Denain (Epoch AI)
works.what_measured: Composition of SWE-bench Verified: annotated human time to fix, task type, repository mix.
works.method_plain: Analysis of OpenAI's annotator difficulty labels plus Epoch's own classification of the 500 issues.
key_numbers: 39% of tasks under 15 min, 52% 15 min-1 h, 8% 1-4 h, 3 tasks over 4 h (OpenAI annotations; I could not open OpenAI's page, which returned 403)
About 87% bug fixes, 9% features, 4% refactors; Django is about half the issues; the 5 largest repos are over 80%
Quick fixes average about 5 changed lines; 1-4 h tasks about 50 lines
5-10% of samples flawed or unsolvable (Epoch estimate); scaffold choice moves scores by up to about 20%
works.relevance_to_theta: An annotated distribution of task lengths for bug-fix maintenance work. It is the closest public f_maintenance, but it is selected toward small, well-specified issues. It also lets SWE-bench scores be converted into p at h of about 15-60 min.
works.limitations: Annotated human-time estimates, not measured times; METR found them optimistic. Selected open-source Python repos, not client enterprise code.

works.title: Estimating time spent on work tasks
works.authors: Stephane Hatgis-Kessell, Tomás Aguirre, Alexander Wan, Rishi Bommasani
works.what_measured: Share of working time and per-instance duration for about 18,000 O*NET tasks.
works.method_plain: Combine O*NET's task-frequency ratings with per-instance durations recovered from LLM pairwise judgments of 'which takes longer', solved as a constraint problem, then validated with worker data from several occupations.
key_numbers: Weighting exposure by time share instead of task count widens exposure gaps between occupations
Reshuffles 11 of the 25 occupations commonly reported as most exposed (toward analytical roles, away from clerical)
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly addresses the w_j (time-share) weighting that the exposure literature skipped, and gives task-instance durations, a crude cross-occupation f(h). It supports the working hypothesis: exposure papers weight by task count, not time, and so miss part of the intensive margin.
works.limitations: I read only the abstract page. Durations come from LLMs and are only partly validated. US O*NET, not Indian IT. Data-release status unclear.

works.title: An Alternative Issue Tracking Dataset of Public Jira Repositories; and JOSSE: A Software Development Effort Dataset Annotated with Expert Estimates
works.authors: Lloyd Montgomery, Clara Lüders, Walid Maalej (2022); Mohammed Alhamed, Tim Storer (2022)
works.venue: MSR 2022 Data Showcase (arXiv 2201.08368); Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7022735 (linked to ICSME 2022)
works.what_measured: Public Jira issue data. Montgomery et al.: 16 Jira instances, 1,822 projects, 2.7M issues, with fields including timeestimate, timespent, created and resolutiondate. JOSSE: Apache, JBoss and Spring Jira tasks, all labelled with actual effort and 19% with expert estimates.
works.method_plain: Scrape public Jira instances and release them as a MongoDB dump (Montgomery). Filter issues with logged work and clean them through six quality steps (JOSSE).
key_numbers: Montgomery: 2.7M issues, 32M changes, 9M comments, 1M links; CC BY 4.0; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5882881
JOSSE: actual effort on all issues, expert estimates on 19%; CC BY 4.0; used by Anthropic (2025) as ground truth for 1,000-ticket validation
Neither source page reports summary statistics of durations (not verified)
works.relevance_to_theta: The best public raw material for an hours-weighted f_maintenance(h) and f_development(h) built from logged effort (timespent), not wall-clock resolution time. Issue-type labels (bug, improvement, task) allow splitting by service line, which also gives w_j.
works.limitations: Open-source projects, where time logging is sparse and selective. Effort units and coverage of timespent are not verified. Not Indian client-delivery work, where effort is logged against SOWs.

research.stream_summary:
The way AI capability is measured over time is now fairly well defined for software. The way that capability turns into labor saved is still mostly assumed. METR's time-horizon work supplies a usable p(h,t). Its latest public data (Time Horizon 1.1, frozen Sep 2026) gives a post-2023 doubling time of about 129 days (95% CI 104-158). Frontier models now have 50% horizons of 6-17 hours, but 80% horizons only of about 1-3 hours. For most models the 50% horizon is 4-6x the 80% horizon. That slope matters as much as the level. METR's own March 2026 note shows that reasonable alternative curves move 80% horizons by up to 2x. Ord's constant-hazard model gives T99 of about T50/70; a logistic fit gives about T50/200 (my calculation). Domain matters too: computer-use horizons, the relevant ones for BPO and IT-operations work, run about 40-100x shorter than coding horizons.

On the intensive margin, three pieces of evidence pin down q and rho. METR found that about half of test-passing SWE-bench PRs would not be merged, so q ≈ 0.5. Fixing a passing agent PR took about one-third of the human task time. GDPval's review-and-fix model shrinks a 90x raw speedup to 1.1-1.4x. Anthropic's conversation-based estimate of about 80% time savings leaves review out entirely, so it is an upper bound. Causal evidence on kappa is weak: METR's RCT found a 19% slowdown in early 2025, and its 2026 redesign concedes selection bias. In BPO, AI assistance cut average handle time by about 9% on chats averaging 40 minutes.

The working hypothesis is partly supported. Exposure studies weight tasks by count, not time. New work on time shares and GDPval-style workflows begins to cover the intensive margin, but no study measures net savings as capability rises. The weakest input is f_j: no public dataset of hours-weighted durations exists for Indian IT tickets or BPO transactions.
gaps_noticed: No public, hours-weighted task-duration distribution (f_j) for IT-services maintenance tickets, infrastructure tickets or BPO transactions in Indian firms. The best proxies are open-source Jira timespent (JOSSE, Montgomery), SWE-bench annotations, and the 40-minute chat average from Brynjolfsson et al. Real client data would need firm or vendor access (ServiceNow, Jira Cloud, contact-center average-handle-time distributions).

q is measured only on SWE-bench-type bug fixes, for models up to Sonnet 4.5, with no agent iteration. Nothing measures q for infrastructure changes, testing or BPO outputs, or how q evolves for 2026 frontier models. METR's weak trend result hints q*p grows about 10 pp/yr more slowly than p.

rho (review and fix cost) rests on tiny samples: METR's n=15 estimate of about 26-42 min against 1.3 h tasks, and GDPval's assumed 109-min review. No study measures review time as a function of h and of the reviewer's familiarity.

No time-horizon or success-curve benchmark exists for BPO or back-office transaction work, nor for IT operations such as incident triage, patching and monitoring. Computer-use horizons (OSWorld) are the nearest proxy.
No public 99% horizons. High-reliability tails depend on the curve's functional form (logistic versus exponential), and the choice changes the tail by about 3x. This matters for client-facing SLAs.
Causal evidence for kappa is outdated (early-2025 tools). METR's 2026 RCT broke down because developers who refuse to work without AI select out, so no clean current estimate exists.

Human baseline times in METR come from low-context contractors; in-house professionals are faster, so mapping benchmark h onto offshore delivery h needs a context adjustment that nobody has estimated.

I could not open OpenAI's SWE-bench Verified page (403), the AI Futures interactive model, or the JOSSE paper's summary statistics; numbers from those sources come via Epoch's or Anthropic's summaries.
No India-specific academic field study on AI voice and chat agents in BPO (containment rates, handle times) was found; only vendor claims exist.

datasets.name: METR Time Horizon 1.1 model-level results
datasets.description: p50 and p80 horizons with confidence intervals for about 26 models, release dates, and fitted doubling times (post-2023: 128.7 days). Direct input for p(h,t).

datasets.name: METR Time Horizon 1.1 task-level results
datasets.description: Per-task, per-model success data with human task lengths. Lets you refit p(h) with a shared slope or alternative curves (listed on METR's time-horizons page; I did not download it).

datasets.name: Public Jira Dataset (Montgomery, Lüders, Maalej 2022)
datasets.description: MongoDB dump of 16 public Jira instances: 2.7M issues, with created and resolution dates, timeestimate, timespent, issue type, and change history. Raw material for f_maintenance(h) and f_development(h), and for w_j by issue type.

datasets.name: JOSSE effort dataset (Alhamed & Storer 2022)
datasets.description: Apache, JBoss and Spring Jira tasks with actual effort on every issue and expert estimates on 19%. CC BY 4.0. Used by Anthropic as ground truth for validating LLM time estimates.

datasets.name: SWE-bench Verified with difficulty annotations
datasets.description: 500 bug-fix tasks with annotated human-time buckets (<15 min 39%, 15-60 min 52%, 1-4 h 8%). Gives an f(h) proxy for small maintenance fixes and a way to map benchmark scores onto p.

datasets.name: METR SWE-bench maintainer review data (Whitfill et al. 2026)
datasets.description: 296 maintainer merge decisions on agent PRs plus 47 golden patches. The main q estimate. Whether the data are released is not stated in what I read.

datasets.name: GDPval gold subset
datasets.description: 220 open-sourced expert tasks (of 1,320) with expert completion times (average about 404 min) and values. Useful for review-cost (rho) modelling and long-task f(h).

datasets.name: Remote Labor Index
datasets.description: 240 real Upwork projects with actual human hours (median 11.5 h) and cost. Only 10 are public; the 230-project test set is private.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index task-level time-savings estimates
datasets.description: LLM-estimated time with and without AI, aggregated to O*NET tasks (about 80% median savings, excluding review). Release of task-level estimates was not confirmed on the page I read; earlier Economic Index releases have been public.

datasets.name: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond customer-support data
datasets.description: Chat-level data on 5,179 mostly Philippine support agents (average handle time about 40 min). Proprietary firm data; the paper's replication package is the likely route, but access was not verified.

datasets.name: Time shares for O*NET tasks (Hatgis-Kessell et al. 2026)
datasets.description: Per-instance durations and time shares for about 18,000 O*NET tasks. Candidate w_j and f(h) priors; release status unclear from the abstract page.

works.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (v1 and v2 titled 'Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks')
works.authors: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, Katharyn Garcia, Max Hasin, Sami Jawhar, Megan Kinniment, Nate Rush, Sydney Von Arx, Ryan Bloom, Thomas Broadley, Haoxing Du, Brian Goodrich, Nikola Jurkovic, Luke Harold Miles, Seraphina Nix, Tao Lin, Chris Painter, Neev Parikh, David Rein, Lucas Jun Koba Sato, Hjalmar Wijk, Daniel M. Ziegler, Elizabeth Barnes, Lawrence Chan (METR; 26 authors)
works.what_measured: The '50% time horizon': the length of task (measured by how long skilled humans take) that an AI agent completes with 50% probability. Tasks are software, ML research-engineering and cyber tasks: HCAST (97 tasks), RE-Bench (7) and SWAA (66 short tasks), 170 in total.
works.method_plain: Humans with domain expertise are timed on each task. Each AI agent is run several times per task. For each model, a logistic curve of success against log(human time) is fitted, and the task length where predicted success is 50% (and 80%) is read off. That length is then plotted against model release date.
key_numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 50% horizon 'around 50 minutes' (abstract). Ord (2025) quotes the v1 figures as 59 min at 50% and 15 min at 80%.

The frontier 50% horizon has doubled about every 7 months since 2019 (abstract). The abstract says the trend 'may have accelerated in 2024'. The current HTML (v4) gives 207 days for 2019-2025, and the paper calls its 2024-only estimate not robust. The record's '~4 months' figure was not found in this paper; it comes from Kwa & Cheng (2025).

Task lengths in the paper: SWAA tasks take seconds (about 1-30 s), HCAST tasks run from 1 minute to 30 hours, and RE-Bench tasks are treated as 8 h each. The record's 'up to 16 hours' is not confirmed.
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the source of the functional form and the trend for p(h,t): a logistic curve in log h, with a per-model slope and a doubling time. It says nothing directly about q, rho, kappa or f_j.
works.limitations: Tasks are clean, self-contained, scored automatically and need little context. Contractor baseliners took about 5-18x longer than repository maintainers on internal PR tasks, so h is likely overstated for in-house, high-context work. Few tasks are very long. Success means 'passes the automated scoring', not 'mergeable'. Several numbers changed between v1 and v4, so cite the version.
works.corrections: 1) Task range: the record's '1 second to 16 hours' is not in the paper, which describes HCAST tasks up to 30 hours. 2) The '(about every 4 months)' attached to the 2024 acceleration was not found in this paper; the abstract says only 'may have accelerated'. 3) Removed the unconfirmed limitation 'only about 2 tasks per model-run family at long lengths'. 4) Added the full author list and version dates; the NeurIPS 2025 venue comes from arXiv's journal-ref field. 5) The original title was confirmed through Ord's reference list.

works.title: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models (Time Horizon 1.1 page and data files benchmark_results_1_1.yaml, task_results_1_1.yaml)
works.authors: METR
works.year: 2026 (TH1.1 release post dated 29 Jan 2026; page last updated 8 Sep 2026)
works.what_measured: Updated 50% and 80% horizons, with confidence intervals, for 26 models on the TH1.1 suite (228 unique tasks in the task file), plus fitted doubling times.
works.method_plain: The same method as Kwa et al., on a larger suite with more long tasks. The model-level YAML gives p50 and p80 estimates with CIs. The task-level YAML gives, for each agent and task, the human minutes, successes and runs, plus each agent's fitted logistic coefficient and intercept.
key_numbers: Doubling time from 2023 on: 128.7 days (95% CI 104.4-158.0); all-time stitched: 187.8 days. The file notes that both exclude points whose central p50 estimate is above 16 h. These numbers are in the YAML, not in the page text.
Claude Opus 4.6 (released 2026-02-05): p50 718.8 min (about 12.0 h), p80 69.9 min
Claude Mythos Preview early (2026-04-07): p50 1044.8 min (about 17.4 h, above the 16 h reliability limit), p80 185.9 min
p50/p80 ratio: 18 of 26 models fall between 4.0x and 6.0x (verifier's tabulation). The full range is 2.3x to 10.3x. Opus 4.6 is the highest at 10.3x; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) is 7.9x.
Claude 3.7 Sonnet under TH1.1: p50 60.4 min, p80 12.1 min
The page says measurements above 16 h are unreliable with the current task suite, and that it is no longer actively updated. No 99% horizons are reported.
31 of the 228 tasks have human time of 8 h or more, and 5 have 16 h or more (verifier's count from the task file)
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the most current machine-readable input for p(h,t). The task-level file holds the raw success counts and human times, so p(h) can be refit with a slope shared across models or with other curve shapes. The 4-6x gap between p50 and p80 shows how much theta_j depends on the slope.
works.limitations: Recent-model p50 values are fragile (see Barry 2026); Opus 4.6 falls about 40% on private-only tasks. Few long tasks. The page is frozen as of Sep 2026. Doubling times exclude models above 16 h.
works.corrections: All numbers were checked against the downloaded YAML. Minor clarifications: the doubling times are in the YAML, not the page text; 'mostly 4-6x' is 18 of 26 models, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct) at 7.9x is a second outlier besides Opus 4.6; the 'about 31 long tasks' is confirmed only if 'long' means 8 h or more.

works.title: Impact of modelling assumptions on time horizon results
works.authors: Alexander Barry (METR)
works.what_measured: How sensitive 50% and 80% horizons are to: the curve family (logistic, fixed-slope logistic, logistic with a reliability ceiling, beta-binomial, Cauchy, Weibull, minimum-squared-error fits, and nonparametric LOESS, spline, isotonic and rolling-average fits); regularization; task weighting; private versus public tasks; and noise in task lengths.
works.method_plain: Refit the same success data under many curve shapes and data choices, then compare the resulting horizons and the out-of-sample fit (leave-one-family-out cross-validation).
key_numbers: Reasonable alternative fits cut recent models' 50% horizons by up to 35% and raise their 80% horizons by up to 100%
For Opus 4.6, reasonable methods vary by about 1.5x at 50% and about 2x at 80%

Correcting for noisy task lengths (SIMEX) could cut frontier 50% horizons by about 30% (0-60% cannot be ruled out) and raise 80% horizons by about 20% (range 0-50%). For Opus 4.6 specifically, the 50% horizon falls 25-40% under the logistic model.
Opus 4.6 on private-only tasks: the 50% horizon falls 40%, from 11h59m to 7h11m
The fixed-slope logistic, one slope shared by all models, performed best on both cross-validation metrics
The logistic model is very sensitive to performance on very easy tasks. This tends to give shallow slopes, which lower 80% horizons and raise 50% horizons
works.relevance_to_theta: theta_j integrates p over the whole task-length distribution, so it depends on the slope and the curve shape, not only on the 50% point. The note shows that the high-reliability region moves by up to 2x across reasonable methods. Implication for the recipe: fit one shared slope, and report theta_j under at least the logistic and constant-hazard (or Weibull) curves.
works.limitations: A research note, not peer reviewed. Software tasks only. No doubling-time estimates.
works.corrections: Minor: the SIMEX 80% effect has a stated range of 0-50%. The note attributes shallow slopes to the logistic model in general, not only to per-model fits. The '35%/100%' figures come from 'reasonable alternative fits', which include more than curve shape.

works.title: Is there a half-life for the success rates of AI agents?
works.authors: Toby Ord (Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, University of Oxford)
works.what_measured: Whether the success-versus-length data in Kwa et al. fit a constant-hazard model (exponential survival), in which each minute of human-equivalent work carries a fixed chance of failure.
works.method_plain: Overlay a one-parameter exponential decay, p(h) = 0.5^(h/T50), on Kwa et al.'s per-model success curves and compare it visually with their log-logistic fit. Then derive the implied high-reliability horizons. Ord does no formal statistical comparison and says one should be done.
key_numbers: T80 ≈ 1/3 T50; T90 ≈ 1/7 T50; T99 ≈ 1/70 T50; T99.9 ≈ 1/700 T50 (each additional nine divides the horizon by 10)
Assuming a 7-month doubling time, T80 reaches a given length about 1 year after T50 does, T90 about 2 years after, T99 about 4 years after and T99.9 about 6 years after
Kwa et al.'s 80% horizon for Claude 3.7 Sonnet was 0.25 of its 50% horizon (15 vs 59 min), close to the constant-hazard prediction of 0.322
Human success decays more slowly than constant hazard predicts: still above 20% at 12 h, against a predicted 6.25%
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a one-parameter, interpretable alternative form for p(h,t) and makes the reliability tails explicit. The record's own derivation was checked and is arithmetically correct: a logistic in log h with T80 = T50/5 implies T99 ≈ T50/207, against T50/70 under constant hazard.
works.limitations: A short note that has not been peer reviewed. The comparison of fits is visual only. It covers one task suite, and generalization is left open.
works.corrections: Clarified the method: Ord fits an exponential curve and compares it with the log-logistic by eye; he runs no formal model comparison. All key numbers match the PDF text.

works.title: How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains?
works.authors: Thomas Kwa, Vincent Cheng (METR)
works.what_measured: Time horizons and their growth rates across '9 existing benchmarks'. The table lists 11 entries: METR-HRS, SWE-bench Verified, OSWorld, WebArena, Mock AIME, MATH, LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, Video-MME, Tesla FSD Tracker and RLBench.
works.method_plain: Estimate human task lengths for each benchmark. Fit success-versus-length curves, or assume a slope when only overall scores are available. Then compare horizon levels and doubling times.
key_numbers: Software and reasoning domains: 50-200+ minute horizons, currently doubling every 2-6 months. METR-HRS shows about 100-minute horizons doubling every about 4 months since 2024.
Visual computer use (OSWorld, WebArena): horizons 40-100x shorter than the software/reasoning cluster (the text also says about 50x), with similar growth rates, about 2 years behind
Tesla FSD: about 0.6 doublings per year (about 20 months per doubling)
Default slope when only overall scores are available: beta ≈ 0.6, the METR-HRS average. A benchmark is excluded from the main analysis when more than half its models have beta < 0.25.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that p(h,t) depends on the domain. BPO and IT-operations work done through GUIs resembles computer use, whose horizons are about 40-100x shorter than coding, so theta_BPO likely needs its own, lower p curve rather than the METR-HRS coding curve.
works.limitations: Mapping benchmarks onto human time is rough, and many slopes are assumed rather than fitted. No BPO or IT-operations benchmark is included. Mid-2025 data.
works.corrections: Corrected the exclusion rule: a benchmark is excluded from the main analysis when more than half of its models have beta < 0.25; it is not true that any benchmark with beta < 0.25 is excluded. Noted that the post says 9 benchmarks but tables 11 entries, and that the computer-use multiple appears as 40-100x, about 50x and about 100x in different places.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: How often AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests would be merged by the real repository maintainers.
works.method_plain: Four maintainers (2 scikit-learn, 1 Sphinx, 1 pytest) reviewed 296 AI-generated PRs without being told who wrote them. The PRs came from Claude 3.5 Sonnet (old), Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. Of 47 original human 'golden' PRs, a random half were reviewed to set a noise baseline. Scores are normalized to the golden-patch merge rate. Agents could not iterate on feedback.
key_numbers: After normalization, the automated grader's score exceeds the maintainer merge rate by about 24.2 pp (SE 2.7); unnormalized, by 34.9 pp (SE 2.2)
About 68% of the golden (human) patches were merged

Maintainer-judged scores improve 9.6 pp/yr more slowly than grader scores (SE 5.5). This is weak evidence, significant only at the 10% level, and it falls to 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1) when only state-of-the-art models are kept.
Claude Sonnet 4.5: about a 50-minute horizon under the grader versus about 8 minutes under maintainer review, which the authors call roughly a 7x overstatement
The summary says 'roughly half' of test-passing PRs would not be merged
Coverage: 3 of 12 repos and 95 of 500 issues
works.relevance_to_theta: The direct source for q ≈ 0.5, though the value depends on normalization. Whether q is constant is unclear, because the slower-trend result is fragile. The roughly 7x shrink in horizon under the maintainer standard suggests modelling q*p as a shifted p(h) curve.
works.limitations: 3 of 12 repos and 95 of 500 issues. Static review, with no chance for the agent to iterate. Older issues. The latest model tested is Sonnet 4.5. The authors explicitly do not claim a fundamental capability limit, and say better elicitation could fix many problems. Release of the data is not mentioned.
works.corrections: Minor: the authors describe the horizon gap as roughly 7x, not 6x. Added the state-of-the-art-only robustness figure (4.1 pp/yr, SE 12.1).

works.title: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation (URL slug: 'towards-reconciling-slowdown-with-time-horizons')
works.authors: David Rein (METR)
works.year: 2025 (Aug; the page shows 13 Aug 2025, the URL says 2025-08-12)
works.what_measured: On 18 real tasks from two repositories used in METR's RCT (15 from stdlib-js, 3 from hypothesis): the agent's pass rate on the human-written tests, whether its PRs could be merged as-is, and the estimated human time to fix them.
works.method_plain: Run Claude 3.7 Sonnet in an Inspect ReAct agent on the tasks and score its patches against the human PR's tests. Then review 15 PRs by hand against five failure modes and estimate how long a human would need to bring each to mergeable quality.
key_numbers: Test pass rate 38% (±19%, 95% CI); none of the 15 manually reviewed PRs was mergeable as-is
Estimated fix time: about 42 min on average across reviewed PRs, and about 26 min for PRs that passed the tests (minimum 15 min)
Human task length averaged 1.3 h (range 20 min-4 h), so fixing a passing PR costs about one-third of the task
All 15 reviewed PRs had at least 3 of the 5 failure modes: core functionality, test coverage, documentation, linting/formatting/typing, and other code quality
works.relevance_to_theta: An empirical anchor for review-plus-fix cost: about 0.33 of h for passing PRs on mature repositories. It suggests replacing the binary q with a fix-cost term, because rejected output is not worthless.
works.limitations: Tiny sample (n=15 reviewed; 3 tasks not reviewed). One older model with a basic scaffold. Two high-standard repositories. Fix times are estimates, not measurements.
works.corrections: Title corrected to the page's title, 'Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation'; 'Towards Reconciling Slowdown with Time Horizons' appears only in the URL slug. The page date is 13 Aug 2025. All numbers confirmed.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity (plus the 24 Feb 2026 update, 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design')
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (2025); Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (2026 update)
works.what_measured: The causal effect of allowing AI tools (mainly Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on task completion time for experienced developers working in their own mature repositories.
works.method_plain: A randomized controlled trial: 246 real issues were each randomly assigned 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed', and completion times were compared.
key_numbers: AI increased completion time by 19% (a slowdown). Developers forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and believed afterward that AI had given a 20% reduction.
Economics experts predicted 39% shorter times and ML experts 38%
16 developers (about 5 years' prior experience in their projects), 246 tasks

2026 update (late-2025 study: 57 developers, 800+ tasks): newly recruited developers show a -4% change in completion time, i.e. about 4% faster (CI -15% to +9%); returning developers -18% (CI -38% to +9%). METR calls the data unreliable because developers who do not want to work without AI select out (30-50% said they skipped tasks). It believes speedups are probably higher now, but says its data are only very weak evidence of how much.
works.relevance_to_theta: The best causal evidence on kappa (assistant-mode speedup) for expert maintenance-type work: about zero or negative in early 2025, and uncertain since. The gap between self-reported and measured speed warns against taking kappa from surveys or from LLM-estimated time savings.
works.limitations: Expert developers in their own large, familiar repositories, unlike Indian IT services teams working on client code. Early-2025 tools. The 2026 redesign shows that selection problems now dominate these RCTs.
works.corrections: The 2026 update was opened in full, not just seen in a search excerpt. Fixed the sign wording: '-4%' is a change in completion time, meaning about a 4% speedup, not a 'speedup of -4%'. Added the returning-developer estimate and the sample size of the 2026 study. Added arXiv version dates.

works.title: Estimating AI productivity gains from Claude conversations
works.authors: Alex Tamkin, Peter McCrory (Anthropic)
works.year: 2025 (Nov; the page header says 25 Nov 2025, the citation block says 2025-11-05)
works.what_measured: For 100,000 Claude.ai conversations, Claude's estimate of how long each task would take a professional without AI and how long it took with AI, aggregated to O*NET tasks and occupations.
works.method_plain: An LLM estimates time without AI and time with AI for each conversation; time saved = 1 - ratio. The duration estimates were validated on a set of open-source JIRA tickets. The page links to Zenodo record 7022735, which is the JOSSE dataset, but does not name it.
key_numbers: Tasks would take 'on average about 90 minutes' without AI (1.4 h is also stated in places, which is slightly inconsistent)
Median time savings about 80% (84% in the results text, 81% in a figure caption)
Implied US labor productivity growth of 1.8%/yr over 10 years at universal adoption (an exercise, not a forecast); implied TFP growth about 1.1%/yr

Validation on 1,000 JIRA tasks: Claude Sonnet 4.5 Spearman 0.44 (r_log 0.46) versus human developer estimates 0.50 (r_log 0.67). Claude's estimates are compressed: it overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones.
Software developers account for 19% of the aggregate gain; customer service representatives about 4%
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest existing attempt at a task-level 'fraction of time saved'. It is a template for theta_j, but it leaves out time spent validating or refining output outside the chat (rho) and acceptance failures (q), so it likely overstates net savings. Its JIRA validation shows that LLM-estimated h is noisy (Spearman 0.44), which matters if f_j is built from LLM estimates.
works.limitations: Excludes time outside the chat, such as review and iteration. Claude.ai users only. No ground truth for the savings estimates. The authors note that RCTs find smaller gains. Task-level estimates are not released; the page says aggregate datasets will be shared in future.
works.corrections: The page does not name 'JOSSE'. It links to zenodo.org/records/7022735, which is JOSSE, so the identification is correct but inferred. Noted the date discrepancy on the page and the 90-minute versus 1.4-hour inconsistency.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, et al. (OpenAI; 19 authors)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded head-to-head comparisons of model versus human deliverables on 1,320 real work tasks from 44 occupations in the top 9 US GDP sectors (220 of them open-sourced as a gold subset), plus a speed and cost model that includes expert review and fixing.
works.method_plain: Professionals with an average of 14 years' experience wrote tasks from their own work, and completion times were recorded. Other experts compared AI and human outputs blind. A 'try the model, review, then fix or resample' workflow converts win rates into net speed and cost factors.
key_numbers: Gold-subset expert time: 404 min (HT, appendix). Table 3 lists a 9.49 h mean for the gold subset and Table 4 lists 8.63 h for the full set, so the paper is internally inconsistent.
Average task value $398.46 (gold) and $391.44 (full)
Claude Opus 4.1: 47.6% of gold deliverables rated as good as or better than the expert's (wins plus ties). GPT-5: 39.0% wins.
Expert review averages 109 min, costing $86 (RT/RC in the workflow model)
GPT-5 speed factors: 90x (naive), 1.12x (try once then fix), 1.39x (try n times then fix). Cost factors: 474x, 1.18x and 1.63x.
About 29% of GPT-5 ratings were 'bad or catastrophic', with about 3% of failures marked catastrophic
works.relevance_to_theta: A published workflow model that turns raw quality into net time saved once review and fix costs are included. It is conceptually close to the draft max{...} expression. A 90x raw speedup becomes 1.12-1.39x, i.e. about 11-28% of time saved, once review is counted. A 109-minute review against a 404-minute task gives rho ≈ 0.27.
works.limitations: US occupations with one-shot deliverables, not maintenance tickets. Review and fix times are inputs to a stylized model. Speed and cost factors are reported for OpenAI models.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Added a fourth named author and the author count (19). The claim in the record that this is 'the only published workflow model' and is 'structurally almost identical' to the draft formula is an overstatement and was softened.

works.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
works.authors: Mantas Mazeika, Alice Gatti, Cristina Menghini, ... Dan Hendrycks (Center for AI Safety and Scale AI; 47 authors)
works.what_measured: End-to-end completion of 240 real freelance projects by AI agents, judged by whether the AI deliverable is at least as acceptable as the human one.
works.method_plain: Collect real paid freelance projects together with their actual human time and cost, have agents attempt them, and have trained evaluators judge whether the result is acceptable.
key_numbers: Human time per project: mean 28.9 h, median 11.5 h. Cost: mean $632.6, median $200.
Over 6,000 hours of work worth over $140,000 in total
Automation rates: Manus 2.5%; Grok 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 2.1%; GPT-5 (CLI) 1.7%; ChatGPT agent 1.3%; GPT-5 (CUA) and Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.8%
Failure reasons (not mutually exclusive): poor quality 45.6%, incomplete 35.7%, corrupted files 17.6%, inconsistencies 14.8%
Inter-annotator agreement 94.4%
230 projects form the private test set; 10 are public
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a client-acceptance standard on long, real projects (median 11.5 h), which amounts to q*p at long h. Near-zero rates are consistent with p(h) falling to almost nothing at the long end of f_j. The project durations are a rare real distribution of outsourced-work lengths, but only 10 projects are public.
works.limitations: Late-2025 models only. The category mix leans toward creative and design work (video and animation, 3D/CAD, graphic design, audio); the exact shares were not confirmed. Little software maintenance or BPO. The test set is private.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. The category mix is described in the appendix but shares were not checked, so 'dominated by' is softened.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2): 889-942
works.what_measured: Productivity of 5,179 customer-support agents (89% outside the US, mainly in the Philippines) at a firm selling software to small businesses, before and after a staggered rollout (Nov 2020-Feb 2021) of a GPT-based tool that suggests replies.
works.method_plain: Difference-in-differences and event-study comparisons of agents who got the tool at different times. Outcomes: resolutions per hour, average handle time, chats per hour, resolution rate and customer satisfaction.
key_numbers: Resolutions per hour +14% on average (+13.8% with agent and tenure fixed effects); +34% (0.29 log points) for the lowest skill quintile; no gain for the most skilled
Support chats average about 40 minutes; post-treatment agents average 35 minutes (raw difference)
Average handle time falls 3.8 min (-9%); chats per hour +0.37 (+14% from a baseline of 2.6)
Agents with under 1 month of tenure: +0.38 log points (46%) in resolutions per hour
works.relevance_to_theta: The canonical offshore-support estimate of kappa (assistant mode): about 9% less time per chat, or about 12% in time-per-resolution terms (1 - 1/1.14), with a 2020-21 GPT model. The average of about 40 minutes per chat is a concrete anchor for f_BPO. Caution: if BPO uses the computer-use p curve (horizons 40-100x shorter than coding), p at 40 minutes is low, not high. The record's statement that p is 'already high' there contradicts its own BPO mapping.
works.limitations: Old model, assistant mode only (no full automation). One firm. Philippine agents serving a US software firm's customers, not Indian IT-BPO. No transaction-level distribution of handle times.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the NBER PDF. The relevance text was corrected: it says BPO p is 'already high' at short h under the computer-use curve, which contradicts the 40-100x shorter computer-use horizons.

works.title: AI 2027 Timelines Forecast; and AI Futures Model: Dec 2025 Update
works.authors: Eli Lifland, Nikola Jurkovic, with FutureSearch (Apr 2025); Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, Brendan Halstead, Alex Kastner (31 Dec 2025 update)
works.what_measured: Forecasts of when AI reaches a 'superhuman coder' (SC) or 'automated coder' (AC), made by extrapolating METR time horizons and adding gap adjustments.
works.method_plain: Monte Carlo simulation over subjective parameter distributions: the current horizon, the doubling time, the probability of super-exponential growth, the horizon needed for full automation, and the gaps between benchmarks and real work.
key_numbers: AI 2027 inputs: 80% horizon 15 min (Claude 3.7 Sonnet); doubling time 4.5 months (80% CI 2.5-9); P(superexponential) 0.45 (Eli) / 0.4 (Nikola)
80% horizon required for SC: Eli 10 years (80% CI 1 month-1,200 years); Nikola 1.5 months (16 h-2 work-years)
Gap medians: engineering complexity 3 months (FutureSearch 11); feedback loops 6 (Eli) / 3 (Nikola) months (FutureSearch 18.3)

Dec 2025 model: SC median Dec 2031 at median parameters. Eli's all-things-considered distribution: 10th percentile 2027.5, median 2032.5, 90th percentile 2085. About 3-5 years later than the previous model.
Kokotajlo: with the roughly 4-month 'RL-era' doubling and an exponential trend, AC arrives in 2030; with a pure exponential and his other parameters fixed, in 2034
The AI 2027 timelines page notes a code bug in the intermediate speedup calculation that had 'about a 9 month impact' on the SC median
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows how to put a probability distribution over the future path of p(h,t), including a super-exponential branch and explicit discounts for the gap between benchmarks and real work. These discounts play the same role as q and the domain discounts in the theta recipe. Useful for scenario bands on theta_j(t).
works.limitations: Mostly subjective parameters (the authors say the forecast relies substantially on intuitive judgment). Aimed at automating AI R&D, not services labor. The FutureSearch figures are described inconsistently on the page (2 versus 3 forecasters).
works.corrections: The 9-month bug-fix note is on the AI 2027 timelines page and refers to the SC median. The Dec 2025 update post gives no 9-month figure, and the date of the bug note was not confirmed as Dec 2025. Added the dates of both pieces.

works.title: What skills does SWE-bench Verified evaluate?
works.authors: Florian Brand, Jean-Stanislas Denain (Epoch AI)
works.what_measured: Composition of SWE-bench Verified: annotated human time to fix, task type, repository mix and age.
works.method_plain: Analysis of the SWE-bench Verified annotators' difficulty (time) labels, plus Epoch's own classification of the 500 issues.
key_numbers: 39% of tasks under 15 min, 52% 15 min-1 h, 8% 1-4 h, 3 tasks over 4 h (time estimates by the SWE-bench Verified annotators; the labels are in the 'difficulty' field of the Hugging Face dataset)
87% bug fixes, 9% feature requests, 4% refactors. Django is nearly half the issues; the 5 largest of the 12 repos make up over 80%.
Quick fixes average about 5 changed lines; 1-4 h tasks about 50
5-10% of samples flawed or unsolvable (Epoch's estimate); the scaffold can change scores by up to about 20%
works.relevance_to_theta: An annotated distribution of task lengths for bug-fix maintenance work, the closest public f_maintenance proxy, though selected toward small, well-specified issues. It also allows SWE-bench scores to be mapped onto p at h of about 15-60 min.
works.limitations: Time buckets are annotators' estimates, not measured times; METR found them optimistic. Selected open-source Python repositories; half the issues are from 2020 or earlier.
works.corrections: Authors and date confirmed (13 Jun 2025). The time labels were confirmed directly in the Hugging Face dataset (princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified, 'difficulty' field, 500 rows), so they no longer rest only on Epoch's summary. Citation confidence raised to high.

works.title: Estimating time spent on work tasks
works.authors: Stephane Hatgis-Kessell, Tomás Aguirre, Alexander Wan, Rishi Bommasani
works.what_measured: Time shares, and the time per single instance, for nearly 18,000 tasks covering nearly all US jobs.
works.method_plain: Split each task's time into its expected frequency (from O*NET) and the time one instance takes. The per-instance time is estimated by solving a constraint satisfaction problem built on language-model pairwise judgments of which task takes longer. The estimates are validated by characterizing the solution space and by collecting data from workers in several occupations.
key_numbers: Weighting AI exposure by share of working time instead of share of tasks widens the gap between the least and most exposed jobs: measured exposure falls for most occupations but rises for the most exposed
Reshuffles 11 of the 25 occupations widely reported as most exposed, moving the top of the list away from clerical work toward analytical roles
works.relevance_to_theta: Directly addresses the time-share weighting (w_j) in aggregation and gives per-instance durations, a rough cross-occupation f(h). It shows that the choice of weights matters. It is evidence about aggregation, not about the intensive margin (how much labor AI removes within an exposed task). The abstract also notes that 'recent work suggests weighting tasks by time spent', so prior work is not uniformly count-weighted.
works.limitations: Verified at the abstract level only. Durations come from LLMs and are partly validated. US O*NET, not Indian IT. Data release not mentioned on the abstract page. Odd metadata: the ID prefix 2608 implies Aug 2026, but the page shows v1 on 26 Jun 2026.
works.corrections: Abstract, authors and date confirmed from the arXiv page metadata. The relevance claim was rewritten: time weighting concerns aggregation (w_j), not the intensive margin, and the paper itself says some recent work already weights by time.

works.title: An Alternative Issue Tracking Dataset of Public Jira Repositories; and JOSSE: A Software Development Effort Dataset Annotated with Expert Estimates
works.authors: Lloyd Montgomery, Clara Lüders, Walid Maalej (2022); Mohammed Alhamed, Tim Storer (2022)
works.venue: MSR '22 (19th International Conference on Mining Software Repositories), DOI 10.1145/3524842.3528486, arXiv 2201.08368; JOSSE: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7022735 (record lists ICSME 2022)
works.what_measured: Public Jira issue data. Montgomery et al.: 16 public Jira instances, 1,822 projects, 2.7M issues, with fields including timeestimate, timespent and created/resolution timestamps. JOSSE (JIRA Open-Source Software Effort): Apache, JBoss and Spring Jira tasks, all annotated with actual effort and 19% with expert estimates.
works.method_plain: Montgomery et al. scraped public Jira instances through the Jira API V2 and released them as a MongoDB dump (5.8 GB ZIP; current Zenodo version v7, Jun 2025). JOSSE filtered issues that had logged effort and applied six data-quality refinement steps.
key_numbers: Montgomery: 2.7M issues, 32M changes, 9M comments, 1M issue links; CC BY 4.0; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5882881
JOSSE: actual effort on all issues and expert estimates on 19%; CC BY 4.0 per Zenodo (the Glasgow page lists no license). Anthropic (2025) links to it for its 1,000-ticket validation.
Neither source page reports summary statistics of durations (not verified)
works.relevance_to_theta: The best public raw material for hours-weighted f_maintenance(h) and f_development(h) built from logged effort (timespent) rather than wall-clock resolution time. Issue-type labels allow a split by service line, and hence w_j.
works.limitations: Open-source projects, where time logging is sparse and selective. Coverage and units of timespent are unverified. Not Indian client-delivery work.
works.corrections: Venue corrected to the MSR '22 proceedings (DOI 10.1145/3524842.3528486); the 'Data Showcase' track label was not confirmed on the pages read. Noted that the Montgomery Zenodo record is now v7 (23 Jun 2025), and that the Glasgow repository page states no license while Zenodo states CC BY 4.0. The field is spelled 'resolutionedate' (sic) in the paper's table.

summary_flags: 'Three pieces of evidence pin down q and rho' overstates it. q ≈ 0.5 comes from 3 repos and 95 issues, models up to Sonnet 4.5, no iteration, and depends on normalization (24.2 pp normalized vs 34.9 pp unnormalized gap). rho comes from n=15 PRs (Rein) and a stylized GDPval workflow. They are anchors, not pinned values.

Frontier 50% horizons 'of 6-17 hours' need caveats. The 17.4 h Mythos figure is above METR's 16 h reliability limit. Opus 4.6's 12 h falls to about 7.2 h on private-only tasks and could be about 30% lower after the noise correction (Barry 2026).
'For most models the 50% horizon is 4-6x the 80% horizon' is accurate for 18 of 26 models, but the full range is 2.3-10.3x.
'T99 ≈ T50/200 under a logistic' is the researcher's own calculation (checked: about T50/207 when T80 = T50/5), not a published figure. Label it as derived.

'Exposure studies weight tasks by count, not time' is too broad. Hatgis-Kessell et al. say prior weights are 'idiosyncratic' and that some recent work already weights by time. Their paper is about aggregation weights (w_j), not the intensive margin.

'No study measures net savings as capability rises' is an absence claim that was not verified. Whitfill et al. track maintainer-judged quality across model generations, and GDPval reports net speed and cost factors by model. Better: 'no study measures net labor savings by task-length band for IT-services work as capability rises'.
Gap: 'q*p grows about 10 pp/yr more slowly than p' rests on a result significant only at 10%, which falls to 4.1 pp/yr (SE 12.1) with state-of-the-art models only. Treat it as suggestive at most.

Gap: 'q is measured only on SWE-bench-type bug fixes' is too strong. Rein (2025) measures mergeability on RCT-repository tasks, and GDPval and RLI measure acceptance of deliverables in other domains, though none covers IT services or BPO.

The Anthropic ~80% savings is called an 'upper bound'. It excludes review time, so it likely overstates net savings, but it is LLM-estimated with no ground truth, so 'likely overstated' is safer than 'upper bound'.

The Brynjolfsson relevance text says BPO p is 'already high' at short h under the computer-use curve. That contradicts the summary's own claim that computer-use horizons are 40-100x shorter than coding horizons.
The GDPval relevance text calls it 'the only published workflow model' and 'structurally almost identical' to the draft formula. Neither claim was verified, so both were softened.

Kwa et al. key numbers: the 'about every 4 months' 2024 acceleration and the '1 second to 16 hours' task range are not in the paper as stated. The paper gives no figure for the acceleration, and HCAST tasks run up to 30 h. The 4-month figure for METR-HRS is from Kwa & Cheng (2025).
The METR uplift update was listed as 'seen via search excerpt only'. It has now been opened and verified. The '-4%' is a change in completion time (about 4% faster), not a 'speedup of -4%'.
The 9-month bug fix belongs to the AI 2027 timelines page (SC median), not the Dec 2025 model update.
verify.corrected_summary:
AI capability over time is now fairly well measured for software, but how that capability turns into labor saved is still mostly assumed. METR's time-horizon work gives a usable form for p(h,t): a logistic curve in log task length. Its latest public data (Time Horizon 1.1, page frozen Sep 2026) gives a post-2023 doubling time of about 129 days (95% CI 104-158), excluding points above 16 h. The most recent frontier models have 50% horizons of roughly 6-12 hours, with one model at about 17 h, above METR's 16 h reliability limit. Their 80% horizons are about 1-3 hours. For 18 of 26 models the 50% horizon is 4-6x the 80% horizon (full range 2.3-10.3x). That slope matters as much as the level. METR's March 2026 note shows that reasonable alternative fits change 80% horizons by up to 2x and could cut frontier 50% horizons by about 30% after correcting for noisy task lengths. Ord's constant-hazard model implies T99 ≈ T50/70; a logistic fit with typical TH1.1 slopes implies about T50/200 (our own calculation). Domain matters too: computer-use horizons, the closest proxy for BPO and IT-operations work, run about 40-100x shorter than software horizons.

On the intensive margin, a few small studies give rough anchors for q and rho but do not pin them down. METR maintainers would not merge roughly half of test-passing SWE-bench PRs (3 repos, models up to Sonnet 4.5, no iteration), which suggests q ≈ 0.5, depending on normalization. In 15 reviewed agent PRs, fixing a test-passing PR was estimated at about one-third of the human task time. GDPval's review-and-fix model shrinks GPT-5's 90x raw speedup to 1.12-1.39x (about 11-28% time saved). Anthropic's LLM-estimated median time saving of about 80% excludes review and validation, so it likely overstates net savings. Causal evidence on kappa is weak and dated. METR's early-2025 RCT found a 19% slowdown, and its late-2025 follow-up (about 4% faster for new recruits, wide CI) is compromised by developers who would not work without AI opting out. In offshore customer support, AI assistance cut average handle time by about 9% on chats averaging 40 minutes, using a 2020-21 model.

The working hypothesis is partly supported. Exposure measures mainly answer whether AI can touch a task. Recent work shows that weighting tasks by time instead of count changes the results (an aggregation, w_j, issue), and workflow models such as GDPval's begin to net out review costs. Still, no study we found measures net labor saved by task-length band for IT-services or BPO work as capability rises. The weakest input is f_j: no public dataset of hours-weighted durations exists for Indian IT tickets or BPO transactions. Open-source Jira effort logs and SWE-bench time labels are the best public proxies.
verify.dataset_notes:
- **METR TH1.1 model-level (benchmark_results_1_1.yaml):** public; downloaded and confirmed. 26 models with p50 and p80 estimates and CIs, and doubling times of 128.7 days (post-2023) and 187.8 days (stitched).
- **METR TH1.1 task-level (task_results_1_1.yaml):** public; downloaded and confirmed (about 686 KB). It holds 228 unique tasks, and for each agent and task the human_minutes, n_successes, n_runs and task_weight, plus each agent's fitted logistic coefficient and intercept. Human times run from 0.02 to 1,800 min; 31 tasks are 8 h or longer and 5 are 16 h or longer. Analysis code is at GitHub METR/eval-analysis-public.
- **Public Jira Dataset (Montgomery et al.):** public, CC BY 4.0. The DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5882881 resolves to the Zenodo record, now version v7 (23 Jun 2025), a 5.8 GB MongoDB dump.
- **JOSSE:** the Zenodo record 7022735 states CC BY 4.0. The Glasgow repository page (researchdata.gla.ac.uk/1723) lists no files or license. Whether the files can be downloaded from Zenodo was not checked.
- **SWE-bench Verified time labels:** a better primary URL is https://huggingface.co/datasets/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified. The 'difficulty' field holds the time buckets for 500 rows (public). The Epoch blog is a secondary summary.
- **METR maintainer review data (Whitfill et al.):** access unknown; the note does not mention a data release.
- **GDPval gold subset:** public (220 tasks, per the abstract).
- **Remote Labor Index:** partly public, not 'lab-internal'. 10 projects are public; the 230-project test set is private.
- **Anthropic task-level time savings:** not released. The page says aggregate datasets will be shared going forward.
- **Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond data:** proprietary firm data; access is unverified, and 'on-request' is not confirmed.
- **Hatgis-Kessell et al. time shares:** release status not stated on the abstract page.
- **WebSearch limit:** the web-search budget for this turn ran out partway through. All verification was done by opening the pages listed directly, but no independent search was run for alternative versions or errata.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (lead), with Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
works.venue: Anthropic research report (with data release on Hugging Face)
works.what_measured: Five 'primitives' for each sampled Claude conversation (Nov 2025): task complexity (years of schooling needed), user and AI skill, autonomy, task success, and work/personal/education use. Also estimated human time with and without AI, which gives a speedup.
works.method_plain: Claude reads privacy-protected samples of real Claude.ai and first-party API transcripts and labels each one with a classifier. Labels include whether the task succeeded and how long a human would take with and without AI. Success labels were spot-checked against a human researcher. Speedup = human-alone time / human-with-AI time. The task-level results are then fed into a macro productivity calculation.
key_numbers: Task success (Claude-judged): about 67% on Claude.ai and about 49% on the 1P API; software development requests 61%

API success falls from about 60% on tasks under 1 human-hour to about 45% on tasks of 5+ human-hours. A 50% success rate is reached at about 3.5 human-hours on the API. The Claude.ai linear extrapolation gives about 19 hours.

Mean human-alone time is about 3.1 h (Claude.ai) and 1.7 h (API). Mean human-with-AI time is about 15 min (Claude.ai) and 5 min (API). Software development is about 3.3 h alone vs. about 15 min with AI.
Speedup is about 9x for tasks needing 12 years of schooling and about 12x for 16 years (Claude.ai)

Implied US labor productivity uplift is about 1.8 pp/yr over a decade. Adjusting for success brings it to about 1.2 pp (Claude.ai) and 1.0 pp (API). With CES elasticity 0.5 it is about 0.6-0.8 pp success-adjusted.
API traffic is 74% work-related and 64% directive, vs. 46% and 32% on Claude.ai
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the closest public analogue to the integral formula. It gives a task-length-conditioned success curve from real deployment, a field counterpart to p(h,t), and per-task time-with-AI vs. time-alone, a crude kappa/theta. Its success adjustment cuts the uplift by about 40%, which is the same logic as multiplying by p. It does not separate review time (rho) or reviewer acceptance (q). The model also self-grades its success, so the numbers are gross of human verification.
works.limitations: Success and times are judged by Claude, not observed. The sample is selected: users bring tasks they expect AI to handle. The data are conversation-level, not hours-weighted occupational task shares, so they are not f_j(h). There is no India- or firm-specific breakdown. The 'time with AI' measures interaction time, not the full workflow including integration and review.

works.title: Many SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged into main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether real repo maintainers would merge AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests. This measures the gap between 'passes checks' and 'accepted by a reviewer'.
works.method_plain: Four active maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest blind-reviewed 296 grader-passing AI patches from five models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet through Sonnet 4.5, plus GPT-5). They also reviewed 47 original human 'golden' patches to measure how noisy their own merge decisions are. Results are reported relative to that golden baseline.
key_numbers: About 68% of the human golden patches were merged, which is the maintainer noise baseline
Golden-normalized, the grader overstates maintainer merges by about 24.2 pp (SE 2.7). Roughly half of passing PRs would not be merged.
The raw gap is 34.9 pp (SE 2.2). Raw maintainer merge rates are about one-third to one-half of grader pass rates.
Maintainer merge rates improved about 9.6 pp/yr less than grader scores (SE 5.5, significant only at 10%)
Claude Sonnet 4.5's 50% time horizon is about 50 min under the grader vs. about 8 min under maintainer review, roughly a 7x overstatement
By repo the gap is 18.3 pp (scikit-learn), 23.3 pp (Sphinx) and 43.1 pp (pytest)
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the source of the project's q of about 0.5. It also shows that q is not a constant: horizons shrink about 7x rather than 2x under maintainer acceptance, so acceptance falls with task length. The trend gap is weakly negative, so q may drift over time. A better approach would be to refit p(h) using maintainer acceptance as the success criterion rather than multiplying by a scalar q.
works.limitations: Agents got one static attempt with no feedback or iteration, so the result overstates rejection relative to a real workflow. It covers one benchmark, one harness and three Python OSS repos, with small, older issues (golden patches average about 17 changed lines). Reviewers had no CI. The newest model was Sonnet 4.5. The setting is not enterprise maintenance work.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: The causal effect of allowing AI tools on completion time for real issues in developers' own large repositories.
works.method_plain: A randomized controlled trial. Each of 246 real issues was randomly assigned to 'AI allowed' or 'AI not allowed', and completion time was compared across the two arms. Developers mainly used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet.
key_numbers: 16 experienced developers worked on repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code
Tasks averaged about 2 hours each. Developers were paid $150/hr.
Allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (95% CI +2% to +39%)
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believed in a 20% speedup afterward
works.relevance_to_theta: This is a direct, causal measurement of kappa (assistant-mode speedup) on roughly 2-hour tasks. In early 2025 it was negative (about -0.16 as time saved), so the floor in max{...,kappa} could be below zero. It also shows that self-reports overstate time savings by about 40 pp, which matters if theta is built from surveys.
works.limitations: A small sample of elite OSS maintainers on familiar codebases, which is very unlike Indian IT services staff on client codebases. Uses early-2025 tools. METR itself labels the result out of date. The study does not separate review time from generation time.

works.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
works.authors: METR (post; study team incl. Becker, Rush)
works.what_measured: A follow-up RCT on late-2025 AI tools (started Aug 2025), and why the design failed.
works.method_plain: The same task-level randomization with 57 developers (10 returning, 47 new), 143 repos and 800+ tasks. Developers increasingly refused to work without AI and held back tasks they did not want to do unaided. METR therefore judged the estimate unreliable and is moving to other designs.
key_numbers: Returning developers: -18% time (a speedup), CI -38% to +9%
New developers: -4%, CI -15% to +9%
30-50% of developers withheld some tasks from possible no-AI assignment
Pay was cut from $150/hr to $50/hr
Data are public on GitHub (METR/Measuring-Late-2025-AI-on-OSS-Devs)
works.relevance_to_theta: kappa is moving from negative to probably positive, but the size is not identified. This is a methods warning for any theta_j measurement: task-level RCTs break once AI is the default, because of selection into tasks and multi-agent parallel work that makes clock time ill-defined. It argues for fixed-task experiments, time-use diaries and observational telemetry, which are exactly the designs a theta_j recipe would need.
works.limitations: METR calls the data 'only very weak evidence' on the size of the speedup. Both CIs include zero. Headlines that report '+18%' misread the sign convention (negative = faster).

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, et al. (19 authors, OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Expert-graded quality of model deliverables vs. human expert deliverables on 1,320 real work tasks from 44 occupations in the top 9 GDP sectors. Also expert review time and the resulting speed and cost of a 'model, then human review, then fix' workflow.
works.method_plain: Professionals averaging 14 years of experience wrote tasks from their real work. Other experts compared model and human outputs blind. Review time was clocked with monitoring software. A 'try n times' model assumes the expert samples the model up to n times, reviews each attempt, and does the task themselves if all attempts fail. Expected time and cost are then compared with unaided expert time.
key_numbers: 1,320 tasks in the full set and a 220-task open gold subset
Best win-or-tie rate vs. experts: Claude Opus 4.1 at 47.6% (gold subset)
Average expert completion time is about 404 min (about 6.7 h) at about $361 per task
Average expert review time is 109 min (about $86) per deliverable, about 27% of task time
Speed multipliers under 'Try n times': gpt-4o 0.46x, o4-mini 1.06x, o3 1.28x, gpt-5 1.39x. Cost multipliers: 0.53x, 1.22x, 1.47x, 1.63x.
Software Developers is among the included occupations
works.relevance_to_theta: The 'try n times' calculation is structurally almost identical to the project's integrand: success probability (p*q as expert win rate), review cost (rho about 0.27 for roughly 7-hour tasks), and a fallback to human labor. A 1.39x speedup implies theta of about 1 - 1/1.39 = 0.28 for GPT-5 on this task mix. It is the best public template for measuring rho, and a direct theta estimate for long tasks.
works.limitations: The tasks are one-shot, self-contained deliverables chosen by OpenAI-recruited experts, not an hours-weighted sample of real work (not f_j). Speed and cost figures are reported only for OpenAI models. The authors say the try-n model over-penalizes AI because experts adapt. Grading is preference-based and noisy. There is no Indian IT services mix.

works.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (Aug 2026 revision)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper + ADP/DEL Canaries Dashboard
works.what_measured: US employment by age and AI-exposure quintile, using ADP payroll microdata through June 2026.
works.method_plain: Occupations are ranked by exposure (Eloundou et al. measures, plus a split between AI usage that automates and AI usage that complements). Employment of exposed and less-exposed groups is compared over time, controlling for firm-level shocks. This is a descriptive event-study, not a causal estimate.
key_numbers: Workers aged 22-25 in highly exposed occupations are about 19% below the employment path of less-exposed peers (June 2026). The gap was 15% at the July 2025 vintage.
From Nov 2022 to Jun 2026, employment of 22-25-year-olds fell about 11% in the top-2 exposure quintiles and grew about 10% in the bottom 3
The Aug 2025 version reported a 13% relative decline and the Nov 2025 version 16%, so the figures are vintage-specific and should not be mixed
The authors report no economy-wide displacement. The gap runs through reduced hiring, not separations, and is concentrated where usage is automating rather than complementary.
