works.relevance_to_theta: This is the Digital Economy Lab's flagship 'measure the outcome' agenda. It operates on employment outcomes, downstream of theta, and uses extensive-margin exposure scores. It helps confirm the hypothesis: even the leading lab still proxies the intensive margin with exposure plus an automation/augmentation split. It is useful as a validation target, since it shows the realized labor effect is hiring-margin and junior-heavy, which matters for w_j in Indian IT pyramids.
works.limitations: Descriptive, not causal. The gap attenuates with education controls, and some pre-trends exist. It is US-only. ADP gaps are larger than national survey benchmarks. It contains no task-level time-saved measure.

works.title: A Research Agenda for the Economics of Transformative AI
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Anton Korinek, Ajay K. Agrawal
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 34256 (also introduction to NBER volume 'The Economics of Transformative AI')
works.what_measured: Nothing empirical. It is an agenda that sets nine 'Grand Challenges': growth, innovation, income distribution, decision-making power, geoeconomics, information flows, safety risks, well-being, and transition dynamics.
works.method_plain: A position paper that lays out open questions and methods, including new indicators, task-level assessments and AI-agent simulations. Those method details come from an earlier draft summary in search results. The NBER landing page I opened lists only the nine challenges.
key_numbers: 9 Grand Challenges
works.relevance_to_theta: Mainly for framing. It legitimizes 'task-level assessment' as a priority, but the landing page I verified gives no recipe for measuring intensive-margin labor savings. It does not supply any parameter.
works.limitations: I opened only the NBER abstract page, not the full PDF, so I cannot confirm specific measurement proposals in the text.

works.title: Making AI Count: The Next Measurement Frontier
works.authors: Diane Coyle, John Lourenze S. Poquiz
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 34330; chapter in 'The Economics of Transformative AI' (NBER/U. Chicago Press)
works.what_measured: Conceptual. It covers how national accounts (SNA 2025) and official statistics miss AI's effects: AI as an asset, cross-border AI inputs, quality change, and process change.
works.method_plain: A review of statistical frameworks that identifies measurement gaps and recommends that statistical agencies move to more granular, task-based, outcome-focused measurement.
key_numbers: No quantitative estimates. Its main recommendation is 'granular, task-based, and outcome-focused' official measurement.
works.relevance_to_theta: It supports the claim that official data do not measure theta. It specifically flags cross-border AI inputs, which is exactly the Indian IT case: US clients consume AI-augmented Indian services, and AI compute is imported. Relevant to how phi and output deflators would be mismeasured.
works.limitations: Conceptual. I verified only the abstract and landing page. It contains no labor-time measurements.

works.title: Incorporating AI impacts in BLS employment projections: occupational case studies
works.authors: Christine Machovec, Michael J. Rieley, Emily Rolen
works.venue: Monthly Labor Review (US Bureau of Labor Statistics)
works.what_measured: How BLS adjusts its 2023-33 occupational projections for generative AI, with case studies of computer, legal, business/financial and engineering occupations.
works.method_plain: Analyst judgment based on published research as of June 2024. BLS adjusts its staffing-pattern models only where research gives 'clear expectations' of impact. It explicitly reasons about productivity gains leading to lower prices and higher demand, which is the eps*phi channel.
key_numbers: Software developers projected 1,692.1k to 1,995.7k (+17.9%), 2023-33, vs. +4.0% for all occupations
Customer service representatives projected -5.0% through 2033
No numeric productivity or time-savings adjustment is stated for software developers. BLS says there is 'no clear evidence' that productivity gains will outweigh demand.
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows the official statistical agency has no theta-type parameter. It makes qualitative calls and uses the same decomposition as the project (replacement vs. demand response). This is a gap the project's bottom-up theta_j could fill. The 'customer service' call parallels the BPO line.
works.limitations: Judgmental. There are no quantitative task-time estimates, and BLS says its methods are not designed for rapid technological change. US only.

works.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (earlier title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects)
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 33777 (earlier version BFI WP 2025-56)
works.what_measured: AI chatbot adoption, self-reported time savings and new AI tasks among Danish workers in exposed occupations, linked to administrative earnings and hours.
works.method_plain: Two large adoption surveys (late 2023 and 2024) are linked to Danish register data. Difference-in-differences compares adopters and non-adopters and workplaces over time.
key_numbers: Precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours. Effects larger than 2% are ruled out two years after ChatGPT (NBER revised abstract).

Earlier version: average time savings of 2.8% of work hours, from about 25,000 workers in 11 occupations at 7,000 workplaces. This comes from the earlier abstract as quoted in search results; I could not parse the BFI PDF, so treat it as medium-confidence.
Employers reorganize tasks toward content generation, AI oversight and AI integration
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few measured intensive-margin numbers: time saved at actual adoption. It is far below capability ceilings of 15-56% of tasks (Eloundou). The gap between realized and capability values is what the project's 'adoption dropped' theta is a ceiling on. It also documents new oversight tasks, an rho-type cost that raises review labor.
works.limitations: Danish, 2023-24, chatbots only (not agents). Time savings are self-reported (compare METR's 40-pp perception gap). The occupations are not IT services.

works.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
works.authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
works.year: 2023 (Mar; v5 Aug 2023; later published in Science 2024)
works.what_measured: Whether each O*NET task could be done at least 50% faster at equal quality with LLM access, or with LLM-powered tools. This is binary exposure labeled by humans and GPT-4.
works.method_plain: Annotators and GPT-4 label every O*NET task E0/E1/E2 (no exposure, direct LLM exposure, exposure via LLM-based software). Labels are aggregated to occupations, weighted by task.
key_numbers: About 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected
About 19% of workers could have at least 50% of their tasks affected
About 15% of all US worker tasks could be done significantly faster at the same quality with direct LLM access, rising to 47-56% with LLM-powered software
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the classic extensive-margin benchmark. Its threshold is binary ('at least 50% faster'), so it says nothing about the size of savings, review cost or failure rates. That supports the working hypothesis. The task-to-occupation weighting is a template for w_j, but O*NET task weights are not hours shares.
works.limitations: Static (GPT-4 era). Binary and threshold-based. No verification cost. US O*NET tasks are not Indian IT service lines.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Szymon Sacher, Zoe Hitzig, Shaoyi Zhang, Ryan Heller, Peter McCrory
works.what_measured: AI autonomy by product (Claude Code vs. chat/Cowork) and output type, timing of usage, and a new linked Anthropic Economic Index Survey of users.
works.method_plain: Daily and hourly privacy-preserving telemetry samples (Apr 10 to Jun 10, 2026), an output-type classifier with more than 30 artifact categories, and an autonomy score on a 1-5 scale. Survey responses are linked to the same users' usage.
key_numbers: Claude Code averages 0.37 points more AI autonomy (1-5 scale) than chat/Cowork. The gap is 0.53 for scripts/code. Claude Code is more autonomous in 26 of 31 output types.
About two-thirds of the autonomy gap comes from more delegation on the same tasks
54% of Claude Code sessions run on Opus vs. 10% of chat/Cowork
Survey: about 9,700 linked respondents. In separate interviews of 81k users, 86% report speed gains, 69% quality gains and 27% cost savings.
The report does not estimate task success or time savings
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that the delegate-vs-assistant split (the p*q term vs. the kappa term) depends on product, not just on the model. Agentic harnesses shift work into the delegated branch. It does not give time saved or review cost.
works.limitations: No time-savings or success estimates in this release. Survey respondents are heavily computer/math (about 30% vs. 4% of US employment). The report describes no separate downloadable dataset.

research.stream_summary: The measurement agenda is moving fast, but no one yet publishes the object the project needs: hours of labor saved per task, net of failures and review, at a given capability level. Three groups come closest. (1) GDPval (OpenAI) uses a 'try the model n times, have an expert review each attempt, then do it yourself if all fail' calculation. It measured expert review time directly: 109 minutes against about 404 minutes of expert task time, so review costs roughly 27% of the task. For GPT-5 the result is a 1.39x speedup, about 28% time saved. That is essentially the project's integrand, measured on long one-shot tasks. (2) METR provides the reviewer-acceptance correction: about half of SWE-bench-passing patches would not be merged, and Sonnet 4.5's 50% time horizon drops from about 50 to about 8 minutes under maintainer review. So q shrinks with task length rather than being a constant 0.5. METR's randomized trials measured the assistant-mode speedup, kappa, at -19% (a slowdown) for early-2025 tools. Its late-2025 trial broke down because developers refused to work without AI, a warning for any experimental recipe. (3) The Anthropic Economic Index (Jan 2026) gives a field version of p(h): API success falls from about 60% to about 45% as tasks lengthen from under 1 hour to 5+ hours. Adjusting for success cuts implied productivity growth from 1.8 to about 1.0 pp per year. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Canaries) and BLS measure outcomes and still rely on extensive-margin exposure scores, so the working hypothesis largely holds. Funding: Anthropic's Economic Futures awards ($10-50k plus $5k credits) are currently closed. OpenAI's Economic Research Exchange (deadline July 5, 2026) is closed. The OpenAI Foundation's $250M program promises open calls but has no dates yet. Stripe's fellowship (2025: $10k, grad students) has no 2026 date. UChicago's AI in the Workplace fellowship targets PhDs and faculty. No undergraduate-eligible open call was found.
gaps_noticed: No source measures hours-weighted task-length distributions f_j(h) for any service line, let alone Indian IT. The Anthropic Index gives conversation-level human-time estimates, not workforce time use.

Review cost rho is measured in only one place (GDPval: 109 of about 404 minutes, one-shot deliverables). There is nothing for maintenance tickets, test writing or BPO transactions, and nothing on how rho scales with h.

q (reviewer acceptance) is measured only on small Python OSS patches with one-shot agents. There is no enterprise or client-acceptance data. METR's horizon result (50 min to 8 min) implies q depends on h, which a scalar q of 0.5 misses.
kappa estimates are either negative (early-2025 RCT) or unidentified (late-2025 RCT broke down from selection). No credible current number exists.
All lab telemetry (Anthropic, OpenAI 'How People Use ChatGPT') judges success and time with the model itself, not with observed outcomes.

No India-specific or IT-services-firm-specific measurement program was found at any of the labs, BLS, OECD or Windfall Trust. The OpenAI Foundation explicitly lists low- and middle-income-country evaluation as a priority but has not yet funded anything there.
Could not open OpenAI's Economic Research Exchange RFP page (HTTP 403). Its July 5, 2026 deadline and the econresearch@openai.com contact come from search snippets only.
Could not open the full NBER w34256 PDF to confirm its specific measurement proposals.
Could not verify the Humlum-Vestergaard 2.8% time-savings figure in the PDF itself (the BFI PDF would not parse). The NBER revised abstract reports only null earnings/hours effects (bound below 2%).
Windfall Trust: no fellowships, grants or data products with deadlines found. Its 'Measure' initiative is undocumented.
OECD AI-WIPS and ONS: no specific generative-AI task-time survey found in this pass.

datasets.name: Anthropic Economic Index (all releases, Feb 2025 to Jun 2026)
datasets.description: Aggregated Claude usage mapped to O*NET tasks: automation vs. augmentation, plus Jan 2026 primitives (task success, human time with and without AI, complexity, autonomy). Raw Claude.ai and API splits for Nov 13-20, 2025, with geography. Licensed CC-BY. The best public source for a field p(h) and per-task speedups.

datasets.name: GDPval gold subset (220 tasks) + automated grader
datasets.description: Expert-written real-work tasks with reference deliverables in 44 occupations, including software developers. The paper reports expert completion time (about 404 min), review time (109 min) and cost. The full 1,320-task set is not public.

datasets.name: METR early-2025 developer RCT data
datasets.description: Task-level data from 246 issues with AI-allowed/disallowed assignment, completion times and developer forecasts. Usable to estimate kappa by task length.

datasets.name: METR late-2025 developer RCT data
datasets.description: 57 developers, 800+ tasks, 143 repos. METR flags it as selection-biased, but it is usable for bounding kappa.

datasets.name: METR time-horizon task suite and model results
datasets.description: Logistic p(h) fits by model, the source of p(h,t). The underlying task suite is partly private.

datasets.name: ADP payroll microdata (Canaries) / Canaries Dashboard
datasets.description: High-frequency US payroll by age and occupation exposure. The microdata are available only to the ADP/Stanford team; the dashboard is public.

datasets.name: BLS Employment Projections + AI exposure classification
datasets.description: Occupational projections with qualitative AI adjustments, plus a 2025-35 exposure tier. Useful as a comparison for the demand (eps*phi) channel.

datasets.name: Danish AI adoption surveys linked to registers (Humlum-Vestergaard)
datasets.description: About 25,000 workers in 11 exposed occupations with self-reported time savings, linked to admin earnings and hours. Access runs through Statistics Denmark and the authors.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Economic primitives
works.authors: Ruth Appel, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory (lead authors); Miles McCain, Ryan Heller, Tyler Neylon, Alex Tamkin
works.venue: Anthropic research report (data on Hugging Face, Anthropic/EconomicIndex, release_2026_01_15)
works.what_measured: Five 'primitives' for sampled Claude conversations from Nov 13-20, 2025 (1M Claude.ai Free/Pro/Max conversations and 1M first-party API transcripts): task complexity, human and AI skills, use case (work/personal/education), AI autonomy, and task success. It also has Claude-estimated human time for each task without AI and with AI, which gives a speedup.
works.method_plain: Claude classifiers label privacy-protected transcripts. Success is Claude's own judgment of whether the task was completed. The human-time estimates reuse Anthropic's earlier productivity method, which had shown Claude's time estimates correlate with actual time on software tasks. For Claude.ai, the new classifiers were checked against a human researcher's labels on a small set of transcripts with user feedback. For the API they were checked on internal and synthetic data. The authors call the classifiers 'directionally accurate' and say no single number should be treated as exact. Speedup = estimated time alone / estimated time with AI. Task-level speedups are then aggregated into a macro labor-productivity calculation, with and without a success adjustment.
key_numbers: Task success (Claude-judged): 67% on Claude.ai, 49% on the 1P API, 61% for software development requests

API success falls from about 60% on tasks under 1 human-hour to about 45% on tasks of 5+ human-hours. It crosses 50% at about 3.5 hours. On Claude.ai, a linear extrapolation reaches 50% at about 19 hours.

Mean estimated human-alone time: 3.1 h (Claude.ai), 1.7 h (API). Mean human-with-AI time: 15 min (Claude.ai), 5 min (API). Software development: about 3.3 h alone vs about 15 min with AI. All are Claude's estimates, not measured durations.
Speedup on Claude.ai: about 9x for tasks needing 12 years of schooling, about 12x for 16 years

Implied US labor productivity uplift: about 1.8 pp/yr over the next decade. Success-adjusted: 1.2 pp (Claude.ai) and 1.0 pp (API). With CES sigma = 0.5 (tasks are complements): 0.7-0.9 pp unadjusted, 0.8 pp (Claude.ai) and 0.6 pp (API) success-adjusted.
API traffic: 74% work-related and 64% directive. Claude.ai: 46% and 32%.
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest public field analogue to p(h): success conditioned on estimated human task length, from real deployment. The time-alone vs time-with-AI ratio gives a crude theta or kappa per task. Adjusting for success cuts the uplift by roughly 33-44% (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp), which is the same logic as multiplying by p. It separately identifies neither review time (rho) nor reviewer acceptance (q). Both success and time are model-judged, so the figures are gross of human verification. The report acknowledges validation costs could reduce gains but does not net them out.
works.limitations: Success and times are Claude's estimates, not observed outcomes. 'Time with AI' is Claude's estimate of collaboration time, not a measured duration of the whole workflow (integration, testing, review). The sample is selected: users bring tasks they expect AI to handle. Data are conversation-level, not hours-weighted task shares, so they are not f_j(h). There is no India or firm breakdown. Classifier validation used small samples.
works.corrections: All key numbers confirmed on the report page. Clarified the sampling window (Nov 13-20, 2025; 1M + 1M transcripts) and the validation details. Added the unadjusted CES figure (0.7-0.9 pp). Reworded the limitation: 'time with AI' is a Claude estimate, not measured interaction time. Removed f_j from params, because the record's own limitations say these data are not f_j(h).

works.title: Many SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged into main
works.authors: Parker Whitfill, Cheryl Wu, Joel Becker, Nate Rush (METR)
works.what_measured: Whether active repo maintainers would merge AI patches that pass SWE-bench Verified's automated tests. This is the gap between 'passes checks' and 'accepted by a reviewer'.
works.method_plain: 4 active maintainers (2 scikit-learn, 1 Sphinx, 1 pytest) reviewed 296 grader-passing AI patches from 5 models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Old), Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4 Opus, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5. The 3 repos cover 95 of the 500 SWE-bench Verified issues. To measure noise in their own merge decisions, maintainers also reviewed 47 original human 'golden' patches, a random half of the golden set. Results are normalized to the golden merge rate.
key_numbers: About 68% of human golden patches were merged by maintainers (the noise baseline)
Golden-normalized, grader pass rates exceed maintainer merge rates by about 24.2 pp (SE 2.7). The summary says roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged.
Raw (unnormalized) gap: 34.9 pp (SE 2.2). Raw maintainer merge rates are roughly one-third to one-half of grader pass rates (Appendix A4).
Normalized trend: maintainer merge rates improve about 9.6 pp/yr less than grader scores (SE 5.5). The authors call this weak evidence. The raw trend difference is 15.5 pp/yr (SE 4.6).
Claude Sonnet 4.5's 50% time horizon is about 50 min under the grader vs about 8 min under maintainer merge decisions, roughly a 7x overstatement
By repo, level gaps are 18.3 pp (scikit-learn, SE 4.6), 23.3 pp (Sphinx, SE 4.1) and 43.1 pp (pytest, SE 5.2)
works.relevance_to_theta: The source of q of about 0.5. The horizon shrinking about 7x, not 2x, suggests acceptance falls with task length, so q is better modeled as q(h). That is an inference from the horizon refit, not a directly reported q-by-length curve. A cleaner method is to refit p(h) with maintainer acceptance as the success criterion rather than multiplying by a scalar q. The trend evidence on whether q drifts over time is weak and differs by repo (it reverses for scikit-learn).
works.limitations: Agents got one attempt, with no feedback or iteration. There was no CI (no linting or tests) during review. The study covers one benchmark, one harness and 3 Python OSS repos. Issues are small: golden patches average about 17 changed lines. The newest model is Sonnet 4.5. The setting is not enterprise maintenance work.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the SEs by repo, the raw trend difference, the 95/500 issue coverage, and the fact that maintainers reviewed a random half of golden patches. Flagged that 'q falls with h' is an inference.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth (Beth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: The causal effect of allowing AI tools on completion time for real issues in developers' own large repositories.
works.method_plain: A randomized controlled trial at the issue level. Each of 246 issues was randomly assigned 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed', and completion times were compared. Developers mainly used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. 'AI allowed' means developers could use AI as they chose, so the estimate is the effect of permission, not of any single usage mode.
key_numbers: 16 experienced developers on repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines of code
Issues averaged about 2 hours. Pay was $150/hr.
Allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (95% CI +2% to +39%, as restated in METR's Feb 2026 post. The GitHub README gives 0.188 with CI of about 0.013 to 0.395.)
Developers forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and believed afterward that AI had sped them up 20%
The page now carries a banner saying the results are out of date
works.relevance_to_theta: Causal evidence that the AI-assisted speedup could be negative in early 2025 on about 2-hour tasks. It is not a clean measure of kappa, because the treatment mixes assistant and delegate use (and non-use). Converted to the project's units (fraction of labor time saved = 1 - T_AI/T_alone), the estimate is about -0.19, not -0.16. The figure -0.16 is the change in output per hour (1 - 1/1.19). The perception gap (about +20% believed vs -19% measured, roughly 39 pp) warns against building theta from self-reports.
works.limitations: Small sample of elite OSS maintainers on familiar codebases, unlike Indian IT services staff on client code. Early-2025 tools. METR itself labels the result out of date. The public data include initial and post-review implementation times for part of the study, so review time is only partially separable, not entirely absent.
works.corrections: Citation and headline numbers confirmed. Corrected the relevance claim: time saved in the project's units is about -0.19, not -0.16. Noted that the treatment is 'AI allowed', not pure assistant mode. Softened the claim that the study does not separate review time: the dataset has post-review implementation time for part of the sample. The CI is not shown on the July 2025 blog page itself; it was confirmed via METR's Feb 2026 post and the GitHub README.

works.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
works.what_measured: A follow-up issue-level RCT on late-2025 AI tools, started Aug 2025, and why METR judged the design no longer reliable.
works.method_plain: The same issue-level randomization with 57 developers (10 returning, 47 new), 143 repos and 800+ tasks. Many developers declined to submit tasks they did not want to do without AI. That selection makes the estimate unreliable, so METR is changing designs.
key_numbers: Returning developers: -18% time (negative = speedup), 95% CI -38% to +9%
New developers: -4%, 95% CI -15% to +9%
30-50% of developers said they did not submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI
Pay was cut from $150/hr to $50/hr
Data: github.com/METR/Measuring-Late-2025-AI-on-OSS-Devs (public)
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests the assistant-mode speedup has probably turned positive, but its size is not identified. A methods warning for any theta_j recipe: issue-level RCTs break once AI is the default, because people select which tasks to submit. That argues for fixed-task experiments, time-use diaries or telemetry.
works.limitations: METR calls the data 'only very weak evidence' on the size of the speedup. Both CIs include zero. Under the sign convention, negative means faster.
works.corrections: Authors filled in from the page: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud. The record said only 'METR (incl. Becker, Rush)'. All numbers confirmed. Dropped the record's 'multi-agent parallel work makes clock time ill-defined' point, which I did not confirm on the page.

works.title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
works.authors: Tejal Patwardhan, Rachel Dias, Elizabeth Proehl, Grace Kim, Michele Wang, Olivia Watkins, Simón Posada Fishman, Marwan Aljubeh, Phoebe Thacker, Laurance Fauconnet, Natalie S. Kim, Patrick Chao, Samuel Miserendino, Gildas Chabot, David Li, Michael Sharman, Alexandra Barr, Amelia Glaese, Jerry Tworek (OpenAI)
works.what_measured: Blind expert comparisons of model vs human-expert deliverables on 1,320 real work tasks in 44 occupations across the top 9 US GDP sectors. Also expert completion time, monitored expert review time, and the implied speed and cost of a 'model, then human review, then human redo if it fails' workflow.
works.method_plain: Professionals (average 14 years' experience, minimum 4) wrote tasks from their real work. Other experts graded model vs human outputs blind. Human completion time was self-reported and checked by reviewers. Review time was observed from task-monitoring software. 'Try 1 time': expected time = model time + review time + (1 - w) x full human time, where w is the win-or-tie rate. 'Try n times': resample and re-review up to n times, then the human does it. Speed ratio = human time / expected time. All speed and cost figures are computed on the 220-task gold subset.
key_numbers: 1,320 tasks in the full set; 220-task open-sourced gold subset
Best win-or-tie rate vs experts: Claude Opus 4.1 at 47.6% (gold subset)
Average expert completion time 404 min at $361 per task (gold subset)
Average expert review time 109 min ($86) per deliverable, about 27% of completion time
Speed multipliers, Try n times: gpt-4o 0.46x, o4-mini 1.06x, o3 1.28x, gpt-5 1.39x. Cost: 0.53x, 1.22x, 1.47x, 1.63x.
GPT-5 (win rate 39.0%), Try 1 time: 1.12x speed, 1.18x cost
Software Developers is an included occupation (Professional, Scientific and Technical Services)
works.relevance_to_theta: The 'try' formulas are structurally close to the project's delegate branch: success probability (w, the expert win-or-tie rate, standing in for p*q), review cost (rho about 0.27 on tasks averaging about 6.7 h), and a fallback to full human redo. They have no partial-credit or assistant term (no kappa): a failure means the whole task is redone. Implied time saved for GPT-5 is about 1 - 1/1.39 = 0.28 (try n) or 1 - 1/1.12 = 0.11 (try once), on this task mix. It is the best public template for measuring rho directly.
works.limitations: One-shot, self-contained deliverables written by recruited experts, not an hours-weighted sample of real work (not f_j). Speed and cost tables cover OpenAI models only. Footnote 9 says the try-n calculation over-penalizes the model. 'Win' includes ties with the human, a lenient acceptance bar. Grading is preference-based. There is no Indian IT services mix.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed. Added the full 19-author list, the try-once GPT-5 figures (1.12x speed, 39.0% win rate), and the facts that the speed/cost figures are on the gold subset and completion times are self-reported while review time is monitored. Softened 'structurally almost identical to the integrand' to note there is no assistant (kappa) branch.

works.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence (August 2026 version)
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
works.venue: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper. Accompanying news post: 'No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%' (Aug 12, 2026).
works.what_measured: US employment by age and AI-exposure quintile, using ADP payroll data through June 2026.
works.method_plain: Occupations are ranked into AI-exposure quintiles (the Eloundou et al. GPT-4 'beta' measure, plus alternatives). Usage data split occupations into automating vs complementary AI use. The 19% headline is a simple descriptive 'kept-pace' gap: how far young exposed workers' employment is below where it would be had it grown like less-exposed peers. Earlier versions headlined regressions that adjust for firm-level shocks. This is descriptive, not causal.
key_numbers: Employment of workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations is 19% below the kept-pace path (June 2026), up from 15% at the July 2025 data vintage (same descriptive measure)
Nov 2022 to Jun 2026, ages 22-25: employment fell about 11% in the top two exposure quintiles and grew about 10% in the bottom three

Earlier versions headlined a different measure, a firm-shock-adjusted regression: 13% relative decline on July 2025 data and 16% on September 2025 data. Do not mix these with the 15%/19% descriptive figures.

No evidence of economy-wide displacement. The adjustment runs mainly through reduced hiring, not separations. Declines are concentrated where AI use substitutes for tasks, with flat or rising employment where it complements. So far it shows up in employment, not base pay.
works.relevance_to_theta: Measures outcomes downstream of theta, using extensive-margin exposure scores plus an automation/complementarity split. It does not measure labor time saved, which supports the working hypothesis. Useful as a validation target: the realized effect is on hiring and concentrated among juniors, which matters for w_j and the pyramid structure in Indian IT.
works.limitations: Descriptive, not causal. Gaps shrink with education controls. Some divergent trends predate generative AI. Gaps are larger in the ADP sample than in national survey benchmarks. Specifications that account for firm hiring became more sensitive after data-pipeline changes. US only. No task-level time-saved measure.
works.corrections: (1) The 16% figure is from September 2025 data, not a 'Nov 2025 version'. (2) The 13% and 16% are firm-shock-adjusted regression estimates, a different measure from the 15%/19% descriptive kept-pace gap, so mixing them is a measurement mismatch, not just a vintage issue. (3) The method description wrongly said the headline controls for firm-level shocks; the 19% headline is the simple descriptive divergence. (4) Replaced the news-post URL with the paper PDF and gave the paper's exact title ('Six Facts about').

works.title: A Research Agenda for the Economics of Transformative AI
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Anton Korinek, Ajay K. Agrawal
works.what_measured: Nothing empirical. An agenda built around nine Grand Challenges: economic growth, innovation, income distribution, decision-making power, geoeconomics, information flows, safety risks, human well-being, and transition dynamics.
works.method_plain: A position paper. Its methods section includes Section 4.4, 'Task-level Assessments of Potential Impact'. That section proposes moving beyond O*NET's roughly 18,000 tasks by using NLP on job postings and resumes to build a finer, dynamic task taxonomy. Section 4.5 covers simulating economies with LLM agents, and an appendix lists technological and economic indicators (compute, labor, energy, capabilities, productivity, GDP).
key_numbers: 9 Grand Challenges
works.relevance_to_theta: Framing only. Its task-level proposal is about finer task classification (an extensive-margin, exposure-style refinement), not measuring labor time saved net of review. That supports the working hypothesis. It supplies no parameter.
works.limitations: A position paper with no measurement recipe for intensive-margin labor savings.
works.corrections: Removed the unverified claim that it is 'also the introduction to the NBER volume'. Neither the NBER page nor the PDF front matter says so. Opened and read the full PDF, which confirms the task-level-assessment and AI-agent-simulation sections that the record could only attribute to search snippets. Citation confidence raised to high.

works.title: Making AI Count: The Next Measurement Frontier
works.authors: Diane Coyle, John Lourenze S. Poquiz
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 34330; forthcoming in 'The Economics of Transformative AI' (2026, eds. Agrawal, Brynjolfsson, Korinek)
works.what_measured: Conceptual. How national accounts (SNA 2025) and official statistics miss AI's effects: valuing AI as an asset, cross-border inputs, quality change, and process change.
works.method_plain: A review of statistical frameworks. It recommends 'more granular, task-based, and outcome-focused' statistics. It specifically proposes adding detail on tasks, time spent on tasks and technologies used to labor force surveys, plus time-use-at-work data and job-task mapping, triangulated with administrative records and employer surveys.
key_numbers: No quantitative estimates
works.relevance_to_theta: Supports the claim that official data do not measure theta. Its explicit call for task-time and time-use-at-work data is close to a data requirement for f_j(h) and w_j. Its cross-border point concerns geographically dispersed AI infrastructure and investment (data centers, trade statistics, multiregional input-output tables). Applying it to US clients buying AI-augmented Indian services is the researcher's extension, not the paper's claim.
works.limitations: Conceptual. No labor-time measurements.
works.corrections: Citation confirmed. I read the full PDF, not just the abstract. Added the time-use and task-time survey recommendations. Clarified that the cross-border argument is about AI infrastructure and investment, so the Indian IT services application is an inference.

works.title: Incorporating AI impacts in BLS employment projections: occupational case studies
works.authors: Christine Machovec, Michael J. Rieley, Emily Rolen
works.venue: Monthly Labor Review (US Bureau of Labor Statistics)
works.what_measured: How BLS accounted for generative AI in its 2023-33 occupational projections, with case studies of computer, legal, business/financial and engineering occupations.
works.method_plain: Analyst judgment based on information available in June 2024. BLS adjusts its models only where research gives 'clear expectations' of employment impact. It reasons about whether productivity gains will be offset by higher demand.
key_numbers: Software developers: 1,692.1k (2023) to 1,995.7k (2033), +17.9%, vs +4.0% for all occupations
Customer service representatives: projected -5.0% through 2033
On the conjecture that AI productivity gains would cut software developer employment, BLS says there is 'no clear evidence to support this conjecture'
BLS: projection methods 'are not designed to capture extremely rapid technological change'
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows the official statistical agency has no theta-type parameter. It makes qualitative calls that weigh replacement against demand response, the same decomposition as the project. The customer-service call parallels the BPO line.
works.limitations: Judgmental. No quantitative task-time estimates. US only. Information cutoff June 2024.
works.corrections: All numbers and quotes confirmed. The record's paraphrase of the 'no clear evidence' quote ('productivity gains will outweigh demand') was reworded to match its context more closely. Note: this article contains no '2025-35 exposure tier'; see dataset notes.

works.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI (earlier title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects)
works.authors: Anders Humlum, Emilie Vestergaard
works.year: 2025 (May 9; NBER versions May 2025, Oct 2025; revised Mar 2026)
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 33777 (earlier version: BFI Working Paper 2025-56)
works.what_measured: AI chatbot adoption, self-reported time savings and new AI-related tasks among Danish workers in 11 exposed occupations, linked to administrative earnings and hours.
works.method_plain: Two adoption surveys (late 2023 and 2024), each with about 25,000 workers at about 7,000 workplaces, linked to Danish matched employer-employee registers. Difference-in-differences uses employer encouragement policies as quasi-experimental variation. Time savings as a share of work hours = frequency of use x self-reported time saved per day of use.
key_numbers: Revised NBER abstract (Mar 2026): null effects on earnings and recorded hours, ruling out effects 'larger than 2%' two years after ChatGPT. The May 2025 BFI version said CIs rule out effects larger than 1%.

May 2025 BFI version: average time savings of 2.8% of users' total work hours (main text). The abstract rounds this to 3%. Range: 6.8% (marketing professionals at encouraging employers) down to 0.6% (teachers at non-encouraging schools).
On days they use chatbots, users report 6-7% time savings. Typical adopters use chatbots only every third to fourth day.
About 80% of saved time is reallocated to other job tasks. New tasks include content generation, AI oversight and AI integration.
Occupations include software developers and IT support specialists. Software developers at encouraging employers report about 7% time savings.
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few large-sample measures of time saved at actual adoption, and it includes software developers and IT support. It is self-reported and among users only, so it bounds realized savings well below capability ceilings. It documents new oversight and integration tasks, an rho-type cost.
works.limitations: Danish, 2023-24, chatbots only (not agents). Time savings are self-reported (compare METR's perception gap) and measured among users. The record's claim that 'the occupations are not IT services' is wrong: software developers and IT support specialists are among the 11 occupations, though they are not IT-services-firm employees.
works.corrections: Extracted text from the BFI PDF that the record could not parse. 2.8% is confirmed in the May 2025 main text; the abstract of that version says 3%. The 25,000 workers and 7,000 workplaces are per survey round. The earnings bound is 1% in the May 2025 version and 2% in the revised NBER abstract. Fixed the limitation: software developers and IT support are included. Added the occupation range and usage-day savings.

works.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
works.authors: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin, Daniel Rock
works.year: 2023 (arXiv v1 Mar 17; v5 Aug 21, 2023). Published as 'GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs', Science 384(6702):1306-1308, June 2024.
works.what_measured: Whether each O*NET task could be done at least 50% faster at equal quality with direct LLM access (E1) or with LLM-powered software (E2). Binary or threshold exposure labeled by humans and GPT-4.
works.method_plain: Human annotators and GPT-4 label each O*NET task as E0 (no exposure), E1 (direct LLM exposure) or E2 (exposure via LLM-based tools). Labels are aggregated to occupations.
key_numbers: About 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected
About 19% of workers may have at least 50% of their tasks affected
About 15% of all US worker tasks could be done significantly faster at the same quality with direct LLM access, rising to 47-56% with LLM-powered software
works.relevance_to_theta: The classic extensive-margin benchmark. The threshold is binary (at least 50% faster), so it says nothing about the size of savings, review cost or failure rates, which supports the working hypothesis. The task-to-occupation aggregation is a template for w_j, but O*NET tasks are not weighted by hours.
works.limitations: Static (GPT-4 era). Binary, threshold-based. No verification cost. US O*NET tasks, not Indian IT service lines.
works.corrections: Abstract numbers and the arXiv versions are confirmed. Science publication details confirmed via Crossref metadata: Science 384(6702):1306-1308, published online June 20, 2024, with a shortened title. The record's 'weighted by task' aggregation detail was not checked in the full text and has been dropped.

works.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences
works.authors: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Szymon Sacher, Zoe Hitzig, Shaoyi Zhang, Ryan Heller, Peter McCrory
works.what_measured: AI autonomy by product (Claude Code vs chat/Cowork) and by output type, timing of usage, and a new Anthropic Economic Index Survey linked to the same users' usage.
works.method_plain: Privacy-preserving samples of chat and Cowork conversations (Apr 10 to Jun 10, 2026), an output-type classifier, and an autonomy rating on a 1-5 scale ('none' to 'extreme'). Survey responses (survey launched Apr 2026) are linked to usage from mid-May to early June 2026.
key_numbers: Claude Code averages 0.37 points more autonomy (1-5 scale) than chat/Cowork. The gap is 0.53 for scripts/code snippets. Claude Code is more autonomous in 26 of 31 output types.
About two-thirds of the gap comes from more delegation on the same tasks; about one-third from a different mix of outputs
54% of Claude Code sessions are served by Opus vs 10% of chat/Cowork conversations
About 9,700 respondents in the linked survey sample. In separate 81k-user interviews: 86% report speed gains, 82% scope gains, 69% quality gains, 27% cost savings.
About 30% of survey respondents are in computer/math occupations vs 4% of US employment
Task success and time savings are not directly estimated
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that the delegate vs assistant split (the p*q branch vs the kappa branch) depends on the product and harness, not only on the model: agentic tools shift work into delegation. It gives no time saved or review cost.
works.limitations: No time-savings or success estimates. Survey respondents are heavily computer/math. Self-reported gains.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed. Corrected the limitation 'no separate downloadable dataset': the Hugging Face EconomicIndex README lists a 2026-06-26 release ('Artifacts and monthly aggregates'). Added the 82% scope-gains figure and the one-third mix component.

summary_flags: GDPval described as 'essentially the project's integrand': overstated. It has a delegate branch (win rate, review cost, full human redo on failure) but no assistant or partial-credit (kappa) term. 'Win' includes ties. Figures cover OpenAI models only, on the 220-task gold subset. The 28% (1.39x) is the lenient try-n case; try-once for GPT-5 is 1.12x (about 11% time saved).

'METR's randomized trials measured kappa at -19%': imprecise. The RCT measures the effect of being allowed to use AI (any mode, including non-use), not pure assistant-mode speedup. In the project's units, time saved is about -0.19. The record's '-0.16' elsewhere is output per hour, not time saved.

'q shrinks with task length rather than being a constant 0.5' is an inference from the 50 min to 8 min horizon refit, not a directly reported q-by-length curve. The time-trend evidence is weak (SE 5.5) and reverses for scikit-learn.

'Adjusting for success cuts implied productivity growth from 1.8 to about 1.0 pp': 1.0 is the API figure; Claude.ai is 1.2 pp. Also, Anthropic's p(h) is Claude-judged success against Claude-estimated human time on a self-selected sample, so calling it a 'field version of p(h)' needs that caveat.
'Stanford DEL and BLS still rely on extensive-margin exposure scores': true for Canaries, but the BLS article uses analyst case-study judgment, not exposure scores.

Canaries vintage claim was wrong: 16% was from September 2025 data, not a 'Nov 2025 version'. The 13%/16% (firm-shock-adjusted regressions) and the 15%/19% (descriptive kept-pace gap) are different measures. The record also wrongly said the 19% headline controls for firm shocks.

Gap claim 'rho is measured in only one place (GDPval)' is overstated. METR's early-2025 public data include initial vs post-review implementation time for part of the sample. Humlum-Vestergaard report time spent editing chatbot output and new oversight tasks. GDPval remains the only direct monitored review-time measure found.
Humlum-Vestergaard limitation 'occupations are not IT services' is wrong: software developers and IT support specialists are among the 11 occupations.

Working hypothesis 'largely holds' needs nuance. Intensive-margin time savings ARE measured (Humlum-Vestergaard self-reports; Anthropic model estimates; GDPval workflow ratios; METR RCTs), but not net of review and failure, by task length, for IT-services work. The exposure literature itself (Eloundou; the Brynjolfsson-Korinek-Agrawal agenda's task-level section) stays on the extensive margin.

Funding claims partly unverified. Confirmed: Anthropic Economic Futures awards are $10-50k plus $5k API credits and closed ('not currently accepting applications'), and eligibility language names academic economists, data scientists and PhD students. Also confirmed: the OpenAI Foundation's $250M (May 27, 2026 post) promises open calls with no dates and names low- and middle-income countries as a focus. NOT verified: the OpenAI Economic Research Exchange July 5, 2026 deadline and contact (page 403), Stripe fellowship details (403), and the UChicago AI in the Workplace fellowship (not opened by the record or by me).

The claim that OpenAI's 'How People Use ChatGPT' judges success and time with the model was not verified (the paper was not opened by the record). The Windfall Trust, OECD AI-WIPS and ONS negative findings were not re-checked; my web-search budget was exhausted mid-check, so these remain unverified absence-of-evidence claims.
Coyle-Poquiz's cross-border point concerns AI infrastructure and investment. Applying it to Indian IT services exports is the researcher's extension.
verify.corrected_summary: No one publishes exactly what the project needs: hours of labor saved per task, net of failures and review, as a function of task length and capability, for IT-services work. Several sources supply pieces. (1) GDPval (OpenAI, Oct 2025) models a 'model attempt, then expert review, then human redo if it fails' workflow. On the 220-task gold subset, monitored expert review averaged 109 minutes against 404 minutes of self-reported expert completion time (review is about 27% of task time). For GPT-5 this implies a 1.12x speedup if the model is tried once (about 11% time saved) and 1.39x if it is retried up to n times (about 28%). This is a template for the delegate branch of the integrand, with a full-redo fallback and no assistant (kappa) term. It covers OpenAI models only and one-shot expert-written tasks. (2) METR provides the reviewer-acceptance correction. Normalized to maintainers' own 68% merge rate for human patches, roughly half of SWE-bench-passing patches from mid-2024 to late-2025 agents would not be merged (24.2 pp normalized gap; raw merge rates are one-third to one-half of pass rates). Claude Sonnet 4.5's 50% time horizon falls from about 50 to about 8 minutes under maintainer review, which suggests (but does not directly show) that acceptance falls with task length. METR's early-2025 RCT found that allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (CI +2% to +39%). This measures the effect of AI permission, not a pure assistant-mode kappa, and corresponds to about -0.19 time saved. The late-2025 follow-up (point estimates -18% and -4% time, CIs including zero) was judged only very weak evidence because developers withheld tasks they would not do without AI. (3) The Anthropic Economic Index (Jan 2026) gives a model-judged, deployment-based analogue of p(h). API success falls from about 60% on sub-hour tasks to about 45% on 5+ hour tasks, crossing 50% near 3.5 hours. Adjusting for success lowers implied US productivity growth from about 1.8 to 1.2 pp/yr (Claude.ai) or 1.0 pp/yr (API). Both success and time are Claude's estimates. (4) Humlum and Vestergaard's Danish survey-register study, which includes software developers and IT support, finds self-reported time savings of about 2.8% of users' work hours (6-7% on usage days) and no detectable earnings or hours effects. The exposure literature (Eloundou et al.) and outcome trackers (Canaries: the employment of 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs is 19% below the kept-pace path as of June 2026, mostly through reduced hiring) stay on the extensive margin or on outcomes. BLS uses qualitative case-study judgment. So the hypothesis holds in a refined form: intensive-margin savings are measured, but not net of review and failure, by task length, for IT-services task mixes. On funding, Anthropic's Economic Futures awards ($10-50k plus $5k API credits) are closed. The OpenAI Foundation's $250M program (announced May 2026) promises open calls with no dates yet and names low- and middle-income countries as a priority. Details of OpenAI's Economic Research Exchange, Stripe's fellowship and UChicago's fellowship could not be verified from primary pages.
verify.dataset_notes: Anthropic EconomicIndex (Hugging Face): public, CC-BY data, MIT code. Releases confirmed: 2025-02-10, 2025-03-27, 2025-09-15, 2026-01-15, 2026-03-24 (Opus 4.5/4.6 and learning curves, missing from the record), and 2026-06-26 (artifacts and monthly aggregates). The Jan 2026 config has raw Claude.ai and 1P API files for Nov 13-20, 2025; oddly, the API file sits under the release_2025_09_15 path. The README does not say which primitive fields (success, human time, schooling, autonomy) or geography the Jan 2026 files contain, so check the files before relying on them. GDPval: the URL given is the paper, not the data. The gold subset (220 tasks) is described as open-sourced, but I did not open its data host, and I did not verify the 'automated grader' or whether per-task times are released. The 404/109-minute figures are paper-level averages. METR early-2025 RCT (github.com/METR/Measuring-Early-2025-AI-on-Exp-OSS-Devs): confirmed public. data_complete.csv has 246 issues with pre-randomization time forecasts, treatment, initial and post-review implementation times (post-review only for part of the study), plus regression.py, which gives 0.188 (CI about 0.013 to 0.395). METR late-2025 RCT (github.com/METR/Measuring-Late-2025-AI-on-OSS-Devs): confirmed public; README says to interpret 'with a major grain of salt'. The repo page does not state counts; 57 developers, 143 repos and 800+ tasks come from the blog. METR time horizons: metr.org/research is a listing page with no dataset links. Cite the specific posts instead (e.g., metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/ and metr.org/blog/2026-01-29-time-horizon-1-1/). The public data location was not verified in this check. ADP/Canaries: the microdata are not public (restricted to the ADP-Stanford team). The paper says it provides a public set of 'AI Economic Indicators'. Better URL: digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/08/Canaries_August2026.pdf. BLS: the cited MLR article covers only the 2023-33 projections and contains no '2025-35 exposure tier', so that part of the description is unverified and should be removed or sourced separately. Danish Humlum-Vestergaard data: about 25,000 workers per survey round, linked to Statistics Denmark registers. The 'on-request via Statistics Denmark and authors' access route was not verified (register microdata typically require authorized institutional access). Mark access as restricted/unverified.

streams.name: HCI studies of AI-assisted work: where the time goes, verification behaviour, and over-reliance

works.title: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14306 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.14306, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Share of session time spent in 12 'CUPS' states (e.g. verifying a suggestion, writing new code, prompt crafting, waiting) while programmers code with GitHub Copilot; acceptance rates; true verification time per suggestion, including checking done after accepting.
works.method_plain: 21 Microsoft programmers each did one roughly 12-minute coding task with Copilot while the screen was recorded. Right afterwards they replayed the video and labelled every segment with what they were doing (3,137 labels). There was no no-AI control group.
key_numbers: Mean task time 12.23 min (sd 3.98); 1,024 suggestions shown, 34.0% accepted (mean of per-person acceptance rates 36.5%, range 14.3%-60.7%)
'Thinking/Verifying Suggestion' is the largest state: 22.4% of session time (sd 12.97)

Other states: Writing New Functionality 14.05%, Editing Last Suggestion 11.90%, Prompt crafting 11.56%, Debugging/Testing 11.31%, Thinking about new code 10.91%, Looking up documentation 7.45%, Waiting for suggestion 4.20%, Editing written code 4.28%, Deferring thought 1.39%
Copilot-specific states (verifying, deferring, waiting, prompt crafting, editing a suggestion) together take 51.5% of session time (sd 19.3); every participant spent more than 21% there
Paper's conclusion: 34.3% of session time goes to double-checking and editing Copilot suggestions

Hidden verification: when a programmer defers thought and accepts first, they verify afterwards 53.2% of the time. Adjusted mean verification time is 15.21 s (median 6.48 s) against an unadjusted 3.25 s (median 1.99 s), about 5x higher. So raw acceptance rates and time-to-accept understate review cost
Suggestions shown while the user was crafting a prompt were accepted only 10.7% of the time

By experience: acceptance 30.0% (+/-14.5) for programmers with more than 6 years professional experience vs 37.6% (+/-14.6) for less experienced ones; 37.6% for prior Copilot users vs 29.3% for new users. The authors say n is too small to conclude
Survey: 17/21 agreed they finished faster with Copilot
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the closest existing template for splitting AI-assisted work into authoring, verifying and waiting time. The 22.4% verify share and the 34.3% verify-plus-edit share bound rho for short, autocomplete-style tasks (h of a few seconds to minutes). Acceptance of about 34% is an observed acceptance rate, not q (q is acceptance conditional on passing checks). The finding that verification continues after acceptance warns that acceptance-based measures understate rho.
works.limitations: n=21 from a single firm; short (about 12 min) self-contained tasks, mostly Python; 2022-era inline completion, not agents; no no-AI control, so kappa cannot be computed directly; labels are self-reported after the fact.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09089, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Effect of allowing AI tools (mainly Cursor with frontier models) on completion time for real issues in large open-source repos, plus a screen-recording breakdown of time by activity: coding, testing, reading, prompting, waiting on AI, reviewing AI output, idle.
works.method_plain: A randomized controlled trial. 16 experienced maintainers each listed real issues from their own repositories (246 tasks, about 2 hours each on average). Each issue was randomly assigned to 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed'. Researchers hand-labelled 143 hours of screen recordings at about 10-second resolution, of which 84 hours (74 recordings) were valid.
key_numbers: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (regression estimate); the raw ratio difference was 34%
Forecast speedups: developers expected a 24% time reduction before the study and believed in a 20% reduction afterwards; economics experts predicted 39% and ML experts 38%
Developers accepted fewer than 44% of AI generations

With AI allowed, about 9% of time went to reviewing and cleaning AI output and about 4% to waiting on AI generations (labelled subset). Time actively coding and reading/searching fell, and idle time rose
75% of developers report reading every line of AI code; 56% often need major changes to clean it up; 100% report needing to modify AI code
No clear learning effect over the first 30-50 hours of Cursor use; underpowered positive speedup beyond 50 hours
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a direct kappa-type measurement in a high-context setting, and kappa can be negative (a slowdown of about 19%) for long tasks in familiar codebases where tacit knowledge matters. It is the only study found with an activity-level time split (review about 9%, waiting about 4%) under a randomized counterfactual. The acceptance rate below 44% bounds q times p. The gap between perceived and measured speed warns against using self-reported savings for theta_j.
works.limitations: 16 developers, all expert maintainers on very familiar repos with high quality standards. This is close to the worst case for AI and unlike Indian IT services maintenance, which is staffed by less senior engineers on client code. Early-2025 models. Time shares come from a subset of recordings.

works.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
works.authors: Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.03622, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Security and correctness of code written with vs without an AI assistant (codex-davinci-002); participants' confidence and trust; how often AI output was copied.
works.method_plain: A between-subjects user study: 47 participants (33 with AI, 14 control) solved 5 security-relevant tasks (encryption, signing, sandboxed paths, SQL, C strings). Solutions were graded secure or insecure, and confidence was surveyed afterwards.
key_numbers: Q1 encryption: 67% of AI-group answers correct vs 79% of control; the AI group was significantly more likely to be insecure (p=0.017)
Q2 signing: 3% of the AI group wrote a secure solution vs 21% of control (p=0.039), while correctness was similar (55% vs 64%)

Among AI-group participants with insecure answers, trust in the AI to write secure code was higher (e.g. mean Likert 4.0 vs 1.5 on Q3), and belief that they solved the task securely exceeded insecure control participants (3.5 vs 2.0 on Q1)
Share of AI outputs copied directly, without vs with security experience: Q1 22.4% vs 9.2%; Q4 SQL 25.3% vs 6.67%
Insecure answer rate for participants who did not adjust temperature vs those who did: Q1 70% vs 20%; Q3 81% vs 50%
87% of secure responses required significant user edits to the AI output
Long prompts led to acceptance 42.7% of the time vs 15.7% for short prompts
Tasks took about 11-14 min each (Q5 31 min)
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that 'passing the checks the user ran' is not the same as acceptable quality. Users accept output that is functionally correct but insecure, and less expert, more trusting users accept more. So q in practice is too high for some error classes, and the labour saved is partly a quality cost pushed downstream. Secure outcomes needed heavy editing, which implies a higher true rho once hidden defects are counted.
works.limitations: Small sample, mostly university students; a 2022 model; narrow security tasks; copying is a crude proxy for acceptance; no time-share data.

works.title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
works.authors: Helena Vasconcelos, Matthew Joerke, Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin, Tobias Gerstenberg, Michael Bernstein, Ranjay Krishna
works.venue: Proc. ACM HCI Vol. 7, CSCW1, Article 129 (CSCW 2023)
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06823 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.06823, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Overreliance (the rate of agreeing with the AI when it is wrong) as a function of task difficulty, the cost of reading the explanation, and monetary reward for accuracy.
works.method_plain: Five preregistered online experiments (N=731 in total) in which people solved mazes with a simulated AI that was right 80% of the time. The researchers varied maze difficulty, the type of explanation, and the bonus per correct answer, and fitted Bayesian mixed models.
key_numbers: Study sizes: S1 N=340, S2 N=340, S3 N=286, S4 N=114, S5 N=76
AI accuracy fixed at 80%; human pilot accuracy 83.5%
S1: overreliance rises as tasks get harder (easy minus medium = -3.967 in model units, 95% CI [-5.48, -2.53]); explanations do not reduce overreliance on easy tasks but do on hard tasks
S4: a high bonus ($0.50 per correct maze) vs a low bonus ($0.01) lowered overreliance (difference 0.93, CI [0.414, 1.46])
The most salient explanation condition reached an average overreliance of 0% (S3)
S5: people place higher monetary value on explanations that are easier to understand and on explanations in harder tasks
works.relevance_to_theta: Formalizes reliance as a cost-benefit choice. People verify when verification is cheap relative to doing the task and when the stakes are high. In theta_j terms, q and rho are jointly chosen, not fixed: making verification cheaper (good tests, diffs) or raising the penalty for errors (client SLAs) lowers false acceptance at the cost of more review time. On hard, long tasks, unaided verification is costly, so overreliance rises.
works.limitations: A toy maze task with a simulated AI, using crowd workers; overreliance is reported as model coefficients more than raw rates; no coding or professional setting.

works.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
works.authors: Zana Bucinca, Maja Barbara Malaya, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
works.venue: Proc. ACM HCI Vol. 5, CSCW1, Article 188 (CSCW 2021); DOI 10.1145/3449287
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09692 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.09692, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Overreliance, correctness and subjective ratings under 'cognitive forcing' designs (e.g. the person must decide before seeing the AI, or the AI answer appears only on request) vs simple explainable-AI designs vs no AI.
works.method_plain: An online experiment with 199 people on a nutrition-judgement task (identifying the main carbohydrate source in a meal) with a simulated AI that was 75% accurate. Several interface designs were compared.
key_numbers: N=199; AI accuracy 75%

Carb-source detection on trials where the AI was wrong (my reading of Table 2 marginal means): overreliance 0.64 with simple explainable AI vs 0.48 with cognitive forcing; correct answers 0.08 vs 0.27 (significant)
Overall decision: overreliance about 0.68 vs 0.65 (not significant)
Users rated the designs that most reduced overreliance least favourably; trust was 3.72 in both categories (n.s.)
The benefit was concentrated among people high in 'need for cognition'
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the false-acceptance rate (1 minus q, applied to wrong output) depends on workflow design: forcing independent thinking cuts overreliance, but users dislike it and it costs time. Firms choosing review processes therefore trade rho against q. It also shows overreliance stays high (about 0.5-0.65 of wrong AI answers accepted) even under the better designs.
works.limitations: A non-programming toy task with crowd workers; the table values here were extracted from PDF text and the column alignment should be confirmed against the original table; no timing data on review cost.

works.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
works.authors: Gagan Bansal, Tongshuang Wu, Joyce Zhou, Raymond Fok, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Daniel S. Weld
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14779 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.14779, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Accuracy of human-AI teams and agreement with the AI, with and without explanations, when the AI is about as accurate as the human.
works.method_plain: Mechanical Turk experiments on sentiment classification (Beer, Amazon book reviews) and LSAT logic questions, with about 100 participants per condition and an AI fixed at 84% accuracy on sentiment. Conditions compared showing only confidence against several explanation styles.
key_numbers: Beer: the team with AI confidence reached accuracy 0.89+/-0.05, above both the AI (0.84) and unassisted humans (0.82+/-0.09)
Complementary gains for Team (Conf) of 2.2% (Amzbook) and 20.1% (LSAT) over unassisted workers
Explanations did not beat the confidence-only baseline (Beer 0.89 vs 0.88, p=.24)
Explanations increased the chance humans accepted the AI's recommendation regardless of its correctness: accuracy improved when the AI was right and worsened when it was wrong
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that persuasive presentation raises acceptance of both correct and incorrect outputs. If AI coding agents produce fluent PR descriptions or rationales, the observed acceptance q may rise without any rise in true quality, inflating measured theta_j.
works.limitations: Short classification tasks with crowd workers; a 2020-era setting; no timing breakdown.

works.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
works.authors: Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee, Advait Sarkar, Lev Tankelevitch, Ian Drosos, Sean Rintel, Richard Banks, Nicholas Wilson
works.what_measured: When knowledge workers report doing critical thinking (verification, integration) while using GenAI, how their effort changes, and how this relates to confidence in the AI vs in themselves.
works.method_plain: An online survey of 319 knowledge workers, who described 936 real examples of using GenAI at work. Regressions link confidence measures to self-reported critical thinking and effort, supplemented by qualitative coding.
key_numbers: 936 examples: 39.96% Creation, 32.37% Information, 27.67% Advice tasks
Critical thinking was reported as enacted in about 60% (555/936) of examples

Confidence in AI doing the task is negatively associated with enacting critical thinking (beta=-0.69, p<0.001); self-confidence (beta=0.26, p=0.026) and confidence in evaluating AI (beta=0.31, p=0.046) are positive
'Less' or 'much less' effort reported for 72% (Knowledge), 79% (Comprehension), 69% (Application), 72% (Analysis), 76% (Synthesis) and 55% (Evaluation) of examples
Qualitatively, effort shifts toward information verification, response integration and task stewardship
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests that rho is endogenous to trust: as confidence in AI rises (for example, as p(h,t) improves), workers check less. That lowers measured rho but may lower effective quality. This is a time-varying channel in the model: rho(t) falls with capability partly through less scrutiny, not only through cheaper verification.
works.limitations: Self-reported and cross-sectional; recalled examples; no time measurement; a convenience sample of Prolific workers; not specific to software or IT services.

works.title: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models
works.authors: Shraddha Barke, Michael B. James, Nadia Polikarpova
works.venue: arXiv:2206.15000, formatted as a Proc. ACM Program. Lang. submission. I did not confirm the final OOPSLA publication from an opened page
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.15000 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.15000, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: Qualitative patterns of how programmers prompt, validate and use Copilot suggestions.
works.method_plain: Grounded-theory observation of 20 participants with varied Copilot experience working on tasks in four languages, including a two-part task designed to separate familiar work from unfamiliar work.
key_numbers: 20 participants, 4 programming languages

Use is 'bimodal': acceleration mode (the programmer knows the next step; quick visual 'pattern-matching' validation; short suggestions) vs exploration mode (the programmer is unsure; more extensive validation, e.g. running code and comparing alternatives)
No time shares or rates reported (qualitative study)
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests kappa and rho differ by mode. Acceleration means low rho and modest kappa on familiar work; exploration means high rho with possibly large savings on unfamiliar work. For f_j this means task familiarity, not only length h, matters. Service lines heavy on routine maintenance would sit in acceleration mode.
works.limitations: Qualitative, with no numbers; small sample; 2022 inline completion.

works.title: The RealHumanEval: Evaluating Large Language Models' Abilities to Support Programmers
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Valerie Chen, Mohammed Alsobay, Subhro Das, Sebastian Zhao, Dennis Wei, Manish Nagireddy, Prasanna Sattigeri, Ameet Talwalkar, David Sontag
works.venue: arXiv:2404.02806 (venue not confirmed from opened page)
works.url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02806 (and full PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.02806, text extracted locally)
works.what_measured: How benchmark gains in LLMs translate into human productivity (time per task, tasks completed) with autocomplete vs chat assistance vs no LLM, and suggestion acceptance and copy rates.
works.method_plain: 243 participants (80% CS students) worked in a web IDE for about 35 minutes on short coding tasks, randomly assigned to one of 7 LLMs (autocomplete or chat) or no LLM, with full telemetry logged.
key_numbers: Average time per task 358 s (std 153 s)
5,204 autocomplete suggestions shown with an average 11.3% acceptance rate; 35.8% of chat messages had code copied
GPT-3.5, CodeLlama-34b and GPT-4 cut time per task by an average of 78, 64 and 60 s against about 400 s with no LLM (p=0.04, 0.12, 0.10); CodeLlama-7b added about 10 s

Benchmark gains translate less than one-for-one: GPT-3.5 (chat) beats CodeLlama-34b by 85% on HumanEval, but users were only 8.3% faster (95% CI [-11.2, 24.6]); 34b vs 7b, a 19% HumanEval gap, gave users 22.8% faster times
User preferences (acceptance rates) did not track actual productivity
works.relevance_to_theta: The only study found that maps benchmark capability (a proxy for p) to the human time saved (kappa) across models of different quality. The mapping is concave and noisy, which supports modelling kappa as a function of p rather than a constant. Also warns that acceptance rates are poor proxies for savings.
works.limitations: Mostly students; very short tasks (minutes); 2023-24 models; no split of time into verification and authoring.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Saffron Huang, Bryan Seethor, Esin Durmus, Kunal Handa, Miles McCain, Michael Stern, Deep Ganguli (Anthropic Societal Impacts)
works.what_measured: Self-reported share of work done with Claude, productivity gains, how much work can be fully delegated, and how engineers verify output; plus Claude Code transcript analysis.
works.method_plain: An internal survey (132 engineers and researchers, Aug 2025), 53 interviews, and about 200,000 Claude Code transcripts from Feb and Aug 2025.
key_numbers: Claude used in about 59-60% of work, up from 28% a year earlier
Self-reported productivity gain of about +50%, up from +20%; 14% report more than +100%
More than half say they can 'fully delegate' only 0-20% of their work
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done
Engineers prefer delegating tasks that are easy to 'sniff-check' for correctness
works.relevance_to_theta: Separates delegation from assistance. Most work is assisted (the kappa route), and only a small slice is fully delegated (the q*p route). The finding that delegation is chosen by how cheap verification is supports making rho a function of task verifiability in f_j. The 27% figure on new work warns that time 'saved' partly becomes extra output, which is the demand-side d term rather than labour replacement.
works.limitations: Self-reported; a frontier-lab workforce, highly unrepresentative; not anonymous; the authors themselves flag METR's finding that developers overestimate speedups.

research.stream_summary: The HCI literature does measure the behavioural pieces of theta_j, but in small, short-task lab settings. Mozannar et al. (CUPS, CHI 2024) is the best template. Programmers with Copilot spent 22.4% of session time verifying suggestions and 34.3% verifying plus editing. About half of all time went to AI-specific activity. True verification time per suggestion was about 5x the naive estimate, because people accept first and check later. METR's 2025 randomized trial is the only study combining a randomized counterfactual with a minute-level time split. Expert developers on their own repos were 19% slower with AI, accepted fewer than 44% of generations, and spent about 9% of time reviewing and cleaning AI output plus about 4% waiting. So kappa can be negative on long, context-heavy tasks. RealHumanEval links benchmark strength (a proxy for p) to time saved and finds the link weaker than one-for-one. The over-reliance studies (Bansal 2021, Bucinca 2021, Vasconcelos 2023) show acceptance of wrong AI output is common. In Bucinca's task, about 0.5-0.65 of wrong AI answers were accepted. Over-reliance also rises with task difficulty, falls with higher stakes and cheaper verification, and is inflated by fluent explanations. So q and rho are a joint choice, not constants. Perry et al. show the cost in code: AI users wrote less secure code while believing it more secure. For example, 3% vs 21% wrote a secure signing solution. Lee et al. (CHI 2025) find that higher confidence in AI predicts less critical thinking (beta=-0.69). That implies rho falls over time partly because scrutiny falls, not only because checking gets cheaper. Bottom line for the working hypothesis: HCI does address the intensive margin, but only for minute-scale coding tasks, Western samples and pre-agent tools. Nothing measures rho or q on hour-to-day tasks, in services firms, or as capability rises.
gaps_noticed: No study measures rho (review time as a share of task length h) across a range of task lengths; CUPS covers seconds-to-minutes and METR about 2-hour tasks, with no curve linking them
No HCI time-use study in an IT services or BPO firm, or in India; samples are Microsoft or US developers, students, and crowd workers

q is never measured as defined in the model (acceptance conditional on passing tests). Studies report raw acceptance rates (Copilot about 34%, RealHumanEval autocomplete 11.3%, METR below 44%) that mix p and q
Over-reliance studies use toy tasks (mazes, nutrition, sentiment) with simulated AI at a fixed 75-84% accuracy; how overreliance changes as AI accuracy rises toward 95%+ is not mapped
No longitudinal study tracks how rho and q change as the same workers use better models over time; METR finds no learning effect over 30-50 hours, but this is underpowered
Downstream quality cost (defects escaping review) is measured only for security (Perry) and is not converted into hours of later rework
Agentic workflows (multi-file PRs, autonomous agents) lack a CUPS-style time breakdown; most evidence is inline autocomplete or chat

Dell'Acqua et al. 'Jagged Technological Frontier' (BCG consultants, outside-frontier accuracy drop) is highly relevant to q, but the HBS and SSRN pages returned 403, so I could not verify its numbers and it is excluded
Peng et al. 2023 (55.8% faster with Copilot) is cited inside Mozannar et al. but I did not open it; my web-search budget ran out mid-task, so the 2026 literature was not searched

datasets.name: CUPS dataset (Copilot session labels and telemetry, Mozannar et al.)
datasets.description: 21 sessions with 3,137 CUPS state labels plus telemetry. The paper says the data and labelling tool are released, but I did not open the repository to confirm.

datasets.name: METR early-2025 developer RCT data
datasets.description: 246 tasks with completion times, AI-allowed flags and labelled screen-recording activity categories (27 fine-grained labels). I did not confirm the public release terms.

datasets.name: RealHumanEval interaction logs
datasets.description: Telemetry from 243 participants: suggestions shown and accepted, chat copies, code snapshots every 15 s, and task times across 7 LLMs. The paper describes releasing the data, but I did not open the repository.

datasets.name: Perry et al. user-study instrument
datasets.description: The authors release the UI as a research instrument; participant-level data release is not confirmed.

datasets.name: Anthropic Claude Code internal transcripts
datasets.description: About 200,000 transcripts and the internal survey; only aggregate results are published.

works.title: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
works.venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2024), pp. 1-16, DOI 10.1145/3613904.3641936
works.what_measured: Share of session time in 12 'CUPS' activity states (e.g. verifying a suggestion, writing new code, prompt crafting, waiting) while programmers code with GitHub Copilot; acceptance rates; verification time per suggestion including checking done after accepting.
works.method_plain: 21 programmers recruited through internal developer mailing lists at Microsoft each did one coding task with Copilot (about 12 minutes on average) while the screen was recorded. Afterwards they replayed the recording and labelled every segment with what they were doing (3,137 labels). 19 of 21 used Python. No no-AI control group.
key_numbers: Mean task time 12.23 min (sd 3.98); 1,024 suggestions shown, 34.0% accepted overall; mean of per-person acceptance rates 36.5% (median 33.8%, range 14.3%-60.7%)
