'Verifying suggestion' is the largest state: 22.4% of session time (sd 12.97); 'Writing new functionality' is second at 14.05%

Other states (Figure 1 values): Editing last suggestion 11.90%, Prompt crafting 11.56%, Debugging/Testing 11.31%, Thinking about new code 10.91%, Looking up documentation 7.45%, Editing written code 4.28%, Waiting for suggestion 4.20%, Deferring thought 1.39%

Copilot-specific states (verifying, deferring, waiting, prompt crafting, editing a suggestion) together take 51.5% of session time (sd 19.3); every participant spent more than 21% there; half spent more than 47%
Conclusion section: 34.3% of session time goes to double-checking and editing Copilot suggestions (= 22.4% verifying + 11.90% editing)

When a programmer defers thought on a suggestion they accepted, they verify it immediately afterward 53.2% of the time. Adjusted mean verification time 15.21 s (sd 20.68; median 6.48 s) vs unadjusted 3.25 s (sd 3.33; median 1.99 s): about 5x higher mean, 3x higher median
Of 234 suggestions shown while the user was crafting a prompt, only 10.7% were accepted

Acceptance 30.0% (+/-14.5) for programmers with more than 6 years' professional experience vs 37.6% (+/-14.6) for the rest; 37.6% (+/-15.3) for prior Copilot users vs 29.3% (+/-13.7) for new users. Authors say n is too small to conclude
Survey: 17/21 agreed they completed the task faster with Copilot; 16/21 agreed they were more productive
works.relevance_to_theta: Closest existing template for splitting AI-assisted work into authoring, verifying and waiting time. The 22.4% verify share and the 34.3% verify-plus-edit share bound rho for short, autocomplete-style work (suggestions of seconds, sessions of minutes). The 34% acceptance is an observed acceptance rate that mixes p and q, not q itself. The post-acceptance verification finding warns that acceptance-based measures understate rho.
works.limitations: n=21 from one firm; short (about 12 min) self-contained tasks, mostly Python; 2022-era inline completion, not agents; no no-AI control, so kappa cannot be computed; labels are retrospective self-reports; 6.5% of session time was labelled 'I don't know' and dropped.
works.corrections: All numbers match the v5 PDF. Added final venue details from Crossref (CHI 2024, pp. 1-16, DOI 10.1145/3613904.3641936). Clarified that the 10.7% is of 234 suggestions shown during prompt crafting.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth (Elizabeth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.venue: arXiv:2507.09089 (METR report; no journal venue confirmed)
works.what_measured: Effect of allowing AI tools (mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on completion time for real issues in mature open-source repos, plus screen-recording labels of time by activity: coding, testing/debugging, reading/searching, Git/environment, prompting, waiting on AI, reviewing AI output, idle/other.
works.method_plain: Randomized controlled trial. 16 experienced developers (about 5 years on their repository on average) listed real issues from their own projects: 246 tasks, about 2.0 hours each on average. Each issue was randomly assigned to 'AI allowed' or 'AI disallowed'. Researchers labelled 128 screen recordings (143 hours) at about 10-second resolution into 27 fine-grained categories; after filtering, 74 recordings (84 hours) were analysed.
key_numbers: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19% (regression estimate); the raw ratio of average times differed by 34% because AI-allowed issues happened to be slightly harder
Forecasts: developers expected a 24% time reduction beforehand and believed afterwards in a 20% reduction; economics experts predicted 39% shorter and ML experts 38% shorter
Developers accepted fewer than 44% of Cursor generations (excludes 3 developers whose data could not be collected)

On the 44 AI-allowed issues with valid labelled recordings, about 9% of time went to reviewing and cleaning AI output and about 4% to waiting on AI generations. With AI, the share of time actively coding and reading/searching fell, and idle time rose
75% of developers report reading every line of AI code; 56% often need major changes to clean it up; 100% report needing to modify AI code

No clear learning effect over the first 50 hours of Cursor use (and no change when dropping each developer's first eight AI-allowed issues). The positive speedup beyond 50 hours comes from a single developer; a footnote says that after publication a second developer corrected their Cursor experience to more than 100 hours, and including them moves that bucket from roughly 25% speedup to roughly 0%
works.relevance_to_theta: The only randomized estimate in this stream of the net time effect of AI on realistic, roughly 2-hour tasks. It shows the net effect of allowing AI can be negative (about 19% slower) for experts in very familiar codebases with high quality standards. It is not a clean kappa: it mixes assistance, delegation and developers' own choices about when to use AI. It provides an activity-level split under a randomized counterfactual (review about 9%, waiting about 4%). The <44% acceptance rate is a raw acceptance rate (mixes p and q). The gap between perceived and measured speed warns against self-reported savings for theta_j.
works.limitations: 16 developers, all expert maintainers on repositories they know very well, with high quality standards: close to a worst case for AI and unlike Indian IT services work by less senior engineers on client code. Early-2025 models. Time shares come from a filtered subset of recordings (44 AI-allowed issues). Learning analysis is underpowered and its one positive point is fragile (see footnote 15).
works.corrections: Corrected the learning-effect claim: the >50-hour positive speedup rests on one developer and the paper's own footnote 15 says a corrected second developer moves it to about 0%. Specified that the 9% and 4% shares come from 44 AI-allowed issues with valid recordings, and that 143 hours came from 128 recordings. Noted that the <44% acceptance figure excludes 3 developers. First author list name is 'Beth Barnes' on the paper. Softened the relevance claim that this is a 'direct kappa' measurement.

works.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
works.authors: Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh
works.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS '23), pp. 2785-2799, DOI 10.1145/3576915.3623157
works.what_measured: Security and correctness of code written with vs without an AI assistant (OpenAI codex-davinci-002); participants' confidence and trust; how often AI output was copied; how prompts and parameters relate to security.
works.method_plain: Between-subjects user study: 47 participants (33 with AI, 14 control) did 5 security-related tasks in Python, JavaScript and C (encryption, signing, sandboxed directory, SQL, C strings). Answers were graded for correctness and security; a survey followed.
key_numbers: Q1 encryption: 67% of AI-group answers correct vs 79% of control; the AI group was significantly more likely to write an insecure solution (p=0.017)
Q2 signing: 3% of the AI group wrote a secure solution vs 21% of control (p=0.039), while correctness was similar (55% vs 64%)

Within the AI group, participants with insecure answers trusted the AI to write secure code more than those with secure answers (mean Likert 4.0 vs 1.5 on Q3; 3.53 vs 1.0 on Q2). Insecure AI-group participants were also more likely to believe they solved the task securely than insecure control participants (3.5 vs 2.0 on Q1)
Share of AI outputs copied directly, without vs with security experience: Q1 22.4% vs 9.2%; Q4 SQL 25.3% vs 6.67%
Insecure answer rate for participants who did not vs did adjust temperature: Q1 70% vs 20%; Q3 81% vs 50%
87% of secure responses required significant user edits from the closest AI output (normalized edit distance)
Long prompts led to participant acceptance 42.7% of the time vs 15.7% for short prompts
Tasks took about 11-14 min each, except Q5 (31 min)
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that passing the checks a user actually ran is not the same as acceptable quality: users accept output that is functionally correct but insecure, and more trusting users accept more. So q in practice can be too high for some error classes, and part of the labour 'saved' is a quality cost pushed downstream. Secure outcomes needed heavy editing, suggesting a higher true rho once hidden defects are counted.
works.limitations: Small sample (87% aged 18-24, mostly students); a 2022 model; narrow security tasks; copying is a crude proxy for acceptance; no time-share data; control group only 14 people.
works.corrections: No numerical errors. Clarified that the 4.0 vs 1.5 trust comparison is between insecure and secure answers within the AI group, and added the Q2 figure. Page range and DOI confirmed via Crossref.

works.title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
works.authors: Helena Vasconcelos, Matthew Jörke, Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin, Tobias Gerstenberg, Michael S. Bernstein, Ranjay Krishna
works.venue: Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 7, CSCW1, Article 129 (April 2023), DOI 10.1145/3579605
works.what_measured: Overreliance (rate of agreeing with the AI when it is wrong) as a function of task difficulty, the cost of using the explanation, and monetary reward for accuracy; plus the subjective value of explanations.
works.method_plain: Five online experiments (N=731 total) in which people solved mazes with a simulated AI that was right 80% of the time. Researchers varied maze difficulty, explanation type and the bonus per correct answer, and fitted Bayesian linear mixed-effects models. Studies 1, 2, 4 and 5 were preregistered; Study 3 was exploratory.
key_numbers: Study sizes: S1 N=340, S2 N=340, S3 N=286, S4 N=114, S5 N=76
AI accuracy fixed at 80%; human pilot accuracy 83.5%

S1: overreliance rises as tasks get harder (Easy Pred minus Medium Pred = -3.967, 95% CI [-5.48, -2.53]); explanations do not change overreliance on easy tasks (0.164, CI [-1.678, 2.17]) but reduce it on hard tasks (1.74, CI [0.889, 2.76])
S4: high bonus ($0.50 per correct maze) vs low bonus ($0.01) lowered overreliance (Low minus High = 0.93, CI [0.414, 1.46])
In exploratory Study 3, the most salient explanation condition had an average overreliance rate of 0%
S5: people assign higher utility to explanations in harder tasks and to easier-to-use (highlight) explanations over written ones
works.relevance_to_theta: Frames reliance as a cost-benefit choice: people verify when verification is cheap relative to doing the task, and when stakes are high. In theta_j terms, q and rho are chosen together rather than fixed: cheaper verification (good tests, diffs) or higher penalties for errors (client SLAs) lower false acceptance at the cost of more review time. On hard tasks, unaided verification is costly and overreliance rises.
works.limitations: Toy maze task with a simulated AI and crowd workers; results reported mainly as model coefficients rather than raw rates; the 0% result comes from an exploratory study; no coding or professional setting.
works.corrections: Not all five studies were preregistered: Study 3 is explicitly exploratory with no preregistration, and the 0% overreliance result comes from it. Author name spelled Jörke on the paper (Joerke is a transliteration); middle initial for Michael S. Bernstein added. Added DOI. Models are Bayesian linear mixed-effects models.

works.title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
works.authors: Zana Buçinca, Maja Barbara Malaya, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
works.venue: Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 5, CSCW1, Article 188 (April 2021), DOI 10.1145/3449287
works.what_measured: Overreliance, correctness and subjective ratings under three 'cognitive forcing' designs (e.g. decide before seeing the AI, AI shown only on request, waiting) vs two simple explainable-AI designs vs no AI.
works.method_plain: An online experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk with 199 retained participants on a nutrition task (find the ingredient highest in carbs and pick a lower-carb substitute) with a simulated AI that was 75% accurate.
key_numbers: N=199; AI accuracy 75%
Carb-source detection on trials where the AI was wrong (Table 2 marginal means): overreliance 0.64 with simple explainable AI vs 0.48 with cognitive forcing (p=.003); correct 0.08 vs 0.27 (p<<.0001)

Overall decision on trials where the AI was wrong: overreliance 0.30 vs 0.26 (not significant); correct 0.03 vs 0.09 (p=.003); the remaining 0.68 vs 0.65 is 'human error' (wrong in a different way from the AI), not overreliance
Trust: 3.91 (simple explainable AI) vs 3.72 (cognitive forcing), not significant
Users gave the least favourable subjective ratings to the designs that reduced overreliance most
Cognitive forcing benefited people higher in 'need for cognition' more, on average
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the false-acceptance rate on wrong AI output depends on workflow design: forcing independent thinking cuts overreliance on the key sub-decision, but users dislike it. Firms choosing review processes trade review effort against acceptance quality. On the carb-source sub-decision about half to two-thirds of wrong AI answers were still accepted; on the full decision the overreliance rate was lower (about 0.26-0.30) because many errors were the human's own.
works.limitations: Non-programming toy task with crowd workers; simulated AI; no timing data on review cost.
works.corrections: Two errors in the record. (1) The overall-decision figure '0.68 vs 0.65' is the 'human error' row of Table 2, not overreliance; overall overreliance is 0.30 vs 0.26 (n.s.). (2) Trust was not '3.72 in both categories': it was 3.91 (SXAI) vs 3.72 (CFF), n.s. The carb-source numbers (0.64 vs 0.48; 0.08 vs 0.27) are correct. The relevance claim that overreliance stays at 0.5-0.65 'even under the better designs' holds only for the carb-source sub-decision.

works.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
works.authors: Gagan Bansal, Tongshuang Wu, Joyce Zhou, Raymond Fok, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Daniel S. Weld
works.venue: CHI '21 (CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems), Yokohama; DOI 10.1145/3411764.3445717
works.what_measured: Accuracy of human-AI teams and reliance on the AI, with and without explanations, when the AI is about as accurate as the human.
works.method_plain: Mechanical Turk experiments on sentiment classification (Beer reviews, Amazon book reviews) and LSAT logic questions, with about 100 participants per condition (93-101 after filtering) and AI accuracy fixed at 84%. Compared showing only AI confidence against several explanation styles.
key_numbers: Beer: team with AI confidence reached accuracy 0.89 +/- 0.05, above both the AI (0.84) and unassisted humans (0.82 +/- 0.09)
Team (Conf) also reached complementary performance on Amzbook and LSAT, with relative gains of 2.2% and 20.1% over unassisted workers
Explanations did not beat the confidence-only baseline (Beer 0.89 vs 0.88, p=.24; similar for Amzbook p=.22)
Explanations increased the chance humans accepted the AI's recommendation regardless of its correctness: they helped when the AI was right and hurt when it was wrong
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that persuasive presentation raises acceptance of both correct and incorrect outputs. By extension (not tested in the paper), fluent PR descriptions from coding agents could raise observed acceptance without raising true quality, inflating measured theta_j.
works.limitations: Short classification tasks with crowd workers; 2020-era setting; no timing breakdown; no generative or coding tasks.
works.corrections: No errors found. Added DOI from the paper's ACM reference.

works.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
works.authors: Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee, Advait Sarkar, Lev Tankelevitch, Ian Drosos, Sean Rintel, Richard Banks, Nicholas Wilson
works.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25), DOI 10.1145/3706598.3713778 (article number not confirmed)
works.what_measured: When knowledge workers report doing critical thinking (e.g. verification, integration) while using GenAI, how their effort changes, and how this relates to confidence in the AI and in themselves.
works.method_plain: An online survey on Prolific of 319 knowledge workers who described 936 real examples of using GenAI at work. Regressions link confidence measures to self-reported critical thinking and effort, plus qualitative coding of free-text answers.
key_numbers: 936 examples: 374 (39.96%) Creation, 303 (32.37%) Information, 259 (27.67%) Advice
Critical thinking was self-reported as enacted in 555 of 936 examples (59.29%)

Confidence in AI doing the task is negatively associated with enacting critical thinking (beta=-0.69, p<0.001); self-confidence (beta=0.26, p=0.026) and confidence in evaluating AI responses (beta=0.31, p=0.046) are positively associated
'Less' or 'much less' effort reported in 72% (Knowledge), 79% (Comprehension), 69% (Application), 72% (Analysis), 76% (Synthesis) and 55% (Evaluation) of examples
Qualitatively, effort shifts toward information verification, response integration and task stewardship
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests rho may be endogenous to trust: people who are more confident in the AI report less critical checking. If confidence rises with capability, measured rho could fall partly through less scrutiny rather than cheaper verification, possibly at a quality cost. This is a hypothesis from cross-sectional self-reports, not a measured time trend.
works.limitations: Self-reported and cross-sectional; recalled examples; no time measurement; Prolific convenience sample; not specific to software or IT services; associations, not causal effects.
works.corrections: Could not confirm 'Article 1121': Crossref lists the paper in the CHI '25 proceedings (pp. 1-22, DOI 10.1145/3706598.3713778) but gives no article number, and the ACM page returned 403; article number removed. Removed 'time-varying' from margins because the study is cross-sectional. The MSR publication landing page was not re-opened; the PDF was.

works.title: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models
works.authors: Shraddha Barke, Michael B. James, Nadia Polikarpova
works.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 7 (OOPSLA1), pp. 85-111, 2023; DOI 10.1145/3586030
works.what_measured: Qualitative patterns in how programmers prompt, validate and use Copilot suggestions.
works.method_plain: Grounded-theory observation of 20 participants (15 from academia, 5 from industry; 9 had used Copilot before) solving tasks in four languages, including a two-part 'Benford's Law' task built to separate a familiar part (Fibonacci) from an unfamiliar part (plotting).
key_numbers: 20 participants (15 academia, 5 industry), 4 programming languages

Interaction is 'bimodal': acceleration mode (programmer knows the next step; quick visual 'pattern-matching' validation; short suggestions) vs exploration mode (programmer is unsure; more extensive validation such as running code and comparing alternatives)
No time shares or rates reported (qualitative study)
works.relevance_to_theta: Suggests kappa and rho differ by mode: acceleration means light review and modest savings on familiar work; exploration means heavier review with possibly larger savings on unfamiliar work. For f_j, task familiarity, not only length h, may matter.
works.limitations: Qualitative, no numbers; small, mostly academic sample; 2022 inline completion.
works.corrections: Final venue confirmed via Crossref: Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 7(OOPSLA1), pp. 85-111, 2023, DOI 10.1145/3586030 (the arXiv PDF carries a placeholder ACM template reference). Added participant composition (15 academia, 5 industry).

works.title: The RealHumanEval: Evaluating Large Language Models' Abilities to Support Programmers
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Valerie Chen, Mohammed Alsobay, Subhro Das, Sebastian Zhao, Dennis Wei, Manish Nagireddy, Prasanna Sattigeri, Ameet Talwalkar, David Sontag
works.what_measured: How benchmark gains in LLMs translate into programmer productivity (time per task, tasks completed) with autocomplete vs chat vs no LLM, and whether preference metrics (acceptance, copy rates) track productivity.
works.method_plain: 243 participants (80% CS undergraduate or graduate students) worked in a web IDE for 35 minutes on short Python tasks, randomly assigned to a no-LLM control or one of several autocomplete or chat LLM conditions (CodeLlama-7b, CodeLlama-34b, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4o for chat), with telemetry including code snapshots every 15 s.
key_numbers: 888 coding tasks completed; average time per task 358 s (std 153 s)
5,204 autocomplete suggestions shown with an average 11.3% acceptance rate; 1,055 chat messages, 35.8% with at least one copy event

Against about 400 s per task with no LLM, GPT-3.5, CodeLlama-34b and GPT-4(o) models cut time per task by an average of 78, 64 and 60 s (p=0.04, 0.12, 0.10); CodeLlama-7b added about 10 s; no significant differences in number of tasks completed

Benchmark gains are not proportional to user gains: CodeLlama-34b (chat) is 19% better than 7b on HumanEval and users were 22.8% faster (95% CI [2.8, 38.7]); GPT-3.5 (chat) beats CodeLlama-34b by 85% on HumanEval but users were only 8.3% faster (95% CI [-11.2, 24.6])
Programmer preferences (acceptance and copy rates) did not correlate with actual performance
works.relevance_to_theta: Links benchmark capability (a proxy for p) to human time saved across models of different quality, and finds the link positive but far from one-for-one and noisy. Supports treating kappa as a function of capability rather than a constant, but the data are too noisy to pin a functional form. Also warns that acceptance rates are poor proxies for savings.
works.limitations: Mostly students; very short tasks (minutes); 2023-24 models; only one significant time reduction (GPT-3.5, p=0.04, before correction); no split of time into verification and authoring.
works.corrections: Clarified the conditions: the 'GPT-4' model in the results is GPT-4o (chat), which the appendix says was added post hoc; the paper describes 'seven LLMs' and also 'seven conditions', so the exact condition count is inconsistent in the paper itself. Added 888 tasks, the 34b-vs-7b confidence interval, and the null result on tasks completed. Venue not confirmed (no journal-ref on arXiv; web search budget exhausted). Removed the word 'concave' from relevance: the paper only says gains are 'not proportional', and the 7b model was slower than no LLM.

works.title: How AI is transforming work at Anthropic
works.authors: Saffron Huang, Bryan Seethor, Esin Durmus, Kunal Handa, Miles McCain, Michael Stern, Deep Ganguli (Anthropic)
works.what_measured: Self-reported share of work done with Claude, productivity gains, how much work can be fully delegated, and how engineers choose what to delegate; plus Claude Code transcript analysis.
works.method_plain: An internal survey of 132 engineers and researchers (August 2025), 53 in-depth interviews drawn from respondents, and about 200,000 internal Claude Code transcripts from February and August 2025.
key_numbers: Claude used in about 59% of work (60% in the key-findings summary), up from 28% a year earlier
Self-reported productivity gain about +50%, up from +20% a year earlier; 14% report gains above 100%
More than half say they can 'fully delegate' only 0-20% of their work (authors note respondents interpreted 'fully delegate' differently)
27% of Claude-assisted work would not otherwise have been done
Engineers tend to delegate tasks they can relatively easily 'sniff-check' for correctness, plus low-stakes, repetitive work and tasks where validation effort is small relative to creation effort
works.relevance_to_theta: Separates delegation from assistance: most work is assisted (the kappa route) and only a small slice is fully delegated (the q*p route). Delegation chosen by how cheap verification is supports making rho depend on task verifiability within f_j. The 27% new-work figure warns that 'saved' time partly becomes extra output, which belongs to the demand term d rather than labour replacement.
works.limitations: Self-reported; a frontier-lab workforce, highly unrepresentative of IT services; the authors themselves cite METR's finding that developers overestimate speedups.
works.corrections: Numbers match the page. The page's contributors section names five people and its suggested citation adds Miles McCain and Michael Stern. Removed the limitation 'not anonymous' because I could not confirm it on the page.

summary_flags: Bucinca et al. 2021: the summary's 'about 0.5-0.65 of wrong AI answers were accepted' holds only for the carb-source sub-decision (0.64 simple XAI vs 0.48 cognitive forcing). For the full decision, overreliance on wrong AI answers was 0.30 vs 0.26 (n.s.). The record's '0.68 vs 0.65 overreliance' is actually the 'human error' row, and its 'trust 3.72 in both' is wrong (3.91 vs 3.72, n.s.).

METR learning effect: the record's 'underpowered positive speedup beyond 50 hours' rests on one developer, and the paper's own footnote says a corrected second developer moves that bucket from about +25% to about 0%. This should not be cited as evidence of learning.

'METR's 2025 randomized trial is the only study combining a randomized counterfactual with a minute-level time split' is overstated: the search was cut short (no 2026 literature, Peng et al. and Dell'Acqua et al. not opened). Labels are at about 10-second resolution, and the 9% / 4% shares come from only 44 AI-allowed issues.

'So kappa can be negative on long, context-heavy tasks' over-generalizes. METR measures the net effect of allowing AI (assistance, delegation and the developer's choices combined), for expert maintainers on their own repos. It does not isolate kappa, and it does not show the effect is driven by task length.
Vasconcelos et al.: the 0% overreliance result comes from Study 3, which was exploratory and not preregistered; the record called all five studies preregistered.

'Inflated by fluent explanations' (Bansal 2021) extrapolates. The paper shows explanations raise acceptance regardless of correctness on classification and LSAT tasks; fluency of generated rationales was not tested.
Lee et al. 2025: 'implies rho falls over time' turns a cross-sectional, self-reported association into a time trend. At most it suggests a hypothesis.
RealHumanEval: 'concave' mapping from benchmark to time saved is not a claim the paper makes ('not proportional'); CodeLlama-7b was slower than no LLM, and only one time reduction had p<0.05.

Internal inconsistency: the bottom line says HCI evidence is 'only for minute-scale coding tasks' and 'nothing measures rho on hour-to-day tasks', yet METR's tasks average about 2 hours and report a review share. Rephrase to: one study at about 2 hours, none at day scale.

Gaps list: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023) and Peng et al. (2023) remain unverified. METR follow-up work and the 2025-2026 literature were not searched; my own web-search budget was also exhausted, so I could not fill these gaps.
verify.corrected_summary: The HCI literature measures some behavioural pieces of theta_j, mostly in small, short-task settings. Mozannar et al. (CUPS, CHI 2024) is the best template. 21 Microsoft programmers using Copilot on about 12-minute tasks spent 22.4% of session time verifying suggestions and 34.3% verifying plus editing them, and about half of all time (51.5%) on Copilot-specific activity. True verification time per suggestion was about 5x the naive estimate, because people often accept first and check afterwards. METR's 2025 randomized trial (16 expert maintainers, 246 tasks of about 2 hours on their own repositories) found that allowing early-2025 AI tools increased completion time by 19%. Developers accepted fewer than 44% of generations. On 44 AI-allowed issues with labelled recordings, about 9% of time went to reviewing and cleaning AI output and about 4% to waiting. So the net effect of AI can be negative for experts on very familiar code. This is not a clean kappa measurement, and the study's apparent learning effect beyond 50 hours is fragile by the authors' own footnote. RealHumanEval (243 mostly-student participants, minute-scale tasks) finds that stronger benchmark models save more user time, but far less than one-for-one, and that acceptance rates do not track productivity. The over-reliance studies show that acceptance of wrong AI output is common and depends on design and incentives. In Bucinca et al., 48-64% of wrong AI answers were followed on the key sub-decision, and 26-30% on the full decision. In Vasconcelos et al., over-reliance rises with task difficulty and falls with higher rewards and cheaper-to-use explanations. In Bansal et al., explanations raise acceptance whether or not the AI is right. Together these suggest q and rho are jointly chosen rather than constants. Perry et al. show the cost in code: AI users wrote less secure code while believing it more secure (e.g. 3% vs 21% secure signing solutions). Lee et al. (CHI 2025) find in a cross-sectional survey that higher confidence in AI is associated with less self-reported critical thinking (beta=-0.69). This is consistent with, but does not show, rho falling over time through reduced scrutiny. Bottom line for the working hypothesis: HCI does touch the intensive margin, including review time. The evidence comes from minute-scale coding sessions plus one roughly 2-hour RCT, from Western or lab samples, and from pre-agent tools. Nothing found measures rho or q on day-scale tasks, inside IT services or BPO firms, or as capability rises for the same workers. This search did not cover the 2026 literature.
verify.dataset_notes: CUPS: the paper names https://github.com/microsoft/coderec_programming_states as its code and data location. The page loads (HTTP 200), but I did not inspect its contents or license, so access stays 'public (unconfirmed contents)'; use the GitHub URL, not the arXiv URL. RealHumanEval: the paper releases data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/hsseinmz/realhumaneval (loads, HTTP 200) and code at https://github.com/clinicalml/realhumaneval. Access is likely public, but I did not check the license. Perry et al.: the abstract says the authors release their user-study apparatus AND anonymized data to researchers, so the record's 'participant-level data release not confirmed' understates it. Access mode (public vs on request) not confirmed. METR RCT: I found no data-release statement in the paper text, so access remains unknown. Anthropic transcripts: lab-internal, with only aggregates published (consistent with the page).

streams.name: Selective automation, learning to defer, and human-AI triage (operations research, ML, economics)

works.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
works.authors: Maithra Raghu, Katy Blumer, Greg Corrado, Jon Kleinberg, Ziad Obermeyer, Sendhil Mullainathan
works.what_measured: Diagnostic error on diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading under three regimes: human doctors only, the algorithm on every case (full automation), and per-case triage where some cases go to the algorithm and human effort goes to the rest.
works.method_plain: A CNN is trained to grade eye photos. A second model predicts, for each case, how likely the algorithm and the doctors are to be wrong. Cases are ranked by this 'triage score'. The easiest share alpha goes to the algorithm and the remaining human budget goes to the hardest cases. Evaluation uses an adjudicated gold-standard set, plus a second holdout set in the appendix.
key_numbers: Error rate: about 5.5% for human doctors, about 4% with full automation, about 3.5% with optimal triage (abstract/intro of the PDF)
On roughly 40% of instances the algorithm makes zero errors
A simple triage score finds a zero-error subset equal to 35% of the data; a separate error-prediction model raises this to 44% (averaged over 3 repetitions)
Doctors have a lower error probability than the model on a nontrivial share of cases, about 5%
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that the automation ceiling depends on predicting algorithm (and human) error for each instance, not on the average. In the draft this means p should be p_i (instance-level) rather than p(h). Because max{.} is convex, E[max(q p_i(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa)] >= max evaluated at E[p|h] (Jensen's inequality), so integrating over h alone understates theta_j. The zero-error subset (35-44%) is a share of work that could be handed off with little review, which points to rho close to 0 on a predictable slice.
works.limitations: Medical image classification, not generative or agentic work; 2019 CNN; error is measured, not labor time; the human-effort budget is stylized; preprint.

works.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, David Sontag
works.what_measured: How to jointly train a classifier and a 'rejector' that decides, per input, whether to predict or defer to a human expert, using only samples of the expert's past decisions.
works.method_plain: The learning-to-defer problem is reduced to cost-sensitive learning, with a new consistent surrogate loss that generalizes cross-entropy. 'Consistent' means that optimizing the surrogate recovers the best possible defer/predict rule given enough data.
key_numbers: No headline numbers verified: only the abstract page was opened, and its experiments are not summarized there
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives the statistical machinery (the canonical learning-to-defer, or L2D, formulation) for estimating the routing rule implied by the draft's max{} operator per instance. It needs data on AI correctness and human correctness/cost for the same instances, which is a dataset requirement for estimating theta_j rigorously.
works.limitations: Classification only; the expert's cost is an accuracy loss, not time; no labor-time or generative-task evidence.

works.title: Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology
works.authors: Nikhil Agarwal, Alex Moehring, Pranav Rajpurkar, Tobias Salz
works.what_measured: Accuracy and active time of 227 professional radiologists reading chest X-rays with or without AI predictions and clinical history (2x2 design). Also estimates how radiologists weight AI against their own signal, and the optimal case-level delegation among AI alone, human alone and human+AI.
works.method_plain: A randomized information experiment. A structural model of belief updating is estimated by GMM. Its weights show whether people over-trust AI (automation bias) or under-trust it (automation neglect). A policy then routes each case by the AI's predicted probability to minimize diagnostic loss plus human time cost (radiologist wage $3.6/minute).
key_numbers: 227 radiologists; they match the diagnostic standard in 73.2% of patient-pathology pairs; 2.79 minutes per patient on average (2.8 in the delegation section)
AI predictions do not improve average performance; the AI tool beats about three-quarters of radiologists
AI assistance slows radiologists by about 4% (a time cost, not a saving)
Weight on the AI signal b = 0.26 (s.e. 0.02) vs weight on own information d = 0.88 (s.e. 0.01) in the selected model, i.e. automation neglect
48% of radiologists improve on average with AI assistance

Optimal delegation: AI decides almost all cases if a false negative costs less than $100. With a high false-negative cost, humans are involved in 51% of cases, mostly without AI assistance. Even for a Bayesian at $10,000, 21% of cases go to AI alone
Moving from unassisted radiologist to the frontier can cut decision loss while saving $4.9 per case in time costs
works.relevance_to_theta: Direct evidence that kappa, the assistant-mode speedup, can be zero or negative: AI slowed experts by 4% with no average accuracy gain. It also shows that the best design is either/or routing by case. In the draft, kappa should not be assumed positive, and the max{} should compare 'delegate to AI' against 'human alone', not against 'human with AI'.
works.limitations: Classification of X-rays, not generative or coding work; the AI gives a probability, not a draft artifact; an experiment, not production; radiology has liability and regulatory constraints unlike IT services.

works.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
works.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas Malone
works.what_measured: Whether human+AI teams beat the better of human alone or AI alone ('synergy'), and whether they beat the human alone ('augmentation'), across published experiments.
works.method_plain: A meta-analysis pooling standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g = difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation, bias-corrected), with moderator regressions by task type and by which party is better alone.
key_numbers: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes
Synergy (human+AI vs best of the two alone): g = -0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07)
Augmentation (human+AI vs human alone): g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.74)
Decision tasks: synergy g = -0.27; creation tasks: g = 0.19 (n.s., 34 effect sizes)
When AI alone beats the human: synergy g = -0.54; when the human beats AI: g = 0.46
Only 3 experiments used a predetermined delegation of subtasks; synergy g = 0.22, not significant
works.relevance_to_theta: Generalizes the Agarwal result. Where AI outperforms people, adding a human to the loop tends to make results worse than AI alone, so the max{} rule should often choose pure delegation or pure human. Creation tasks, which are closer to code, show positive but imprecise synergy, so kappa for generative work may be positive. Measures quality, not time saved.
works.limitations: Outcomes are quality or accuracy, not labor time; mostly lab studies with lay participants; few coding or agentic tasks; heterogeneous metrics.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein
works.what_measured: Task completion time for experienced open-source developers on their own repositories when AI tools (mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) are allowed vs disallowed, with screen-recording time breakdowns.
works.method_plain: An RCT at the task level: each real GitHub issue is randomly assigned AI-allowed or not, and the time to complete it is compared. 143 hours of screen recordings are labeled to see where time goes (prompting, waiting, reviewing AI output, idle).
key_numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks, 2.0 hours average task length
AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer
Developers forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and believed afterwards that AI had reduced time by 20%; economics experts predicted 39% shorter, ML experts 38% shorter
Developers accept <44% of AI generations; 75% report reading every line of AI code; 56% often make major changes to clean it up
No clear learning effect across the first 30-50 hours of Cursor use (underpowered)
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest coding analogue of the radiology finding. For roughly 2-hour tasks in mature codebases, assistant mode gave a negative speedup (kappa about -0.19 in time terms) for early-2025 tools. The <44% acceptance rate gives a rough value for q at the generation level. Time spent reviewing and waiting is a direct input to rho.
works.limitations: Small sample of very experienced developers on familiar, high-standard repos, which may differ from Indian IT services maintenance work; early-2025 models; assisted mode only, with no agent-delegation arm.

works.title: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
works.what_measured: How programmers using GitHub Copilot split their session time across activities (verifying suggestions, writing, prompting, waiting, editing suggestions), and their acceptance rates.
works.method_plain: 21 programmers completed coding tasks with Copilot, then retrospectively labeled their own session segments using a taxonomy (CUPS). Time shares are averaged per participant.
key_numbers: 21 participants
'Verifying suggestion' is the largest state at 22.4% of session time (s.d. 12.97)
Copilot-specific states (verifying, deferring thought, waiting, prompt crafting, editing suggestion) total 51.5% of session time; all participants spend more than 21% there
Average acceptance rate 36.5% (median 33.8%, range 14.3%-60.7%)
Waiting for suggestions is 4.2% of session time
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few direct measurements of review time as a share of work in AI-assisted coding, giving a rough value for rho (about 0.22 of session time on verification alone) and for suggestion-level q (about 0.35).
works.limitations: Small lab sample; completion-style (line-level) suggestions, not agentic PRs; no counterfactual time without AI; self-labeled.

works.title: Learning to Defer in Congested Systems: The AI-Human Interplay
works.authors: Thodoris Lykouris, Wentao Weng
works.what_measured: Theory and algorithms for AI-human pipelines (content moderation) where the AI classifies items and decides which to send to a capacity-limited human review queue.
works.method_plain: A contextual queueing model: jobs arrive, the AI classifies each and chooses whether to admit it for review, and human capacity varies over time. Congestion delays both decisions and the training labels the AI receives. Humans see only AI-filtered items. An online learning algorithm balances misclassification loss, loss on unreviewed jobs and delay loss, and is tested on online comment datasets.
key_numbers: No quantitative results recorded: only the abstract page was opened
works.relevance_to_theta: The operations-research piece for queueing with human review. When review capacity is fixed, the share of AI output that can be checked (and hence the realized q and rho) depends on arrival rates and congestion. This matters for aggregation from task-level theta_j to firm-level labor: review is a bottleneck resource, not a per-task constant.
works.limitations: Theory plus simulations on moderation data; no labor-time numbers; not coding.

works.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
works.authors: Yonatan Geifman, Ran El-Yaniv
works.venue: arXiv 1705.08500 (commonly cited as NeurIPS 2017; venue not shown on the page opened)
works.what_measured: The risk-coverage trade-off: how much error can be guaranteed if the model is allowed to abstain on some inputs.
works.method_plain: Take a trained network, use its confidence score to choose an abstention threshold so that the error on accepted inputs stays below a target with high probability, and report coverage (the share not abstained).
key_numbers: ImageNet top-5: 2% error guaranteed with 99.9% probability at nearly 60% coverage
works.relevance_to_theta: The classic selective-prediction tool. A risk-coverage curve is exactly the object needed to replace a single q with a schedule: what share of instances can be auto-accepted (rho near 0) at a target error rate. Applied to coding agents, coverage at a target defect rate would be a direct input to theta_j.
works.limitations: Image classification; abstention on the AI side only, with no human cost model; 2017.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER WP 31161; Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2): 889-942 (2025)
works.what_measured: Issues resolved per hour by customer-support agents after a staggered rollout of an AI conversational assistant.
works.method_plain: A staggered-rollout difference-in-differences: agents who got the tool earlier are compared with those who got it later, over time.
key_numbers: 5,179 customer support agents
+14% issues resolved per hour on average
+34% for novice/low-skilled workers; minimal gains for experienced/highly skilled workers
works.relevance_to_theta: Field evidence on kappa in BPO-type work (assistant mode, not delegation): positive and about 0.14 on average, but heterogeneous by skill. This contrasts with the negative kappa in radiology and the METR coding study, so kappa should be indexed by task and worker.
works.limitations: Single firm; assistant mode only, with no routing to AI alone; throughput rather than labor-time saving per unit; 2020-21 era model.

works.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
works.authors: Gagan Bansal, Tongshuang Wu, Joyce Zhou, Raymond Fok, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Daniel S. Weld
works.what_measured: Whether AI explanations help human-AI teams beat both human and AI alone (complementary performance), on three datasets with an AI of human-comparable accuracy.
works.method_plain: Mixed-method user studies that vary whether the AI recommendation comes with an explanation.
key_numbers: No numeric results verified; only the abstract page was opened. Qualitative: explanations raised acceptance of AI recommendations whether or not they were correct
works.relevance_to_theta: Reviewer acceptance (q) is not a fixed fraction of correct outputs. Interface features can raise acceptance of wrong outputs, so q*p overstates net labor saved if downstream rework is ignored.
works.limitations: Lab classification tasks; no time measures recorded here.

works.title: Learning to Route LLMs with Confidence Tokens (Self-REF)
works.authors: Yu-Neng Chuang, Prathusha Kameswara Sarma, Parikshit Gopalan, John Boccio, Sara Bolouki, Xia Hu, Helen Zhou
works.what_measured: Whether LLMs can be trained to emit confidence tokens that support routing a query to another expert, or rejecting it, when the output is unreliable.
works.method_plain: Lightweight fine-tuning adds confidence tokens trained on the model's own errors. The resulting score is compared with verbalized confidence and token probabilities on routing and rejection tasks.
key_numbers: No numbers verified: only the abstract page was opened; the abstract claims the tokens beat verbalized confidence and token-probability baselines
works.relevance_to_theta: An example of the 2024-25 extension of learning-to-defer to generative LLMs. A working per-instance confidence signal is what lets a firm route each ticket or code change to AI or human, which lifts achievable theta above the h-average.
works.limitations: QA-style benchmarks, not agentic coding; no human time cost; preprint.

works.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
works.authors: Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M Waleed Kadous, Ion Stoica
works.what_measured: The cost and quality of routing each query between a strong (expensive) and a weak (cheap) LLM using learned routers.
works.method_plain: Routers are trained on human preference data with augmentation to predict when the weak model's answer is good enough. Cost is compared at matched quality.
key_numbers: Costs reduced 'over 2 times in certain cases' without loss in response quality (abstract); share routed not recorded
works.relevance_to_theta: Model-to-model rather than human-AI routing, but it shows per-query difficulty prediction for generative tasks is feasible and economically large. The same router logic applied to 'AI vs human' would raise theta_j above the h-averaged formula and would lower the AI running cost netted out of theta.
works.limitations: No human in the loop; chat benchmarks; quality judged by preference models; preprint.

research.stream_summary:
This literature treats automation as a routing problem: for each piece of work, decide whether the AI does it alone, a human does it alone, or a human does it with AI help. It reshapes the draft formula in three ways.

First, routing happens per instance, not per task length. Raghu et al. (2019) find that a diabetic-retinopathy algorithm makes zero errors on about 40% of cases. Error-prediction models can pick out a zero-error 35-44% slice in advance, so triage beats full automation (about 3.5% vs 4% error, compared with 5.5% for humans). The max function in the draft is convex. So averaging the pass rate p over all tasks of length h and then taking the max understates the ceiling. The right object is the average of the max over instances, and it needs a per-instance confidence signal. Learning-to-defer (Mozannar & Sontag 2020), selective prediction (Geifman & El-Yaniv 2017) and newer LLM routers (RouteLLM, Self-REF) supply the estimators.

Second, assisted mode is often worse than either party alone. In Agarwal et al.'s experiment with 227 radiologists, AI help gave no average accuracy gain and slowed readers by about 4%. Radiologists put weight 0.26 on the AI against 0.88 on their own signal. The optimal policy sends cases to AI alone or to a human alone, rarely to both. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments (Vaccaro et al. 2024) finds human+AI teams do worse than the better of the two alone (g = -0.23), and much worse when AI is the stronger party (g = -0.54). In coding, METR's 2025 RCT found AI made experienced developers 19% slower. Customer-support field data, by contrast, show +14%. So the assistant-mode speedup kappa can be negative, and its sign depends on the task.

Third, review is a congestible, measurable cost. Copilot users spend 22.4% of session time verifying suggestions. Queueing models (Lykouris & Weng) show that review capacity limits how much AI output can be accepted.

No source I could verify measures routing between a coding agent and a human with labor-time outcomes. That is the key gap.
gaps_noticed: The web-search budget was exhausted early in this stream (the tool reported the 200-search limit), so 2025-2026 work on deferral or escalation for coding agents and customer-service bots could not be searched. Coverage of that sub-area is thin and relies on arXiv IDs fetched directly.

No verified study measures labor time under per-instance routing between a coding agent and a human. The existing evidence is either assisted-mode time (METR RCT, CUPS) or classification accuracy (radiology, retinopathy). Agentic delegation with a human fallback and a time outcome is the missing experiment.

No source gives within-length variance of AI success, i.e. how predictable p_i is beyond h. This determines how much the Jensen gap (instance-level routing vs h-averaging) raises theta_j. METR task-level success data could in principle estimate it.

kappa estimates conflict in sign by domain: -4% time in radiology, -19% in METR coding, +14% throughput in BPO customer support. There is no IT-services-specific estimate, and none for Indian delivery teams.
q is measured only at the suggestion or generation level (Copilot acceptance about 36.5%, Cursor <44%), not at the task or PR level for agentic output in enterprise maintenance work.

Review cost rho is measured as a share of session time with AI (22.4% verifying), not as a share of the human-only task length h, which the draft needs. A conversion requires a no-AI counterfactual on the same tasks.
Queueing and review-capacity effects (Lykouris & Weng) are theory and simulation; no empirical estimate exists of how review bottlenecks cap realized automation in software firms.

Bansal et al. suggest acceptance can rise regardless of correctness, so q may include accepted-but-wrong outputs whose rework cost is not netted out. No study found quantifies downstream rework for AI code in services firms.
The Mozannar & Sontag, RouteLLM, Self-REF and Bansal entries were checked at abstract level only; their experimental numbers were not verified.
