Weight on the focal AI signal b = 0.26 (s.e. 0.02) vs weight on own information d = 0.88 (s.e. 0.01) in the selected model, i.e. automation neglect
48% of radiologists improve on average with AI assistance

Optimal delegation: AI decides almost all cases if a false negative costs less than $100. Using observed behavior and a high false-negative cost, humans are involved in 51% of cases, mostly without AI assistance. For a Bayesian decision-maker even at $10,000, 21% of cases go to AI alone
Moving from the unassisted radiologist to the frontier can reduce decision loss while saving $4.9 per case in time costs
Radiologist wage of $3.6 per minute (footnote / Appendix C.8.2)
works.relevance_to_theta: Evidence that kappa, the assistant-mode speedup, can be zero or slightly negative: AI slowed experts by about 4% with no average accuracy gain. It also shows that, given observed (biased) human updating, the best design is either/or routing by case. For the draft, kappa should not be assumed positive, and with biased reviewers the max{} should compare 'delegate to AI' with 'human alone'. Note that for a fully Bayesian reviewer the optimal policy does use human+AI, so this depends on reviewer behavior.
works.limitations: Classification of X-rays, not generative or coding work; the AI gives a probability, not a draft artifact; an experiment on retrospective cases, not production; radiology has liability and regulatory constraints unlike IT services.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the August 2026 revision PDF. Added the s.e. and source table for the 4% slowdown. Added the nuance that the main delegation model sets human time with and without AI equal, and that $3.6/minute is used in a footnote and appendix variant. Clarified that b is the weight on the focal AI signal.

works.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
works.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas Malone
works.what_measured: Whether human+AI teams beat the better of human alone or AI alone ('synergy'), and whether they beat the human alone ('augmentation'), across published experiments.
works.method_plain: A meta-analysis pooling standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g: difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation, with a small-sample correction), with moderator regressions by task type and by which party performs better alone.
key_numbers: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes
Synergy (human+AI vs best of the two alone): g = -0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07)
Augmentation (human+AI vs human alone): g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.74)
Decision tasks: synergy g = -0.27 (95% CI -0.44 to -0.10); creation tasks: g = 0.19 (95% CI -0.09 to 0.48, not significant, n = 34)
When the AI alone beats the human: synergy g = -0.54; when the human beats the AI: g = 0.46
Only 3 experiments (4 effect sizes) used a predetermined delegation of separate subtasks; synergy g = 0.22 (95% CI -0.42 to 0.87), not significant
works.relevance_to_theta: Generalizes the Agarwal result. Where AI outperforms people, adding a human to the loop tends to make results worse than AI alone, so the max{} rule should often choose pure delegation or pure human. Creation tasks, which are closer to code, show positive but imprecise synergy, so kappa for generative work may be positive. Outcomes are quality, not time saved, so this bears on the sign of kappa only indirectly.
works.limitations: Outcomes are quality or accuracy, not labor time; lab and online experiments with a mix of crowdworkers and experts (e.g. doctors); few coding or agentic tasks; heterogeneous metrics.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the v2 PDF; added confidence intervals. Softened the limitation 'mostly lay participants': the paper includes both crowdworker and expert samples.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein
works.what_measured: Task completion time for experienced open-source developers on their own repositories when AI tools (mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) are allowed vs disallowed, with screen-recording time breakdowns.
works.method_plain: An RCT at the task level: each real GitHub issue is randomly assigned AI-allowed or not, and completion times are compared. 143 hours of screen recordings (128 recordings, about 29% of total hours) are labeled to see where time goes.
key_numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks, 2.0 hours average task length; developers had on average 5 years of experience on their repositories
AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer
Developers forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and estimated afterwards that AI had reduced time by 20%; economics experts predicted 39% shorter, ML experts 38% shorter

Developers accept <44% of Cursor generations (Cursor analytics; excludes 3 developers with their own subscriptions); 75% report reading every line of AI code; 56% report often needing major changes to clean it up
No clear learning effect across the first 30-50 hours of Cursor use (underpowered)
works.relevance_to_theta: The closest coding analogue to the radiology finding. For roughly 2-hour tasks in mature codebases, assistant mode with early-2025 tools gave a negative speedup (time ratio about 1.19, i.e. kappa about -0.19). The <44% acceptance rate is a rough generation-level value for q, not a task-level q. Time spent reviewing and waiting is a direct input to rho.
works.limitations: Small sample of very experienced developers on familiar, high-standard repos, which may differ from Indian IT services maintenance work; early-2025 models; assisted mode only, with no agent-delegation arm.
works.corrections: Author name: the paper lists 'Beth Barnes', not 'Elizabeth Barnes'. Added that the <44% figure comes from Cursor analytics for 13 of 16 developers. All other numbers confirmed in the v2 PDF. Whether METR has published a later follow-up with newer tools was not checked (search budget exhausted).

works.title: Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming
works.authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
works.what_measured: How programmers using GitHub Copilot split their session time across activities (verifying suggestions, writing, prompting, waiting, editing suggestions), and their acceptance rates.
works.method_plain: 21 programmers at one large organization completed a short coding task with Copilot (about 12 minutes on average), then retrospectively labeled their own session segments with a taxonomy (CUPS). Time shares are normalized to each session's length and averaged.
key_numbers: 21 participants; average task time 12.23 minutes
'Verifying suggestion' is the largest state at 22.4% of session time (s.d. 12.97)
Copilot-specific states (verifying, deferring thought, waiting, prompt crafting, editing suggestion) total 51.5% of session time; all participants spend more than 21% there
1,024 suggestions shown, 34.0% accepted overall; average per-participant acceptance rate 36.5% (median 33.8%, range 14.3%-60.7%)
Waiting for suggestions is 4.2% of session time
works.relevance_to_theta: One of the few direct measurements of review time as a share of AI-assisted coding time: about 0.22 of session time on verification alone, and suggestion-level acceptance about 0.35. Both are for line-level completions in ~12-minute tasks, so they do not map directly to rho (a share of human-only task length h) or task-level q.
works.limitations: Small lab sample at one organization; short tasks; completion-style suggestions, not agentic PRs; no counterfactual time without AI; self-labeled.
works.corrections: Numbers confirmed in the v5 PDF. Added the 12-minute task length and the overall 34.0% acceptance figure, which bound how far these numbers transfer.

works.title: Learning to Defer in Congested Systems: The AI-Human Interplay
works.authors: Thodoris Lykouris, Wentao Weng
works.venue: arXiv 2402.12237 (preprint; no venue listed on arXiv)
works.what_measured: Theory and an online learning algorithm for AI-human content-moderation pipelines, where the AI classifies items and decides which to send to a capacity-limited human review queue.
works.method_plain: A contextual queueing model: jobs arrive, the AI classifies each and decides whether to admit it for review, and human review capacity is limited. Congestion delays both decisions and the training labels the AI receives, and humans see only AI-filtered items. An online learning algorithm balances misclassification loss, loss on unreviewed jobs and delay loss. Numerical experiments use comment data from Wikipedia and the Civil Comments platform.
key_numbers: No quantitative results checked; the abstract says the algorithm substantially reduces misclassifications relative to existing moderation practice in experiments on online comment data (Wikipedia, Civil Comments)
works.relevance_to_theta: The operations-research piece on queueing with human review. When review capacity is fixed, the share of AI output that can be checked depends on arrival rates and congestion. This matters for aggregating from task-level theta_j to firm-level labor: review is a bottleneck resource, not a per-task constant. It is a model, not an empirical estimate.
works.limitations: Theory plus numerical experiments on moderation data; no labor-time numbers; not coding.
works.corrections: Added the named datasets (Wikipedia and Civil Comments) from the PDF.

works.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
works.authors: Yonatan Geifman, Ran El-Yaniv
works.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017); arXiv 1705.08500
works.what_measured: The risk-coverage trade-off: how low an error rate can be guaranteed if the model may abstain on some inputs.
works.method_plain: Take a trained network, use its confidence score to choose an abstention threshold so that the error on accepted inputs stays below a target with high probability, and report coverage (the share not abstained).
key_numbers: ImageNet top-5: 2% error guaranteed with 99.9% probability at nearly 60% coverage (abstract)
works.relevance_to_theta: The classic selective-prediction tool. A risk-coverage curve is the object needed to replace a single q with a schedule: what share of instances can be auto-accepted (rho near 0) at a target error rate. For coding agents, coverage at a target defect rate would be a direct input to theta_j; no such curve for coding was found here.
works.limitations: Image classification; abstention on the AI side only, with no human cost model; 2017.
works.corrections: Venue confirmed as NIPS 2017 (NeurIPS proceedings vol. 30) on the proceedings page; the record had left it unconfirmed. Confidence raised to high.

works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 31161 (April 2023, revised November 2023); Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2): 889-942 (2025)
works.what_measured: Issues resolved per hour by customer-support agents after a staggered rollout of an AI conversational assistant.
works.method_plain: A staggered-rollout difference-in-differences: agents who got the tool earlier are compared with those who got it later, over time.
key_numbers: 5,179 customer support agents
+14% issues resolved per hour on average
+34% for novice and low-skilled workers; minimal impact for experienced and highly skilled workers
works.relevance_to_theta: Field evidence on kappa in BPO-type work (assistant mode, not delegation): positive on average and heterogeneous by skill. A 14% throughput rise corresponds to roughly a 12% cut in time per resolved issue if quality is held fixed; it is not directly the same unit as the time effects in the radiology and METR studies.
works.limitations: Single firm; assistant mode only, with no routing to AI alone; throughput rather than labor-time saving per unit of work. The model vintage and data period were not checked here.
works.corrections: Removed the unverified limitation '2020-21 era model' (not checked on the page opened). Added the revision date from the NBER page. Abstract numbers confirmed.

works.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
works.authors: Gagan Bansal, Tongshuang Wu, Joyce Zhou, Raymond Fok, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Daniel S. Weld
works.what_measured: Whether AI explanations help human-AI teams beat both the human and the AI alone (complementary performance), in user studies on three datasets with an AI of roughly human-level accuracy.
works.method_plain: Mixed-method user studies that vary whether the AI recommendation comes with an explanation.
key_numbers: No numeric results checked. Qualitative (abstract): AI help produced complementary gains, but explanations did not add to them; explanations made people more likely to accept the AI recommendation whether or not it was correct
works.relevance_to_theta: Reviewer acceptance (q) is not a fixed fraction of correct outputs. Interface features can raise acceptance of wrong outputs, so q*p overstates net labor saved if downstream rework is ignored.
works.limitations: Lab classification-style tasks; no time measures recorded here.
works.corrections: Added from the abstract that AI help did produce complementary gains (only explanations failed to add to them); the record left this out.

works.title: Learning to Route LLMs with Confidence Tokens
works.authors: Yu-Neng Chuang, Prathusha Kameswara Sarma, Parikshit Gopalan, John Boccio, Sara Bolouki, Xia Hu, Helen Zhou
works.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267; arXiv 2410.13284
works.what_measured: Whether LLMs can be trained to emit confidence tokens that support routing a query to another model, or rejecting it, when the output is unreliable.
works.method_plain: Lightweight fine-tuning (the method is called Self-REF) adds confidence tokens, trained on labels of whether the base model was right or wrong. The resulting score is compared with verbalized confidence and token probabilities on routing and rejection tasks.
key_numbers: No numbers checked; the abstract claims the confidence tokens beat verbalized-confidence and token-probability baselines on routing and rejection
works.relevance_to_theta: An example of extending learning-to-defer to generative LLMs. A working per-instance confidence signal is what would let a firm route each ticket or code change to AI or human, which could lift achievable theta above the h-average.
works.limitations: QA-style benchmarks, not agentic coding; routing is between models, with no human time cost.
works.corrections: Title on arXiv is 'Learning to Route LLMs with Confidence Tokens' ('Self-REF' is the method name, not part of the title). Venue corrected from 'preprint' to ICML 2025 (PMLR 267), per the proceedings footer in the v3 PDF.

works.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
works.authors: Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M Waleed Kadous, Ion Stoica
works.what_measured: The cost and quality of routing each query between a strong (expensive) and a weak (cheap) LLM using learned routers.
works.method_plain: Routers are trained on human preference data, with data augmentation, to predict when the weak model's answer is good enough. Cost is compared at matched quality.
key_numbers: Costs reduced by over 2 times in certain cases without substantially compromising response quality (abstract); share routed not recorded
works.relevance_to_theta: Model-to-model rather than human-AI routing, but it shows that per-query difficulty prediction for generative tasks is feasible and can matter for cost. The same router logic applied to 'AI vs human' could raise theta_j above the h-averaged formula and lower the AI running cost netted out of theta.
works.limitations: No human in the loop; chat benchmarks; quality judged by preference models and benchmarks.
works.corrections: Venue corrected from 'preprint' to ICLR 2025 (the v4 PDF header reads 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025'). Abstract cost figure confirmed.

summary_flags: Raghu et al.: 'error-prediction models can pick out a zero-error 35-44% slice in advance' is true only on the adjudicated set, averaged over 3 repetitions. On the appendix holdout set the zero-error shares fall to roughly 10-24%. State both.

Jensen argument: E[max] >= max(E) is a bound for an oracle that knows p_i. The achievable gain depends on how well p_i can be predicted beforehand. 'Averaging understates the ceiling' should read 'understates the oracle ceiling; the achievable gain depends on predictor quality, which no source here measures for coding'.
'rho close to 0 on a predictable slice' is the record's inference, not a result of Raghu et al. (they measure errors, not review time).

Agarwal et al.: the 4% slowdown is real (about +5.9 s on about 154 s, significant), but the authors call human time with and without AI similar and set them equal in the delegation model. The 'either/or' result depends on observed biased updating; for a Bayesian reviewer the optimal policy does use human+AI.

The kappa comparison mixes units: Agarwal (-4%) and METR (-19%) are time per task, while Brynjolfsson et al. (+14%) is resolutions per hour (about 12% less time per resolution if quality is unchanged). Vaccaro et al. measure quality, not time. The sign conflict is real, but the magnitudes are not directly comparable.
Brynjolfsson et al.: the record's '2020-21 era model' limitation was not verified on any page opened; removed.
Copilot 22.4% verifying comes from 21 programmers at one organization on ~12-minute tasks with line-level completions. It should not be read as a general review-cost share.

Lykouris & Weng 'show that review capacity limits how much AI output can be accepted' overstates a model plus numerical experiments on Wikipedia and Civil Comments moderation data; it is not an empirical estimate.

'No source I could verify measures routing between a coding agent and a human with labor-time outcomes' reflects a search that hit the search budget, not a full survey. Call it 'not found', not 'does not exist'.
Venue errors in the record: RouteLLM is ICLR 2025 and the confidence-token paper is ICML 2025, not preprints. Geifman & El-Yaniv is confirmed NIPS 2017. METR author is listed as 'Beth Barnes'.

Dataset entry for Agarwal et al. gives https://www.nber.org/data-appendix/w31422. That URL was not opened, and the paper's 'Data Appendix' is an appendix section (balance tests etc.), not a data release. Treat it as unverified.

This stream does not directly test the working hypothesis about the exposure literature (extensive vs intensive margin); it supplies intensive-margin and routing evidence but no exposure-literature comparison.
This verification pass also hit the shared web-search limit, so no newer (2025-2026) work on agent deferral or escalation was searched for; only primary pages reached by direct URL were checked.
verify.corrected_summary:
This literature treats automation as a routing problem: for each piece of work, decide whether the AI does it alone, a human does it alone, or a human does it with AI help. It suggests three changes to the draft formula. None is yet backed by coding-specific labor-time evidence.

First, routing can happen per instance, not just per task length. On an adjudicated diabetic-retinopathy set, Raghu et al. (2019, arXiv preprint) find that the algorithm makes zero errors on about 40% of cases. Triage scores pick out a zero-error subset of 35-44% (averaged over three repetitions), and triage beats full automation (about 3.5% vs 4% error, against 5.5% for doctors). On a noisier holdout set the zero-error shares shrink to roughly 10-24%. Because the max function in the draft is convex, taking the max at the average pass rate for length h is below the average of instance-level maxima. That is an upper bound for an oracle. How much of it a firm can capture depends on how well instance-level success can be predicted in advance, which nothing here measures for coding work. Learning-to-defer (Mozannar & Sontag, ICML 2020), selective classification (Geifman & El-Yaniv, NIPS 2017) and LLM routers (RouteLLM, ICLR 2025; confidence tokens, Chuang et al., ICML 2025) supply estimators. The LLM routers route between models, not between AI and humans.

Second, assisted mode is often no better than either party alone. In Agarwal et al.'s experiment with 227 radiologists (NBER WP 31422, revised 2026), AI predictions gave no average accuracy gain, even though the AI beat about three-quarters of radiologists, and active time rose by about 4%. Radiologists put weight 0.26 on the AI signal against 0.88 on their own. Given this biased updating, the optimal policy sends cases to AI alone or to a human alone and rarely to both. A Bayesian reviewer would use AI help more. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments (Vaccaro et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2024) finds human+AI teams do worse than the better of the two alone on average (g = -0.23), and worse still when the AI is the stronger party (g = -0.54). Creation tasks show positive but non-significant synergy (g = 0.19). In coding, METR's 2025 RCT (16 developers, 246 tasks) found tasks took 19% longer when early-2025 AI tools were allowed. In customer support, Brynjolfsson et al. (QJE 2025) found 14% more issues resolved per hour. The assistant-mode speedup kappa can therefore be negative or positive depending on the task. These estimates use different units (time per task, throughput, quality), so their magnitudes are not directly comparable.

Third, review is a measurable and possibly congestible cost. In a 21-person lab study of short Copilot tasks, verifying suggestions took 22.4% of session time, and about 36% of suggestions were accepted. A queueing model by Lykouris & Weng (preprint), tested on moderation data, shows how limited review capacity can constrain what AI output gets checked. It is theory, not an empirical estimate for software firms.

This search found no study that measures labor time when work is routed per instance between a coding agent and a human. The search was cut short by a tool limit, so this is a gap in what was found, not proof that no such study exists.
verify.dataset_notes:
1) Agarwal et al. radiology experiment: pre-registration AEARCTR-0009620 is confirmed in the paper. The listed URL https://www.nber.org/data-appendix/w31422 was not opened and is unverified. The paper's 'Data Appendix' (Appendix C) is a section of the PDF (balance tests, robustness), not a microdata release. Access: unknown; no public microdata confirmed.
2) Vaccaro-Almaatouq-Malone meta-analysis: the paper's Data Availability and Code Availability statements say data and code are on the project's OSF repository, https://osf.io/wrq7c/ (a view-only link is given in the paper). Access: open per the paper; the OSF page itself was not opened.
3) METR early-2025 developer RCT: no data-release statement was found in the v2 PDF text. Access: unknown.
4) CUPS Copilot study: the paper says code and data are at https://github.com/microsoft/coderec_programming_states. Access: open per the paper; the repository itself was not opened. Use this URL instead of the arXiv page.
5) Raghu et al. adjudicated diabetic-retinopathy set: no data-availability statement was found in the arXiv text. 'On-request' is unsupported. Mark access unknown (likely restricted, with Google and clinical partners).

streams.name: Software-engineering research on code review: baseline review cost, defect detection, and review of AI-generated code

works.title: Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
works.authors: Caitlin Sadowski, Emma Soderberg, Luke Church, Michal Sipko, Alberto Bacchelli
works.venue: ICSE 2018, Software Engineering in Practice (SEIP) track
works.what_measured: Logs of about 9 million reviewed changes (Jan 2014 to Jul 2016) and about 13 million comments, from more than 25,000 authors and reviewers. Also measures reviewer time from logged tool interactions over 5 weeks in Oct 2016, plus interviews and a survey of 98 engineers.
works.method_plain: Log analysis of Google's review tool (Critique). A 'review session' is a run of interactions by a non-author on one change with gaps of no more than 10 minutes. Session hours are summed per user per week.
key_numbers: Reviewer time: mean 3.2 hours/week, median 2.6 hours/week, spent reviewing others' changes (from logs, not self-report)
Median developer authors about 3 changes/week (80% author fewer than 7). Median developer reviews 4 changes/week (80% review fewer than 10)
Median change size: 24 lines modified. Over 10% of changes modify a single line. Over 35% touch one file and about 90% touch fewer than 10 files
Median wait for first feedback: under 1 hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large changes. Median latency for the whole review: under 4 hours
Median reviewer count is 1, and fewer than 25% of changes have more than one reviewer
Comments per change rise with change size up to a peak of 12.5 comments/change at about 1,250 lines

Comparison numbers cited from Rigby & Bird: median time to approval 17.5 h (AMD), 15.7 h (Chrome OS), 14.7/19.8/18.9 h (three Microsoft projects). Median change size 44 lines (AMD) and 263 lines (Lucent)
Derived by me, not stated in the paper: 3.2 h/week divided by about 4 changes/week gives roughly 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change. That is crude, because it divides a mean by a median
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the best large-scale baseline for rho on human-written code. Review takes about 3 hours per 40-hour week (about 8% of time) at a median change of 24 lines. It also shows that review effort (comments) grows with change size up to about 1,250 lines, which matters because agent PRs tend to be larger. The 'latency' numbers are elapsed calendar time, not effort, so they must not be used directly as rho.
works.limitations: Single firm with unusually small changes and one reviewer. Review time per change has to be inferred and is not reported directly. There is no defect-detection measure and nothing on AI code. Latency means elapsed time, not hours worked.

works.title: Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review
works.authors: Alberto Bacchelli, Christian Bird
works.what_measured: Why developers review code and what reviews actually produce at Microsoft. Methods were observation, interviews, surveys (165 managers, 873 programmers) and a card sort of 570 review comments from 200 threads.
works.method_plain: Asked people what they expect review to do, then hand-classified real review comments to see what it actually does.
key_numbers: 'Finding defects' is the first motivation for 383 programmers (44%) and the top reason for 44% of managers
Only 78 of 570 comments (14%) concern defects. 65 of those are logic issues and 5 are security
Most frequent category: 'code improvements', 165 comments (29%)
Survey response rates: 28% (managers) and 44% (programmers)
works.relevance_to_theta: Review outcomes are mostly about maintainability and understanding, not catching bugs. So passing review is a weak test of correctness, and q (the share of passing output that reviewers accept) partly measures style and fit. Defects that slip past review show up later as downstream costs. The paper also identifies understanding the change as the bottleneck, which suggests rho rises when the author (an AI) cannot explain its intent.
works.limitations: Microsoft only, 2012 data, and a small comment sample (570). Comments are an imperfect proxy for what review catches. No time measurements.

works.title: Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs: How the Current Code Review Best Practice Slows Us Down
works.authors: Jacek Czerwonka, Michaela Greiler, Jack Tilford
works.what_measured: Microsoft data on what review comments contain, how useful authors find them, and how review time and usefulness relate to reviewer experience and review size.
works.method_plain: A short experience report built on Microsoft's internal engineering data and earlier Microsoft studies.
key_numbers: Only about 15% of review comments indicate a possible defect. At least 50% concern long-term maintainability
Reviewers new to a part of the code base: about 33% of their comments are judged useful by the author. By the third review of the same area this rises to about 67%
Usefulness falls as review size grows, with the drop noticeable at 20 or more changed files
Developers spend on average 6 hours/week reviewing others' changes (cited from an earlier study)
Median time from review request to all sign-offs is about 24 hours, often days or weeks
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives rho as a time share: about 6 of roughly 40 hours, or about 15% of developer time, goes to reviewing, about twice Google's figure. Supports a low effective defect catch rate, which links q to downstream rework. The finding that usefulness depends on reviewer familiarity suggests rho is higher for unfamiliar code, and AI-written code is unfamiliar to everyone.
works.limitations: Two pages with few methods details. Several numbers are cited from other studies rather than measured here. Comment usefulness is not the same as defects found.

works.title: The Impact of Design and Code Reviews on Software Quality: An Empirical Study Based on PSP Data
works.authors: Chris F. Kemerer, Mark C. Paulk
works.url_opened: https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1109/TSE.2009.27 (abstract only; the IEEE landing page did not render; open-access copy listed at https://hdl.handle.net/11059/14085, not opened)
works.what_measured: How review speed (lines of code per hour) affects the share of defects that review removes, using Personal Software Process (PSP) training data from 371 and 246 programs.
works.method_plain: Regression and mixed models of defect-removal effectiveness on review rate, controlling for developer ability and other process variables.
key_numbers: Review rate significantly affects defect-removal effectiveness, even after controlling for developer ability
At the recommended rate of 200 LOC/hour or less, individual code reviews found more than half of defects and design reviews found nearly two-thirds
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a speed-quality tradeoff for rho. At about 200 LOC/hour a reviewer catches a bit over half of defects, and going faster catches fewer. For an AI change of L lines, a careful review costs about L/200 hours, which pins rho in hours per line rather than as a share of h. It also shows that cutting review time (lower rho) raises escaped defects (worse effective q).
works.limitations: Classroom PSP exercises in which developers review their own code, so this is not team review of production code. I read the abstract only. Effectiveness numbers beyond the abstract were not verified.

works.title: Best Practices for Peer Code Review (SmartBear guide summarizing the SmartBear/Cisco review study)
works.authors: SmartBear Software (corporate)
works.year: undated web page (the underlying Cisco study is commonly dated to about 2006; year not confirmed on the page)
works.what_measured: Rules of thumb on review size, inspection rate and session length, drawn from a SmartBear study of a Cisco programming team.
works.method_plain: Vendor summary of data collected with its own review tool. The page gives no methods detail.
key_numbers: Review no more than 200-400 LOC at a time
Defect density drops significantly at rates faster than 500 LOC/hour
Do not review for more than 60 minutes at a time. A 200-400 LOC review takes 60-90 minutes
Claims a 200-400 LOC review 'should yield 70-90% defect discovery'. That is the page's claim, not a measured rate in a peer-reviewed study
The page does not give the number of reviews in the Cisco study. The often-quoted '2,500 reviews / 3.2 million LOC' figure was NOT confirmed in the page I opened
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives an industry norm of about 300-500 LOC/hour for review speed, so rho for a change of L lines is about L/400 hours. Its 70-90% defect-discovery claim is much higher than the academic estimates (Kemerer & Paulk: just over half), so it should not be used as the catch rate.
works.limitations: Vendor marketing material with no methods or sample sizes on the page. Its numbers are widely repeated without the underlying data. Low evidential weight.

works.title: Resolving code review comments with ML
works.authors: Alexander Frommgen, Lera Kharatyan (Google)
works.what_measured: Deployment of an ML model that proposes edits resolving reviewer comments in Google's review tool.
works.method_plain: Offline evaluation plus production usage logs.
key_numbers: Authors spend an average of about 60 minutes of active 'shepherding time' per change between sending it for review and submitting it
Offline, the model addresses 52% of comments at a target precision of 50%
40-50% of previewed suggested edits are applied by authors. The preview rate rose from about 20% in beta to about 40% at launch
Savings of 'hundreds of thousands of hours annually' are a projection, not a measurement
works.relevance_to_theta: The author-side cost of review (about 60 minutes per change) belongs in the review-loop cost on top of reviewer time. Combined with Sadowski et al., total review overhead per median 24-line Google change is roughly 1.5-2 person-hours (my combination, not stated in either source). The 40-50% apply rate is a q-like acceptance rate for a narrow AI task.
works.limitations: Blog post, not peer-reviewed. Time savings are projected. Specific to Google.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.what_measured: Randomized trial: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real tasks, each task randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI. Includes time-use coding from screen recordings.
works.method_plain: Randomize AI access per task and compare completion times. Label screen recordings into activity categories, including reviewing AI output.
key_numbers: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%. Developers forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and believed afterwards that AI had cut time by 20%
Developers accept fewer than 44% of AI generations
On 44 issues with valid labeled recordings, about 9% of time with AI was spent reviewing and cleaning AI outputs, and about 4% waiting on generations
75% report reading every line of AI code. 56% often need major changes. 100% report needing to modify AI code
works.relevance_to_theta: The most direct measurement of review cost for AI output: about 9% of total task time with AI, plus 4% waiting. The acceptance rate below 44% is a q analogue for assistant-mode output. The 19% slowdown is a direct estimate of net kappa (negative) for expert developers on familiar codebases.
works.limitations: Small sample of experts in mature open-source repositories with high quality standards. Early-2025 tools. The 9% applies to the recording subset only. It may not carry over to Indian IT maintenance work on unfamiliar client code.

works.title: Automated Code Review In Practice
works.authors: Umut Cihan, Vahid Haratian, Arda Icoz, Mert Kaan Gul, Omercan Devran, Emircan Furkan Bayendur, Baykal Mehmet Ucar, Eray Tuzun
works.venue: ICSE 2025, Software Engineering in Practice track; arXiv:2412.18531
works.what_measured: Effects of an LLM-based automated reviewer (built on Qodo PR Agent) in an industrial firm. 4,335 PRs across three projects, 1,568 of which received automated reviews. About 238 practitioners had access, and 22 were surveyed in depth.
works.method_plain: Before/after comparison of PR metrics plus practitioner surveys.
key_numbers: 73.8% of automated review comments were resolved
Average PR closure time rose from 5 h 52 min to 8 h 20 min, with trends varying by project
Most practitioners reported a minor improvement in code quality, alongside faulty reviews, unnecessary corrections and irrelevant comments
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that AI on the review side does not automatically cut rho: elapsed review time rose about 42% after adoption. This matters for any assumption that AI review offsets the extra review burden of AI-written code. It is an industrial (non-Big-Tech) setting closer to IT-services firms.
works.limitations: Before/after design with no control group. Closure time is elapsed time, not effort. One company, and I read only the abstract page.

works.title: The Rise of AI Teammates in Software Engineering (SE) 3.0: How Autonomous Coding Agents Are Reshaping Software Engineering (AIDev dataset)
works.authors: Hao Li, Haoxiang Zhang, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.what_measured: More than 456,000 agent-authored PRs (OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) across 61,000 repositories and 47,000 developers, compared with human PRs on acceptance and turnaround time.
works.method_plain: Mining GitHub PR metadata and timelines. Compares merge rates and time to close.
key_numbers: Agent PR acceptance: Codex 64%, Devin 49%, Copilot 35%. That is 15-40 percentage points below human PRs, with the largest gaps on features and bug fixes
Accepted Codex PRs close in a median of 0.3 h vs 3.9 h for accepted human PRs
Accepted Copilot PRs take a median of 17.2 h to review, more than 4x accepted human PRs (3.9 h). Rejected Copilot PRs take 4.6 h vs 27.6 h for human rejections
Copilot completes half its PR jobs within 12.8 minutes and 75% within 18.5 minutes
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives q-like merge rates for agent PRs and shows review latency differs widely by agent (some much faster, Copilot much slower). The authors warn that very fast closes may mean shallow review, so effective rho may be low at the cost of escaped defects. AIDev is a public dataset for estimating review time against PR size.
works.limitations: Turnaround is elapsed time, not reviewer effort. Many repositories are personal or low-stakes (Codex PRs are often self-merged). Selection effects. Early snapshot (mid-2025).

works.title: On the Use of Agentic Coding: An Empirical Study of Pull Requests on GitHub
works.authors: Miku Watanabe, Hao Li, Yutaro Kashiwa, Brittany Reid, Hajimu Iida, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.what_measured: 567 Claude Code-assisted PRs in 157 open-source projects, matched to 567 human PRs. Measures merge rates, PR size, time to merge, and the kinds of revisions needed before merge.
works.method_plain: Manual and statistical comparison of matched agent and human PRs.
key_numbers: Merged: 83.8% of agent PRs (475/567) vs 91.0% of human PRs (516/567), a statistically significant difference
Median lines added: 48 (agent) vs 24 (human). Median files: 2 for both
Median time to merge: 1.23 h (agent) vs 1.04 h (human), not significantly different
45.1% of merged agent PRs needed revision. Of those, 47.7% involved bug fixes and 29.0% documentation. Median of 2 revision commits for both groups
64.1% of rejected agent PRs were closed with no explanatory comment
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that agent PRs are about twice as large in added lines, which raises review cost per PR under a lines-per-hour review model. Nearly half of merged agent PRs needed human fixes, so a pass/merge is not the same as zero rework. That rework sits between q and rho. Matched human baselines make it a useful calibration source.
works.limitations: Open-source only, with self-selected Claude Code users. No reviewer-effort hours. Elapsed time only.

works.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
works.authors: Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh
works.what_measured: A user study (54 recruited, 47 analyzed) of security-related programming tasks with and without an AI assistant (codex-davinci-002).
works.method_plain: Randomized lab study. Two raters coded each answer for correctness and security (Cohen's kappa 0.68-0.96).
key_numbers: Encryption task: 67% of AI-group participants gave correct solutions vs 79% of controls. The AI group was significantly more likely to write insecure solutions (p = 0.017)
Signing task: 3% of the AI group wrote secure solutions vs 21% of controls (p = 0.039)
The AI group was more likely to believe its code was secure
works.relevance_to_theta: AI output can pass functional checks while hiding security defects, and authors become overconfident. Combined with low defect-detection rates in review (14-15% of comments concern defects; just over half of defects caught at careful speed), this suggests the effective q falls below the nominal merge rate. It supports adding a downstream defect-cost term rather than treating review as fully catching errors.
works.limitations: Old model (2022 Codex), small sample with many students, and lab tasks focused on crypto. It does not measure review.

research.stream_summary:
The human code-review literature gives fairly solid baselines for rho on human-written code, but almost nothing that is measured on AI-written code in terms of effort (hours) rather than elapsed time. At Google (Sadowski et al. 2018), reviewers spend 3.2 hours/week (median 2.6) reviewing about 4 changes/week with a median size of 24 lines. That is about 8% of working time, or very roughly 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change, plus about 60 minutes of author-side work per change (Google 2023 blog). At Microsoft, the figure is about 6 hours/week, or about 15% (Czerwonka et al. 2015). Inspection-speed studies give a per-line cost: careful review runs at 200 LOC/hour or less (Kemerer & Paulk 2009) and should stay below about 500 LOC/hour (SmartBear). Faster review catches fewer defects.

Review is a weak correctness filter. Only 14-15% of review comments are about defects (Bacchelli & Bird 2013; Czerwonka et al. 2015). Even careful individual review catches only just over half of defects, so passing review does not make code correct, and q should be discounted for escaped defects. AI output makes this worse: users with AI wrote less secure code and trusted it more (Perry et al. 2023). In METR's 2025 trial, experts spent about 9% of their time reviewing and cleaning AI output, accepted fewer than 44% of generations, and were net 19% slower. Agent PRs add about twice as many lines as human PRs, and 45% of merged ones needed human fixes (Watanabe et al. 2025). Their merge rates trail humans by 15-40 points (AIDev). Using an AI reviewer increased PR closure time in one industrial study (Cihan et al. 2025).

Implication for the draft: model rho as review hours per line (about 1/200 to 1/500 hours per line) times AI change size, not as a fixed share of h. Add an escaped-defect term, because review catches only part of the errors.
gaps_noticed: My web search budget ran out at the very first search, so later sources were reached only by known URLs, DOI metadata lookups and arXiv. Several 2025-2026 MSR/ICSE papers on reviewer effort for agentic PRs were probably missed. A follow-up search pass is recommended.

Fagan (1976, IBM Systems Journal 15(3), DOI 10.1147/sj.153.0182) could NOT be opened (the IEEE page did not render and Semantic Scholar has no record). Its inspection-rate norms are unverified here and should not be cited from this pass.

Mantyla & Lassenius (2009, IEEE TSE, 'What Types of Defects Are Really Discovered in Code Reviews?') was found in metadata, but its open-access PDF link was dead. The commonly quoted figure, that about 75% of review findings are evolvability rather than functional defects, is unverified.
McIntosh et al. (MSR 2014), on review coverage and participation vs post-release defects, was confirmed in metadata only (closed access). Numbers not extracted.
SmartBear/Cisco: the sample size (often quoted as 2,500 reviews, 3.2M LOC) was not on the page I opened. The 70-90% defect-discovery figure is a vendor claim.
No study measures reviewer EFFORT (active hours, as opposed to elapsed latency) per line for AI-written vs human-written code. The AIDev and Watanabe numbers are elapsed time to merge.

No study measures review time or defect escape in Indian IT services or offshore maintenance contexts, where reviewers often work on unfamiliar client code (Czerwonka suggests reviewing unfamiliar code is much less effective).
No study shows how review cost scales with AI capability over time (time-varying rho), or how review cost depends on the human-time length h of the task rather than on lines changed.
No link from the passed-review rate to downstream defect cost for AI code in production (escaped-defect rate per merged AI PR).

datasets.name: AIDev (agentic PR dataset)
datasets.description: More than 456,000 PRs from 5 coding agents across 61,000 repos, with timelines, review events, code changes and merge outcomes. Usable to regress review latency and merge probability on PR size and task type. Hosting location not verified in this pass (the paper says it is public).

datasets.name: Watanabe et al. Claude Code PR sample
datasets.description: 567 agent PRs plus 567 matched human PRs with revision-type labels. Replication package availability not verified.

datasets.name: Google Critique review logs
datasets.description: About 9M changes and 13M comments with interaction-level timing. Internal to Google, with only aggregates published.

datasets.name: METR early-2025 RCT task and screen-recording labels
datasets.description: 246 tasks with per-task timings and labeled activity categories (reviewing AI output, waiting, etc.). Public release status not verified, so treat as on request.

datasets.name: PSP review data (Kemerer & Paulk)
datasets.description: Review-rate and defect-removal data for 371 and 246 PSP programs. SEI data, availability unverified.

works.title: Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
works.authors: Caitlin Sadowski, Emma Söderberg, Luke Church, Michal Sipko, Alberto Bacchelli
works.venue: ICSE-SEIP '18 (40th International Conference on Software Engineering, Software Engineering in Practice track), Gothenburg
works.what_measured: Review logs for about 9 million reviewed changes (Jan 2014 to Jul 2016) from more than 25,000 authors and reviewers. About 13 million comments (Sep 2014 to Jul 2016). Reviewer time from logged tool interactions over five weeks starting in October 2016. Also 12 interviews and a survey sent to 98 engineers, with 44 valid responses (45% response rate).
works.method_plain: Log analysis of Google's review tool (Critique). A 'review session' is a run of interactions on one uncommitted change by someone other than the author, with no more than 10 minutes between interactions. Session hours are summed and averaged per user per week. Users without data for all 5 weeks are dropped.
key_numbers: Reviewer time: mean 3.2 hours/week, median 2.6 hours/week, spent reviewing changes (from logs, not self-report). The paper contrasts this with 6.4 hours/week self-reported for open-source projects (Bosu & Carver 2013)
Median developer authors about 3 changes/week (80% author fewer than 7). Median developer reviews 4 changes/week (80% review fewer than 10)
Median change size: 24 lines modified. Over 10% of changes modify a single line. Over 35% modify one file and about 90% modify fewer than 10 files
Median wait for first feedback: under 1 hour for small changes and about 5 hours for very large changes. Overall median latency of the whole review process: under 4 hours (elapsed time, not effort)
Fewer than 25% of changes have more than one reviewer, and the median reviewer count is 1
Average comments per change rise with lines changed, peaking at 12.5 comments/change for changes of about 1,250 lines

Cited from Rigby & Bird: median time to approval 17.5 h (AMD), 15.7 h (Chrome OS), 14.7/19.8/18.9 h (three Microsoft projects). Median change size 44 lines (AMD) and 263 lines (Lucent). Another study (Czerwonka et al.) gives 24 h at Microsoft
Over 80% of changes involve at most one iteration of resolving comments

Derived by the stream, not stated in the paper: 3.2 h/week divided by about 4 changes reviewed/week gives roughly 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change. This is crude because it divides a mean by a median
works.relevance_to_theta: The best large-scale, log-based baseline for reviewer effort on human-written code (rho). About 3 hours per week goes to review, roughly 8% of a 40-hour week (the 40 hours is an assumption). That is at a median change size of 24 lines and one reviewer. Review effort, measured by comments, grows with change size up to about 1,250 lines, which matters because agent PRs are larger. The latency numbers are elapsed calendar time and must not be used directly as rho. Note: if about 45-50 minutes goes to a 24-line change, the implied rate is about 30 lines/hour. That is far slower than the 200-500 LOC/hour inspection norms, so a fixed per-change overhead probably dominates for small changes.
works.limitations: Single firm with unusually small changes and usually one reviewer. Review time per change is not reported directly and has to be inferred. There is no defect-detection rate (only 2 survey respondents said review comments had found a bug) and nothing on AI-written code. Latency is elapsed time, not hours worked.
works.corrections: Sample sizes fixed: the survey was SENT to 98 engineers and got 44 valid responses (45%), plus 12 interviews. The record said 'a survey of 98 engineers'. Added the date range for the comments (Sep 2014 to Jul 2016), the paper's own comparison figure of 6.4 h/week self-reported for open source, and the 24 h Microsoft median it cites. All other key numbers were checked against the PDF text and match.

works.title: Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review
works.authors: Alberto Bacchelli, Christian Bird
works.venue: ICSE 2013 (35th International Conference on Software Engineering), pp. 712-721
works.what_measured: Why developers at Microsoft review code, and what reviews actually produce. Methods: observation, interviews, surveys (165 managers with a 28% response rate, 873 programmers with 44%), and a card sort of 570 comments from 200 randomly sampled review threads.
works.method_plain: Asked people what they expect review to do, then hand-classified real review comments to see what it actually does.
key_numbers: 'Finding defects' is the first motivation for 383 programmers (44%), second for 204 (23%) and third for 96 (11%). It is the top reason for 44% of managers

Only 78 of 570 comments (14%) concern defects, the fourth most frequent of nine categories. Of these, 65 are logic issues, 6 high-level issues, 5 security and 3 exception handling (these sum to 79, a small inconsistency in the paper)
Most frequent category: 'code improvements', with 165 comments (29%)
Survey response rates: 28% (managers, 165 answers) and 44% (programmers, 873 answers)
Understanding the change is reported as the main challenge of review
works.relevance_to_theta: Review comments are mostly about maintainability and understanding rather than bugs. So passing review is a weak test of correctness, and q (the share of passing output that reviewers accept) partly reflects style and fit. A low share of defect comments does not by itself tell us the catch rate, because it could also mean few defects were present. The finding that understanding is the bottleneck suggests rho rises when the author (an AI) cannot explain its intent. That is an inference, not a result in the paper.
works.limitations: Microsoft only, with a small comment sample (570). Comment counts are an imperfect proxy for what review catches. No time or effort measurements.
works.corrections: No changes to the numbers; all match the PDF. Added the second and third motivation counts and the full breakdown of defect comments. Removed the claim of '2012 data' from limitations, because the data year was not confirmed in this check. Added page numbers (712-721, as cited in Czerwonka et al. 2015).

works.title: Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs: How the Current Code Review Best Practice Slows Us Down
works.authors: Jacek Czerwonka, Michaela Greiler, Jack Tilford
works.venue: ICSE 2015, Software Engineering in Practice (SEIP) track. It is a 2-page talk abstract (an experience report), not a full research paper
works.what_measured: A short experience report from Microsoft on what review comments contain, how useful authors find them, and how usefulness relates to reviewer experience and review size. Several figures are cited from other studies rather than measured here.
works.method_plain: Experience report using Microsoft's internal engineering data (CODEMINE) and earlier studies. Gives no methods detail.
key_numbers: Only about 15% of review comments indicate a possible defect, 'much less a blocking defect'. At least 50% concern long-term maintainability

Reviewers with no prior exposure to that part of the code base: on average about 33% of their comments are judged useful by the author. On the third review of the same area this rises to about 67%, and by the fourth it matches the project's long-term average
Usefulness falls as the number of files in a review grows, but the drop only becomes noticeable at 20 or more changed files

'Developers spend on average six hours a week reviewing changes of others'. This is CITED from Bosu & Carver (ESEM 2013), a self-report survey that Sadowski et al. describe as covering open-source projects (6.4 h/week). It is not a Microsoft measurement
Median time from review request to all sign-offs is about 24 hours, with many reviews lasting days or weeks. This is cited from Rigby & Bird (ESEC/FSE 2013) and is elapsed time
works.relevance_to_theta: It supports the view that review rarely catches functional defects, which links q to downstream rework. The finding that usefulness depends on reviewer familiarity suggests review is less effective, and possibly more costly, on unfamiliar code. That is relevant to offshore maintenance of client code and to AI-written code; the second point is an inference. Its 6 h/week figure must NOT be used as a Microsoft measurement of rho, because it is a self-reported survey number from another study.
works.limitations: A two-page talk abstract with no methods. Most headline numbers are cited from other studies (Bosu & Carver 2013; Rigby & Bird 2013). Comment usefulness is not the same as defects found.
works.corrections: Main correction: the record and the stream summary present '6 hours/week, about 15% of time' as a Microsoft figure. The PDF cites it to Bosu & Carver 2013 (reference 6), a self-reported survey that Sadowski et al. 2018 characterize as open-source (6.4 h/week). It is not comparable to Google's log-based 3.2 h/week. The 24 h median sign-off time is cited to Rigby & Bird 2013. Venue clarified as a SEIP talk abstract. The MSR landing page lists only Czerwonka and Greiler, but the PDF and Sadowski et al. list all three authors.

works.title: The Impact of Design and Code Reviews on Software Quality: An Empirical Study Based on PSP Data
works.authors: Chris F. Kemerer, Mark C. Paulk
works.venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, vol. 35, pp. 534-550 (DOI 10.1109/TSE.2009.27)
works.what_measured: How review rate (lines of code reviewed per hour) affects defect-removal effectiveness (the share of defects present that review removes). Uses Personal Software Process (PSP) training data from two datasets of 371 and 246 programs.
works.method_plain: Regression and mixed models of defect-removal effectiveness on review rate, controlling for developer ability and other process variables. In PSP, each developer reviews their own design and code.
key_numbers: PSP review rate significantly affects defect-removal effectiveness, even after accounting for developer ability and other significant process variables (abstract)
At the recommended rate of 200 LOC/hour or less, individual reviews found nearly two-thirds of defects in design reviews and more than half in code reviews (abstract)
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives a speed-quality tradeoff for rho. At 200 LOC/hour or slower, an individual code review removes a bit over half of the defects present, and faster review removes fewer. This supports modelling review cost per line and adding an escaped-defect term. But 200 LOC/hour is a recommended upper limit on speed in a classroom self-review setting, not an observed rate in modern team review.
works.limitations: Classroom PSP exercises in which developers review their OWN code, so this is not team review of production code. Only the abstract was read. The open-access handle listed by Semantic Scholar (hdl.handle.net/11059/14085) redirects to a Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira repository behind a bot-check page, so it was not confirmed to host this paper.
works.corrections: Venue detail: Semantic Scholar confirms vol. 35, pp. 534-550. The issue number '(4)' was not confirmed in this check and has been removed. The primary URL should be the DOI (https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2009.27, which resolves to IEEE Xplore document 4815279). The open-access handle redirects to a Colombian university repository behind a bot challenge and is unverified. The abstract numbers match. Nothing beyond the abstract was checked.

works.title: Best Practices for Code Review (SmartBear 'learn' guide citing a SmartBear study of a Cisco Systems programming team)
works.authors: SmartBear Software (corporate; no named author on page)
works.year: Undated web page. The year of the underlying Cisco study is not stated on the page
works.what_measured: Rules of thumb on review size, inspection rate and session length, attributed to a SmartBear study of a Cisco Systems programming team.
works.method_plain: Vendor summary of data collected with its own review tool. The page gives no methods, sample size or date.
key_numbers: Review no more than 200-400 LOC at a time. Beyond 400 LOC the ability to find defects diminishes
'Significant drop in defect density at rates faster than 500 LOC per hour'
Do not review for more than 60 minutes at a time, because performance drops off after about 60 minutes
'A review of 200-400 LOC over 60 to 90 minutes should yield 70-90% defect discovery'. This is the vendor's claim, not a peer-reviewed measured rate
The page gives no sample size, line count or year for the Cisco study, so the often-quoted '2,500 reviews / 3.2 million LOC' is not confirmed here
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives an industry norm for careful inspection speed (at most about 500 LOC/hour, ideally slower). Its 70-90% defect-discovery claim is far above the academic estimate (Kemerer & Paulk: just over half for individual code review), so it should not be used as the catch rate. Low evidential weight.
works.limitations: Vendor marketing material with no methods, sample sizes or dates on the page. The numbers are widely repeated without the underlying data.
works.corrections: The quotes match the page as fetched. The page heading does not use the word 'Peer' (the URL slug does), so the title is adjusted to describe the page. Year and sample size remain unconfirmed.

works.title: Resolving code review comments with ML
works.authors: Alexander Frömmgen, Lera Kharatyan (Google Core Systems & Experiences)
works.what_measured: Deployment of an ML model in Google's code review tool that suggests edits to resolve reviewer comments.
works.method_plain: Offline evaluation plus production usage statistics.
key_numbers: Change authors need an average of about 60 minutes of active 'shepherding time' between sending a change for review and submitting it
Offline, the model addresses 52% of comments at a target precision of 50%
40-50% of previewed suggested edits are applied by authors
About 20% of generated suggestions were previewed during the beta. This rose to about 40% at launch after a prominent 'Show ML-edit' button was added
'Hundreds of thousands of hours annually' of saved review time is a projection, not a measurement
works.relevance_to_theta: The author's side of the review loop (about 60 minutes per change) is a cost on top of reviewer time. Combining it with Sadowski et al. gives roughly 1.5-2 person-hours per median Google change. That is the stream's own combination: the two figures come from different years and definitions, and shepherding time may include work other than responding to comments. The 40-50% apply rate is a q-like acceptance rate for a narrow AI task.
works.limitations: Blog post, not peer-reviewed. Time savings are projected. Specific to Google.
works.corrections: All numbers match the post. Clarified that the 20% to 40% figures are preview rates of generated suggestions.

works.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
works.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth (Beth) Barnes, David Rein (METR)
works.venue: arXiv:2507.09089 (METR report; v1 12 Jul 2025, v2 25 Jul 2025)
works.what_measured: Randomized trial: 16 experienced open-source developers and 246 real issues in mature repositories they know well (about 5 years of experience on average). Each issue was randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI, mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. A subset of screen recordings was labeled by activity.
works.method_plain: Randomize AI access per task and compare completion times. Hand-label screen recordings into activity categories, including reviewing AI output and waiting on generations.
key_numbers: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%. Developers forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and estimated afterwards that AI had cut time by 20%. Experts forecast 39% (economics) and 38% (ML) reductions
Developers accept fewer than 44% of Cursor generations
On the subset of 44 issues with valid labeled screen recordings, about 9% of time with AI went to reviewing and cleaning AI output, and about 4% to waiting on generations
75% report reading every line of AI code. 56% often need major changes to clean it up. 100% report needing to modify AI code

The acceptance rate below 44% is a q analogue for assistant-mode output. The 19% slowdown is a direct estimate of net assistant-mode speedup (kappa) for experts on familiar codebases, and it is negative.
works.limitations: Small sample of experts in mature open-source repositories with high quality standards, using early-2025 tools. The 9% and 4% come from a 44-issue subset of the recordings. It may not carry over to Indian IT maintenance work on unfamiliar client code, where the AI's relative advantage may differ.
works.corrections: All numbers were confirmed in the PDF (Section C.1.4, the factor table, and the abstract). The third author is listed on arXiv as Elizabeth Barnes (known as Beth Barnes). Added the expert forecasts.
