works.authors: Umut Cihan, Vahid Haratian, Arda İçöz, Mert Kaan Gül, Ömercan Devran, Emircan Furkan Bayendur, Baykal Mehmet Uçar, Eray Tüzün
works.venue: ICSE 2025 (47th International Conference on Software Engineering), Software Engineering in Practice track; arXiv:2412.18531
works.what_measured: Effects of an LLM-based automated reviewer built on Qodo PR Agent at one industrial firm. About 238 practitioners across ten projects had access. Three projects were analyzed: 4,335 PRs, of which 1,568 received automated reviews. Also per-PR developer surveys and a broader survey of 22 practitioners.
works.method_plain: Before/after comparison of PR metrics, plus practitioner surveys.
key_numbers: 73.8% of automated review comments were resolved
Average PR closure time rose from 5 h 52 min before adoption to 8 h 20 min after, with trends varying by project
Most practitioners reported a minor improvement in code quality, alongside faulty reviews, unnecessary corrections and irrelevant comments
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that putting AI on the review side does not automatically cut review cost: elapsed closure time rose about 42% after adoption. This matters for any assumption that AI reviewers offset the extra review burden of AI-written code. It is an industrial, non-Big-Tech setting somewhat closer to IT services firms.
works.limitations: Before/after design with no control group. Closure time is elapsed time, not effort. One company. Only the abstract page was read.
works.corrections: Authors, venue (arXiv comments field: to be presented at ICSE 2025 SEIP) and all abstract numbers match. Added that the roughly 238 practitioners span ten projects.

works.title: The Rise of AI Teammates in Software Engineering (SE) 3.0: How Autonomous Coding Agents Are Reshaping Software Engineering (AIDev dataset)
works.authors: Hao Li, Haoxiang Zhang, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.venue: arXiv:2507.15003 (v1 20 Jul 2025; marked 'Manuscript submitted to ACM')
works.what_measured: The full AIDev dataset has 456,535 agent-authored PRs (OpenAI Codex, Devin, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) from 47,303 developers across 61,453 repositories, collected 1 Jan to 22 Jun 2025. The acceptance and turnaround comparisons use AIDev-pop, a filtered subset of 7,122 PRs from 856 repositories with at least 500 GitHub stars, compared with 6,628 human PRs from the same repositories.
works.method_plain: Mining GitHub PR metadata and timelines. Compares merge rates and time to close for agent PRs against human PRs in popular repositories.
key_numbers: In AIDev-pop (repositories with at least 500 stars), agent acceptance rates are Codex 64%, Devin 49% and Copilot 35% (text). These are 15 to 40 percentage points below human PRs, with the largest gaps on features, bug fixes and performance work. Table 5 shows slightly different figures (65.3%, 48.9%, 38.2%; human 76.8%)
Accepted Codex PRs close in a median of 0.3 h vs 3.9 h for accepted human PRs. Rejected Codex PRs close in 2.4 h vs 27.6 h
Accepted Copilot PRs take a median of 17.2 h to review, more than 4x accepted human PRs (3.9 h). Rejected Copilot PRs take 4.6 h vs 27.6 h for human rejections
Copilot completes half its PR jobs within 12.8 minutes and 75% within 18.5 minutes
works.relevance_to_theta: Gives q-like merge rates for agent PRs in popular repositories, and shows that review latency varies widely by agent: Codex is much faster, Copilot much slower. The authors warn that very fast closes may reflect superficial review. AIDev is a public dataset that can be used to regress review latency and merge probability on PR size and task type.
works.limitations: Turnaround is elapsed time, not reviewer effort. The headline acceptance and latency numbers cover only the 7,122-PR popular-repository subset and three of the five agents, not the full 456k. Selection effects. Early snapshot (to June 2025). The record's claim that 'Codex PRs are often self-merged' was not found in the text checked.
works.corrections: The acceptance and turnaround numbers come from the AIDev-pop subset (7,122 PRs, 856 repositories with at least 500 stars), not the full 456k dataset. The record implied the latter. Exact full-dataset counts added (456,535 / 47,303 / 61,453). Noted the gap between the text and Table 5 acceptance rates, and added Codex's rejected-PR latency (2.4 h). The 'often self-merged' limitation is unverified and has been rephrased. Dataset hosting confirmed at github.com/SAILResearch/AI_Teammates_in_SE3, which links to huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev.

works.title: On the Use of Agentic Coding: An Empirical Study of Pull Requests on GitHub
works.authors: Miku Watanabe, Hao Li, Yutaro Kashiwa, Brittany Reid, Hajimu Iida, Ahmed E. Hassan
works.what_measured: 567 Claude Code-generated PRs across 157 open-source projects, compared with 567 human PRs by the same authors in the same repositories. The human sampling window was extended back to April 2024, so only 42% of human PRs fall in the same timeframe. Measures merge rates, PR size, time to merge, revisions before merge, and rejection reasons.
works.method_plain: Manual classification and statistical tests (chi-squared, log-rank, Mann-Whitney) comparing agent PRs with matched human PRs.
key_numbers: Merged: 83.8% of agent PRs (475/567) vs 91.0% of human PRs (516/567). The difference is statistically significant (chi-squared, p<0.05)
Median lines added at initial submission: 48 (agent) vs 24 (human). Median files modified: 2 for both
Median time to merge: 1.23 h (agent) vs 1.04 h (human). A log-rank test finds no significant difference

45.1% (214/475) of merged agent PRs were modified between submission and merge, vs about 41.5% of human PRs (58.5% of human PRs were merged without revision, vs 54.9% of agent PRs). When revisions were needed, the revision effort (commits, lines, files) was not significantly different between the groups
Revision types for agent PRs (multi-label): bug fixes 47.7%, documentation 29.0%, refactoring 27.1%, code style 23.4%. 34.1% of revision commits were themselves co-authored by Claude Code
64.1% of rejected agent PRs were closed with no explanatory comment
works.relevance_to_theta: Agent PRs add about twice as many lines, which raises review cost per PR under a lines-per-hour model. About 45% of merged agent PRs were revised before merge, often for bug fixes. But human PRs were revised at a similar rate with similar effort, so this is NOT evidence of a large extra rework burden specific to AI. Also, many revisions were themselves AI-assisted. Matched human baselines make it a useful calibration source for q.
works.limitations: Open-source only, with self-selected Claude Code users. The human baseline partly comes from an earlier period. No reviewer-effort hours, only elapsed time. Revisions are not necessarily made by humans.
works.corrections: Removed 'median of 2 revision commits for both groups', which was not found. The paper says only that revision effort was not significantly different. Added the human comparison: 41.5% of human PRs were also revised, which undercuts reading 45% as an AI-specific rework rate. Added that 34.1% of revision commits were co-authored by Claude Code, so 'needed human fixes' is inaccurate. Added the replication package: https://github.com/mmikuu/OnTheUseOfAgenticCoding (the repository exists; contents not inspected).

works.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
works.authors: Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh
works.what_measured: User study: 54 recruited, 47 analyzed (33 experiment, 14 control). Participants did five security-related programming tasks in Python, JavaScript and C, with or without an AI assistant (codex-davinci-002).
works.method_plain: Randomized user study. Two raters manually coded each answer for correctness and security, with Cohen's kappa of 0.7-0.96 for correctness and 0.68-0.88 for security. Logistic regression of security outcomes on group.
key_numbers: Encryption task: 67% of AI-group participants gave correct solutions vs 79% of controls. The AI group was significantly more likely to write insecure solutions (p = 0.017)
Signing task: 3% of the AI group wrote secure solutions vs 21% of controls (p = 0.039)
Participants with AI access were more likely to believe their code was secure
works.relevance_to_theta: AI output can pass functional checks while hiding security defects, and authors become overconfident. Together with evidence that review rarely catches functional defects, this suggests effective q may be below the nominal merge rate. That is an inference: the study does not measure review.
works.limitations: Old model (2022 Codex), small sample with many students, lab tasks focused on crypto. It does not measure code review.
works.corrections: Minor: Cohen's kappa is reported separately (correctness 0.7-0.96; security 0.68-0.88), not as one range of 0.68-0.96. Added the group sizes (33 experiment, 14 control). Other numbers match the PDF.

summary_flags: MISATTRIBUTION: 'At Microsoft, the figure is about 6 hours/week, or about 15% (Czerwonka et al. 2015)'. Czerwonka et al. cite this to Bosu & Carver (ESEM 2013), a self-reported survey that Sadowski et al. describe as covering open-source projects (6.4 h/week). It is not a Microsoft measurement and is not comparable to Google's log-based 3.2 h/week.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY: the summary recommends rho of about 1/200 to 1/500 hours per line, but its own Google baseline (about 45-50 reviewer-minutes on a median 24-line change) implies about 30 LOC/hour. That is roughly 7-15x slower per line. The inspection-rate norms (Kemerer & Paulk's recommended maximum of 200 LOC/h in PSP self-review; SmartBear's 500 LOC/h vendor threshold) are for careful line-by-line inspection, not observed modern review. For small changes a fixed per-change cost seems to dominate, so a pure per-line model would understate rho.

OVERSTATED: 'Agent PRs ... 45% of merged ones needed human fixes (Watanabe et al. 2025)'. About 41.5% of matched human PRs were also revised, revision effort did not differ significantly, and 34.1% of revision commits were co-authored by Claude Code. This is not evidence of a large AI-specific rework burden, and the fixes were not all human.

SCOPE: AIDev's '15-40 points below humans' merge-rate gap is measured on the AIDev-pop subset (7,122 PRs in repositories with at least 500 stars) for three agents (Codex, Devin, Copilot), not on the full 456k-PR dataset or all five agents.

OVERINFERENCE: 'Only 14-15% of review comments are about defects' is a share of comments, not a defect catch rate. A low share could also mean few defects were present. The catch-rate evidence comes from Kemerer & Paulk (PSP classroom self-review) and the SmartBear vendor claim, neither of which is modern team review.

OVERSTATED GENERALITY: 'Even careful individual review catches only just over half of defects' comes from PSP classroom data where developers review their own code at 200 LOC/h or slower. It is not a measured catch rate for peer review of production code.

DERIVED NUMBERS: the 8% of working time (assumes a 40-hour week), the 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change (a mean divided by a median), and the 60-minute author-side figure (Google's 2023 'shepherding time', which may include work beyond answering review comments) are the stream's own combinations of sources with different years and definitions. They should be labelled as rough.
'AI output makes this worse' (Perry et al.) rests on a 2022 Codex model and crypto lab tasks, and the study does not measure review. It supports a hypothesis but not a parameter value.
Cihan et al.'s closure-time increase is a before/after comparison without a control, measuring elapsed time, not effort. It should not be read as evidence that AI review raises reviewer hours.
METR's 9% review/cleanup share and 4% waiting share come from a 44-issue subset of labeled recordings, not all 246 tasks.

The web-search budget was also exhausted during this verification pass, so the stream's gap remains: 2025-2026 MSR/ICSE work on reviewer EFFORT for agent PRs was not searched systematically. The unopened works (Fagan 1976; Mäntylä & Lassenius 2009; McIntosh et al. 2014) were not checked here either and should not be cited from this stream.
verify.corrected_summary:
The code-review literature gives reasonable baselines for reviewer effort on human-written code. Almost nothing measures review EFFORT (hours) on AI-written code; the agent-PR studies report elapsed time.

Human baseline. At Google (Sadowski et al. 2018, log-based), reviewers spend a mean of 3.2 hours/week (median 2.6) reviewing a median of about 4 changes/week, with a median change size of 24 lines. That is roughly 8% of a 40-hour week. Our crude division gives about 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change. Google's 2023 blog adds about 60 minutes of active author 'shepherding time' per change. The often-quoted '6 hours/week' (Czerwonka et al. 2015) is a self-reported survey figure cited from Bosu & Carver (2013), not a Microsoft measurement, so it is not comparable.

Inspection-speed studies give a per-line view. In PSP classroom self-review, Kemerer & Paulk (2009) find that reviewing at 200 LOC/hour or slower removes just over half of code defects, and faster review removes fewer. SmartBear's vendor guide warns against going faster than about 500 LOC/hour. But Google's numbers imply about 30 LOC/hour for small changes. This suggests rho has a sizeable fixed cost per change plus a per-line component, not a per-line rate taken from inspection norms.

Review as a filter. Only about 14-15% of review comments concern defects (Bacchelli & Bird 2013; Czerwonka et al. 2015). Review is mostly about maintainability and understanding. This, together with the PSP catch rates, suggests passing review does not guarantee correctness, so an escaped-defect term is worth modelling. The comment-share evidence does not by itself pin down a catch rate.

AI-specific evidence:
- METR's 2025 RCT (16 experts, 246 tasks): developers were 19% slower with AI and accepted fewer than 44% of generations. On a 44-issue subset, they spent about 9% of their time reviewing and cleaning AI output and 4% waiting.
- Claude Code PRs (Watanabe et al. 2025) add about twice as many lines as matched human PRs (median 48 vs 24) and merge less often (83.8% vs 91.0%). Merge time is similar, and the share needing revision before merge is similar (45% vs about 41%).
- In popular GitHub repositories, three agents' merge rates trail humans by 15-40 points (AIDev-pop subset, Li et al. 2025). Review latency varies widely by agent.
- Perry et al. (2023) found users of a 2022 Codex assistant wrote less secure code and were more confident in it.
- One industrial before/after study found an AI reviewer raised average PR closure time (elapsed) from 5.9 to 8.3 hours (Cihan et al. 2025).

Implications for the draft: model rho as a fixed per-change cost plus a per-line cost scaled by AI change size, calibrated to observed modern review rather than to inspection norms alone. Treat q as merge-rate-like evidence, discounted for escaped defects. Measure reviewer effort on AI output directly, because none of the agent-PR studies do.
verify.dataset_notes:
AIDev: public. The canonical location is the GitHub repo https://github.com/SAILResearch/AI_Teammates_in_SE3 (named in the paper's abstract), which links to the Hugging Face dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev (versioned; v3 and v5 tags seen). Use those rather than the arXiv page as the dataset URL. The headline comparisons in the paper use the AIDev-pop subset (7,122 PRs from repositories with at least 500 stars).

Watanabe et al.: a replication package exists at https://github.com/mmikuu/OnTheUseOfAgenticCoding (the repo returned HTTP 200; its contents were not inspected), so access is likely public rather than unknown.

Google Critique logs: internal; only aggregates are published (correct as listed).

METR early-2025 RCT: public release of the task-level timings and recording labels was not verified in this pass; keep as on-request/unknown.

Kemerer & Paulk PSP data: SEI PSP data. The listed handle https://hdl.handle.net/11059/14085 is an open-access copy of the PAPER (per Semantic Scholar), not a dataset. It redirects to a Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira repository behind a bot-check page and was not confirmed. Access to the data is unknown; use the DOI https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2009.27 for the paper.

streams.name: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)

works.title: How Many U.S. Jobs Might Be Offshorable?
works.authors: Alan S. Blinder
works.venue: Princeton University CEPS Working Paper No. 142 (March 2007); later version in World Economics 2009 (not opened)
works.what_measured: An ordinal 0-100 offshorability index for 817 detailed US occupations (799 SOC codes plus 18 subdivided ones), and the share of 2004 US employment that is 'potentially offshorable' within a decade or two.
works.method_plain: Blinder and an RA read O*NET occupation descriptions and work-activity scores and asked two questions in sequence: does the worker need to be physically near a specific US location, and does the work need face-to-face contact? Occupations were sorted into four categories (533 were judged plainly non-offshorable, Category IV), then the 284 in Categories I-III were given rank numbers by hand. He also builds an objective O*NET-based ranking and compares it with an independent subjective one.
key_numbers: 22.2% of 2004 US employment (210 occupations, about 28.9 million jobs) potentially offshorable under the most conservative cutoff (index 51-100)
25.6% (240 occupations, 33.4 million jobs) under the moderate cutoff (index 37 and above)
about 29% under the most aggressive cutoff (all of Category III); the abstract states the range as 22% to 29%

Computer programmers and data entry keyers share the top rating (100). Computer systems analysts, computer support specialists and applications and systems software engineers are near the top of the list of large occupations
Little or no correlation between offshorability and skill (education or wages); controlling for education, highly offshorable occupations already paid significantly lower wages in 2004
He compares his conservative figure with McKinsey's 11% and says his is roughly double
Explicitly NOT a forecast of jobs actually offshored; the scale is ordinal, not a probability
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the template for the extensive margin: a binary or ordinal judgment of whether a task can be done by a remote, cheaper supplier, with nothing on how much labor is saved. It is the direct ancestor of AI exposure indices, and it shows the same gap the project hypothesizes: 'potentially offshorable' (22-29%) is not 'offshored', just as 'exposed' is not theta_j. The occupation list (programmers, systems analysts and support specialists at the top) maps onto the service lines in w_j. The ordinal-not-cardinal warning carries straight over to exposure scores.
works.limitations: Subjective and ordinal, US 2004 occupations, no task-length or intensive-margin information, and no realized-offshoring data. Says nothing about review or coordination costs, which the offshoring literature treats as the actual barrier.

works.title: Alternative Measures of Offshorability: A Survey Approach
works.authors: Alan S. Blinder and Alan B. Krueger
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 15287 (Aug 2009); published in Journal of Labor Economics 31(S1): S97-S128 (2013), per the NBER page
works.what_measured: How offshorable US jobs are, measured from a household survey (Princeton Data Improvement Initiative). Self-reports are compared with ratings by professional coders.
works.method_plain: Workers were asked about their job duties, for example whether the work must be done on site or face to face. Researchers built several offshorability measures from the answers, both from workers' own judgments and from trained coders reading the job descriptions, then checked how far the measures agree and whether offshorability predicts wages or layoffs.
key_numbers: All measures find about 25% of US jobs offshorable
The three preferred measures agree 70% to 80% of the time
Professional-coder assessments look the most accurate
More educated workers hold somewhat more offshorable jobs
Offshorability has no systematic effect on wages or layoff probability
Routine work is no more offshorable than other work
works.relevance_to_theta: The methods lesson: exposure classifications from different raters agree only 70-80% of the time, and exposure does not predict layoffs. This is a direct warning against reading theta_j off an exposure score, and it supports the working hypothesis that the extensive margin does not identify the intensive one. It also suggests a recipe step: have expert coders (not workers' own reports) label task requirements, then measure agreement between raters.
works.limitations: US only; measures potential offshorability, not the labor saved. The published JOLE version was not opened, so page numbers come from the NBER page.

works.title: Tradable Services: Understanding the Scope and Impact of Services Offshoring
works.authors: J. Bradford Jensen and Lori G. Kletzer
works.venue: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper 05-9 (September 2005); prepared for the Brookings Trade Forum 2005 (the Brookings volume itself was not opened)
works.what_measured: Which US service industries and occupations are tradable (could be supplied from elsewhere), the share of employment in them, wage premia, employment growth and displacement.
works.method_plain: An activity whose output can be shipped will be geographically concentrated (produced in a few places and sold everywhere), while a non-tradable activity follows local demand. Using the 2000 Census 5% PUMS, they compute a locational Gini (how unevenly employment is spread across metro areas relative to demand) for each industry and occupation. Activities with Gini of 0.1 or more are classed as tradable, with the cutoff calibrated on manufacturing.
key_numbers: Employment share in tradable professional/business service industries (NAICS 51-56): 13.7% of total US employment, larger than tradable manufacturing (12.4%)

Share of each occupation group's employment classed as tradable: computer and mathematical 100%, legal 96%, life/physical/social science 83%, business and financial operations 68%, architecture and engineering 63%
Workers in tradable service industries earn about 6% more than those in non-tradable ones, controlling for demographics; almost 15% more within professional services
Little evidence that tradable services grew more slowly overall, but some evidence of slower growth at the low-skill end and higher displacement rates
works.relevance_to_theta: An objective, outcome-based exposure measure that complements Blinder's judgment-based one. Every computer and mathematical occupation is classed as tradable, so essentially the whole Indian IT/BPO workforce sits in what the offshoring literature already treated as fully exposed. The useful idea for the project is identification by revealed behavior (where work actually sits) rather than by judgment. The AI analogue would infer theta_j from where firms actually route tickets to AI, not from rubric scores.
works.limitations: Measures tradability, not how much labor is saved; the threshold is arbitrary (the share falls as the cutoff rises); US data from 2000. The Brookings Trade Forum published version was not opened.

works.title: Introduction to 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization' (summarizing van Welsum and Reif, 'We Can Work It Out: The Globalization of IT-enabled Services')
works.authors: Marshall Reinsdorf and Matthew J. Slaughter (introduction); the underlying chapter is by Desirée van Welsum and Xavier Reif
works.venue: NBER volume 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization', University of Chicago Press, May 2009 (conference April 2006), chapter c11604
works.what_measured: The editors' summary of the volume. It reports van Welsum and Reif's estimate of the share of OECD employment that is potentially offshorable.
works.method_plain: Van Welsum and Reif count employees in occupations with four attributes: (a) intensive use of ICT, (b) output that can be sent over ICT, (c) highly codifiable knowledge content, and (d) no need for face-to-face contact.
key_numbers: 18 to 20 percent of total employment potentially offshorable in OECD countries with detailed enough data (an upper bound, per the editors)
Editors note this is slightly above Jensen and Kletzer's US tradable-services employment share
works.relevance_to_theta: Its criteria (codifiable knowledge, output transmittable digitally, no face-to-face) read almost as a definition of current LLM exposure, and they are the traits that let Indian IT/BPO firms ticketize work. The link to f_j(h): codified, modular work is broken into short, well-specified units, the region where p(h,t) is highest.
works.limitations: Only the editors' introduction was read; the van Welsum-Reif chapter itself was not opened, so its details are second-hand. Extensive margin only.

works.title: Reputation Effects and the Limits of Contracting: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works.authors: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo
works.what_measured: How contract terms (fixed-price vs. time-and-materials, i.e., who bears cost-overrun risk) and ex post outcomes after renegotiation depend on a vendor's reputation, in Indian customized-software projects.
works.method_plain: The authors collected their own data on 230 software projects done by 125 Indian firms for clients. They estimate how ex ante contract terms and outcomes after overruns vary with firm characteristics plausibly tied to reputation (such as firm age), controlling for project, client and firm characteristics, and interpret the results with a model of reputation.
key_numbers: 230 projects
125 Indian software firms
Main finding (abstract): both ex ante contract terms and ex post outcomes vary with reputation-related firm characteristics, after controls
Effect sizes are not reported here because the full text is paywalled and was not read
works.relevance_to_theta: Not about theta_j directly, but it is the classic micro evidence on how Indian IT contracts allocate cost risk. That allocation governs pass-through phi: under time-and-materials, AI labor savings flow to the client automatically through fewer billed hours (phi near 1), while under fixed-price the vendor keeps them until renegotiation. The project dataset needs each firm's revenue split between fixed-price and T&M by year, which TCS and Infosys disclose in their annual reports. Project-level overrun data of this kind is also a natural source for how often delivered work fails client acceptance (q) and how much rework it needs (rho).
works.limitations: Data from the late 1990s; only the abstract and metadata were read (paywalled), so specific coefficients, including the fixed-price/T&M split, are not confirmed here.

works.title: Quality Certification and the Economics of Contract Software Development: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works.authors: Ashish Arora and Jai Asundi
works.what_measured: Whether ISO 9001 certification raises growth, revenue per unit of size and implied price or quality for Indian contract-software firms.
works.method_plain: A stylized model of a firm developing software for others under contract, data on 95 Indian software firms and their US clients, and field interviews.
key_numbers: 95 Indian software firms
ISO certification increases firm growth
Partial evidence that certified firms earn more revenue for a given size, implying higher prices per unit of output
Firms mostly see ISO as a marketing tool, though some adopted more systematic, better-defined development processes
works.relevance_to_theta: Documents that Indian IT competed by making its process verifiable to distant clients, through certification and later CMM levels. Verification cost is the core problem for remote delivery, and the same problem now limits AI delegation (q and rho). Industrialized, process-heavy delivery also means tasks arrive pre-specified, which pushes f_j(h) toward short h. This is the companion paper to Arora, Arunachalam, Asundi and Fernandes (2001, Research Policy), whose full text was not opened.
works.limitations: Old data and a working paper; only the abstract was read, and it reports no coefficients.

works.title: The Service Sector as India's Road to Economic Growth
works.authors: Barry Eichengreen and Poonam Gupta
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 16757 (Feb 2011); also India Policy Forum 7(1): 1-42 (2011), per the NBER page
works.what_measured: India's services growth compared with international norms, the role of modern services (business services, communications, banking), and the skill mix of service employment.
works.method_plain: Cross-country comparison of services' share of output and employment against income levels, plus Indian sectoral and household data on who works in modern services.
key_numbers: Services' share of Indian output has roughly converged to international norms after starting about 15 years earlier from unusually low levels
Continued above-norm growth depends on modern services and on applying IT to traditional services; the authors say the latter helps output more than employment
The skill mix in manufacturing and services is increasingly similar, so modern services are not only a destination for the highly skilled
Abstract gives no further quantitative figures
works.relevance_to_theta: Macro context for demand d and for why job losses in IT/BPO matter in aggregate. It does not inform theta_j, but it frames the services-led-growth route that AI substitution would threaten. Their remark that IT in traditional services raises output more than employment is an early version of the s versus eps*phi question.
works.limitations: Pre-AI; only the abstract was read, with no task-level content.

works.title: Do Labor Market Opportunities Affect Young Women's Work and Family Decisions? Experimental Evidence from India
works.authors: Robert Jensen
works.what_measured: Effects of a randomized expansion of BPO job opportunities on young women's employment, schooling, marriage and fertility in rural India.
works.method_plain: BPO recruiting services were provided for three years in randomly chosen villages. The industry was new and largely unknown there, so this exogenously expanded women's perceived job options, and outcomes are compared with control villages.
key_numbers: Young women in treatment villages were significantly less likely to marry or have children during the study period, and more likely to work or pursue more schooling or post-school training
They reported wanting fewer children and more steady work over their lifetimes
Coefficients and sample sizes not recorded: paywalled, only the abstract was read
works.relevance_to_theta: No bearing on theta_j itself. It matters for the welfare reading of g_L: BPO is the service line most exposed, and where AI pass rates on short, scripted tasks are likely highest. The losses would fall partly on entry-level workers, including women for whom these jobs changed schooling and marriage decisions. The paper also shows the information channel: perceived opportunity changes human-capital investment, so the expectation of AI shrinking BPO could reduce investment even before any layoffs.
works.limitations: Recruitment intervention from the 2000s, not a labor-demand shock; only the abstract was read.

research.stream_summary: The offshoring literature of 2005-2013 asked almost the same question the project now asks about AI: which jobs could a cheaper, remote supplier do? Blinder (2007) hand-ranked 817 US occupations and found 22-29% 'potentially offshorable'. Blinder and Krueger (2009/2013) used a survey and found about 25%. Jensen and Kletzer (2005) inferred tradability from geographic concentration and classed 100% of computer and mathematical occupations as tradable. Van Welsum and Reif's OECD criteria (codifiable knowledge, output sent digitally, no face-to-face contact) put 18-20% of employment as potentially offshorable. Two lessons carry over. First, the measures are extensive-margin and ordinal: Blinder warns his index is not a probability or a forecast, and Blinder-Krueger find exposure does not predict wages or layoffs, while their measures agree only 70-80% of the time. That supports the working hypothesis that exposure indices do not identify theta_j. Second, the Indian IT/BPO workforce sits at the very top of every offshorability ranking, alongside programmers and data-entry keyers. Its work was made codifiable and verifiable across distance (Arora-Asundi on ISO certification) and is governed by contracts that allocate cost risk (Banerjee-Duflo on fixed-price vs. time-and-materials). Those features push task lengths f_j(h) short, where AI succeeds, and contract mix largely determines pass-through phi. Eichengreen-Gupta give the services-led-growth context, and Jensen (2012) shows that BPO jobs change women's schooling and marriage decisions, which matters for who bears losses. Nothing found here measures the intensive margin, meaning hours saved net of review, for Indian IT work.
gaps_noticed: The web-search budget for this turn ran out after the first queries. Several targets could not be located and are NOT verified: the IMF working paper 'AI and Services-Led Growth: Evidence from Indian Job Adverts' (Copestake, Marczinek, Pople, Stapleton), which I could not confirm, so do not cite it until verified; the Brookings Trade Forum 2005 published version of Jensen-Kletzer (the PIIE WP 05-9 version was opened instead); and Gopal, Sivaramakrishnan, Krishnan and Mukhopadhyay, 'Contracts in offshore software development' (Management Science 2003), whose page returned 403, so its content is unconfirmed.
Arora, Arunachalam, Asundi and Fernandes (2001, Research Policy) was not opened in this pass; the DOI I tried returned 404.

No intensive-margin evidence for Indian IT/BPO: no study measures hours saved per ticket, review time, or acceptance rates for offshore or AI-delivered work. The offshoring literature never measured coordination or verification cost directly either. That is the analogue of rho and q, and it is the gap the project's recipe would fill.

No public data on the hours-weighted distribution of task or ticket lengths (f_j(h)) in Indian IT service lines. Ticket-level data (ServiceNow or JIRA exports from vendors) would be lab-internal or on-request at best.

Contract-type evidence (fixed-price vs. T&M share) is dated (late 1990s micro data); recent pass-through evidence linking contract mix to AI-driven price cuts is missing. Firm annual reports disclose the revenue split and could fill this.

Peer-reviewed micro evidence on Indian IT/BPO labor markets after 2015 is thin in what was found here; most recent evidence comes from industry bodies (NASSCOM) and job-posting data rather than journals.

datasets.name: Blinder (2007) offshorability index by occupation (appendix table, 817 SOC occupations)
datasets.description: Ordinal 0-100 offshorability ranks for US occupations; can be crosswalked to O*NET or ISCO and compared with AI exposure scores, to test whether offshorability and AI exposure pick out the same tasks.

datasets.name: Princeton Data Improvement Initiative survey (used by Blinder-Krueger)
datasets.description: Household survey with job-duty questions and professional-coder offshorability ratings; access terms were not checked.

works.title: How Many U.S. Jobs Might Be Offshorable?
works.authors: Alan S. Blinder
works.venue: Princeton University CEPS Working Paper No. 142 (March 2007). A later journal version (World Economics, 2009) is reported but was not opened or confirmed in this check.
works.what_measured: An ordinal 0-100 offshorability index for 817 US occupations (799 BLS SOC codes, some split into parts), and the share of 2004 US employment that is 'potentially offshorable' within a decade or two.
works.method_plain: Blinder, with research assistant Yanliang Miao, used O*NET descriptions and work-activity scores. He asked whether the work must be done near a specific US location and whether it needs face-to-face contact. Each occupation went into one of four categories. 533 occupations were judged highly non-offshorable (Category IV, index 0-25). The 284 occupations in Categories I-III were then given index numbers by hand. He also builds an objective O*NET-based ranking and compares it with an independent subjective ranking by a second rater, using 799 occupations.
key_numbers: Table 1: Category I 59 occupations (8.2 million workers, index 100-76); Category II 151 (20.7 million, 75-51); Category III 74 (8.8 million, 50-26); Category IV 533 (92.6 million, 25-0); total 817 (130.3 million)
Most conservative cutoff (Categories I+II, index 51-100): 210 occupations, 22.2% of 2004 US employment, about 28.9 million jobs
Moderate cutoff (index 37 and above): 240 occupations, 25.6%, 33.4 million jobs
Most aggressive cutoff (all of Category III, index 26 and above): 284 occupations, 29.0%, 37.8 million jobs. The abstract gives the range as 22% to 29%. Blinder's own best guess is 26-29%

Computer programmers and data entry keyers both get index 100. In Table 2, the major-occupations list: computer systems analysts 93 (Category I), computer support specialists 92/68 (split between I and II), applications and systems software engineers 74 (Category II)
Little or no correlation between offshorability and skill, measured by education or wages. Controlling for education, the most offshorable occupations already paid significantly lower wages in 2004
Says even the conservative estimate is roughly double McKinsey's 11%. McKinsey's figure covers worldwide private-sector service employment, so the two numbers measure different things
States the scale is ordinal, not cardinal; the index numbers are not probabilities; and the paper makes no estimate of how many jobs will actually be offshored
works.relevance_to_theta: This is the template for an extensive-margin measure. It judges, on an ordinal scale, whether a remote supplier could do the work, and says nothing about how much labor that saves. It is a direct ancestor of AI exposure indices and makes the same distinction the project needs: 'potentially offshorable' is not 'offshored', just as 'exposed' is not theta_j. Its warning that the scale is ordinal, not a probability, carries over to exposure scores. It informs no theta_j parameter directly. It could at most give rough US occupation weights, not w_j for Indian service lines.
works.limitations: Subjective and ordinal. Uses US 2004 occupations. Has no information on task length or the intensive margin, and no data on realized offshoring. Says nothing about review or coordination costs. Only 284 of the 817 occupations were individually hand-ranked; the other 533 were placed as a block in Category IV. The World Economics version was not opened.
works.corrections: All numbers confirmed in the PDF text. Added detail: the aggressive cutoff is 29.0% (284 occupations, 37.8 million jobs), and the author's best guess is 26-29%. Clarified that software engineers sit at index 74 (Category II), not at the very top. Added that the McKinsey 11% is a worldwide service-sector figure, so 'roughly double' compares different bases. Removed w_j from params: the index is US occupation-level and does not give Indian service-line labor shares. The World Economics 2009 version is still unconfirmed.

works.title: Alternative Measures of Offshorability: A Survey Approach
works.authors: Alan S. Blinder and Alan B. Krueger
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 15287 (August 2009); Journal of Labor Economics 31(S1): S97-S128 (2013), per the NBER page
works.what_measured: How offshorable US jobs are, measured with a household survey. Workers' own reports are compared with ratings by professional coders.
works.method_plain: A household survey asked workers about their job duties. The authors built several offshorability measures, some from workers' own answers and some from professional coders reading the job descriptions. They checked how often the measures agree and whether offshorability is related to education, wages, layoffs and routine work.
key_numbers: All measures suggest about a quarter of US jobs are offshorable
The three preferred measures agree 70% to 80% of the time
Professional coders appear to be the most accurate, so the Census Bureau could collect this without adding survey questions
More educated workers hold somewhat more offshorable jobs
Offshorability has no systematic relationship with wages or layoff probability
Routine work is no more offshorable than other work
works.relevance_to_theta: A methods lesson: different raters of the same jobs agree only 70-80% of the time, and offshorability does not line up with layoffs or wages. That warns against reading theta_j straight off an exposure score, and it is consistent with the project's working hypothesis, though it does not prove it. It also suggests a recipe step: have expert coders label task requirements and report agreement between raters.
works.limitations: US only. Measures potential offshorability, not labor saved. The finding that offshorability is unrelated to layoffs is a correlation from a single cross-section. Only the NBER abstract page was read; the JOLE article and the survey details were not opened.
works.corrections: No factual changes; the abstract and journal citation match the NBER page. Removed w_j from params because nothing here gives labor shares by service line. Changed 'no systematic effect' to 'no systematic relationship' to avoid a causal reading.

works.title: Tradable Services: Understanding the Scope and Impact of Services Offshoring
works.authors: J. Bradford Jensen and Lori G. Kletzer
works.venue: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper 05-9 (September 2005). Published as 'Tradable Services: Understanding the Scope and Impact of Services Outsourcing' in Brookings Trade Forum 2005: Offshoring White-Collar Work, eds. S. M. Collins and L. Brainard, pp. 75-116 (Brookings, 2006). The published-version details come from the reference list of Reinsdorf and Slaughter (2009); the volume itself was not opened.
works.what_measured: Which US service industries and occupations are tradable, their share of employment, wage differentials, employment growth from 1998 to 2002, and displacement.
works.method_plain: Work that can be shipped tends to be geographically concentrated, while non-tradable work follows local demand. Using the 2000 Census 5% PUMS (place-of-work metro areas), they compute a demand-weighted locational Gini for each industry and occupation. An industry or occupation with Gini of 0.1 or more is classed as tradable. The 0.1 cutoff was chosen by checking it against goods-producing industries, which are known to be mostly tradable.
key_numbers: Employment in tradable professional and business service industries (NAICS 51-56): 13.7% of total US employment, more than tradable manufacturing (12.4%)

Share of employment classed as tradable, by occupation group: computer and mathematical 100%, legal 96%, life/physical/social sciences 83%, business and financial operations 68%, architecture and engineering 63%

Across ALL industries, workers in tradable industries earn 6% more, controlling for demographics and industry and region fixed effects. Within professional services, tradable-industry workers earn almost 15% more

Mean tradable service industry employment growth was 7.6%, against 6.7% for non-tradable services. There is some evidence of lower growth at the low-skill end and higher displacement rates in tradable services
works.relevance_to_theta: An objective, outcome-based exposure measure that complements Blinder's judgment-based one. It classes all US computer and mathematical occupations as tradable. It is still an extensive-margin, yes/no classification and says nothing about labor saved. Its useful idea for the project is identifying exposure from revealed behavior rather than judgment. The AI analogue (inferring theta_j from where firms actually send work to AI) is the researcher's suggestion, not something in the paper.
works.limitations: Measures tradability, not labor saved. The 0.1 threshold is a judgment call. Uses US 2000 data. Covers US occupations, so mapping to Indian IT/BPO roles is an inference: BPO roles such as call centre and data entry sit in office/admin support and sales groups, not in computer and mathematical.
works.corrections: The 6% wage premium is for tradable vs. non-tradable industries across ALL industries, not specifically service industries; the 'almost 15%' figure is within professional services. Added the 7.6% vs 6.7% service growth figures. Added published-version details (Brookings Trade Forum 2005, published 2006, pp. 75-116, eds. Collins and Brainard), taken from a reference list and not independently opened; that version's title says 'Outsourcing' where the WP says 'Offshoring'. Removed w_j from params. Toned down the relevance claim that 'essentially the whole Indian IT/BPO workforce' is fully exposed, because BPO occupations are not in the computer and mathematical group. The WP number 05-9 comes from the PDF filename and the September date from the cover; the PIIE landing page was not found (404).

works.title: Introduction to 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization' (summarizing van Welsum and Reif, 'We Can Work It Out: The Globalization of ICT-enabled Services', chapter 9)
works.authors: Marshall Reinsdorf and Matthew J. Slaughter (introduction); the underlying chapter is by Desirée van Welsum and Xavier Reif
works.venue: NBER volume 'International Trade in Services and Intangibles in the Era of Globalization', eds. Reinsdorf and Slaughter, University of Chicago Press, May 2009 (conference April 28-29, 2006); introduction is chapter c11604, pp. 1-24
works.what_measured: The editors' summary of the volume, including van Welsum and Reif's estimate of the share of employment in OECD countries that is potentially offshorable.
works.method_plain: Per the editors, van Welsum and Reif count employees in detailed occupations with four attributes: (a) intensive use of ICT; (b) output that can be transmitted by ICT; (c) highly codifiable knowledge content; and (d) no need for face-to-face contact.
key_numbers: 18 to 20 percent of total employment is potentially offshorable in the OECD countries with detailed enough data; the editors call this an upper bound
The editors say this is slightly above the US tradable-services employment share found by Jensen and Kletzer
works.relevance_to_theta: Its four criteria (codifiable knowledge, output sent digitally, no face-to-face contact) resemble the features used in LLM exposure rubrics. It is extensive-margin only. The link to f_j(h), that codified work comes in short units where p(h,t) is highest, is the researcher's hypothesis and is not in the source.
works.limitations: Only the editors' introduction was read; the van Welsum-Reif chapter itself was not opened, so its details are second-hand. Extensive margin only.
works.corrections: No numeric changes; the four attributes, the 18-20% figure and the Jensen-Kletzer comparison all match the PDF. The introduction refers to the chapter as 'We can Work it Out: The Globalization of IT-enabled Services'. Marked the f_j(h) link as the researcher's speculation.

works.title: Reputation Effects and the Limits of Contracting: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works.authors: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo
works.what_measured: How ex ante contract terms and ex post outcomes after renegotiation in Indian customized-software projects vary with firm characteristics linked to reputation. The abstract does not mention fixed-price vs. time-and-materials contracts, so that framing is not confirmed here.
works.method_plain: The authors collected their own data on 230 software projects carried out by 125 Indian firms. They relate contract terms and outcomes to reputation-related firm characteristics, controlling for project, client and firm characteristics, and interpret the results with a model in which reputation shapes contracts.
key_numbers: 230 projects
125 Indian software firms
Abstract: both ex ante contract terms and ex post outcomes vary with reputation-related firm characteristics, after controls
No effect sizes confirmed; the full text was not read
works.relevance_to_theta: Not about theta_j. It is classic micro evidence on how Indian IT contracts handle risk and reputation, which bears on pass-through phi. The researcher's argument that savings pass to the client under time-and-materials (phi near 1) but stay with the vendor under fixed price until renegotiation is a plausible hypothesis, not a finding of this paper as far as could be checked. Using this kind of data to measure q or rho is speculative.
works.limitations: Late-1990s data. Only the abstract and metadata were read (paywalled), so no coefficients and no fixed-price/T&M results are confirmed.
works.corrections: The citation is correct; added the August 2000 issue date. Removed 'fixed-price vs. time-and-materials' from what_measured as a confirmed feature, because the abstract does not mention it. It may be in the full text, but that was not checked. Marked the phi, q and rho arguments as the researcher's hypotheses. The claim that TCS and Infosys report a fixed-price/T&M revenue split in their annual reports was not checked.

works.title: Quality Certification and the Economics of Contract Software Development: A Study of the Indian Software Industry
works.authors: Ashish Arora and Jai Asundi
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 7260 (July 1999); no published version listed on the NBER page
works.what_measured: Whether ISO 9001 certification is associated with firm growth and with higher revenue for a given firm size (implying higher price or quality) for Indian contract-software firms.
works.method_plain: A simple model of a firm that develops software for others under contract, plus data on 95 Indian software firms and their US clients, plus field interviews.
key_numbers: 95 Indian software firms
ISO certification increases firm growth
Partial evidence that certified firms earn more revenue for a given size, implying higher prices per unit of output and so higher quality
Field interviews: most firms see ISO mainly as a marketing tool, though some adopted more systematic, better-defined development processes
works.relevance_to_theta: Shows that Indian IT firms signalled quality to distant clients through certification, a verification problem similar to the one now facing AI delegation (q, rho). The paper does not measure verification cost or task length. The ideas that process-heavy delivery pushes f_j(h) toward short tasks, and that this feeds q, are the researcher's inference.
works.limitations: Old data; a working paper; only the abstract was read, and it gives no coefficients. Interviews suggest certification was often a marketing signal rather than a real process change, which weakens the 'made verifiable' reading.
works.corrections: Citation and abstract claims confirmed. Removed q from params: the paper does not estimate acceptance rates. Noted that the 'pre-specified tasks push f_j(h) short' link is the researcher's inference. The companion Research Policy 2001 paper (Arora, Arunachalam, Asundi, Fernandes) was not verified.

works.title: The Service Sector as India's Road to Economic Growth
works.authors: Barry Eichengreen and Poonam Gupta
works.venue: NBER Working Paper 16757 (February 2011); published as 'The Service Sector as India's Road to Economic Growth?' in India Policy Forum 7(1): 1-42 (NCAER, 2011), per the NBER page
works.what_measured: India's services growth compared with international norms, the roles of modern services (business services, communications, banking) and of IT in traditional services, and the skill mix of service employment.
works.method_plain: Compares India's services share with cross-country norms, and uses Indian sectoral and household data to see who works in modern services.
key_numbers: India's services growth started about 15 years earlier from unusually low levels, and the services share has roughly converged to international norms

Continued above-norm growth depends on modern services and on applying IT to traditional services (retail and wholesale trade, transport and storage, public administration). The abstract says the latter helps output more than employment
Modern service employment is not simply manufacturing in disguise. The skill mix in manufacturing and services is increasingly similar, so modern services are not only for the highly skilled
works.relevance_to_theta: Macro context for demand d and for why IT/BPO jobs matter for India's growth model. It does not inform theta_j. Its remark that IT in traditional services raises output more than employment loosely echoes the s versus eps*phi question.
works.limitations: Pre-AI and macro-level; only the abstract was read.
works.corrections: The published India Policy Forum title ends with a question mark ('...Road to Economic Growth?'). The other content matches the abstract.

works.title: Do Labor Market Opportunities Affect Young Women's Work and Family Decisions? Experimental Evidence from India
works.authors: Robert Jensen
works.what_measured: Effects of BPO recruiting services, offered in randomly chosen rural Indian villages, on young women's employment, schooling, marriage and fertility.
works.method_plain: For three years, recruiting services for BPO jobs were provided to young women in randomly selected villages. The industry was new and little known, so this shifted households' perceived job options for women in a way they had not anticipated. Outcomes are compared with control villages.
key_numbers: Young women in treatment villages were less likely to marry or have children during the study period, and more likely to enter the labor market or get more schooling or post-school training
They reported wanting fewer children and expecting to work more continuously over their lives
Sample sizes and coefficients not recorded: paywalled, only the abstract was read
works.relevance_to_theta: No bearing on theta_j. Relevant to who bears losses if BPO employment shrinks, and to the idea that perceived job prospects change human-capital investment. The claims that BPO is the most exposed service line and has the highest AI pass rates are the researcher's speculation, not from this paper.
works.limitations: A recruitment intervention from the 2000s, not a labor-demand shock; only the abstract was read.
works.corrections: Citation confirmed. Marked as speculation the relevance claims about BPO being most exposed and having the highest pass rates.

summary_flags: 'Blinder (2007) hand-ranked 817 US occupations': only 284 were individually hand-ranked; 533 were placed as a block in Category IV (index 0-25).

'The Indian IT/BPO workforce sits at the very top of every offshorability ranking': overstated. These are US occupation rankings, not Indian ones. Software engineers sit at index 74 (Category II) in Blinder's list, not at the top. Blinder-Krueger's occupation ranking was not checked. BPO roles fall in office/admin support and sales, not in Jensen-Kletzer's 100%-tradable computer and mathematical group.

'Its work was made codifiable and verifiable across distance (Arora-Asundi on ISO certification)': overstated. Arora-Asundi's interviews say most firms treated ISO mainly as a marketing tool, and only some changed their processes.

'governed by contracts that allocate cost risk (Banerjee-Duflo on fixed-price vs. time-and-materials)': the abstract does not mention fixed-price or T&M. That framing is not confirmed from what was read.
'Those features push task lengths f_j(h) short, where AI succeeds, and contract mix largely determines pass-through phi': no source here supports either claim. Both are hypotheses to test.
Jensen-Kletzer's 6% wage premium is for tradable industries across all industries, not tradable service industries specifically.

Gap claim 'the offshoring literature never measured coordination or verification cost directly' is too strong and was not checked. Contract studies such as Gopal et al. (2003) and offshoring-cost models exist. Say instead 'none found in this pass'.

Missing classics: the stream omits trade-in-tasks theory, which defines this field and is the closest analogue to a task-level, cost-weighted theta_j: Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg, 'Trading Tasks: A Simple Theory of Offshoring' (AER 2008). Not verified in this pass because the search budget ran out; check it before citing.

The IMF paper 'AI and Services-Led Growth: Evidence from Indian Job Adverts', Gopal et al. (Management Science 2003) and Arora et al. (Research Policy 2001) all remain unverified. A guessed IMF URL returned 404, and the search budget for this turn ran out.
Note on this check: the web-search budget ran out partway through. Primary pages and PDFs were still opened directly for all eight works.
verify.corrected_summary:
The offshoring literature of 2005-2013 asked a question close to the one this project asks about AI: which jobs could a cheaper, remote supplier do? Blinder (2007) sorted 817 US occupations into four categories, hand-ranking the 284 judged at least somewhat offshorable. He found 22-29% of 2004 US employment 'potentially offshorable' (22.2%, 25.6% or 29.0% depending on the cutoff). Blinder and Krueger (2009/2013), using a household survey, found about a quarter of US jobs offshorable. Jensen and Kletzer (2005) inferred tradability from geographic concentration and classed 100% of US computer and mathematical employment as tradable. Van Welsum and Reif, as summarized by Reinsdorf and Slaughter (2009), used four criteria (ICT-intensive, output sent digitally, codifiable knowledge, no face-to-face contact) and put 18-20% of employment in OECD countries as potentially offshorable, an upper bound.

One lesson carries over directly. These are extensive-margin measures, and Blinder's is explicitly ordinal. Blinder warns his index is neither a probability nor a forecast. Blinder and Krueger find their preferred measures agree only 70-80% of the time and that offshorability is unrelated to wages or layoff probability. This is consistent with, though it does not prove, the working hypothesis that exposure indices do not identify theta_j.

On India, the classic micro studies are about contracting and quality signalling, not labor saved. Banerjee and Duflo (2000) show that contract terms and renegotiated outcomes in 230 Indian software projects vary with firm reputation. Arora and Asundi (1999) find that ISO certification is associated with faster growth among 95 firms, though firms mostly saw it as marketing. The ideas that these features shorten task lengths f_j(h), or that contract mix sets pass-through phi, are hypotheses these papers do not test. Eichengreen and Gupta (2011) give the services-led-growth context. Jensen (2012) shows that BPO job opportunities changed young rural women's schooling, work and marriage decisions, which matters for who bears losses. Nothing found here measures the intensive margin (hours saved net of review) for Indian IT/BPO work. Trade-in-tasks theory (Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg 2008) and several India-specific papers named in the gaps still need to be checked.
verify.dataset_notes: 1) Blinder (2007) index: confirmed public. The appendix table in the CEPS PDF lists every occupation with SOC code, rank, index and employment (817 rows, since some SOC codes are split). 2) Princeton Data Improvement Initiative: the URL is the NBER paper page, not a data page, and access remains unknown. 3) 2000 Census 5% PUMS: the dataset is public, but the URL given is the Jensen-Kletzer paper, not the Census data page, so a primary data URL is still needed. The proposal to replicate the locational Gini on PLFS is unchecked: PLFS records where people live, not clearly where they work, and the district identifiers were not checked against the MoSPI data terms. 4) Banerjee-Duflo project data: 'on-request' is unconfirmed; treat access as unknown. 5) Indian IT firm annual reports/20-F: the URL field is WRONG. It points to the Blinder-Krueger NBER page, which has nothing to do with these filings. Remove it until an actual filing (e.g., Infosys 20-F on SEC EDGAR, TCS annual report on tcs.com) is opened. Whether each firm discloses a fixed-price vs. T&M revenue split was not checked.

missing_streams.name: HCI studies of AI-assisted work: where the time goes, verification behaviour, and over-reliance
missing_streams.why_missing_matters: Three of the four behavioural parameters in theta_j are kappa (speedup when AI assists), rho (review time as a share of h) and q (share of passing output a reviewer accepts). HCI is the field that measures these directly, by logging what people do minute by minute while working with AI. The current map has economics RCTs that report only total time saved, plus benchmarks that report only pass rates. Nothing in it splits a session into writing, waiting, reading and verifying. The over-reliance literature also shows q is not fixed: reviewers accept wrong AI output, more so when they trust the AI. So some 'labor saved' net of review may be quality cost pushed downstream. Perry et al. show this for security bugs, and Lee et al. show verification effort falls as confidence in AI rises. For an AI-safety reader this is the familiar 'scalable oversight' problem, observed in the workplace.
missing_streams.brief: Look for studies that time how long people spend verifying AI output, and how verification effort and accuracy change with trust, task difficulty and explanation cost. Seed works, all opened: (1) Mozannar, Bansal, Fourney, Horvitz, 'Reading Between the Lines: Modeling User Behavior and Costs in AI-Assisted Programming' (arXiv 2210.14306, CHI 2024). It introduces the CUPS taxonomy of programmer states with Copilot, including time spent verifying suggestions, and is the closest existing template for measuring rho and kappa. (2) Barke, James, Polikarpova, 'Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models' (arXiv 2206.15000, 2022). It finds use splits into 'acceleration' mode and 'exploration' mode, which suggests kappa differs by mode. (3) Vasconcelos et al., 'Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making' (arXiv 2212.06823, CSCW 2023). People weigh the cost of verifying against the cost of just relying on the AI, which makes q a choice rather than a constant. (4) Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos, 'To Trust or to Think' (arXiv 2102.09692, 2021; DOI 10.1145/3449287). (5) Bansal et al., 'Does the Whole Exceed its Parts?' (arXiv 2006.14779; submitted to CHI'21): explanations raised acceptance of AI advice whether or not the advice was correct. (6) Lee, Sarkar, Tankelevitch et al., 'The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking' (CHI 2025; 319 knowledge workers): AI shifts effort toward verification and integration. (7) Perry, Srivastava, Kumar, Boneh, 'Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?' (arXiv 2211.03622, CCS 2023). Extract any reported time shares (verification vs. authoring), acceptance rates of correct vs. incorrect suggestions, and how these vary with developer experience.

missing_streams.name: Selective automation, learning to defer, and human-AI triage (operations research, ML, economics)
missing_streams.why_missing_matters: The draft formula max{q*p*(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa} is a routing rule: for each task, hand it to AI or keep the human with AI assistance. This literature works out how to route optimally, and it changes theta_j in two ways. First, routing is done per task instance using an estimate of AI error on that instance, not by task length h alone. If difficulty varies within a given h and that variation can be predicted, the achievable theta is above the h-average the draft integrates. Averaging p(h) before taking the max understates the ceiling. Second, Agarwal et al. find that AI-assisted humans can do worse than either the human or the AI alone, because people underweight the AI's prediction. So kappa (the assistant-mode speedup) could be zero or negative, and the best design is often either/or rather than assisted. Neither point appears in the current map. The nearest item, Huang, Xiao, Vishnoi 'Delegation and Verification under AI', is theory without empirical triage evidence.
missing_streams.brief: Look for (a) learning-to-defer and selective prediction methods, (b) empirical studies of when AI-assisted humans beat or lose to AI alone, and (c) any extension to generative or agentic tasks such as code. Seed works, all opened: (1) Raghu, Blumer, Corrado, Kleinberg, Obermeyer, Mullainathan, 'The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort' (arXiv 1903.12220, 2019). It shows automation gains depend on estimating human and algorithm error per instance. (2) Mozannar & Sontag, 'Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert' (arXiv 2006.01862, ICML 2020). (3) Agarwal, Moehring, Rajpurkar, Salz, 'Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology' (NBER WP 31422, July 2023, revised August 2026). Radiologists underweight AI, and the optimal design routes cases either to the AI or to the human, rarely to an AI-assisted human. Also search for 2024-2026 work on deferral and selective routing for LLM agents (for example, routing coding tasks between an agent and a human, or confidence-based escalation in customer-service bots), and for the operations-research literature on queueing with human review. Specific 2024-2026 titles could not be confirmed here because the web-search budget ran out.

missing_streams.name: Software-engineering research on code review: baseline review cost, defect detection, and review of AI-generated code
missing_streams.why_missing_matters: rho (review time as a share of h) is the parameter the draft is least able to pin down. The 'benchmark-to-reality gap' stream covers acceptance of agent pull requests (Nakashima et al., Pinna et al., METR's merge study) but not the established empirical literature on human code review. That literature says how long review takes per change, what review actually catches, and how review effort grows with change size. A key finding: reviews find fewer defects than developers expect (Bacchelli and Bird). So passing review does not mean correct. That links rho to q and to the downstream quality costs in x1. For the Indian IT case, review and QA are themselves a large share of billed hours in maintenance and testing, so a higher review burden partly offsets the authoring time AI saves within the same w_j.
missing_streams.brief: Collect empirical numbers on review time per change and per line of code, review latency, defect-detection rates, and how they scale with change size, then any 2024-2026 studies of reviewing AI-written code. Seed works, opened: (1) Bacchelli & Bird, 'Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review' (ICSE 2013, Microsoft). Finding defects is the main motive for review, but reviews find fewer defects than expected, and understanding the change is the bottleneck. (2) Sadowski, Soderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli, 'Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google' (ICSE SEIP 2018). It analyzes logs of 9 million reviewed changes and is a candidate source for review-time distributions; the landing page does not give the numbers, so read the paper. (3) Frommgen & Kharatyan, 'Resolving code review comments with ML' (Google Research blog, 23 May 2023). It reports about 60 minutes of active author shepherding time per change, and that 40-50% of previewed ML-suggested edits are applied. Its time saving is a projection, not a measurement. (4) Perry et al. (CCS 2023; see x1) on security defects in AI-assisted code. Also look up Fagan's 1976 IBM Systems Journal paper on code inspections (the classic origin of inspection-rate norms; not opened in this pass), the SmartBear/Cisco review-rate study, and 2025-2026 MSR/ICSE papers on review effort for AI-generated or agentic pull requests.

missing_streams.name: Offshoring and task-trade economics, and the economics of the Indian IT/BPO industry (developing-country evidence)
missing_streams.why_missing_matters: The project studies Indian IT/BPO firms, whose whole business model rests on tasks that are codifiable, modular and deliverable remotely. Those are the traits the offshorability literature measured, and they overlap heavily with AI exposure. The map has Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg's theory of task trade but none of the empirical offshorability measures, and nothing on how Indian IT work is organized and priced. Both matter for the parameters. First, offshore work is broken into ticketed, specified units, which pushes f_j(h) toward short h, where AI pass rates p(h,t) are highest. Second, contract structure (time-and-materials vs. fixed-price) largely decides pass-through phi. Third, the long-run substitution story, AI vs. Indian labor, is Blinder's offshoring question with a machine as the low-cost supplier. Developing-country evidence is also thin: the map has World Bank and ILO reports but little peer-reviewed micro evidence on Indian IT/BPO labor markets.
missing_streams.brief: Seed works, opened: (1) Blinder, 'How Many U.S. Jobs Might Be Offshorable?' (Princeton CEPS WP 142, March 2007). It ranks more than 800 occupations by how offshorable they are and estimates 22-29% of US jobs are potentially offshorable. (2) Blinder & Krueger, 'Alternative Measures of Offshorability: A Survey Approach' (NBER WP 15287, Aug 2009; published in the Journal of Labor Economics, though the published version was not opened here). About 25% of US jobs are offshorable. Both are direct ancestors of task-exposure indices. (3) Arora, Arunachalam, Asundi, Fernandes, 'The Indian software services industry' (Research Policy 30(8):1267-1287, 2001). It describes how Indian firms specialized in low-risk, well-specified tasks under particular contract types; the full text is paywalled and only the bibliographic record was opened. (4) Jensen, 'Do Labor Market Opportunities Affect Young Women's Work and Family Decisions? Experimental Evidence from India' (QJE 127(2):753-792, 2012). It is a randomized BPO-recruitment experiment showing how BPO jobs change labor supply, schooling and marriage in rural India, which matters for who loses if BPO employment shrinks. Also look for: Jensen & Kletzer on tradable services (Brookings Trade Forum 2005); Eichengreen & Gupta on India's services-led growth; work on IT-services contract types and pricing; and an IMF working paper, recalled but NOT confirmed here, 'AI and Services-Led Growth: Evidence from Indian Job Adverts' (Copestake, Marczinek, Pople, Stapleton, around 2023). Verify it before citing.

This is the founding paper of the task approach, and the 'Task-based theory' stream skips it. URL opened: https://www.nber.org/papers/w8337

Agarwal, Moehring, Rajpurkar, Salz, 'Combining Human Expertise with Artificial Intelligence: Experimental Evidence from Radiology', NBER WP 31422 (July 2023, revised August 2026). URL opened: https://www.nber.org/papers/w31422

completeness_critic.notes:
How this was checked: the shared web-search budget was already used up when this agent started (the first WebSearch call was refused). Every work named above was therefore confirmed by opening its landing page with WebFetch, not from search snippets. Pages opened: arxiv.org/abs/2210.14306, nber.org/papers/w31422, arxiv.org/abs/2206.15000, arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622, arxiv.org/abs/2006.01862, nber.org/papers/w15287, the Microsoft Research page for Bacchelli & Bird 2013, research.google/pubs/modern-code-review-a-case-study-at-google/, academic.oup.com/qje/article/127/2/753/1826429 (Jensen 2012, abstract only), arxiv.org/abs/2212.06823, the Microsoft Research page for Lee et al. CHI 2025, arxiv.org/abs/2006.14779, arxiv.org/abs/1903.12220, ideas.repec.org/a/eee/respol/v30y2001i8p1267-1287.html (Arora et al. 2001, bibliographic record only), princeton.edu/~ceps/workingpapers/142blinder.pdf (first page extracted from the PDF), research.google/blog/resolving-code-review-comments-with-ml/, arxiv.org/abs/2102.09692.

Not confirmed: Copestake et al., IMF 'AI and Services-Led Growth: Evidence from Indian Job Adverts' (a guessed IMF URL returned 404). Also not opened: Frey & Osborne (2017), Fagan (1976), Jensen & Kletzer (2005), Eichengreen & Gupta, and the published JOLE version of Blinder & Krueger. Treat all of these as leads to verify before citing. Frey & Osborne, 'The future of employment' (Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 2017), is another classic missing from the exposure stream, but it was not checked this session.

Note on the working hypothesis: it largely holds, but it should be stated carefully. The map already contains some intensive-margin work: Svanberg et al. on cost-effective automation, Tamkin & McCrory on time savings per conversation, and Merali on how productivity scales with model capability. What is genuinely missing is the measurement of net-of-review labor saving (streams x1 and x3) and of routing (x2).

A substantive point for the recipe, from x2: the draft takes the max{delegate, assist} at each task length h after averaging p over all tasks of that length. If AI success varies predictably within a given h, routing each task instance separately gives a higher theta, because the average of a max is at least the max of the averages. The recipe should either justify routing on h alone or model the spread of difficulty within each h. Agarwal et al. also suggest kappa can be at or below zero for some tasks.

Duplicates noticed across the streams provided: METR's merge-rate note, GDPval, and Tamkin & McCrory each appear in 5-7 streams. Organizers may want to de-duplicate so the map does not overstate how much evidence there is.

skeptic.lens_summary:
Skeptic lens. I tried to refute the claim that "the intensive margin is under-measured", and it is mostly refuted in its broad form. Many studies measure how much labor AI removes per task.
- Experiments and RCTs: Noy-Zhang 37-40%, Peng 55.8%, Dell'Acqua 22-28%, Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond about 8-13%, Alibaba 4% of chat time at full use, METR -19% and then +4 to 18%.
- Field throughput studies: Cui et al. +26% PRs; Microsoft's agentic rollout +24% merged PRs.
- Usage-based estimates: Anthropic's roughly 80% gross saving. Its January 2026 report adjusts for task success and links success to task length.
- Survey series: Bick-Blandin-Deming find about 0.35 hours saved per assisted hour; Humlum-Vestergaard find about 3% of hours.
- Workflow calculations that net out review and redo: GDPval, where 90x falls to 1.12-1.39x.
- Capability slopes: Merali within one design, GDPval across model generations.
- Macro plug-ins: Acemoglu's 27%. Firm case disclosures: Infosys 60% and 18%, TCS 25-30% targets.

Even 'net of review' and 'net of failure' are partly measured: GDPval's monitored 109-minute review, METR's 9% review share and fix-time estimates, the CUPS study's 22.4% of time spent verifying, METR's maintainer merge test, and Anthropic's success adjustment. The exposure literature (Eloundou et al.) does stay on the extensive margin, but the hypothesis that 'nobody measures the intensive margin' is false.

What survives is narrower, and I think it is real. No study measures the integrand jointly on one task population: p, q, rho and kappa together, stratified by task length h, for delegated agentic work, and tracked against a capability index. Review cost rho as a function of h, and acceptance q for agents that iterate on enterprise code, are essentially unmeasured. Task types other than coding (testing, IT operations, BPO back-office) and Indian delivery settings have no net intensive-margin measurements. Hours-weighted f_j(h) and w_j for Indian service lines are absent; the public proxies are Jira effort logs, SWE-bench difficulty labels, Hatgis-Kessell et al. and the Anthropic Economic Index histograms. Downstream rework is documented but never converted into hours.

Process note: the shared web-search budget ran out (limit hit on my first query), so I could not search for new 2026 work. I relied on the verified digest and opened two primary pages directly by URL:
- https://metr.org/notes/2026-02-17-exploratory-transcript-analysis-for-estimating-time-savings-from-coding-agents/ (Amy Deng, Feb 2026). On 5,305 Claude Code transcripts from 7 staff, it finds a 1.5x-13x time-savings factor, called a 'soft upper bound'. Human review time is not explicitly netted out.
- https://metr.org/notes/2026-01-22-time-horizon-limitations/ (Kwa, Jan 2026). It says converting horizons to speedup needs data on time spent 'prompting AIs, waiting for generations, checking AI output', which requires 'Cursor logs or screen recordings'.

Absence claims below should therefore read as 'not found in the digest plus direct fetches', not as proof that nothing exists.

gaps.title: No joint measurement of the whole integrand on one task population, by task length
gaps.plain_explanation: The draft formula needs, for the same tasks: the chance AI output passes (p), the share of passing output a reviewer accepts (q), review time as a share of the task (rho), and the speedup when AI only assists (kappa). Each is measured somewhere, but always on different tasks, models and populations, and almost never broken down by how long the task takes a human (h). Combining parameters from different studies assumes they are independent and comparable, which nobody has checked.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval (Patwardhan et al. 2025, arXiv 2510.04374) combines a win rate (a stand-in for q*p), monitored review time (109 of 404 min) and full redo on failure into a net speedup (GPT-5: 1.12x try once, 1.39x try n). The Anthropic Economic Index 'Economic primitives' report (Jan 2026) gives success as a function of estimated human hours (50% at about 3.5 h on the API). METR (Whitfill et al., Mar 2026) gives q of about 0.5 on SWE-bench-passing PRs.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: GDPval reports no breakdown by h, has no assistant (kappa) branch, uses grading time rather than production review, and covers only OpenAI models on one-shot deliverables with few software tasks. In the Anthropic data, both success and time are judged by Claude, the tasks are ones users chose, and there is no rho or q. METR's q comes from 3 Python repos with one-shot agents and no review-time results, even though review times were collected.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j integrates max{q p(h)(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa} over f_j(h). If q and rho vary with h, and the GDPval-style collapse from 90x to 1.4x depends on task length, then multiplying constants taken from different studies can misstate theta_j by a factor of 2 or more. The 7x horizon shrink under maintainer review suggests q depends on h.
gaps.survived_refutation: I checked GDPval, the Anthropic Jan 2026 primitives report, METR's maintainer note and Rein (2025) fix-time estimates, the CUPS study, METR's RCT and Feb 2026 update, and the METR transcript note (fetched directly). Each measures one or two pieces. None measures p, q, rho and kappa on the same tasks stratified by h.
