The METR time-horizon limitations note (fetched) says explicitly that this conversion needs data on prompting, waiting and checking time that METR does not have.

gaps.title: Review/verification cost rho as a function of task length, for production review
gaps.plain_explanation: We do not know how much reviewer time a piece of AI output costs, relative to doing the work by hand, as the task gets longer. The few numbers come from very different settings: seconds-long autocomplete suggestions, a grader's time on 7-hour deliverables, and fix-time guesses for 4 pull requests.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval's monitored expert grading time (109/404 min, rho about 0.27); CUPS (Mozannar et al., CHI 2024): 22.4% of session time verifying on about 12-minute tasks; METR RCT (2025): about 9% of AI-allowed time reviewing and cleaning output (44-issue subset); Rein (METR, Aug 2025): estimated fix time about one-third of h, based on n=4 passing PRs; Google (Sadowski et al. 2018): baseline of 3.2 h/week of review on human code; Faros telemetry: elapsed review time rising with adoption.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: There is no curve of rho against h. Most figures are shares of time spent with AI, not of human-only time h. GDPval's figure is grading time on pairwise comparisons. METR's maintainer study recorded review time and from-scratch time but did not publish them. Agent-PR studies (AIDev, Watanabe et al.) report elapsed time to merge, not reviewer effort. Theory (Demirer et al. 2026) suggests a fixed cost per verified chunk rather than a cost proportional to h, but this has not been tested.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: rho enters theta_j linearly and directly. At rho of about 0.27, a model that passes 50% of tasks with q=0.5 saves almost nothing on delegated work. Whether rho rises, falls or stays flat with h decides whether long tasks are ever worth delegating.
gaps.survived_refutation: The digest covers GDPval, CUPS, METR's RCT and fix-time note, the AIDev and Watanabe merge-latency studies, Faros and Cihan et al. All of them measure either a single point, an elapsed time, or a share of AI-session time. The METR transcript note (fetched) counts only 10-minute windows with typed messages, so silent review is not measured. No source gives reviewer effort hours plotted against task length.

gaps.title: Acceptance q for agents that iterate, on enterprise or client-style code, and how it changes over time
gaps.plain_explanation: The q of about 0.5 comes from agents that got one attempt, with no feedback, on three strict open-source Python projects, using models up to Sonnet 4.5. Real delivery work lets agents revise after review, on client codebases with different quality standards. Nobody has measured acceptance under those conditions, or how it is changing as models improve.
gaps.closest_existing_work: METR (Whitfill, Wu, Becker, Rush, Mar 2026): 24.2 pp normalized gap between test-pass and merge rates, and a weak 9.6 pp/yr trend (falling to 4.1 pp/yr, SE 12.1, with state-of-the-art models only). AIDev and Nakashima et al. (2026): deployed agent PR merge rates of 55-86% against 82.6% for humans. Pinna et al. (2026): merge rates by task type.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: METR's numbers are one-shot and lower bounds. Deployment merge rates are not conditioned on passing tests or on task length, are shaped by which tasks people choose to delegate and by self-merging, and come from open-source repos. Nothing covers enterprise or offshore maintenance repos or 2026 frontier agents.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: q multiplies p in the delegate branch. Values between 0.5 and 0.9 move theta for delegated tasks by up to about 2x, and whether q rises more slowly than p decides how theta_j(t) grows.
gaps.survived_refutation: Candidates checked were METR's maintainer note, AIDev v5 (7.69M PRs), Nakashima and Pinna, Watanabe et al., and Google's ML-edit apply rates. Deployment data exist and are public, so a q(h,t) estimate could be built from AIDev. But no published study conditions on test-passing and task length with iterating agents, so the gap survives as unestimated rather than unmeasurable.

gaps.title: Net intensive margin indexed to a capability measure (theta as a function of t)
gaps.plain_explanation: Several studies show time savings rising with newer models. But none links measured, review-net labor savings on a fixed task set to a capability index such as METR's time horizon. So the slope of theta_j(t) is extrapolated rather than measured.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Merali (arXiv 2409.02391; 2512.21316): randomized over 13 LLMs, about 12% faster per 10x compute in translation and about 8%/yr less task time in consulting and analysis, with smaller gains on agentic workflows. GDPval: try-n speedup rises from 0.46x (GPT-4o) to 1.39x (GPT-5), across models but not experimentally. METR RCT repeated: -19% then +4 to 18%, with selection problems. RealHumanEval: benchmark gains translate less than one-for-one into user time saved. The Bick-Blandin-Deming quarterly series: self-reported saving per assisted hour flat at about 0.35.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Merali is assistant mode on short non-IT tasks, indexed to compute rather than a horizon. GDPval covers few models, OpenAI only, with no breakdown by h. METR's repeat is unreliable by METR's own account. RPS is self-reported, top-coded and gross. None jointly maps net savings onto p(h,t) for software or BPO tasks.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: The recipe derives theta_j(t) from METR's p(h,t) trend (50% horizon doubling about every 129 days). If net savings rise more slowly than p, because q and rho lag (as Merali's agentic finding and METR's q trend hint), then the bottom-up S(t) will overshoot.
gaps.survived_refutation: This is the weakest surviving gap, because Merali and GDPval do give capability slopes for the intensive margin. It survives only in its specific form: a review-net theta for IT task types tied to a horizon-type capability index. I could not search for 2026 follow-ups because the search budget ran out.

gaps.title: No net intensive-margin measurement for non-coding IT-services task types or Indian delivery settings
gaps.plain_explanation: Almost all measured savings are for writing or changing code, short writing tasks, or chat support. Testing, infrastructure and IT operations (incident triage, patching), application maintenance on legacy client systems, and BPO back-office transactions (claims, invoices, KYC) have no measured time-saved figures net of review. Nothing is measured inside TCS, Infosys, Wipro or HCLTech teams.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (QJE 2025; Philippine chat support, assistant mode, about 8-13% time saved); Alibaba RCT (arXiv 2603.29888; 4% of chat time at full use, new agents only); Cui et al. (Accenture Southeast Asia, Copilot, +26% PRs pooled); TheAgentCompany (p by role, no human times); METR computer-use horizons 40-100x shorter; ICRIER 2026 survey (direction of change only, 651 respondents); Infosys and TCS case claims (60%, 18%, 25-30% targets); Stanford talk (brownfield/legacy about 0-7%).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The chat studies are assistant mode with 2020-24 models. The firm claims are selected showcase cases or targets, with no portfolio average and no review netting. ICRIER reports no magnitudes. TheAgentCompany has no human time baselines. No study measures delegated agentic work in BPO with review time recorded.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j for j = testing, infrastructure, BPO and maintenance cannot be borrowed from coding results. Computer-use p is far lower, and the legacy-language results point to near-zero gains. These lines carry a large share of w_j in Indian IT (application managed services alone is 22-45% of revenue by press estimates).
gaps.survived_refutation: Checked the digest streams s02, s03, s10 and s11 (customer service, Alibaba, Accenture, WDR Table 4.1, ICRIER, firm transcripts, Cognizant). None gives a review-net time saved for testing, IT operations or back-office BPO, or for an Indian delivery team. Firm disclosures exist but are selected cases, which matches the 'firm-level effort-reduction disclosures' the brief asked me to check.

gaps.title: Hours-weighted task-length distributions f_j(h) and time weights w_j for Indian IT service lines
gaps.plain_explanation: To add up savings across tasks you need to know how working hours in each service line split across short and long tasks, and across service lines. Public proxies exist for US or open-source work, but none for Indian delivery work. Analysts use revenue shares instead of hours.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Montgomery et al. (MSR'22) Jira dataset (2.7M issues with timespent) and JOSSE effort data; SWE-bench Verified difficulty buckets (39% <15 min, 52% 15-60 min); Hatgis-Kessell et al. (arXiv 2608.05172), per-instance durations for about 18,000 O*NET tasks; Anthropic Economic Index human_only_time histograms per O*NET task; GDPval and RLI human times; Brynjolfsson et al. 40-minute chats; Jefferies/ICICI/HCLTech revenue splits.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The Jira data are sparse, selective open-source effort logs. The Anthropic histograms count conversations users chose to bring, not hours of work. Hatgis-Kessell uses LLM-estimated durations on US O*NET. None reflects the client-ticket mix, the onsite/offshore split or legacy maintenance in Indian firms. Revenue shares differ from hours shares.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j is an integral over f_j(h). With p logistic in log h, moving hours mass between 15-minute and 8-hour tasks can change theta_j several-fold. w_j weights the sum S = sum w_j theta_j.
gaps.survived_refutation: Strictly this is a data gap, not an intensive-margin gap, but it is a binding input. Public proxies were found and should be used as priors (they refute 'no f(h) data exist anywhere'). None is specific to IT services or India, and ITSM ticket data are held by firms.

gaps.title: Downstream rework and quality cost not converted into labor hours
gaps.plain_explanation: Time saved today may be partly paid back later as bug fixing, incidents or technical debt, or as rework pushed onto colleagues. Studies document these effects but none puts them in hours per unit of accepted output, so 'net' savings are net of review at most, never of later rework.
gaps.closest_existing_work: He et al. (MSR'26) Cursor study: persistent complexity about +9% net of codebase growth; Faros Q2 2026: bugs per PR +28.7%, incidents per PR +242.7% (correlational); Perry et al. (CCS'23): more insecure code; BetterUp/Stanford 'workslop' survey (about 2 h per incident, self-reported); DORA (lower stability).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The evidence is correlational or self-reported, measured in proxy units (static-analysis warnings, incidents, elapsed time), with no conversion into maintenance labor hours and no client-delivery setting.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j is meant to be net of failure and review. If AI-written code raises later maintenance labor, net theta_dev is overstated and w_maintenance rises later. This matters especially for Indian application managed services, which inherit code that others wrote.
gaps.survived_refutation: I checked the CMU Cursor panel, Faros, DORA, Perry et al., Watanabe et al. (revision rates similar to humans) and workslop. All document the direction but give no hours figure, and the Watanabe result shows that a simple 'AI PRs need more fixes' claim does not hold. The gap survives as unquantified rather than unrecognized.

refuted_gaps: REFUTED: 'Nobody measures how much labor AI removes per task (intensive margin)'. Filled by RCTs and field studies: Noy & Zhang 2023 (37-40% time saved on writing); Peng et al. 2023 (55.8% faster, greenfield code); Dell'Acqua et al. (22-28% less time inside the frontier); Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond QJE 2025 (+15% resolutions/hr, -8.5% handle time); Alibaba RCT arXiv 2603.29888 (-32% on the diagnosis step, -4% of chat time at full use); Google RCT arXiv 2410.12944 (about 21% faster, CI includes 0); Cui et al. (+26% PRs); METR RCT arXiv 2507.09089 (-19%); Dillon et al. (17% less email time); Lukac et al. NEJM AI (scribes -9.5% ITT).

REFUTED: 'The intensive margin is not estimated at scale'. Filled by Tamkin & McCrory (Anthropic, Nov 2025; about 80% gross saving across 100k conversations, with O*NET aggregation and JIRA validation); Bick-Blandin-Deming RPS on FRED (RPSGENAITSALL; about 0.35 hours saved per assisted hour, quarterly 2024Q4-2026Q3); Humlum & Vestergaard NBER w33777 (2.8% of users' hours, 6-7% on usage days); METR transcript note (Deng, Feb 17 2026, fetched: 1.5x-13x time-savings factor, a 'soft upper bound').

REFUTED: 'Nobody nets savings for failure or success probability'. Filled by Anthropic Economic Index 'Economic primitives' (Jan 15 2026: success-adjusted uplift falls from 1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr); GDPval try-1x and try-n workflows (redo on failure); Remote Labor Index (2.5% automation rate under client acceptance, 21% on the Oct 2026 leaderboard).

PARTLY REFUTED: 'Nobody nets out review/verification time'. GDPval measures expert review time with monitoring software (109 of 404 min); METR RCT time breakdown (about 9% review/cleanup, 4% waiting; the public repo has post-review implementation times); CUPS (Mozannar et al. CHI 2024: 22.4% verifying, 34.3% verifying plus editing); Rein, METR Aug 2025 (fix time about one-third of h for passing PRs). What survives is rho as a function of h for production review (G2).

REFUTED: 'Nobody links AI success to task length outside benchmarks'. Anthropic Jan 2026 primitives give success by estimated human hours on real API traffic (about 60% for sub-hour tasks, about 45% at 5+ h, 50% at about 3.5 h). The caveat is that both success and time are judged by the model.

REFUTED: 'Nobody measures how savings change with capability'. Merali arXiv 2409.02391 and 2512.21316 randomize 13 LLMs (12% faster per 10x compute; about 8%/yr less task time). GDPval speedups rise across model generations (0.46x to 1.39x). METR re-ran its RCT (Feb 2026 update). RealHumanEval arXiv 2404.02806 relates benchmark gains to user time. The narrower horizon-indexed version survives as G4.

REFUTED: 'The acceptance rate q is unmeasured'. METR (Whitfill et al., Mar 2026; about half of passing PRs not mergeable, 24.2 pp normalized gap); AIDev arXiv 2507.15003 plus HF dataset v5; Nakashima et al. arXiv 2602.04226; Pinna et al. arXiv 2602.08915; Watanabe et al. arXiv 2509.14745. The narrower q(h,t) for iterating agents on enterprise code survives as G3.

REFUTED: 'Delegated or agentic mode has no field evidence'. Murphy-Hill et al. arXiv 2607.01418 (Microsoft, +24% merged PRs per engineer after Claude Code and Copilot CLI, synthetic control); METR transcript note (Feb 2026); the Anthropic internal study (0-20% of work fully delegable for more than half of respondents).

REFUTED: 'Macro work has no intensive-margin number'. Acemoglu (Economic Policy 2025) uses a 27% labor cost saving (36% with Peng); the OECD (Filippucci et al., IPM 2025) uses 30%; PWBM assumes 25% rising to 40%; Aghion-Bunel use 27-40%. These are plugged-in experimental values, so the macro literature is evidence of reliance on external intensive-margin estimates, not of their absence.

REFUTED: 'Firms disclose nothing on effort reduction'. Infosys Q4 FY26 (Hertz COBOL migration 60% lower cost and timeline; BP 18% IT-ops efficiency); TCS Q2 FY27 (25-30% faster S/4HANA target; 2x HR-ops efficiency target); Cognizant CEO, Feb 2025 (17-34% developer productivity); HCLTech Q4 FY26 (3-5%/yr shrink of the at-risk 40% of spend). These are selected cases rather than portfolio averages, so they feed G5 rather than filling it.

PARTLY REFUTED: 'The exposure literature is purely extensive'. Eloundou E1 is a binned intensive threshold (at least 50% time saved, believed rather than measured); ILO WP140 gives continuous 0-1 task scores; Hatgis-Kessell et al. arXiv 2608.05172 weight tasks by time. The core point still holds: no exposure index measures review-net time saved.

PARTLY REFUTED: 'No public task-length data exist'. Montgomery et al. Jira dataset (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5882881), JOSSE (Zenodo 7022735), SWE-bench Verified difficulty labels (HF princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified), METR task_results_1_1.yaml, Anthropic EconomicIndex human_only_time histograms (Jan and Mar 2026 releases). The India and IT-services-specific hours-weighted version survives as G6.

measurement.lens_summary:
Measurement lens. For each parameter I asked three questions: is there a credible estimate, is it from 2025-26 agentic tools or from 2023-24 assistant/autocomplete tools, and is it measured in a setting like Indian IT services or BPO?

**Coverage of what I could check.** The shared web-search budget was exhausted before my first query. I could not run new searches. I opened two primary pages directly:
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05352 (ITBench, IBM/UIUC, Feb 2025): 94 IT-automation scenarios. Agents resolve 13.8% of SRE, 25.2% of CISO and 0% of FinOps scenarios. No human completion times are reported.
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045 (tau-bench, Yao et al., Jun 2024): simulated customer-service agent conversations with a pass^k reliability metric (gpt-4o pass^8 below 25% in retail). No human time baselines.

Everything else rests on the verifier-corrected digest. Absence claims below mean "not found in the digest plus these two fetches". They do not mean "does not exist". A follow-up search pass is recommended, especially for 2026 work on reviewer effort for agent PRs and for BPO agent field trials.

**Status by parameter:**
- **p(h,t):** the best-measured parameter. METR TH1.1 is agentic and current to April 2026, but covers software, ML and cyber tasks only. Its h is contractor time. Its high-reliability tail is poorly identified.
- **q:** a single credible source (METR, March 2026, about 0.5). It is one-shot, covers 3 Python OSS repositories, uses models up to Sonnet 4.5/GPT-5, and appears to depend on h, so a single scalar is the wrong form.
- **rho:** no direct measurement of reviewer effort hours on agentic output as a function of h. The available numbers are GDPval grading time, n=4 estimated fix times, assistant-mode screen shares, or elapsed latency.
- **kappa:** every clean estimate is pre-agent (2020-24 assistants and autocomplete), or comes from early-2025 tools where the AI-allowed arm mixes modes. The late-2025 RCT broke down because developers withheld tasks.
- **f_j(h) and w_j:** essentially unmeasured for Indian IT or BPO. Only US or OSS proxies, LLM-estimated proxies, and revenue-share proxies exist.
- **theta_j directly:** gross, model-estimated values (Anthropic, about 80%), net benchmark workflow values (GDPval, about 11-28%), and selected firm showcase cases. No net, audited, service-line-level measure exists to validate against.

**Verdict on the working hypothesis.** It survives in refined form. Intensive-margin numbers do exist. What does not exist is a measurement that is net of review, failure and AI cost, resolved by task length, indexed to capability, and set in IT-services or BPO task mixes.

gaps.title: No hours-weighted task-length distribution f_j(h) for any Indian IT or BPO service line
gaps.plain_explanation: The recipe needs, for each service line (maintenance, testing, development, infrastructure, BPO, consulting), the share of labour hours spent on tasks of each length h. Nobody has measured this for Indian delivery work. Existing length data are counts of conversations, tickets or projects, not hours. They come from US, open-source or freelance settings, and lengths are often guessed by an LLM or an annotator.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Anthropic Economic Index Jan/Mar 2026 HF releases: per-O*NET-task human_only_time histograms, Claude-estimated, conversation-weighted, units not stated. SWE-bench Verified difficulty buckets: 39% under 15 min, 52% 15-60 min, 8% 1-4 h (annotator estimates, OSS bug fixes). Public Jira Dataset (Montgomery et al. 2022) and JOSSE: logged OSS timespent. RLI: 240 projects, median 11.5 h, only 10 public, creative-heavy. Hatgis-Kessell et al. 2026: LLM-estimated per-instance durations for about 18k US O*NET tasks. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond: about 40-minute mean chat. Alibaba: 466 s chat with a 36 s diagnosis step.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: None of these is hours-weighted over a firm's actual workload. Anthropic's histograms are selected on tasks users chose to bring to Claude. Claude's time estimates are compressed: it overestimates short tasks and underestimates long ones (Spearman 0.44 on JIRA). SWE-bench buckets are optimistic annotator guesses for small fixes. OSS time logging is sparse and selective. Nothing covers testing cycles, infrastructure tickets, AMS incident queues or BPO transactions in Indian client delivery.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j is an integral of the delegation payoff over f_j(h). METR's fitted slope is shallow (roughly 0.6-0.95 per log unit of h), so p falls slowly with h. That means where the mass of hours sits, especially the long tail, largely sets theta_j. Two service lines with the same mean ticket length but different tails can have very different theta_j. Alibaba shows the point: a 32% cut on a sub-step became a 4% cut on the whole chat.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked all f_j entries in streams s01, s06, s10, s12, s13 and x3. Also fetched ITBench and tau-bench; neither reports human task times.

gaps.title: Task length h is measured on the wrong human: METR h is low-context contractor time
gaps.plain_explanation: METR measures task length as how long skilled outside contractors take. On internal PRs, repository maintainers were 5-18x faster than contractors. Indian IT staff working on long-running client accounts fall somewhere in between. No one has estimated the right conversion for them. The same task can look like a 4-hour task (low success) or a 20-minute task (high success) depending on whose clock is used.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Kwa et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.14499): contractors took 5-18x longer than maintainers. AI performance looked consistent with contractor time. Anthropic JIRA validation shows LLM time estimates are compressed. Whitfill et al. 2026: Sonnet 4.5's horizon is about 50 min under the grader vs about 8 min under maintainer review.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The 5-18x figure is one internal comparison on METR's own PRs. There is no estimate of the h-mapping for vendor staff with intermediate context on client codebases, nor for BPO process work.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Plugging Indian-firm f_j(h) (measured in staff hours) into METR's p(h,t) (measured in contractor hours) without a context adjustment can shift every h-bin's p by a large factor. At the frontier that is equivalent to shifting t by more than a year.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Searched the s04, s12 and s13 records; only the METR internal-PR comparison exists.

gaps.title: No capability curve p(h,t) with human time baselines for testing, IT operations or BPO work
gaps.plain_explanation: METR's time-horizon curves cover software, ML and cyber tasks. For computer-use tasks, the closest proxy for BPO and IT operations, horizons are 40-100x shorter. Benchmarks for IT operations and customer-service agents exist and report success rates, but they never record how long a human takes. So they cannot be placed on the h axis.
gaps.closest_existing_work: METR TH1.1 YAML (228 tasks, software/ML/cyber). Kwa & Cheng 2025: visual computer use 40-100x lower horizons. OSWorld: 369 tasks, humans 72.36%, best model 12.24% in 2024. TheAgentCompany: per-role success, no human times. ITBench (opened): SRE 13.8%, CISO 25.2%, FinOps 0%, no human times. tau-bench (opened): retail customer-service agents, pass^8 below 25% for gpt-4o, no human times. Anthropic Jan 2026: API success-by-length curve, about 60% under 1 h falling to about 45% at 5+ h.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No IT-ops, test-writing or BPO-transaction benchmark pairs agent success with human completion times. The Anthropic usage curve is model-judged, selected by users and not split by service line. Software-maintenance p cannot simply be reused for BPO or infrastructure.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Testing, infrastructure and BPO are probably most of Indian IT/BPO headcount. Without a domain-specific p_j(h,t), theta for those lines is extrapolated from coding curves, possibly off by 1-2 orders of magnitude in horizon.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Fetched ITBench and tau-bench abstracts directly; both lack human baselines. TheAgentCompany and OSWorld records in the digest confirm the same.

gaps.title: The high-reliability tail of p(h,t) and its slope are poorly identified
gaps.plain_explanation: Full delegation needs an AI that succeeds 90-99% of the time. Benchmarks pin down the 50% point reasonably well. They pin down the 80% point badly: across reasonable fitting methods it moves by up to 2x. The 99% point cannot be measured with current task suites. Whether the curve is logistic or constant-hazard changes the 99% horizon by about 3x.
gaps.closest_existing_work: METR TH1.1 p50/p80 by model: the p50/p80 ratio is 2.3-10.3x, mostly 4-6x. Barry (METR, Mar 2026): reasonable fits move p80 by up to 2x and p50 by up to 35%, and noise on short tasks flattens slopes. Ord 2025: constant hazard implies T99 ≈ T50/70. Kwa (METR, Jan 2026): 99% horizons would need about 300 diverse tasks per time bucket.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No 90/95/99% horizons are published. Per-model slopes must be backed out from p50/p80. Horizons above 16 h are officially unreliable, and the dashboard was frozen in September 2026.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Through q and the max{} kink, the delegate branch only pays off where q·p is high. That high-p region is exactly the poorly identified part of the curve. theta_j is therefore sensitive to an untested choice of curve shape.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Based on the verified Barry, Ord and Kwa notes and the TH1.1 YAML.

gaps.title: Reviewer acceptance q comes from one small, one-shot, pre-2026 study, and appears to depend on h
gaps.plain_explanation: q, the share of test-passing AI output a reviewer would accept, comes almost entirely from one METR note. Four maintainers judged one-shot patches from three Python open-source repositories, with models no newer than GPT-5 and Sonnet 4.5. Agents could not revise after feedback. The same note implies acceptance falls with task length: the horizon shrinks about 7x under the maintainer standard. So a constant q = 0.5 is the wrong form. Deployment merge rates exist but are not conditioned on passing tests or on task length.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Whitfill et al. (METR, Mar 2026): normalized gap 24.2 pp, roughly half of passing PRs not mergeable; 50 to 8 min horizon. Rein (METR, Aug 2025): 0 of 15 reviewed PRs mergeable as-is. AIDev / Nakashima et al.: agent PR acceptance 55-86% vs human 82.6%. Pinna et al.: docs 82.1%, features 66.1%. Watanabe et al.: Claude Code PRs merged 83.8% vs 91.0%. GDPval win rate as a q·p proxy. RLI client acceptance about 2.5% (late-2025 agents).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No frontier 2026 models are covered, and no agent-plus-feedback loop. There is no conditioning on passing checks in deployment data, and no enterprise or client acceptance standard. Nothing covers testing artefacts, infrastructure changes or BPO outputs. The trend in q relative to p is significant only at the 10% level, and is not significant for state-of-the-art models alone.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: q multiplies the whole delegate branch. Moving q from 0.5 to 0.8, or treating it as a 7x horizon shift rather than a multiplier, can change theta_j by tens of percentage points at current horizons.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s03, s04, s05, s12, s13 and x3. AIDev and related data refine but do not fill the gap, because they are not conditioned on test-passing or h.

gaps.title: No direct measurement of reviewer effort rho (hours, as a share of h) on agentic output across task lengths
gaps.plain_explanation: rho is how much human review and clean-up time AI output costs, as a share of the task's human length. The available numbers are grading time in a benchmark, estimated fix times on 4 PRs, screen-recording shares in assistant mode, or calendar time to merge, which is not hours of effort. METR collected maintainer review times in its 2026 study but did not publish them. No one has measured how review time scales with h, or whether it behaves like a fixed cost per change plus a per-line cost.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval: 109 min grading on 404-min tasks (rho ≈ 0.27; measured grading time; OpenAI models; one-shot deliverables). Rein 2025: about 26 min estimated fix on 1.3 h tasks (n=4). METR early-2025 RCT: about 9% of AI-allowed time reviewing and cleaning (44 issues, assistant mode). CUPS (Mozannar et al.): 22.4% of session time verifying in 12-min Copilot sessions (2022 tools). Google human-code baseline: 3.2 h/week, roughly 45-50 reviewer-min per 24-line change (derived). Faros, AIDev, Watanabe: elapsed latency only. Cihan et al.: closure time 5.9 h to 8.3 h after adopting an AI reviewer.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Only GDPval measures review time in hours on substantial tasks, and that is benchmark grading, not production review. All software figures are pre-agent or early 2025. None is from IT-services delivery, where reviewers often work on unfamiliar client code (Czerwonka: reviews of unfamiliar code are much less useful). None varies h. Agent PRs are about 2x larger than human PRs (Watanabe), so per-change review cost may grow.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: rho is subtracted one-for-one from the delegate payoff. Moving rho from about 0.1 to about 0.3 can erase the delegate branch at mid-range p. If rho is mostly fixed per change, short tasks lose most and the shape of theta over h changes.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s05 and x3 (code-review literature) and x1 (HCI). The METR note confirms review times were collected but not reported.

gaps.title: No q or rho for non-code BPO and back-office outputs (tickets, documents, reconciliations, KYC, claims)
gaps.plain_explanation: BPO work produces documents, ticket resolutions and data entries, not code. No study measures how often such AI output is accepted, or how long checking and fixing it takes. The closest evidence is a self-report survey about low-quality AI work passed to colleagues, and a radiology calibration of a theory model.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Workslop survey (BetterUp/Stanford, HBR 2025): 1,150 US desk workers, 40% received workslop, about 2 h per incident, self-reported. Huang, Xiao & Vishnoi (ICML 2026): verification-cost model calibrated on one radiologist. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond: 35-38% suggestion adherence (2020-21 assistant). Alibaba: Qwen assistant for new agents, opening stage only. Lukac et al. AI scribes: 9.5% ITT at about 30% usage. RLI failure modes: poor quality 45.6%, incomplete 35.7%.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: There is no randomized or logged measurement of delegated (not assisted) BPO work with review time recorded separately. Nothing is India-based. The scribe and assistant studies measure assistant mode and mix in partial adoption.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: BPO is a service line in its own right, with possibly the highest exposure (IMF Philippines; SADU call-centre postings -24%). Without q_BPO and rho_BPO, theta_BPO must be borrowed from code or customer-support assistance numbers.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s02, s05, s10 and x2. tau-bench (opened) measures agent task success in simulated customer service, but has no human acceptance or review-time measures.

gaps.title: Assistant-mode speedup kappa: all clean estimates are pre-agent, and current RCT designs break
gaps.plain_explanation: kappa is the time saved when a human uses AI as a helper rather than handing the task off. Credible estimates come from 2020-24 tools: chat assistants and autocomplete. The 2025 METR trial mixed helper and delegate use, and found a 19% slowdown for experts. Its late-2025 rerun was compromised: developers withheld tasks they would not do without AI. No clean estimate exists for 2025-26 tools, for IT-services staff, or for testing, infrastructure or BPO with current tools.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (2020-21; about 8-13% time per chat). Alibaba RCT (early 2024; -4.2% chat time at full use, new agents only). Cui et al. (2022-23 Copilot; +26% PRs, about 21% labour saved per PR; Accenture Southeast Asia n=320). Google RCT (mid-2024; about 21% faster, CI includes 0). Peng et al. (2022; 55.8% on a toy task; Indian/Pakistani freelancers). METR 2025 (+19% time) and Feb 2026 (point estimates -4% to -18%, CIs include 0, selection). Murphy-Hill et al. 2026 (Microsoft CLI agents +24% merged PRs; synthetic control; mixes modes). Merali (consulting -8% task time per year of progress; agentic tasks gain less; abstract only).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Old tools, or modes not separated, or selection-biased. Outcomes are throughput rather than labour hours per accepted unit. There is no India delivery-team sample. The Accenture offices are in Southeast Asia, not India.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: kappa is the floor of the max{} and the redo-assist term inside the delegate branch. Its sign (negative for experts on familiar code in 2025, positive for novices in support work) sets theta_j wherever delegation does not pay, which is most of h today.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s02, s03, s07, x2 and x4.

gaps.title: No measurement separates the delegate and assist branches on the same tasks, so the form of the max{} is untested
gaps.plain_explanation: The formula assumes each task either goes to the AI (with review, and a helper-mode redo on failure) or is done with AI help, whichever saves more. There are other plausible rules: retry and re-verify (Demirer et al.), or a human redoes the task from scratch after a failure (GDPval, Huang et al.). These give different answers for the same p. No dataset records, on the same tasks, the time under delegation with fallback versus time under assistance.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval try-once and try-n scenarios (delegate plus full human redo, no kappa). Demirer et al. 2026 (chained steps, retry until success). Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi (caught errors redone manually, uncaught ones accepted silently). Anthropic internal survey (about 59% of work uses Claude; more than half can fully delegate only 0-20%). Anthropic EI automation vs augmentation shares. Agarwal et al. radiology (optimal routing is either/or under biased updating). Vaccaro et al. meta-analysis (human+AI worse than the better alone, g = -0.23).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: These are a benchmark workflow model, theory, usage shares or classification tasks. None times both branches on the same coding or BPO task set with 2025-26 agents.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: The fallback rule decides how much a failed delegation costs. With p around 0.5 at typical h, theta_j can differ by a large fraction between 'redo with kappa' and 'redo from scratch'.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s09 (theory), x2 (triage and deferral) and s13.

gaps.title: Labour-time weights w_j by service line are unmeasured for Indian IT (only revenue shares exist)
gaps.plain_explanation: S = sum of w_j·theta_j needs each task type's share of labour hours. For Indian IT and BPO firms only revenue shares and analyst guesses exist. The national labour survey cannot separate the relevant occupations. Inside a job, much time goes to meetings, coordination and client communication that no task type j captures. That share is also unmeasured.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Jefferies/5paisa: application managed services 22-45% of revenue (narration, not attributed). HCLTech Q4 FY26 call: about 40% of spend AI-disrupted. ICICI: 30% of revenue at risk. ICRIER 2026 division mentions (development 72%, infra 48%). PLFS: NCO 3-digit only (from search results, not opened). O*NET importance/frequency weights. Hatgis-Kessell et al. (US time shares). Anthropic: developers about 23% of time writing code (Claude-estimated). Dillon et al.: email about 29% of the week.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Revenue shares differ from hours because of pricing and the onsite/offshore mix. ICRIER reports no magnitudes. Nothing measures within-role time allocation for Indian delivery staff.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Errors in w_j pass straight into S. Leaving out unclassified time (meetings, coordination) overstates S, because those hours have theta near 0.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s01, s10, s11 and x4. The PLFS 3-digit limit is unopened and flagged in the digest.

gaps.title: No net theta tracked across model generations on a fixed task mix (theta_j(t) is extrapolated)
gaps.plain_explanation: The recipe makes theta change over time through p(h,t). No one has measured net labour saved, after review and failure, for the same task set as models improve. The few time series are self-reported, gross, or limited to one vendor's models. One self-report series even suggests saving per AI-touched hour has been flat.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval try-n speed: 0.46x (GPT-4o) to 1.39x (GPT-5), OpenAI only. Merali 2024: about 12% faster per 10x compute in translation. Merali 2025: about -8% task time per year (abstract only). METR maintainer-vs-grader trend: 9.6 pp/yr slower (10% significance only). RPS/FRED: hours saved per hour assisted about 0.34-0.39 from 2024Q4 to 2026Q3, roughly flat (self-report, top-coded). Anthropic EI Jan, Mar and Jun 2026 releases (gross; success dropped in June). METR uplift 2025 vs 2026 (design broke).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: There is no panel with fixed tasks, varying model, and measured review time. The RPS ratio is gross and top-coded. GDPval covers one vendor's models on one-shot deliverables.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: The project's value lies in theta_j(t) rising with capability. If q and rho do not improve along with p, the measured path may be much flatter than the p(h,t) extrapolation. Only a capability-indexed panel can tell.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s02, s04, s06, s07 and s12.

gaps.title: No net, service-line-level theta for Indian IT or BPO to validate the bottom-up recipe against
gaps.plain_explanation: Every direct theta number is one of four things. Model-estimated and gross (Anthropic, about 80%). Benchmark-workflow-based (GDPval, about 11-28%). Self-reported, with known perception errors (METR: about +20% believed vs -19% measured). Or a company showcase or target (Infosys, TCS). The one India-wide firm survey reports only directions of change. The top-down 2.3 pp/yr mixes theta with adoption and demand, and HCLTech management says AI has barely shown up in reported numbers.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Tamkin-McCrory Nov 2025 (gross, excludes validation). Anthropic Jan 2026 success-adjusted (1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr). GDPval. Humlum-Vestergaard (about 3% of hours, self-report, includes software developers and IT support). ICRIER 2026 (651 respondents, direction only). Infosys Hertz COBOL migration 60% and BP IT ops 18%. TCS ERP target 25-30%. EY projections (development about 60%, BPO 52%; method undisclosed).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Selected cases, targets or projections. No audited portfolio effort reduction. Self-reports are unreliable in both directions (METR overstated; Peng understated).
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Without an external net anchor for at least one service line, errors in p, q, rho and kappa cannot be told apart. The bottom-up S(t) can only be checked against an aggregate that also contains adoption and eps·phi.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s07, s10 and s11; ICRIER and the firm transcripts are the closest.

gaps.title: Downstream costs of accepted AI output (escaped defects, technical debt, incidents) are never converted into labour hours
gaps.plain_explanation: theta should be net of all the extra work AI output causes. Studies show that accepted AI code is linked to more complexity, more warnings, more incidents and less secure code. None of them converts this into later hours of maintenance labour.
gaps.closest_existing_work: He et al. MSR '26 (Cursor): complexity +42% headline, about 9% net of codebase growth; warnings +30%. Faros Q2 2026: incidents per PR +243%, bugs per developer +54% (correlational, vendor). Perry et al. CCS '23 (less secure code, more confidence). DORA 2024/2025 (stability negatively associated with AI adoption). Kemerer-Paulk (self-review at ≤200 LOC/h catches just over half of defects; PSP classroom).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The quality metrics are proxies such as static-analysis warnings and incident counts, not hours. Most data are correlational or open-source. Nothing is from client delivery under SLAs.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: If accepted AI work raises future maintenance hours, net theta_dev is lower and w_maintenance rises over time. The gross per-task saving overstates multi-year replacement.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s03, s05 and x3.

gaps.title: AI running cost relative to Indian labour cost is unmeasured
gaps.plain_explanation: The definition of theta deducts the cost of running the AI. Cost-versus-human comparisons exist only against US wages and only for OpenAI models (GDPval), or for computer vision (Svanberg). Indian wages are lower, so the AI's share of total cost is higher and the US ratios cannot be borrowed. Agentic tasks also use many more tokens. No study prices AI cost per task for IT-services task mixes against vendor labour cost.
gaps.closest_existing_work: GDPval cost ratios (GPT-5 try-n 1.63x cheaper; US OEWS wages; OpenAI only). Anthropic API cost and token indices per O*NET task (Jan 2026 release; not converted to a share of labour cost). Svanberg et al. (computer vision, US). TheAgentCompany ($4.2 per task, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Borri et al. (agentic tokens over half of OpenRouter consumption).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No India wage base. No IT-service task mix. Runs with many agent retries are not priced.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: Under 'try n times then fix', each retry adds AI cost. At Indian wage levels the cost deduction may bind on long or retry-heavy tasks and lower theta_j relative to US-calibrated estimates.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s01, s04, s06 and s08.

gaps.title: q, rho and kappa by reviewer or worker seniority are unmeasured, though Indian delivery pyramids are junior-heavy
gaps.plain_explanation: How well and how fast people check AI output depends on their skill. In theory, weak checkers verify less and over-delegate. Empirically, gains are largest for novices, and experienced users get somewhat higher success. Indian IT firms have many junior staff and few senior reviewers. No one has measured acceptance quality or review time by seniority in software delivery, or whose hours (junior or senior) are saved versus added.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi 2026 (theory; radiology calibration). Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (+34% for novices, about 0 for top agents). Cui et al. (short-tenure +27-39% vs long-tenure +8-13%; imprecise). Anthropic Mar 2026 (6+ month users about 3-4 pp higher success). Garicano and Ide-Talamas (hierarchy theory). Czerwonka et al. (unfamiliar reviewers give fewer useful comments).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No IT-delivery measurement by seniority. No hours-versus-cost split for saved junior hours against added senior review hours.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: An hours-weighted theta_j can differ from a cost-weighted one. Junior-heavy reviewing may raise accepted-but-wrong output (effective q too high) and push costs downstream (see M13).
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked s05, s09, s10 and x1.

gaps.title: How predictable AI success is for an individual task (spread of p within a length bin) is unmeasured for coding and IT work
gaps.plain_explanation: The formula uses the average success rate at each task length. If a firm can predict in advance which individual tasks the AI will get right, it can route only those to the AI and save more. Averaging hides this gain (Jensen's inequality), and the size of the gain depends on how good the prediction is. Tasks of the same length can also sit inside or outside the AI's 'frontier' (Dell'Acqua et al.). No one has measured this predictability for coding or IT tickets.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Raghu et al. 2019 (retinopathy: zero-error triage slice of 35-44% on the adjudicated set, about 10-24% on a noisier holdout). Mozannar-Sontag (learning-to-defer estimators). RouteLLM and Self-REF (model-to-model routing). Dell'Acqua et al. (outside-frontier task: correctness -19 pp). METR TH1.1 task_results YAML (per-task successes; could in principle estimate within-h dispersion).
gaps.why_it_falls_short: There are classification or medical examples and model-to-model routers. Nothing measures human-AI routing with a labour-time outcome in software or BPO.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: The size of the gap between h-averaged theta and theta under instance-level routing is an unmeasured upward adjustment. It could be substantial if per-task success is predictable from ticket features.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a (measurement lens). Checked x2; the METR task-level file is confirmed public in the s12 dataset notes.

refuted_gaps: 'No source measures the intensive margin at all.' Refuted: Tamkin-McCrory (Anthropic, Nov 2025; gross, about 80%), GDPval try-once/try-n (about 11-28% net of grading time), METR RCTs, Humlum-Vestergaard (about 2.8% of users' hours) and Bick-Blandin-Deming RPS (saved per assisted hour about 0.35) all measure intensive-margin quantities. The remaining gap is narrower: net of review and failure, by h, for IT-services work (M6, M11, M12).

'No source nets out task failure.' Refuted: the Anthropic Economic Index Jan 2026 'economic primitives' report multiplies time savings by Claude-judged success, cutting the estimate from 1.8 to 1.0-1.2 pp/yr.

'Nothing outside METR ties AI success to task length.' Refuted: the Anthropic Jan 2026 report gives API success falling from about 60% (under 1 h) to about 45% (5+ h), crossing 50% near 3.5 h. It is model-judged and selected, so only a usage-based analogue.

'rho is measured only in GDPval.' Refuted in part: METR's early-2025 RCT reports about 9% of AI-allowed time reviewing and cleaning, and its public data have post-review implementation time for part of the sample. Rein (METR, Aug 2025) estimates fix time at about a third of h for test-passing PRs (n=4). Mozannar et al. CUPS measures 22.4% of session time verifying. The gap that survives is reviewer effort for agentic output across h (M6).

'q is measured only on SWE-bench.' Refuted in part: Rein 2025 (mergeability on RCT repositories), AIDev-derived deployment merge rates (Nakashima et al.; Pinna et al.; Watanabe et al.), GDPval win rates and RLI client acceptance all measure acceptance. None is conditioned on passing tests and length for IT-services output (M5).

'No benchmark exists for IT operations or customer-service agent tasks.' Refuted: ITBench (arXiv 2502.05352, opened: SRE 13.8%, CISO 25.2%, FinOps 0%), tau-bench (arXiv 2406.12045, opened: retail customer service, pass^k), TheAgentCompany and OSWorld exist. The gap survives only as 'no human time baselines, so no p(h)' (M3).

'No public raw material exists for maintenance and development task lengths.' Refuted in part: the Public Jira Dataset (Montgomery et al. 2022, Zenodo 5882881) and JOSSE (Zenodo 7022735) provide logged OSS effort, and SWE-bench Verified has annotator time buckets. They are not Indian client delivery and not hours-weighted (M1).

'The Anthropic Economic Index has no intensive-margin time series after Feb 2026.' Refuted: the 2026-03-24 HF release keeps task_success and both time fields, and the 2026-06-26 release has monthly human_only_time_mean and human_with_ai_time_mean for April-May 2026 (without success).

'No theory gives labour time as a continuous function of a capability index net of verification.' Refuted: Demirer et al. 2026 (q = alpha^d, verification per chain) and Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi 2026 do this. What is missing is calibration to METR horizons and IT/BPO workflow data, which is a measurement gap (M9, M11).

context.lens_summary: Context lens: what is missing for Indian and Philippine IT services and BPO. The shared web-search budget was used up on my first query, so this lens relies on primary documents I opened directly or had already saved. Those are: the Infosys FY2026 20-F (SEC EDGAR, infy-20260331.htm), the Infosys Q4 FY26 call transcript (SEC exhibit 99.5), the ICRIER 'AI and Jobs' report (PDF fetched and parsed), and the HCLTech Q4 FY26 and TCS Q2 FY27 transcripts. I also used saved PDFs of WDR 2026, the World Bank India Development Update 2026, Chandar and Klein Teeselink (2026), Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (arXiv v2) and the Betai-Chen slides. Ravanilla (2026, Philippine BPO, SSRN 7313383) is cited in Chandar and Klein Teeselink, but SSRN returned 403, so it is unverified. Overall finding: the developing-country evidence is about outcomes. There are surveys (ICRIER: direction of change only), postings studies (World Bank SADU), firm-level employment studies (Chandar and Klein Teeselink, which includes India), and management statements. Almost nothing measures the inputs to theta_j for Indian or Philippine delivery work. Specifically missing are hours-weighted task mixes, task-length distributions, review cost and client acceptance in outsourced settings, AI running cost relative to Indian labor cost, and p(h) for legacy stacks, BPO processes and non-native-English or code-mixed settings. Several contextual facts are now disclosed, and the recipe should use them: Infosys reports 54% fixed-price revenue (FY25 and FY26), 76.8% offshore effort in FY26, and a shift to outcome and transaction pricing that its 20-F attributes to 'AI disruptions'. Its CFO says productivity 'will get passed back to the client largely'. These facts mean the bridge from theta to observed headcount runs through contract structure and the staffing pyramid. That bridge is needed to validate theta against the top-down 2.3 pp/yr, and no study builds it. Procedural note for the user: when I downloaded the Infosys 20-F from SEC EDGAR with curl, I put the user's email address in the HTTP User-Agent header (SEC asks for a contact). That was a mistake, because the email should not be sent to outside services, and the user should be told.

gaps.title: No hours-based task mix (w_j) for Indian IT and BPO service lines
gaps.plain_explanation: To add up labor savings across service lines (maintenance, testing, development, infrastructure, BPO, consulting), you need the share of labor HOURS each one takes. For Indian vendors these shares are available only as revenue shares or rough directions, never as measured hours by service line, seniority or onsite/offshore location.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Infosys FY26 20-F: onsite effort 23.2% vs offshore 76.8%, with no split by service line. ICRIER 2026 (651 respondents, 620 firms): divisions most affected (software development 72%, infrastructure/cloud 48%, project management 37%), direction of change only. HCLTech Q4 FY26 call: about 40% of industry spend is 'AI disrupted'. Jefferies via 5paisa: AMS is 22-45% of revenue. Hatgis-Kessell et al. 2026: O*NET time shares, US only.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: Revenue shares are not hours shares. Pricing, onsite rate premiums and fixed-price margins all drive them apart. ICRIER reports no magnitudes. O*NET's task taxonomy does not match how Indian vendors split delivery into AMS, testing, infra managed services and BPO towers.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: S = sum_j w_j theta_j is linear in w_j. Moving 10 points of hours from maintenance to development can change S by as much as the theta_j estimates themselves differ. Weights are also needed to compare against the top-down 2.3 pp/yr, which is measured per head.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: No task-length distributions (f_j(h)) for Indian delivery work: tickets, test cases, BPO transactions
gaps.plain_explanation: The recipe integrates AI success over how long tasks take. Nobody has published how long an AMS ticket, a test-automation task or a claims or KYC transaction takes in an Indian delivery center, weighted by hours.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Public Jira datasets (Montgomery et al. 2022; JOSSE): open-source effort logs. SWE-bench Verified time buckets (39% under 15 min). Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond: about 40-minute average chats, mostly Philippine agents. Alibaba RCT: about 466-second chats. RLI: freelance projects with a median of 11.5 h.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: All of these come from open source, US or Chinese consumer support, or freelance markets. None describes ITSM tickets under SLAs at Indian vendors. Those are held by vendors or clients in ServiceNow, Jira or Remedy and have never been released.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: p(h) is logistic in log h. Whether the typical AMS ticket takes 20 minutes or 6 hours puts it in very different parts of the curve, and that decides whether theta_maintenance is near its ceiling or near kappa.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: AI running cost has never been compared with Indian labor cost, so 'net of AI cost' is not calibrated for India
gaps.plain_explanation: theta is meant to be net of the cost of running the AI. In the US, labor costs so much that agent compute is a rounding error. In India, fully loaded labor is far cheaper, so the cost of an agent run, especially with many retries, could take a real share of the savings, and some tasks may not be worth automating at Indian wages even when AI can do them.
gaps.closest_existing_work: WDR 2026 (PDF p.121): developing countries rationally skip automation, such as checkout systems or sewing equipment, when wages are below the cost of the equipment. WDR 2026 (PDF p.104): the price per million tokens at GPT-3.5 level fell from about $20 to $0.07 (late 2022 to late 2024). Chandar and Klein Teeselink 2026: junior employment losses are deeper in richer countries (r = -0.37 with income, not individually significant). Svanberg et al.: a US cost test for computer vision. GDPval: cost ratios at US wages. TheAgentCompany: about $4.2 per task for the best agent. My own derivation from the Infosys FY26 20-F: employee benefit costs ($9,739M in cost of sales plus $766M in S&M) over 328,594 employees is about $32k per employee per year, roughly $16/hour. This average includes the pricier onsite staff, so the offshore hourly cost is lower.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No study computes the cost-effectiveness threshold for LLM or agent work at Indian or Philippine wages. WDR's wage-versus-automation-cost point is qualitative and about physical capital. GDPval and SWE-Lancer cost ratios use US wages and bounties. Who pays for tokens is also unknown: TCS says it helps clients 'manage AI token costs', which suggests the cost may sit with the client.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_j(net) is roughly the gross time saved minus AI cost divided by labor cost per hour. At about $16/h, a $4 agent run on a 1-hour task removes about a quarter of the saving. At US wages it removes almost nothing. Without this term, theta for India is biased upward, most for long, retry-heavy delegated tasks.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: Contract structure (fixed-price, T&M, outcome-based) is not linked to whether time savings show up as headcount or as price cuts
gaps.plain_explanation: Under time-and-materials, saved hours become fewer billed hours and lower revenue, which is pass-through to the client. Under fixed-price, the vendor keeps the saving as margin and may cut staff without revenue falling. The same theta therefore produces different realized replacement, depending on contract mix and when contracts renew.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Infosys FY26 20-F: 54% of revenue from fixed-price contracts in both FY25 and FY26. The 20-F also says 'AI disruptions have led us to deviate from our standard pricing policies' toward output, outcome and transaction pricing, and lists 'AI led compression' and 'clients moving the work to offshore based GCCs' as risks. Infosys CFO (Q4 FY26): productivity 'will get passed back to the client largely'. HCLTech Q4 FY26: pre-AI renewals already carried 10-15% price cuts over a deal's life, and a Q1 'productivity pass-through' seasonality. Banerjee and Duflo (2000): reputation and contracting in Indian software, pre-AI. Betai-Chen slides: the platform data record whether each project is fixed-price or hourly, but no split results are reported.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No study estimates how contract type governs the timing and size of pass-through, or of headcount response, to AI savings. Disclosures give the mix only at firm level, not by service line or by renewal year.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta is a capability ceiling, but validating it against the top-down 2.3 pp/yr (revenue or headcount per unit of work) means stripping out the contract-driven pass-through (phi) and its timing. Without the contract mix, a low realized rate cannot be told apart from a low theta or from savings retained under fixed-price.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: The staffing pyramid: whose hours are saved, who reviews, and how reviewer skill changes q and rho
gaps.plain_explanation: Indian delivery teams are junior-heavy. Infosys onboarded more than 20,000 freshers in FY26 and plans a similar number in FY27, and TCS onboarded about 10,000 graduates this year. If AI removes cheap junior hours but adds expensive senior review hours, the hours saved and the money saved differ. If juniors review AI output themselves, acceptance quality may suffer.
gaps.closest_existing_work: ICRIER 2026 and the World Bank India Development Update 2026 (p.41): 55% of firms report lower entry-level hiring vs 25% mid-level and 14% senior. Chandar and Klein Teeselink 2026: junior share -1.9 pp at affiliates of adopters, covering 41 countries including India. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond and Cui et al.: larger gains for novices and short-tenure staff. Theory: Garicano (2000), Ide and Talamas (2025), and Huang, Xiao and Vishnoi (2026), where weak verifiers over-delegate.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No study measures review time or acceptance by reviewer seniority in delivery teams. None tracks pyramid ratios (seniors per junior) as AI use rises, and none links the theory to Indian staffing data. The evidence describes outcomes (hiring), not parameters.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta is hours-weighted, but the wage bill and headcount respond to a cost-weighted saving. rho and q depend on who reviews. A junior-heavy pyramid may mean higher kappa for juniors, higher review demand on seniors, and a q that is either too lenient or too strict. Ignoring this misstates both theta_j and its link to headcount.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: Outsourced work is low-context and reviewed twice, and nobody measures acceptance by the client
gaps.plain_explanation: Vendors work on the client's codebase and processes with partial context. Output often passes internal vendor review and then client acceptance (UAT, change boards). Benchmarks measure acceptance by owners (repo maintainers) or by algorithms, not by a client accepting a vendor's delivery.
gaps.closest_existing_work: METR (Kwa et al.): contractors took about 5-18x longer than repository maintainers on the same PRs, so h depends on context. METR maintainer review (Whitfill et al. 2026): q of about 0.5, from owners. SWE-Lancer: Expensify freelance tasks with manager selection. RLI: client acceptance, but on mostly creative freelance work. Anthropic Sept 2025 report: 'context' offered as a possible bottleneck for enterprise deployment.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No q or rho is measured in a vendor-client setting, and none in Indian IT. The context adjustment to h (low-context vendor vs high-context owner) has not been estimated for vendor staff, who sit between contractors and maintainers.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: The right h for Indian staff, and so p(h,t), needs a context adjustment. Two review layers may stack rho. Client acceptance criteria (SLAs, compliance) set the effective q, which may differ from open-source merge standards in either direction.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: BPO back-office and voice work in India and the Philippines has no task-level capability or time-saved measurement
gaps.plain_explanation: BPO towers (finance and accounting, claims, KYC, order-to-cash, voice support) are run through GUIs, documents and phone calls. The only measured BPO productivity evidence is an assistant for chat support at one firm with a 2020-21 model. Nothing measures delegation to agents on these processes in Indian or Philippine centers.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (QJE 2025; mostly Philippine agents): handle time -8.5%, resolutions per hour +15%. Alibaba RCT (China): chat time -4% at full use. METR horizon note: computer-use horizons are 40-100x shorter than software horizons. TheAgentCompany: admin and finance tasks hardest. WDR 2026 (ch. 4 vignette, PDF p.137): a Philippine BPO agent who discards inappropriate AI suggestions, and clients who still prefer human voice. Ravanilla (2026), on Philippine BPO labor displacement, is cited by Chandar and Klein Teeselink but I could not open it.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The evidence is assist-only, single-firm and from older models. There is no p(h) curve for BPO transactions and no measured q or rho for document or ticket outputs. The Philippine displacement paper (if verified) measures labor demand, not time saved per task.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta_BPO probably needs its own, much lower p curve than coding (computer-use horizons), and the delegate-vs-assist split may differ sharply. BPO is a large hours share in Indian and Philippine IT-BPM, so errors here move S a lot.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: Language effects: English quality, accents, and Indic or code-mixed work
gaps.plain_explanation: Part of what offshore BPO sells is fluent English. AI may substitute for that directly (polishing text, AI voice), or may close the gap for offshore workers. Domestic Indian BPO serves customers in Hindi or code-mixed language, where models perform worse. Neither channel has been measured in terms of time saved.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond section 5.4.1: AI raised LLM-scored English comprehensibility and native fluency, with a larger gain for Philippine-based agents than US-based ones. Betai-Chen slides: English spelling, English grammar and English translation are among the most GenAI-automatable skills (scores about 9.0-9.3 out of 10). WDR 2026: AI performs better on public-service queries in English-speaking countries, and low-resource languages are underserved.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The fluency result is a quality outcome, not time saved, and comes from a 2020-21 text-chat tool. Nothing measures voice-agent containment or accuracy on Indian or Philippine accents, or on Hindi and code-mixed queries, apart from vendor claims (none verified here).
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: For export BPO, AI may raise quality more than it saves time, so kappa is small but substitution pressure on demand is large. For domestic or Indic-language work, p may be lower than English benchmarks imply. Using English benchmark p overstates theta there.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: Legacy and niche technology stacks in Indian AMS lack a p(h) curve
gaps.plain_explanation: A large share of Indian maintenance work is on mainframe/COBOL, SAP/ERP and proprietary client platforms. Capability benchmarks are almost all Python, JavaScript and open-source repositories.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Stanford talk (Denisov-Blanch 2025): gains of about 0-5% for niche languages such as COBOL (thin support). Betai-Chen: COBOL among the least automatable skills (2.82, rank 2728 of 2742). Infosys Q4 FY26: one showcase COBOL-to-microservices migration with 60% lower cost and 60% shorter timeline. TCS Q2 FY27: target of 25-30% faster S/4HANA implementation.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: The firm figures are selected showcases and targets, and the academic or market evidence is thin and contradictory. There are no benchmark tasks with human time baselines on legacy or ERP stacks.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: If AMS hours are concentrated on legacy stacks with low p, theta_maintenance is far below what Python benchmarks imply. Large migration projects are the opposite case: a one-off task where AI may save a lot.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

gaps.title: Time zones and offshore latency: how delegation interacts with overnight, follow-the-sun delivery
gaps.plain_explanation: Offshore teams work across time zones. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond note that many agents work overnight to cover US business hours. Review and iteration cycles with the client therefore cost elapsed days, and the number of rounds needed can change both labor and whether clients bother to offshore at all. Agents that work asynchronously could make this better or worse.
gaps.closest_existing_work: Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond: overnight shifts noted descriptively. Infosys FY26 20-F: 'clients moving the work to offshore based GCCs' is a stated pricing risk. World Bank India Development Update 2026 (p.41): the six largest IT firms shed about 64,000 workers while the rest of tech services, including GCCs, added about 700,000. The global software engineering literature on temporal distance was not verified in this pass, because search was unavailable.
gaps.why_it_falls_short: No study measures how time-zone separation changes the number of AI-output review rounds (q iterations), coordination labor, or the incentive for clients to do AI-assisted work in-house rather than offshore.
gaps.why_it_matters_for_theta: theta counts labor time, not elapsed time, so latency matters through extra review rounds and coordination hours (rho) and through lower q when feedback is slow. Shifts of work to GCCs or in-house also contaminate the top-down 2.3 pp/yr used to validate theta.
gaps.survived_refutation: n/a

refuted_gaps: 'There is no India-specific evidence on AI and IT employment': refuted. ICRIER (Mishra et al. 2026; 651 respondents from 620 firms; directional, division-level), World Bank SADU Oct 2025 and India Development Update 2026 (55% / 25% / 14% lower entry / mid / senior hiring), and Chandar and Klein Teeselink 2026 (41 countries including India) all exist. What is missing is parameter-level data (w_j, f_j, rho, q), not outcome evidence.

'Contract mix (fixed-price vs T&M) is not disclosed': refuted for Infosys. The FY26 20-F reports fixed-price revenue at 54% in both FY25 and FY26, and a shift toward output, outcome and transaction pricing attributed to AI disruptions. The split by service line is still not disclosed.
'Onsite/offshore mix is unknown': refuted for Infosys. The FY26 20-F gives onsite effort 23.2% and offshore 76.8% (FY25: 23.9% / 76.1%).

'No evidence on English or language effects of AI in offshore BPO': partly refuted. Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond (section 5.4.1) find that AI raised English comprehensibility and native-fluency scores, with larger gains for Philippine-based agents. Time-saved and voice-channel effects are still unmeasured.

'The wage-versus-automation-cost logic has never been applied to developing countries': partly refuted. WDR 2026 makes the argument qualitatively for physical automation (cashier systems, garment equipment), and Chandar and Klein Teeselink find junior losses deeper in richer countries (r = -0.37, not significant). No LLM- or agent-specific calibration at Indian wages exists, so gap C3 stands.

ideas.title: From time horizons to net labor saved: a calibrated theta_j(h,t) with a value-of-information ranking of the missing data
ideas.what_youd_do: Plainly: turn METR's capability curve into labor saved net of review and failure, then measure which unknown input contributes most to the uncertainty. That ranking is the 'dataset requirement' the mentor asked for. Steps: (1) Download METR's per-task file task_results_1_1.yaml (228 tasks; for each agent, human_minutes, successes and runs). Refit p(h,t) two ways: a logistic in log h with one slope shared across models (Barry, METR, Mar 2026, found this cross-validates best), and Ord's constant-hazard curve. Bootstrap the h50 trend. Measurements above 16 h are flagged as unreliable, so cap or flag them. (2) Code q two ways: as a scalar of about 0.5, and as a horizon shift. The shift uses Whitfill et al. (METR, Mar 2026), where Sonnet 4.5's horizon is about 50 min under the grader and about 8 min under maintainers. (3) Model rho as a fixed cost per change plus a part proportional to h. The anchors are weak: Google's log-based review baseline (a rough derived 45-50 reviewer-minutes per change), GDPval review at about 0.27 of task time, Rein's n=4 fix-time estimate at about 0.33 of h, and CUPS at 22.4% of session time. Use kappa in a range from about -0.19 (METR 2025 RCT) to about +0.2. Treat the gap between contractor and in-house h (5-18x per Kwa et al.) as an explicit parameter. (4) Build hours-weighted f_j(h) proxies. For maintenance: SWE-bench Verified difficulty buckets, reweighted from counts to hours. For maintenance vs development vs test: timespent fields in the Montgomery et al. public Jira dump, split by issue type. (5) Integrate the draft formula to get theta_j(t). Run a global sensitivity analysis (Sobol indices) and report which parameter dominates and what precision on it would pin theta_j within ±5 pp. (6) Cross-check against the Anthropic Economic Index success-by-length curve (API 50% near 3.5 h) and, loosely, the top-down 2.3 pp/yr. Deliverables: a 6-8 page note, a notebook, and one interactive chart. The note also states the recipe formally, with a data-requirements table.
ideas.data_needed: METR TH1.1 per-task and per-model YAML. SWE-bench Verified 'difficulty' field (500 rows). Montgomery et al. Public Jira Dataset (2.7M issues, timeestimate/timespent). Optionally JOSSE effort data. Published anchors for q, rho and kappa (Whitfill et al. 2026; Rein 2025; GDPval; Mozannar et al. CUPS; METR RCT). Anthropic Economic Index Jan/Mar 2026 releases, for the cross-check.
ideas.data_access: All public. I opened https://metr.org/time-horizons/: it links /assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml and /assets/task_results_1_1.yaml, and says it is 'no longer actively updated' (Sep 8, 2026) and that measurements above 16 h are unreliable. SWE-bench Verified is on Hugging Face (princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified). The Jira dump is Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5882881 (CC BY 4.0, 5.8 GB MongoDB). One correction to the digest: I opened the Economic Index release_2026_01_15 data_documentation.md, and the per-O*NET-task intersections carry mean, median, SD and CIs for human_only_time and human_with_ai_time, but NOT histograms. Histograms exist only for the standalone numeric facets, and time units are not stated. So f(h) per task cannot be read off directly.
ideas.weeks_effort: 4-5 weeks at 5-8 hrs/week (about 30-40 hrs). Week 1: refit p(h). Week 2: f(h) proxies from Jira and SWE-bench. Week 3: integration and Sobol. Weeks 4-5: write-up and chart.
ideas.gap_addressed: Measurement M4 (poorly identified high-reliability tail and curve shape), M5 (q depends on h), M6 (rho form), M2 (contractor vs in-house h), plus M1 via proxies. Skeptic G1 (no joint integrand) and G4 (theta not indexed to capability). Directly answers the mentor's 'dataset requirement and recipe' by ranking which missing measurement matters most.
ideas.who_would_care: METR: Kwa's Jan 2026 note says converting horizons to speedup needs prompting, waiting and checking time data METR does not have. This shows how much each of those matters. Epoch AI: GATE treats automation as all-or-nothing per task. This gives a partial-automation, review-net version of 'share automated as capability rises', and the mentor co-authored GATE. Anthropic Economic Research: their Jan 2026 success-adjusted estimate has no rho or q term. It is also a clean writing sample, because it shows that the applicant can combine benchmark methodology with an economic aggregation and is honest about uncertainty.
ideas.risks: Priors on rho and kappa may drive the answer. That is partly the point, since the output is a sensitivity ranking, but it must be presented that way. The f(h) proxies are open-source US work, not Indian delivery work. The METR h is contractor time, and the context multiplier is unknown. The top of the horizon curve is unreliable above 16 h and the dashboard is frozen. The Sobol ranking depends on the chosen prior ranges, so show it under two sets of ranges.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Download task_results_1_1.yaml and benchmark_results_1_1.yaml. Reproduce Claude 3.7 Sonnet's p50 (about 60 min under TH1.1) from the stored logistic coefficients. Then run a shared-slope refit across all 26 models and plot both curves on one log-h axis.

ideas.title: q(h,t) in the wild: reviewer acceptance and fix-up share of coding-agent PRs by task size and month, from AIDev
ideas.what_youd_do: Plainly: measure, on real GitHub deployment data, how often agent-written changes get accepted, and how much human fixing they need, as the change gets bigger and as agents improve. Steps: (1) Pull the AIDev-pop tables: pull_request, pr_reviews, pr_review_comments, pr_commits, pr_commit_details and pr_timeline. (2) Define acceptance strictly: merged by someone other than the PR opener. This removes self-merges, which inflate Codex's numbers. Add a stricter version: merged with no later human revision commits. (3) Define a 'fix-up share': the fraction of final changed lines that came from human (non-agent) commits after the agent's first push. This is the deployment analogue of Rein's fix-time estimate and a proxy for the q/rho mix. Also count review rounds and review comments as a rough effort proxy. (4) Proxy task length h by the size of the initial diff (lines and files). On a 200-300 PR subsample, add an LLM-estimated human time, and calibrate that estimator on JOSSE/Jira logged effort, as Anthropic did. (5) Fit logistic merge probability against log size by agent and calendar month, mirroring the METR curve. Compare with matched human PRs in the same repositories (the Watanabe et al. design). Read off a size at which acceptance falls to 50% and track it over time. (6) Report selection explicitly: compare agent vs human PR size distributions in the same repos, because people delegate easy tasks. Deliverable: a short empirical note on 'q(h,t) in deployment vs the METR maintainer study', with the code.
ideas.data_needed: AIDev v5 (PRs, reviews, review comments, timeline, commits with diffs). JOSSE or Montgomery Jira effort logs to calibrate an LLM time estimator. Published comparison points: Whitfill et al. 2026 (normalized gap about 24.2 pp), Nakashima et al. 2026 (agent merge rates 55-86% vs 82.6% human), Pinna et al. 2026 (by task type), Watanabe et al. 2025 (83.8% vs 91.0%, agent PRs about 2x larger).
ideas.data_access: Public. I opened https://huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev. v5 has 7,685,281 PRs across 961,168 repositories and six agents (Codex, Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Jules, Devin), CC-BY-4.0, cutoff Mar 31, 2026. The detailed review, timeline and commit tables are in the AIDev-pop subset (repos with more than 100 stars), so the analysis is laptop-scale. The card does not mention CI or check status, so test-passing cannot be conditioned on directly. JOSSE is on Zenodo record 7022735 (CC BY 4.0). LLM time estimation needs a few dollars of API calls.
ideas.weeks_effort: 4-5 weeks (about 30-40 hrs). Week 1: load data and compute descriptive merge rates by agent and size. Week 2: fix-up share and self-merge filtering. Week 3: size-to-time calibration on a subsample. Week 4: logistic fits and trends. Week 5: write-up.
ideas.gap_addressed: Measurement M5 and skeptic G3: q comes from one small one-shot study and probably depends on h, and nothing measures acceptance for agents that iterate. Partly M6 (fix-up share as a rho proxy) and M13 (reverts after merge can be detected in the timeline). Supplies the 'q(h)' row of the dataset requirement with a real-world estimate.
ideas.who_would_care: METR: a deployment-side complement to the maintainer study, which had one-shot agents on 3 repos with models up to Sonnet 4.5. This one has iterating agents through Mar 2026. Lab economics teams (Anthropic, OpenAI): agent quality in the wild by product. The MSR/software-engineering community. A good writing sample, because it shows empirical care with selection problems on a large messy dataset.
ideas.risks: No test-passing condition, so this is roughly q*p at the delegated task mix, not q. Strong selection into which tasks get delegated: small diffs may simply be easier tasks. Open-source norms differ from client delivery. Diff size is a poor proxy for human time, which is why the calibration step exists. 'Fix-up share' can be contaminated by the agent being re-invoked, since about 34% of revision commits in Watanabe et al. were Claude-co-authored, so agent commits must be identified via author or trailer metadata. Results may say more about repo norms than capability.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Download the AIDev-pop pull_request and pr_commit_details tables. Compute merge rate by agent × deciles of lines added, with and without excluding PRs merged by their own opener, and check that the overall rates roughly match Nakashima et al.

ideas.title: A review-cost and acceptance primitive for agentic coding logs: measurement spec plus a consented pilot on local Claude Code transcripts (LAB-INTERNAL DATA for the full version)
ideas.what_youd_do: Plainly: the Anthropic Economic Index and METR's transcript note both measure AI time but not the human time spent checking and fixing AI output, or whether the output survives. Design that missing measurement, and test it at small scale on data you can legitimately access. Steps: (1) Write a measurement spec with four session-level quantities. (a) Agent working time. (b) Human active time after the agent's last edit: prompting, reading and hand edits. (c) Whether the agent's diff survives in git after 7 and 30 days, as an acceptance and downstream-rework signal. (d) Estimated human-only task length h. These give rho(h) and an observed q(h). The spec includes classifier prompts, privacy design (aggregates only) and a power calculation for what a lab would need. (2) Pilot on your own local Claude Code transcripts and those of 3-5 consenting peers, joined to their git history. Use timestamps of user turns, tool calls and file edits, plus git log and blame for survival. (3) Validate the time inference against a one-week self-timed diary on a subset of sessions, because silent reading time is invisible in logs, which is the gap METR's Feb 2026 transcript note leaves. (4) Report pilot rho and survival rates by task size, clearly labelled as illustrative. Deliverable: a 5-page proposal-style paper.
