It doubles as an Anthropic Fellows or Economic Futures application and specifies exactly what the lab-scale version (Claude Code session telemetry) would estimate.
ideas.data_needed: Lab version: Claude Code or agent session telemetry at scale, with timestamps and repo outcomes. LAB-INTERNAL, held by Anthropic (and similar for OpenAI Codex, GitHub). Pilot version: local Claude Code JSONL transcripts and git repos from the student and consenting peers, plus a short time diary. Methodological anchors: METR transcript note (Deng, Feb 17, 2026: 5,305 transcripts from 7 staff, 1.5x-13x 'soft upper bound', silent review not netted out), METR's Jan 2026 limitations note, Anthropic EI Jan 2026 primitives, and Huang-Xiao-Vishnoi 2026 (verification effort as a choice).
ideas.data_access: Pilot: local data that the participants own, used with explicit consent, and only aggregate statistics leave their machines. Code contents must never be shared. I did not inspect the local transcripts, because this session's permission policy blocked reading them as potential personal data. So whether every record carries timestamps still needs checking by the student. Full version: lab-internal. The Economic Futures page I opened (https://www.anthropic.com/economic-futures/program) offers $10k-50k plus $5k API credits and consultation on Economic Index data, does not mention raw-data access, and says 'We are not currently accepting applications.' I could not verify the current Anthropic Fellows call, because the web-search budget was exhausted.
ideas.weeks_effort: 4-6 weeks (about 30-45 hrs). Week 1: spec and parser. Weeks 2-3: recruit peers and run the diary week. Week 4: survival join and estimates. Weeks 5-6: write the proposal paper.
ideas.gap_addressed: Measurement M6 and skeptic G2 (no measurement of reviewer effort on agentic output as a function of h), M5 (acceptance), M13 (downstream rework never converted to hours), and M11 (a capability-indexed panel becomes possible if run across model versions). Specifies the rho and q rows of the dataset requirement and how a lab could fill them.
ideas.who_would_care: Anthropic Economic Research. Its Jan 2026 report proxies verification only through success rates, and its June 2026 data dropped task_success. This proposes the next primitive. Also the Anthropic Fellows economics track and METR, which is redesigning its uplift studies. The strongest 'application-shaped' option, because it ends with a concrete ask for lab data and a ready protocol.
ideas.risks: Pilot n will be tiny and from students or AI-adjacent users, not IT-services staff. Treat it as a feasibility demo, not an estimate. Idle gaps in logs mix silent review with unrelated work. Git survival is confounded by later refactors. Privacy: transcripts can contain secrets or others' code, so use consent and on-device aggregation. Labs may already measure this internally, which makes novelty uncertain, but a public spec still has value. Do not rely on getting lab access within the fellowship window.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Draft the one-page spec (the four quantities and their definitions). Write a parser that turns one of your own Claude Code session files into a timeline of user turns, tool calls and file edits. Check whether timestamps are present and whether edited files can be matched to commits in that repo's git log.

ideas.title: A fixed-task mini-panel: delegate vs assist vs manual on IT-services-style tasks, with timed review, across two model generations
ideas.what_youd_do: Plainly: run the draft formula as a tiny experiment. Take real-looking IT-services tasks of known length, let agents try them, time the human review and fix, and see how net saving moves with task length and with a newer model. Steps: (1) Assemble 12-18 tasks across three lines, spanning roughly 10 min to 4 h: maintenance bug fixes from open-source Jira issues with logged timespent (Montgomery or JOSSE), unit or regression test writing, and a BPO-style data-reconciliation or document-extraction task. h comes from the logged effort or from a timed human baseline. (2) For each task, run the same harness with an older and a current model (e.g. via API), allowing up to n retries, and record pass or fail on hidden checks (p). (3) A reviewer, ideally two, one of them a working engineer and if possible someone in Indian IT, times review plus fix with a stopwatch and records accept or reject (q, rho). Separately time the 'assist' branch on a subset (human does the task with AI chat help) to get kappa. Record the fallback rule used after failure, to test the max{} form (M9). (4) Compute net theta per task, fit it against log h and model generation, and compare with GDPval's try-once and try-n arithmetic. Deliverable: a pilot dataset with a protocol document, which is literally 'the recipe', and a short note on what n is needed to estimate theta_j within ±5 pp.
ideas.data_needed: Task sources: public Jira issues with logged effort plus reproducible repos, and synthetic BPO-like spreadsheets or documents. API access for two model generations (budget roughly a few hundred dollars; this is an estimate). Reviewer time from the student plus 1-3 volunteers. Comparison anchors: GDPval (review 109 of 404 min), METR RCT data (public repo with initial_implementation_time and post_review_implementation_time), Rein 2025.
ideas.data_access: Mostly public or self-generated. I opened https://github.com/METR/Measuring-Early-2025-AI-on-Exp-OSS-Devs. It has data_complete.csv with ai_treatment, developer time forecasts, initial_implementation_time and post_review_implementation_time (the last missing for some issues). No screen-recording labels are included and no license is stated, so it can serve as a benchmark for the review-time protocol. Jira and JOSSE data are CC BY 4.0. The volunteer reviewers' time is the binding constraint. Indian IT reviewers depend on the student's network and, if recruited, would need informed consent.
ideas.weeks_effort: 5-6 weeks (about 40-48 hrs). This is the tightest of the four. Week 1: pick tasks and baselines. Weeks 2-3: agent runs. Weeks 3-4: timed reviews. Week 5: analysis. Week 6: protocol and write-up. Cut to 12 tasks if behind.
ideas.gap_addressed: Measurement M9 (delegate and assist never timed on the same tasks, so the max{} form is untested), M11 (no net theta on fixed tasks across model generations), M6 (rho by h), M3 and M7 (no p or q for testing or BPO-type outputs), and skeptic G1 (no joint integrand on one task population). This is the mentor's recipe executed at pilot scale.
ideas.who_would_care: METR: its Feb 2026 post says it is redesigning uplift studies and considering fixed-task experiments, which this pilots, with IT-services and BPO-style tasks they do not cover. OpenAI's GDPval team (the same try-then-fix logic, extended to an assist branch and length bins). Epoch, for a capability-indexed net-saving slope. A strong writing sample, because it shows the ability to design and run an evaluation with real human-time measurement, a skill AI-lab economics teams prize.
ideas.risks: Very small n, so estimates will be noisy. Frame it as a protocol and power study. If the student is the main reviewer, they lack client context and know the task set, which biases rho and q. Logged Jira effort is sparse and self-selected. Tasks or issues may be in model training data. API cost and harness setup can eat the time budget. BPO tasks built by the student may be unrealistically clean. Timing your own review introduces Hawthorne effects.
ideas.first_step_this_week: From the Montgomery Jira dump or JOSSE, shortlist about 20 resolved issues with non-null timespent between 15 min and 4 h in repos that build locally. Pick 12 spread across log-h. Write a one-page protocol fixing the retry budget, accept/reject criteria and how review time is recorded.

ideas.title: A working theta_j calculator plus a value-of-information ranking that becomes the 'dataset requirement' for the mentor
ideas.what_youd_do: Build the recipe end to end with the numbers that exist today, then find out which missing number matters most. Steps: (1) Code theta_j(t) = integral of max{q*p(h,t)*(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, kappa} f_j(h) dh in Python, with each input given a prior range taken from the digest. p(h,t) comes from METR TH1.1 (p50/p80 by model). q: 0.5 as a scalar, or a roughly 7x horizon shift (Whitfill et al. 2026). rho: 0.1-0.33 of h (METR RCT about 9%; Rein 2025 about 1/3; GDPval about 0.27). kappa: -0.19 to +0.2 (METR 2025; Cui et al.; Google RCT). f_j(h): SWE-bench Verified buckets and RLI as two extremes. (2) Add the three competing fallback rules the literature uses when the AI fails: redo with assistance (the draft), full human redo (GDPval), and retry-and-reverify (Demirer et al. 2026). (3) Run a Monte Carlo and a variance decomposition (Sobol indices or a simple binned correlation ratio) to see how much of the spread in theta_j, and in S = sum w_j theta_j, comes from each parameter. (4) Back-solve: given an adoption band, which parameter combinations reproduce the top-down 2.3 pp/yr (range 1.5-3.6)? (5) Turn the ranking into a one-page dataset specification. For each ticket or task: service line, logged effort hours, an AI-used/delegated flag, whether the output passed automated checks, reviewer hours, accept/reject, rework hours, model and tool version, and date. Add the minimum sample size per h-bin needed to cut the dominant uncertainty in half.
ideas.data_needed: Published parameter values only: METR benchmark_results_1_1.yaml (p50/p80 by model), Whitfill et al. 2026 (q), Rein 2025 and the METR RCT (rho), the METR, Google and Cui RCTs (kappa), SWE-bench Verified difficulty buckets, RLI hour distribution (median 11.5 h), and the project's own top-down 2.3 pp/yr series. Revenue-share proxies for w_j (AMS 22-45%, about 40% 'AI-disrupted' per HCLTech).
ideas.data_access: All public. I opened the METR TH1.1 task-level YAML and the SWE-bench Verified HF card (500 rows, 'difficulty' field, values '<15 min fix', '15 min - 1 hour', '1-4 hours' plus a fourth). The other values come from the verified digest. No firm data needed.
ideas.weeks_effort: 2-3 weeks at 5-8 hrs/week (week 1: code plus priors; week 2: Monte Carlo, variance decomposition and back-solve; week 3: write the dataset spec)
ideas.gap_addressed: Directly answers the mentor's request for 'a dataset requirement and a recipe'. Covers skeptic/G1 (no joint measurement of the integrand), measurement/M9 (the fallback rule is untested) and M12 (no net anchor), by showing which measurement would most narrow S(t). Also makes the M10/C1 w_j problem concrete: how wrong can revenue-share weights be before they dominate?
ideas.who_would_care: Andrei Potlogea first, since this is literally the deliverable. Also METR: Kwa's Jan 2026 note says converting horizons to speedup needs prompting, waiting and checking time, which this specification names. Anyone writing to an Indian IT firm, NASSCOM or ICRIER to request data would use the one-page spec as the ask.
ideas.risks: Garbage-in: the priors are borrowed from different tasks, models and populations, so the absolute theta_j level is not credible. The value of this project is the ranking and the specification, and it should be framed that way. The variance decomposition depends on prior ranges you choose, so report it under two or three prior sets. The fallback-rule comparison may show the formula's shape matters more than any parameter, which is a useful finding but not a number.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Write the theta_j function (about 50 lines) with p(h) as a logistic in log h fed by one model's p50 and p80 from benchmark_results_1_1.yaml. Plot theta against t for one service line under the three fallback rules at the central priors, and show Andrei the plot.

ideas.title: Refit METR's task-level data to pin down the shape and tail of p(h,t), how predictable success is task by task, and whether q is a multiplier or a horizon shift
ideas.what_youd_do: Use METR's public per-task, per-model success counts, not just the published 50%/80% horizons. Steps: (1) Load task_results_1_1.yaml (per agent: release date and fitted coefficient/intercept; per task: human_minutes, n_successes, n_runs, task_weight). (2) Refit p(h) under a logistic in log h with a slope shared across models (Barry 2026 found this cross-validates best), a constant-hazard/exponential curve (Ord 2025), and a Weibull curve. Report 80/90/95/99% horizons with bootstrap CIs by task family, so the 'unidentified tail' is quantified rather than asserted. (3) Measure overdispersion within an h-bin. Model success with a beta-binomial and estimate how much tasks of the same length differ in success probability. Convert that into an oracle upper bound on the gain from per-task routing: the Jensen gap between the average of max{} and max{} at the average (the measurement/M16 question). Add a realistic version by asking how much of that spread is predictable from task family plus length. (4) Implement q in two ways: a scalar 0.5 multiplier, and a shift of h50 by about 7x (Sonnet 4.5: 50 min under the grader vs 8 min under maintainers, Whitfill et al. 2026). Show how far theta_j diverges between them across f_j. (5) As a scenario, apply the 40-100x computer-use horizon discount (Kwa and Cheng 2025) to obtain a provisional p_BPO and p_infra.
ideas.data_needed: METR task_results_1_1.yaml (228 tasks, all TH1.1 models). benchmark_results_1_1.yaml for cross-checks. Whitfill et al. 2026 horizon numbers. Kwa and Cheng 2025 domain multipliers. METR's public eval-analysis code (named in the digest; not opened by me) to replicate their fit before deviating.
ideas.data_access: Public. I fetched task_results_1_1.yaml (about 670 KB). It has the fields above, e.g. GPT-4 0314 on acdc_bug/fix_checkpointing: human_minutes 877, 0 of 6 successes. A copy was saved locally at /Users/ndeshpande/.claude/projects/-Users-ndeshpande-Documents-2-misc-1-AI-SPAR---Andrei-0--Exploratory-Analysis/bceada8d-afbe-4309-8489-b0945fd4a342/tool-results/webfetch-1793050910388-6afst7.bin. The page does not say what the per-agent coefficient and intercept parameterize; check against METR's code. The dashboard was frozen in September 2026, so the data end with models released by 7 April 2026.
ideas.weeks_effort: 2-3 weeks (week 1: replicate METR's p50/p80 for a few models; week 2: alternative curves, tail CIs and overdispersion; week 3: the q-form comparison, written up as a recipe module)
ideas.gap_addressed: measurement/M4 (high-reliability tail and slope poorly identified), M16 (predictability of success within a length bin), M5 (q as a scalar vs a function of h), and a first-pass placeholder for M3 (no p(h) for BPO or IT ops). This is the most 'AI-safety-native' project: an evals re-analysis whose output is an economic parameter.
ideas.who_would_care: METR. Their Barry (Mar 2026) and Kwa (Jan 2026) notes flag exactly these issues: about 300 tasks per bucket are needed for 99% horizons, and curve choice moves p80 by up to 2x. Also forecasters such as AI Futures, whose timelines depend on the 80% horizon, and the mentor, because theta_j's sensitivity to curve shape decides whether METR's data can anchor the recipe at all.
ideas.risks: Few long tasks: 31 tasks are 8 h or more and only 5 are 16 h or more, so tail estimates will have wide CIs. That is itself a finding, but expect no sharp 99% number. Task-length labels are noisy (Barry's SIMEX analysis), which mechanically inflates apparent within-bin dispersion and will overstate the routing gain unless corrected. The 7x horizon shift rests on 3 Python repos and one model. The computer-use discount is a cross-benchmark rough guess, not a BPO measurement. Contractor-time h (measurement/M2) remains uncorrected.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Parse the YAML into a tidy table (agent, release_date, task_id, family, human_minutes, n_successes, n_runs, task_weight). Refit a weighted logistic for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and check that you recover METR's TH1.1 values (p50 about 60 min, p80 about 12 min). If you do not, read METR's eval-analysis code before going further.

ideas.title: Re-analyse METR's two public developer RCTs to estimate kappa and post-review rework as functions of task length
ideas.what_youd_do: The METR RCT data are public at the issue level and include a pre-randomization length forecast, which no published analysis has used to give a curve against h. Steps: (1) Early-2025 data (246 issues): regress log(total time) on AI-allowed x log(predicted_time_no_ai), using the developer's pre-randomization forecast as h, with developer fixed effects. This gives an assistant-mode effect as a function of task length (a kappa(h) curve, with honest CIs) rather than one -19% number. (2) Compute post_review_implementation_time / h by arm and by h-bin. This is the author-side cost of fixing work after review, one measurable component of rho, and shows whether it behaves like a fixed cost per PR or scales with h (the skeptic/G2 question). (3) Repeat on the late-2025 data (57 developers, 800+ issues). Use estimatedTimeOtherTreatment and perceivedEffort. Bound the selection problem: issues 'ditched' or not submitted. Use the incomplete/ditched status for a Lee-bounds-style sensitivity check, and run panel-only vs new developers separately. (4) Compare forecast vs realized speedup by h to quantify how self-reports err (the 'self-reports are wrong in both directions' warning), which matters for any survey-based theta. Optional stretch: in AIDev v5, merge rate of agent PRs vs PR size by agent and month, as a deployment-side q proxy (not conditioned on tests).
ideas.data_needed: METR early-2025 RCT data_complete.csv. METR late-2025 RCT data.csv. Optionally the AIDev v5 pull_request and pr_commit_details tables.
ideas.data_access: Public on GitHub; I opened both repos. Early-2025 (github.com/METR/Measuring-Early-2025-AI-on-Exp-OSS-Devs) columns: dev_id, issue_id, predicted_time_no_ai, predicted_time_ai_allowed, prior task exposure, external resource needs, ai_treatment, initial_implementation_time, post_review_implementation_time (missing for some issues). The excerpt did not state units for the implementation-time columns, and no license was visible. Late-2025 (github.com/METR/Measuring-Late-2025-AI-on-OSS-Devs) columns: treatmentAssignment, status (incomplete/complete/ditched), estimatedTimeWithAI/WithoutAI, initial and post-review implementation time in minutes, estimatedTimeOtherTreatment, perceivedEffort, isPanelDeveloper. Its README asks readers to interpret it 'with a major grain of salt'. AIDev v5 is on Hugging Face (hao-li/AIDev; CC-BY-4.0, 7.69M PRs, six agents); the card does not list a line-count field, but it can probably be derived from patches.
ideas.weeks_effort: 1.5-2 weeks (small CSVs; most of the time goes to careful specification and writing up the caveats). Add 1-2 weeks for the AIDev stretch.
ideas.gap_addressed: measurement/M8 (kappa is pre-agent or broken by selection; this gives its dependence on h within those limits), M6 and skeptic/G2 (no rho against h; this measures the post-review fix component), and M9 partially (the AI-allowed arm mixes modes, so the shape tells you where assistance helps or hurts).
ideas.who_would_care: METR, who released the data but reported pooled effects. The mentor, because kappa is the floor of the max{} and its sign across h decides theta wherever delegation does not pay. Economists using RCT numbers as the 'intensive margin' input in Acemoglu-style aggregation.
ideas.risks: Small n: 246 issues across 16 developers gives wide CIs on an interaction term, so expect 'suggestive' rather than 'significant'. h is the developer's own forecast and is noisy and correlated with familiarity. Use prior task exposure as a control and an errors-in-variables check. post_review_implementation_time is author rework, not reviewer hours, so it is a lower bound on review cost, not rho itself. Expert maintainers on their own repos are far from Indian vendor staff on client code (M2, C6). The late-2025 data are selection-biased by METR's own account. The AI arm mixes assistance and delegation, so this is not a pure kappa.
ideas.first_step_this_week: Clone both repos, run METR's regression.py to reproduce +19% (early) and -18%/-4% (late), and confirm the time units. Then add the interaction ai_treatment x log(predicted_time_no_ai) and plot the fitted effect against h with a 95% band.

ideas.title: Hours-weighted task-length distributions f_j(h) from public Jira effort logs, plus a calibrated LLM duration labeller for later use on firm ticket text
ideas.what_youd_do: Build the best public prior for f_maintenance(h), f_development(h) and f_testing(h), and a tool to estimate h where hours are not logged. Steps: (1) From JOSSE (all issues carry actual effort, 19% also have expert estimates) and the Public Jira Dataset, extract issues with logged time spent. Map Jira issue types, components and labels to service lines (bug/maintenance, new feature/development, test, build/infra), using an LLM classifier on summary text where labels are missing, and spot-check 100 by hand. (2) Plot count-weighted vs hours-weighted histograms of h for each line and fit lognormal or mixture models. Report how much of total hours sits above 4 h, 8 h and 16 h, the region where p(h) is weakest. (3) Calibrate an LLM labeller. Have an LLM estimate hours from issue text for a few hundred held-out JOSSE issues and compare with logged effort and with the expert estimates. Replicate the compression Anthropic reported (Spearman about 0.44; long tasks underestimated, short ones overestimated), then fit a correction (isotonic or quantile mapping). (4) Apply the corrected labeller to SWE-bench Verified problem statements and compare with its annotator buckets (39% under 15 min, 52% 15-60 min, 8% 1-4 h), to see which is optimistic. (5) Deliver per-service-line f_j(h) curves with uncertainty, plus a documented labelling protocol that can be run on an Indian firm's ticket export if one is ever obtained. Optional: ITSM incident event logs (the BPI Challenge 2013 Volvo IT and 2014 Rabobank logs on 4TU) for an infrastructure/AMS proxy using elapsed times. I could not verify these (4TU refused the connection and the search budget was exhausted).
ideas.data_needed: JOSSE (Apache, JBoss and Spring Jira issues with actual effort). The Public Jira Dataset (16 public Jira instances, 2.7M issues with timeestimate and timespent fields per Montgomery et al. 2022). SWE-bench Verified with the difficulty field. LLM API access for classification and duration labelling.
ideas.data_access: Public. I opened both Zenodo records. JOSSE (zenodo.org/records/7022735): CC BY 4.0, one 193 MB zip; the page does not state effort units. Public Jira Dataset (zenodo.org/records/5882881): v7 (23 Jun 2025), CC BY 4.0, a 5.8 GB MongoDB dump; the Zenodo page does not document field names, so timespent units and coverage must be checked in the dump. SWE-bench Verified on Hugging Face: 500 rows with a 4-value difficulty field. The BPI ITSM logs are unverified.
ideas.weeks_effort: 3-4 weeks (week 1: load JOSSE, which is small, and do the service-line mapping; week 2: hours-weighted f_j and fits; week 3: LLM labeller calibration; week 4: the Public Jira Dataset at scale, or skip it and write up)
ideas.gap_addressed: measurement/M1 and context/C2 (no hours-weighted f_j(h) for any service line). The public open-source version is the best available prior, and the labeller is the bridge to firm data. Partially M2: logged effort is in-context developer time, a different 'whose clock' from METR's contractors, and comparing the two quantifies the gap. Also C1/M10 in a small way: the hours split across issue types gives a within-engineering w_j proxy.
ideas.who_would_care: The mentor, since f_j is the input the integral depends on most, given METR's shallow slope. The Anthropic Economic Index team, who use JOSSE-type data to validate Claude's time estimates and whose compression bias this would correct. Anyone at TCS, Infosys or ICRIER who could run the labeller on internal ServiceNow or Jira exports and share only the aggregate histograms. That fits MoSPI-style aggregate-only norms and firm confidentiality.
ideas.risks: Open-source time logging is sparse and self-selected: the people who log hours are not typical, and logged hours may be rounded or estimated. Neither source covers Indian client delivery, legacy stacks (COBOL, SAP) or BPO transactions, so this is a prior, not an estimate for TCS. Testing and infrastructure are thinly represented in open-source Jira. The 5.8 GB MongoDB dump is a real time sink, so start with JOSSE. An LLM labeller calibrated on open-source code issues may not transfer to enterprise ticket language.

ideas.what_youd_do:
Goal: turn the revenue shares the firms already published into hours shares w_j for maintenance, testing, development, infrastructure, BPO and consulting, with bounds. This is the 'dataset requirement' half of the mentor's request, for w_j.

1) Extract every service_line row from data/tidy/panel_long.csv into one table, plus a crosswalk column mapping each firm's labels to the six j. The repo already holds the most detailed public splits these firms ever reported:

- TCS 2017Q1: ADM 37.9, Assurance (testing) 9.0, Infrastructure 16.1, BPS 11.7, Enterprise Solutions & Consulting 17.5, Engineering 4.9.

In 2018Q1, offshore was 71.3% of effort but only 45.4% of revenue, so an onsite hour billed roughly 3x an offshore hour (my arithmetic from repo data).

- Use segment revenue per employee where both are disclosed, to bound BPO rates relative to IT rates.
- Report w_j as intervals.

3) Add a non-task bucket w_0 (bench, training, sales and support, coordination), where theta is about 0. Source it from Infosys person-months, 2010-18 (billed onsite/offshore, non-billable, trainee, sales and support), plus the utilisation series already used for M1. Leaving this out overstates S.

4) Roll the weights forward to FY26 using the coarser recent splits:
- HCLTech ITBS/ER&D;
- TechM IT/BPS;

- Infosys Core/Digital to 2023Q1;
- the press-reported AMS share of 22-45% of revenue;

State plainly that the FY26 vector is extrapolated.

5) Write the dataset-requirement spec: what an ideal firm dataset would contain (timesheet hours by service line × task type × ticket length × AI-assist flag × reviewer hours × reopen rate), and which of today's public disclosures substitutes for each field.

Service-line revenue shares, onsite/offshore effort and revenue shares, person-month breakdowns, utilisation, segment headcount where reported, and fixed-price shares. All of these are already in data/tidy/panel_long.csv and data/corrected/core_quarterly_final.csv.

It also fixes a known bias: omitting non-task time (w_0) overstates S. The verified literature has no hours-weighted service-line mix for Indian delivery. Hatgis-Kessell et al. (arXiv 2608.05172, opened) estimate time shares for about 18,000 US O*NET tasks, but on a US task taxonomy that does not match AMS, testing and infrastructure towers.

ideas.title: Ceiling-versus-realized test: does a bottom-up θ ceiling fit the 2.3 pp/yr, and what adoption does it imply?
ideas.what_youd_do:
Goal: use the top-down estimate as a validation constraint on the bottom-up recipe, in the partial-identification style of ESTIMATION_PLAN.md (bounds plus breakdown points).

1) Implement θ_j(t) = ∫ max{q·p(h,t)(1−κ)+κ−ρ, κ} f_j(h) dh as a function.
- Build p(h,t) from METR's public TH1.1 file (https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml; I downloaded it to the scratchpad). Back out each model's logistic slope from β = ln4 / ln(p50/p80).
- Add two alternative curve shapes: Barry's shared-slope fit, and Ord's constant-hazard model.
- Add a context multiplier on h, since METR's h is low-context contractor time.

2) Put prior ranges on each input:
- q: 0.5 (Whitfill et al., METR, 10 Mar 2026, opened) to about 0.85;
- ρ: about 0.1-0.33 (Rein 2025; GDPval 109/404 min);
- κ: by tool vintage, from −0.19 (METR 2025 RCT) to about +0.25;
- f_j: public proxies. These are the SWE-bench Verified time buckets, the Public Jira Dataset (Zenodo 5882881, CC BY 4.0, opened), and the per-O*NET-task human_only_time means in the Anthropic Economic Index 2026-01-15 and 2026-03-24 releases (data documentation opened: task-level mean, median and CIs, no units, no task-level histograms);
- BPO and infrastructure p: shifted down by the 40-100x computer-use horizon gap.
For weights, use w_j from firmdata-1.

3) Compute S_ceiling(t) at each model release date from GPT-4 (Mar 2023) to Claude Opus 4.6 (Feb 2026).

4) Validation identity. The realized cumulative replacement over FY24-26 is about 3 × 2.3 ≈ 7 pp (about 4.5-11 pp across the 1.5-3.6 identification bounds). It must satisfy:
- (a) realized ≤ ΔS_ceiling over the window;
- (b) realized ≈ Σ w_j A_j θ_j, which gives an implied average adoption A.
Check A against adoption evidence already in the repo's call corpus. For example, Infosys reported 30,000+ developers on GitHub Copilot (Q4 FY26) and 'over 80,000' on Claude Code or Codex (Q1 FY27), against about 328,000 staff.

5) Report the region of (q, ρ, κ, h-multiplier, curve shape) that passes both checks, plus breakdown points: how wrong would q or ρ have to be for the ceiling to fall below what was realized?

6) Handle contracts explicitly. On time-and-materials work (43-48% of revenue at the firms that report it), savings reach clients as fewer billed hours. M1+M2 partly miss that, so treat 2.3 as closer to a lower bound on realized s.

Preliminary illustration (my own calculation, with an assumed f, not a finding). Assumptions: hours-weighted lognormal ticket lengths with medians of 1-4 contractor-hours, q = 0.5, ρ = 0.27, κ = 0.1. Under these, θ stays at the κ floor of 0.10 from GPT-4 through Claude 3.7. It reaches only 0.11-0.15 by Opus 4.6. With ρ = 0.1 it reaches 0.21-0.31.

Implication: the FY24-26 data mostly constrain κ × adoption, not q, ρ or p. The test only bites on the delegation branch once FY27-28 filings arrive. Saying that clearly is itself a useful result for Andrei.
ideas.data_needed:
- METR TH1.1 benchmark_results_1_1.yaml and task_results_1_1.yaml (both linked from https://metr.org/time-horizons/, opened; the page says it is no longer updated, and horizons above 16 h are unreliable).
- SWE-bench Verified difficulty labels (HF princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified).
- Public Jira Dataset (Zenodo 5882881). I could not confirm from the page that timespent is populated, so inspect the dump.

- Repo inputs: the round4 M1/M2 outputs (m1_summary.csv, m2_aggregate.csv, robustness/m1_scope_subcon), audit/calls_statements.csv for adoption disclosures, Wipro fixed-price share 2013-2026 and Infosys effort shares from panel_long.
ideas.data_access: All public. METR files are open downloads. Hugging Face data are CC-BY. The Jira dump is CC BY 4.0 (5.8 GB). Everything else is already in the repo.
ideas.weeks_effort: 3-4 weeks at 5-8 hrs/week: about 1 week for the integral code and curve alternatives, 1 week to assemble priors and f_j proxies, and 1-2 weeks for the identification region, adoption cross-check and write-up. It can start in parallel with firmdata-1, using placeholder weights.
ideas.gap_addressed:
- Measurement M12: there is no net, service-line θ anchor. This project uses the firm aggregate as the anchor and is explicit that it also contains adoption.
- M11 and skeptic G4: θ_j(t) is extrapolated, never checked against outcomes.
- Context C4: contract structure links θ to observed numbers.

It also turns the working hypothesis into something testable. Whatever the exposure literature says about the extensive margin, a recipe for the intensive margin is only credible if it can be reconciled with a realized replacement rate. METR's own limitations note (Kwa, Jan 2026) says converting horizons into speedups needs data it does not have.
ideas.who_would_care:
- Andrei and the checkpoint: it links Part A (diagnosis) to Part B (scenarios) through a single tested mapping, rather than plugging in capability numbers by assumption.

ideas.title: Cross-firm and cross-segment dose-response test of the θ_j ordering, with a power check first
ideas.what_youd_do:
Goal: test whether the across-j pattern of the recipe (not just its total) shows up in outcomes. If θ differs by service line, firms and segments with more hours in high-θ lines should show larger M1 residuals (faster growth in revenue per busy employee).

0) Power check before any estimation. data/explore/round4/residual/noise_check.csv gives a within-firm SD of the annual residual of about 2.2-3.4 pp, so a firm's 3-year mean has an SE of roughly 1.3-2 pp. Using firmdata-2's priors and each firm's last disclosed mix, compute the predicted spread of firm-level ΔS over FY24-26. Examples of mix: HCLTech infrastructure-heavy (38.9% in 2019Q1), TCS ADM-heavy (37.9%), TechM IT vs BPS, the mid-tier firms in data/explore/midtier, and the BPO firms. If the predicted spread is under about twice the SE, stop and record that as the result. The round4 M6 elasticity test failed for exactly this reason: line-specific demand noise of about 3 pp/yr against tiny predicted gaps.

1) If the test has power, estimate with three contrasts that net out common shocks:
- within-firm segment contrasts: HCLTech ITBS vs ER&D, TechM IT vs BPS, Accenture Consulting vs Managed Services, Cognizant Consulting & Technology vs Outsourcing;
- BPO-firm vs IT-firm revenue per employee;
- across firms, regressing the M1 residual on predicted S_firm.
Use sign-flip and leave-one-out inference, reusing the existing scripts in round4/elasticity_xsec.

2) Pre-register a version for FY27-28. After the summer-2026 agent step change, the recipe predicts the delegation branch starts to differ sharply across j, so predicted gaps may become large enough to detect. Commit to the predictions now and test them as quarterly results arrive.

scores.title: Working theta_j calculator plus value-of-information ranking that becomes the dataset requirement
scores.rationale: This is the closest to what the mentor literally asked for, and the first step is concrete: about 50 lines of code fed by numbers already on disk. I confirmed that the METR TH1.1 benchmark YAML is in the scratchpad, with p50/p80 for 26 models from GPT-2 to the early Mythos preview, and that metr.org/time-horizons links both YAMLs and says it is frozen (Sep 8, 2026) and unreliable above 16 h. Gap score is held at 6 because it is synthesis, not new measurement. A variance decomposition only ranks uncertainty inside prior ranges you choose yourself, and a referee will say so. My own quick calculation shows why it still earns its place. Under the draft formula, a scalar q puts a hard cap on theta at q(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, which is 0.28 at q=0.5, kappa=0.1, rho=0.27, no matter how capable models become. Treating q instead as a 7x horizon shift removes that cap: for Opus 4.6 on hours-weighted lognormal tasks with a 1 h median, theta is about 0.19 under the multiplier vs about 0.35 under the shift. So the q functional form and the fallback rule are first-order modelling choices, and this idea is the cheapest way to show that. Career value is moderate: a sensitivity notebook is a useful tool but not, on its own, a writing sample.

scores.title: Ceiling-versus-realized test against the 2.3 pp/yr
scores.rationale: This is the validation half of the recipe. Without it, the bottom-up theta is unfalsifiable. I partly reproduced its illustration with the same YAML. With q=0.5, rho=0.27, kappa=0.1 and hours-weighted lognormal tasks with 1-4 h medians, theta is about 0.10-0.12 for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 0.14-0.19 for Opus 4.6. The exact value depends on the assumed spread of task lengths, so their 0.11-0.15 is in range. Its most valuable insight is honest: FY24-26 mainly constrains kappa times adoption, not q or rho. A second issue it underplays: kappa is held constant in the formula, so all of the change in S over time comes from the delegation branch. Validation must compare the CHANGE in adoption-weighted S with the cumulative 7 pp (4.5-11), not the level of S, and kappa needs a vintage index. Feasibility is docked because it depends on firmdata-1 weights and on a model-to-fiscal-quarter mapping of which models were actually in use, which is guesswork. Adoption head-counts come from the repo's call corpus; I did not re-verify the Infosys 30k/80k figures. Career value is good: a horizons-to-labour mapping checked against firm outcomes is something Epoch and METR have not published.

scores.title: Labour-hour weights w_j from the firms' service-line disclosures
scores.rationale: The data really are in the repo. I checked data/tidy/panel_long.csv. Infosys Q4FY18 (the idea's '2018Q1') shows App Development 15.5, App Maintenance 15.6 and BPM 5.4. Offshore effort is 71.3 vs offshore revenue 45.4. TCS Q4FY17 shows Assurance 9.0, BPS 11.9, Infra 16.2 and ADM 37.7; the idea says 37.9, so some quarter or vintage is slightly off and needs re-checking. HCLTech Q4FY19 shows Application 32.6, Infra 38.9, Business Services 4.5. Infosys person_months cover Q1FY11-Q4FY18. Adding w_0 (bench, training, sales) is a real fix: leaving it out mechanically inflates S. Weaknesses: the splits end in 2017-19, the revenue-to-hours conversion applies one firm-level onsite premium to every line, and the FY26 roll-forward is mostly narrative. Career value toward AI labs is low, since this is India-specific accounting, but Andrei needs it.

scores.title: Refit METR task-level data: curve shape, tail, within-bin dispersion, q as multiplier vs horizon shift
scores.rationale: This is the most evals-native idea and the best signal to METR and Epoch. The data are public, and the task YAML was already fetched. The parts with real economic leverage are step 4 (the q form, see feasible-1) and step 3 (within-bin dispersion as an upper bound on the gain from routing tasks to AI). The curve-shape and tail work largely repeats what Barry (Mar 2026) and Kwa (Jan 2026) already flagged. I opened Kwa's note: it says 99% horizons need about 300 diverse tasks per time bucket, so the TH1.1 suite (31 tasks of 8 h or more) cannot deliver a sharp tail. The finding is mostly 'wide CIs'. Feasibility risk: the meaning of the per-agent coefficient and intercept in the YAML is undocumented, and replicating METR's task weighting is fiddly. Do the q-form comparison inside feasible-1 this week. Do the refit only to the depth needed to put bootstrap bands on p(h).

scores.title: Re-analyse METR's public developer RCTs for kappa(h) and post-review rework
scores.rationale: Cheap and concrete. I opened the early-2025 repo: data_complete.csv has dev_id, issue_id, predicted_time_no_ai and predicted_time_ai_allowed (stated in minutes), ai_treatment, initial_implementation_time and post_review_implementation_time (units not stated; partly missing), plus regression.py. No license is stated. I did not open the late-2025 repo. Gap is held at 5 for four reasons. (a) 246 issues and 16 developers give an interaction term with very wide CIs. (b) These are 2025 assistant-era tools on experts' own repos, far from Indian vendor staff. (c) Post-review time is author rework, not reviewer hours, so it is only a lower bound on rho. (d) The abstract of arXiv 2507.09089 does not mention a breakdown by forecast length, but the full paper's subgroup figures may already show one, so check before claiming novelty. Its real value to the recipe is that it gives the kappa row an honest prior with a length gradient, and it shows how much self-reported forecasts err, which matters for any survey-based theta.

scores.title: From horizons to net labor saved: calibrated theta_j(h,t) with VOI ranking (umbrella)
scores.rationale: This is essentially feasible-1 + feasible-2 + feasible-4 bundled together, with Sobol indices and a 6-8 page note. As a frame for the final write-up it is right. As a 6-week plan at 5-8 hrs/week it is overscoped. The Montgomery Jira MongoDB dump (5.8 GB, field names undocumented on Zenodo) alone could eat two weeks. Its correction about the Anthropic Economic Index (task-level means, medians and CIs but no task-level histograms) is useful and should be carried into the recipe. Do not run it as a separate project; use it as the table of contents for the deliverable.

scores.title: Fixed-task mini-panel: delegate vs assist vs manual across two model generations
scores.rationale: This targets the truest gap: nobody measures p, q, rho and kappa jointly on one task set, stratified by h (skeptic G1, measurement M9 and M11). The design is what a lab economics team would want to see. But it cannot be done well in 5-6 weeks at 5-8 hrs/week by one student. It needs volunteer reviewers, harness setup, timed baselines and contamination checks, and with 12-18 tasks and the student as reviewer, rho and q are biased and very noisy. Score it high on gap and low on feasibility. The protocol document and power calculation (what n per h-bin would pin theta_j within ±5 pp) are worth writing in week 6 as the 'ideal experiment' appendix. Do not run the experiment.

scores.title: q(h,t) in the wild from AIDev agent PRs
scores.rationale: I confirmed the AIDev card: 7,685,281 PRs, 961,168 repos, six agents, CC-BY-4.0, cutoff Mar 31 2026. The AIDev-pop tables include pull_request, pr_reviews, pr_review_comments, pr_commits, pr_commit_details and pr_timeline. The visible card text mentions no CI or check status, so you cannot condition on passing tests, and the estimate is of q*p at a self-selected delegation mix, not q. Given that the q form decides whether theta saturates, a deployment-side q(size, month) curve would be valuable, and labs would read it. But defining 'fix-up share' (separating agent from human commits) is the hard step, and diff size is a weak proxy for h. Recommended scope: one week of descriptive merge rate by agent x size decile x month, excluding self-merges. Treat it as a sanity band on q, not a parameter estimate.

scores.title: Hours-weighted f_j(h) from public Jira effort logs plus a calibrated LLM duration labeller
scores.rationale: f_j is probably the input theta depends on most, given METR's shallow slopes (p50/p80 ratios of about 4-10x in the YAML), so the gap is real. I opened the JOSSE record: Alhamed and Storer 2022, CC BY 4.0, 193.1 MB, 'annotated with actual effort', 19% with expert estimates. The page does not give units (story points vs hours is unresolved). That is the first thing that could kill the idea. Open-source logged effort is sparse and self-selected and says nothing about Indian AMS, testing, infrastructure or BPO. The LLM-labeller calibration duplicates work Anthropic has published. The bridge value, a labelling protocol a firm could run on its own ticket exports and share only aggregates from, is real but speculative. Scope it down to JOSSE-only count-weighted vs hours-weighted histograms (one week).

scores.title: Coding management disclosures into per-j theta envelopes
scores.rationale: The corpus exists: audit/calls_statements.csv has about 2,087 rows. The day-one keyword filter is cheap and worth doing. But firms showcase their best cases and announce targets, so almost no claim is realized, portfolio-wide and about labour effort, which is the only kind the 'lower bound on the ceiling' logic works for. Expect a handful of usable numbers per service line at best. Use it as a qualitative per-j cross-check in the write-up. Do not build the full two-coder codebook.

scores.title: Review-cost and acceptance primitive from agentic coding logs; local transcript pilot
scores.rationale: It is shaped like a fellowship application, which helps career value, but it is off the mentor's critical path. Users of local Claude Code are not IT-services staff. Recruiting peers, running a diary week, getting consent and handling privacy all eat time. Idle gaps in logs mix silent review with unrelated work. It also needs lab data for the real version, and the Economic Futures page (as reported by the idea's author) is not taking applications. Labs may already measure this internally. Park it as a post-fellowship proposal.

scores.title: Cross-firm/cross-segment dose-response test of the theta_j ordering
scores.rationale: The idea itself predicts that the test is underpowered. noise_check.csv shows a within-firm SD of the annual residual of 3.39 pp (2.23 excluding FY21), against predicted mix-driven gaps probably under 1 pp/yr, with N of about 6-12 firms and stale mix data. The round4 M6 elasticity test already failed for the same reason. The only part worth keeping is the 2-hour pre-registration of FY27-28 predictions, which belongs in the firmdata-2 write-up.

judge.remaining_weeks_plan:
The plan assumes about 5 weeks after this one, at 5-8 hrs/week (about 30-40 hours). One rule throughout: every week ends with a figure or table that goes into the final note.

Week 2: recipe core (feasible-1). Put prior ranges on q, rho and kappa, the context multiplier m on h (1 to 18), and the curve shape. Run a Monte Carlo and a simple variance decomposition: binned correlation ratios are enough, Sobol indices are optional. Report it under two prior sets. Finish the firmdata-1 revenue-to-hours conversion and the w_0 estimate from Infosys person-months (Q1FY11-Q4FY18 are in the panel). Output: the parameter ranking.

Week 3: p(h,t) module (trimmed feasible-2).
- Parse task_results_1_1.yaml.
- Replicate METR's p50 for 2-3 models.
- Fit the shared-slope logistic and bootstrap bands on p(h) by model.
- Optionally, one overdispersion number per h-bin, as the bound on the gain from routing tasks to AI.
Skip the Weibull curve and the computer-use extrapolation beyond a single scenario line.

Week 4: validation (firmdata-2).
- Build the adoption series A(t) from the call corpus and a model-vintage map.
- Compute the change in S_ceiling over FY24-26.
- Find the region of (q, rho, kappa, m, curve) consistent with 7 pp cumulative (4.5-11), with breakdown points and implied adoption.
In parallel, if time allows, run the feasible-3 interaction regression and use it to tighten the kappa prior.

Week 5: one data module, chosen by the week-2 ranking.
- If f_j or the context multiplier dominates: JOSSE only. Check units, then plot count-weighted vs hours-weighted effort for bug and feature issues and fit lognormals.
- If q dominates: an AIDev-pop descriptive analysis of merge rate by agent x size decile x month, excluding self-merges.
Do one, not both.

Week 6: write up.
- A 5-7 page note with the recipe stated formally and the identified set.
- A one-page firm data request.
- A pre-registered FY27-28 prediction table (the useful residue of firmdata-4).
- A half-page appendix with the lab-4 fixed-task protocol and power calculation as 'the ideal experiment'.

Explicitly dropped: lab-3 (park as a post-fellowship proposal), lab-4 execution, firmdata-4 estimation, the Montgomery 5.8 GB dump, LLM-labeller calibration, and the firmdata-3 full codebook. For firmdata-3, do only the one-day keyword filter and quote any portfolio-level realized claims in the write-up.

Contingency: if week 2 shows the q form and fallback rule swamp every data-driven parameter, say so as the main result. Then spend week 5 on AIDev, because q is the row where public data can move the answer.

1. Recipe plus validation spine: feasible-1 + firmdata-2 + firmdata-1. They share one theta function. feasible-1 ranks what is unknown, firmdata-1 supplies the weights including w_0, and firmdata-2 checks the result against the 2.3 pp/yr. Together they are exactly 'a dataset requirement and a recipe', and the result is the backbone of the deliverable. lab-1 is the right title and table of contents for this bundle; do not run it as a separate project.

judge.dataset_requirement_and_recipe:
DATASET REQUIREMENT AND RECIPE FOR theta_j (draft for Andrei)

Target. theta_j(t) is the share of labour hours in service line j removed at full adoption with the AI available at date t. It is net of failure, review, assistant-mode redo and AI running cost. The aggregate is S(t) = sum_j w_j theta_j(t), plus a non-task bucket w_0 with theta_0 = 0.

Core formula (draft, with the choices made explicit):
theta_j(t) = integral of max{ q(h,t)·p(h/m,t)·(1-kappa_v) + kappa_v - rho(h) - c(h,t)/wage, kappa_v } f_j(h) dh

- m is the context multiplier converting firm-staff hours into METR contractor hours.
- kappa_v is the assistant-mode speedup for tool vintage v.
- c/wage is AI running cost as a share of labour cost.

Three structural choices must be reported as alternatives, not hidden:
- (i) q as a scalar multiplier, or as a horizon shift (q=1 with h50 divided by about 7). Under a scalar q=0.5, theta per task is capped at q(1-kappa)+kappa-rho, which is about 0.28 at the central values. Under a horizon shift the cap is 1-rho.
- (ii) The fallback after failure: redo with assistance, full human redo, or retry and re-verify.
- (iii) The curve shape: a logistic in log h with a shared slope, or constant hazard.

A. Public data now (each row: dataset, fields, how the parameter is estimated)

1. p(h,t). Dataset: METR TH1.1 task_results_1_1.yaml and benchmark_results_1_1.yaml (linked from metr.org/time-horizons; frozen Sep 8 2026; unreliable above 16 h).
   - Fields: agent, release_date, task_id, task family, human_minutes, n_successes, n_runs, task_weight.
   - Estimate: weighted logistic of success on log h with a shared slope across models and a model-specific intercept. Bootstrap over tasks. Cross-check that p50/p80 match the benchmark file (for example Claude 3.7 Sonnet 60.4/12.1 min; Opus 4.6 718.8/69.9).
   - Testing, infrastructure and BPO have no human-timed benchmark, so use scenario multipliers only (computer-use horizons 40-100x shorter, flagged as a guess).

2. m (context). There is no dataset. Prior range 1 to 18, from METR's 5-18x contractor-vs-maintainer comparison. Report theta under m = 1, 3 and 10.

3. q. Anchor: Whitfill et al., METR, 10 Mar 2026. 296 PRs, 4 maintainers, 3 repos. Merge rate is 24.2 pp (SE 2.7) below the grader; Sonnet 4.5's horizon is about 50 min under the grader vs about 8 min under maintainers.
   - Deployment band: AIDev-pop (HF hao-li/AIDev v5, CC-BY-4.0) tables pull_request, pr_reviews, pr_commits and pr_commit_details. Fields: agent, created/merged timestamps, merged_by vs author, additions/deletions/files, and commit author.
   - Estimate: logistic of non-self merge on log diff size by agent and month. This estimates q·p at the self-selected delegation mix and serves as a bound, not a point.

4. rho(h). Model it as rho(h) = a/h + b, a fixed cost per change plus a part proportional to length. Anchors:
   - GDPval: 109 of 404 min (about 0.27);
   - Rein 2025: about 1/3, n=4;
   - METR early-2025 RCT: about 9% of AI-allowed time reviewing and cleaning;
   - post_review_implementation_time from the RCT's data_complete.csv, as a lower bound on author-side rework;
   - CUPS: 22.4% of session time verifying.
   Report the a=0 and b=0 corners.

5. kappa_v. Dataset: METR early-2025 RCT data_complete.csv. Fields: dev_id, issue_id, predicted_time_no_ai (minutes), ai_treatment, initial_implementation_time and post_review_implementation_time (units to confirm), prior task exposure.
   - Estimate: log(time) on ai_treatment x log(predicted_time_no_ai) with developer fixed effects, giving kappa(h) for the 2025 vintage.
   - Other vintages from the published Google RCT, Cui et al. and the late-2025 METR rerun, the last flagged as selection-biased.

6. f_j(h). Use JOSSE (Zenodo 7022735, CC BY 4.0; check effort units first) for maintenance (bug) and development (feature): hours-weighted histograms and lognormal fits. Use SWE-bench Verified's 4-level difficulty field (500 rows) as an optimistic short-task extreme.
   - For BPO, the only anchors are chat lengths: about 40 min in Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond, about 466 s at Alibaba.
   - Run theta under at least two f_j per line, because f_j and m interact.

7. w_j and w_0. Dataset: data/tidy/panel_long.csv, rows with dim_type=='service_line'. Examples: Infosys Q4FY18 AD 15.5, AM 15.6, BPM 5.4; TCS Q4FY17; HCLTech Q4FY19.
   - Convert revenue to hours using offshore effort vs revenue shares (Infosys Q4FY18: 71.3 vs 45.4, so onsite hours are billed at about 3x offshore hours) and per-line onsite-intensity ranges.
   - w_0 from Infosys person_months (Q1FY11-Q4FY18: billed, non-billable, trainee, sales).
   - Report intervals, and flag the FY26 roll-forward as extrapolated.

8. c/wage. AI cost per task (tokens times price, times number of retries) divided by the loaded wage. The context lens derives about $16/h average loaded cost from the Infosys FY26 20-F (I did not re-check it). Include this term only in the long-task, many-retry scenario.

B. Estimation procedure
- (1) Monte Carlo over the parameter priors and the three structural choices.
- (2) Variance decomposition of theta_j and S under two prior sets. The output is a ranking of which missing measurement most narrows S.
- (3) Report S(t) at each model release date as an identified band, not a point.

C. Validation against the top-down estimate (about 2.3 pp/yr, range 1.5-3.6, FY24-26)
- (a) Compare changes, not levels. The realized cumulative replacement over FY24-26 (about 7 pp, range 4.5-11) should roughly equal the change over the window in sum_j w_j·A_j(t)·theta_j(t), where A(t) is adoption, built from disclosed tool head-counts in audit/calls_statements.csv with a lag from model release to enterprise use.
- (b) Ceiling test: the realized change must be no larger than the change in S_ceiling over the same window. Report the breakdown points (for example, the smallest q or largest rho at which the ceiling falls below what was realized).
- (c) Implied adoption A = realized / change in S. Check it against disclosures, for example Infosys tool counts relative to about 328k staff, taken from the repo corpus and not re-verified here.
- (d) Contract adjustment: on time-and-materials work, savings show up as fewer billed hours, so measured replacement is closer to a lower bound.
- (e) Per-line sanity checks from any realized, portfolio-wide firm claims (firmdata-3 filter).
- (f) Pre-register the FY27-28 predictions, when the delegation branch should start to separate the service lines.
State plainly that the FY24-26 data mostly identify kappa x adoption, and have little power over q and rho.

D. The ask: ideal firm or partner dataset (one row per ticket or task)
- service line j and task type, client and account (hashed);
- logged effort hours (staff time) and an estimate made before the work started;
- AI mode (none / assist / delegate), tool and model version, and date;
- whether automated checks passed;
- reviewer ID or seniority band and reviewer minutes;
- accept or reject at vendor review and at client review (UAT);
- rework hours before and after acceptance; reopen or incident within 30 days;
- AI cost (tokens or $);
- onsite/offshore flag; contract type (fixed-price, T&M, outcome).

Plus timesheet hours by service line and non-task category, to give w_j and w_0.

Rough sample size: if per-ticket net saving has an SD of about 0.4 (an assumption), estimating theta_j within ±5 pp needs about 250 tickets per line per mode at 95% confidence, and about 500 per arm for an AI-vs-no-AI difference, in each of roughly 4 h-bins. Only aggregates by line x h-bin x mode need to leave the firm.

Sources I opened for this judgment:
- metr.org/time-horizons/
- metr.org/notes/2026-03-10-many-swe-bench-passing-prs-would-not-be-merged-into-main/
- metr.org/notes/2026-01-22-time-horizon-limitations/
- arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089
- github.com/METR/Measuring-Early-2025-AI-on-Exp-OSS-Devs
- huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev
- huggingface.co/datasets/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified
- zenodo.org/records/7022735

Local files checked: data/tidy/panel_long.csv, data/explore/round4/residual/noise_check.csv, audit/calls_statements.csv, and the scratchpad METR bench.yaml.

Not opened by me, so the values are taken from the ideas and the digest: GDPval, Rein 2025, CUPS, Cui et al., the late-2025 METR repo, the Montgomery Jira dump, the Anthropic Economic Index releases, and the Infosys 20-F wage derivation.
